For many of us, our phones are not just a means of communication, but also a tool for organization, research, and creativity. By permitting their use during lunch and other free periods, students can stay connected with family and friends, access important information, and even utilize educational apps that can supplement our learning.

One of the primary concerns about allowing phones in school is that they can be a distraction during class time. However, with the caveat that phones must be turned off during lessons, this risk can be mitigated. In fact, by allowing students to use their phones during breaks, they are less likely to feel the need to sneakily check them during class, which can be a more significant distraction. Moreover, with the rise of mobile technology, it is inevitable that students will be using their phones regularly; by incorporating them into our school routine, we can teach responsible phone use and digital citizenship. This approach also acknowledges that students are capable of self-regulation and can be trusted to use their phones judiciously.

On the other hand, a blanket ban on phones, as proposed by Policy 2, may be overly restrictive and even counterproductive. In today's digital age, phones are an essential part of our lives, and denying students the opportunity to use them at all can be seen as out of touch with reality. I am writing to share my thoughts on the proposed policy that would require students to maintain at least a B average to take part in sports and other extracurricular activities. While I recognize that this idea comes from a good place—wanting everyone in our school to achieve their highest academic potential—I strongly believe that raising the bar to a B average would do more harm than good, particularly for the large number of students who currently hold a solid C average.

For many of us, school activities are not merely hobbies; they are the primary reason we stay engaged and show up every single day. Being part of a sports team, marching band, or theater production gives students a sense of belonging and purpose. A student working at a C level is still passing their classes, and that C often reflects real effort in a subject they find genuinely difficult. Stripping away the one part of the school day they love will not suddenly turn them into straight-A students. If anything, it risks doing the opposite: students who feel alienated or defeated are far more likely to tune out, fall behind, or even consider dropping out altogether.

Furthermore, education extends well beyond tests and textbooks. When students participate in athletics, they learn resilience, teamwork, and accountability. In clubs, debate, or student council, they develop leadership and communication skills. These are the exact qualities that colleges, trade programs, and employers search for. Denying a student these growth opportunities because their grade sits just a few points below an arbitrary cutoff limits their long-term potential. A grade point average reflects only one dimension of a young person’s abilities.

We also have to consider that students do not all start from the same place outside of school. Many students balance their schoolwork with part-time jobs, family caregiving responsibilities, or learning differences that make earning high marks an uphill battle. These classmates often work every bit as hard as top academic performers, yet their circumstances make a B average exceptionally difficult to achieve. A blanket requirement unfairly penalizes them for challenges beyond their control. For these students in particular, staying after school for an activity provides a positive, safe, and supervised environment that they might not have elsewhere.

If our true objective is to raise academic achievement, support will always be more effective than punishment. Instead of locking the door to activities, our school could implement mandatory study halls before practices, peer tutoring programs, or regular academic check-ins with coaches and club advisors. Students struggling with their grades could be given a probationary period with clear benchmarks and dedicated help rather than being immediately cut from their teams.

Academics are undeniably important, but excluding capable, hardworking students from school life is the wrong way to foster achievement. I respectfully ask you to maintain the current eligibility standard and focus on lifting students up rather than shutting them out. Thank you for listening to our voices on this important decision.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

Students would benefit from having the option to attend classes from home, although distance learning should not completely replace traditional schools. For many students, being physically present in a classroom is valuable because it encourages social interaction, routine, and direct contact with teachers. Still, online attendance can make education more accessible and flexible for students whose circumstances make daily travel to school difficult.

One major advantage of learning from home is that it can prevent students from falling behind when they cannot safely or reasonably attend school in person. A student recovering from surgery, managing a chronic illness, or caring for a family member may miss weeks of instruction under a system that requires physical attendance. With video conferencing, that student can listen to lessons, ask questions, submit assignments, and remain connected to classmates. Instead of returning to school overwhelmed by missed material, the student can continue learning at a manageable pace.

Distance learning can also help students who live far from school or have demanding schedules outside the classroom. In rural areas, some students spend a large portion of each day riding a bus. Others may work after school to support their families or participate seriously in athletics, music, or other activities. Attending certain classes online could save commuting time and allow these students to organize their days more effectively. The benefit is not simply convenience; it is the chance to devote more energy to learning rather than to transportation and scheduling problems.

In addition, some students learn better in a quieter, more controlled environment. A crowded classroom can be distracting for a student with anxiety, attention difficulties, or sensory sensitivities. At home, the student may be able to pause a recorded explanation, review a difficult lesson, or take short breaks without embarrassment. Online tools can also make participation easier. A shy student who rarely raises a hand in class may feel more comfortable asking questions through a chat feature or discussion board.

However, schools should be careful not to assume that every student will thrive at home. Young people often need structure, supervision, and face-to-face friendships. In-person classes teach cooperation in ways that are difficult to reproduce through a screen: students work in groups, read body language, resolve disagreements, and build relationships with adults outside their families. Not every home has reliable internet, a quiet workspace, or an adult available to help. If online learning became the only model, it could widen inequalities between students.

For these reasons, the best approach is to offer distance learning as a meaningful choice rather than a universal requirement. Schools could allow students to attend remotely during illness, family emergencies, or temporary scheduling conflicts, while also providing regular opportunities for in-person meetings and support. They should lend devices, improve internet access, and ensure that online students can still speak with teachers and participate in school activities. Used thoughtfully, learning from home can give students greater access to education without sacrificing the important benefits of a real school community.

Extracurricular activities have long been celebrated as an essential component of a well-rounded education. From athletics and debate to student council and theater, these programs provide students with opportunities to build leadership skills, pursue passions, and forge lasting friendships. Recognizing these benefits, the principal has recently decided to mandate that every student participate in at least one extracurricular activity. While this policy is rooted in good intentions, mandating participation is fundamentally misguided. Compulsory involvement overlooks students’ diverse personal responsibilities, destroys the intrinsic motivation that makes these clubs thrive, and places an unsustainable burden on school resources.

First and foremost, a mandatory activity policy fails to account for the complex lives students lead outside the classroom. Many teenagers carry significant responsibilities that cannot be neatly postponed for after-school practices or club meetings. For example, some students work part-time jobs to help support their families, while others must care for younger siblings until their parents return home from work. Furthermore, students grappling with heavy academic coursework or personal health challenges require their afternoon hours for studying, rest, and doctor appointments. Imposing a mandatory extracurricular requirement punishes students who already balance demanding schedules, ultimately heightening stress and forcing them to compromise their academic performance or family welfare.

In addition to disregarding external duties, compulsory participation undermines the very spirit of extracurricular activities. The defining feature of any club or team is voluntary engagement fueled by genuine enthusiasm. When students choose to join the robotics team or the school newspaper, they bring passion, energy, and a willingness to collaborate. Conversely, when participation becomes a bureaucratic requirement, clubs are flooded with reluctant participants who attend solely to fulfill an administrative checklist. These apathetic members often disrupt meetings, lower morale, and diminish the experience for genuinely invested peers. True engagement cannot be manufactured through institutional mandates; forced passion inevitably yields resentment.

Finally, a universal mandate would overwhelm the school’s limited resources and faculty. Most extracurricular programs operate on modest budgets and rely on teachers who volunteer their time as advisors and coaches. If every student in the school suddenly requires a roster spot, the institution must drastically expand its offerings, secure additional funding, and compel already overburdened teachers to supervise more after-school programs. Overcrowded clubs and underfunded sports teams would compromise the quality of instruction and mentoring, leaving both students and staff frustrated by diluted experiences.

While the administration’s desire to foster student involvement is commendable, enforcement is the wrong approach. Education should guide students toward discovering their interests, not dictate how they spend every hour of their lives. Instead of issuing an inflexible mandate, the school should focus on removing barriers to access, offering transport options, and expanding the variety of available clubs to attract students organically. By respecting students’ autonomy and time, the school can cultivate authentic involvement that enriches students rather than exhausts them.

As I consider the proposal to require all students to perform community service, I am reminded of the diverse perspectives within our school community. On one hand, I have friends who are passionate about giving back to the community, and their experiences have not only benefited the recipients of their service but also enriched their own lives. On the other hand, I also have friends who are concerned that mandatory community service would encroach upon their already demanding schedules. While I understand their concerns, I firmly believe that incorporating community service into our school's curriculum can have a profoundly positive impact on our students and the community at large. By requiring students to participate in community service, we can foster a sense of social responsibility, empathy, and civic engagement that will benefit them throughout their lives.

One of the primary advantages of mandatory community service is that it provides students with opportunities to develop valuable skills, such as teamwork, problem-solving, and leadership. For example, a group of students who volunteered at a local food bank not only helped to sort and distribute food to those in need but also learned about the complexities of food insecurity and the importance of addressing this issue in our community. Moreover, by working together towards a common goal, they developed strong bonds and a sense of camaraderie that transcended their differences. These experiences can be transformative, helping students to become more confident, resilient, and compassionate individuals.

Furthermore, requiring community service can also help to address the needs of our local community. For instance, a friend who volunteers at an animal shelter has helped to care for abandoned pets, assist with adoption events, and raise awareness about animal welfare issues. By supporting these organizations, we can help to create a more just and equitable society, where everyone has access to the resources and opportunities they need to thrive.

In conclusion, while I understand the concerns about the potential impact of mandatory community service on students' schedules, I firmly believe that the benefits far outweigh the costs. Making significant choices is an inevitable part of human life, whether one is selecting a career path, purchasing a home, or navigating a personal crisis. In moments of uncertainty, individuals instinctively turn to others for guidance. While relying on a single confidant may seem straightforward, consulting multiple sources is far more advantageous. Seeking a variety of perspectives leads to superior decision-making because it mitigates personal bias, illuminates critical blind spots through specialized knowledge, and encourages the decision-maker to think more deeply before taking action.

First, collecting diverse viewpoints helps neutralize subjective bias. Every adviser filters reality through their unique fears, preferences, and personal values. Consequently, relying on a single individual means inheriting their unexamined prejudices. For instance, consider a professional deciding whether to leave a stable corporate job to launch a startup. A parent, motivated by an instinct to protect, might counsel against the move out of anxiety over financial instability. Conversely, an ambitious colleague might urge immediate risk-taking while downplaying practical hazards. By listening to both, the decision-maker can separate excessive caution from reckless optimism, arriving at a balanced assessment that neither adviser could have offered in isolation.

Furthermore, different people possess distinct domains of experience, allowing them to reveal factors that one person would inevitably overlook. Complex decisions are rarely one-dimensional; they contain emotional, practical, and financial facets. When an individual prepares to buy a first home, for example, consulting only a real estate agent might center the conversation on neighborhood charm and resale potential. However, speaking with a home inspector could uncover aging plumbing systems, while an accountant might illuminate the long-term impact of local property taxes. Each contributor evaluates the dilemma through a different analytical lens. Gathering these varied insights provides a comprehensive picture, transforming an uninformed gamble into a well-calculated choice.

Finally, the process of reconciling contrasting opinions cultivates personal agency and critical thinking. When an individual seeks counsel from only one authority figure, there is a temptation to defer passively to their judgment. In contrast, when presented with competing recommendations, the decision-maker cannot simply follow orders. They are compelled to compare conflicting rationales, verify facts, and determine which advice aligns best with their core values. This intellectual friction dismantles flawed assumptions and clarifies priorities, ultimately empowering the individual to take genuine ownership of their ultimate path.

The collective wisdom of several advisers serves as a vital safeguard against poor judgment. While sorting through conflicting counsel requires patience and discernment, the rewards are profound. By exposing personal biases, assembling diverse expertise, and demanding active engagement from the chooser, multiple opinions illuminate the safest and most rewarding path forward. Sound decisions are rarely forged in an echo chamber; they emerge when varied viewpoints challenge, refine, and elevate an individual's judgment.

Dear Principal,

Our school is considering whether all students should be required to perform community service. I believe we should adopt this requirement. Some students may worry that service would take time away from homework, jobs, sports, or other activities. However, the benefits to both students and the community make a reasonable service requirement worthwhile.

Community service teaches responsibility, empathy, and practical skills that students cannot learn from a textbook alone. For instance, a student who tutors an elementary school child must prepare, explain ideas clearly, and be patient when the child struggles. Through that experience, the tutor develops communication skills and gains a sense of accomplishment from helping someone improve. In the same way, students who clean up litter in a park learn that public spaces do not stay clean by themselves. Someone has to notice a problem and take responsibility for fixing it. A service requirement would make sure that every student, not just those who already volunteer, has the chance to learn these lessons.

Community service would also benefit the people around our school. We have many students, and even a few hours of service from each person could make a real difference. More young children could receive tutoring, parks and sidewalks could be cleaner, and elderly residents could have visitors or help with simple tasks. Each activity may seem small by itself, but together they would have a meaningful effect. Our community supports the school through taxes, donations, and local programs, so it makes sense for students to give something back.

I understand why some students are concerned about finding the time. Many students already balance classes, sports, part-time jobs, and family responsibilities. Still, the requirement could be designed to be flexible. Students could complete service hours on weekends, during study halls, after school, or over the summer. The school could also offer different types of projects so that students could choose opportunities that fit their schedules and interests. A limited requirement, such as twenty hours per year, would not be overwhelming. Instead, it could help students learn to plan ahead and manage their time, which are important skills for college and future jobs.

Some people may say that service is not meaningful if it is required. While that is understandable, many valuable experiences begin as requirements. Students may not choose to take every class, such as math or science, but they still learn useful information from them. In the same way, a student who is required to tutor a child or help clean a park might discover an interest in teaching, environmental work, or another kind of service. Even if students do not continue volunteering afterward, they will have learned what it means to contribute to the people around them.

For these reasons, I strongly support requiring students to perform community service. A thoughtful and flexible program would build character, strengthen our community, and teach students important life skills. I hope you will consider adopting a reasonable service requirement for our school.

Sincerely,  
A Student

Modern life encourages an illusion of seamless multitasking. We answer emails while waiting in line, listen to podcasts while folding laundry, and trade text messages while walking down the street. Yet this fluidity collapses entirely the moment an individual steps into the driver’s seat of an automobile. Operating a vehicle demands uninterrupted visual, manual, and cognitive attention. Because mobile devices fundamentally undermine all three, drivers should be barred from using cell phones in any capacity while their vehicles are in motion.

Much of the legislative discourse over the past two decades has centered on the physical mechanics of phone use, leading to widespread bans on handheld devices while explicitly sanctioning hands-free alternatives. This distinction, however, rests on a dangerous misunderstanding of human cognition. The primary hazard of a phone call is rarely the mechanical act of holding plastic to one’s ear; it is the mental load required to converse with a disembodied voice. Cognitive psychologists refer to the resulting impairment as inattentional blindness. When a driver’s mind is engaged in deciphering speech and projecting a mental image of the person on the other end of the line, the brain narrows its field of visual processing. Drivers using hands-free setups frequently look directly at hazards—red lights, braking vehicles, pedestrians stepping into crosswalks—without actually registering them. A passenger in the car naturally modulates conversation based on the traffic environment, pausing when conditions grow treacherous; a remote interlocutor cannot adjust to a sudden icy patch or an erratic lane-changer.

The counterarguments often appeal to practicality. Smartphones serve as our primary navigators, and completely eliminating them seems anachronistic, if not impossible. Furthermore, emergencies inevitably arise. Yet these realities do not necessitate active engagement while operating a vehicle. Turn-by-turn navigation can be programmed prior to shifting out of park, operating purely as an audio guide that requires zero interaction from the driver. If an emergency occurs or a route must be adjusted, pulling over into a designated parking area or onto the shoulder takes seconds. The minor inconvenience of stopping completely pales beside the catastrophic consequences of a split-second distraction. At highway speeds, glancing down at a notification for just four seconds means traveling the length of an entire football field entirely blind.

Treating the open road as a mobile office or entertainment hub is a cultural habit born of convenience, not necessity. Decades ago, society viewed driving under the influence of alcohol with a degree of casual tolerance that seems unthinkable today; it required strict legal boundaries and sustained public campaigns to reframe the behavior as reckless endangerment. Mobile phone use behind the wheel requires an identical reckoning. When piloting two tons of steel and glass at high velocity, divided attention is an unacceptable gamble. A total, uncompromising prohibition on cell phone use while operating a vehicle is the only standard that respects the sheer lethality of the machine and the shared vulnerability of everyone on the road.

The widespread ownership of cell phones has made constant communication a normal part of modern life, but it has also created a serious danger on the road. Although mobile devices offer convenience, connection, and a sense of security, allowing drivers to use them in any capacity while operating a vehicle creates unacceptable risks. Because even hands-free use impairs attention and because the consequences of divided focus are often fatal, drivers should not be permitted to use cell phones at all while driving.

The strongest reason for a complete ban is that cell phone use causes cognitive distraction, even when the driver’s hands remain on the wheel. Driving requires continuous observation, judgment, and quick reaction. When a person is engaged in a phone conversation, the brain focuses on listening and responding rather than fully processing the road. Research on inattention blindness shows that a driver can look directly at a hazard and still fail to recognize it because his or her mind is elsewhere. Unlike listening to the radio, a phone call is interactive and demands mental effort. As a result, a driver on a hands-free call may miss a pedestrian stepping into a crosswalk or a vehicle braking suddenly ahead. Therefore, “in any capacity” must include hands-free use, since the danger is mental rather than purely physical.

In addition, the manual and visual actions of dialing, texting, or glancing at a screen combine several forms of distraction. Texting is especially hazardous because it can take a driver’s eyes off the road for several seconds, long enough to travel the length of a football field at highway speed. While some argue that voice commands and built-in systems reduce these risks, such technologies still require the driver to divide attention among the phone, the vehicle, and traffic. The safest approach is to remove the option entirely rather than allow partial use that may encourage risky behavior.

Finally, the public cost of distracted driving justifies a strict prohibition. Thousands of deaths and injuries each year are attributed to distracted driving, many involving cell phones. Unlike unavoidable hazards, this risk is voluntary and preventable. A total ban sends a clear message that driving is a full-time activity requiring undivided concentration. It also gives law enforcement a straightforward standard: if the vehicle is moving, the phone should not be in use. Genuine emergencies can be handled by pulling over safely before making a call.

In conclusion, the convenience of cell phone communication cannot outweigh the responsibility to protect human life. Because phone use impairs attention even when hands are free, and because divided attention leads to avoidable crashes, drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle. A total ban would reinforce responsible driving, reduce injuries and deaths, and keep every driver’s focus where it belongs: on the road.

Seeking advice from more than one person can lead to better decisions because different people notice different risks, values, and possibilities. No individual sees every side of a problem, especially when the person making the choice is stressed, excited, or uncertain. Multiple opinions do not guarantee a perfect answer, but they can provide a fuller picture and help someone make a decision with greater confidence.

For example, consider a student deciding whether to attend a college far from home. A parent might focus on safety, cost, and the emotional difficulty of moving away. A teacher may consider the school’s academic reputation and whether its programs match the student’s strengths. A friend who has already moved away for college might offer practical advice about roommates, homesickness, and independence. Each person is responding to the same question, yet each brings a different kind of knowledge. If the student listened only to a parent, they might overlook an excellent academic opportunity. If they listened only to a friend, they might underestimate the financial burden. Hearing several perspectives makes it easier to compare the benefits and drawbacks honestly.

Multiple opinions can also protect people from emotional or impulsive choices. When someone is excited about a new job offer, for instance, they may focus mainly on the higher salary or impressive title. A trusted mentor could point out that the position requires frequent travel, has limited opportunities for advancement, or may not fit the person’s long-term goals. On the other hand, a family member might remind them that a demanding schedule could affect their health or relationships. These comments may not be what the person wants to hear, but advice is most valuable when it reveals a problem that has been ignored.

Another advantage is that consulting several people can help identify reliable patterns. One opinion may simply reflect personal preference. If three experienced mechanics warn that a used car has unusually high repair costs, however, that repeated concern deserves attention. Similarly, if several employees describe a workplace as supportive and fair, their agreement may be more meaningful than one glowing online review. Comparing responses helps a person separate isolated opinions from useful evidence.

Still, asking for many opinions does not mean surrendering responsibility for the final choice. Advice can become confusing when people have conflicting priorities. A person choosing a career may receive one recommendation to pursue stability, another to follow passion, and another to choose the highest-paying option. Rather than treating any adviser as completely right, the individual should consider which values matter most to them. The goal is not to collect votes but to gain information.

In the end, major decisions usually affect more than one part of life, so they deserve more than one viewpoint. After weighing those perspectives, a person is better prepared to make a choice that is informed, realistic, and truly their own.

Second, lunch and free periods are appropriate times for students to use phones. Students already use their free time to talk with friends, finish homework, read, or relax. Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge you to support keeping the Electoral College as the method for electing the President of the United States. I understand that many people are frustrated with this system, especially after recent elections, but I believe it still plays an important role in protecting federalism and encouraging national unity.

One of the strongest arguments against the Electoral College is that a candidate can lose the national popular vote and still become president. This happened in 2000 and 2016, which understandably made many Americans question whether the system is fair. However, Judge Richard A. Posner offers a helpful defense: the Electoral College prevents a candidate from winning simply by running up huge margins in densely populated urban areas or in one part of the country. Instead, it pushes candidates to create broad coalitions that include voters from different states and regions. That requirement helps ensure the president has support across the country, not just in a few concentrated areas.

Critics also point out that the Electoral College encourages campaigns to spend most of their time in a handful of swing states, while safe Democratic and Republican states seem to be ignored. There is some truth to this, and I do not want to dismiss that concern. Still, the focus on swing states can be seen another way: it forces candidates to pay attention to states that are politically divided and to appeal to a range of voters rather than simply energizing one base. Under a national popular vote, campaigns might focus even more narrowly on large population centers, where the most efficient path to a majority would likely be found.

Another concern involves faithless electors, or electors who do not vote for the candidate who won their state. While this possibility sounds troubling, it is rare and has not decided a modern presidential election. The process described by the Office of the Federal Register shows that the Electoral College has operated for more than two centuries, providing stability and a reliable method for choosing the president. A popular vote system, by contrast, could create new problems. A close national election would likely lead to a nationwide recount, with disputes in every county and no clear framework for resolving them. The Electoral College keeps recounts and controversies largely within individual states, which is more manageable and produces a clearer result.

In short, I recognize that the Electoral College is not perfect, but it encourages candidates to build broad, geographically diverse support and helps avoid the uncertainty of a nationwide popular-vote recount. I ask you to oppose replacing it with a direct popular vote and to support keeping this constitutional system.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

Dear Principal Harmon,

I am writing about the proposal to require all students to perform community service. After thinking it over, and after talking with friends on both sides of the question, I believe a service requirement would be a good addition to our school, provided it is designed with some care.

The strongest argument against the idea is one I hear often. My friend Marcus works twenty hours a week at his uncle's garage and helps raise two younger siblings. When he hears "required service," he hears one more demand on a day that is already full. I take that seriously. A requirement that ignores students like Marcus would be unfair, and it would probably breed resentment instead of generosity.

But I think the answer is to build flexibility into the requirement, not to abandon it. Consider what my friends who already volunteer have gotten out of it. Priya tutors second graders in reading on Thursday afternoons, and she talks about it with more energy than she brings to almost anything else. She has learned patience, and she has discovered that she wants to teach. Another friend, Daniel, joined a weekend creek cleanup out of boredom, and now he organizes one every spring. Neither of them would have stumbled into these experiences without a nudge. Many students simply never think of volunteering until someone puts it in front of them, and a requirement can be that push.

There is also a practical benefit our school should not overlook. Students who spend a few hours in a food pantry or a nursing home see parts of our town that school never shows them. It is hard to stay indifferent to hunger or loneliness once you have met someone who lives with it. That kind of understanding is difficult to teach from a textbook, and it makes us better neighbors and, eventually, better citizens.

As for time, the numbers are modest if we plan sensibly. Suppose the requirement were forty hours over four years. That is ten hours a year, less than an hour a month. Students could complete hours during the summer, on weekends, or through projects organized at school during advisory periods. Those with jobs or family responsibilities could count some of that work, such as caring for a relative or helping at a family business that serves the community, so that students like Marcus are not penalized for obligations they already carry.

I would also suggest letting students choose where they serve. Someone who loves animals might walk dogs at the shelter, while someone who is shy might sort donations behind the scenes. Choice makes the work meaningful instead of a box to check. Teachers or counselors could help match students with organizations, and a short reflection, a paragraph or a brief conversation, would help students notice what they learned.

Not every student will embrace the requirement at first, and a few will grumble all the way through. Still, many things we require, from gym class to group projects, feel like a chore until they turn into something we value. Service is likely to be one of them.

I hope you will consider adopting a requirement that is reasonable in size, flexible in how it can be met, and respectful of the students who already have too much on their plates. Thank you for taking the time to read my thoughts.

Sincerely,
Jordan Ellis
Grade 10

Summer break can lead to the “summer slide,” when students lose some of the academic skills they worked hard to develop during the school year. To prevent this, many schools assign summer projects. Although student-designed projects can allow young people to explore their interests, summer projects should mostly be teacher-designed. Teachers can make sure the work is academically useful, fair to all students, and connected to clear learning goals, while still offering some choices.

First, teacher-designed projects can match curriculum standards and focus on the skills students will need in the next grade. Teachers understand which topics are most important for future classes. For example, an eighth-grade math teacher could create a summer assignment that reviews linear equations and basic geometry because both are necessary for success in Algebra I. A student might choose to create a cooking blog involving fractions, which could be interesting, but it might not review the full range of math skills required. In the same way, an English teacher could assign summer reading that prepares students for a fall unit on American literature. Reading novels such as *To Kill a Mockingbird* or *The Great Gatsby*, along with answering guided questions, would give students useful background for class discussions later. When teachers design the project, they can make sure it reinforces the right material.

Teacher-designed projects also promote equity by giving students clear expectations and structure. Not every student has a parent, tutor, computer, or other resources available during the summer. If students are simply told to create their own academic project, some may receive a great deal of help and produce complicated presentations or experiments. Others may not know where to begin. This could make existing achievement gaps even wider. A teacher-designed assignment gives everyone the same directions, rubric, and materials list. For instance, a teacher could assign a summer journal with daily writing prompts that requires only a notebook and pencil. Templates, checklists, and examples could also help students who need more support. Providing this structure makes the assignment more accessible and gives every student a fair chance to succeed.

Of course, supporters of student-designed projects may argue that students work harder when they can choose subjects that matter to them. That is a reasonable point, since interest can increase motivation. However, teacher-designed projects do not have to remove all student choice. A history teacher might ask students to select any decade from the twentieth century and create an annotated timeline. A science teacher could allow students to choose between tracking weather patterns and conducting a simple plant-growth experiment. In both cases, students have ownership over part of the assignment, but the teacher still sets academic expectations and makes sure the project teaches important skills.

Ultimately, summer projects should be teacher-designed because teachers can connect them to needed curriculum, create fair expectations for all students, and provide helpful structure. At the same time, including limited choices can make the work more interesting and personal. By relying on teachers to design meaningful summer assignments, schools can better reduce learning loss and help students return prepared for the year ahead.

I think students would benefit from having the option to attend classes from home, although it should not completely replace going to school. Online learning can help students who are sick, have transportation problems, or need a quieter place to focus. At the same time, schools should make sure that students still have chances to interact with teachers and classmates.

One reason distance learning can be helpful is that students do not always have control over their situation at home. For example, a student might have the flu or another illness that makes it hard to get to school, but they may still feel well enough to listen to a lesson online. Instead of missing several days of work and becoming stressed about catching up, they could join the class from home. This would also keep sick students from spreading germs to other people at school.

Distance learning could also help students with difficult schedules. Some students have long bus rides, family responsibilities, or medical appointments. If a student has to help take care of a younger sibling after school or has physical therapy during the day, attending online could make it easier for them to stay involved in class. It might also help students who feel unsafe traveling to school during bad weather. Rather than canceling learning completely because of snow or flooding, classes could continue through video conferencing.

Another benefit is that some students learn better in a calm environment. Classrooms can be loud, especially during group work or when many students are talking. At home, a student may be able to use headphones, sit in a comfortable workspace, and avoid distractions from crowded hallways. They could also replay recorded lessons if the school allows it. For example, if someone does not understand a math problem the first time, being able to watch the explanation again could be very useful.

However, I do not think all students should be required to learn from home. School is not only about academic subjects. Students make friends, join clubs, play sports, and learn how to work with other people in person. It can also be harder to stay motivated at home when there is no teacher nearby. Some students may start checking their phones, playing games, or leaving the screen while class is happening. Teachers might also have a harder time noticing when someone is confused.

Because of these problems, distance learning should be an option instead of the normal way students attend school. Schools could let students attend remotely for short periods, such as when they are sick or dealing with a family issue. They should also set clear rules, like keeping cameras on when possible, participating in discussions, and completing assignments on time.

Overall, being able to attend classes from home would benefit many students because it gives them flexibility when life gets complicated. As long as schools still encourage in-person learning and social connection, distance learning can be a helpful choice rather than a replacement for school.

Extracurricular activities can be some of the most valuable parts of a student’s education. Sports teach teamwork, yearbook develops writing and design skills, and student council gives students experience with leadership. However, requiring every student to participate in at least one activity is not the best decision. Schools should strongly encourage involvement and make activities accessible, but participation should remain a choice because students have different responsibilities, interests, and needs.

First, not every student has the same amount of free time after school. Many students have obligations that are just as important as school clubs or teams. Some students care for younger siblings while their parents work. Others have part-time jobs to help their families pay for food, rent, or transportation. A student who works several evenings each week may not be able to attend football practice, drama rehearsals, or student council meetings without becoming exhausted. Requiring that student to join an activity could create unnecessary stress and even harm academic performance. Education should recognize students’ real lives rather than assume that everyone has the same schedule.

In addition, students should have the freedom to choose how they spend their time outside the classroom. A student may be passionate about an activity that the school does not offer, such as painting, coding, caring for animals, or helping at a community center. Another student may use free time to practice music independently or take care of mental health needs. These experiences can be meaningful and educational even if they do not appear on an official school list. If the school requires participation only in approved extracurricular activities, it may send the message that students’ personal interests and family responsibilities do not count.

Mandatory involvement could also cause students to join activities without genuine interest. For example, a student who dislikes sports might sign up for a team only to meet the requirement. That student may attend irregularly, contribute little, and take attention away from teammates who truly want to participate. Similarly, a student forced onto the yearbook staff might not be motivated to complete assignments carefully. Clubs and teams tend to be stronger when members choose to be there and share a common purpose. Enthusiasm cannot be created simply by making attendance compulsory.

This does not mean schools should ignore students who are not involved. Instead, schools could offer activity fairs, provide late buses, reduce fees, and help students find clubs that match their interests. Teachers and counselors could personally invite quiet or uncertain students to try an activity for a few weeks. Schools could also recognize community service, jobs, and family caregiving as valuable forms of involvement. These approaches would remove barriers while still respecting students’ choices.

Extracurricular activities offer important opportunities for friendship, leadership, and personal growth, so schools should make them welcoming and available to everyone. Nevertheless, requiring every student to participate would be unfair to those with demanding responsibilities or different goals. Encouragement, support, and flexibility will inspire more meaningful participation than a rule ever could.

Dear Principal Miller,

As our school community re-evaluates its technological guidelines, the question of how to manage mobile devices has become central to our daily learning environment. Between the two proposed options, I strongly urge you to adopt Policy 1, which permits students to bring phones to campus and access them during lunch periods and free time, provided they remain turned off during instructional hours. This balanced approach addresses the practical realities of modern communication, fosters essential habits of self-regulation, and avoids the contentious enforcement challenges associated with an outright ban.

First and foremost, mobile phones serve as an indispensable link between students and their families. Many students manage complicated schedules involving extracurricular activities, after-school employment, or caretaking responsibilities for younger siblings. Permitting phone access during lunch allows students to coordinate transportation, confirm family logistics, and respond to urgent messages without disrupting class time or placing an administrative burden on the main office. In unpredictable circumstances, such as sudden weather cancellations or family emergencies, the ability to communicate directly provides reassurance to both students and parents.

Furthermore, Policy 1 offers a valuable opportunity to cultivate digital literacy and personal responsibility. High school serves as a transitional stage designed to prepare young adults for higher education and the modern workplace—environments where mobile devices are ubiquitous, yet personal discipline is strictly expected. An absolute ban operates on total deprivation rather than guided practice. By requiring devices to be powered off during academic instruction while allowing their use during leisure hours, the school establishes a clear professional boundary. This expectation teaches students how to compartmentalize personal distractions and focus on the task at hand, a skill far more enduring than forced compliance.

Finally, attempting to enforce a total ban, as proposed in Policy 2, would severely damage the school climate. Total prohibitions inevitably drive behavior underground, turning teachers and administrators into surveillance agents who must constantly police pockets and confiscate hidden devices. This dynamic breeds mutual distrust and diverts valuable instructional energy toward minor disciplinary infractions. In contrast, Policy 1 offers a reasonable compromise that students are far more willing to honor. When policies reflect fairness and mutual respect, compliance naturally increases, allowing staff to focus on education rather than confrontation.

In conclusion, maintaining an undistracted classroom environment does not require the complete exclusion of mobile technology from our campus. Policy 1 strikes the ideal balance by safeguarding the integrity of academic time while recognizing students' practical needs and capacity for maturity during personal breaks. Thank you for your leadership and for thoughtfully considering the student body’s perspective as you make this important decision.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

Dear Senator,

As your constituent, I am writing to urge you to oppose efforts to dismantle the Electoral College. In an era marked by intense political division, calls to replace this foundational institution with a direct national popular vote have grown louder. Yet, while the impulse to simplify the presidential selection process is understandable, abolishing the Electoral College would erode the federalist design of our Republic and introduce profound administrative instability into our elections. 

Critics, such as Bradford Plumer, frequently argue that the system is fundamentally undemocratic. Plumer notes that the mechanism allows a candidate to secure the presidency while losing the national popular vote, as occurred in 2000 and 2016. Detractors further contend that the widespread "winner-take-all" allocation utilized by forty-eight states and Washington, D.C., reduces general election campaigns to a narrow set of swing states, leaving millions of voters in reliably partisan states feeling sidelined. These criticisms are not without merit; voter alienation is a real concern in modern American politics. 

However, moving to a direct popular vote would merely substitute one set of geographic distortions for another, far more damaging one. As the Office of the Federal Register documents, the Framers deliberately established the Electoral College as a constitutional compromise between legislative selection and direct democratic voting, ensuring every state retained a voice equal to its total congressional delegation. This structure prevents candidates from treating less populous regions as political irrelevancies. 

Legal scholar Richard A. Posner emphasizes that the Electoral College serves as a vital safeguard of federalism. By requiring a candidate to secure a distribution of electoral votes across diverse jurisdictions, the current system forces campaigns to assemble broad national coalitions rather than catering exclusively to high-density metropolitan corridors. Without the discipline imposed by the state-by-state contest, candidates could easily win the White House simply by running up exorbitant margins in a handful of populous cities and coastal states, wholly ignoring the agricultural, industrial, and civic interests of the interior.

Equally compelling is the institutional stability the system provides in moments of electoral crisis. A nationwide popular vote would turn every close contest into an administrative nightmare. As Judge Posner points out, the existing framework confines contested tallies and potential recounts to individual states, insulating the broader nation from widespread legal paralysis. In contrast, an election decided by a razor-thin national margin would necessitate a recount across thousands of decentralized county election boards nationwide, straining our democratic infrastructure to the breaking point.

The Electoral College is not an antiquated obstacle to democracy; it is the structural anchor of our federal system. It tempers the tyranny of mere population density and compels our leaders to build geographic consensus across our sprawling continent. For these reasons, I respectfully ask that you defend our constitutional system and reject any legislative measures aimed at bypassing the Electoral College.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Constituent

When our principal announced that every student must join at least one extracurricular activity, groans echoed through the auditorium. I get it. Some students already juggle jobs, family responsibilities, or hours of homework. Adding another obligation can feel like one more demand on an already stretched schedule. Yet I believe this decision is not only reasonable but necessary. Schools should push us beyond the classroom walls, because that is where confidence, collaboration, and a sense of belonging actually take root.

The quietest kid in my biology class joined the yearbook staff last fall. At first, he only carried a camera and avoided the planning meetings. Within weeks, though, he was haggling over photo layouts and suggesting a spread about the robotics team. He had found a role that did not depend on raising his hand in a lecture. A mandatory extracurricular policy creates thousands of those opportunities. Without a nudge, many students never sample drama, debate, or intramural soccer, and they miss the chance to discover a talent or a community.

Critics often say that forced participation breeds resentment and half-hearted effort. That concern is real. But mandatory does not mean forced into a single activity; it means required to choose something. A student who hates basketball can join the environmental club. Someone who freezes on stage can manage lights for the winter musical. This flexibility preserves student agency while still opening doors. For some, the first reluctant step into a club meeting turns into the first place they feel at home.

There is also a practical argument. Employers and colleges constantly ask for more than grades. They want evidence of teamwork, initiative, and commitment. A transcript full of A’s tells only part of the story. Serving on student council, editing the literary magazine, or volunteering as a peer tutor demonstrates that a student can set goals, resolve conflicts, and follow through outside the pressure of tests. By making one activity mandatory, the school ensures that every graduate leaves with at least one concrete example of that growth.

I understand the worry about overbooked students. Some teenagers work to help support their families, care for younger siblings, or manage health challenges. A rigid policy could punish them unfairly. That is why the school should offer low-time-commitment options, such as a monthly book club or a Saturday park cleanup, and should grant exceptions on a case-by-case basis. A thoughtful version of this policy would not ignore real hardships; it would simply set the default expectation that everyone belongs to something beyond their class schedule.

What finally convinces me is a memory from my freshman year. I almost did not try out for the school play because I was afraid of forgetting lines. My friend dragged me to auditions. I ended up with a small role, a terrible stage accent, and a group of friends I still eat lunch with two years later. That experience taught me more about discipline and vulnerability than any worksheet. Not every student will have a friend pushing them through the door. A school-wide requirement can be that push. It should not be the only nudge in a young person’s life, but it can be the one that matters.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge you to support preserving the Electoral College. At a time when partisan division dominates the national conversation, our constitutional mechanisms face intense scrutiny. While the idea of a direct national popular vote possesses an intuitive, democratic appeal, the framework established by the framers remains an essential safeguard for the stability of our federal republic.

As detailed by the Office of the Federal Register, the Electoral College was born out of a deliberate compromise between a congressional selection of the executive and a purely popular vote. By tying each state’s allotment of electors to its total congressional representation—combining members of the House of Representatives with two senators—the system guarantees that every state retains a constitutional baseline of influence. This design ensures that smaller states are not rendered entirely irrelevant by more populous neighbors.

Critics like Bradford Plumer raise understandable concerns, pointing out that the mechanism can elevate a candidate who lost the aggregate national vote, as occurred in 2000 and 2016. Furthermore, detractors argue that the winner-take-all model used by forty-eight states and Washington, D.C. distorts campaigning, encouraging candidates to pour time and money into a narrow tier of swing states while taking noncompetitive regions for granted. 

Yet, replacing this system with a national popular vote would create far more dangerous distortions. As legal scholar Richard A. Posner notes, the Electoral College compels candidates to assemble broad geographic coalitions rather than simply racking up lopsided majorities in a handful of high-density metropolitan corridors. Without the discipline imposed by state-by-state tallies, a campaign could run up astronomical margins in major coastal cities while ignoring rural and regional concerns across middle America entirely. The current structure demands that an aspiring president appeal to diverse constituencies across multiple cultural and economic landscapes.

Beyond coalition building, the practical virtues of the Electoral College during disputed elections cannot be overstated. When an election yields an agonizingly close outcome, our current process confines the inevitable friction of legal challenges and recounts to individual states, as Judge Posner highlights. A nationwide popular vote, by contrast, would expose the entire country to the administrative nightmare of a 50-state recount, where every precinct from Alaska to Florida would be litigated under differing local ballot standards. Such a scenario would inevitably delay the transfer of power and corrode public trust in the final outcome.

The Electoral College is not an obsolete relic, but a cornerstone of American federalism designed to balance local sovereignty with national unity. It tempers raw majoritarianism with regional moderation and ensures decisive transitions of power. For the enduring health of our republic, I ask that you oppose any efforts to dismantle this vital institution.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Constituent

Imagine getting into a car, sitting back, and letting a computer do all the steering while you do your homework or take a nap. In the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," the author explains that tech companies and automakers are working hard to make this technology part of everyday life. People like Google cofounder Sergey Brin think this could completely change how we travel. However, even though the idea sounds cool and futuristic, companies should not rush into developing and deploying driverless cars right now. Autonomous vehicles still have too many dangerous flaws, software risks, and confusing legal problems to be trusted on real roads.

First of all, the technology behind driverless cars is simply not reliable enough to handle bad weather or unexpected road conditions. The article states that these vehicles rely on laser radar, cameras, GPS, and sensors to detect obstacles and lane markings. But it also points out that these sensors struggle during heavy rain, snow, fog, and in unmarked construction zones. When human beings drive, they can use their judgment to navigate around an orange cone or slow down when it is pouring rain. If a computer gets confused by bad weather, it could lead to terrible accidents. On top of that, the software can glitch or get hacked by cybersecurity threats, which is a scary thought when you are traveling at sixty miles per hour on a highway.

Another major problem is how people interact with semi-autonomous systems. Supporters in the article mention that over 90 percent of car crashes are caused by human error, like texting or falling asleep. While that might make computers sound safer, the article also explains that semi-autonomous cars still need humans to take over during emergencies. The problem is that studies show people quickly lose focus when a machine is driving for them. If a driver zones out because the car is steering itself, their reaction time will be way too slow when something suddenly goes wrong. Instead of eliminating human error, these vehicles might actually make drivers less alert and less prepared to react safely.

Finally, there are huge unresolved questions about what happens when a crash actually occurs. The article mentions that nobody knows who should be held legally responsible. Should the blame go to the person sitting in the car, the company that wrote the software, or the automaker that built the vehicle? Our legal system is not set up to answer these questions yet. Until there are clear laws and real accountability, putting these cars on public roads puts regular drivers and pedestrians at unfair risk.

In conclusion, autonomous vehicles are not ready for the real world. While the promise of fewer accidents and better mobility for disabled people sounds great, the current reality involves failing sensors, distracted drivers, hacking risks, and confusing legal issues. Developers need to slow down and fix these serious problems before replacing regular drivers with computers.

Dear Principal Johnson,

I am writing to respectfully oppose the proposed policy requiring students to maintain at least a B average in order to participate in sports and other school activities. I understand that the purpose of this rule would be to encourage stronger academic performance. However, I believe it would harm many students instead of helping them. A student with a C average is still passing, yet this policy would take away opportunities that often help students stay motivated, connected, and successful in school.

Extracurricular activities should not be viewed only as rewards for students with the highest grades. Sports, music, drama, student government, and clubs are important parts of a well-rounded education. They teach skills that cannot always be learned in a classroom, including teamwork, responsibility, leadership, discipline, and communication. For example, a student who earns Cs in algebra may still be a dedicated basketball player who learns how to work under pressure and encourage teammates. Another student who has difficulty writing essays may discover confidence through the robotics club, band, or school play. Taking those opportunities away could make students feel that their strengths do not matter.

In addition, activities can actually improve students’ grades. Being on a team or involved in a club requires students to plan ahead, attend school, and balance homework with practices or meetings. For many students, an activity gives them a reason to stay focused in class and keep trying when school becomes difficult. If participation is taken away until a student reaches a B average, the school may remove the motivation that student needs to improve. Rather than excluding students with Cs, the school could require them to attend study hall, receive tutoring, or meet regularly with a teacher to check their progress. This would make academics a priority without cutting students off from valuable activities.

A strict B-average rule also ignores the different challenges students may face. Some students work extremely hard but earn Cs because they have learning differences, are still developing English skills, care for siblings, work after school, or deal with difficult situations at home. These students may need sports and clubs even more because activities can provide structure, friendships, and a healthy way to deal with stress. Removing those supports could lead to more isolation and frustration, not better grades.

The policy could also discourage students from taking challenging classes. A student might avoid honors science or advanced math because earning a C in a difficult course could make them ineligible. Grades are important, but they do not always show how much effort a student is making or how much they are learning.

I agree that academic success should remain a major priority at our school. Still, a more supportive policy would be better than requiring a B average. Students could be expected to pass all of their classes, attend school regularly, and participate in academic support when their grades fall below a certain level. This approach would hold students accountable while giving them the help they need to improve.

Thank you for considering student opinions on this important issue. I hope you will choose a policy that encourages academic growth without taking away the activities that help many students succeed.

When students are given the freedom to design their own projects, they are more likely to pursue topics that genuinely interest them, leading to a more engaging and enjoyable learning experience. For instance, a student passionate about environmental conservation might design a project that involves conducting a local park cleanup, researching sustainable practices, and creating a public awareness campaign. This type of project not only develops important skills such as research, critical thinking, and problem-solving but also allows students to explore their passions and interests in a meaningful way. In contrast, teacher-designed projects can often feel rigid and restrictive, limiting students' ability to explore and express their individuality.

Moreover, student-designed projects help students develop essential life skills such as self-directed learning, time management, and self-discipline. When students are responsible for designing and completing their own projects, they must prioritize tasks, set deadlines, and manage their time effectively to ensure successful completion. These skills are invaluable in today's fast-paced, ever-changing world, where individuals are expected to be adaptable, resourceful, and proactive. Furthermore, student-designed projects provide students with the opportunity to reflect on their own learning, identifying areas of strength and weakness, and stretching their abilities to tackle complex challenges. This metacognitive awareness is critical for students' long-term success, as it enables them to develop a growth mindset, set realistic goals, and navigate the complexities of an increasingly rapidly evolving world.

Another significant advantage of student-designed projects is that they allow teachers to gain a deeper understanding of their students' interests, strengths, and learning styles. By reviewing student-designed projects, teachers can identify areas where students may need additional support or enrichment, informing their instruction and assessment strategies for the upcoming academic year. Additionally, student-designed projects can help bridge the gap between school and real-world learning, as students apply theoretical concepts to practical problems and scenarios. For example, a student interested in entrepreneurship might design a project that involves developing a business plan, creating a marketing campaign, and launching a small-scale venture. Dear Principal Reynolds,

I appreciate that you are looking for ways to push us toward academic excellence. Raising expectations is a natural instinct for any school leader, and the idea that requiring a B average will motivate students to study harder sounds reasonable in theory. In practice, however, barring students with a C average from sports and clubs would do far more harm than good. I strongly urge you to keep the current eligibility standard in place.

A grade of C is, by definition, satisfactory. It means a student has demonstrated a functional grasp of the curriculum and met the district's baseline requirements for graduation. For many of our classmates, earning that C is not a sign of laziness or indifference; it is the result of exhausting effort. Some juggle part-time jobs to help support their families, others care for younger siblings after the bell rings, and many battle genuine learning differences or severe test anxiety. Telling these students that meeting grade-level standards is no longer good enough to wear a jersey, join the robotics team, or perform in the spring play sends an alienating message: if you aren't naturally gifted in the classroom, you don't fully belong to our school community.

Just as importantly, extracurriculars are not a distraction from academics—they are often the very engine that keeps students engaged. Coaches, directors, and club advisors demand discipline, monitor attendance, and hold participants accountable in ways that regular classroom teachers rarely have the time to do. For a struggling sophomore, the promise of stepping onto the soccer pitch or tuning an instrument at the end of the day is often what makes six hours of difficult coursework bearable. Take that outlet away, and you remove their primary anchor to the school. Experience shows that when struggling students lose their connection to after-school programs, their grades do not magically climb to a B. Instead, their attendance drops, their frustration mounts, and they drift toward failing entirely.

If our shared goal is truly to raise student achievement, the answer lies in support rather than exclusion. Instead of sidelining students who hold a C average, the school could mandate study tables or peer tutoring sessions for any participant whose GPA sits between a 2.0 and a 3.0. This approach would preserve the positive accountability of teams and clubs while providing the concrete academic assistance these students actually need to improve

Dear Senator [Last Name],

My name is [Name], and I am a student in your district. I am writing because I think our country should change to electing the president by popular vote instead of using the Electoral College. I hope you will support this change when it comes up in the Senate.

The biggest reason is that the Electoral College does not always go with what most Americans want. According to Bradford Plumer, a candidate can win the national popular vote and still lose the presidency, which happened in 2000 and 2016. That seems really unfair to me. In school we learn that every vote should count the same, but in those elections millions more people voted for one candidate and that candidate still lost. If the point of an election is to find out what the people want, the system should do that.

Another problem is how campaigns are run. The Office of the Federal Register explains that forty-eight states and Washington, D.C. use a "winner-take-all" system, meaning the candidate who wins a state by even a tiny amount gets all of its electoral votes. Plumer says this causes candidates to focus almost completely on a few swing states and ignore everyone else. If I lived in a state that is safely one party, my vote would hardly matter to the campaigns, and they would not visit or talk about my concerns. Plumer also says this can lower voter turnout, since people may think there is no point in voting. A popular vote would make every voter in every state worth the same to a candidate.

I know there are good arguments on the other side. Judge Richard Posner defends the Electoral College by saying it protects federalism and makes candidates build broad coalitions across large and small states. He worries that without it, candidates would just run up huge vote totals in big cities or one region. I understand this concern, but I do not think it is very convincing. Under a popular vote, a candidate would still need votes from all over the country, and every vote in a small state or a rural area would count just as much as one in a city. Right now, candidates can ignore whole states, so the current system does not really force them to care about everyone either.

Posner also says the Electoral College gives a clear winner quickly and keeps recounts limited to single states instead of one giant national recount. That is a fair point, and a national recount in a very close race could be messy. However, close elections already cause problems under the current system, like in 2000, when the whole result depended on one state. Also, recounts are rare, and we could create clear national rules for them. Fixing a possible recount problem is not a good enough reason to keep a system that can pick the candidate with fewer votes. The Electoral College also has "faithless electors," who Plumer says could vote against their state's popular choice. That adds one more way the result might not match what voters chose.

The Federal Register points out that the Electoral College was created as a compromise by the Founding Fathers. A compromise made a long time ago does not have to stay forever, especially when it causes problems today. The country has changed a lot since then, and our voting system should change too.

For these reasons, I urge you to support moving to a national popular vote for president. It would be fairer, it would make every voter matter, and it would make sure the person with the most votes becomes president. Thank you for your time and for considering my opinion.

Sincerely,
[Name]

Cell phones have become essential tools for communication, navigation, work, and emergencies. Because they are so common, many drivers assume they can use them safely behind the wheel, especially when the phone is hands-free or mounted on the dashboard. Still, drivers should not use cell phones in any capacity while actively driving, except in a true emergency when stopping is impossible. Even hands-free use divides attention, slows reactions, and creates needless risk for drivers, passengers, cyclists, and pedestrians.

The most serious problem is cognitive distraction. Safe driving demands constant awareness of traffic signals, nearby vehicles, road hazards, weather, pedestrians, and the unpredictable choices of other drivers. A person can be looking straight at the road while talking on the phone, yet part of that person's mind is still on the conversation. Research and everyday experience both show that drivers on calls miss exits, overlook changes in traffic, and react late when the car ahead brakes. Bluetooth headsets, voice commands, and speakerphones do not solve this. The driver's hands may stay on the wheel, but their attention is still split.

Visual and manual distractions make the danger even greater. Reading or sending a text means taking your eyes off the road and usually using one or both hands. At highway speed, a car can travel the length of a football field in just a few seconds. In that time, a child could step into a crosswalk, a vehicle could stop short, or traffic could merge into another lane. No message, social media update, or phone call is important enough to justify losing sight of the road, even briefly. Navigation apps can be just as risky when drivers keep glancing at maps, changing settings, or searching for destinations while the car is moving.

Some people argue that they need their phones for directions, work, or contact with family. Those needs are real, but they do not require using a phone while driving. Drivers can enter their route before leaving, pull over to answer a call, or ask a passenger to handle the device. Employers also should not pressure workers to answer messages or calls from the road. If something is urgent, the safest option is to stop in a legal parking area before responding. The one reasonable exception is an emergency, such as needing to contact emergency services when no safe alternative exists. Even then, the driver should use the quickest and safest method available.

Laws against handheld phone use are a good start, but they may not go far enough. Society should treat distracted driving as unacceptable in the same way it treats driving without a seat belt. Drivers can help by silencing notifications, keeping phones out of reach, and setting automatic replies that tell people they are on the road. These habits reduce temptation and make attention to driving the priority.

In the end, operating a vehicle is a serious responsibility, not an opportunity to multitask. Cell phones are useful, but whatever they offer can wait until the car is safely parked. To protect everyone who shares the road, drivers should avoid using cell phones in any capacity while driving.
