Driverless Cars: A Future Worth Pursuing

Imagine a world where no one has to worry about a drunk driver swerving across the center line, a distracted teenager reading a text, or an exhausted commuter drifting off at the wheel. According to the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," this world may be closer than we think. Although the technology faces real obstacles, the development of driverless cars should continue because of their potential to save lives, expand mobility, and make transportation more efficient.

The strongest argument for driverless cars is safety. The article points out that human error causes over 90 percent of traffic accidents, often because of texting, drowsiness, or impaired driving. These are not problems of bad roads or faulty engineering; they are problems of human limitation. A computer does not get tired, does not check its phone, and does not drink alcohol. Driverless vehicles are equipped with laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors that detect obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals, so they can monitor their surroundings constantly. If these machines remove even a portion of the human mistakes behind crashes, thousands of lives could be saved each year, and the article notes that insurance costs could fall as well.

Driverless cars could also help people who are currently left behind by the automobile. Elderly and disabled people often cannot drive, which limits their independence and their access to doctors, stores, and friends. The article explains that autonomous vehicles could provide mobility for these passengers. Beyond that, Google cofounder Sergey Brin envisions driverless public transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. Such a system could reduce pollution, ease congestion, and free up city land now devoted to parking lots.

Critics raise serious concerns, and they deserve a fair response. Current sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or unmarked construction zones, and software may be vulnerable to glitches or hackers. The article also warns that semi-autonomous cars require drivers to stay alert and take over in emergencies, yet studies show that passengers quickly lose focus when a computer is driving. Finally, it is unclear who should be legally responsible after an accident: the owner, the software developer, or the automaker.

These problems are real, but they are reasons to keep developing the technology carefully, not to abandon it. Sensor limitations and software flaws are engineering challenges, and engineers are exactly the people who solve such challenges through testing and refinement. The danger of distracted "backup" drivers actually supports the case for fully autonomous systems, since the risk comes from asking humans to supervise a machine they have stopped paying attention to. The best answer may be to perfect cars that do not depend on human reaction at all. As for legal responsibility, laws have adapted to every major technological change, from airplanes to the internet. Lawmakers can establish rules for liability just as they once created traffic codes and insurance requirements for the first cars.

Stopping development now would also mean accepting the status quo, in which human error continues to cause the vast majority of crashes. That is a cost measured in injuries and deaths, and it is happening today. Imperfect technology under development is not more dangerous than the imperfect drivers already on the road.

In conclusion, driverless cars offer remarkable benefits: fewer accidents, greater independence for the elderly and disabled, and more efficient, environmentally friendly transportation. The weaknesses described in the article, from bad-weather performance to legal uncertainty, are significant but solvable. With careful testing, strong security, and thoughtful laws, society can overcome these hurdles. The development of driverless cars should go forward, because the road ahead promises to be safer than the one we travel now.

Distance learning, once a limited alternative, has become a significant option in modern education. Although some people worry that learning from home isolates students or weakens the quality of instruction, I believe students can benefit greatly from the opportunity to attend classes from home because it offers flexibility, expands access to educational opportunities, and helps students develop independence.

One major benefit of distance learning is flexibility. In a traditional classroom, all students must follow the same pace, even if some need more time to understand a concept while others are ready to move ahead. Online and video-based classes often allow students to review recorded lessons, pause lectures, and rewatch difficult sections. For example, a student struggling with a complicated chemistry lesson can replay the teacher’s explanation several times, which is impossible in a regular classroom. Distance learning also helps students with demanding schedules, such as athletes, performers, or young people with family responsibilities, because they can complete their studies at times that fit their lives.

Another important advantage is increased access to education. Some students cannot attend school regularly because of chronic illness, mobility challenges, or severe anxiety. For these students, attending classes from home can mean the difference between falling behind and staying on track. A student recovering from surgery, for instance, can still participate in class discussions through video conferencing instead of missing weeks of instruction. Distance learning can also help students in rural or underfunded schools take advanced courses, such as AP Physics or foreign languages, that are not offered locally. In this way, online learning can help equalize educational opportunity.

Distance learning also encourages students to become more independent and responsible. Without a teacher physically supervising them all day, students must learn to manage their time, keep track of assignments, and ask for help when needed. These skills are valuable preparation for college and the workforce, where self-direction is essential. For example, a high school student who learns to organize a digital calendar, meet deadlines, and communicate professionally by email is building habits that will serve them well after graduation.

Of course, critics are right that distance learning can reduce face-to-face socialization and make hands-on activities more difficult. However, distance learning does not have to be all-or-nothing. Many schools use hybrid models in which students attend some classes at home and some in person. This approach preserves social interaction and practical learning while still offering the flexibility and accessibility of online education.

In conclusion, distance learning is not a perfect solution for every student or every subject, but the benefits are clear. It allows students to learn at their own pace, gives more young people access to quality education, and builds independence. When offered thoughtfully, especially in combination with in-person experiences, attending classes from home can be a powerful tool that helps students succeed.

The widespread use of cell phones has transformed the way people communicate, access information, and navigate their daily lives. However, one aspect of cell phone usage has sparked intense debate: their use while operating a vehicle. With millions of people around the world using cell phones on a daily basis, it is crucial to examine the implications of allowing drivers to use these devices while behind the wheel.

Driving is a complex task that requires attention, concentration, and quick reflexes. When a driver uses a cell phone, their focus is diverted from the road, and their reaction time is significantly impaired. Even hands-free devices, which are often touted as a safer alternative, can still lead to cognitive distraction, as the driver's brain is preoccupied with the conversation rather than the task of driving. This distraction can have devastating consequences, including accidents, injuries, and even fatalities. Furthermore, the risk of an accident increases exponentially when a driver is texting or browsing on their phone, as this requires manual dexterity and visual attention, taking their eyes off the road for extended periods.

Proponents of cell phone use while driving argue that it is a matter of personal freedom and convenience. They claim that responsible drivers can multitask and use their phones safely, without compromising their driving abilities. However, this argument is based on a flawed assumption that drivers can accurately assess their own abilities and behavior. In reality, studies have shown that drivers tend to overestimate their skills and underestimate the risks associated with cell phone use while driving. Moreover, the risks are not limited to the individual driver; other road users, including pedestrians, cyclists, and passengers, are also put in harm's way when a driver is distracted by their cell phone.

In addition to the safety concerns, allowing cell phone use while driving can also have broader societal implications. If drivers are permitted to use their phones without restriction, it can create a culture of complacency and normalize reckless behavior. This can lead to a rise in accidents and near-misses, which can have significant economic and social costs. On the other hand, banning or restricting cell phone use while driving can send a strong message about the importance of road safety and responsible behavior.

In conclusion, the risks associated with cell phone use while driving far outweigh any perceived benefits. While it may be convenient to make calls, send texts, or browse the internet while on the move, the consequences of distracted driving are too severe to ignore. Drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle, except in emergency situations or when the vehicle is safely parked. By restricting cell phone use, we can promote a safer, more responsible driving culture and reduce the number of accidents and fatalities on our roads. Ultimately, the safety of all road users should take precedence over personal convenience, and it is our collective responsibility to prioritize responsible driving practices.

When summer assignments are designed entirely by teachers, they often become little more than boxes to check. Students read a prescribed novel, answer generic questions, or complete a math packet, and by August much of that work is forgotten. I believe summer projects should be student-designed, with teachers providing a clear framework and final approval, because ownership transforms the project from an obligation into an extension of a student’s genuine curiosity.

The most obvious advantage is relevance. A teacher cannot know every student’s passion. One teenager might spend hours tinkering with robotics; another might be fascinated by fashion history. If both are handed the same worksheet on ecosystems or the same research paper prompt, neither is likely to stretch beyond what is required. But when a student designs a project around something they already care about, the work stops feeling like school. A student who loves basketball could analyze shooting statistics across a season and create a data presentation. Another drawn to music could compose three short pieces and record a reflection on how key and tempo affect mood. These projects demand the same core skills—research, writing, math, critical thinking—but the student invests more because the topic is their own.

Student-designed projects also teach planning and accountability, which are often absent from teacher-designed packets. When a student proposes a project, they must break it into manageable steps, anticipate obstacles, and set deadlines. A teacher can require a one-page proposal before summer begins, a mid-summer check-in, and a final presentation in the fall. This structure preserves rigor without dictating content. For example, a student interested in environmental science might propose testing water quality at three local sites and comparing the results. To do that well, she has to learn proper sampling methods, organize data, and write up her findings. If she simply filled out a pre-made lab report, she would miss the experience of designing her own investigation.

Critics might argue that teenagers, left to their own devices, will aim too low or choose projects that do not build academic skills. That is a fair concern, but it is solved by teacher guidance rather than teacher control. A teacher can approve proposals, set minimum expectations, and require evidence of learning. A student who wants to “learn cooking” might be pushed to connect it to chemistry, write a cost analysis, or research the nutritional science behind ingredients. The project remains student-designed, but it is not directionless. In contrast, teacher-designed projects often fail even the students who complete them because they feel impersonal. A student may do the work, but never truly engage.

Summer should be a break from the rigid routines of the school year, not a break from learning. When students are given the responsibility to design a meaningful project with guidance from teachers, they practice the kind of self-directed learning that college and careers demand. They return in the fall with something to show that reflects who they are, not just a stack of completed worksheets. That is the difference between work done for a teacher and work done for oneself.

Summer projects should be mostly student-designed, because students learn more deeply when they can tie academic skills to their own interests, questions, and communities. Teachers should still set clear expectations, deadlines, and grading criteria, but they shouldn't hand every student the same assignment. A well-planned project that lets students choose can prevent learning loss while also building independence, curiosity, and responsibility.

The first reason is motivation. During the school year, students often do their work simply because it is required. Summer is supposed to be a break from that routine, so a long teacher-designed packet on topics a student doesn't care about can feel more like punishment than learning. A student who loves sports, on the other hand, could study the mathematics behind baseball statistics, and a student who loves animals could volunteer at a shelter and keep a journal about their care. Both would practice research, writing, and analysis, but they would do it through subjects they actually enjoy. When students are interested, they spend more time on their work and produce more thoughtful results.

Student-designed projects also teach life skills. In college and in many careers, people are expected to identify a problem, set goals, manage their time, and finish work without constant supervision. A summer project gives students a chance to practice all of this. Imagine a student curious about local history who decides to interview older residents, visit a museum, and put together a short documentary. To succeed, that student would have to schedule interviews, organize notes, judge the reliability of sources, and meet a final deadline. A uniform worksheet rarely demands that much planning.

Another benefit is that these projects connect learning to the real world. A teacher-designed assignment might ask everyone to read the same novel or solve the same set of equations. Those tasks have value, but they don't always match the varied experiences and needs of students. Consider a student worried about pollution in a nearby park. That student could collect data on litter, research recycling policies, and write a proposal to the town council. The project would involve science, math, persuasive writing, and civic engagement, and it would show that schoolwork can help solve problems that matter.

Some people argue that teacher-designed projects are fairer because every student is held to the same academic level. Fairness, however, doesn't require identical assignments. Teachers can create a shared rubric requiring every project to include research, evidence, reflection, and a final product. They can also approve proposals before summer begins and offer a list of suggested topics for students who struggle to decide. That kind of structure protects academic standards without taking away student choice.

In the end, summer projects should be student-designed within a framework guided by teachers. When students own what they study, they become more engaged and creative, and they are more likely to keep learning outside the classroom. Instead of assigning one project to everyone, schools should let students turn their individual interests into meaningful academic experiences.

Dear Principal,

As I consider the proposed policy change that would require students to maintain at least a B average to participate in sports and extracurricular activities, I strongly believe it is not in the best interest of our school community. While I appreciate your dedication to fostering academic excellence, I urge you to reconsider this policy. By barring students with a C average from participating in activities, we risk inadvertently harming the very students who need these programs the most.

For many students, extracurricular activities serve as a primary motivator, encouraging them to stay engaged in school and maintain a connection to our community. These programs provide a sense of belonging and accountability, requiring participants to attend classes, respect school rules, and earn passing grades. By setting the bar at a C average, we establish a realistic and attainable baseline for students who struggle with academics. Raising the threshold to a B average could lead to disheartenment among students who work hard to earn a C, causing them to disengage from their coursework and potentially leading to higher rates of absenteeism and dropouts.

Extracurricular activities are not simply privileges, but rather essential educational spaces where students develop critical life skills. Through sports, music, theater, and clubs, students learn valuable lessons about teamwork, leadership, resilience, and time management. Denying these opportunities to students with satisfactory academic standing – which a C average represents – would deprive them of well-rounded growth and essential stress relief. Moreover, physical activities and creative arts promote mental health and provide a much-needed outlet for students who are already working hard academically. Removing these outlets could increase anxiety and lower overall well-being.

Implementing a B average requirement could also have unintended negative consequences for our classroom culture. In an effort to maintain a high GPA, students might avoid challenging courses, opting instead for easier classes that guarantee a high mark. This could disproportionately affect students with learning disabilities, language barriers, or demanding family responsibilities, who may be putting forth their best effort despite facing significant challenges.

Rather than excluding students with a C average, I propose that our school implement targeted support systems to help students succeed. Mandatory study halls, peer tutoring sessions, and academic counseling could provide students with the resources they need to improve their grades while still allowing them to participate in extracurricular activities. By maintaining the current eligibility standard and pairing it with academic support, we can encourage students to strive for higher achievement without taking away the activities that give their high school experience meaning.

In conclusion, extracurricular activities are a vital part of our school's fabric, fostering character, community, and scholastic discipline. I urge you to consider the potential consequences of this policy change and instead focus on providing support and resources to help students succeed. By doing so, we can create a more inclusive and supportive environment that benefits all students, regardless of their academic standing.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

I agree with the principal’s decision to require every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. Academics are an important part of education, but they do not completely prepare students for the challenges they will face outside the classroom. Activities such as sports, yearbook, drama, student council, or community service teach valuable skills, help students feel connected to school, and allow them to discover interests they might otherwise never explore.

To begin with, extracurricular activities teach lessons that are difficult to learn from textbooks alone. Students on a sports team learn teamwork, discipline, and how to respond to both winning and losing. Yearbook staff members must meet deadlines, pay attention to details, and cooperate with photographers, writers, and editors. Student council members practice leadership, public speaking, and negotiation. For example, a student helping organize a school fundraiser may need to communicate with teachers, divide jobs among classmates, and solve problems when plans change. These experiences build confidence and responsibility in ways that tests and lectures cannot always provide.

Extracurricular activities can also make students feel like they belong at school. Some students feel invisible during the regular school day, especially if they are shy, new to the school, or struggling in class. Joining a club or team gives them a smaller group where they can contribute and make friends. A shy freshman who joins drama club, for instance, may become more comfortable speaking in front of others while finding supportive classmates. Likewise, a student who writes for the school newspaper might feel proud when their article is published. Feeling connected to a group can improve a student’s attitude, attendance, and overall well-being. Requiring participation gives students who might not sign up on their own the opportunity to experience that connection.

In addition, activities help students manage their time and discover talents they did not know they had. When students have practice, meetings, or projects in addition to homework, they often learn to plan ahead instead of procrastinating. Although being busy can be challenging, it can also teach students how to organize their priorities. More importantly, a required activity may encourage someone to try something outside their comfort zone. A student who joins robotics only to meet the requirement could discover an interest in engineering. Another student who helps with the school musical might realize they enjoy designing sets or working with lights. Without a small push, many students might never take that first step.

Some people may argue that mandatory activities would burden students who already have jobs, family responsibilities, or demanding classes. That is a reasonable concern, but the policy could be flexible. Schools could offer short-term projects, community service opportunities, lunch clubs, or activities that meet only once a week. Students should be able to choose an option that fits their schedule and interests. The goal should not be to punish students or make their lives more stressful. Instead, it should encourage them to become more involved in their school community.

Overall, requiring each student to participate in an extracurricular activity is a positive decision. It teaches practical life skills, creates stronger connections among students, and helps young people discover their strengths. With flexible choices and thoughtful planning, this policy could make school a richer experience for everyone.

I agree with the principal’s decision to require every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. Some people may think this is an unnecessary rule, but it can help students develop important life skills, feel more connected to school, and discover opportunities they might not otherwise try.

Extracurricular activities teach lessons that are difficult to learn only in a classroom. A student who joins a sports team can learn discipline, teamwork, and how to deal with both winning and losing. Someone working on the yearbook has to meet deadlines, cooperate with classmates, and pay close attention to details. Student council members practice public speaking, negotiation, and leadership. These activities build time-management, responsibility, and problem-solving skills that will be useful in college, careers, and adult life.

They can also help students grow in unexpected ways. For example, a shy student who joins drama club may become more confident through rehearsals and performances. A student in robotics might learn to keep trying after a design fails several times. Not every student will be comfortable at first, but trying something new can reveal talents and interests they did not know they had. Requiring students to participate gives them a reason to step outside their usual routines.

Another benefit is that activities help students feel like they belong at school. Being part of a club, team, or organization gives students a chance to make friends with people who share their interests. They also get to know teachers, coaches, and mentors in a different setting. A student who looks forward to debate practice, art club, or soccer after school may feel more motivated to attend classes and stay involved. Students who spend time in constructive activities are also surrounded by supportive adults and peers who want them to succeed.

A required extracurricular policy can promote fairness as well. When activities are completely optional, the students most likely to join are often already confident, outgoing, or supported by families with extra time and money. A school requirement can encourage all students to participate, including those who may not have transportation, private lessons, or encouragement outside school. If the school offers many choices—such as sports, music, theater, community service, coding, gardening, academic clubs, and student government—every student has a better chance of finding something meaningful.

Of course, some people may argue that forcing students to join an activity will create resentment or lead to half-hearted participation. However, the policy does not mean every student must play a sport or join the same club. It only asks each student to choose one activity that interests them. Schools can also allow students to switch activities after a season or semester if their first choice is not a good fit. For students with jobs, family responsibilities, or other serious commitments, schools should be flexible and count structured activities outside of school when appropriate.

A school should educate the whole person, not just teach academic subjects. Requiring at least one extracurricular activity can help students gain skills, make connections, and receive opportunities more equally. With enough choices and reasonable flexibility, the principal’s decision is practical and beneficial. It gives every student a better chance to grow both inside and outside the classroom.

Students should have the option to attend classes from home, but it should remain an option rather than a replacement for the classroom. Distance learning helps a surprisingly wide range of students, and the schools that offer it are acknowledging something true: not every learner thrives in the same environment.

Consider the students for whom a physical classroom is an obstacle. A teenager recovering from surgery, a child with a chronic illness like Crohn's disease, or a student with severe anxiety may be perfectly capable of doing the work but unable to sit through a seven-hour school day. Without a remote option, these students fall behind, then fall further behind, and eventually some give up entirely. With one, they can follow along from a couch or a bed, ask questions through a chat window, and rejoin their classmates when they are ready. The difference between staying enrolled and dropping out can be that simple.

Geography matters too. In rural parts of the country, a student may live an hour or more from the nearest school, and a long bus ride eats into time that could go toward sleep, homework, or family responsibilities. Small rural schools also struggle to staff advanced courses. A school with only a handful of students interested in calculus or Mandarin cannot easily justify hiring a full-time teacher, but it can connect those students to a live online class taught elsewhere. Distance learning, in this sense, widens opportunity instead of narrowing it.

There is also the matter of flexibility. Some students are competitive athletes who travel for tournaments, young actors with irregular schedules, or teens who work part-time to help support their families. Recorded lectures and video sessions let them keep up without sacrificing the commitments that shape their lives. Others simply learn better at home, where there are fewer distractions, less social pressure, and room to move at a comfortable pace. A student who is bullied at school, for example, may finally be able to concentrate on learning rather than on getting through the hallway.

Critics raise fair concerns, and I do not want to wave them away. Many students need the structure that a classroom provides. Without a teacher physically present, it is easy to mute the microphone, open another tab, and drift. The pandemic showed how uneven remote learning can be, especially for younger children and for families without reliable internet or a quiet place to study. Schools also play a social role that no screen fully replicates; friendships, teamwork, and casual conversations with teachers are part of education, too.

But these problems argue for careful design, not for eliminating the option. Schools can require regular check-ins, set clear attendance expectations, and provide laptops and internet hotspots to families who lack them. They can limit remote enrollment for younger children, who need more supervision, while offering it more freely to older students who have shown they can manage their time. And they can build in occasional in-person meetings so that remote students stay connected to their school community.

Ultimately, the goal of education is to help each student learn, and a single format cannot accomplish that for everyone. Offering distance learning as one choice among several acknowledges the real differences in students' health, circumstances, and learning styles. For many, it is a lifeline; for others, a useful supplement. Schools that provide it, with sensible support and safeguards, are not lowering their standards. They are making sure that more students have a genuine chance to meet them.

Dear Principal,

I am writing because I do not think students should need a B average to participate in sports and other school activities. I understand that grades are important and that school should come before games, clubs, and events. However, requiring a B average would hurt many students who are trying their best, and it could actually make some students do worse in school instead of better.

First, not every student who has a C average is lazy or does not care about learning. Some students struggle with one subject, such as math or English, while doing well in others. A student might have Bs and As in most classes but get a D in a difficult class, which could lower the average. Other students have learning differences, family responsibilities, jobs, or problems at home that make school harder. It would not be fair to take away the activities they enjoy just because they are not earning a B average.

Sports and activities can also help students improve their grades. Being on a team teaches students how to manage time, work with others, and stay responsible. For example, a student on the basketball team has to finish homework before practice and cannot miss class without consequences. Students in band, drama, robotics, and student council also have reasons to stay organized and come to school. If they are removed from these activities, they may lose motivation and feel like there is nothing positive connecting them to school.

Activities are important for students’ mental health too. Not everyone is good at sitting in a classroom all day. Some students feel successful for the first time when they play a sport, perform in a play, or help with a club. Taking that away could make them feel like failures. It could especially affect students who do not have many friends or safe places to go after school. Activities give them a group where they belong.

Instead of requiring a B average, the school could make a policy that encourages improvement. For example, students with a C average could still participate but be required to attend tutoring, get extra help from teachers, or make a plan to raise grades in the classes they are struggling with. Students who are failing multiple classes could have temporary limits until they show improvement. This would keep academics important without punishing students who are honestly working hard.

A B average is a good goal, but it should not be the only way a student can be part of school life. Students learn valuable lessons through activities that cannot always be measured by grades. I hope you will choose a policy that supports students in improving instead of excluding them.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

Summer projects, when required, should be teacher-designed. Students may dream up ambitious ideas in June, but without adult architecture, their plans often dissolve into last-minute scrambles or shallow busywork. Teacher-designed assignments provide the structure, clarity, and curricular connection that make summer learning meaningful rather than merely mandatory.

Consider a typical middle school science class. A teacher might design a project asking students to observe a local ecosystem over several weeks: record temperature, rainfall, and wildlife sightings in a log, then write a short analysis of patterns. Students can choose which park, backyard, or vacant lot to study, but the scientific method, data table, and final questions are provided. That balance matters. The student who would independently design a rigorous field study is rare; most need the scaffold of specific prompts and models. Without it, one child returns with a half-empty notebook, another with a poster copied from the internet, and a third with nothing at all because the open-ended task felt overwhelming.

Teacher-designed projects also protect equity. When a school says, “Design your own summer project,” students with educated parents, museum memberships, and quiet study spaces often thrive. Their peers, left to interpret vague instructions, may flounder. A well-designed teacher project can be completed with common household materials, a library card, or a walk around the neighborhood. For example, a high school English teacher might assign students to interview an older relative or neighbor about a historical event, using a provided list of questions and a reflection template. The assignment is rigorous, but it does not require travel or expensive technology. Every student can return with a meaningful oral history.

Skeptics argue that student-designed projects build ownership and creativity. Those are worthy goals, but they do not require abandoning teacher design. A teacher can set the learning targets—practice persuasive writing, collect data, analyze a novel—while allowing students to choose topics, formats, or presentation styles. In that model, creativity operates inside a frame solid enough to guarantee effort and growth. For instance, a math teacher might require students to track personal spending or sports statistics over the summer, but let them decide whether to present findings as a spreadsheet, a graph-heavy poster, or a short video. The core skills remain intact; the vehicle varies.

Ultimately, summer assignments exist to prevent learning loss and extend classroom habits. Teachers know which skills students have just begun to master and which gaps need reinforcement. A student, however motivated, cannot design a project that targets those academic needs with the same precision. Teacher-designed summer work, enriched with choices within boundaries, respects student voice without sacrificing rigor. It turns the long break into a bridge rather than a blank void.

Dear Principal Johnson,

I am writing to share my view on the proposed policy that would require students to maintain at least a B average to take part in sports and other school activities. I understand that the goal is to encourage academic achievement, and I respect that goal. However, I believe this policy would hurt many students, including the ones it is meant to help. I urge you to reconsider.

First, activities often give students the motivation to do well in school. Many students with a C average stay engaged because they love basketball, band, drama, or student council. Those activities give them a reason to show up every day, to stay out of trouble, and to feel connected to the school. If we take those activities away, we risk removing the very thing that keeps some students trying. A student who feels left out of school life is more likely to lose interest in classes, not less. Instead of raising grades, the policy could push them lower.

Second, a B requirement is a high bar for many students, and a C is not a failing grade. A C average means a student is meeting expectations and passing their classes. Some students work extremely hard for their Cs because certain subjects are difficult for them, or because they have jobs, family responsibilities, or learning differences. It seems unfair to punish a student who is putting in real effort simply because their results do not reach a certain number. Since many students currently have a C average, this rule would shut out a large part of the student body from activities that are supposed to be open to everyone.

Third, activities teach valuable skills that are not measured by grades. Teamwork, discipline, time management, leadership, and perseverance are learned on the field, on the stage, and in clubs. Employers and colleges value these qualities. A student who learns to balance practice with homework is gaining real-world experience. Taking away that opportunity would deprive students of lessons that classrooms alone cannot provide.

Fourth, there are better ways to encourage good grades. The school could offer free tutoring, study halls, or peer mentoring for students whose grades fall. It could set a reasonable minimum, such as a C average, and give students a probation period to improve before they lose eligibility. Coaches and advisors could also check in on their members' progress. These solutions support students rather than punish them, and they would improve grades without cutting anyone off from the activities they care about.

Some people may argue that students should treat school as the top priority, and I agree that academics matter. But a policy that removes support instead of adding it is not the best way to reach that goal. Students who are struggling need encouragement and help, not exclusion.

In conclusion, requiring a B average would discourage students who rely on activities for motivation, penalize those who work hard for their Cs, and take away important learning experiences. A policy built around academic support and a more realistic standard would better serve our school. Thank you for taking the time to consider students' opinions on this important issue.

Respectfully,

A Concerned Student

Activities often give students a reason to stay connected to school. Sports and activities also teach skills that grades do not always measure. Students learn responsibility by arriving on time for practice, cooperation by working with a team, perseverance by preparing for performances or competitions, and leadership by helping younger members. A student taking advanced math, honors science, or a challenging writing course may earn a C while working harder than another student who earns a B in less demanding classes. Students whose grades fall below a certain level could attend tutoring, meet regularly with a teacher or counselor, complete missing assignments, or participate in study hall before practice. This approach would make activities an incentive to improve, rather than a privilege that disappears when students need motivation most.

Of course, students should not ignore their schoolwork. Those who are failing several classes or refusing to complete assignments should be required to make a clear plan for improvement. However, setting the standard at a B average would exclude a large number of students who are capable, hardworking, and still developing academically.

Our school should expect students to do their best while also providing support when they struggle. Keeping students involved in activities, along with holding them accountable for their work, would be a more effective and compassionate policy than requiring a B average.

The development of driverless cars has been a topic of intense debate in recent years, with proponents arguing that they could revolutionize the way we travel and opponents raising concerns about their safety and reliability. As I consider the issue, I firmly believe that the development of driverless cars should be supported and encouraged. In the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," the author presents a compelling case for the benefits of autonomous vehicles, and I agree that their potential to reduce traffic accidents, provide mobility for elderly or disabled passengers, and lower insurance costs makes them an attractive solution to many of the problems associated with traditional cars.

One of the most significant advantages of driverless cars is their potential to reduce traffic accidents. As the article notes, human error is responsible for over 90 percent of traffic accidents, often due to texting, drowsiness, or impaired driving. By removing the human element from the driving process, autonomous vehicles could dramatically reduce the number of crashes on our roads, saving lives and reducing the financial burden of accidents on individuals and society as a whole. Furthermore, driverless cars could provide mobility for elderly or disabled passengers who are currently unable to drive themselves, giving them a new level of independence and freedom. This is a particularly important benefit, as it could help to address issues of social isolation and inequality that are often faced by these groups.

Despite the concerns raised by critics and safety experts, I believe that the benefits of driverless cars outweigh the risks. While it is true that current sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or unmarked construction zones, and software systems remain vulnerable to glitches or cybersecurity threats, these are technical challenges that can be addressed through further research and development. In fact, many of the automakers and tech companies working on autonomous vehicles are already investing heavily in the development of more advanced sensors and software systems that can mitigate these risks. Additionally, the potential benefits of driverless cars are so significant that it is worth taking a calculated risk to pursue their development.

In conclusion, the development of driverless cars is a concept that holds tremendous promise for improving road safety, providing mobility for elderly or disabled passengers, and reducing the environmental impact of transportation. While there are certainly challenges to be addressed, I firmly believe that the benefits of autonomous vehicles outweigh the risks. As Sergey Brin's vision of a future with driverless public transportation becomes a reality, I have no doubt that we will see a significant reduction in traffic accidents, a decrease in fuel consumption and parking space requirements, and a new level of independence and freedom for millions of people around the world. Ultimately, the development of driverless cars is an opportunity that we cannot afford to miss, and I strongly support their continued development and deployment.

Dear Senator,

As the debate over the Electoral College continues to garner attention, I am writing to express my support for preserving this vital institution in our democratic process. While some argue that it is undemocratic and outdated, I firmly believe that the Electoral College plays a crucial role in ensuring that presidential candidates build broad national coalitions and cater to the interests of all states, regardless of their population size.

One of the primary concerns raised by critics of the Electoral College is that it can lead to a situation where a candidate wins the presidency without receiving the most popular votes. As Bradford Plumer notes in "The Indefensible Electoral College," this has happened in two elections since 2000. However, this argument overlooks the fact that the Electoral College is designed to prevent candidates from winning solely by accumulating votes in densely populated urban areas. By requiring candidates to secure a majority of electoral votes, the system ensures that they must appeal to voters across multiple states and regions. This promotes a more nuanced and inclusive campaign strategy, one that takes into account the diverse interests and needs of different parts of the country.

Another criticism of the Electoral College is that it can lead to a disproportionate focus on "swing states" at the expense of other states. However, as Judge Richard A. Posner argues in "In Defense of the Electoral College," this is a necessary consequence of a system that prioritizes the interests of all states, not just those with large populations. By giving each state a minimum number of electoral votes, the system ensures that even small states have a voice in the election process. This is particularly important for states with unique economic or cultural interests that might be overlooked in a purely popular vote system.

Some argue that the Electoral College is undemocratic because it can lead to "faithless electors" who vote against their state's popular choice. However, this is a rare occurrence and one that does not undermine the overall integrity of the system. In fact, the Electoral College has a number of built-in safeguards to prevent such abuses, including the requirement that electors be chosen by each state's voters.

In contrast to a purely popular vote system, the Electoral College produces a clear and decisive winner quickly, avoiding the chaos of a nationwide recount. As Posner notes, this is particularly important in a country as large and diverse as the United States, where a disputed election could have significant consequences for national stability. By confining any disputed vote recounts to individual states, the Electoral College helps to prevent the kind of national crisis that could arise from a contested election.

In conclusion, while the Electoral College may have its flaws, I firmly believe that it plays a vital role in promoting federalism and ensuring that presidential candidates build broad national coalitions. Rather than abandoning this institution, we should work to reform it and make it more responsive to the needs of all states and voters. I urge you to oppose any efforts to abolish the Electoral College and instead support reforms that would make it more effective and inclusive.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

In today's world, smartphones have become an integral part of daily life, offering unparalleled connectivity and convenience. However, when it comes to driving, the use of cell phones poses a significant threat to road safety. Operating a vehicle requires undivided attention, quick reflexes, and a high level of situational awareness. The distractions caused by mobile devices, including visual, manual, and cognitive distractions, make it clear that drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while behind the wheel.

One of the most obvious hazards of phone use while driving is the physical distraction it causes. Engaging in activities like texting, browsing, or dialing a number takes a driver's eyes off the road and their hands off the steering wheel. For instance, a mere five-second glance at a screen while driving at highway speeds is equivalent to driving the length of a football field blindfolded. In that brief moment, a pedestrian could step into the crosswalk, traffic could come to a sudden halt, or an unexpected obstacle could appear. By prohibiting the use of handheld devices altogether, drivers can maintain the physical readiness needed to react to unexpected hazards.

Moreover, cognitive distraction is a significant threat that is often underestimated. Many drivers believe that using hands-free technology, such as Bluetooth headsets or voice-activated systems, eliminates the risks associated with mobile communication. However, research has shown that this is not the case. Engaging in a conversation, even hands-free, requires a significant amount of mental bandwidth, drawing resources away from the visual processing centers needed for safe driving. This can lead to a phenomenon known as inattentional blindness, where a driver may look directly at a hazard without actually perceiving it. In fact, studies have found that drivers using hands-free devices exhibit delayed braking responses similar to those of intoxicated drivers. Therefore, to ensure that drivers maintain their full cognitive focus on the road, even hands-free use should be prohibited.

Some argue that banning phone use altogether is unnecessary, as many drivers rely on their phones for essential functions like GPS navigation or handling emergency situations. While it is true that these are important uses, they do not outweigh the risks associated with phone use while driving. Convenience should never take precedence over public safety. Instead, drivers can use alternative methods, such as built-in GPS systems or pulling over to a safe location to make a call or send a message. By taking these simple precautions, drivers can minimize the risks associated with phone use and ensure a safer driving experience for themselves and those around them.

Ultimately, the risks associated with phone use while driving are too great to ignore. By prohibiting the use of cell phones in any capacity, we can significantly reduce the number of accidents and near-misses on the road. It is our responsibility as drivers to prioritize safety and minimize distractions, and banning phone use is a crucial step in achieving this goal. By staying focused on the road and avoiding the temptations of our phones, we can create a safer and more responsible driving environment for everyone.

The rise of autonomous vehicles has generated considerable excitement, promising a future in which cars drive themselves and traffic accidents plummet. However, while driverless cars may offer long-term possibilities, their current development should be opposed or at least paused. The article “Driverless Cars Are Coming” reveals serious unresolved problems in sensor reliability, human attention, and legal accountability that make the rapid push toward autonomous vehicles unsafe.

First, the technology itself is not dependable enough for real-world conditions. The article notes that current sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or unmarked construction zones. A car that cannot reliably navigate common weather or roadwork cannot be trusted with passengers’ lives. In addition, software systems remain vulnerable to glitches and cybersecurity threats. A brief computer malfunction at highway speed or a hacker gaining control of a vehicle could turn a promised safety improvement into a new source of danger.

Second, the transition period between human-driven and fully autonomous cars creates a dangerous gray area. Many vehicles now use semi-autonomous features that still require a human driver to stay alert and take over in emergencies. Yet the article reports that studies show passengers quickly lose focus when a computer is driving, slowing their reaction times. This means the very design of driverless cars encourages inattention while demanding sudden, high-stakes intervention. That combination is a recipe for crashes rather than prevention.

Third, legal and ethical questions remain dangerously unanswered. According to the article, when an accident inevitably occurs, it is unclear whether the vehicle owner, the software developer, or the automaker should be held legally responsible. Without clear accountability, victims may struggle to receive compensation, and manufacturers may have little incentive to fix flaws. A technology that cannot yet define responsibility for its failures should not be deployed on public roads.

Proponents argue that because human error causes over 90 percent of traffic accidents—often from texting, drowsiness, or impaired driving—driverless cars could dramatically reduce crashes, save lives, lower insurance costs, and help elderly or disabled passengers. These are worthy goals. However, they assume that autonomous systems will be reliable enough to replace human judgment, and the article shows that this reliability does not yet exist. The promised benefits cannot be realized if sensors fail in bad weather, drivers do not pay attention during the transition, and no one is legally accountable when something goes wrong.

In conclusion, the development of driverless cars should be opposed in its current form. Until sensors can handle all driving conditions, software is secure against glitches and cyberattacks, semi-autonomous systems no longer depend on distracted human supervisors, and legal responsibility is clearly established, autonomous vehicles are not ready for widespread use. We should not trade the known risks of human driving for new, unresolved risks

Dear Principal,

After thinking carefully about the two proposed cell phone policies, I believe Policy 1 is the better choice. Students should be allowed to bring phones to school and use them during lunch or other free periods, as long as they are turned off and put away during class. This policy creates a fair balance between protecting learning time and recognizing that phones can be useful in students’ everyday lives. A complete ban might seem simpler, but it would ignore important benefits and would not help students learn to manage technology responsibly.

One important reason to allow phones is safety and communication. Many students need to contact parents or guardians about rides, after-school activities, jobs, or changes in family plans. Lunch and free periods are reasonable times for students to check messages or make quick calls without interrupting instruction. In an emergency, having a phone nearby can also help students reach family members quickly. If phones were banned completely, students could feel disconnected from their families, and everyday scheduling problems could become much more difficult.

Policy 1 would also help students develop responsibility. High school is a time when students should begin learning how to handle distractions and make good choices. If students are allowed to use phones only during appropriate times, they learn that there is a difference between personal time and class time. In college and in many workplaces, people will have access to phones, but they will still be expected to focus when they have important responsibilities. A total ban may prevent some problems in the short term, but it does not prepare students to manage technology on their own.

In addition, phones can give students a useful break during lunch or free time. Students sometimes need a few minutes to listen to music, read something they enjoy, play a short game, or connect with friends and family. These activities can help relieve stress after a difficult class or before a busy afternoon. When students have a chance to relax during their free time, they may return to class more focused and ready to learn. Since the policy would require phones to be off during instruction, these benefits would not have to interfere with academics.

Of course, there is a valid concern that phones can be distracting in class. Students may be tempted to text, scroll through social media, or use their phones when they should be listening. However, Policy 1 addresses that concern with a clear and reasonable rule: phones must be turned off and put away during instructional time. Teachers can enforce this expectation with consistent consequences, just as they do with other classroom rules. A complete ban, on the other hand, could lead to more arguments, hidden phones, and unnecessary punishment.

For these reasons, I strongly believe the school should adopt Policy 1. It keeps classrooms focused while still supporting student safety, communication, responsibility, and well-being. Allowing phones during lunch and free periods is a balanced approach that respects students while protecting the learning environment.

Sincerely,  
[Student Name]

Summer projects should be student-designed. I know some people argue that teachers need to design them to make sure we don’t just slack off or pick something too easy, but in my experience, a teacher-designed project usually ends up feeling like extra homework, not actual learning. When students get to choose their own topic or format, they actually care about what they’re doing, and that makes them put in more effort.

Last summer, my school required everyone going into ninth grade to read the same novel and complete a packet of questions about theme and character. I did it the last week before school started, mostly copying quotes I found online, because I had no interest in the book. I didn’t remember much by September. But my friend’s family let her design her own summer project: she loves baking, so she decided to test how different substitutions—like applesauce instead of eggs—changed a muffin recipe. She kept notes, took photos, made a chart of results, and even baked samples for our first week back. She learned about variables and ratios without being forced to, and she actually talked about it for weeks. That’s real learning.

Student-designed projects also teach responsibility and planning. If a teacher gives you a detailed rubric with due dates, you’re just following instructions. But if you design your own project, you have to figure out what you want to learn, break it into steps, and manage your time over the summer. For example, a kid in my grade is into old video games. He designed a project where he learned basic pixel art and coded a simple platformer game in Scratch. He had to set his own deadlines, debug his code, and decide what counted as “done.” We saw his game at the back-to-school showcase, and it was way more impressive than a worksheet. No teacher would have assigned that, but it still used math, logic, and creativity.

Some people might say student-designed projects can be too easy or off-track, like a student just playing basketball and calling it a physics project. But that’s why there should be some light guidelines—maybe students write a short proposal or check in once over the summer. The point isn’t to eliminate all teacher input; it’s to let the main ideas and format come from the student. If I choose something I’m already curious about, I won’t treat it like a chore.

In the end, summer should be a break from the normal school routine, but that doesn’t mean our brains have to shut off. Student-designed projects let us learn in a way that feels more like life and less like busywork. When we have a say in what we study, we don’t just finish the project; we actually remember it.

Seeking advice from multiple individuals is a common practice when faced with a difficult decision. This approach can significantly enhance the decision-making process, ultimately leading to a better choice. By consulting with various people, an individual can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the situation, uncover potential pitfalls, and develop a more informed perspective.

One of the primary benefits of seeking multiple opinions is that it allows individuals to consider different perspectives and insights. When people from diverse backgrounds and experiences share their views, they bring unique knowledge and expertise to the table. For instance, if someone is contemplating a career change, they may consult with a career counselor, a friend in the desired field, and a family member who has undergone a similar transition. Each of these individuals can provide distinct advice, highlighting various aspects of the career change, such as the job market, required skills, and personal fulfillment. By weighing these different perspectives, the individual can develop a more nuanced understanding of the situation and make a more informed decision.

Another advantage of seeking multiple opinions is that it can help individuals identify potential risks and pitfalls. When people share their experiences and concerns, they can alert others to potential dangers or downsides that may not have been immediately apparent. For example, if someone is thinking of investing in a business venture, they may consult with a financial advisor, a lawyer, and a entrepreneur who has started a similar business. Each of these individuals can provide valuable insights into the potential risks and challenges associated with the investment, such as market volatility, regulatory hurdles, and cash flow management. By being aware of these potential pitfalls, the individual can take steps to mitigate them and make a more informed decision.

Furthermore, seeking multiple opinions can also help individuals develop a sense of confidence and clarity in their decision-making. When people receive validation and support from others, they are more likely to feel assured in their choices. Conversely, if they receive conflicting advice or warnings, they can re-evaluate their decision and consider alternative options. For instance, if someone is deciding whether to pursue a graduate degree, they may consult with an academic advisor, a professional in their desired field, and a friend who has completed a similar program. If all of these individuals recommend pursuing the degree, the person is likely to feel more confident in their decision. On the other hand, if they receive mixed advice, they may need to reassess their goals and priorities.

In conclusion, seeking multiple opinions is a valuable strategy for making better choices. By consulting with various individuals, people can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the situation, uncover potential pitfalls, and develop a sense of confidence and clarity in their decision-making. Whether it's a career change, investment decision, or personal choice, seeking multiple opinions can provide a more informed and nuanced perspective, ultimately leading to a better outcome. By recognizing the benefits of seeking multiple opinions, individuals can make more informed decisions and navigate complex situations with greater ease and confidence.

When people face an important decision, they often ask more than one person for advice. This is usually a smart move, because different people notice different risks, draw on different experiences, and question assumptions that might otherwise go unchallenged. Too many opinions can feel confusing at times, but advice from several trustworthy sources generally leads to a more informed and balanced choice.

For one thing, multiple opinions give a person access to a wider range of knowledge. No one understands every part of a complicated decision. A high school student choosing a college, for example, might talk with a parent, a teacher, a current college student, and a financial aid counselor. The parent may be most concerned with safety and cost, while the teacher can tell which school would best support the student's academic interests. A current student can describe what daily campus life is really like, and the counselor can explain scholarships, loans, and long-term costs. If the student listened only to a friend who picked a college because of its attractive dormitories, more important issues like affordability or available programs could easily be missed.

Several opinions can also help people notice their own biases. We tend to favor choices that feel familiar, exciting, or easy. Someone shopping for a car, for instance, might be drawn to a stylish model with impressive technology. A mechanic, though, might warn that the car is expensive to repair, and a family member might remind the buyer about fuel efficiency and insurance rates. These extra viewpoints do not necessarily stop the buyer from choosing the car he or she loves, but they make the decision more realistic. Instead of acting on impulse, the buyer can weigh excitement against practical concerns.

Different opinions can also bring out consequences that one person might never have considered. Suppose someone is deciding whether to take a job in another city. A close friend may urge the move because of the higher pay and the chance for adventure. A mentor, however, might ask whether the position offers room for advancement, and a relative might raise concerns about housing costs and living far from family. By listening carefully to all of these responses, the person can consider both short-term benefits and long-term effects. The final answer may still be to move, but it will rest on a fuller understanding of what that choice involves.

Of course, asking many people for advice does not mean handing the decision over to them. Some advice is poorly informed, overly emotional, or shaped by the other person's own preferences. The one seeking help has to judge which opinions are relevant. It makes more sense to ask people who are knowledgeable, honest, and genuinely concerned than to collect as many answers as possible.

In the end, seeking multiple opinions leads to better decisions because it broadens perspective, reduces the pull of bias, and prepares a person for different outcomes. Important choices are rarely simple, and no one sees every side of a situation alone. By listening to several thoughtful voices and then making an independent judgment, people can choose more wisely and with greater confidence.

Dear Principal,

I believe students should be required to complete some community service, although the requirement should be reasonable and flexible. School is not only a place to learn algebra, grammar, and science facts. It is also where students learn how to be responsible members of the community. A small amount of service can teach lessons that are difficult to learn from a textbook.

First, community service helps students recognize that their actions affect other people. When a student tutors an elementary school child, for example, that child may become more confident about reading or math. The tutor also learns patience, communication, and the satisfaction of seeing someone improve. A friend of mine volunteered at an after-school program and originally thought she would simply help children finish homework. Instead, she discovered that some of the children needed someone to listen to them and encourage them. That experience changed the way she thought about younger students in our town.

Service can also make students more aware of problems they might otherwise ignore. It is easy to complain about littered parks or crowded animal shelters without doing anything about them. Picking up trash, sorting donated food, or helping at a shelter shows students that community problems are not solved only by adults or government officials. Even a few hours of work from each student could make a visible difference. If an entire grade participated in a neighborhood cleanup, local parks and sidewalks could become safer and more welcoming.

Some students argue that they are already too busy with homework, sports, jobs, and family responsibilities. This concern is understandable. A requirement should not demand so many hours that students lose time for studying or important commitments. However, requiring a limited number of hours over the course of a year would be manageable for most students. The school could also offer choices. Students could volunteer on weekends, work with younger children, assist teachers, help senior citizens, participate in environmental projects, or complete service connected to clubs they already belong to. Flexibility would make the program fairer while still ensuring that every student contributes.

A required program may seem less meaningful than voluntary service at first. Yet many students would never try volunteering if it were not encouraged by school. Once they begin, they may find a cause they genuinely care about. A student who reluctantly spends one afternoon at a food pantry might later return because he understands how much families depend on it. The requirement would be the introduction, not the only reason to help.

For these reasons, I hope you will require community service in a balanced way. A modest, flexible program would strengthen our community while helping students become more thoughtful, capable, and compassionate citizens.

Sincerely,  
A Student

Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge you to support a national popular vote for president. The Electoral College began as a constitutional compromise, but a system designed more than two centuries ago deserves a second look when it can put in office a president who was rejected by most voters. A citizen's vote should carry the same weight no matter which state that citizen calls home.

Under the current system, a candidate can win the presidency without winning the national popular vote. Bradford Plumer points out in "The Indefensible Electoral College" that this happened in both 2000 and 2016. Results like these shake public confidence, since voters naturally expect the candidate backed by the most Americans to win. Yet the real goal under the Electoral College is not to collect the most votes nationwide. It is to reach 270 of the 538 electoral votes. Because each state's electors equal its number of House members plus its two senators, voters in sparsely populated states end up with more influence per person than voters in large ones.

The winner-take-all rule makes matters worse. According to the Office of the Federal Register, forty-eight states and Washington, D.C. give all their electoral votes to whoever wins the state's popular vote. A candidate who takes 49 percent of a state's vote therefore usually earns nothing from it, while the winner takes everything. Plumer argues that this pushes campaigns to concentrate on a few "swing states" and overlook voters in states that are safely Democratic or Republican. Someone living in a noncompetitive state should not matter less simply because the outcome there seems predictable. A national popular vote would give candidates a reason to seek support everywhere, from rural communities and small towns to suburbs and big cities in every state.

Defenders of the Electoral College raise serious points. Judge Richard A. Posner argues that it preserves federalism and forces candidates to build broad coalitions instead of piling up huge margins in cities or a single region. He also observes that because elections are run state by state, a disputed result can be contained within one state rather than triggering a nationwide recount. These are real advantages, and they deserve consideration.

Still, a popular vote would not require candidates to ignore rural or small-state voters. Since every vote would count equally, candidates would have reason to campaign in all regions rather than a handful of battlegrounds. In fact, the present system already neglects many rural voters in reliably partisan states, just as it neglects urban voters there. As for recounts, close elections can already cause turmoil under the Electoral College, as the disputed 2000 election showed. Clear national standards for ballots, recounts, and election administration could limit confusion while still honoring equal representation.

The Federal Register reminds us that the Founders created the Electoral College as a compromise between selection by Congress and election by popular vote. Compromises are sometimes necessary, but they should not permanently stand in the way of equal political participation. The president should reflect the choice of the greatest number of Americans. I respectfully ask you to support efforts to move our nation toward electing the president by national popular vote.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Constituent

Cell phones are now a regular part of daily life, used for communication, directions, work, and emergencies. However, driving is an activity that requires constant attention and quick decision-making. Distracted driving causes thousands of deaths each year, and cell phones are one of its most common causes. For that reason, drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle, including hands-free calls. Even when a phone is not being held, it can divide a driver’s attention, create enforcement problems, and place other people on the road at unnecessary risk.

The main problem with cell phone use is not just the act of holding or looking at a device. It is the mental distraction that comes with using it. Hands-free technology may prevent drivers from taking their hands off the wheel, but it does not eliminate the need to listen, think, and respond. A phone conversation requires a driver to process what another person is saying and decide how to answer. The brain cannot fully focus on driving and carry on a separate conversation at the same time; instead, it shifts attention between the two tasks. During those moments of reduced attention, a driver may miss a changing traffic light, a pedestrian entering the road, or a vehicle braking suddenly.

Studies of distracted driving have shown that hands-free phone use can lead to “inattention blindness,” meaning that drivers may look directly at something without truly noticing it. Research also suggests that reaction times for drivers using phones can be similar to those of impaired drivers. This is especially concerning because a driver may believe that he or she is being safe simply because both hands are on the wheel and the phone is connected through Bluetooth. In reality, the mind may still be elsewhere. Safe driving requires more than looking ahead; it requires actively noticing and responding to everything happening on the road.

Allowing limited phone use also makes distracted-driving laws harder to enforce. If only handheld devices are banned, police officers may have trouble determining whether someone is holding a phone, adjusting a GPS mount, or speaking through a hands-free system. Partial bans can also send a confusing message by suggesting that certain kinds of phone use are harmless. A complete prohibition would be simpler and clearer. It would establish the expectation that drivers should focus entirely on the road while the vehicle is moving. Missing a call, waiting to reply to a message, or delaying a route adjustment is a small inconvenience compared with the possible consequences of a crash.

Some people may argue that phones are necessary for navigation, emergencies, or work. These concerns are understandable, but they do not justify using a phone while driving. A driver can pull over safely to make a call, send a text, or enter directions into a GPS application. Many phones also include “do not disturb while driving” settings that silence notifications and automatically respond to messages. In an actual emergency, stopping in a safe location before using the phone is still the responsible choice.

Others may claim that speaking to a passenger is just as distracting as talking on the phone. However, passengers can see the road and often pause or change the conversation when traffic becomes difficult. A person on the other end of a phone call cannot recognize dangerous conditions or know when the driver needs to focus.

Ultimately, any cell phone use while driving, whether handheld or hands-free, creates avoidable danger. A full ban would encourage safer habits, make laws easier to enforce, and help prevent crashes. No call, text, or notification is worth risking a life.
