Distance learning should be available as an option for students who need or prefer to attend classes from home. Although traditional classrooms provide important opportunities for social interaction and direct support from teachers, online or video-based instruction can give many students greater access to education. When it is offered thoughtfully rather than imposed on everyone, learning from home can improve flexibility, safety, and academic opportunity.

One major benefit of attending classes from home is that it helps students whose circumstances make regular school attendance difficult. For example, a student with a chronic illness may be physically unable to travel to school every day, even though the student is fully capable of completing academic work. Similarly, students recovering from injuries or living with disabilities may find transportation, crowded hallways, and long school days exhausting. Distance learning allows such students to remain connected to their classes instead of falling behind or missing large amounts of instruction. In this way, online attendance can make education more inclusive.

Learning from home can also help students balance school with other serious responsibilities. Some teenagers care for younger siblings, work part-time to support their families, or participate in demanding activities such as athletic training or music programs. A flexible online schedule may allow them to watch recorded lessons, complete assignments during available hours, and communicate with teachers electronically. This does not mean that students should have fewer expectations. In fact, distance learning requires responsibility, time management, and self-discipline. However, for motivated students, the ability to organize their work around real-life obligations can prevent them from choosing between education and family responsibilities.

In addition, online learning can expand the courses available to students. A small school may not have enough teachers or students to offer advanced computer science, foreign languages, or specialized art classes. Through video conferencing, students could join courses taught at another school or by qualified instructors in other locations. A student interested in engineering, for instance, might take an advanced programming class online even if that course is unavailable in the local building. Distance learning therefore can provide opportunities that would otherwise be limited by geography or school budgets.

Critics rightly point out that students may feel isolated at home and may be distracted by games, social media, or family noise. These concerns are real, especially for younger students who benefit from structure and face-to-face guidance. For this reason, distance learning should not completely replace schools. Schools should provide regular live meetings, office hours, counseling, group projects, and optional in-person activities. Parents and teachers should also help students establish routines and quiet places to work. With these supports, many of the disadvantages of remote learning can be reduced.

Overall, students would benefit from having the choice to attend classes from home. It can keep vulnerable students connected to school, accommodate complicated family situations, and provide access to a wider range of courses. Traditional classrooms will remain valuable, but a flexible education system recognizes that students do not all learn best under identical circumstances.

Dear Principal Johnson,

I am writing to share my opinion about the possible policy that would require students to have at least a B average to play sports or join other activities. I am against this change. I understand that grades are important, but I think this rule would hurt more students than it would help.

First, a lot of students have a C average, and a C is not a failing grade. It means a student is doing average work and understanding most of the material. If we take away activities from all of those students, we are basically punishing people who are passing. Some students work really hard for their C. A person might study for hours and still struggle in math or science. Telling that student they can't be on the track team because they didn't hit a B feels unfair.

Second, activities are often the reason students want to come to school at all. I know people who barely care about class, but they show up every day because they have practice or rehearsal or a club meeting. If they lose that, they might stop trying completely. Their grades could actually get worse instead of better. Being on a team also teaches things that classes don't always teach, like working with others, being on time, and not giving up when something is hard.

Third, activities can help students keep their grades up. When you play a sport, you have to manage your time. I have noticed that I do my homework faster and more carefully during basketball season because I know I only have a small amount of time before practice. Some coaches and club advisors also check on grades and encourage their students to do better. If students are kicked out of these groups, they lose those adults who are pushing them. They might also have more free time to spend on their phones or video games instead of studying.

Another problem is that some students need activities for their future. A student who is good at a sport might hope for a scholarship, and a student in band or art might want to build a portfolio. Missing a whole season over a grade that is just a little under a B could hurt those chances.

I do think grades matter, and I'm not saying students should be able to ignore school. Maybe there is a better way to handle this. The school could keep the current rule of needing a C average, or students who are below it could be put on a warning period first. They could also get free tutoring, study hall, or help from teachers before they lose their spot. That way students are being supported instead of just being punished.

In conclusion, requiring a B average is too strict for a school where so many students have a C. It could push students away from school, take away something that motivates them, and make them feel like their effort doesn't count. I hope you will think about the students who would be affected and choose a solution that helps them improve their grades without taking away their activities.

Thank you for taking the time to listen to student opinions.

Sincerely,
A concerned student

Distance learning has evolved from a rare alternative into a familiar part of modern education. While a computer screen cannot completely recreate the energy of a physical classroom, students benefit greatly when schools offer the choice to attend classes from home. Offering this route introduces flexibility, expands accessibility, and allows for a more personalized approach to learning.

Perhaps the biggest advantage of distance learning is the flexibility it provides. Realistically, students lead very different lives outside of school. Some train as competitive athletes and travel frequently, while others care for younger siblings, look after sick relatives, or work part-time jobs to help their families get by. In those situations, a rigid seven-hour school day inside a brick-and-mortar building can force someone to fall behind or even consider dropping out. With video conferencing and online portals, an athlete on the road can still tune into a live discussion, and a working student can catch up on recorded lectures late at night. Instead of forcing teenagers to choose between their personal responsibilities and their diplomas, remote classes help them balance both.

Distance learning also breaks down serious physical and geographical barriers. A student recovering from major surgery, managing a chronic illness, or dealing with mobility issues can stay on track without suffering through an exhausting daily commute. Geography matters just as much. For teenagers in rural districts, the nearest high school might be an hour away, and small local schools often lack the resources to offer electives like advanced physics, specialized coding, or less common foreign languages. Online coursework bridges that gap, giving students access to specialized or college-level classes they simply would not have had otherwise.

Beyond logistics, some people simply absorb material better outside of a traditional classroom. Crowded hallways and noisy rooms can be overwhelming, and students dealing with severe social anxiety or bullying often spend more energy surviving the school day than actually learning. At home, they can create a quiet, low-stress study space. When working with digital materials, they can pause a recording to jot down notes or replay a tricky math problem until it finally clicks. That kind of autonomy does not just improve grades; it also builds the self-discipline and time-management habits needed for college and future jobs, where remote and self-directed work are now ordinary.

Of course, critics point out that remote schooling can feel isolating and cut young people off from everyday social development. Others worry that without direct supervision or steady internet access, students might lose motivation and slip through the cracks. These are fair points, but they highlight the need for thoughtful implementation rather than an outright ban. Schools can combat isolation by requiring interactive video sessions, organizing virtual group work, and still welcoming remote students to join sports teams, theater productions, or on-campus clubs. Districts can also lend out laptops and Wi-Fi hotspots to make sure technology is never a roadblock. Most importantly, distance learning works best as an option, not a mandate. Students who thrive on the social hustle of a campus can always stay right where they are.

Ultimately, giving students the opportunity to learn from home meets diverse needs that a one-size-fits-all classroom cannot always address. It creates breathing room for those with heavy commitments, extends opportunities to isolated learners, and provides a gentler environment for students who struggle in crowds. By offering remote education as a choice, schools are not giving up on traditional teaching; they are simply opening another door for students who need a different way to succeed.

When our principal announced that every single student would have to join at least one extracurricular activity, I know the intention was probably good. Teachers and administrators want us to make friends, learn new skills, and feel connected to the school. But even though joining a club or a sports team can be a great experience, making it mandatory is a mistake. High school students already have different lives, responsibilities, and limits, and forcing everyone to participate will cause more problems than it solves.

The biggest issue is that many students have serious responsibilities outside of school that take up their afternoons. For example, some students have to work part-time jobs at grocery stores or fast-food restaurants to help their families pay rent or save for college. Other students go straight home after the final bell to watch their younger brothers and sisters so their parents can work late shifts. If the school forces these students to stay after for track practice or student council meetings, it puts them in an impossible situation. They shouldn’t have to choose between getting in trouble at school or letting down their families.

Another big problem is transportation and logistics. The regular yellow buses run right after the final bell rings. For students whose parents work late or who don't have their own cars, getting a ride home at 5:00 or 6:00 p.m. is not easy. Not every school has late activity buses, and even when they do, those buses usually drop kids off far from their houses. Forcing students into clubs when they have no reliable way to get home safely just isn't fair.

On top of that, making activities mandatory actually ruins the clubs themselves. Extracurriculars are fun and productive because the people there genuinely want to participate. If you fill the yearbook room or the drama club with twenty kids who are only there to check off a graduation requirement, the energy completely changes. People who don't care will just sit in the back on their phones, complain, or distract the students who are actually passionate about the work. It makes the experience worse for everyone, including the teachers who have to sponsor the clubs and deal with discipline issues.

High school is already stressful enough with heavy homework loads, tests, and personal lives. While schools should definitely encourage everyone to try new things and make clubs accessible, they should not make them compulsory. Extracurricular means "outside the curriculum" for a reason. Keeping clubs voluntary respects our time outside of school and ensures that the people who join are there because they truly want to be.

Imagine a world where thousands of fatal car crashes simply never happen because no one behind the wheel is distracted by a smartphone, nodding off, or driving while impaired. That is the kind of future autonomous vehicles offer. While the transition will not be simple, the development of driverless cars should definitely continue. As shown in the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," autonomous technology has the potential to save countless lives, cut down on environmental waste, and give non-drivers greater freedom. The obstacles critics bring up are genuine, but they are technical hurdles to overcome through better engineering, not reasons to shut the project down.

The most convincing case for driverless technology comes down to safety. According to the article, human error causes more than 90 percent of all traffic accidents, largely due to everyday issues like texting, exhaustion, or intoxication. Unlike human drivers, computer systems do not get tired, emotional, or careless. Using a combination of laser radar, cameras, GPS, and advanced sensors, autonomous vehicles can track lane markings, obstacles, and traffic lights at all times. Replacing even a fraction of human drivers with automated systems would cause accident numbers to plunge, saving thousands of lives and lowering insurance costs across the board.

Beyond crash prevention, autonomous vehicles offer practical daily benefits. Google cofounder Sergey Brin points out that automated public transportation could get by on half the fuel and half the parking room that regular cars demand today. In packed metropolitan areas, swapping oversized parking lots for green spaces and housing while cutting emissions would make cities cleaner and much more livable. Autonomous transportation would also be life-changing for elderly individuals and people with disabilities who cannot drive themselves. For them, driverless vehicles mean personal independence rather than relying on family members or specialized transit services.

Of course, skeptics raise sensible doubts that deserve attention. The article points out that current sensors often struggle during snowstorms, heavy downpours, thick fog, or poorly marked construction zones. There are also genuine concerns about software glitches, cybersecurity hacks, and the legal headache of determining whether a crash is the fault of the car owner, the software programmer, or the manufacturer. On top of that, studies reveal that drivers quickly lose focus when a computer takes the wheel, leaving them unprepared to grab control during an emergency.

Yet none of these problems are impossible to fix. Sensor performance in bad weather is a technical challenge that will improve as engineers run more real-world tests and refine the hardware. In fact, the dangerous drop in human attention during semi-autonomous driving actually proves we need fully autonomous vehicles, since the riskiest part is relying on an inattentive human backup. Cybersecurity and liability questions are tricky, but our society already handles similar issues in commercial aviation, digital banking, and medical technology by updating regulations and establishing clear legal frameworks. 

Stopping development today would mean accepting the status quo, where human error regularly causes tragic, preventable deaths. The safe path forward is to keep testing autonomous vehicles carefully under strict government oversight. Driverless cars promise safer highways, cleaner cities, and greater freedom for people who cannot drive, making this technology well worth the effort to get right.

Almost everywhere you look today, people have their phones in their hands. Whether it is teenagers checking social media or parents taking calls for work, cell phones have become an essential part of daily life. However, just because we rely on our phones so much does not mean they belong everywhere. In my opinion, drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle, because any type of phone use creates a serious danger for everyone on the road.

The most obvious reason why phones and driving do not mix is visual and manual distraction. When a driver looks down to read a text, answer a call, or skip a song, their eyes are off the road and at least one hand is off the steering wheel. In driver’s ed, we learn that taking your eyes off the road for even five seconds at highway speed is like driving the entire length of a football field completely blind. A lot can happen in that short amount of time. A car could brake suddenly, a deer could run across the road, or a pedestrian could step into a crosswalk. If you are looking at a screen, you cannot react fast enough to stop a crash.

Some people argue that hands-free technology, like Bluetooth or speakerphone, solves this problem because your hands stay on the wheel. While it might seem safer, research shows that cognitive distraction is still a major issue. When you are engaged in an intense phone conversation, your brain is focused on the person you are talking to rather than what is happening around your car. It is different from talking to a passenger because a passenger can see the traffic and will naturally stop talking if things get dangerous. A person on the other end of a phone call has no idea what is happening on the road, so they keep talking and demanding your attention.

Another common argument is that drivers need their phones for GPS navigation. It is true that digital maps are helpful, especially for new drivers or when traveling somewhere unfamiliar. However, this can still be handled safely without using the phone while actively driving. A driver should set their destination before they put the car into drive, mount the phone on the dashboard, and only listen to audio directions. Actively typing in addresses, searching for music, or holding the phone while the car is moving should be completely off-limits.

In conclusion, using a cell phone while driving is just too risky, no matter how skilled someone thinks they are behind the wheel. Driving requires a person’s complete physical and mental focus. A text message, social media notification, or phone call is never important enough to risk someone’s life. If something is truly an emergency, the driver can easily pull over into a parking lot to handle it. Until a car is safely parked, phones should be put away so that the roads are safer for everyone.

I believe that students should be required to perform community service, although the requirement should be flexible enough to accommodate students’ schedules and responsibilities. Community service helps students understand the needs of others, strengthens the school’s connection to the community, and teaches skills that cannot always be learned in a classroom.

First, community service encourages students to become more responsible and caring citizens. Many students spend most of their time thinking about grades, sports, jobs, or social activities. These things are important, but students also need opportunities to recognize that other people may need help. For example, students who tutor elementary school children can see how difficult learning to read or solve math problems can be for younger students. A high school student may take reading for granted, but after helping a child sound out words or complete a homework assignment, that student can better appreciate the value of patience and education. This experience can make students more thoughtful and compassionate.

Community service also makes a real difference in neighborhoods. A group of students cleaning litter from a park may seem like a small contribution, but it can improve a shared space for children, families, and older residents. Similarly, students who volunteer at food drives, animal shelters, or senior centers can provide help to organizations that often have too few workers. If every student completed even a modest number of service hours, the combined effort could have a meaningful impact. Schools should not only prepare students for college or careers; they should also prepare them to contribute to the places where they live.

In addition, required service can help students discover interests and abilities they did not know they had. A student who reluctantly begins tutoring might realize that he or she enjoys teaching. Another student who volunteers at an animal shelter might develop an interest in veterinary medicine. Service can also build practical skills, such as communication, teamwork, planning, and problem-solving. These skills are valuable in future jobs and relationships. In this way, community service is not simply time taken away from students’ lives; it can be an investment in their personal growth.

Some students may argue that they are already too busy with homework, jobs, family duties, or extracurricular activities. This concern is reasonable, so the requirement should not be excessive. For instance, the school could require a limited number of hours each semester and allow students to choose from many approved activities. Students with jobs or family responsibilities could receive flexible deadlines or participate in service projects connected to their existing commitments. The goal should be to make service meaningful, not to create unnecessary stress.

For these reasons, I strongly support requiring community service for all students. A fair and flexible program would help students develop empathy, improve the community, and gain valuable experience. By making service part of education, our school would show that success is not only about what we achieve for ourselves, but also about how we help others.

Cell phones have become essential tools for communication, navigation, work, and emergencies. Because they are so common, many drivers assume they can safely use them while operating a vehicle, especially if they use hands-free features. However, driving requires constant attention, quick judgment, and awareness of changing conditions. Drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle, except in a genuine emergency when the vehicle cannot first be safely stopped. Even hands-free phone use creates dangerous mental distractions that can increase the risk of crashes.

The most obvious danger of cell phone use is physical distraction. Holding a phone, typing a message, scrolling through a playlist, or entering an address into a navigation application requires drivers to remove at least one hand from the wheel and their eyes from the road. A vehicle can travel a significant distance in only a few seconds, meaning that a driver who looks down briefly may fail to notice a stopped car, pedestrian, cyclist, traffic signal, or hazard. Texting is particularly dangerous because it combines visual, manual, and mental distraction. No message is important enough to justify placing other road users at risk.

Some people argue that hands-free technology solves this problem because drivers can keep both hands on the steering wheel and their eyes facing forward. While hands-free devices reduce physical distraction, they do not eliminate cognitive distraction. A driver engaged in a conversation may miss important details in the driving environment because part of their attention is focused on listening, responding, and thinking about the discussion. Unlike speaking with a passenger, a phone conversation involves a person who cannot see the road and therefore cannot pause naturally when traffic becomes difficult. Even a voice-controlled phone or navigation system can cause a driver to concentrate on commands rather than road conditions.

A complete restriction on phone use while driving would also create clearer and more enforceable rules. Laws that permit certain forms of hands-free use can be confusing, and drivers may wrongly believe that any use is safe if they are not holding the device. A simple rule—pull over before using a phone—would be easier to understand and would encourage safer habits. Drivers who need directions can program their route before leaving or stop in a safe location to make changes. Those expecting an important call can wait until they arrive, use a passenger to respond, or pull over when practical.

There should be limited exceptions for emergencies, such as reporting a collision, calling for medical assistance, or seeking help when a driver is in immediate danger. Even then, drivers should stop the vehicle whenever possible before making the call. The purpose of such an exception is not convenience but protection of life.

Ultimately, operating a vehicle is a serious responsibility, not a task that can be safely combined with constant digital communication. Because cell phones distract drivers physically and mentally, their use should be prohibited while a vehicle is in operation. Waiting a few minutes to make a call or send a message is a small inconvenience compared with the potential consequences of a preventable crash.

Driverless cars, on the other hand, are equipped with laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors that can detect obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals, making them much safer than human-driven cars.

Another benefit of driverless cars is that they could provide mobility for elderly or disabled passengers who are currently unable to drive themselves. Dear Senator [Last Name],

I am writing to urge you to support moving the United States from the Electoral College to a national popular vote for president. Whatever virtues the founders saw in the system, it now allows the loser of the national vote to win the White House, and it leaves tens of millions of Americans on the sidelines of presidential campaigns.

The first problem is the plainest. In 2000 and again in 2016, a candidate won the most votes nationwide and still lost the presidency. Bradford Plumer points to both cases as proof that the system can override the will of the majority. No other office in this country is decided that way. We would not accept a governor or a senator taking office after finishing second in the count, and it is hard to explain why the one office that represents the whole nation should be the exception.

The second problem is how the system shapes campaigns. The Office of the Federal Register explains that forty-eight states and Washington, D.C. award all of their electoral votes to whoever wins the state's popular vote. Under that winner-take-all rule, a candidate who is certain to carry or lose a state gains nothing from courting its voters. Plumer notes that campaigns therefore pour their time, advertising, and promises into a handful of swing states and largely ignore everyone else. A Republican in California or a Democrat in Alabama knows that his or her vote will almost certainly not change the outcome. That is hardly an incentive to participate. Under a national popular vote, every ballot would count equally no matter where it was cast, and candidates would have reason to seek votes in every community.

I do take the opposing arguments seriously. Judge Richard Posner defends the Electoral College as an expression of federalism, one that forces candidates to build broad coalitions across large and small states rather than piling up votes in a few dense cities. That concern deserves a response. But the current system does not really force candidates to appeal to all regions; it forces them to appeal to the few states that are competitive. Many small states are ignored just as thoroughly as large ones. A national vote, by contrast, would reward a candidate for gaining votes in rural Wyoming, suburban Ohio, and urban Texas alike, since each voter would be worth the same. A candidate could not win by running up totals in a couple of cities, because even the largest cities hold only a small share of the national electorate.

Posner also argues that the Electoral College produces a quick, clear winner and confines recounts to individual states, sparing us a chaotic nationwide recount. This is a fair point about administration, but I think it is overstated. The 2000 election showed that a recount in a single pivotal state can be just as bitter and drawn out as anything we might fear nationally, and it ended with the presidency hanging on a few hundred votes in Florida. Moreover, a national margin is usually far larger than a margin in one state, so a close enough race to require a nationwide recount would be extremely rare. The Electoral College also carries risks of its own. As Plumer observes, faithless electors can in theory vote against their state's popular choice, adding a small but real chance of subverting the voters' decision.

Finally, the Federal Register reminds us that the Electoral College was a compromise, designed in the Constitution to bridge the eighteenth-century divide between election by Congress and election by the people. Compromises suit the circumstances that produce them. Today, with the franchise broadened and a mobile, national electorate, the case for choosing the president directly is much stronger.

I ask that you support a national popular vote, whether through a constitutional amendment or through an interstate compact. Every citizen's vote should carry the same weight, and the candidate with the most votes should win.

Respectfully,

[Your Name]
[Your Address]

The rapid advancement of automotive technology has brought humanity to the threshold of a major transportation revolution. As detailed in the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," innovators like Google cofounder Sergey Brin envision a future dominated by autonomous public transit that significantly reduces fuel consumption and parking requirements. Although critics highlight legitimate engineering hurdles and ethical dilemmas, the development of autonomous vehicles should be actively pursued and supported. The immense potential of driverless cars to save thousands of lives, dramatically lower societal costs, and provide independence to underserved populations far outweighs the transitional challenges.

The most compelling argument in favor of developing driverless cars is the unprecedented improvement in public safety. According to the article, human error is responsible for more than 90 percent of all traffic accidents, largely due to preventable behaviors such as texting, drowsy driving, and intoxication. Human beings are inherently vulnerable to distractions, emotional volatility, and fatigue. In contrast, autonomous vehicles utilize an interconnected network of laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors specifically engineered to constantly track obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals without succumbing to lapses in judgment. By removing human error from the equation, autonomous technology has the power to eliminate the vast majority of collisions, sparing countless families the grief of fatal crashes and substantially reducing insurance costs for everyday commuters.

In addition to enhanced roadway safety, autonomous vehicles offer crucial social and environmental advantages. For decades, the elderly and individuals with disabilities have faced restricted personal freedom due to an inability to operate standard automobiles. Autonomous vehicles offer these marginalized groups newfound mobility and autonomy. Furthermore, the environmental efficiency projected by industry leaders—including a 50 percent reduction in both fuel usage and parking footprint—promises to make cities cleaner, more walkable, and less congested.

Opponents of autonomous transit often cite technological and legal limitations, pointing out that sensors can malfunction in heavy rain, snow, or fog, and that liability remains ambiguous following a collision. Others note that human drivers lose focus during semi-autonomous operations. However, these criticisms describe growing pains typical of any nascent technology rather than inherent, permanent flaws. Sensors can be upgraded, software resilience against cyber threats will strengthen through continued research, and legal frameworks can be adapted by policymakers to assign clear product liability. Haulting innovation out of fear of unresolved questions would merely preserve the deadly status quo, where tens of thousands of people die annually due to human mistakes.

Ultimately, the advent of driverless technology represents a vital step forward for public safety, urban efficiency, and human equity. While the technical and legal challenges identified by critics require rigorous oversight, the societal benefits of saving lives, cutting emissions, and expanding mobility are simply too significant to abandon. Society must embrace the development of driverless cars and actively steer this revolutionary technology toward a safer and more accessible future.

Although some students may initially resist the idea of mandatory extracurricular activities, I strongly agree with the principal’s decision. Requiring every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity—whether a sport, the yearbook, student council, or another club—builds essential life skills, strengthens the school community, and helps students discover hidden talents. Far from being a burden, this policy is an investment in the whole student.

First, extracurricular activities teach skills that cannot be learned from a textbook. When a student joins a sports team, for example, they learn discipline, teamwork, and resilience. A basketball player must attend early-morning practices, work with teammates who have different strengths, and learn to bounce back after a tough loss. Similarly, a student who works on the yearbook develops time management and attention to detail while meeting strict deadlines. These are exactly the habits employers and colleges look for, yet they are rarely practiced in a traditional classroom setting where individual test scores often take priority over collaboration and persistence.

Second, mandatory participation strengthens the school community. When all students share at least one common extracurricular experience, social barriers begin to break down. A shy freshman who joins the student council may find herself planning a charity drive alongside a senior she would never have spoken to otherwise. The football player and the debate club member might discover mutual respect while volunteering at a school event. If extracurricular activities are optional, too many students miss these opportunities. They may go home immediately after school, never forming meaningful connections beyond their immediate friend group. By requiring participation, the school ensures that every student has a place to belong and a reason to feel invested in the school’s success.

Of course, some critics argue that forcing students into activities will create resentment and half-hearted effort. They claim that students should be free to choose how they spend their free time. However, the policy only requires one activity, and students still have the freedom to choose which one suits them. A student who hates sports can join the drama club, the robotics team, the school newspaper, or a community service group. With a wide enough range of options, nearly every student can find something they genuinely enjoy. Often, students who are required to try an activity discover a passion they would never have explored on their own. The reluctant freshman who is pushed onto the track team may become the varsity captain by senior year.

Finally, extracurricular involvement has concrete academic and personal benefits. Studies consistently show that students who participate in structured after-school activities tend to have better attendance, higher grades, and lower dropout rates. Being part of a team or club gives students a reason to come to school and a support system when they struggle.

In conclusion, requiring all students to participate in at least one extracurricular activity is a wise and forward-thinking decision. It teaches practical skills, builds a stronger and more inclusive school culture, and opens doors to new interests and friendships. Rather than limiting students, this policy expands their opportunities and prepares them for success both inside and outside the classroom.

Driverless cars should continue to be developed because they have the potential to make transportation safer, more efficient, and more accessible. Although the technology still has important weaknesses, especially in bad weather and emergency situations, those concerns are reasons for careful testing and regulation rather than reasons to abandon the idea. If autonomous vehicles are introduced responsibly, they could solve many of the problems caused by human drivers.

The strongest argument for driverless cars is safety. According to the article, human error causes more than 90 percent of traffic accidents. People text while driving, fall asleep at the wheel, speed, or drive after using alcohol or drugs. A computer does not become distracted by a phone notification or make a reckless decision because it is angry or tired. Driverless vehicles use laser radar, cameras, GPS, and sensors to detect obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals. These systems could react consistently to dangers that a human driver might not notice in time. Even if autonomous vehicles are not perfect, they may eventually be much safer than the human drivers who cause most crashes today.

Driverless cars could also improve life for people who cannot easily drive themselves. Elderly people, disabled passengers, and those with medical conditions often depend on relatives, buses, or expensive transportation services. An autonomous vehicle could give them greater independence. Instead of being isolated at home or relying on another person for every trip, they could travel to school, work, appointments, or stores more easily. This technology could make transportation available to many people who are currently limited by their ability to drive.

In addition, the article describes Sergey Brin’s vision of driverless public transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today’s cars. If fewer people need to own individual vehicles, cities may have less traffic and less land wasted on large parking lots. Lower fuel use could reduce pollution, while fewer accidents could lower insurance costs and save families from the emotional and financial pain caused by crashes.

Critics are right to point out that autonomous cars are not ready to operate without limits everywhere. Sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, and construction zones with unclear lane markings. Software can also fail or become vulnerable to cybersecurity threats. These risks are serious, particularly because semi-autonomous systems may cause drivers to lose attention and react slowly when they suddenly need to take control. However, the answer is not to stop development. Automakers and governments should require extensive testing in difficult conditions, strong protections against hacking, and clear instructions about when human drivers must remain alert. Laws should also establish who is responsible when an autonomous vehicle causes an accident.

Driverless cars will not create a perfect transportation system overnight. Still, the dangers of the current system are already clear: human mistakes injure and kill people every day. By developing autonomous vehicles carefully and holding companies accountable for their safety, society can move toward a future with fewer crashes, greater independence, and cleaner, more efficient travel.

As the proposal to introduce a minimum grade B average requirement for participation in sports and other activities gains momentum, it is essential to consider the potential consequences of such a policy change. While the intention behind this initiative may be to promote academic excellence, it is crucial to weigh the potential benefits against the potential drawbacks. In my opinion, implementing a grade B average threshold would be misguided and ultimately detrimental to the well-being and development of many students.

One of the primary concerns with this policy is that it would unfairly penalize students who, despite their best efforts, struggle to achieve high grades. Many students at our school have a grade C average, which, while not exceptional, still demonstrates a satisfactory understanding of the subject matter. By barring these students from participating in activities, we risk depriving them of valuable opportunities for personal growth, socialization, and skill development. Extracurricular activities provide a platform for students to explore their passions, develop teamwork and communication skills, and build meaningful relationships with their peers. Denying students access to these experiences would not only be demotivating but also potentially damaging to their self-esteem and overall educational experience.

Moreover, introducing a grade B average requirement would create a culture of exclusivity, where students who are already struggling academically are further marginalized. This could lead to a decline in student morale, increased absenteeism, and a higher dropout rate. Instead of fostering a supportive and inclusive environment, we would be creating a system that rewards only the highest achievers, while leaving behind those who need guidance and encouragement. It is essential to recognize that every student has unique strengths and weaknesses, and that academic performance is not the sole indicator of a student's potential or worth.

Another significant issue with this policy is that it would place undue pressure on students to prioritize academics over other aspects of their lives. While academic achievement is undoubtedly important, it is not the only factor that contributes to a student's overall development. By making participation in activities contingent upon a high grade point average, we would be sending a message that academic success is the only thing that matters. This could lead to an unhealthy obsession with grades, at the expense of other essential aspects of student life, such as mental health, physical well-being, and creative pursuits.

Rather than introducing a rigid grade-based threshold, I propose that we focus on providing support and resources to help students improve their academic performance. This could include tutoring programs, academic counseling, and mentorship initiatives that cater to the diverse needs of our student body. The widespread use of cell phones has revolutionized the way people communicate, access information, and navigate their daily lives. However, this ubiquitous technology has also introduced a significant risk to road safety, as the temptation to use cell phones while driving can be overwhelming. The question of whether drivers should be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle is a complex one, with proponents on both sides presenting compelling arguments.

On one hand, the convenience and potential benefits of using cell phones while driving are undeniable. For instance, hands-free devices and voice-activated systems can enable drivers to make emergency calls, receive important updates, or access GPS navigation without taking their eyes off the road or hands off the wheel. Furthermore, the ability to use cell phones can be a vital tool for certain professions, such as truck drivers or delivery personnel, who rely on real-time communication to navigate their routes and manage their logistics. In these cases, the use of cell phones can enhance productivity, efficiency, and overall safety.

On the other hand, the dangers associated with using cell phones while driving are well-documented and alarming. The distraction caused by texting, browsing, or talking on a cell phone can significantly impair a driver's reaction time, judgment, and ability to respond to unexpected situations on the road. Moreover, the cognitive load imposed by cell phone use can lead to a phenomenon known as "inattention blindness," where drivers fail to notice critical events or hazards, even if they are looking directly at them. The consequences of this distraction can be devastating, resulting in accidents, injuries, and fatalities that could have been prevented if the driver had remained focused on the road.

In light of these findings, it is reasonable to conclude that the risks associated with using cell phones while driving far outweigh any potential benefits. While there may be certain exceptions, such as the use of hands-free devices or voice-activated systems, the general rule should be that drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle. This is not to say that drivers should be completely disconnected from the world while driving, but rather that they should be able to stay focused on the road and avoid distractions that could put themselves and others at risk.

Ultimately, the solution to this problem lies in a combination of education, legislation, and personal responsibility. Governments and regulatory agencies can establish and enforce strict laws and guidelines that prohibit the use of cell phones while driving, while also promoting public awareness campaigns to educate drivers about the dangers of distraction. At the same time, drivers themselves must take ownership of their actions and make a conscious decision to stay focused on the road, avoiding the temptation to use their cell phones while driving. By working together, we can reduce the risks associated with cell phone use while driving and create a safer, more responsible driving culture.

The widespread use of cell phones has become an integral part of daily life, with many individuals relying on these devices for communication, navigation, and entertainment. However, the question of whether drivers should be allowed to use cell phones while operating a vehicle is a contentious issue. While some argue that cell phone use is a necessary aspect of modern life, even while driving, others claim that it poses a significant risk to road safety. In this essay, I will argue that drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

The primary concern with cell phone use while driving is the distraction it causes. When a driver is engaged in a conversation, texting, or browsing on their phone, their attention is diverted from the road, increasing the likelihood of accidents. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), distracted driving claims thousands of lives each year, with cell phone use being a leading cause of distraction. The brain cannot multitask as effectively as previously thought, and attempting to do so while driving can have devastating consequences. Furthermore, the physical act of holding and manipulating a phone while driving can also impede a driver's ability to react quickly to changing road conditions, making it even more hazardous.

Another argument against cell phone use while driving is that it can lead to a decrease in reaction time. A study by the University of Utah found that drivers who used their cell phones while driving had a slower reaction time than those who did not, making them more likely to be involved in a collision. This decreased reaction time can have severe consequences, especially in emergency situations where quick decision-making is crucial. Moreover, the use of cell phones can also lead to a lack of situational awareness, making drivers less likely to notice pedestrians, cyclists, or other vehicles on the road.

Some may argue that hands-free phone use or the use of voice-activated systems eliminates the distraction caused by cell phones. However, research suggests that even hands-free phone use can be distracting, as the brain is still engaged in a conversation and not fully focused on the road. Additionally, voice-activated systems can be flawed, and drivers may still need to take their eyes off the road to operate them. Therefore, it is essential to ban all forms of cell phone use while driving to minimize the risk of distraction.

In conclusion, the risks associated with cell phone use while driving far outweigh any potential benefits. The distraction caused by cell phones can lead to a significant increase in accidents, and the decrease in reaction time can have severe consequences. To ensure road safety, it is essential to prohibit all forms of cell phone use while driving. By doing so, we can reduce the number of accidents and save lives. Ultimately, the convenience of using a cell phone while driving is not worth the risk of harm to oneself or others. As such, drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

Dear Principal Ramirez,

I am writing to share my opinion on whether students should be required to perform community service. Some of my friends tutor elementary school children or clean up litter, and they believe deeply in giving back. Other friends worry that a requirement would take time away from homework, jobs, and family responsibilities. After considering both sides, I believe our school should require community service, as long as the requirement is reasonable and flexible.

The strongest reason to require service is that it teaches skills and values that classrooms alone cannot. My friend Daniel tutors third graders in reading every Thursday afternoon. He has learned to be patient, to explain ideas clearly, and to stay responsible for someone who depends on him. These are the same skills employers and colleges look for, yet no textbook can fully teach them. If every student had a similar experience, more of us would graduate with real-world confidence and a stronger sense of empathy.

A requirement would also help students who would never volunteer on their own. Many teenagers are not against service; they simply never get around to it. They may not know where to begin, or they may assume someone else will do the work. A school requirement removes that barrier. I have a friend who was unenthusiastic about a neighborhood cleanup until she actually participated. Afterward, she was proud to see a clean park and began organizing weekend cleanups with her family. Without the push, she might never have discovered how much she cared.

In addition, the community benefits when hundreds of students work together. Our school has more than a thousand students. If each of us gave even thirty hours over four years, that would be tens of thousands of hours of tutoring, cleanup, food-bank sorting, and support for senior citizens. Local organizations that are short on volunteers would gain tremendous help, and students would see that they can improve the place where they live.

I understand the concern that service takes time away from what students need or want to do. Some students play sports, work after school, or care for younger siblings, and their schedules are already full. This is a fair point, and it is why the policy must be designed carefully. The requirement should be modest, such as twenty to thirty hours over four years, so that it can be completed gradually. Students should be allowed to choose where they serve, which lets them pick activities connected to their interests. The school could also count service done on weekends, during summer, or through family and religious organizations. Students who already work or care for relatives could receive credit for approved forms of that responsibility. With these options, service becomes an opportunity rather than a burden.

Finally, a requirement would send a message about the kind of school we want to be. Academic success matters, but so does character. When a school says that serving others is part of a complete education, students take that idea seriously, and it shapes how they treat their neighbors long after graduation.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge you to adopt a community service requirement that is manageable and flexible. It would benefit students, strengthen our community, and help us grow into responsible adults. Thank you for considering my perspective.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

Dear Principal Reyes,

I am writing to urge you to adopt Policy 1, which lets students carry phones and use them during lunch and other free periods, provided they stay off during class. A total ban sounds tidy, but I think it would cause more problems than it solves, and the middle path asks students to practice something they will need for the rest of their lives: self-control.

Start with safety. Parents worry, and not without reason. If there is a lockdown, a bus breakdown, or a sudden change in after-school pickup, a phone is the fastest way for a family to reach a student and for a student to reach help. Under a ban, the only line of communication is the front office, which can be swamped within minutes of any real emergency. I would rather know that my mother can reach me, and that I can reach her, than depend on a single phone line that everyone is trying to use at once.

Then there is the practical side of student life. Many of us juggle jobs, younger siblings, and sports practices that shift without warning. A quick text to say that I need to be picked up at 4:30 instead of 3:45 can save a parent a wasted trip. Phones also hold things teachers increasingly ask us to use: calendars, assignment portals, and photos of the whiteboard before it gets erased. Allowing phones during free time means students can handle these small logistics at lunch rather than sneaking a glance in class.

I understand the strongest argument against my position, which is distraction. Nobody can honestly claim that phones help anyone concentrate on algebra. But Policy 1 already addresses that: phones must be off during class. The real question is enforcement, and here I think a ban may be harder to maintain than a limited allowance. Bans tend to create a cat-and-mouse game in which students hide phones in sleeves and backpacks, and teachers spend precious minutes policing pockets. When phones are permitted at lunch, the rule has a reasonable boundary, and students lose little by following it. People tend to respect limits that feel fair.

There is also something to be said for lunch itself. After four hours of sitting still and being told where to focus, students need a break, and for many of us that break includes checking in with friends, listening to music, or simply decompressing. Some students who are shy or new find it easier to ease into a social setting when they have something familiar in their hands. A ban would not turn the cafeteria into a salon of lively conversation overnight; it would likely just make lunch feel more like another class.

Finally, I believe schools should prepare us for the world outside them. Adults are constantly deciding when to put their phones away: in meetings, at dinner, behind the wheel. If we never carry phones at school, we never practice making those choices. Policy 1 gives us a daily chance to learn when a phone belongs in a pocket and when it is fine to take it out.

If you do choose Policy 1, I would suggest a clear consequence for violations, such as having the phone held in the office until the end of the day for a first offense, so that the rule has teeth. I believe most students will rise to the trust you show them.

Thank you for taking the time to consider a student's perspective.

Respectfully,
Jordan Ellis
Grade 10

The question of whether summer projects should be teacher-designed or student-designed has long divided educators. Teacher-designed projects can certainly keep students focused on specific skills, but I believe student-designed projects are the stronger option because they encourage independence, boost motivation, and let students explore what genuinely interests them.

One major reason to favor student-designed projects is that they build self-directed learning. When students design their own projects, they have to take ownership: setting goals, planning steps, and managing their time. That process strengthens critical thinking and problem-solving. For example, a student curious about environmental science might choose to study how pollution affects local wildlife, collecting data and presenting the findings. Because the project is theirs, they are more likely to invest real effort and develop a deeper understanding of the topic.

Student-designed projects also tend to increase motivation. Students are far more engaged when they can pursue their own interests. Teacher-designed assignments, by contrast, can sometimes feel irrelevant or forced, which leads to boredom. A student who loves photography, for instance, might document the natural beauty in their area, while a coding enthusiast might create an app that helps people learn a language. When students choose their own focus, educators can tap into their natural curiosity and help them see learning as something enjoyable, not just a classroom requirement.

Finally, giving students control over their summer projects lets them explore their passions more deeply. Instead of being limited to a predetermined topic, students can investigate issues that matter to them and see how their learning connects to the real world. A student passionate about social justice might research inequality in their community and propose solutions, while a student interested in engineering might build a prototype to solve an everyday problem. This kind of ownership gives students a sense of purpose and direction.

In short, summer projects should be student-designed because they promote independence, increase motivation, and allow students to follow their passions. When students have the freedom to shape their own projects, they practice valuable skills like critical thinking, problem-solving, and time management. They also develop a lasting love of learning that reaches beyond the classroom. As the world grows more complex, giving students room to pursue their interests is an important step in preparing them for the future.

I agree with the principal’s decision to require every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. Although some people believe that after-school activities should remain voluntary, I am convinced that making them a requirement benefits students academically, socially, and personally. Extracurricular activities are not simply add-ons to the school day; they are essential experiences that teach lessons classrooms cannot always provide.

One important benefit of extracurricular participation is that it teaches teamwork and responsibility. When students join a sports team, work on the yearbook staff, or serve on student council, they must learn to cooperate with others to achieve a common goal. A basketball player, for example, quickly discovers that winning depends on passing, communication, and trusting teammates rather than individual talent alone. Similarly, yearbook staff members must divide tasks, meet deadlines, and solve problems together. These experiences prepare students for college and future careers, where collaboration and reliability are essential.

In addition, extracurricular activities help students discover hidden talents and build confidence. A quiet student who joins the drama club may find that she loves performing on stage. A student who reluctantly tries debate may become a confident public speaker. Student council offers opportunities to plan events, manage budgets, and speak in front of the entire school. Without a requirement, many students would never take the risk of trying something new, and they might miss discovering a passion or strength they did not know they had.

Furthermore, participation in extracurricular activities often improves academic performance by teaching time management. Students who know they have soccer practice or a robotics club meeting after school learn to use their time wisely. They are more likely to complete homework during study hall, avoid procrastination, and stay organized. Many schools report that involved students have better attendance and higher grades than students who go straight home every afternoon. The discipline developed through activities carries over into the classroom.

Some critics argue that requiring participation forces students into activities they do not enjoy and may create stress. However, schools can address this concern by offering a wide variety of clubs and teams, from art and music to community service and academic competitions. A single requirement is flexible, and students can choose an activity that matches their interests. Summer break gives students something the normal school calendar rarely allows: long stretches of unstructured time. When schools assign summer homework, they want to prevent learning loss, but who actually designs the project makes a huge difference. While teacher-assigned work provides an easy, predictable structure, summer projects should ultimately be student-designed. Letting students take the lead builds genuine motivation, fosters independence, and produces much deeper learning than work finished simply to earn a grade.

The strongest argument for student-designed projects comes down to motivation. During the school year, teachers rely on daily deadlines, regular reminders, and classroom routines to keep everyone on task. Over the summer, those guardrails vanish. If an assignment feels like mindless busywork, it inevitably gets put off until the final weekend before school starts. When students choose their own topics, however, they actually have a reason to get started. A student fascinated by baking might study how humidity, proofing times, and yeast ratios alter bread texture, recording each test in a lab notebook. A standard, assigned book report usually results in a rushed Sunday evening panic, but the baking experiment can spark a summer-long inquiry that weaves together chemistry, measurement, and technical writing.

Student-directed projects also cultivate skills that canned assignments ignore. Planning an independent project requires identifying a goal, mapping out intermediate steps, hunting down resources, and managing time without a supervisor hovering. Colleges and workplaces constantly emphasize these self-starter habits, yet typical classroom rubrics leave little room to practice them. For example, a student who decides to create a volunteer portal for a local animal shelter has to figure out what the organization needs, teach herself basic web design, and troubleshoot code when things inevitably break. That kind of real-world problem-solving teaches resilience far better than any packet of worksheets ever could.

Some educators worry that students, left to their own devices, will pick trivial topics to skate by without doing real work. While this is a fair concern, the answer is not to take away student ownership. Schools can simply require a short proposal in June that outlines a research question, a schedule, and an expected end product. Teachers can review and approve these plans, offering advice and setting up an occasional check-in over the break. In this model, the teacher acts as a mentor and editor rather than a taskmaster. Students still hold the reins, but the school ensures the work remains academically challenging.

Equity is another valid concern, since some families have more money for materials, lessons, or museum visits. Yet student-driven work does not need to be expensive. A student can record oral histories by interviewing relatives, document native plant species in a local green space, or learn Python through free public library courses. Open-ended projects can actually level the playing field, allowing kids to draw on their own communities and lived experiences instead of forcing everyone into a rigid, one-size-fits-all mold.

When September arrives and students present what they worked on, the atmosphere is completely different. Instead of turning in thirty identical posters, classmates get to share projects they actually care about, learning from each other's diverse interests. If the real goal of summer learning is to nurture thoughtful, curious minds, we should trust students to chase the questions that matter to them.

As the principal considers whether to require all students to perform community service, I strongly believe that it should be mandatory. Not only does community service foster a sense of social responsibility, but it also provides students with invaluable skills and experiences that can benefit them throughout their lives. While some may argue that community service takes away from other activities, I firmly believe that the benefits far outweigh the drawbacks.

One of the primary advantages of requiring community service is that it helps students develop a sense of empathy and compassion for others. By volunteering at local food banks, nursing homes, or animal shelters, students gain a deeper understanding of the challenges faced by vulnerable populations. For example, a friend of mine who tutored elementary school children discovered that many of them struggled with basic reading skills due to lack of resources at home. This experience not only improved her teaching skills but also instilled in her a sense of responsibility to give back to her community. Similarly, students who participate in community clean-up initiatives learn about the importance of environmental conservation and the impact of their actions on the community.

Another significant benefit of community service is that it provides students with opportunities to develop essential life skills, such as communication, teamwork, and problem-solving. By working together to address community needs, students learn to collaborate effectively, think critically, and adapt to new situations. For instance, a group of students who organized a charity event to raise funds for a local hospital learned how to plan, execute, and evaluate a project, skills that will serve them well in their future careers. Moreover, community service experiences can also enhance students' college applications and future job prospects, as they demonstrate a commitment to social responsibility and civic engagement.

Some may argue that requiring community service would take away from students' already packed schedules, leaving them with insufficient time for other activities. However, I would counter that community service can be integrated into existing curricula and extracurricular programs, minimizing the impact on students' schedules. Additionally, many community service activities can be completed during weekends, holidays, or summer breaks, ensuring that students have ample time to balance their commitments.

In conclusion, requiring students to perform community service is essential for fostering a sense of social responsibility, developing valuable life skills, and promoting civic engagement. While some may view community service as a time-consuming obligation, I firmly believe that the benefits far outweigh the drawbacks. By incorporating community service into our school's curriculum, we can empower students to become active, informed, and compassionate citizens who are equipped to make a positive impact in their communities. Cell phones have become so ordinary that many people barely notice when they reach for one. A driver may glance at a message while stopped at a light, change a song through a dashboard connection, or answer a call using a hands-free system. Because these actions seem brief or convenient, they are often treated as harmless. Yet driving requires continuous attention, judgment, and physical control. Drivers should not use cell phones in any non-emergency capacity while operating a vehicle because even limited phone use divides attention and creates risks for everyone on the road.

The most obvious danger is visual and manual distraction. Reading a notification or typing a response requires a driver to take eyes off the road and, usually, at least one hand off the wheel. At highway speeds, a vehicle can travel the length of a football field in only a few seconds. During that time, traffic can slow, a pedestrian can enter a crosswalk, or another driver can change lanes unexpectedly. A person who looks down “just for a moment” may have too little time to react safely. The fact that many drivers believe they can multitask does not change the physical limits of human attention.

Hands-free calling is sometimes presented as a reasonable compromise, but it is not entirely safe either. A driver engaged in an emotional conversation, a complicated work call, or a disagreement may still be mentally removed from the task of driving. This kind of cognitive distraction can lead people to miss signs, overlook hazards, or make poor decisions at intersections. Speaking with a passenger is different because a passenger can see the traffic conditions and may pause the conversation when the situation becomes demanding. Someone on the other end of a phone call cannot do that.

Banning routine phone use would also establish a clearer social expectation. Current rules often distinguish between texting, holding a phone, and using hands-free technology, but complicated laws can be difficult to enforce and easy to rationalize around. A simple principle—phones should remain out of use while the vehicle is moving or temporarily stopped in traffic—would be easier for drivers to remember. People could pull into a safe parking area before responding to messages, setting navigation, or making calls. Modern phones also offer “do not disturb while driving” settings that can silence alerts and send automatic replies.

There should, however, be limited exceptions for genuine emergencies. Calling emergency services after a crash, reporting an immediate threat, or seeking urgent medical help may be necessary when no safer option exists. Navigation can also be useful if it is programmed before the trip begins and operated without handling the phone. These exceptions should not become excuses for casual scrolling, answering messages, or adjusting playlists at red lights.

Driving is not a background activity that can safely be combined with every other part of modern life. It is a responsibility that affects passengers, cyclists, pedestrians, and other motorists. For that reason, drivers should avoid cell phone use in any ordinary capacity until they have safely parked.

Dear Principal Johnson,

I am writing to share my opinion on whether students should be required to perform community service. I think our school should require it, but with some flexibility so it does not become a burden. I have friends on both sides of this, and I understand why they feel the way they do, but I believe the benefits are bigger than the problems.

First, community service teaches students things we don't always learn in class. My friend Marcus tutors second graders at Lincoln Elementary twice a week. At first he only did it because his older sister told him it would look good on college applications. Now he talks about those kids all the time. He said he learned patience, and he even got better at explaining math because he has to break it down for little kids. You can't really get that from a worksheet. If every student had a chance like that, I think more people would find out what they're good at or what they care about.

Second, service helps the community in ways that really add up. Another group of my friends spends some Saturday mornings cleaning litter at the park near our school. Before they started, the park was covered in wrappers and bottles. Now families actually use it, and my little cousin plays there. If the whole school helped out, we could do much more than a few volunteers can. Our town has a lot of needs, like food drives, helping older neighbors, and cleaning up, and students are a big group of people who could help.

I do know the other side. Some of my friends say service takes too much time. One of them plays on the soccer team, works part time at a grocery store, and still has to keep up his grades. When he comes home, he barely has time to sleep, so adding more hours of service sounds stressful to him. I think that is a fair point. Nobody wants a rule that makes students fall behind in their classes or lose their jobs.

That's why I think the requirement should be reasonable. Instead of asking for a huge number of hours, the school could ask for something small, like fifteen or twenty hours a year. Students should also get to pick what kind of service they do, so it fits their schedule and interests. A student who is busy during the week could do a weekend project, and someone who likes animals could help at a shelter. We could even count things we already do through the school, like helping at school events or tutoring younger students on campus. This way the rule is not just one more thing to stress about.

Some people say that service only means something if you choose to do it. I see that, but sometimes people need a push to get started. Many students never volunteer simply because they never thought about it or didn't know where to begin. A requirement would give them that first step, and I bet many of them would end up liking it, the way Marcus did.

In conclusion, I believe students should be required to do community service as long as the amount is small and students have choices. It helps our community, and it helps us grow as people. Thank you for taking the time to consider my opinion.

Sincerely,
A concerned student

Dear Principal,

When I hear my friends argue about community service, I notice something strange. The ones who volunteer often sound proud and energized, even when they originally signed up only because a club required it. The ones who resist have rarely tried it. I believe that is exactly why you should require all students to perform community service.

I understand the objection. Homework, sports, part-time jobs, and family responsibilities already eat up our afternoons. Mandatory service can feel like one more demand. Yet I have watched a reluctant friend start tutoring a fourth grader in math and change completely. At first she counted the minutes. Then the student finally solved a fraction problem on his own, and she talked about it for a week. That hour stopped being a chore and became something she looked forward to. If service had been optional, she would never have discovered that satisfaction.

Another friend spent a Saturday cleaning litter along a creek near our school. She was annoyed about the early alarm, but she came home with a muddy jacket and a sharp sense of injustice about the plastic tangled in the roots. She now carries a trash bag on her walks. Again, the requirement turned an abstract idea about caring for the community into a direct, personal experience.

This is not to say that forty hours of forced labor would be good for everyone. A rigid program would breed resentment. But a thoughtful requirement—twenty hours spread across a year, with choices like tutoring, park cleanup, assisting at a senior center, or working at a food pantry—gives students freedom while making sure everyone steps outside their own schedule. The time cost is real, but it is modest compared with the habits it builds. Service teaches patience, humility, and collaboration in ways a classroom lecture cannot.

Requiring community service also sends a clear message: our school belongs to the community, and the community belongs to us. That message should not depend on whether a student happens to be motivated. I have seen too many classmates avoid volunteering simply because they do not know where to start or assume they will hate it. A requirement gives them a beginning. After that, many will keep going on their own.

Please adopt a flexible community service requirement. It will not turn every student into a saint, but it will open a door that many would otherwise never push.

Sincerely,
Maya Chen

I think summer projects should be student-designed. When students get to choose what they work on, they're more likely to be interested in it and actually learn something. This is a lot like what we'll have to do in college and in our future careers, so it's good practice. Teachers can still provide guidelines and requirements for student-designed projects, and even offer suggestions for topics or approaches. This way, we can still make sure we're meeting the standards, but we also get to have some autonomy and choose something we're interested in. For example, a teacher might say that our project has to be related to a particular subject, like science or history, but we get to choose the specific topic and how we want to approach it.

Finally, student-designed projects can be a great way to discover new passions and interests. When we're forced to do a project on a certain topic, we might not learn anything new about ourselves. This can be really valuable, because it can help us figure out what we want to study in college or pursue as a career. In conclusion, I think summer projects should be student-designed. This approach allows us to take ownership of our learning, develop important skills, and discover new passions and interests. This is a better approach than having teachers design the projects, because it's more engaging, motivating, and relevant to our lives.
