As our school re-evaluates its policies on mobile devices, the question of how to manage them has become increasingly important. After considering the two proposed options, I strongly believe that Policy 1 is the better choice. This policy allows students to bring their phones to school and use them during lunch and free periods, as long as they are turned off during class time. By adopting this approach, our school can strike a balance between acknowledging the practical role of mobile phones in modern life and maintaining a distraction-free learning environment.

One of the primary advantages of Policy 1 is that it recognizes the importance of mobile phones as a means of communication between students and their families. For many students, phones are not just a luxury, but a necessity. They help students coordinate their schedules, stay in touch with family members, and respond to emergencies. By allowing phone use during lunch, students can take care of personal matters without disrupting class or placing an unnecessary burden on the school administration. This is particularly important in situations where students need to confirm transportation arrangements, respond to family emergencies, or deal with unexpected events like weather cancellations.

In addition to providing a practical solution, Policy 1 also offers an opportunity to teach students about digital literacy and personal responsibility. As we prepare for higher education and the workforce, it is essential that we learn how to use mobile devices responsibly. By setting clear expectations for phone use during school hours, we can help students develop the skills they need to stay focused and avoid distractions. This approach is more effective than a total ban, which can be seen as overly restrictive and may lead to students finding ways to circumvent the rules. Instead, by trusting students to use their phones responsibly during designated times, we can promote a sense of maturity and accountability.

Another significant benefit of Policy 1 is that it can help maintain a positive school climate. A total ban on phones, as proposed in Policy 2, can create an adversarial relationship between students and teachers, with staff members feeling like they need to police students' behavior. This can lead to a culture of mistrust and undermine the educational experience. In contrast, Policy 1 offers a more collaborative approach, where students are treated as responsible individuals who can be trusted to make good choices. By working together to establish clear expectations and consequences, we can create a more supportive and inclusive learning environment.

In conclusion, I believe that Policy 1 is the better choice for our school. By allowing students to use their phones during designated times, we can promote digital literacy, personal responsibility, and a positive school climate. This approach recognizes the importance of mobile phones in modern life while maintaining a distraction-free learning environment. I appreciate your leadership and willingness to consider the student body's perspective on this issue. I am confident that by working together, we can find a solution that benefits everyone involved.

I think students would really benefit from being able to attend classes from home. There are a lot of reasons why I believe this, and I've seen it work well for some of my friends who have had to stay home from school for various reasons. One of the main reasons I think distance learning is a good idea is that it allows students to learn at their own pace. When you're in a regular classroom, the teacher has to teach at a pace that works for the majority of the students, which can be really slow for some kids or too fast for others. But with distance learning, students can review the material as many times as they need to, and they can even speed up or slow down the video if they need to.

Another reason I think distance learning is beneficial is that it reduces the stress and pressure of being in a traditional classroom. Some students get really anxious about speaking up in class or participating in discussions, and distance learning eliminates that pressure. Students can just focus on learning the material without worrying about what their classmates think of them. Plus, if a student is feeling sick or having a bad day, they can still attend classes from home and not fall behind.

Distance learning also provides more flexibility for students who have other commitments, such as sports or family obligations. For example, I have a friend who is really into dance, and she has to attend practice every day after school. With distance learning, she could attend her classes from home and then go to practice without having to worry about missing any schoolwork. This would be especially helpful for students who have to take care of a family member or have a part-time job.

In addition, distance learning can be more cost-effective for schools and families. Schools wouldn't have to spend as much money on maintaining classrooms and other facilities, and families wouldn't have to spend as much money on transportation or lunch. This could be especially helpful for families who are struggling financially.

Some people might argue that distance learning lacks the social interaction and face-to-face communication that is essential for learning. But I don't think this is necessarily true. With video conferencing, students can still interact with their teachers and classmates, and they can even participate in virtual discussions and group work. Plus, many online learning platforms have built-in tools for collaboration and communication, such as chat rooms and discussion boards.

I also think that distance learning can help students develop important skills, such as time management and self-motivation. When you're attending classes from home, you have to be really disciplined and organized to stay on top of your work. This can be really helpful for students who are planning to go to college or enter the workforce, where they will be expected to work independently and manage their time effectively.

Overall, I think that distance learning is a great option for students, and it can provide a lot of benefits, from flexibility and reduced stress to cost-effectiveness and skill-building. Of course, it's not for everyone, and some students might prefer the traditional classroom experience. But for students who are self-motivated and disciplined, distance learning can be a really great way to learn and succeed.

Dear Principal Davis,

When I first heard about the proposal to raise the academic eligibility cutoff for extracurricular activities to a B average, I understood the good intentions behind it. We all want our peers to excel academically, and our primary mission here is to learn. Yet, after discussing this proposal with classmates, teammates, and teachers, I strongly urge you not to adopt this policy. Setting the bar at a B average risks alienating the very students who rely on school activities the most.

A grade of C represents satisfactory mastery of course material. While we should always encourage students to strive for higher marks, treating a C as an unacceptable failure sends a demoralizing message. It tells students who work tirelessly just to pass a challenging chemistry or algebra class that their honest effort counts for nothing if it falls short of an arbitrary standard. For students with learning differences, or those who balance jobs and family responsibilities after the final bell rings, maintaining a consistent B average is an enormous hurdle. Disqualifying them from sports, theater, or robotics will not magically unlock higher grades; it will simply convince them that our school has no room for their talents.

Extracurricular activities are not merely rewards for academic brilliance—they are frequently the engine driving it. Countless students show up on time, stay out of trouble, and keep their grades from slipping into failing territory specifically because they want to remain eligible for Friday night games or the spring musical. Coaches and club advisors act as vital mentors, tracking report cards and demanding accountability. If you strip these outlets away from students holding a C average, you remove their primary incentive to stay focused. Deprived of their teams, creative outlets, and mentors, many will drift further from academic investment, not closer to it.

There is also the matter of student well-being. Extracurriculars teach resilience, leadership, and collaboration—skills that no textbook can replicate. For many teenagers, an hour on the track or in the art studio provides essential relief from anxiety and daily stress. Eliminating that release valve will foster resentment and burnout rather than scholarly ambition.

Drivers should not be permitted to use cell phones in any capacity while their vehicles are in motion.

As the debate over the Electoral College continues to simmer, I strongly believe that this institution should be preserved as a vital component of our democratic system. While critics argue that it is undemocratic and outdated, I firmly believe that the Electoral College plays a crucial role in ensuring that presidential candidates build broad national coalitions and do not solely focus on densely populated urban areas.

One of the primary arguments against the Electoral College is that it can lead to a situation where a candidate wins the national popular vote but loses the presidency, as happened in 2000 and 2016. However, this argument overlooks the fact that the Electoral College is a deliberate design of the Founding Fathers, intended to balance the interests of large and small states. As Judge Richard A. Posner notes in "In Defense of the Electoral College," the Electoral College prevents candidates from winning solely by running up massive vote totals in single regions, forcing them to build broad national coalitions. This ensures that presidential candidates must appeal to a diverse range of voters across the country, rather than simply focusing on one or two densely populated areas.

Another criticism of the Electoral College is that it can lead to "faithless electors" who vote against their state's popular choice. However, this criticism is overstated, and the risk of faithless electors is extremely low. Moreover, as the Office of the Federal Register notes in "What Is the Electoral College?", the Electoral College consists of 538 electors, and a majority of 270 electoral votes is required to elect the President. This means that even if a few electors were to vote against their state's popular choice, it is unlikely to change the outcome of the election.

In contrast to the criticisms, I believe that the Electoral College has several benefits. For example, it produces a clear, decisive winner quickly, avoiding the chaos of a nationwide popular-vote recount. As Judge Posner notes, this confines any disputed vote recounts to individual states, making it easier to resolve disputes and ensure a smooth transition of power. Additionally, the Electoral College preserves federalism, giving smaller states a voice in the election process and preventing larger states from dominating the outcome.

Some may argue that the Electoral College is unfair because it can lead to a situation where a candidate wins the presidency without receiving the most popular votes. However, this argument assumes that the popular vote is the only measure of a candidate's legitimacy. As Bradford Plumer notes in "The Indefensible Electoral College," the winner-take-all rule in most states can lead to a situation where presidential campaigns focus almost exclusively on a handful of "swing states" while ignoring voters in safely Democratic or Republican states. However, this criticism can be addressed by reforming the Electoral College system, rather than abolishing it altogether. For example, states like Maine and Nebraska allocate electors proportionally by congressional district, which can help to reduce the impact of the winner-take-all rule.

In conclusion, while the Electoral College is not perfect, I firmly believe that it should be preserved as a vital component of our democratic system. Its benefits, including the promotion of broad national coalitions and the preservation of federalism, outweigh its drawbacks. Rather than abolishing the Electoral College, we should focus on reforming it to address the criticisms and ensure that it continues to serve the interests of all Americans. I urge you to consider the importance of the Electoral College and work to preserve it for future generations.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

When our principal announced that every single student would be required to participate in at least one extracurricular activity, I know the intention was good. High school is supposed to be about getting involved, making friends, and building up a resume for college or a job. However, making after-school activities mandatory is the wrong move. Students already have complicated lives, and turning extracurriculars into another requirement will only create more stress and do more harm than good.

First of all, this policy completely overlooks the real-world responsibilities that many students have once the final bell rings. Not everyone has the luxury of staying after school until five o’clock for soccer practice or sitting in a classroom to work on the yearbook. A lot of kids have part-time jobs because they need to help their families pay for groceries, or they are trying to save money for college. For example, my friend Marcus works four days a week at a local grocery store right after school. Other students have to rush home immediately to babysit younger brothers and sisters so their parents can work late shifts. Forcing these students to stay at school for an extra hour or two puts an unfair burden on their families.

Second, academic pressure is already high enough as it is. Between regular homework, studying for tests, and trying to keep grades up, most students are already overwhelmed and not getting enough sleep. Extracurricular activities are supposed to be an outlet where you go to relax and do something you actually enjoy, like playing an instrument or joining the art club. The moment the school forces you to do it, the fun disappears. It just turns into another assignment on your to-do list, which makes burnout even worse. 

Finally, forcing everyone to join will end up hurting the clubs and teams themselves. Right now, groups like the student council or the drama club work well because the members actually want to be there. They are excited and put in real effort. If you suddenly flood those groups with dozens of kids who only signed up because they were forced to, it ruins the experience for everyone. People will just sit in the back, look at their phones, and drag down the energy of the students who genuinely care about the project or the sport.

Instead of forcing everyone into an activity, the administration should focus on encouraging participation naturally. The school could offer late activity buses so transportation is not an issue, or create new clubs that match hobbies students actually care about. The word "extra" is right there in the title: extracurricular. It should always be a personal choice, not a graduation requirement.

Summer projects should be student-designed, not teacher-designed. When students choose their own focus, the work becomes an extension of curiosity rather than a box to check. Teacher-designed assignments often assume one size fits all; a student who dislikes physics may dutifully complete a packet on motion, but the learning evaporates by September. By contrast, a student who spends July building a skateboard ramp and measuring launch angles has absorbed the same concepts without coercion.

Consider reading. A teacher might assign the same novel to thirty students. Some will love it, some will skim it, and many will forget it. If students design their own summer reading plan around a question that matters to them—how families survive crisis, why revolutions fail, what makes a villain compelling—they read more deeply because the inquiry is theirs. One ninth grader spent last summer reading memoirs of immigrants after hearing her grandmother’s stories. She returned to school with a portfolio of notes and a proposal for an oral history project. No teacher could have prescribed that exact path. The project grew out of her own life.

Skeptics say students lack the judgment to design rigorous summer work. But student-designed does not mean unsupervised. A teacher can provide a framework: the project must include research, a product, and a reflection. Students then fill that frame with their own questions. A reluctant writer might create a graphic novel about a local ecosystem. A future engineer might design and test a water filter from household materials. A musician might compose three pieces inspired by different historical periods and explain the connections. Each project demands planning, revision, and evidence. The difference is that the student cares about the outcome.

This ownership also reduces summer learning loss. The problem with most summer packets is not that they are too hard or too easy; it is that they feel like schoolwork without school. When the task belongs to the student, deadlines become personal. A boy who builds a computer from used parts over the summer is not counting down until the assignment is finished. He is troubleshooting because he wants the machine to boot. That persistence transfers to the classroom in the fall: he has practiced solving open-ended problems, not just completing worksheets.

Of course, some students will flounder without more direction. For them, teachers can offer menus of possible projects or require periodic check-ins. The goal, however, should remain choice. A teacher-designed project may look neat in August, but a student-designed one is more likely to leave a lasting mark. Schools should trust students to ask their own questions and then hold them accountable for answering well.

Important decisions are rarely improved by relying on a single viewpoint. Whether someone is choosing a college, accepting a job, facing a medical question, or working through a conflict with a friend, asking several people can lead to a better choice. Each person notices different risks, brings different experience, and questions assumptions that might otherwise go unchallenged. Advice can't replace personal responsibility, but hearing more than one perspective gives a person better information and more confidence in the final decision.

For one thing, multiple opinions can reveal details that a single adviser might miss. Everyone's knowledge is limited, and everyone has biases. A student deciding between two colleges might start with a guidance counselor, who can explain graduation rates, financial aid, and academic programs. Current students, on the other hand, can describe the dorms, the social life, and how approachable the professors really are. Parents may focus on cost and safety, while a favorite teacher may think about which school best suits the student's interests. No one person is likely to know all of this. By putting the pieces together, the student can choose based on a fuller picture instead of one glossy brochure or one person's preference.

Asking around also helps a person spot bias. Advice usually grows out of personal experience. A friend who loves a certain company may urge someone to apply because the workplace matched that friend's personality. A former employee, however, may say the same company demands long hours and offers little flexibility. Neither person is necessarily wrong. The job might be perfect for someone who thrives in a fast-paced setting and miserable for someone who values free time. When the job seeker hears both accounts, he or she can measure them against personal priorities rather than assuming one person's experience applies to everyone.

Different voices can also push people to think more carefully. If someone hears only advice that matches what he or she already wants, it is easy to rush ahead without considering the consequences. Take a person thinking about buying an expensive car. A friend who is passionate about cars might talk about style, speed, and new technology. A cautious relative, though, might ask about monthly payments, insurance, repairs, and savings goals. That second opinion may not stop the purchase, but it could lead the buyer to pick a cheaper model or wait until the car is truly affordable. Competing viewpoints, then, do not simply cause confusion; they can make a person examine the decision more responsibly.

Naturally, asking many people does not mean following every suggestion. Too much advice can be overwhelming, and some advisers simply do not know enough about the situation. The decision-maker has to judge how credible each source is and decide which advice actually fits. Even so, gathering several thoughtful opinions is usually wiser than depending on one voice.

Dear Principal Martinez,

Thank you for giving students the opportunity to share our thoughts on the proposed policy change. I understand that your goal is to push us to do our best academically, but I am writing to strongly urge you not to raise the minimum GPA requirement for sports and clubs to a B average. I believe that making this change would actually end up hurting a lot of students instead of helping them.

First, a C average represents passing work. High school classes are challenging, and for many students, maintaining a C in tough subjects like Algebra II or Chemistry is already an uphill battle that takes genuine effort. If you suddenly tell someone who is working as hard as they can for a C that their effort is no longer good enough to play soccer or participate in the school play, they are not going to feel inspired. In fact, most of them will probably just give up. When a goal feels completely out of reach, people stop trying altogether. Keeping the bar at a C gives struggling students an achievable goal that keeps them motivated to pass their classes.

Second, for a lot of kids at our school, extracurricular activities are the main reason they stay focused and look forward to coming to class every day. Being on a team or in a club gives people a sense of belonging and keeps them out of trouble after school. Coaches and club advisors are like second parents to many of us; they check our grades, hold us accountable, and push us to do better. If you ban C students from these activities, they will have nowhere to go from 3:00 to 5:00 p.m. Cutting them off from their teammates and positive mentors will only make them feel disconnected from school, which could cause their grades to drop even further.

Finally, school is supposed to be about learning life skills, not just getting top marks on a report card. Things like discipline, communication, leadership, and time management are taught on the field, in the band room, and through student council. Students who get C grades deserve the chance to build those skills just as much as students who get straight A’s. 

Instead of banning students with a C average, maybe the school could offer mandatory after-school study halls or peer tutoring for athletes and club members who need extra help. That way, the school is actually supporting them in raising their grades instead of just punishing them.

I appreciate how much you care about our academic success, but extracurriculars are often the glue that holds our school community together. Please keep the requirement at a C average so all students have a reason to stay engaged and do their best. 

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

Summer break often causes the “summer slide,” the loss of academic skills students worked hard to build during the school year. To prevent this, many schools require summer projects. While some argue that students should design their own projects to follow their interests, I believe summer projects should be teacher-designed. Teacher-designed projects ensure academic rigor, equity, and clear learning goals while still allowing for limited student choice.

First, teacher-designed projects align with curriculum standards and target the specific skills students need for the next grade level. Teachers know what knowledge and abilities are essential for success in their upcoming courses. For example, an eighth-grade math teacher can design a summer packet reviewing linear equations and introductory geometry because those skills are prerequisites for Algebra I. A student-designed project, such as a cooking blog that uses fractions, might be engaging but may not cover all the necessary math standards. Similarly, an English teacher can assign a summer reading list that builds background for the fall study of American literature, selecting novels like *To Kill a Mockingbird* or *The Great Gatsby* and pairing them with guided questions. This purposeful alignment helps ensure that summer work reinforces the right knowledge.

Second, teacher-designed projects promote equity and provide clear structure. Not all students have parents or resources to help them design meaningful academic projects. An open-ended “create your own project” assignment can widen achievement gaps: affluent students might produce elaborate science experiments with parental guidance, while other students may struggle to find direction or choose tasks that are not academically challenging. A teacher-designed project gives every student the same clear instructions, rubric, and list of required materials. For instance, a teacher might create a summer journal with daily prompts and require only a notebook and pencil, making the work accessible to all learners. Teachers can also provide templates and checklists that support students who need extra scaffolding. This shared structure is fairer and more likely to keep all students learning.

Some may object that student-designed projects increase engagement because students choose topics they care about. This concern is valid, but teacher-designed projects can include meaningful choice within clear boundaries. For example, a history teacher might ask students to choose any decade of the twentieth century and create an annotated timeline, or a science teacher might allow students to select between a plant-growth experiment and a weather observation log. This approach gives students a sense of ownership while preserving the teacher’s expert learning objectives. Motivation and academic rigor can therefore coexist.

In conclusion, summer projects should be teacher-designed. Teachers possess the curricular knowledge to target essential skills, the ability to create equitable structures for all learners, and the flexibility to include student choice within a well-crafted assignment. By trusting teachers to design summer work, schools can more reliably prevent summer learning loss and prepare students for the year ahead.

Dear Principal,

I am writing to express my strong support for requiring all students to complete community service before graduation. Some students already tutor elementary school children, volunteer at local events, or help clean up litter in parks. Others worry that service would take time away from homework, jobs, sports, or family responsibilities. Those concerns are understandable, but I believe a flexible community service requirement would benefit students, our school, and the larger community far more than it would inconvenience us.

Community service teaches responsibility and empathy in ways that students cannot always learn from a textbook. For example, students who tutor younger children must be patient, explain ideas clearly, and encourage someone who may be struggling. A friend of mine tutors elementary students in math. She told me that helping children understand basic problems has made her think more carefully about how people learn. It has also helped her become more confident in her own classes. In the same way, students who pick up litter around parks or streets can see the results of their effort immediately. They learn that clean, safe public spaces depend on people who are willing to care for them. These experiences can create habits of citizenship that continue long after students graduate.

A community service requirement could also bring our school closer to the surrounding neighborhood. Students might volunteer at food banks, senior centers, libraries, animal shelters, or community events. By doing so, they would see needs that may not be obvious in their daily lives. Volunteering can help students appreciate what they have while also showing them that small actions can make a real difference. It would also reflect positively on our school. Rather than being known only for academics or sports, our school could be recognized as a place where students contribute to the community.

Another benefit is that service could help students connect with people outside their usual friend groups. Students from different grades, backgrounds, and interests could work together on a common project. Someone who usually spends time with teammates or classmates might get to know students they would not otherwise meet. Working together at a food drive or neighborhood cleanup could improve school spirit and reduce some of the divisions between social groups.

Of course, the requirement should be reasonable. Many students have busy schedules, especially those who take advanced classes, play sports, work part-time jobs, or care for family members. For that reason, the school should allow students to complete a set number of hours over all four years of high school instead of requiring too many hours at once. Students should also have choices about where and when they serve. They could volunteer on weekends, during the summer, or over school breaks. The school might even provide some opportunities during the school day, such as helping with recycling drives or tutoring younger students after classes.

Learning to manage time and balance responsibilities is an important skill for adulthood. Community service would not simply take time away from students’ lives; it would add something valuable to them. It would teach us to care about others, take responsibility for our community, and recognize that our actions matter.

For these reasons, I urge you to require community service for all students, while keeping the program flexible enough for different schedules and needs. Every student should have the opportunity to experience the value of giving back.

Sincerely,  
A Student

The decision to require all students to participate in at least one extracurricular activity has sparked significant debate among educators and students alike. While some argue that this mandate will foster a more well-rounded and engaged student body, I firmly believe that it is a misguided policy that neglects the diverse needs and interests of individual students. By forcing students to participate in extracurricular activities, the principal risks stifling their autonomy and creativity, rather than encouraging them to explore their passions.

For instance, students who are already struggling to balance their academic workload with part-time jobs or family responsibilities may find it challenging to dedicate the necessary time and energy to an extracurricular activity. This could lead to undue stress and decreased academic performance, ultimately undermining the very purpose of the policy. Moreover, some students may simply not be interested in the extracurricular activities offered by the school, and forcing them to participate could result in a lackluster experience that fails to provide any meaningful benefits. In contrast, students who are genuinely passionate about a particular activity should be encouraged to pursue it, but this should be a voluntary choice, rather than a mandatory requirement.

Proponents of the policy argue that extracurricular activities provide students with valuable skills, such as teamwork, communication, and leadership, that are essential for success in the real world. While this is undoubtedly true, it is also important to recognize that these skills can be developed through other means, such as volunteer work, internships, or even solo projects. By limiting the definition of extracurricular activities to those offered by the school, the principal may be overlooking other opportunities that could be more relevant and engaging for certain students. For example, a student who is passionate about environmental conservation may find it more fulfilling to participate in a local community garden project, rather than joining the school's debate team or soccer club.

Furthermore, the policy raises concerns about the potential for unequal access to resources and opportunities. Students from low-income families or those with disabilities may face significant barriers to participating in extracurricular activities, such as lack of transportation, equipment, or accommodations. By mandating participation, the school may inadvertently exacerbate existing inequalities, rather than promoting greater inclusivity and diversity. In order to create a more level playing field, the school should focus on providing support and resources to help all students access extracurricular activities, rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all approach.

In conclusion, while the intention behind the principal's decision may be to promote student engagement and development, it is a policy that requires careful reconsideration. By allowing students to choose their own extracurricular activities, or to opt out altogether, the school can foster a more inclusive and supportive environment that values individual differences and promotes genuine passion and interest. Ultimately, the goal of education should be to nurture the unique talents and abilities of each student, rather than trying to fit them into a predetermined mold.

Dear Principal,

I am writing to support requiring all students to complete community service before graduation. Although I understand that some students are concerned about losing time for homework, jobs, sports, or other activities, I believe a reasonable service requirement would improve our education, build character, and help the community.

Community service teaches important lessons that are difficult to learn only by sitting in a classroom. For example, some of my friends tutor elementary school students. Through tutoring, they learn patience, responsibility, and how to explain ideas clearly. They have to prepare for each meeting, respond to the younger students’ questions, and keep encouraging them even when they do not improve right away. Those skills will be useful in college, at work, and in everyday life.

Other friends participate in neighborhood litter cleanups. Their work may seem simple, but it has an obvious effect. After spending an afternoon picking up trash in a park or along a sidewalk, students are more likely to care about keeping public spaces clean. They also begin to understand that a community does not improve by itself. People have to notice problems and take action. If service is only optional, students who already care about volunteering will participate, but many others may never have the chance to discover how rewarding it can be.

A community service requirement would also benefit organizations that need help. Local schools, food banks, parks, libraries, and senior centers often depend on volunteers, yet they do not always have enough people available. If every student completed even a modest number of service hours each year, our school could make a meaningful difference. Students could help with tutoring programs, food drives, park cleanup projects, or activities for elderly residents. One person volunteering for a few hours may not seem like much, but the combined effort of an entire student body could have a major impact.

Of course, some students have busy schedules. They may have after-school jobs, family responsibilities, demanding classes, or extracurricular activities. For that reason, the requirement should be flexible and realistic. The school could require something like twenty hours per year and provide a variety of ways to complete those hours. Students could volunteer during school-sponsored service days, on weekends, during study halls, or through approved community organizations. They should also be able to choose opportunities connected to their interests. A student who enjoys reading might help at a library, while someone interested in sports could assist with a youth recreation program.

In my experience, volunteering does not always take away from important responsibilities. Instead, it can encourage students to manage their time better and spend some of it on something meaningful. It also helps us look beyond our own schedules and concerns. As students, we are part of this community, and we should learn that we have a responsibility to contribute to it.

For these reasons, I encourage you to require community service for all students. With thoughtful planning and flexible options, the time commitment would be manageable, while the benefits to students and the community would last much longer.

Sincerely,  
A Student

Every few seconds, somewhere on a highway, a driver glances down at a glowing screen. The glance feels harmless, a flicker of attention spent on a text or a map. Yet at fifty-five miles per hour, a five-second look away from the road covers roughly the length of a football field with no one watching it. Because of this, drivers should not be allowed to use handheld cell phones while operating a vehicle, though a narrow exception for hands-free navigation and emergency calls is reasonable.

The case against phone use begins with how human attention actually works. People like to believe they can multitask, but research in cognitive psychology consistently shows that what we call multitasking is rapid switching, and each switch carries a cost. A driver reading a message is not simply doing two things at once; she is repeatedly pulling her mind away from the road and then rebuilding her awareness of it. Reaction times slow. Lane position drifts. Brake lights ahead go unnoticed until the last moment. Studies using driving simulators have found that texting drivers perform worse on some measures than those with a blood alcohol level at the legal limit, a comparison that most people find startling because we already treat drunk driving as unacceptable.

The human toll is not abstract. Distracted driving contributes to thousands of deaths in the United States each year, and the victims are often not the people holding the phones. They are pedestrians in crosswalks, cyclists on shoulders, children in the back seats of other cars. A personal habit becomes a public hazard the moment it happens at speed on shared roads, and that is precisely where the government has traditionally been justified in setting rules. We require seat belts, license drivers, and prohibit speeding for the same reason.

Critics sometimes argue that a ban is unenforceable, since a police officer cannot easily see what a driver is doing behind the wheel. There is some truth to this, but the argument proves too little. Laws shape norms even when enforcement is imperfect. Seat belt use rose dramatically after mandates were adopted, not because police caught every offender, but because the rule changed what people considered normal. Stronger penalties, along with technology that can lock or limit phone features while a car is in motion, could help make a ban more than symbolic.

Others point out that phones are also useful tools. A driver lost in unfamiliar territory benefits from GPS, and someone witnessing an accident may need to call for help immediately. These are fair points, and they argue for a thoughtful law rather than no law. Voice-activated navigation set before the trip begins, or a quick emergency call made when pulling over is not possible, poses a very different risk from scrolling social media at a red light that turns green. Even hands-free calling is not entirely safe, since the cognitive distraction of conversation persists, so the most responsible policy would discourage it while recognizing that an absolute prohibition on every function would be difficult to defend.

Ultimately, the question is about what we owe one another on the road. A text can wait ten minutes; a life cannot be returned. Drivers should be required to put the phone down, mount it for navigation if necessary, and treat the act of driving as the demanding responsibility it is.

As our school reconsiders its cell phone policy, I would like to share my thoughts on the two proposals. After thinking through both options carefully, I believe Policy 1—allowing students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times, as long as they are off during class—is the stronger choice. It balances the role phones play in our daily lives with the need to keep classrooms focused.

First, Policy 1 reflects how many students actually live. We often use our phones to coordinate with family members, confirm after-school plans, and respond to emergencies. Letting us keep phones during the day, even with clear limits, shows that the school understands these practical needs. At the same time, it gives us a chance to practice responsible phone use. That kind of trust often encourages better behavior, because students are more likely to respect boundaries when they feel respected themselves. A complete ban, as described in Policy 2, could feel overly strict and create resentment instead of cooperation.

Another reason I support Policy 1 is safety. In an emergency, having a phone allows students to contact parents, guardians, or emergency services quickly. I understand the concern that phones can be distracting, but Policy 2 may not actually solve that problem. If phones are banned entirely, some students will still find ways to bring them, which could lead to more rule-breaking and hidden use. Rather than simply removing phones, the school could focus on teaching students when and how to use them appropriately. That approach seems more realistic and more lasting.

In the end, Policy 1 is a balanced and practical policy. It respects students, supports safety, and encourages responsibility while still protecting class time. I hope you will consider adopting it for our school.

As the world hurtles towards a future where technology dominates every aspect of our lives, the development of driverless cars has become a highly debated topic. While some envision a utopian future where autonomous vehicles revolutionize transportation, others raise concerns about the potential risks and uncertainties associated with this technology. In my opinion, the development of driverless cars is a step in the wrong direction, and we should exercise caution before embracing this technology.

One of the primary concerns with driverless cars is their ability to navigate through challenging environments. As the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming" points out, current sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or unmarked construction zones. This limitation raises serious concerns about the safety of passengers, pedestrians, and other road users. For instance, if a driverless car is unable to detect a pedestrian crossing the road in heavy rain or fog, the consequences could be disastrous. Furthermore, the article highlights the vulnerability of software systems to glitches or cybersecurity threats, which could have catastrophic consequences if not addressed.

Another issue with driverless cars is the requirement for human drivers to stay alert and take over in emergencies. However, studies have shown that passengers quickly lose focus when a computer is driving, slowing their reaction times. This phenomenon, often referred to as "automation complacency," could lead to a false sense of security among passengers, making them less vigilant and more prone to accidents. The article also raises important questions about legal and ethical responsibility in the event of an accident. If a driverless car is involved in a crash, it is unclear whether the vehicle owner, the software developer, or the automaker should be held legally responsible. This lack of clarity could lead to a regulatory nightmare, with victims and their families facing significant challenges in seeking compensation.

Despite the potential benefits of driverless cars, such as reducing crashes and providing mobility for elderly or disabled passengers, I believe that the risks and uncertainties associated with this technology outweigh its advantages. The article quotes Google cofounder Sergey Brin as envisioning a future of driverless public transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. However, this vision is still a long way off, and we need to prioritize the safety and well-being of passengers and road users over the potential benefits of autonomous vehicles.

In conclusion, while the idea of driverless cars may seem exciting and futuristic, we need to approach this technology with caution. The limitations of current sensors, the vulnerability of software systems, and the lack of clarity around legal and ethical responsibility all raise significant concerns about the safety and viability of driverless cars. Rather than rushing to develop and deploy this technology, we should focus on addressing these concerns and ensuring that driverless cars are safe, reliable, and beneficial for all road users. Only then can we consider embracing this technology and reaping its potential benefits.

Summer projects should be primarily student-designed, with teachers providing clear expectations and guidance. Although teacher-created assignments can ensure that students practice particular skills, student-designed projects are more likely to encourage genuine curiosity, responsibility, and long-term learning. A summer break should not become a second version of the school year; instead, it should give students the chance to connect academic ideas to their own interests and experiences.

First, students work harder when they have ownership over a project. A teacher-designed assignment may ask every student to read the same novel, complete the same packet, or create the same presentation. Some students will benefit, but others may see the task as another requirement to finish as quickly as possible. In contrast, a student who chooses a topic usually has a personal reason to explore it. For example, a student interested in basketball could collect statistics from professional games and use them to investigate percentages, averages, and probability. Another student who enjoys cooking could research nutrition, test recipes, and write a report about how ingredients affect health. Both projects develop academic skills, but they do so through topics that matter to the students.

Student-designed projects also teach important habits that traditional assignments may not develop as well. To complete an independent project, students must set goals, manage time, locate reliable information, and solve problems when their original plans do not work. These are valuable skills for high school, college, and future careers. For instance, a student who decides to build a small garden may need to research soil conditions, create a budget for supplies, record plant growth, and revise the plan after pests or bad weather cause difficulties. The student is learning science and mathematics, but also perseverance and planning.

In addition, allowing choice makes summer projects more fair and realistic. Students spend their vacations in different circumstances. Some travel, attend camps, help care for siblings, work part-time jobs, or stay close to home. A single teacher-designed project may assume that every student has the same books, technology, money, and free time. A flexible student-designed project can fit many situations. A student working in a family restaurant, for example, could interview relatives about the business and create a report on food costs or customer service. A student without internet access could keep a journal, read library books, or observe nature in a local park.

This does not mean teachers should simply assign a project and offer no structure. Teachers should provide a menu of possible formats, a rubric describing expectations, checkpoints, and examples of strong projects. They can require every project to include research, writing, reflection, or a presentation so that academic standards are still met. However, the central topic and product should remain the student’s choice.

Summer learning is most meaningful when students see that education extends beyond worksheets and classrooms. By designing their own projects within teacher-guided expectations, students can continue building academic skills while discovering what they genuinely care about.

Dear Principal,

I believe students should be required to perform community service, as long as the requirement is flexible enough to fit their schedules and responsibilities. Service helps students understand the needs of others, connects our school to the community, and teaches skills that a classroom can't always provide.

To begin with, community service encourages students to become more caring and responsible citizens. Many of us spend most of our time worrying about grades, sports, jobs, or social plans. Those things matter, but we also need chances to notice that other people need help. A student who tutors elementary school children, for instance, sees how hard it can be to learn to read or work through a math problem. A high schooler may take reading for granted, but after helping a child sound out words or finish a homework assignment, that student gains a new appreciation for patience and education. Experiences like this can make us more thoughtful and compassionate.

Service also makes a real difference in our neighborhoods. A group of students picking up litter in a park may seem like a small effort, yet it can improve a space shared by children, families, and older residents. Students who volunteer at food drives, animal shelters, or senior centers can also help organizations that often have too few workers. If every student completed even a modest number of hours, the combined effort would add up quickly. Schools should prepare students for college and careers, but they should also prepare them to contribute to the places where they live.

Required service can also help students discover interests and talents they never knew they had. Someone who reluctantly starts tutoring might find out that he or she enjoys teaching. A student volunteering at an animal shelter might become curious about veterinary medicine. Along the way, students build practical skills such as communication, teamwork, planning, and problem-solving, all of which are useful in future jobs and relationships. Seen this way, community service is not just time taken away from our lives. It is an investment in our personal growth.

I understand that some students feel they are already overloaded with homework, jobs, family duties, and extracurricular activities. That concern is reasonable, which is why the requirement should not be excessive. The school could ask for a limited number of hours each semester and let students choose from a wide range of approved activities. Students with jobs or family obligations could be given flexible deadlines or the option to complete projects that fit with what they already do. The goal should be to make service meaningful, not to add needless stress.

For these reasons, I strongly support requiring community service for all students. A fair and flexible program would help us develop empathy, improve our community, and gain valuable experience. By making service part of our education, our school would show that success is not only about what we achieve for ourselves, but also about how we help others.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

When I was trying to decide whether to try out for the school soccer team or keep my weekends free for a part-time job, I asked my best friend first. She said I should definitely go for soccer because I loved it and I’d regret not trying. Then I asked my older cousin, who works and goes to community college. He told me the job would teach me responsibility and give me spending money for things I actually want. At first, I felt more confused because I got two different answers. But after thinking about both, I realized that each person pointed out something I cared about. That’s when I understood why asking multiple people can actually help you make a better choice.

One reason getting advice from different people helps is that no single person sees your whole situation. My friend cared about my happiness and knew how much I liked playing soccer, so she focused on that. My cousin cared about my future and independence, so he focused on money and building a resume. Neither of them was wrong, but they each only saw one part of my life. When I listened to both, I could weigh what mattered more to me: fun and passion or responsibility and cash. In the end, I chose soccer, but I also babysat on weeknights instead of taking the weekend job. That compromise came from hearing both perspectives.

Another reason is that people have different experiences, so they can warn you about things you never considered. Last year, I was deciding between two classes for my schedule. I asked three people. One told me the teacher for one class rarely gives homework, but the tests are hard. Another student said the same teacher is strict about phones. My guidance counselor told me the class would look better on a college application. If I had only asked one person, I would have known about the homework or the strict rules, but not both. With all that information, I knew what I was signing up for and could prepare instead of being surprised.

Sometimes people also ask for advice because they already have a gut feeling, and they want to see if anyone challenges it. When my friend wanted to quit band, she asked a bunch of us. Most of us said she should stay because she was a strong player, but one person said quitting might give her more time to sleep and focus on grades, which she was really worried about. That one different opinion made her pause and think about why she really wanted to leave. She ended up staying in band but dropping one other club. Getting different views helped her find a middle ground instead of making a rushed choice.

In the end, asking more than one person doesn’t mean you’ll get one perfect answer. Sometimes it makes things messier at first. But the different viewpoints help you see more of the picture. You learn about risks, benefits, and options you might not have thought of on your own. Then you can make a choice that fits more parts of your life, not just one person’s idea of what you should do.

When my cousin Dana was deciding between two college offers, she asked her father first. He urged her toward the state university, which was cheaper and only an hour from home. Her high school counselor, though, thought the smaller private school offered better advising in her intended field, nursing. A third voice, an older friend who had attended the private school, mentioned something neither adult had raised: the nursing program there guaranteed clinical placements in its first year, while the state school's students often waited until their second. Dana ended up choosing the private school, with a scholarship appeal in hand, and she says the decision felt solid precisely because she had heard the argument from three directions.

Her experience shows the most basic benefit of asking around. Any single adviser sees a situation through a narrow window. Parents tend to weigh safety and cost, friends tend to weigh social life and fun, and a professional in the field tends to weigh career outcomes. None of these views is wrong, but each is incomplete. Gathering several of them is a bit like assembling a map from separate surveyors, each of whom measured only the territory he knew best.

Multiple opinions also expose bias, including the kind advisers cannot see in themselves. A salesperson recommending a particular laptop may sincerely believe in it, yet the commission lurks in the background. A relative who urges you to stay in your hometown may be reacting partly to his own fear of losing you. When you hear the same suggestion from people with unrelated motives, you can trust it more. When one voice disagrees sharply with the rest, that disagreement is worth examining. It might reveal a blind spot in the majority, or it might reveal the outlier's agenda.

Then there is the matter of information itself. People know different things. Someone considering knee surgery might hear one orthopedist recommend operating immediately and another suggest six weeks of physical therapy first. The conflict can be unsettling, but it carries real value: it tells the patient that the question is not settled, that reasonable experts differ, and that further research or a third consultation is warranted. A person who consulted only the first surgeon would never know there was a choice to make.

Of course, more opinions are not automatically better. Ask ten people and you may drown in contradiction, or drift toward whichever answer you secretly wanted all along. Some people shop for approval rather than advice, polling friends until someone says yes. The practice works best when the person asking chooses advisers who differ in experience and temperament, listens for reasons rather than verdicts, and remembers that the final call belongs to them. An adviser who says "do this" offers less than one who explains what he would weigh and why.

Used that way, outside opinions do something subtle. They rarely hand over the answer. Instead, they sharpen the question. Dana did not simply pick the option that won a vote; her father's worry about debt pushed her to negotiate for aid, and her friend's detail about clinical placements gave her something concrete to value. Each conversation added a consideration she could weigh for herself.

In the end, a good decision is less about finding the one wise person than about widening what you can see before you commit. Several perspectives won't remove the risk from a hard choice, but they make it far less likely that the thing that undoes you is something you simply never heard about.

Although extracurricular activities can enrich a student’s education, schools should not require every student to participate in one. Sports teams, clubs, student government, and publications offer valuable opportunities to build friendships and develop leadership skills. However, making participation mandatory ignores the different responsibilities, interests, and personal circumstances students have outside the classroom. Schools should encourage involvement and make activities accessible, but they should not force every student to join.

First, many students already have significant obligations beyond school. Some students work part-time jobs to help their families pay bills or save for college. Others care for younger siblings while parents work late shifts. A student who spends several hours each afternoon at a job may not be able to attend soccer practice, yearbook meetings, or student council events. Requiring that student to add another commitment could create stress and lower academic performance. Education should help students succeed, not punish them for responsibilities they cannot control.

In addition, mandatory participation may cause students to join activities without genuine interest. Extracurricular programs are most successful when students choose them because they care about the activity. A student who loves writing may devote energy to the school newspaper, while a student interested in science may enjoy robotics club. In contrast, a student who is forced to join a club merely to meet a requirement may attend meetings reluctantly, contribute little, and take space from students who truly want to participate. Clubs depend on enthusiasm and teamwork; unwilling members can weaken the experience for everyone.

Some people argue that requiring an extracurricular activity would help shy or isolated students make friends. This can be true in some cases. A student who joins drama club or a basketball team may discover talents and relationships that would otherwise remain hidden. However, forcing participation is not the best way to create belonging. Students who are anxious, overwhelmed, or uncomfortable in group settings may feel even more isolated if they are required to attend an activity they did not choose. Instead, counselors and teachers should personally recommend programs that match students’ interests and should create low-pressure opportunities, such as occasional activity fairs or short trial sessions.

Furthermore, students can develop important skills outside official school activities. Volunteering at a community center, caring for family members, taking music lessons, participating in religious organizations, or pursuing independent art projects can all teach responsibility, communication, and perseverance. A school should recognize that learning does not happen only on campus or through an official club roster. If the goal is to help students become well-rounded citizens, schools should value these different forms of involvement.

Rather than imposing a requirement, the principal should invest in making extracurricular activities more welcoming and practical. The school could offer late buses, reduce participation fees, advertise clubs more clearly, and schedule some meetings before school or online. These changes would allow more students to participate voluntarily.

Extracurricular activities are valuable, but their value comes from choice and commitment. Students should be encouraged to explore sports, clubs, and leadership opportunities, yet they should also be free to balance school with work, family, and personal interests. A supportive school gives students opportunities without taking away their ability to choose.

Phones can also be helpful during larger emergencies by allowing students to receive important information and reassure worried family members. If phones are not allowed at school at all, students would lose an important way to communicate when they may need it most.

Policy 1 would also help students learn responsibility. In the real world, people are expected to manage technology without letting it interfere with work, school, or other responsibilities. Students should have the chance to practice those skills now. A rule that allows phones during free time but requires them to be off during class sets clear boundaries. It teaches students that there is an appropriate time and place for using a phone.

A total ban, on the other hand, may create more problems than it solves. Some students would probably still bring their phones secretly, especially if they need them before or after school. That could lead to arguments, confiscated phones, and unnecessary distrust between students and staff. Policy 1 is more practical because it recognizes that phones are already an important part of many students’ daily lives while still placing reasonable limits on their use.

Lunch and other free periods are also appropriate times for students to use their phones in positive ways. Students could listen to music, read, check messages from family, look at assignments, or set reminders for upcoming tests and deadlines. Sometimes a short break helps students relax and return to class feeling more focused. Phones can even be useful for taking a picture of homework instructions or quickly checking information for a project.

Of course, some people may worry that phones cause distractions or make cheating easier. Those are reasonable concerns, but Policy 1 addresses them by requiring phones to be turned off during class. Teachers would still be able to enforce the rule, and students who misuse their phones could face consequences. The solution is not to ban phones completely, but to set clear expectations and hold students accountable when they do not follow them.

In conclusion, Policy 1 provides the best balance between safety, responsibility, and learning. It allows students to stay connected when necessary, gives them useful choices during free time, and protects classroom instruction. I respectfully urge you to choose Policy 1.

A Concerned Student

As the debate surrounding the Electoral College continues to unfold, I am writing to express my support for retaining this institution as a means of electing the President of the United States. While some argue that the Electoral College is undemocratic and outdated, I firmly believe that it serves as a vital component of our federal system, ensuring that presidential candidates build broad national coalitions and engage with voters across diverse regions.

One of the primary criticisms leveled against the Electoral College is that it can lead to a situation where the winner of the national popular vote does not win the presidency, as occurred in 2000 and 2016. Critics, such as Bradford Plumer, argue that this outcome is inherently undemocratic and that the Electoral College should be abolished in favor of a popular vote system. However, this perspective overlooks the fact that the Electoral College was established as a compromise between election by Congress and election by popular vote, with the aim of balancing the interests of large and small states. By requiring candidates to secure a majority of electoral votes, the system ensures that successful candidates must demonstrate a broad base of support across multiple states, rather than simply relying on vote totals in densely populated urban areas.

In addition to preserving federalism, the Electoral College also helps to prevent the kind of regionalism that can arise when candidates focus solely on winning votes in specific areas. As Judge Richard A. Posner notes, the Electoral College forces candidates to build national coalitions, engaging with voters in both large and small states. This helps to promote a more nuanced understanding of the diverse needs and concerns of different regions, ultimately leading to more effective governance. Furthermore, the Electoral College produces a clear and decisive winner, avoiding the potential chaos of a nationwide popular-vote recount. By confining any disputed vote recounts to individual states, the system helps to ensure a smooth transition of power and maintain stability in the electoral process.

Some may argue that the Electoral College depresses voter turnout in safely Democratic or Republican states, as presidential campaigns tend to focus on a handful of swing states. However, this criticism ignores the fact that voters in these states still have a critical role to play in shaping the national debate and influencing the direction of the campaign. Moreover, the Electoral College provides an important incentive for candidates to engage with voters in states that might otherwise be overlooked, helping to ensure that the needs and concerns of these states are represented in the national dialogue.

In conclusion, while the Electoral College may have its flaws, I firmly believe that it remains a vital institution in American democracy. By preserving federalism, promoting national coalitions, and ensuring a clear and decisive winner, the Electoral College helps to safeguard the integrity of the electoral process and promote effective governance. Rather than abolishing the Electoral College, we should work to refine and improve it, exploring ways to address concerns around voter turnout and faithless electors while preserving the system's core benefits. Ultimately, the Electoral College remains an essential component of our democratic system, and it is crucial that we continue to support and defend it.

I’ll admit it: when the announcement crackled over the intercom, my first reaction was annoyance. Another requirement, another box to check. But after watching my classmates drift through the halls with earbuds in and eyes down, I’ve changed my mind. Requiring every student to join at least one extracurricular activity is not an overreach; it’s a necessary push toward belonging, growth, and real-world skills.

High school can be brutally isolating. Many students go from class to class, eat lunch alone, and head straight home. A mandatory activity breaks that cycle. Consider the quiet sophomore who would never try out for the school play on her own. Once she is required to choose something, she might end up painting sets for the drama club. There, she learns to use a drill, collaborates with seniors she never would have met, and suddenly has a reason to stay after school. That single connection can transform her entire experience. The same is true for the boy who joins the robotics team not because he loves engineering but because his friends did—and then discovers he has a gift for coding. Without the requirement, neither student would have taken the risk.

Extracurriculars also teach what classrooms often cannot. A group project in history class is temporary; a yearbook staff is a months-long commitment with real deadlines and a final product that hundreds of people will see. Students on the yearbook learn to manage their time, edit photos under pressure, and accept criticism when a layout is rejected. Student council members navigate budgets, negotiate with administrators, and learn that democracy is messy. An athlete on the cross-country team discovers that showing up to practice on a cold, rainy Tuesday matters even when no one is watching. These lessons—responsibility, resilience, teamwork—are exactly what colleges and employers say they want. Mandating participation ensures that every student, not just the naturally outgoing or ambitious ones, has access to them.

Of course, some argue that forcing students to join an activity ruins the spirit of volunteering. They say a reluctant participant will just sulk in the corner and bring down the group. That risk exists, but it is smaller than we fear. The requirement is not to love the activity; it is to show up. And showing up is often the hardest part. Once a student is in the room, surrounded by people working toward a common goal, enthusiasm can grow. I have seen it happen. A friend of mine joined the chess club only because he needed to fulfill the new rule. Within a month, he was staying late to analyze games and teaching openings to beginners. He didn’t need to be forced to love chess—he just needed a reason to walk through the door.

The principal’s decision may feel heavy-handed at first. But schools already require math, science, and physical education because we believe those subjects matter. We should treat involvement in a community the same way. By making extracurricular participation universal, we push students past their comfort zones and into spaces where they can fail safely, learn deeply, and discover who they are beyond a report card.
