I agree with the principal's decision, though I think its success depends on how generously the school defines "extracurricular." Required participation sounds like one more burden for students who already juggle homework, jobs, and family duties. But a school that asks every student to join something is really asking each of them to step outside the classroom and become part of a community, and that is worth the small cost.

Consider what happens in a school where participation is optional. The same faces fill the soccer field, the drama club, and the student council. Meanwhile, a large group of students goes home at 3:15 and is rarely seen again until the next morning. Some of them are shy. Some assume they have no talent worth showing. Others have never been invited. A requirement removes the excuse and the awkwardness at once. Nobody has to wonder whether they are "the kind of person" who joins things, because everyone does.

I have seen how this can change a person. My cousin spent his freshman year eating lunch alone and barely speaking in class. When his school nudged him toward the yearbook staff, he complained for weeks. Then he discovered he had a good eye for photographs. By spring he was running around the gym during pep rallies with a camera, trading jokes with seniors he would never have met otherwise. His grades went up, too, which surprised him more than anyone. Belonging gave him a reason to care about showing up.

That example points to a broader benefit: activities teach what textbooks cannot. A student on the debate team learns to build an argument and then hear it dismantled without taking it personally. A member of the robotics club learns that a project can fail six times before it works. Even a modest commitment, like helping organize a canned-food drive, teaches scheduling, cooperation, and follow-through. Employers and colleges say they value these traits, yet we rarely grade them.

Critics will say that forcing students into clubs defeats the purpose, since enthusiasm cannot be mandated. There is some truth in that. A student who sits through meetings resentfully gains little. But the requirement is only one activity, and the range of choices is wide. Chess, choir, recycling committee, intramural volleyball, tutoring younger children: surely something on that list will not feel like punishment. And many teenagers who begin out of obligation stay out of interest, the way people often come to like a sport only after they have been dragged to practice a few times.

The other fair worry is time. Students who work after school to help support their families cannot simply add a three-hour commitment. The principal should therefore build in flexibility, perhaps counting activities that meet during lunch or once a week, or crediting work in a community organization outside school. A rule that ignores real hardship would be unjust, but a rule with sensible exceptions would not.

In the end, school is supposed to prepare young people for more than tests. It should teach them how to work with others, how to try something unfamiliar, and how to find a place among people who are not already their friends. Requiring one activity is a modest step toward that goal. I would rather see a few students grumble in September and find a home by December than let hundreds drift through four years without ever feeling they were part of the school.

I agree that every student should participate in at least one extracurricular activity, although schools should offer enough variety and flexibility to make the requirement fair. Classes are essential, but they are not the only place where students learn. Activities after school can teach responsibility, cooperation, confidence, and practical skills that are difficult to develop through textbooks alone.

For many students, extracurricular activities provide a chance to discover abilities they did not know they had. A quiet student who rarely speaks in class might become an excellent photographer for the yearbook. Someone who struggles to stay focused during a long lecture may thrive on a soccer field, in a robotics club, or while helping organize a charity event. These experiences can change how students see themselves. When a student realizes that hard work helped the debate team win a competition or that their artwork improved the school newspaper, they gain confidence that can carry over into academic work.

Activities also teach students how to work with other people. In a classroom, students often complete individual assignments and receive grades based on their own performance. On a team, however, each person’s effort affects everyone else. A basketball player who skips practice lets teammates down. A student council member who does not finish a poster can make an entire event less successful. Students learn to communicate, solve disagreements, and keep commitments because real people are depending on them. Those are valuable lessons for future jobs, college group projects, and adult life.

Some people may argue that requiring extracurricular participation would create stress for students who already have heavy homework loads, jobs, or family responsibilities. This concern is reasonable. Not every student has the time or money to join an expensive travel team or attend meetings several evenings a week. That is why the policy should not be limited to traditional clubs and sports. Schools could allow students to fulfill the requirement through low-cost, flexible options such as library volunteering, tutoring younger students, helping with school events, joining a lunchtime club, or completing a community service project. Students who work to support their families could even receive credit for structured volunteer or leadership responsibilities connected to their workplace.

Requiring one activity would also encourage students to become more connected to their school. When students feel that they belong, they are more likely to attend regularly, care about school events, and treat classmates with respect. A student who plays in the band may attend football games to support friends. A student who joins the environmental club may meet peers from different grades whom they would never encounter in class. These connections can make a large school feel less anonymous and more welcoming.

The purpose of a requirement should not be to fill every student’s schedule or force everyone to become an athlete. It should be to make sure that each student has an opportunity to contribute, explore an interest, and belong to a community. With flexible choices and support for students with busy lives, requiring at least one extracurricular activity would help students grow in ways that grades alone cannot measure.

Driverless cars should continue to be developed because they have the potential to make transportation safer, more efficient, and more accessible. Although the technology still has serious limitations, the benefits are too important to ignore. Instead of abandoning autonomous vehicles because of current risks, companies and lawmakers should improve the technology carefully and create strong safety rules before these cars become common on public roads.

The strongest argument for driverless cars is that they could prevent many traffic accidents. According to the article, human error causes more than 90 percent of crashes. Drivers may text while driving, fall asleep, speed, or get behind the wheel while impaired. A computer does not become tired, distracted, or drunk. Autonomous vehicles use laser radar, cameras, GPS, and sensors to detect obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals. If these systems work reliably, they could react to dangerous situations more consistently than many human drivers. Fewer crashes would mean fewer injuries and deaths, and it could also lower insurance costs for families.

Driverless cars could also help people who cannot easily drive themselves. Elderly people, people with disabilities, and others who are unable to operate a vehicle could gain greater independence. Rather than depending on relatives, public buses, or expensive taxi services, they could travel to medical appointments, jobs, stores, and social events. This change would give many people more freedom and make communities easier to navigate.

In addition, autonomous public transportation could reduce waste. Sergey Brin imagines driverless transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today’s cars. If fewer people needed to own individual vehicles, cities might have less traffic congestion and fewer parking lots. Land currently used for parking could become housing, parks, or businesses. Reducing fuel use would also benefit the environment.

Still, critics are right to point out that driverless cars are not ready to replace human drivers everywhere. Sensors may struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or construction zones without clear lane markings. Software can malfunction, and connected vehicles could face cybersecurity threats. The article also explains that people using semi-autonomous features may lose focus and react slowly when they suddenly need to take control. These dangers show that car companies must not rush the technology onto roads simply to make a profit.

However, these concerns are reasons for caution, not reasons to stop development. Autonomous vehicles should be tested in many weather conditions and difficult traffic situations before they are widely used. Manufacturers must create backup systems, protect cars from hacking, and clearly explain when a human driver must remain alert. Lawmakers also need to establish rules about who is responsible when an accident occurs: the owner, the automaker, or the software developer.

Driverless cars offer a promising solution to problems caused by human mistakes, limited mobility, traffic, and fuel use. The technology must be developed responsibly, but its potential to save lives and improve daily life makes continued progress worthwhile.

While I recognize that this initiative is rooted in a sincere desire to promote academic excellence, I strongly urge you to reconsider this change. Excluding students who maintain a C average will inadvertently harm the very individuals who benefit most from school programs, ultimately undermining student engagement, well-being, and academic progress.

First and foremost, extracurricular activities often serve as the primary motivation for students to stay focused and attend school regularly. For many students who currently maintain a C average, earning those grades represents a genuine, daily struggle with demanding coursework. Rather than inspiring these students to reach a B average, an abrupt increase in the eligibility standard risks creating a sense of futility. When the standard feels unattainable, students are more likely to give up entirely. Sports, musical ensembles, and academic clubs provide essential structure, discipline, and accountability. Coaches and club advisors frequently check in on grades and instill habits of time management. Removing students from these supportive networks will weaken their connection to school, likely causing their academic performance to decline further.

Furthermore, extracurricular participation is vital to emotional well-being and character development. High school should nurture the whole person, not merely measure standardized academic output. Athletics and clubs offer students healthy outlets for stress, opportunities to develop leadership abilities, and a profound sense of belonging. For a student who may not excel academically, excelling on the soccer field, on the debate stage, or in the art club provides critical self-esteem. Stripping these opportunities away isolates struggling students, leaving them with fewer positive influences and more unstructured time outside of school, which can lead to negative behaviors.

Rather than enacting an exclusionary policy, the administration should consider proactive, supportive measures. If the goal is to elevate academic standards, the school could implement mandatory study halls or peer-tutoring sessions for athletes and club members whose grades dip toward a C. This approach reinforces the importance of scholarship without severing the positive ties that keep students invested in their education. Conditional eligibility allows students to work toward improvement while remaining part of a team that holds them accountable.

In conclusion, setting high expectations is admirable, but raising the participation threshold to a B average will marginalize a significant portion of our student body. Extracurricular activities are not merely privileges to be enjoyed by high achievers; they are essential educational tools that foster resilience, community, and personal growth. I respectfully ask that you maintain the current policy and instead focus on providing the academic resources students need to achieve their full potential.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

In recent years, distance learning has developed from an emergency solution into a useful educational choice. Although some people believe students need to attend school in person for social growth and participation, students can still benefit greatly from having the option to learn from home. When it is organized well, online and video-conferencing classes offer flexibility, improve access to education, and help students learn in ways that fit their individual needs.

One important benefit of distance learning is flexibility. Students do not have to follow the same rigid schedule every day or spend time commuting to school. This can be especially helpful for students with busy extracurricular schedules, family responsibilities, or health concerns. For example, a student recovering from surgery could continue attending lessons from home rather than missing several weeks of class. In the same way, a competitive athlete traveling for tournaments could join class from a hotel room and stay caught up with assignments. By removing the requirement of physical attendance, schools can help students continue learning even when life circumstances make it difficult to be in the classroom.

Distance learning can also make school more accessible. Students who live far from their schools, have disabilities, or struggle with social anxiety may find it easier to participate from home. Online classes often include features such as live captions, recorded lessons, and screen sharing, which can support students with hearing impairments or difficulties processing information quickly. For instance, a student with a weakened immune system might need to avoid crowded classrooms during an illness outbreak. With an online option, that student could still listen to instruction, complete assignments, and remain connected to classmates without risking their health. Traditional classrooms cannot always meet every student's needs in the same way.

In addition, learning from home can allow for more personalized instruction. Many online platforms let students pause, rewind, and replay recorded lessons. In a regular classroom, if a student does not understand a concept the first time it is explained, the class may move on before the student can catch up. At home, however, the student can review the explanation until it makes sense. Some students may also focus better in a quieter home environment, away from crowded hallways and distractions from classmates. Teachers can use chat boxes, polls, and breakout rooms as well, giving quieter students different ways to ask questions or share ideas.

Of course, distance learning has challenges. Not every student has reliable internet access, and some students may have trouble staying motivated without a teacher physically nearby. However, schools can address these problems by lending devices, providing internet support, and setting clear expectations for attendance and assignments. Teachers can also check in regularly with students who need extra guidance.

Overall, students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home as an option. It should not completely replace in-person learning, since face-to-face interaction remains valuable. Still, distance learning gives students greater flexibility, makes education more accessible, and allows them to learn at a pace that works for them. Schools should continue offering these opportunities so that more students can succeed in ways that fit their lives and needs.

By imposing an after-school requirement, these students are forced to choose between fulfilling their obligations and facing penalties at school. This is not only unfair but also neglects the fact that not all students have equal amounts of discretionary time. True equity requires recognizing and respecting these differences.

Furthermore, mandatory participation can have severe consequences for students' mental health and academic performance. Today's adolescents already face immense pressure, with heavy workloads, hours of homework, and preparation for standardized tests. Adding another obligatory activity to their schedule can lead to sleep deprivation, chronic stress, and a decline in overall well-being. Extracurricular activities are meant to be a source of enjoyment and relief, not an additional burden. When students are forced to participate, these activities lose their appeal and become just another stressful commitment.

When students are coerced into joining, organizations like the student council or school newspaper become filled with disengaged and resentful participants. This not only affects the morale of the group but also places an undue burden on passionate members, who must compensate for the lack of enthusiasm. The unique value of extracurricular activities lies in their ability to bring people together who share common interests and passions. By removing the element of personal choice, we risk diluting the experience for everyone involved.

In light of these concerns, I believe that the administration should reconsider its approach. Rather than resorting to mandates, the focus should be on removing barriers to access and promoting a diverse range of appealing programs. Important decisions are rarely improved by relying on a single viewpoint. Whether a person is choosing a college, accepting a job, making a medical decision, or solving a conflict with a friend, seeking multiple opinions can lead to a better choice. Different people notice different risks, offer different experiences, and challenge assumptions that might otherwise go unquestioned. Although advice should not replace personal responsibility, hearing more than one perspective gives a person stronger information and greater confidence in the final decision.

First, multiple opinions can reveal details that one adviser may overlook. Every person has limited knowledge and personal biases. For example, a student deciding between two colleges might first ask a guidance counselor, who can explain graduation rates, financial aid, and academic programs. The student could also speak with current students, who may describe the quality of dormitories, campus social life, or how easy it is to get help from professors. Parents might focus on costs and safety, while a teacher might consider which school best fits the student’s academic interests. No single person is likely to know all of these things. By combining the information, the student can make a choice based on a fuller picture rather than on one impressive brochure or one person’s preference.

Seeking several opinions also helps people identify bias. Advice is often influenced by personal experience. A friend who loves a particular company may strongly encourage someone to apply there because the workplace suited that friend’s personality. However, another former employee may explain that the same company requires long hours and offers little flexibility. Neither opinion is necessarily wrong; the workplace may be excellent for someone who enjoys a fast-paced environment but frustrating for someone who values free time. Hearing both sides allows the job seeker to compare the advice with personal priorities instead of assuming that one person’s experience will be universal.

In addition, discussing a problem with different people can encourage more careful thinking. When someone hears only advice that agrees with what he or she already wants to do, it is easy to make a quick decision without considering consequences. A person thinking about buying an expensive car, for instance, may ask a friend who is enthusiastic about cars. That friend may emphasize style, speed, and new technology. A financially cautious relative might instead ask about monthly payments, insurance, repairs, and savings goals. The second opinion may not prevent the purchase, but it can lead the buyer to choose a less expensive model or wait until the purchase is affordable. In this way, competing viewpoints do not merely create confusion; they can force a person to examine the decision more responsibly.

Of course, asking many people does not mean following every recommendation. Too much advice can become overwhelming, and some advisers may lack relevant knowledge. The decision-maker must evaluate the credibility of each source and consider which advice fits the situation. Still, gathering several thoughtful opinions is usually wiser than depending on one voice alone.

Ultimately, multiple opinions improve decisions because they provide broader information, expose bias, and encourage reflection. The final choice belongs to the individual, but that choice is likely to be stronger when it has been tested against more than one perspective.

Dear Principal Johnson,

I am writing in response to the proposed policy that would require students to maintain at least a B average to participate in sports and other activities. I understand that the goal is to encourage academic success, and I respect that. However, I strongly believe this policy would do more harm than good, especially for the many students who currently earn a C average.

First, activities often give students the very motivation they need to stay in school and try their best. For many students, a sport, a club, or the school band is the reason they look forward to coming each day. A student who earns a C may not be failing; he or she may simply find certain subjects difficult. If we take away the one thing that makes school enjoyable, that student may lose interest altogether. Instead of working harder, some students might give up, skip class, or even drop out. A C average is a passing grade, and students who meet that standard should not be punished for it.

Second, extracurricular activities teach skills that cannot be learned from a textbook. Team sports teach cooperation, discipline, and leadership. Drama and music teach creativity and confidence. Student government teaches responsibility and public speaking. These are exactly the qualities colleges and employers want to see. Students who are cut off from these opportunities because of a grade of 82 instead of 85 would lose valuable experience that could shape their futures. A single number on a report card does not measure a student's whole potential.

Third, the policy would be unfair to students who face challenges outside the classroom. Some students care for younger siblings, work part-time jobs, or have learning differences that make earning a B much harder than it is for others. These students may work just as hard as a student with straight A's, yet their results look different. Requiring a B average would reward students who have easier circumstances and penalize those who are already struggling. Activities can also be a safe, supervised place for students who might otherwise have nowhere to go after school.

Finally, there are better ways to encourage good grades. The school could offer free tutoring, study halls before practices, or mentoring from older students and teachers. Coaches and advisors could check progress regularly, and students who fall below a C could be placed on a probation period with extra academic support before losing their place on a team. These solutions would help students improve rather than simply shutting them out. A policy that supports students will be far more effective than one that excludes them.

In conclusion, requiring a B average would remove motivation, limit important learning experiences, and treat students unfairly. I agree that academics must come first, but raising the requirement is not the best way to achieve that. I respectfully ask you to keep the current standard, or to consider support programs that help students raise their grades while staying involved. Extracurricular activities can enrich students' lives, build friendships, and teach useful skills. Sports teams encourage cooperation, student council develops leadership, and yearbook staff members practice responsibility and creativity. Even so, I believe schools should strongly encourage participation without requiring every student to join. A mandatory rule would overlook real differences in students' lives, could make activities less meaningful, and might add stress for students who are already stretched thin.

First, many students have responsibilities outside school that make regular participation hard. Some look after younger siblings while their parents work. Others hold part-time jobs to help their families pay bills or to save for college. A student who works several evenings a week may not be able to make it to soccer practice, drama rehearsals, or club meetings. Requiring that student to join an activity would force an unfair choice between family obligations and a school rule. Responsibility does not only happen on campus, after all. Helping at home or holding a job can teach maturity, time management, and commitment just as well.

Activities are also most valuable when students pick them because they truly care about them. A student who loves writing may pour energy into the school newspaper, while another may be thrilled to join the robotics club. That enthusiasm strengthens the group and helps each student discover new talents. A student who is pushed into a club, on the other hand, may show up only to check off a requirement. He or she might contribute very little, feel resentful, and take a spot that a more interested student would have enjoyed. Participation should come from curiosity and motivation, not from fear of punishment or a missing graduation credit.

Finally, a mandatory policy could increase stress. Students already juggle homework, tests, projects, and plans for the future. For those taking difficult classes or dealing with anxiety, a required after-school commitment could become overwhelming. Instead of helping them become well-rounded, the rule might leave them exhausted and hurt their grades. A student who needs the afternoon to study, rest, or get tutoring should not be seen as less connected to the school than a classmate with more free time.

None of this means schools should give up on extracurricular programs. They should offer a wide range of affordable, welcoming activities and make sure everyone knows how to sign up. Club fairs, late buses, waived fees for students who need financial help, and flexible options like occasional service projects or school events would all make involvement easier. These steps open doors without forcing students into commitments they cannot manage.

Extracurricular activities are valuable opportunities, but an opportunity is not the same as an obligation. Students should be encouraged to try sports, clubs, and leadership roles, yet they should keep the freedom to decide how to spend their time. A school that respects its students' different interests and responsibilities will build a stronger, more supportive community than one that expects everyone to participate in the same way.

When my school announced summer projects last year, half my friends got a packet of worksheets and the other half got to pick a topic. The kids with choice actually talked about what they made. The rest just complained. I think summer projects should be student-designed, with some teacher guidance, because students are more likely to actually learn when they care about what they’re doing.

First, student-designed projects let people go deeper into things they already like. For example, my friend Marcus loves fishing. If a teacher assigns a generic research paper on a state’s economy, Marcus will do the minimum. But if he can design a project around fish habitats, he might test water samples at the lake, keep a log of what he catches, and look up why some fish disappear in summer. That’s real science, and he’s not being forced; he’s curious. Last summer I chose to interview my grandmother about her immigration from Mexico for a family history project. I recorded six hours of stories, made a timeline, and even scanned old photos. I never would have done that for a worksheet.

Second, teacher-designed summer work often becomes busywork. I understand why teachers worry that students won’t challenge themselves if left alone. But a packet of math problems or a required book with a five-paragraph essay doesn’t always keep learning alive. Most students copy answers in the last week of August or skim the book online. The work gets done, but it doesn’t mean anything. If the goal is to keep our brains active, a project we design with a clear plan works better because we have a reason to finish besides a grade.

Of course, student-designed doesn’t mean no rules. Teachers should still require a proposal, a timeline, and maybe a final presentation or reflection. That structure stops the “I’ll just build a video game in my head and call it learning” problem. For instance, my English teacher asked us to submit one paragraph explaining our project and one check-in email in July. It was simple, but it kept me on track. A totally open summer assignment might let some kids avoid reading or writing, but with a few checkpoints, student choice can still include those skills. A student who loves basketball could read a biography of a player and write a training log, which involves reading and math without feeling like a punishment.

Some might say teachers know what skills we need to practice, so their projects are more balanced. That’s partly true. But students don’t stop needing to practice skills when they choose; they just practice them in a context they care about. A teacher can look at a student’s project idea and say, “Add a written reflection,” or “Include data from three sources.” That way the project stays challenging but still belongs to the student.

In the end, summer should not feel like a longer version of school. If schools require projects, they should let students design them with teacher check-ins. We’re more likely to read, write, build, and investigate when the question comes from us. That’s the kind of learning that sticks past September.

I am writing to express my concern about the proposed policy requiring students to maintain at least a B average in order to participate in sports and other activities. While I understand the desire to encourage academic excellence, I believe this change would do more harm than good, especially for the many students who currently have a C average. Instead of motivating students, such a strict requirement may discourage them and take away opportunities that could actually help them improve.

First, extracurricular activities often provide the structure and support that struggling students need. A student with a C average may be working hard but facing challenges in one or two subjects. If that student is also on a sports team or involved in a club, those activities give them a reason to stay organized, manage their time, and remain connected to school. Taking away that involvement because they have not reached a B average would remove a powerful source of motivation. For many students, practice schedules and team responsibilities teach discipline that carries over into the classroom. Removing that structure could lead to lower grades, not higher ones.

Second, activities offer a sense of belonging that is especially important for students who do not excel academically. Not every student finds success in the classroom, but they may find it on the field, in the art room, or on stage. These experiences build confidence and a positive identity. When a school tells a student they cannot participate because of their grades, it sends the message that only one kind of success matters. That can lead to frustration, disengagement, and even dropping out. A C average is still a passing average, and it should not be treated as a failure that disqualifies a student from the full school experience.

Finally, a rigid B average requirement does not account for individual circumstances. Students learn at different paces and face different obstacles outside of school. Some students with C averages may be making significant improvement from previous terms, yet the policy would still punish them. A more effective approach would be to provide academic support for students who are struggling, such as tutoring or study halls, while allowing them to remain in activities. Schools could also use a probation system that gives students a chance to raise their grades without immediately losing participation.

In conclusion, I respectfully urge you to reconsider this policy change. Extracurricular activities are not a privilege reserved only for high achievers; they are an essential part of education that helps all students grow. Rather than excluding students with C averages, we should support them and recognize that their involvement in activities can be a path toward improvement.

Sincerely,  
A concerned student

When people have an important decision to make, it can be helpful to ask more than one person for advice. One person may notice something that another person misses. Also, different people have different experiences, so they may give advice from different points of view. Even though a person should still make their own final decision, listening to multiple opinions can help them understand the situation better and avoid making a choice too quickly.

For example, imagine a student deciding whether to join an after-school sports team. The student might ask a close friend who is already on the team. That friend may talk about how fun the practices are, how the team members support each other, and how exciting the games can be. However, the friend may not mention how much time the team takes because they are used to the busy schedule. If the student also asks a parent, the parent might bring up questions about homework, transportation, and whether the student will still have enough time to sleep. A teacher or counselor might add another opinion by explaining that sports can improve confidence and help students make friends, but that the student should be organized with assignments. By hearing all of these opinions, the student can make a more realistic decision instead of only focusing on the fun parts.

Seeking multiple opinions can also help someone recognize possible problems. Sometimes, when people really want something, they only pay attention to advice that agrees with what they already think. This can lead to a bad choice. For instance, if someone wants to spend all of their saved money on a new phone, their friends might say it is a great idea because the phone has cool features. But a sibling or parent might remind them that they may need money later for school supplies, clothes, or an unexpected expense. The person may still decide to buy the phone, but they could choose a less expensive model or wait until they have saved more money. In that case, the extra opinion does not ruin their plan. It helps them make a smarter version of the plan.

Different opinions are especially useful because people have different knowledge. A friend may understand someone’s personality well, while a teacher may know more about college or careers. A parent may have experience with money and responsibilities. None of these people will have every answer, but together they can give a fuller picture. It is like looking at an object from several sides instead of only one side.

Of course, getting too many opinions can sometimes be confusing. People may disagree, and the person asking for advice might feel pressured. That is why it is important to listen carefully but not let other people make the decision for you. The best choice depends on a person’s own goals, values, and situation.

Overall, asking more than one person for advice can lead to better decisions because it gives someone new information, helps them see risks, and shows different viewpoints. By considering several opinions and then thinking for themselves, people are more likely to make choices they will feel good about later.

When facing an important decision, people often turn to others for advice. Although it can be comforting to rely on one trusted friend or advisor, seeking several opinions usually leads to a better choice. Different viewpoints can reveal useful information, expose possible risks, and reduce the influence of personal bias. As a result, the final decision is often more balanced and informed.

One major benefit of asking more than one person is that it gives the decision-maker a wider range of information. People have different experiences, values, and areas of knowledge, so they may notice different parts of the same situation. For example, someone considering a job offer could speak with a former manager about opportunities for advancement, a friend who works in the same field about the company’s culture, and a relative who understands finances about the salary and benefits. A manager may focus on whether the job will build valuable skills, while a friend may know that employees are overworked or unhappy. The relative might point out that a higher salary does not necessarily make up for weak health insurance or an expensive commute. Looking at all of these opinions helps the person see the offer more clearly.

Multiple opinions can also uncover problems that might otherwise be ignored. One person may be excited about an idea and focus only on its advantages. Another person may be more cautious and notice practical challenges. For instance, someone hoping to open a small restaurant could ask a successful restaurant owner, an accountant, and a frequent customer for advice. The owner might explain how difficult it is to manage employees and work long hours. The accountant could warn about costs such as permits, insurance, equipment, and taxes. Meanwhile, the customer might stress the importance of a convenient location, reasonable prices, and appealing food. None of these viewpoints alone gives a complete answer, but together they provide a realistic picture. With that information, the future owner could choose a better location, create a more careful budget, or save extra money for emergencies.

Seeking advice from several people also helps reduce bias. Both the advisor and the person making the decision may have personal preferences that affect their judgment. For example, a parent may encourage a student to attend a nearby university because the parent wants the student close to home. A friend may recommend a different school because of its exciting social life, while a teacher may care most about academic programs and reputation. If the student listened to only one person, the choice might reflect that advisor’s priorities instead of the student’s needs. By comparing different opinions, the student can decide which factors matter most, such as cost, academic opportunities, distance from home, or campus environment.

Of course, asking too many people for advice can become confusing. A person may hear so many conflicting suggestions that making a decision feels even harder. However, this does not mean that consultation is unhelpful. It simply means that advice should come from a small group of people who have relevant experience and who can offer honest perspectives.

In the end, seeking multiple opinions helps people make stronger choices because it broadens their understanding, reveals hidden risks, and balances biased or emotional advice. Whether someone is choosing a career, buying a car, selecting a college, or starting a business, listening to several thoughtful voices can provide valuable clarity before acting.

Summer projects should be primarily student-designed because students are more likely to learn deeply when they can connect academic skills to their own interests, questions, and communities. Teachers should still provide clear expectations, deadlines, and assessment criteria, but they should not prescribe the same project for every student. A well-designed student-choice project can prevent learning loss while also building independence, curiosity, and responsibility.

First, allowing students to choose their projects increases motivation. During the school year, students often complete assignments because they are required to do so. Summer, however, is supposed to provide a break from the normal routine. If a student receives a lengthy teacher-designed packet about topics that do not interest them, the assignment may feel like punishment rather than learning. In contrast, a student who loves sports might investigate the mathematics of baseball statistics, while a student interested in animals could volunteer at a shelter and keep a journal about animal care. Both students would practice research, writing, and analysis, but they would do so through subjects they genuinely enjoy. Interest makes students more likely to spend time on a project and produce thoughtful work.

Student-designed projects also teach valuable life skills. In college and in many careers, people are often expected to identify a problem, set goals, manage time, and complete work with limited supervision. A summer project can help students practice these abilities. For example, a student interested in local history could decide to interview older residents, visit a museum, and create a short documentary or presentation. To finish the project, the student would need to plan interviews, organize notes, evaluate sources, and meet a final deadline. These are skills that cannot always be developed through a uniform worksheet.

In addition, student-designed projects can make learning more connected to the real world. A teacher-designed assignment may ask every student to read the same novel or solve the same group of equations. Those activities can be useful, but they do not always reflect the different experiences and needs of students. A student who is concerned about pollution in a nearby park, for instance, could collect litter data, research recycling policies, and write a proposal to the town council. This project would include science, mathematics, persuasive writing, and civic engagement. It would also show the student that academic learning can help solve meaningful problems.

Some people argue that teacher-designed projects are fairer because they ensure that every student completes work at the same academic level. However, fairness does not require identical assignments. Teachers can create a common rubric that requires all projects to include research, evidence, reflection, and a final product. They can also approve proposals before summer begins and offer several suggested topics for students who need help choosing. This structure would maintain academic standards without eliminating student choice.

Ultimately, summer projects should be student-designed within a teacher-guided framework. When students have ownership over what they study, they are more engaged, more creative, and more likely to continue learning beyond the classroom. Rather than assigning one project to everyone, schools should give students the opportunity to turn their individual interests into meaningful academic experiences.

Driverless cars are coming whether people are ready or not, and I think they should keep being developed. The article shows that there are some real problems, but the benefits are too big to ignore, and the problems are the kind that testing and time can fix.

The biggest reason I support driverless cars is safety. The article says human error causes over 90 percent of traffic accidents. A lot of that comes from things like texting, being drowsy, or driving while impaired. Those are all things a computer doesn't do. A driverless car doesn't get tired after a long day or look down at its phone. If most crashes come from people making bad choices, then taking people out of the driver's seat could save a lot of lives. Fewer crashes would also mean lower insurance costs, which would help families pay less.

Another good reason is that these cars could help people who can't drive. The article mentions elderly and disabled passengers, and I think this is really important. Right now, someone who can't drive might have to depend on other people for every trip to the doctor or the grocery store. A driverless car could give them freedom and let them go places on their own. That is something regular cars can't offer them.

There is also the environmental side. Sergey Brin imagines driverless public transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. If fewer people needed to own cars, cities wouldn't need so many parking lots, and less fuel would be burned. That could be good for both the planet and for crowded cities.

Of course, the article also gives good reasons for people to be worried. Sensors can have trouble in heavy rain, snow, fog, or construction zones where the lanes aren't marked. That is a serious issue because weather and construction happen all the time. The software could also have glitches or be hacked. Another concern is that in semi-autonomous cars, a person is supposed to take over in an emergency, but studies show people stop paying attention when the computer is driving. I can see how that would happen, because it's hard to stay focused when you aren't doing anything. There is also the question of who is responsible in a crash: the owner, the software maker, or the automaker.

Even though these concerns are serious, I don't think they are good enough reasons to stop developing the cars. Most of them are technical problems, and technology gets better with testing. Engineers can keep improving the sensors so they work in bad weather, and they can strengthen the software against hackers. The attention problem could be solved by building fully driverless cars so a human never has to jump in at the last second. The legal question is harder, but laws change all the time when new technology shows up. Lawmakers can decide who is responsible, just like they did with other inventions. Human drivers already cause a huge number of accidents, so waiting for driverless cars to be perfect means more people get hurt in the meantime.

I am writing to share my opinion about whether students should be required to perform community service. After thinking about it and talking with my friends, I believe that our school should require it, as long as the requirement is reasonable and students get some choice in how they complete it.

Some of my friends already do community service, and I have seen how much it helps. One friend tutors elementary school kids at the library on Thursdays. She told me that one of the kids she works with used to hate reading, but now he asks her to pick out new books with him. That is a real change in a kid's life, and it only took an hour or two a week. Another group of my friends cleans up litter at the park near our school. Before they started, there was trash all over the playground. Now little kids can actually play there without stepping on broken glass or wrappers. These are small things, but they make our town a better place.

I also think service teaches students things we do not learn in a classroom. When you tutor someone, you have to be patient and explain things in different ways. When you work on a team picking up litter, you have to cooperate and actually do the work instead of just talking. These skills help later when we have jobs. Colleges and employers also like to see that a student has done something for other people, so a requirement could help students who might not have thought about doing service on their own.

I do understand the other side. Some of my friends say that community service takes too much time. They play sports, have jobs, take care of younger brothers and sisters, or have a lot of homework. The phenomenon known as the "summer slide"—the documented loss of academic skills and knowledge over the extended vacation—has prompted many schools to institute mandatory summer projects. While the goal of keeping young minds engaged during the break is commendable, the execution of these assignments often dictates their success. To foster meaningful intellectual engagement and long-term academic growth, summer projects should be student-designed rather than teacher-designed. Granting learners the autonomy to direct their own summer studies cultivates intrinsic motivation, develops vital executive functioning skills, and transforms education into an authentic, personal pursuit.

First and foremost, student-designed projects overcome the barrier of student resistance by tapping into intrinsic motivation. When teachers assign rigid, standardized tasks over the break, students frequently perceive them as punitive busywork, completing them hastily just days before the autumn term begins. Conversely, when students possess agency over their topics, their work stems from genuine curiosity. For example, a student fascinated by marine biology might choose to design a study on local watershed pollutants, while an aspiring programmer might develop a simple mobile application. Because these undertakings align with individual passions, students are far more likely to invest sustained effort and creative energy throughout the summer months, counteracting academic regression through genuine enthusiasm rather than coerced compliance.

Furthermore, the process of designing an independent project instills critical real-world competencies that prescriptive assignments fail to teach. A teacher-designed project typically supplies the thesis, the methodology, the timeline, and the rubric. While convenient, this approach deprives students of the chance to practice executive functioning and project management. In contrast, conceptualizing an assignment from scratch requires a learner to identify a problem, delineate a realistic scope, establish deadlines, and locate appropriate resources. Navigating these organizational challenges mirrors the demands of university research and professional careers, cultivating resilience, time management, and intellectual self-reliance.

Critics often contend that teacher-designed projects are necessary to guarantee academic rigor and ensure uniform standards across a grade level. Without top-down parameters, skeptics argue, students might choose trivial topics or produce low-quality work. However, autonomy does not necessitate an absence of standards. Schools can easily maintain rigor by providing an overarching evaluative framework—requiring, for instance, a formal research proposal, regular progress logs, and a final presentation—while still leaving the subject and format entirely in the student’s hands. Rigor is not defined by a one-size-fits-all worksheet, but by the depth of thought and execution a student demonstrates.

Ultimately, summer break offers a unique respite from the standardized constraints of the traditional classroom calendar. Requiring students to execute identical, teacher-dictated assignments during this period squanders an ideal opportunity for independent exploration. By empowering students to design their own summer projects, schools not only prevent learning loss but also cultivate lifelong learners who view education not as a series of teacher-imposed obligations, but as an ongoing, self-directed adventure.

The debate over whether summer projects should be teacher-designed or student-designed has sparked intense discussion among educators and students alike. While some argue that teacher-designed projects ensure a consistent level of academic rigor, others claim that student-designed projects foster creativity and autonomy. In my opinion, summer projects should be student-designed, as this approach promotes self-directed learning, increases motivation, and allows students to explore their passions.

Firstly, student-designed projects encourage self-directed learning, which is an essential skill in today's fast-paced, ever-changing world. When students are given the freedom to design their own projects, they must take ownership of their learning, setting goals, and deadlines, and seeking out resources and support as needed. This autonomy allows students to develop a sense of agency and responsibility, which is critical for success in academics and beyond. For instance, a student interested in environmental science might design a project to investigate the impact of local pollution on wildlife, conducting research, collecting data, and analyzing results. This type of project enables students to delve deeper into a subject that genuinely interests them, leading to a more engaging and meaningful learning experience.

Secondly, student-designed projects increase motivation and engagement. When students are allowed to pursue their passions, they are more likely to be invested in their learning, as they are able to explore topics that genuinely interest them. This intrinsic motivation leads to a more enjoyable and productive learning experience, as students are driven to learn and create, rather than simply completing a mandated assignment. For example, a student who loves music might design a project to compose and record an album, exploring the technical and creative aspects of music production. By allowing students to pursue their interests, educators can tap into their natural curiosity and enthusiasm, leading to a more motivated and inspired learner.

Finally, student-designed projects provide an opportunity for students to develop a range of essential skills, including critical thinking, problem-solving, and communication. As students work on their projects, they must navigate obstacles, make decisions, and reflect on their progress, developing a sense of resilience and perseverance. Moreover, student-designed projects allow educators to assess students' learning in a more nuanced and comprehensive way, as they can evaluate not only the final product but also the process and journey that led to its creation. For instance, a student who designs a project to create a documentary film must research, script, film, and edit their work, demonstrating a range of skills, from research and writing to cinematography and storytelling.

In conclusion, while teacher-designed projects may provide a sense of structure and accountability, student-designed projects offer a more effective and engaging way to promote learning during the summer months. By giving students the freedom to design their own projects, educators can foster self-directed learning, increase motivation, and allow students to explore their passions. As we continue to navigate the complexities of education, it is essential that we prioritize student autonomy, creativity, and agency, providing students with the skills and support they need to succeed in an ever-changing world.

Dear Principal,

I believe the school should adopt Policy 1, allowing students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times, while requiring them to be turned off during class. This policy recognizes that phones can be useful tools and important safety devices without allowing them to interfere with learning. A complete ban may sound simpler, but it would be difficult to enforce and would create unnecessary problems for students and families.

First, students often need phones before and after school for safety and communication. Many students walk home, ride public transportation, participate in sports, or wait for rides from parents and guardians. A phone allows them to contact family members if practice ends early, a bus is late, or an emergency occurs. Without phones at school, students might have no easy way to reach a parent when plans change. Parents also benefit from knowing that their children can contact them safely when necessary.

Second, allowing phone use during free times can make the school day more practical and enjoyable without harming class instruction. During lunch, students may want to check messages from family, coordinate rides, look up club information, or use school-approved apps. Phones can also help students organize their schedules by setting reminders for assignments, practices, meetings, and deadlines. These uses are reasonable when they occur outside instructional time. Students are more likely to respect rules when the rules are balanced rather than overly restrictive.

Most importantly, Policy 1 protects learning by clearly requiring phones to be off during class. Teachers should not have to compete with notifications, games, or social media for students’ attention. The policy could include consequences for students who use a phone during instruction, such as having the phone collected until the end of the day or requiring a parent to pick it up after repeated violations. Clear consequences would make expectations fair and consistent. Students would understand that phones are permitted as a privilege during free time, not as a distraction in the classroom.

Some people may argue that a total ban would prevent cyberbullying, cheating, and distractions. However, banning phones entirely would not solve these problems. Cyberbullying can occur before and after school, and cheating can happen with many other tools. Instead of taking phones away from every responsible student, the school should teach digital citizenship and address misuse directly. Teachers can monitor testing situations, and administrators can investigate reports of bullying. A policy that focuses on responsible behavior is more effective than one that assumes every student will misuse a phone.

Policy 1 offers a sensible compromise. It keeps classrooms focused, gives teachers authority to enforce rules, and still allows students access to phones when they may be useful or necessary. By permitting phones during lunch and other free periods while requiring them to be off during class, our school can promote both responsibility and safety. I respectfully encourage you to choose Policy 1.

Dear Principal Harris,

I understand why you are considering a policy that would require a B average for students to take part in sports and other activities. Everyone wants students to take their classwork seriously. Still, I believe this change would hurt many of the students it is meant to help, and I respectfully urge you to reconsider.

Start with the simple fact that a C is not a failing grade. A C means a student is meeting the standard in a class, and many of the students who earn them are working hard. Some are balancing homework with jobs or with caring for younger siblings. Others struggle with one subject, like math or chemistry, that drags down an otherwise solid record. Telling these students that their effort is not good enough to earn a place on a team or in the drama club sends a discouraging message, and it ignores how much they may already be doing.

More importantly, activities are often the reason students stay engaged with school at all. A boy who dreads second period may still show up every morning because he has soccer practice in the afternoon. A girl who feels invisible in class may find her confidence in the band. Take those things away from a student who is already struggling, and I doubt the result will be a burst of studying. It is far more likely that the student will feel disconnected, lose motivation, and slip from a C to a D. Activities give students a sense of belonging, and belonging is one of the strongest motivators there is.

Activities also teach skills that grades do not measure. Playing on a team requires discipline, cooperation, and time management. Students who practice every afternoon learn to use their remaining hours carefully, and many of them do better academically during their busy seasons than they do in their free time. Working on the yearbook or the student council builds responsibility and leadership that colleges and employers value. Cutting off these chances would deprive students of lessons they cannot get from a textbook.

There is also a question of fairness. A B in an advanced class may reflect less mastery than a C in a very demanding one, and teachers grade differently. A policy that rests on one number would treat very different situations as if they were identical. Students with learning differences, or those still learning English, could be shut out through no lack of effort.

I do not think the answer is to do nothing, though. If the goal is to raise grades, there are better ways. The school could set a minimum of a C, so that students who are truly failing must get help before they play. Students who fall below that line could be offered tutoring, study hall, or a meeting with a teacher, with the chance to return once they improve. Coaches and advisers could check progress every few weeks rather than waiting for report cards. These approaches hold students accountable while keeping them connected to the school community.

Raising expectations is a worthy aim, but a B requirement would punish the average student rather than support one. I hope you will consider keeping the current standard or choosing a more flexible approach. Thank you for asking for our opinions and for taking them seriously.

Sincerely,

A concerned student

The idea of distance learning has become increasingly common, with many schools now letting students attend classes from home through online platforms or video conferencing. This shift has sparked debate about whether it truly helps students. In my view, students benefit a great deal from being able to learn from home, and schools should embrace this option.

One major benefit is flexibility. Learning from home allows students to shape their own schedules and balance school with other responsibilities, such as part-time jobs, family obligations, or personal interests. For example, a student caring for a younger sibling or working after school can join live classes or watch recordings without worrying about commuting or rearranging work hours. That kind of control over time is especially valuable for students juggling multiple commitments.

Distance learning also offers a more comfortable learning environment. Traditional classrooms can be intimidating, particularly for shy or anxious students, and that discomfort often discourages participation. At home, however, students can engage in discussions from a familiar setting, which may lower stress and boost motivation. A quiet student who rarely speaks up in person might contribute thoughtfully in an online chat or discussion forum, giving them a voice they might not otherwise have.

In addition, online learning can expand access to resources and expertise. Digital platforms often include interactive tools, recorded lessons, and multimedia materials that make lessons more engaging. Students can also connect with teachers and experts from different parts of the world, gaining perspectives that a single classroom cannot provide. For instance, someone studying a foreign language can take online lessons from native speakers, which can sharpen their skills more effectively than relying only on local resources.

Another important advantage is cost savings. Attending class from home reduces the need for daily transportation, and for some students, it eliminates room and board expenses. Online materials such as e-books, videos, and tutorials can also be more affordable than traditional textbooks. For students on tight budgets, these savings can make education more accessible.

Of course, distance learning is not perfect, and it may not suit every student or subject. Still, the benefits are hard to ignore. Greater flexibility, a more comfortable setting, wider access to resources, and lower costs can all improve the educational experience. As technology improves, I believe distance learning will play an even larger role in schools, and I hope more institutions will offer it as a meaningful option for students.

Dear Senator,

I write to urge you to preserve the Electoral College. While the call for a national popular vote sounds simple and democratic, the Electoral College remains a vital constitutional mechanism that balances competing interests and protects the federal character of our republic.

The Office of the Federal Register reminds us that the Framers created the Electoral College as a compromise between election by Congress and election by a direct popular vote. By assigning each state electors equal to its House seats plus its two Senate seats, the system gives smaller states a meaningful role. Abandoning that structure would shift power toward densely populated urban areas and a few large states. As Judge Richard Posner argues, the Electoral College forces presidential candidates to build broad national coalitions across both large and small states, rather than simply running up enormous vote totals in one region. A direct popular vote would encourage candidates to ignore rural and small-state voters almost entirely.

Critics like Bradford Plumer raise legitimate concerns. The popular-vote winner lost the presidency in 2000 and 2016, and because most states use winner-take-all rules, campaigns focus heavily on a handful of swing states. Faithless electors, though rare, are also troubling. But these flaws do not justify scrapping the entire system. The swing-state problem is largely a result of state-level winner-take-all laws, and states can change those rules themselves—Maine and Nebraska already allocate electors by congressional district. Getting rid of the Electoral College would be a drastic national remedy for a problem that states are able to address individually.

The Electoral College also offers a practical advantage: it confines disputed vote recounts to individual states rather than triggering a chaotic nationwide recount. In a close popular-vote election, every precinct in all fifty states could become a legal battlefield, delaying the result and undermining public confidence.

I understand the appeal of one person, one vote. But the presidency was never designed to be chosen by a simple national majority alone. It is a federal office, and the Electoral College reflects that federal structure. I ask you to defend it.

Respectfully,
[Your Name]

The decision by the principal to mandate participation in at least one extracurricular activity for all students has sparked a heated debate. While some argue that this requirement will enrich the students' overall educational experience, others claim that it will impose undue stress and restrict personal freedom. After careful consideration, I firmly believe that requiring students to participate in an extracurricular activity is a well-intentioned but misguided policy.

On the surface, the idea of encouraging students to engage in extracurricular activities seems beneficial. These activities can foster teamwork, build confidence, and provide a platform for students to explore their passions and interests outside of the classroom. For instance, participating in a sports team can teach valuable lessons about discipline, perseverance, and camaraderie. Similarly, working on the yearbook or serving on the student council can help students develop essential skills in leadership, communication, and problem-solving. However, the issue lies not with the inherent value of these activities, but with the fact that participation is being forced upon all students.

By making extracurricular activities compulsory, the principal's decision may inadvertently create more problems than it solves. For one, it may lead to undue stress and pressure on students who are already struggling to balance their academic workload. Many students have part-time jobs, family obligations, or other responsibilities that demand their time and attention outside of school. By forcing them to participate in an extracurricular activity, the school may be setting them up for failure and creating an unrealistic expectation about what they can handle. Furthermore, some students may simply not be interested in any of the available extracurricular activities, and forcing them to participate may lead to disengagement and a negative experience.

Another concern is that this policy may stifle personal freedom and autonomy. Students should be allowed to make their own choices about how they want to spend their time outside of class. By dictating that they must participate in an extracurricular activity, the school is essentially taking away their ability to make decisions about their own lives. This can be particularly damaging for students who value their independence and prefer to pursue their own interests and hobbies outside of school. For example, a student who is passionate about music or art may want to spend their free time practicing or creating, rather than being forced to participate in a school-sponsored activity.

In conclusion, while the intention behind the principal's decision is laudable, I firmly believe that requiring students to participate in an extracurricular activity is not the right approach. Instead of mandating participation, the school could focus on creating a supportive and inclusive environment that encourages students to explore their interests and passions voluntarily. By doing so, the school can promote a more positive and engaging experience for all students, without imposing unnecessary stress and restrictions on their personal freedom. Ultimately, it is essential to strike a balance between providing opportunities for students to grow and develop, and respecting their autonomy and individuality.

Every year, schools debate whether summer projects should be planned by teachers or by students. Teacher-designed assignments can certainly provide consistency and academic rigor, but I believe student-designed projects are ultimately more valuable. When students create their own projects, they learn to direct their own work, feel more motivated, and get to explore topics they actually care about.

One major benefit of student-designed projects is that they push students to become self-directed learners. Instead of following a teacher’s step-by-step instructions, students set their own goals, create deadlines, and figure out what resources they need. This kind of ownership builds responsibility and independence, which matter far beyond the classroom. For example, a student interested in environmental science could design a summer project investigating how local pollution affects wildlife. They would have to plan their research, collect and analyze data, and draw conclusions. Doing so deepens both their content knowledge and their ability to manage a long-term task.

Student-designed projects also tend to be more motivating. When students choose topics they are genuinely curious about, they are more likely to stay engaged and put in real effort. That internal motivation often leads to a richer experience than simply completing an assignment someone else designed. A student passionate about music, for instance, might compose and record an album, exploring songwriting, audio engineering, and production. Because the project connects to something they love, the work feels meaningful rather than like a chore.

In addition, designing a summer project gives students chances to practice critical thinking, problem-solving, and communication. They have to make decisions, work through obstacles, and reflect on their progress, which builds resilience. Teachers also get a fuller picture of student learning because they can assess both the final product and the process behind it. For example, a student creating a documentary film must research a topic, write a script, conduct interviews, film, and edit. That single project demonstrates research, writing, technical, and storytelling skills all at once.

Teacher-designed projects may provide structure, but student-designed projects offer a more engaging and effective way to keep learning alive over the summer. Allowing students to design their own work encourages independence, boosts motivation, and lets them explore their interests. If schools want summer assignments to be more than busywork, giving students real ownership is the best place to start.

Over the past few years, almost every student has experienced what it is like to take classes online. Even though some people couldn't wait to get back into the physical building, I believe that offering distance learning as an option is definitely beneficial for students. Having the choice to attend classes from home gives students more control over their schedules, helps them focus better, and creates a healthier balance between school and life.

First of all, distance learning allows students to learn at their own pace and avoid common classroom distractions. In a normal high school classroom, there are usually around twenty-five or thirty kids, and it can get really loud. Teachers often have to stop the lesson to manage behavior, or people interrupt with random comments that derail the topic. When you are learning from home, you can set up a quiet study space without someone tapping their pencil next to you or whispering. Also, online classes often provide recorded lectures and digital materials. If you do not understand a tough math problem or a history concept the first time, you can pause the video, rewind it, and watch it again. In a regular class, once the teacher speaks and erases the board, that moment is gone.

Another major benefit is physical and mental well-being. High school starts extremely early for most of us. Waking up at 6:00 a.m. to catch a bus leaves many teenagers chronically sleep-deprived, which makes it really hard to pay attention during first period. When you attend class from home, you cut out the long commute and the stress of rushing out the door. You can get an extra hour of sleep, eat a real breakfast, and start the day feeling actually awake. Additionally, if a student has a mild cold or an injury, they usually have to stay home and miss everything, falling behind on assignments. With distance learning, they could easily log in from their desk, keep up with the work, and avoid spreading germs to their classmates.

Some critics argue that distance learning ruins students' social lives and makes them feel isolated. It is true that sitting in front of a computer all day can get lonely, and you miss out on things like talking to friends in the hallway or doing hands-on science labs. However, having distance learning as an option does not mean school buildings should close down entirely. It just means that students who thrive better at home—such as kids dealing with severe social anxiety, chronic illnesses, or demanding extracurricular schedules—have an alternative that works for their specific situation.

In conclusion, no single learning environment works for every single person. Offering distance learning gives students the flexibility they need to succeed academically and stay healthy. As long as schools provide good resources and keep in-person classes open for those who prefer them, having the option to learn from home is a huge advantage for students today.

Dear Principal Johnson,

I am writing to respectfully oppose the proposed policy that would require students to maintain at least a B average in order to participate in sports and other activities. While I understand the goal of encouraging academic achievement, this rule would hurt many students rather than help them. A C average means a student is passing, yet this policy would treat those students as if they were failing and take away experiences that often keep them connected to school.

First, extracurricular activities are not rewards for top grades; they are essential parts of a complete education. In athletics, music, drama, and clubs, students learn teamwork, responsibility, discipline, and leadership. A student who earns Cs in algebra may be an outstanding point guard learning how to handle pressure and support teammates. A student who struggles with essay writing may find confidence and a reason to attend school through the robotics club or the school play. Excluding these students would remove some of the very experiences that make them feel valued and capable.

Second, participation in activities often improves academic performance. Students who are involved in sports or clubs usually must meet attendance and eligibility standards, and they learn to manage their time between practice, meetings, and homework. For many students, the activity is the reason they keep trying in class. If we take that away until they reach a B average, we may remove the motivation they need to improve. Instead of punishing C students, we should pair participation with academic support, such as required study halls, tutoring, or regular progress checks.

Third, a strict B average does not account for the different challenges students face. Some students work hard and still earn Cs because of learning differences, language barriers, family responsibilities, or personal hardships. These students may need activities as a healthy outlet and a source of stability. Denying them the chance to participate would add stress and isolation, not encourage better grades. A policy based only on letter grades can also create unhealthy pressure and discourage students from taking challenging courses where a C may reflect real effort.

I agree that academic success should be a priority. However, a better approach would be to require students to pass all classes, attend school regularly, and take part in academic support if their grades fall below a certain level. This would keep students eligible while still holding them accountable. It would also give students a reason to stay involved rather than pushing them away.

Thank you for listening to student voices on this important issue. I hope you will consider a more supportive and inclusive policy.

Sincerely,  
[Student Name]
