The widespread use of cell phones has become a routine part of daily life, with most people relying on them for communication, navigation, and entertainment. Yet when it comes to using these devices behind the wheel, the debate grows sharply. Some view cell phone use as a convenient tool for drivers, but others argue it creates serious dangers on the road. In my view, drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

The main issue is distraction. Whenever a driver talks, texts, or scrolls, attention shifts away from the road, raising the chance of a crash. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reported that distracted driving caused 3,166 deaths in the United States in 2017. This danger is not only physical, such as holding a phone or typing; it also involves cognitive distraction. A driver’s mind can remain focused on a conversation or task rather than the road, and that mental split can be just as harmful as taking hands off the wheel. It slows the ability to notice and respond to changing conditions.

Cell phone use also weakens reaction time. Drivers occupied with a phone are less likely to spot and respond to hazards like pedestrians, other vehicles, or debris. Even hands-free devices, often promoted as safer, still create meaningful distraction. Research shows that hands-free phone use can pull a driver’s attention away from the road and increase accident risk, so the problem is not solved simply by keeping both hands on the wheel.

In addition, allowing cell phone use while driving sends a troubling message. If drivers are permitted to use their phones, it may seem like distracted driving is acceptable, which can breed complacency about road safety. A clear ban, on the other hand, signals that safety is a top priority and that distracted driving will not be tolerated.

In conclusion, the risks of cell phone use while driving far outweigh any convenience. Distraction, whether physical or cognitive, can lead to deadly outcomes, and slower reaction times make accidents more likely. Instead of permitting phone use behind the wheel, governments and regulatory agencies should enforce strict laws and penalties to discourage it. That approach can reduce accidents and fatalities and make roads safer for everyone. The safety of drivers, passengers, and pedestrians should come before the convenience of cell phone use, so drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

The idea of driverless cars is exciting. In the article “Driverless Cars Are Coming,” Google cofounder Sergey Brin imagines a future in which autonomous public transportation uses half the fuel and half the parking space required by today’s vehicles. Supporters also point out that human error causes more than 90 percent of traffic accidents, so removing human drivers could save lives, lower insurance costs, and help elderly or disabled people travel more easily. Even with these possible benefits, however, fully autonomous vehicles should not be widely used until major safety, technological, and legal issues are solved. The risks of rushing this technology onto public roads are too serious.

First, the sensors and software in driverless cars are not reliable enough for all real driving conditions. According to the article, current sensors can have difficulty in heavy rain, snow, fog, and unmarked construction zones. These are not unusual situations. Drivers regularly deal with poor weather, detours, and changing road conditions. If an autonomous vehicle cannot clearly detect obstacles, lane markings, or traffic signals in these circumstances, it could make dangerous mistakes. A human driver may also struggle in bad weather, but people can use judgment and adapt to unexpected situations. Until driverless cars can respond safely to these common challenges, they should not replace human drivers.

Another problem is the danger created by semi-autonomous vehicles. These cars can handle some driving tasks, but they still depend on a person to take control during an emergency. The article explains that studies show passengers quickly lose focus when a computer is driving, causing slower reaction times. This creates an unsafe situation: people may believe the car is fully capable of driving itself, while the system still expects them to react instantly if something goes wrong. In reality, drivers may be distracted, tired, or simply unprepared when the vehicle suddenly needs help. Instead of making roads safer, this middle stage of automation could lead to new kinds of accidents.

Driverless cars also face problems involving software failures and cybersecurity. The article notes that autonomous systems can be vulnerable to glitches or cyberattacks. A malfunctioning program could cause a car to misread the road or make the wrong decision. Even more concerning, hackers might interfere with a vehicle’s controls. Because driverless cars rely so heavily on computers, a technical problem could put passengers, other drivers, and pedestrians in danger.

Finally, legal and ethical questions have not been answered. When an accident happens, it may be difficult to decide who is responsible. Is it the owner of the vehicle, the automaker, or the software developer? Without clear laws, victims of crashes may have trouble receiving fair compensation. Manufacturers and insurance companies may also be unsure how to handle responsibility. Before autonomous cars become common, society needs clear rules about accountability.

In conclusion, driverless cars may eventually improve transportation and reduce accidents. They could save fuel, use less parking space, and give more independence to people who cannot drive. However, the technology is not yet ready for widespread use. Sensors still struggle in difficult conditions, semi-autonomous systems can encourage inattention, software may fail or be hacked, and legal responsibility remains unclear. Development and testing should continue carefully, but driverless cars should not become common on public roads until these important problems are resolved.

Dear Principal Davis,

I am writing to share my perspective on the proposed policy that would require students to maintain a B average in order to participate in extracurricular activities. While I know this initiative comes from a genuine desire to raise academic expectations across our school, I strongly believe that shutting out students with a C average will produce the opposite effect, alienating the very students who need our school community the most.

For many students, an after-school sport, the marching band, or the theater troupe is not a distraction from academics—it is the primary reason they show up to school in the morning. When a student who struggles in the classroom knows they have cross-country practice or robotics club waiting at the end of the day, they have a tangible anchor holding them accountable. Strip that away, and you remove their strongest incentive to attend class and complete assignments. Research consistently shows that extracurricular involvement fosters discipline, time management, and a sense of belonging. Denying participation to someone working diligently to hold a C average tells them that their effort counts for nothing unless it meets an arbitrary standard of excellence. 

There are also unintended consequences that this policy would trigger in course selection. If students need a strict 3.0 grade point average to stay on the soccer team or remain in student council, they will naturally avoid challenging classes. A student who might have pushed themselves to take Honors Chemistry or an advanced literature seminar will opt for a less rigorous alternative simply to protect their eligibility. We should be encouraging intellectual risk-taking, not incentivizing students to game the system with an easier schedule. Furthermore, placing such high stakes on letter grades inevitably subjects teachers to intense pressure to bump borderline marks, creating an environment centered on bargaining rather than authentic learning.

We must also recognize that a C average does not always reflect a lack of effort. Many students balance school with part-time jobs to support their families, care for younger siblings, or navigate learning differences that make a B average an uphill battle. For these students, clubs and teams offer a vital outlet for stress relief and emotional support. Cutting them off from positive peer groups during their most vulnerable moments risks pushing them further into isolation or delinquency.

If our collective goal is to help struggling students improve their grades, exclusion is the bluntest and least constructive tool available. A far better approach would be to pair participation with support. Instead of benching students with a C average, we could mandate weekly check-ins, study tables, or peer tutoring sessions. That way, athletics and the arts remain the carrot that draws students toward better academic habits. 

I urge you to keep our current eligibility threshold in place. High expectations matter, but we fulfill them by building bridges of support for our students, not by taking away the activities that give them purpose.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

Dear Principal Williams,

I am writing to share my thoughts on the proposal to require at least a B average for students who participate in sports and clubs. While I understand and respect the desire to raise academic standards across our school, I worry that this particular change would end up hurting many of the students it aims to help. For several reasons, I urge you not to raise the requirement.

To begin with, extracurriculars are often what keep students invested in school in the first place. Many of us with a C average are not falling behind because we lack the ability to learn, but because we feel unmotivated or detached from the classroom. For someone in that position, being part of a team, the marching band, or the drama club provides a clear reason to show up every morning, attend class, and stay out of trouble. Stripping away that outlet rarely inspires a student to suddenly study harder. More often, it leads to frustration, a sense of isolation, and grades that drop even lower.

Furthermore, setting the bar at a B would instantly disqualify a substantial portion of the student body. Because a C average is quite common, this rule would gut rosters and force smaller organizations to shut down entirely. Athletic teams might struggle to field full squads, and productions like the school play or the yearbook might not have enough hands to run effectively. Extracurricular programs foster community spirit and pride, which enrich the entire school environment—including for students who already earn straight A's. Weakening these programs damages our overall culture.

We also should not overlook the critical lessons taught outside of textbooks. On the court or stage, students develop resilience, time management, collaboration, and accountability—qualities that a GPA simply cannot reflect, yet colleges and future employers value deeply. A C is already defined as satisfactory, passing work. Telling students that meeting district standards is not good enough to participate in the broader life of the school sends a discouraging message.

Finally, a rigid B cutoff overlooks the personal realities many students manage outside school hours. Balancing a part-time job to help family, caring for younger siblings, or working through a learning difference makes maintaining high marks far more difficult. A student in those circumstances might be working twice as hard for a C as another does for an easy A, and this policy would unfairly penalize their effort.

Academics should always come first, but there are more constructive ways to encourage growth. Instead of shutting doors, the school could introduce mandatory study tables before practice, offer free peer tutoring, or place struggling students on academic probation with regular check-ins between coaches and teachers. Keeping a C minimum while offering structured support would hold us accountable without cutting off the activities that keep us grounded. 

Thank you for being open to student feedback on this issue. I hope you will consider an approach that focuses on lifting students up rather than leaving them on the sidelines.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

The development of driverless cars has sparked intense debate in recent years, with proponents envisioning a future of enhanced safety and convenience, while critics raise concerns about the potential risks and uncertainties surrounding this technology. After careful consideration of the arguments presented in the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," I firmly believe that the development of driverless cars should be pursued, despite the challenges and complexities that lie ahead. The potential benefits of autonomous vehicles, including a significant reduction in traffic accidents and increased mobility for the elderly and disabled, outweigh the drawbacks, and with continued innovation and refinement, these vehicles can be made safer and more reliable.

One of the most compelling arguments in favor of driverless cars is their potential to drastically reduce the number of traffic accidents on our roads. As the article notes, human error is responsible for over 90 percent of traffic accidents, often due to distracted driving, drowsiness, or impaired driving. By removing the human element from the driving process, autonomous vehicles can minimize the risk of accidents caused by these factors. Furthermore, the use of advanced sensors and computer systems can enable driverless cars to detect and respond to hazards more quickly and effectively than human drivers. For instance, laser radar and cameras can detect obstacles and lane markings, while GPS and computer sensors can monitor traffic signals and adjust the vehicle's speed accordingly. By leveraging these technologies, driverless cars can significantly improve road safety and save countless lives.

Another significant advantage of driverless cars is their potential to provide greater mobility and independence for elderly and disabled individuals. As the article highlights, autonomous vehicles can offer a lifeline to those who are unable to drive themselves, enabling them to travel freely and participate fully in their communities. This is a particularly important consideration, given the growing aging population and the need for innovative solutions to support their mobility and well-being. Moreover, the use of driverless cars can also help to reduce the burden on public transportation systems, by providing a more efficient and personalized mode of transport. For example, autonomous vehicles can be designed to transport individuals directly to their destinations, rather than following a fixed route, which can reduce travel times and increase overall productivity.

Despite the potential benefits of driverless cars, there are also concerns about their safety and reliability, particularly in adverse weather conditions or unmarked construction zones. Critics argue that current sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, or fog, and that software systems remain vulnerable to glitches or cybersecurity threats. However, these challenges can be addressed through continued research and development, as well as the implementation of robust testing and validation protocols. Additionally, the use of semi-autonomous features, which require human drivers to stay alert and take over in emergencies, can help to mitigate these risks and ensure a safe and smooth transition to autonomous vehicles.

In conclusion, while there are valid concerns about the development of driverless cars, I believe that the potential benefits of this technology outweigh the drawbacks. By continuing to innovate and refine autonomous vehicle systems, we can create a safer, more efficient, and more accessible transportation network that enhances the lives of individuals and communities around the world. As Sergey Brin's vision of a future with driverless public transportation suggests, the possibilities are vast and exciting, and with careful planning and execution, we can realize the full potential of this technology and create a better future for all. Ultimately, the development of driverless cars is a complex and multifaceted issue, requiring a nuanced and balanced approach that takes into account the various benefits and challenges involved. By engaging in ongoing research, testing, and evaluation, we can ensure that autonomous vehicles are developed and deployed in a responsible and safe manner, and that their potential is fully realized.

Dear Principal Harris,

I understand why you are considering a B-average requirement for sports and other activities. Every school wants its students to take academics seriously, and no one disputes that grades matter. Still, I believe this policy would do more harm than good, especially for the many students who currently earn Cs, and I would like to explain why.

Start with who would be affected. A C average is not a failing grade. It means a student is passing every class and understanding most of the material. Many of those students are juggling jobs, family responsibilities, or subjects that simply do not come easily to them. Telling them they are not good enough to join the soccer team or the drama club sends a discouraging message. It suggests that only students who already succeed deserve the chance to belong to something.

Activities are also where many students find their reason to show up. A boy who struggles through algebra may still get to school on time every day because he has practice at three o'clock. A girl who is quiet in class may blossom on the stage crew. Take those things away and you do not automatically get a more dedicated student; you often get one who feels disconnected and has more empty hours after school. Research and common sense both suggest that unsupervised time is not usually spent on calculus homework. I worry that some students would drift away from school altogether, and a few might drop out.

There is a practical side as well. Extracurriculars teach skills that no textbook covers: time management, teamwork, leadership, perseverance. A student on the track team learns to plan her evenings around practice and homework precisely because she has to. Colleges and employers value those abilities, and a student who is cut off from activities loses the chance to build them. Some students would also lose athletic or artistic opportunities that could help them earn scholarships, which for certain families is the only realistic path to college.

I do not want to suggest that grades should be ignored. Students who are struggling need support, and I would be glad to see the school offer it. A better approach might be to keep a lower standard, such as a C average or no failing grades, and pair it with help. Teams and clubs could set up supervised study halls before practice, and older students with strong grades could tutor classmates. Coaches and advisers could check in with teachers regularly, and a student who slips could be placed on a short probation period with extra support before losing eligibility. That approach holds students accountable while treating activities as part of the solution rather than a reward to be taken away.

A B requirement might raise a few report cards in the short term, but I suspect it would raise far more resentment. Students who want to stay involved will respond better to encouragement and structure than to exclusion. I hope you will consider keeping activities open to students who are passing their classes and investing in ways to help them improve.

Thank you for asking for our opinions and for taking them seriously.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

Extracurricular activities are undeniably beneficial to the high school experience. Whether taking the field under Friday night lights, designing pages for the yearbook, or debating school policies on the student council, students often find their passions outside the traditional classroom. However, the principal’s recent decision to mandate that every student participate in at least one extracurricular activity is a misstep. Although intended to enrich school culture, this policy fails to account for diverse personal obligations, diminishes the genuine enthusiasm that makes clubs thrive, and introduces unnecessary stress into already demanding schedules.

First and foremost, a blanket mandate ignores the complex realities of students’ lives outside of school. High schoolers do not experience identical circumstances once the final bell rings. Many students must immediately commute to part-time jobs to help support their families financially. Others have critical responsibilities at home, such as caring for younger siblings or assisting elderly relatives while their parents work. Imposing a mandatory after-school commitment places an unfair burden on these individuals, effectively penalizing them for responsibilities beyond their control or forcing them to sacrifice their academic performance to satisfy an administrative requirement.

Furthermore, compelling participation undermines the very nature of what makes extracurriculars valuable: voluntary passion. The prefix “extra” inherently implies something beyond the compulsory curriculum—an avenue where students exercise personal autonomy to pursue their distinct interests. When an activity shifts from an optional opportunity into a graduation requirement, the atmosphere of that organization inevitably deteriorates. A student council populated by apathetic participants will struggle to foster meaningful leadership. Similarly, sports teams and creative clubs rely on dedication and positive energy. Forcing unwilling students into these spaces leads to disengagement and resentment, which directly harms the experience of those who are genuinely committed.

Supporters of the mandate often argue that required involvement prevents social isolation and encourages students to discover talents they might otherwise overlook. While building an inclusive, well-rounded community is a noble goal, compulsion rarely fosters authentic connection. Instead of inspiring personal growth, forced participation makes students feel micromanaged, transforming what should be a creative outlet or stress reliever into just another chore on their to-do lists. True engagement cannot be manufactured through institutional pressure; it must be cultivated by offering diverse, accessible opportunities and encouraging students to participate on their own terms.

In conclusion, while the principal’s intention to foster an active, connected student body is admirable, requiring participation is the wrong approach. It disregards the legitimate responsibilities students balance outside the classroom, threatens to erode the authentic enthusiasm that sustains school organizations, and turns rewarding outlets into bureaucratic obligations. The administration should focus on inspiring and supporting student involvement rather than enforcing it. By keeping extracurricular activities voluntary, our school can ensure that these programs remain spaces of genuine growth, camaraderie, and joy.

Few objects have reshaped daily life as quickly as the cell phone, and few have created a more stubborn problem on the road. The question is whether drivers should be allowed to use phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle. A blanket ban on handheld use is clearly justified. A ban on every function, including voice-activated and hands-free tools, is harder to defend, though the evidence suggests drivers should be far more restricted than most currently are.

Start with what driving demands. It asks for the eyes, the hands, and the mind at once, and a phone competes for all three. Texting is the worst offender because it pulls the eyes from the road for several seconds at a time. At highway speed, a glance of about five seconds covers the length of a football field. Nobody would knowingly close their eyes for that distance, yet people do the equivalent every day to read a message or change a playlist. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration attributes thousands of deaths a year in the United States to distracted driving, and those figures almost certainly understate the problem, since a driver who has just crashed is unlikely to confess to checking a notification.

The harder argument concerns hands-free calling. Many drivers believe that if both hands are on the wheel, they are safe. Research from university driving simulators and from real-world crash studies complicates that belief. A conversation occupies working memory, and drivers on calls tend to miss hazards that fall directly in their line of sight, a phenomenon researchers call inattention blindness. Their reaction times slow, and they brake later. The danger lives partly in the mind, not only in the hands, so legislation that targets the hands alone solves half the problem.

Still, an absolute prohibition has costs and limits. Navigation apps have probably prevented as many dangerous moments as they have caused, sparing drivers from squinting at paper maps or pulling over repeatedly in unfamiliar places. A parent on the road may need to receive an urgent call from a child's school. Someone who witnesses a collision or has a medical emergency should be able to dial for help immediately. A law that criminalized these uses would be difficult to enforce and would likely lose public respect, which is a poor foundation for any safety rule.

The sensible position, then, is a firm distinction between interaction and assistance. Holding a phone, typing, scrolling, watching video, and browsing social media should be prohibited outright, with penalties severe enough to matter, such as meaningful fines and license points rather than a token charge. Several states and countries have seen reductions in violations when enforcement was visible and consistent. Navigation should be set before the car moves, or controlled by voice. Calls should be brief, rare, and avoided in heavy traffic or bad weather. Automakers can help by locking out nonessential functions while a vehicle is in motion, which removes temptation instead of depending on willpower.

Culture matters as well. Drunk driving was once treated as a regrettable but forgivable habit, and it took decades of advocacy to make it socially unacceptable. Phone use behind the wheel deserves the same stigma. A text can wait ten minutes; a life cannot be recovered.

Drivers should therefore not be permitted to use phones in the ways that take their eyes and hands from the road, and they should be discouraged from even hands-free conversation outside of genuine need. Safety is not served by pretending the phone is harmless, nor by pretending the law can erase it entirely. It is served by drawing the line where the evidence points and holding people to it.

The use of cell phones while driving has become a controversial issue in recent years. With the vast majority of people owning and using cell phones daily, it's no surprise that many drivers are tempted to use them while behind the wheel. However, the question remains: should drivers be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle? In my opinion, drivers should not be able to use cell phones while driving, except in emergency situations.

One of the main reasons for this is safety. When drivers use cell phones, they are distracted from the road and other vehicles around them. This can lead to accidents, which can result in injuries or even fatalities. According to statistics, texting and driving increases the risk of a crash by 23 times, and dialing a number increases the risk by 2.8 times. These numbers are alarming and clearly show that using a cell phone while driving is a recipe for disaster. Moreover, even hands-free phone calls can be distracting, as they require the driver to focus on the conversation rather than the road.

Another reason why drivers should not use cell phones is that it can be a significant contributor to reckless driving. When drivers are texting or browsing on their phones, they are not paying attention to the road and may not notice pedestrians, cyclists, or other vehicles. This can lead to reckless driving behaviors such as speeding, tailgating, or running red lights. Additionally, using a cell phone while driving can also lead to a lack of situational awareness, which can cause drivers to miss important traffic signs or signals.

Some might argue that using a cell phone while driving is necessary in emergency situations, such as needing to call for help or navigating through unfamiliar areas. However, this can be achieved through the use of hands-free devices or by pulling over to a safe location. Many cars now come equipped with Bluetooth technology, which allows drivers to make hands-free calls and access GPS navigation. Additionally, many phones have voice-activated assistants that can help drivers with directions or other tasks without requiring them to take their eyes off the road.

In conclusion, drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle, except in emergency situations. The risks associated with using a cell phone while driving are too great, and the consequences can be devastating. By banning the use of cell phones while driving, we can reduce the number of accidents on the road and make our roads safer for everyone. It's our responsibility as drivers to stay focused on the road and avoid distractions, and using a cell phone while driving is a distraction that we can't afford to ignore. By staying off our phones and keeping our eyes on the road, we can ensure that we arrive at our destinations safely and without putting ourselves or others at risk.

I think distance learning can be a good option if it is done right. I know a lot of people say students need to be in a classroom to focus, but attending classes from home has some real benefits.

First, it saves time. At my school, some kids ride the bus for almost an hour each way. If they could log in from home, they would get extra sleep and start the day less stressed. I have to get up at 6:15 to catch the bus. On days when we had online classes during bad weather, I could roll out of bed at 7:50, eat breakfast, and still be ready. I paid attention better because I was not half asleep.

Second, distance learning lets students work at their own pace. In a regular classroom, my math teacher has to keep the whole class together. If I do not understand something, I cannot just pause the teacher. But when lessons are recorded online, I can rewind and watch the hard part again. Last year, my science teacher posted video notes. I watched the section on balancing equations three times before it finally clicked. If I had been in class, I probably would have pretended I got it and fallen behind.

Another reason is that some students feel more comfortable speaking up from home. In class, I sometimes do not ask questions because I do not want to look dumb in front of everyone. Online, I can type a question in the chat or email the teacher privately. My friend who has anxiety said she actually participated more during our virtual days because she did not have to worry about everyone staring at her. That does not mean she wants to stay home forever, but having the option helped her.

Distance learning can also help with scheduling. Students who are serious about sports, music, or family responsibilities could fit school around those things. For example, a kid who takes care of a younger sibling after school could watch a lesson later instead of missing it. My cousin is a competitive swimmer and has practice early in the morning. If her school offered some online classes, she would not have to choose between being exhausted at school and missing practice.

Of course, distance learning is not perfect. It takes self-control, and some kids would just sleep through class or play video games. Internet problems and a lack of quiet space are real issues too. But schools could offer it as an option instead of forcing everyone to do it. Students who learn better in person could stay in the building, while others could use the online option when it helps.

Overall, I believe students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home. It gives more flexibility, lets kids review lessons at their own pace, and can make school less stressful for people who struggle in a regular classroom. It should not replace school completely, but having the choice would help a lot of students learn better.

Requiring every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity may sound like a good way to build school spirit, but I disagree with making it mandatory. Activities such as sports, student council, theater, robotics, and yearbook can be valuable experiences. They help students make friends, discover interests, and develop responsibility. However, the benefits of extracurriculars depend largely on students choosing to be involved. A requirement could create stress, resentment, and unnecessary burdens for students whose lives outside school are already demanding.

Many students have responsibilities that are not visible during the school day. Some care for younger siblings while their parents work. Others have part-time jobs to help support their families, attend appointments, or spend significant time commuting home. For these students, staying after school for a club meeting or practice may not be realistic. Imagine a student who needs to pick up a younger brother from elementary school every afternoon. Even if that student enjoys photography, joining the yearbook staff could mean leaving a sibling without supervision. A school policy should not force students to choose between family responsibilities and graduation requirements.

Mandatory participation could also weaken the quality of activities themselves. Clubs and teams work best when members actually want to contribute. A student who joins the debate team only because it is required may skip meetings, refuse to prepare, or distract others who are committed. The same problem could affect the yearbook staff: if several students are assigned to it unwillingly, they may do little more than meet the minimum expectation. Rather than creating a stronger school community, the policy could turn meaningful opportunities into another box to check.

Students also need time to rest and manage their academic work. High school can already include several hours of homework, major projects, tests, and college or career planning. Not every student handles pressure in the same way. One person may thrive with a packed schedule of classes, soccer practice, and volunteer work, while another may need quiet time at home to stay focused and healthy. Schools should encourage students to challenge themselves, but they should not assume that constant busyness is the same as growth.

A better approach would be to strongly encourage extracurricular involvement and remove barriers that prevent students from joining. The school could hold an activity fair, offer clubs during lunch, provide late buses, and create short-term opportunities such as a one-day service project or a week-long art workshop. Teachers and counselors could help students find activities that fit their interests and schedules. These choices would invite participation without punishing students who have legitimate reasons for being unavailable.

Extracurricular activities are most meaningful when they come from curiosity, commitment, or enjoyment. Students should be given opportunities to explore sports, leadership, creativity, and service, but they should retain the freedom to decide how to use their time. Encouragement builds involvement; requirements often build resentment.

First and foremost, student-designed summer projects promote self-directed learning, a crucial skill in today's fast-paced and ever-changing world. When students are given the freedom to design their own projects, they must take ownership of their learning, set goals, and develop a plan to achieve them. This process helps students develop essential skills such as time management, critical thinking, and problem-solving. For instance, a student interested in environmental science might design a project to investigate the impact of pollution on local wildlife, collecting and analyzing data, and presenting their findings in a report or poster. By allowing students to take the reins, they become more invested in their learning and are more likely to develop a deeper understanding of the subject matter.

Another significant advantage of student-designed summer projects is that they increase motivation and engagement. When students are allowed to pursue their interests and passions, they are more likely to be enthusiastic and motivated to learn. In contrast, teacher-designed projects can sometimes feel forced or irrelevant, leading to a lack of interest and a sense of drudgery. For example, a student who loves photography might design a project to capture and document the beauty of nature, while a student who enjoys coding might create a mobile app to help people learn a new language. By giving students the freedom to choose their own projects, educators can tap into their intrinsic motivation and help them develop a love of learning that extends beyond the classroom.

Furthermore, student-designed summer projects allow students to explore their passions and interests in a more in-depth and meaningful way. When students are given the autonomy to design their own projects, they can delve deeper into topics that truly fascinate them, rather than being restricted to a predetermined set of topics or learning objectives. This approach can help students develop a sense of purpose and direction, as they begin to see the relevance and application of their learning to real-world problems and issues. For instance, a student who is passionate about social justice might design a project to investigate and address issues of inequality in their community, while a student who loves engineering might design and build a prototype to solve a real-world problem.

In conclusion, summer projects should be student-designed, as this approach promotes self-directed learning, increases motivation, and allows students to explore their passions. By giving students the freedom to design their own projects, educators can help them develop essential skills, such as critical thinking, problem-solving, and time management, while also fostering a love of learning that extends beyond the classroom. As we continue to navigate the complexities of the 21st century, it is essential that we provide students with the autonomy and flexibility to pursue their interests and passions, and student-designed summer projects are an excellent way to achieve this goal.

Dear Principal,

If a last-minute practice is canceled or a bus is delayed, a quick text prevents confusion and worry at home. This is not about social media; it is about staying connected to the people responsible for us.

Cell Phones and Driving: Not Worth the Risk

I think drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while they are driving. A lot of people say they can text at a red light or talk on a hands-free call and still be safe, but I don’t buy it. When you’re behind the wheel, your only job should be driving. Anything that takes your eyes, hands, or mind off the road is a risk, and a phone can do all three at once.

The most obvious problem is texting. Even if someone just glances down for a second to see who messaged them, that second can be enough to miss a kid running into the street or the car ahead slamming on its brakes. My driver’s ed teacher told us that reading or sending a text takes your eyes off the road for about five seconds. At 55 miles per hour, that’s like driving the length of a football field with your eyes closed. That image stuck with me. No text message is worth that.

Some people argue that hands-free calling is fine because you aren’t holding the phone. But that doesn’t make it safe. If you’re on a call, your brain is focused on the conversation, not on the road. I’ve seen my mom completely miss a turn while talking to my aunt on speakerphone. She wasn’t texting or holding anything, but she was still distracted. Studies have shown that hands-free calls are not much safer than regular calls because the problem is mental, not just physical. You can be looking right at the road and still not really see what’s happening because you’re thinking about what to say next.

I also think using a phone for GPS or changing music while driving should be done before the car moves. It only takes a few seconds to set up directions or pick a playlist in a parking lot. If you need to change something mid-drive, pull over. It feels annoying, but it’s better than drifting into another lane because you were trying to skip a song. Even at stoplights, I don’t think people should be on their phones. A lot of accidents happen because someone is still looking down when the light turns green, or they don’t notice a pedestrian crossing.

I know people complain that banning all phone use is too strict. They say phones are necessary for emergencies or that drivers should be allowed to answer if their boss calls. But emergencies are rare, and if it’s a real emergency, a driver can pull over safely first. We survived before cell phones existed. People managed to drive without constant connection.

In the end, the risk is just too high. Driving a car is dangerous enough without adding a phone to the mix. I think laws should be clear: no cell phone use while driving, no exceptions. It might be inconvenient, but inconvenience is a small price to pay for keeping people alive.

Summer projects should be primarily student-designed because students are more likely to stay curious, work independently, and connect learning to real life when they have meaningful control over the topic. Teachers should still provide guidance and clear expectations, but a project does not need to look identical for every student in order to be educational.

During the school year, students spend most of their time completing assignments selected by adults. Summer offers a rare opportunity to explore questions that may not fit neatly into a class schedule. A student who loves animals might volunteer at a shelter and create a report about the costs and responsibilities of pet adoption. Another student interested in basketball could track shooting percentages, use statistics to compare players, and design a practice plan based on the results. Both projects involve research, writing, mathematics, and reflection, yet each begins with an interest the student already has.

Choice also encourages persistence. A teacher-designed project may be carefully planned, but if a student sees it as another worksheet packet, it is likely to be completed quickly and forgotten. By contrast, a student building a small garden, interviewing grandparents about family history, or learning to prepare traditional recipes has a personal reason to continue when the work becomes difficult. For example, a student researching the history of a neighborhood might need to read old newspaper articles, organize notes, and revise a presentation. Those tasks can be challenging, but they feel purposeful because the student is investigating a place that matters to them.

Student-designed projects can also accommodate different circumstances. Not every family can afford museum trips, summer camps, or expensive supplies. A single teacher-assigned project may unintentionally favor students with more time, transportation, or financial resources. When students help design their own work, they can choose projects that fit their lives: documenting local plants with a phone camera, reading books from the library, recording oral histories, or studying how a family business operates. Creativity is not limited to students with large budgets.

Of course, student-designed does not mean teacher-free. Teachers can provide a menu of possible formats, establish goals such as research, problem-solving, and communication, and require students to submit a brief proposal before summer begins. They might ask for a journal, photographs, a final product, and a short reflection on what was learned. This structure prevents projects from becoming vague while still leaving room for individual interests.

The best summer learning is not simply an extension of the school year. It is learning that students can carry into their own lives. By allowing students to design their projects within thoughtful guidelines, schools can turn summer work from an obligation into an experience of genuine curiosity and independence.

Dear Principal Thompson,

I am writing in response to your proposal to require a grade B average for students to participate in sports and other activities. I understand that the goal is to encourage academic success, and I respect that. However, I believe this policy would do more harm than good, and I urge you to reconsider it.

First, the policy would punish the students who are already struggling by taking away the very things that keep them engaged in school. For many students with a C average, sports, band, drama, and clubs are the main reasons they look forward to coming to school each day. These activities give them a sense of belonging and purpose. If we remove them, we risk making these students feel disconnected from the school community. A student who feels disconnected is less likely to try hard in class, not more. Removing an incentive to be at school could lead to lower attendance, lower motivation, and even a higher dropout rate.

Second, a grade C is not a failing grade. A C means a student is meeting expectations and understanding an average amount of the material. Many students who earn Cs are working hard but find certain subjects difficult, or they may have learning differences, jobs, or family responsibilities that limit their study time. Telling them they are not good enough to join the track team or the school newspaper sends the wrong message. It suggests that only top achievers deserve opportunities, when in fact all students benefit from them.

Third, activities teach skills that classrooms alone cannot. Athletes learn teamwork, discipline, and time management. Students in clubs learn leadership and communication. Many students actually do better academically during their season or rehearsal period because they have a structured schedule and a reason to manage their time carefully. If we take away that structure, some students may spend their afternoons unsupervised or on screens rather than studying. There is no guarantee that a student barred from soccer will use that time to raise a grade.

Finally, a B average requirement would reduce participation across the school. Many teams and clubs depend on large numbers of students. If a large share of the student body is suddenly ineligible, some programs could struggle to field teams or hold performances. That would hurt school spirit and the students who do qualify as well.

I do believe grades matter, and there are better ways to encourage them. The school could set a lower standard, such as a C average, with a warning period before a student loses eligibility. It could offer free tutoring or required study halls for students whose grades are slipping. Coaches and advisors could work with teachers to monitor progress. These approaches support students rather than excluding them, and they keep the benefits of activities available to everyone.

In conclusion, requiring a B average would take opportunities away from students who need them most and would not necessarily improve their grades. A policy built on support, not exclusion, would better serve our school. Thank you for taking the time to consider the students' views on this important issue.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

Dear Principal,

When I see the students who tutor at the elementary school or spend Saturday mornings picking up litter at the park, I notice something beyond the work itself. They come back looking tired, yes, but also a little more awake to the world. That is why I believe community service should be required, though in a form that respects students’ busy lives.

A good requirement would not simply add hours to our schedules; it would give all of us a chance to learn something that a classroom can only describe. Last fall, my friend Daniel resisted joining the tutoring program. He had basketball practice and a long bus ride home. After a few weeks, however, he told me that explaining multiplication to a fourth grader had forced him to think about math differently. He started planning his homework more efficiently so he could keep tutoring. The time he spent did not disappear from his life; it rearranged his priorities and made him more focused. If the program had been optional, Daniel probably would never have signed up.

Opponents sometimes say that students already have enough demands from classes, jobs, and family responsibilities. That concern is real. A rigid requirement could punish a student who works after school or cares for younger siblings. But the solution is not to abandon the idea. The school could require a modest number of hours, completed over a year, with options during school time or on weekends. Students could choose between tutoring, environmental projects, assisting at a food pantry, or other approved activities. This flexibility would preserve the benefit without ignoring real constraints.

There is another reason to make service a requirement rather than a choice. Optional programs tend to attract students who are already confident and involved. The student who is shy, or who has never been asked to help, may avoid service altogether. A requirement gently pushes that student into a new situation. I watched this happen with my neighbor, who is quiet and usually keeps to herself. She joined a litter cleanup only because her club required it. By the end of the afternoon, she was joking with other volunteers and pointing out how much cleaner the creek looked. She later said she had never thought of herself as someone who could improve the neighborhood. That small shift in identity matters more than the trash bags they filled.

Of course, forced service can feel hollow if it is treated as a box to check. That is why reflection should be part of the process, through short written or spoken responses. Students need a chance to make sense of what they did, not just log hours.

Requiring community service would not solve every problem, but it would teach us that citizenship is not a spectator activity. With reasonable flexibility, it can fit into our lives and expand them at the same time. I urge you to adopt a thoughtful requirement, not as a punishment, but as a shared expectation that every student can contribute.

Sincerely,
A Student

I agree with the principal's decision, though with one condition: the requirement has to be flexible enough that every student can find something that fits. Done well, a participation rule doesn't burden students. It gives them an opening many would never create for themselves.

Think about how a typical student spends the school day. Class periods are fixed, seating is often assigned, and the people around you are mostly the ones who happen to share your schedule. A student who is shy, new to town, or simply unsure of where they belong can go months without a real conversation beyond "Do you have a pencil?" An extracurricular changes the arithmetic. Join the yearbook staff and you are suddenly spending Thursday afternoons arguing about photo captions with sophomores and seniors you would otherwise never have met. Join the robotics club and you learn quickly that a robot with a loose wire is a shared problem, not an individual failure. Friendships form in those moments almost by accident.

There is also a practical benefit that doesn't show up on a report card. Colleges and employers consistently say they want people who can work with others, manage their time, and follow through on a commitment. A student who has spent a season on the track team has learned to show up at six in the morning when they would rather sleep. A student who serves on student council has sat through a budget debate and discovered that persuading a room of classmates takes more than being loud. These are skills a textbook can describe but not really teach.

The strongest objection is that some students already have too much to do. A teenager who works after school to help pay family bills, or who looks after younger siblings, can't simply add a three-hour rehearsal. That concern is real, and a sensible policy should answer it. The requirement could be satisfied by something modest, like a lunchtime chess club, a once-a-week tutoring program, or a service project that meets a few times a semester. The principal could also allow exceptions for students with documented work or family obligations. A rule with that kind of give is far more defensible than one that treats every schedule as identical.

Others argue that forced participation produces halfhearted participation, and that a student who is made to join the drama club will simply stand in the back and wait for the clock. Sometimes that will happen. But I suspect it happens less than critics assume. Many students resist joining things not because they dislike the activity but because walking into an unfamiliar room alone feels risky. A requirement removes that hesitation. Everyone is in the same position, and nobody has to explain why they showed up. Plenty of students who begin out of obligation stay because they discover they are good at something, or simply that they enjoy it.

Finally, school is supposed to prepare young people for more than tests. It should help them figure out what they care about. A student who never leaves the classroom may never learn that they love photography, or that they have a knack for organizing people, or that they can run a mile faster than they believed. Requiring one activity is a small push toward that discovery.

For these reasons, I support the principal's decision. With enough variety on offer and reasonable room for students who truly cannot take on more, the policy would make our school more connected and give students a chance to find out who they are.

Dear Senator,

I write to urge you to oppose any effort to abandon the Electoral College in favor of a direct national popular vote. While the current system has real flaws, the alternatives are worse.

The Electoral College is not a place but a constitutional process designed by the Founding Fathers as a compromise between congressional selection and a pure popular vote. Under this system, each state receives electors equal to its congressional delegation, and forty-eight states plus Washington, D.C., use a winner-take-all rule. Critics rightly point out that this arrangement can produce a president who loses the nationwide popular tally, as happened in 2000 and 2016. They also note that campaigns lavish attention on a handful of swing states while ignoring safe states, and that faithless electors theoretically could overturn a state’s choice.

These criticisms deserve respect, but they ignore what the Electoral College protects. Judge Richard Posner argues that the system preserves federalism and forces candidates to build broad national coalitions rather than simply running up enormous margins in densely populated urban areas or in one region. A direct popular vote would tempt campaigns to focus only on the largest media markets and most concentrated population centers, leaving rural and smaller states without a meaningful voice. Because the Electoral College requires geographic breadth, candidates must appeal to voters in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Arizona, and Georgia, not just California and New York.

Moreover, the Electoral College produces a clear and decisive winner quickly. A nationwide popular vote would invite a single national recount of roughly 150 million ballots, a logistical and legal nightmare. Today, disputed recounts are confined to individual states, as the Office of the Federal Register notes in describing the system’s state-by-state allocation. That containment is a practical advantage that a raw popular vote cannot offer.

Some argue that the winner-take-all rule is undemocratic. But states are free to allocate electors proportionally, as Maine and Nebraska already do, without a constitutional amendment. If more states adopted that approach, the perceived problem of swing-state dominance could be reduced without sacrificing federalism and without empowering a handful of large cities to dictate every presidential election. I am not against reform, but I am against replacing a balanced, state-based process with a simple national tally that would intensify regional polarization.

Please stand against proposals to abolish the Electoral College. It is imperfect, but it remains the better safeguard of our diverse republic.

Sincerely,  
[Your Name]

As the United States continues to grapple with the complexities of its presidential election system, I am writing to argue in favor of keeping the Electoral College. While some critics argue that this system is undemocratic and favors certain states over others, I believe that the benefits of the Electoral College outweigh its drawbacks. In fact, the Electoral College was established by the Founding Fathers as a compromise between election of the President by a vote in Congress and election of the President by a popular vote of qualified citizens, as outlined by the Office of the Federal Register.

One of the primary concerns about the Electoral College is that a candidate can win the national popular vote and still lose the presidency, as happened in 2000 and 2016. Critics like Bradford Plumer argue that this is undemocratic and can lead to a situation where the winner of the popular vote does not win the presidency. However, I would counter that this system actually helps to preserve federalism and ensures that candidates build broad national coalitions across both large and small states. As Judge Richard A. Posner notes, the Electoral College prevents candidates from winning solely by running up massive vote totals in densely populated urban areas or single regions. This forces candidates to campaign and listen to voters in a variety of states, rather than focusing solely on the coasts or urban areas.

Another criticism of the Electoral College is that it can lead to a situation where "faithless electors" can theoretically vote against their state's popular choice. While this is a concern, it is worth noting that this has rarely happened in practice. Additionally, the Electoral College produces a clear, decisive winner quickly and avoids the chaos of a nationwide popular-vote recount, confining any disputed vote recounts to individual states. This is particularly important in a country as large and diverse as the United States, where a national recount could be a logistical nightmare.

Some argue that the Electoral College is unfair because it gives disproportionate weight to the votes of certain states. However, I would argue that this system actually helps to give a voice to smaller states that might otherwise be ignored. Under a popular vote system, candidates might focus solely on the most populous states and ignore the concerns of voters in smaller states. The Electoral College ensures that all states have a minimum number of electoral votes, regardless of their population.

In conclusion, while the Electoral College is not a perfect system, I believe that it is an important part of our democratic process. It helps to preserve federalism, ensures that candidates build broad national coalitions, and produces a clear, decisive winner quickly. Rather than abandoning the Electoral College, we should work to improve it and make it more responsive to the needs of all voters. By doing so, we can ensure that our presidential election system remains fair, democratic, and representative of the will of the American people. I urge you to consider the importance of the Electoral College and to work to preserve this vital institution.

According to the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," tech leaders like Google cofounder Sergey Brin envision a future where autonomous vehicles use less fuel, take up less parking, and make transportation completely public. While this sounds like an exciting vision, the reality is far more dangerous. Driverless cars should not be developed for our roads today because their technology is unreliable in everyday weather, human drivers lose focus when forced to supervise them, and our legal system is not ready to handle who is to blame when crashes happen.

First of all, the technology inside these vehicles simply is not ready for real-world driving. The article explains that autonomous cars rely on laser radar, cameras, GPS, and sensors to detect obstacles and traffic signals. However, safety experts warn that these sensors struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, and unmarked construction zones. Driving conditions are rarely perfect, especially during winter or in areas with constant road work. Cell phones have become so woven into daily life that many people reach for them almost automatically. A notification sounds, a map reroutes, or a call comes in, and the instinct is to respond. Behind the wheel, however, that instinct can have consequences far more serious than a missed message. Drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones actively while operating a vehicle, whether by holding the device, typing, scrolling, or even engaging in a demanding hands-free conversation. The small conveniences offered by a phone are not worth the risk created by divided attention.

The most obvious danger is visual and manual distraction. Reading a text message requires a driver to look away from the road, sometimes for several seconds. At highway speeds, a vehicle can travel the length of a football field in that time. Even a quick glance can prevent someone from noticing a braking car, a pedestrian entering a crosswalk, or debris in the road. Typing, selecting music, searching for directions, and recording videos are similarly hazardous because they take at least one hand from the wheel and focus from driving.

Yet banning only handheld phones does not entirely solve the problem. A driver using a hands-free device may keep both hands on the steering wheel and eyes facing forward, but conversation still consumes mental attention. Research and common experience both suggest that a person deeply involved in a phone call can fail to register details directly in front of them. Speaking to a passenger is not exactly the same: a passenger shares the driving environment and may naturally pause during difficult traffic conditions. Someone on the other end of a phone call cannot see an approaching intersection, heavy rain, or a driver’s need to concentrate.

That does not mean phones must be completely absent from vehicles. They can serve useful purposes when used responsibly. Navigation systems can help drivers avoid getting lost, and a phone may be essential during an emergency or breakdown. The distinction should be between passive, prearranged assistance and active interaction. A driver should set a destination, choose music, adjust settings, and send necessary messages before putting the vehicle in motion. If a change is needed, the driver should pull over safely. Emergency calls should remain permitted, especially when they can bring help quickly to an injured person or dangerous situation.

Laws should reflect this principle clearly. Restrictions are most effective when they are easy to understand: no texting, scrolling, holding a phone, taking video, participating in social media, or conducting nonessential calls while driving. Technology can support these rules through driving modes that silence notifications or automatically respond that the recipient is on the road. Employers also have a responsibility not to pressure workers to answer calls or messages while driving.

Driving is an activity that demands continuous judgment. A cell phone may seem harmless because it is familiar and always nearby, but its distraction can turn an ordinary trip into a preventable tragedy. Drivers should reserve active phone use for after they park, allowing the road—and the people on it—to receive their full attention.

The emergence of autonomous vehicles marks a significant turning point in the history of modern technology. As outlined in the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," the debate surrounding these vehicles is complex, with both proponents and critics presenting valid arguments. While concerns about technological reliability and legal ambiguities are understandable, the benefits of pursuing driverless car development far outweigh the drawbacks. The potential to drastically reduce traffic fatalities, enhance mobility for vulnerable populations, and promote environmental efficiency makes the continued development of autonomous vehicles a worthwhile endeavor.

One of the most persuasive arguments in favor of driverless technology is its ability to minimize traffic accidents. Human error, which accounts for over 90 percent of traffic accidents, is often the result of preventable behaviors such as texting, drowsiness, or impaired driving. In contrast, autonomous vehicles are not susceptible to fatigue, emotional instability, or digital distractions. Equipped with advanced sensors, including laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer systems, these vehicles are designed to continuously monitor their surroundings, detecting obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals with precision. By removing human error from the equation, autonomous vehicles have the potential to significantly reduce the number of accidents on our roads, saving countless lives in the process.

Moreover, the advantages of driverless cars extend beyond safety. For instance, they offer a viable means of transportation for elderly or disabled individuals who may struggle with driving themselves. This not only enhances their mobility but also contributes to a more inclusive and equitable society. Additionally, autonomous vehicles could lead to a reduction in fuel consumption and parking requirements, as envisioned by Google cofounder Sergey Brin. His concept of a future with driverless public transportation, which uses half the fuel and half the parking space of traditional cars, is an intriguing one. By adopting autonomous vehicles, we may be able to create a more sustainable and environmentally friendly transportation system.

Despite these benefits, critics have raised important concerns about the limitations of current technology. For example, sensors can struggle in adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, and software systems remain vulnerable to glitches and cybersecurity threats. Furthermore, the issue of liability in the event of an accident remains unresolved, with questions surrounding who should be held responsible – the vehicle owner, software developer, or automaker. While these concerns are valid, they should not hinder the development of driverless cars. Instead, they should serve as a catalyst for further research and innovation, driving the creation of more sophisticated and reliable technologies.

In conclusion, the development of driverless cars is a pursuit that holds tremendous promise. While there are challenges to be addressed, the potential benefits of autonomous vehicles – from improved safety and increased mobility to enhanced environmental efficiency – make them an exciting and worthwhile endeavor. As we continue to navigate the complexities of this emerging technology, it is essential that we prioritize innovation and collaboration, working towards a future where driverless cars can safely and efficiently transport people, transforming the way we travel and interact with one another.

Dear Principal,

I believe that students should be required to perform community service, as long as the requirement is reasonable and offers different ways to participate. Community service helps students understand the needs of others, improves the school’s relationship with the community, and teaches responsibilities that cannot always be learned in a classroom.

First, volunteering helps students recognize that their actions can make a real difference. It is easy for young people to focus only on homework, sports, friends, and personal goals. Those things are important, but students also benefit from seeing the challenges faced by people outside their usual circles. For example, a student who tutors an elementary school child may realize how difficult reading can be for someone who does not receive much support at home. By spending even one hour a week helping that child practice, the tutor can improve the child’s confidence and academic skills. At the same time, the tutor develops patience, communication skills, and empathy.

Community service can also strengthen the place where students live. When students clean litter from parks, collect food for local families, visit senior citizens, or help at an animal shelter, they make their neighborhoods safer and more welcoming. These activities may seem small, but many small efforts can create significant results. A group of students who spends an afternoon cleaning a playground may make it a healthier place for younger children to use. Students would also be more likely to avoid littering themselves after seeing how much work it takes to clean public spaces.

Some people argue that mandatory service would take time away from studying, jobs, family responsibilities, or activities students enjoy. This concern is understandable. However, a service requirement does not have to be excessive. The school could require a limited number of hours each year, perhaps ten or fifteen, and allow students to complete them during weekends, school-sponsored events, or breaks. Students should also be able to choose from many types of service. A student with limited transportation could help organize a school donation drive, while another student could volunteer at a library or coach younger athletes. Flexible choices would make the program fairer and more meaningful.

In addition, requiring service would encourage students who might never volunteer on their own to give it a chance. Not everyone will immediately enjoy community service, but many students may discover interests or talents through it. Someone who helps at a food pantry might become interested in fighting hunger. Someone who assists younger students might consider becoming a teacher. Even if students do not continue volunteering after graduation, they will have learned that citizenship includes contributing to others.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge you to require a manageable amount of community service for all students. With flexible options and reasonable expectations, the program would benefit both students and the community they call home.

The question of whether summer projects should be teacher-designed or student-designed has sparked considerable debate. While teacher-designed projects can offer structure and alignment with standards, I believe student-designed projects are ultimately more valuable for students’ academic and personal growth. When students shape their own projects, they build autonomy, creativity, and self-motivation—skills that matter far beyond the classroom.

One major advantage is engagement. Students given the freedom to design their own summer work often choose topics that genuinely interest them, which leads to deeper investment. A student passionate about environmental conservation, for example, might study how pollution affects local wildlife by gathering data and running simple experiments. That kind of self-directed project lets students explore what they care about, turning learning into something they want to do rather than something they have to do. Teacher-designed assignments, by contrast, can sometimes feel rigid or disconnected from students’ lives, draining enthusiasm.

Student-designed projects also strengthen critical thinking, problem-solving, and time management. Because students must plan, carry out, and present their work on their own, they face real challenges that require thoughtful solutions. Consider a student who decides to make a documentary about a social issue. To complete it, she has to research, write a script, film footage, and edit everything into a coherent final product. Along the way, she learns to set goals, manage her time, and work through unexpected problems. These are exactly the skills employers and colleges look for, and they develop naturally when students have genuine responsibility for their projects.

Another reason to favor student-designed projects is that they can accommodate different learning styles and strengths. When students choose their own topics and formats, they can play to their abilities while still challenging themselves. A visual learner might create a series of infographics or an art project, while a verbal learner might write a short story or record a podcast. This flexibility helps more students succeed because the project fits how they learn best, rather than forcing everyone into the same mold.

Of course, teacher-designed projects have their merits, especially in ensuring coverage of key skills. Still, I believe the benefits of student-designed summer projects outweigh those advantages. Giving students ownership of their work encourages them to pursue their interests, practice independence, and develop skills that will serve them well in school and beyond. If we want students to become confident, curious, and capable learners, we should trust them to help design their own learning—and summer projects are a great place to start.

Dear Principal Martinez,

Thank you for asking for our feedback on the proposed policy change. While I understand that academics should always come first, I am writing to respectfully urge you not to raise the minimum GPA requirement from a C to a B average for sports and after-school activities. I believe this change would end up hurting more students than it helps.

First of all, extracurricular activities are often the main reason students stay motivated to keep their grades up in the first place. Right now, a C average means a student is passing all their classes. For many kids who struggle in school, maintaining a C average is already a major accomplishment that takes a lot of hard work. If the bar is suddenly moved up to a B, a lot of these students might feel like it is impossible to reach. Instead of working harder, they might just give up entirely, and their grades could drop from a C to an F. Being on a team or in the marching band gives students a sense of belonging and accountability to their coaches and peers. If we take that away, we lose our best leverage to keep them engaged with school.

Secondly, this policy could have the unintended effect of discouraging students from taking challenging classes. If a student wants to stay on the soccer team or participate in the school play, they might decide not to take an honors or AP course because they are worried they will get a C and lose their eligibility. School should be about pushing ourselves and learning, not avoiding tough subjects just to protect a GPA. 

Finally, after-school activities provide benefits that grades simply cannot measure. Sports, drama, debate, and music teach teamwork, discipline, time management, and leadership. They also provide a healthy outlet for stress. High school can be overwhelming, and having an hour or two after school to run on the track or work in the art studio does wonders for our mental health. If students with a C average are banned from these activities, they will likely just go home, sit on their phones, or get into trouble instead of doing something positive and supervised.

Instead of keeping C students off the field or out of clubs, I think a better solution would be to offer them more support. For example, the school could set up mandatory study tables or tutoring sessions for athletes and club members who have a C average. That way, students are pushed to improve academically without losing the activities that make them love coming to school.

Thank you for taking the time to read my letter and for caring about how your decisions affect the student body. I hope you will consider keeping the current C average requirement.

Sincerely,

Jordan Taylor
