Over the past few years, almost every student has experienced what it is like to learn from a computer screen. While some people could not wait to get back into a regular classroom, having the option to attend school from home actually offers a lot of benefits for many students. Even though distance learning is not perfect for everyone, having it available as a real choice can make a huge positive difference in a student's education, health, and daily life.

First of all, distance learning gives students a schedule that works much better for their physical and mental health. A lot of middle and high schools start insanely early, sometimes before 7:30 in the morning. When you add getting ready, packing lunch, and catching a bus or sitting in traffic, teenagers are often waking up before sunrise and functioning on very little sleep. With online classes, students cut out the commute completely. That extra hour of sleep might not sound like a huge deal to adults, but for a tired high schooler, it can completely change how focused you are. You can eat breakfast at your own kitchen table and start first period feeling awake instead of totally exhausted.

Another reason distance learning is beneficial is that regular classrooms are not always the best environment for everyone to concentrate. In-person school has tons of distractions, like noisy hallways, people talking during lectures, and teachers having to stop constantly to manage behavior. On top of that, social pressure and anxiety are very real problems for a lot of kids. When you are working from home, you can create a quiet space where you actually absorb the material without worrying about who is staring at you or getting caught up in school drama. For students who get overwhelmed easily, being in a comfortable setting makes learning way less stressful.

Additionally, online options help students who have special circumstances, like chronic illnesses, doctor appointments, or even busy extracurricular schedules. In a traditional setup, if you get sick or have to travel, you might miss several days and come back completely buried in makeup work. With distance learning, you can log into the video call, listen to the teacher, and stay on top of your assignments without falling behind. It also teaches you how to manage your own time and communicate via email, which are skills people actually need after high school.

Some critics argue that distance learning ruins students' social skills and makes people unmotivated. That can definitely happen if someone is forced into it when they do not want to be. However, the main point is having the option. Students who thrive on sports, clubs, and seeing their friends all day can stay in the physical building. But for the students who work better at their own pace in a calm environment, attending class from home is a lifesaver.

In conclusion, offering distance learning gives students flexibility, better focus, and a healthier routine. Not everyone learns the same way, and school should not be treated like one size fits all. Giving students the choice to attend classes from home would help a lot more of us succeed.

Dear Principal,

As our school evaluates its stance on personal technology, the decision regarding student cell phone usage stands out as a critical choice for our entire community. While I understand that the temptation to eliminate distractions entirely makes a total ban appealing, I firmly believe that Policy 1—allowing students to bring their phones to school and use them during lunch and free periods, while keeping them turned off during class—is the superior, more balanced choice.

First and foremost, allowing students to possess their phones facilitates essential communication between families. Many students manage complex schedules involving extracurricular activities, part-time jobs, and family responsibilities that often require real-time coordination. In the event of an unexpected schedule change or a family emergency, direct communication between parent and child offers vital peace of mind. Under a total ban, the main office would quickly become overwhelmed by parents calling to relay routine logistical messages. Furthermore, students rely on their devices for safety and navigation during their commutes to and from campus. Banning phones from school grounds entirely ignores the daily realities of modern life.

In addition to safety and logistics, Policy 1 serves an educational purpose by helping students develop digital responsibility. The ultimate goal of high school is to prepare young adults for higher education and the professional world. In college and the workplace, individuals are not stripped of their technology; rather, they are expected to exercise self-control by staying off their devices during instructional or meeting times and reserving their usage for designated breaks. A total ban treats students punitively rather than constructively. By enforcing strict boundaries during instructional time while permitting use during social periods, the school provides an environment where students can practice healthy digital habits under realistic conditions.

Finally, Policy 1 is far more practical and enforceable than a total prohibition. A zero-tolerance policy inevitably creates an adversarial dynamic between students and staff. When phones are completely forbidden, students do not stop bringing them; they simply hide them, leading to clandestine use in hallways and restrooms. This forces teachers and administrators to spend valuable time acting as surveillance officers rather than educators. Conversely, when students know they will have legitimate access to their devices during lunch, they are far more inclined to respect classroom rules and keep their phones powered down and stowed away during instructional hours.

Our school’s regulations should reflect the balance and maturity we expect students to demonstrate in their adult lives. Completely barring phones attempts to avoid a modern reality, whereas Policy 1 offers a thoughtful compromise that protects instructional focus while respecting personal autonomy. For these reasons, I respectfully urge you to adopt Policy 1 and help our student body cultivate responsible, lifelong technology habits.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

Summer projects should be student-designed, within a framework set by teachers. The point of assigning work over break is to keep young minds active, and nothing keeps a mind active like genuine interest. A worksheet packet handed out in June is likely to be abandoned by July and rushed through in the last weekend of August. A project a student chose, shaped, and cares about has a far better chance of surviving the pull of video games, sleeping in, and long afternoons at the pool.

Consider what happens with the teacher-designed version. A history teacher assigns a five-page report on the causes of the First World War. Every student gets the same prompt, the same rubric, and the same dull deadline. Some will complete it faithfully, but many will copy from an encyclopedia site or ask a sibling for help. The assignment measures compliance more than learning. Worse, it teaches students that learning is something done to them by an authority, switched on in September and off in June.

Now imagine a student who loves baking. Given the freedom to design a project, she proposes testing how altitude, humidity, or ingredient substitutions change the texture of bread, keeping a log and photographing results. She has to form a question, plan a method, track data, and explain her conclusions, which are the same skills a chemistry teacher hopes to build. Another student who is fascinated by local history might interview his grandfather about the town's closed textile mill and assemble the recordings into a short documentary. Neither project would appear on a standard syllabus, yet both demand research, writing, and critical thinking, and both would likely be remembered long after a worksheet was recycled.

The strongest objection is that students, left alone, will choose something easy or skip the work entirely. That is a fair worry, and it is why pure freedom is not the answer. Teachers should still play a role: requiring a written proposal before school lets out, setting minimum expectations for time and depth, and scheduling a check-in or two over the summer. A teacher can read a proposal for "making a video game" and push the student toward something more rigorous, such as learning basic coding and documenting the process. This arrangement keeps standards intact while leaving the creative decisions with the student.

There is also a practical benefit that rarely gets mentioned. Choosing a project is itself a skill. Adults are rarely handed a detailed prompt; they must decide what is worth pursuing, estimate how long it will take, and manage their own time. Students who practice this at fourteen will be less helpless at twenty. A teacher-designed assignment, however well crafted, removes that practice and leaves the hardest part of the work, deciding what to do, already done.

Teacher-designed projects do have one advantage: they are easy to grade and compare. But ease of grading is a poor reason to shape a child's summer. If the goal is to ensure students keep learning, the better question is not what is simplest to assess, but what students will actually do when no one is watching. They will do what interests them. Schools should build on that instinct rather than fight it, offering structure at the edges and trust at the center.

Every year, thousands of lives are shattered on public roadways, largely because human beings are prone to fatigue, distraction, and poor judgment. The prospect of self-driving vehicles—navigating roads via sophisticated suites of cameras, laser radar, GPS, and computer sensors—offers a radical departure from this grim reality. While skeptics point to weather vulnerabilities and tangled legal questions, halting research and testing would be a grave mistake. The ongoing development of autonomous vehicles is a critical endeavor that promises to dramatically improve road safety, expand societal mobility, and foster a more efficient transportation infrastructure.

The most compelling argument for autonomous vehicles rests on human fallibility. Over ninety percent of vehicular accidents today stem from human error, whether caused by an individual glancing down at a text message, nodding off after a double shift, or driving under the influence of alcohol. Autonomous systems do not suffer from exhaustion, emotional distress, or chemical impairment. By monitoring lane markings, traffic signals, and sudden obstacles without a split second of inattention, driverless technology addresses the root cause of road trauma. Drastically curtailing crashes would save countless lives and substantially ease the burden of astronomical insurance costs for everyday commuters.

Beyond immediate safety dividends, autonomous transit presents transformative societal benefits. Sergey Brin, cofounder of Google, envisions a future where autonomous public transit could cut both fuel consumption and required parking space in half. Such an evolution would free up valuable urban land and reduce the environmental toll of private vehicle ownership. Equally vital is the profound independence this technology offers to populations historically left stranded by conventional transit design. Elderly individuals and people with disabilities, who are frequently shut out from driving standard automobiles, stand to regain unprecedented autonomy and access to essential services.

It is undeniable that significant hurdles remain. Critics correctly note that current sensors can falter when blinded by heavy rain, thick snow, dense fog, or the unpredictable layouts of construction zones. Software glitches and cybersecurity vulnerabilities pose real dangers, and questions of legal liability—whether fault lies with the car owner, software programmer, or manufacturer when a collision occurs—demand clear legislative frameworks. Furthermore, semi-autonomous transitions can leave human drivers dangerously unprepared to retake control on short notice. Yet these issues represent engineering and policy challenges, not permanent road blocks. Abandoning autonomous vehicle research will not resolve these flaws; continued development is the only method by which sensors become weatherproof, networks become secure, and regulators establish sensible accountability protocols.

No transformative technology emerges fully formed, and the automobile was hardly without peril when it first replaced the horse and carriage. Given that the alternative is tolerating an ongoing epidemic of preventable traffic fatalities, the path forward is unmistakable. By continuing to refine autonomous systems with rigorous oversight, society can replace human recklessness with digital vigilance, building a safer and more inclusive transit system for generations to come.

When faced with significant dilemmas, individuals often seek guidance from multiple sources. While consulting a single trusted advisor can provide immediate clarity, relying solely on one person's opinion can be hazardous. Human beings are inherently subjective, with their experiences, biases, and emotions influencing their perspectives. Seeking multiple opinions is a crucial strategy for making better choices, as it helps mitigate personal bias, uncover hidden blind spots, and empower individuals to construct a balanced judgment.

The value of consulting multiple people lies in its ability to counteract individual bias. Every advisor brings their own unique perspective, shaped by their history, fears, and triumphs. For instance, a young professional considering leaving a corporate job to launch a startup may receive cautious advice from a risk-averse parent, while an aggressive venture capitalist might encourage bold action. By gathering counsel from both sources, the entrepreneur can weigh the potential risks and benefits, avoiding the extremes of either perspective. This balanced approach allows individuals to consider multiple facets of a decision, rather than being swayed by a single, potentially skewed viewpoint.

Moreover, seeking diverse opinions provides access to specialized knowledge and expertise. Complex decisions often require input from multiple fields, and consulting various advisors can help individuals assemble a comprehensive understanding of the issue. In healthcare, for example, patients are often encouraged to seek second or third opinions when facing a serious diagnosis. A surgeon, oncologist, and physical therapist may each offer distinct perspectives on the best course of treatment, allowing the patient to make an informed decision. This approach does not indicate a lack of trust in any single professional, but rather a desire to gather a complete understanding of the options and their potential outcomes.

Navigating differing opinions also fosters critical thinking and active ownership of decisions. When individuals rely on a single advisor, they may passively adopt that person's judgment, outsourcing the responsibility of the outcome. In contrast, considering multiple perspectives requires individuals to evaluate evidence, examine rationales, and reconcile contradictions. This process stimulates critical thinking, enabling individuals to distill the underlying wisdom from each advisor and synthesize a customized path that aligns with their core values and objectives.

Ultimately, seeking multiple opinions requires effort and discernment, but the benefits far outweigh the initial expenditure. By tempering subjective bias, uncovering vital information, and promoting rigorous evaluation, a diverse range of perspectives can shield individuals from short-sighted choices. In a complex and uncertain world, wisdom is rarely found in a single voice; it is forged by thoughtfully listening to many perspectives and choosing one's own direction. By embracing this approach, individuals can make more informed, balanced decisions that reflect their unique needs and circumstances.

Dear Principal,

I believe the school should adopt Policy 1, which allows students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times, while requiring them to be turned off during class. This policy creates a fair balance between protecting learning and recognizing that phones are an important part of students’ daily lives.

First, phones can be very useful before and after school. Many students rely on them to contact parents about rides, sports practices, appointments, or changes in plans. If a bus is late or an activity ends early, students can quickly let their families know where they are. Without phones, students may have to wait in the office to use a school phone, which could be inconvenient and create long lines. In some situations, being able to contact a parent immediately also gives students a greater sense of safety.

Allowing phones during free time would also make lunch and study breaks more flexible. Students could check schedules, look up information for assignments, read messages from family members, or listen to music with headphones. Not every student wants to spend every free moment talking to a large group of people. Some students may prefer a quiet break, and a phone can give them a way to relax responsibly. Phones can also help students coordinate group projects, club meetings, and after-school activities.

At the same time, the rule that phones must be turned off during class is important. Classrooms should be places where students listen, participate, and focus on their work. Notifications, games, and social media can easily distract students if phones are available during lessons. A clear rule would make expectations simple: during class, phones stay put away and silent; during approved free periods, students may use them appropriately. Teachers would not have to compete with screens for attention, and students would still have access to their phones when they genuinely need them.

Policy 2 may seem easier because it removes phones entirely, but it is too strict. Students would still bring phones in secret, and teachers would spend time searching for or confiscating them. A complete ban could also create unnecessary conflict between students and staff. Rather than teaching students how to manage technology responsibly, it would simply keep technology out of sight. Learning self-control is an important skill, especially because students will need to use phones appropriately in high school, college, and future jobs.

Of course, Policy 1 should include consequences for students who use phones during class or misuse them during free time. Repeated violations could lead to a phone being held in the office until the end of the day or picked up by a parent. With clear expectations and consistent enforcement, most students would understand the limits.

Policy 1 respects students’ needs while keeping academics as the school’s priority. It is practical, balanced, and more likely to encourage responsible behavior. I hope you will choose this policy for our school.

Sincerely,  
A Concerned Student

Dear Senator,

My name is Jordan, and I am a high school student in your district. I am writing to ask you to support changing the way we elect the president from the Electoral College to a national popular vote. I know this is a big change, but I think it would make our elections fairer and give more people a reason to participate.

The biggest problem with the Electoral College is that the person with the most votes can still lose. According to Bradford Plumer in "The Indefensible Electoral College," this happened in both 2000 and 2016. That doesn't seem right to me. In school we learn that democracy means the majority decides, but the Electoral College can turn that upside down. If millions more people choose one candidate, that candidate should be the one who wins.

Another problem is how the system affects campaigns. The Office of the Federal Register explains that forty-eight states and Washington, D.C. use a "winner-take-all" system. That means if a candidate wins a state by even a small amount, they get all of its electoral votes. Plumer points out that because of this, candidates spend nearly all their time in a few swing states and mostly ignore everyone else. If you live in a state that is safely one party, your vote hardly seems to matter, and that can make people feel like staying home. With a national popular vote, every vote would count the same no matter where a person lives, so candidates would have to care about voters in every state.

I do understand the other side. Judge Richard Posner argues in "In Defense of the Electoral College" that the system protects federalism and makes candidates build broad coalitions across big and small states. He worries that without it, candidates would just run up huge totals in big cities. That is a fair concern, but I am not totally convinced. Under a popular vote, a candidate would still need millions of votes from all kinds of places, because cities alone do not have enough voters to win. Right now, small states are also not really getting attention unless they are swing states. Wyoming and Vermont, for example, get ignored just like big states that are not competitive. So the current system does not actually protect small states the way people say it does.

Posner also says the Electoral College gives a clear winner quickly and keeps recounts inside one state instead of across the whole country. This is probably his strongest point, since a national recount would be hard. However, the Electoral College has not prevented problems either. The 2000 election came down to a recount in one state, and that was still very stressful for the country. Also, Plumer mentions that "faithless electors" could vote against their state's choice, which adds another kind of uncertainty. A national vote would be simpler to understand because the person with the most votes wins. If the race were very close, we could create clear rules for recounts ahead of time.

In conclusion, I believe a national popular vote is the better choice because it respects the idea of one person, one vote. It would stop the situation where the winner of the popular vote loses, it would encourage campaigns to talk to voters everywhere, and it would make people feel their votes matter. I hope you will support efforts in our state to move toward a national popular vote, such as an agreement among states or a constitutional amendment.

Thank you for taking the time to read my letter.

Sincerely,
Jordan

Students should have the option to attend classes from home, provided it remains an option and not a replacement for the classroom. For many students, distance learning solves problems that a traditional school day simply cannot, and the benefits are too real to dismiss.

Consider the student who is sick, or recovering from surgery, or managing a chronic condition like Crohn's disease or severe migraines. In a purely in-person system, that student falls behind with every absence, then spends weeks scrambling to catch up on missed labs and lectures. With a video connection, she can listen to the discussion from her bed on a bad day and still submit the same assignments as everyone else. The difference between staying on track and quietly sliding toward failure can come down to something as simple as a laptop and a stable internet connection.

Health is only one example. Some students live in rural areas where the bus ride takes ninety minutes each way. That is three hours a day spent staring out a window, time that could go to homework, sleep, or helping on the family farm. Others are competitive athletes, young actors, or musicians whose training schedules clash with a standard timetable. A teenage swimmer who rises at 4:30 for practice is not served well by a system that demands she also be physically present at 8:00 for first period. Flexibility lets these students pursue serious talents without abandoning their education.

There is also the matter of learning style and environment. Not everyone thrives in a loud, crowded building. Students with anxiety, or those who are bullied, sometimes find that school itself becomes the obstacle to learning. At home, free from the daily dread of the hallway, they may finally concentrate. I have a cousin who barely passed ninth grade in person and then earned nearly straight A's the following year in an online program. His intelligence hadn't changed; his surroundings had.

Critics are right to raise concerns, of course. School is where children learn to collaborate, argue, and make friends, and no screen fully replicates a lab partner or a hallway conversation. Remote learning also demands self-discipline, and a student without a quiet space or reliable technology can be left worse off. These are serious objections. But they argue for careful design, not for taking the choice away. Schools can lend out laptops and hotspots, require regular check-ins with teachers, and encourage remote students to join clubs or occasional in-person sessions. A student who is struggling online can be moved back into the classroom, just as one who struggles in the classroom might be moved online.

What matters most is that education fits the person receiving it. A single model, applied to every student regardless of circumstance, inevitably fails some of them. Offering distance learning acknowledges that young people have different needs, different homes, and different paths. Giving them the chance to choose, with support and oversight, does not weaken education. It widens the door so that more students can walk through it.

Seeking advice from more than one person can lead to better decisions because different people notice different risks, values, and possibilities. A single opinion may be useful, especially if it comes from someone experienced, but it is still shaped by that person’s background and assumptions. Listening to several perspectives gives someone a fuller picture before making an important choice.

For example, imagine a student deciding whether to attend a university far from home. A parent might focus on safety, cost, and the emotional difficulty of moving away. A teacher may emphasize the school’s academic programs and internship opportunities. Meanwhile, a friend who has already moved away for college could describe practical issues that adults might overlook, such as finding roommates, managing laundry, or dealing with homesickness. None of these opinions is automatically correct, but together they help the student consider both the exciting and difficult parts of the decision.

Multiple opinions are also valuable because they can reveal blind spots. People often seek advice from someone who agrees with them, especially when they already have a preferred answer. This can feel reassuring, but it may not be helpful. Suppose someone wants to quit a stable job to start a small business. An enthusiastic friend might encourage the idea because it sounds brave and creative. A financially cautious relative might point out the need for savings, insurance, and a backup plan. A business owner could offer practical advice about customers, taxes, and long work hours. By hearing all three views, the person can still pursue the business idea, but with more realistic preparation.

At the same time, asking for several opinions does not mean allowing other people to make the decision. Advice can become confusing if a person treats every comment as equally important. Some sources are more informed than others. For medical questions, a trained doctor’s opinion should carry more weight than an online rumor. For a legal problem, speaking with a qualified lawyer is usually wiser than relying on a neighbor’s guess. The goal is not simply to collect the largest number of opinions; it is to seek thoughtful advice from people with relevant experience and different points of view.

Hearing multiple perspectives can also help someone understand what matters most to them. If several people disagree about a choice, the disagreement may reveal competing priorities. For instance, one person may value security, while another values independence or adventure. A young adult deciding whether to accept a high-paying job in another city may realize, after talking with family and mentors, that salary is important but not the only factor. They may care just as much about being near loved ones, having time for hobbies, or working in a field they find meaningful.

Ultimately, good decisions require both information and judgment. Other people can provide knowledge, challenge assumptions, and share lessons from their own lives. The final choice still belongs to the person facing it, but multiple opinions can make that choice more careful, informed, and confident.

As our school reconsiders its cell phone policy, I have thought carefully about the two options. Policy 1 would let students bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free periods, as long as they are turned off during class. Policy 2 would ban phones from campus altogether. Both aim to reduce distractions, but I believe Policy 1 is the stronger choice because it is realistic, promotes responsibility, and still protects learning time.

Policy 1 recognizes how normal phones are in our daily lives. Most students already use them to stay in touch with family, keep track of assignments, and look up information quickly. Allowing phone use during lunch and free time shows that the school trusts us and understands our routines. It also lets phones be useful outside of class. Students could collaborate on projects, check educational apps, or manage their schedules without interfering with lessons.

A full ban, on the other hand, feels unrealistic and overly strict. It would likely lead to more frustration than it prevents and could make students feel that the school does not trust them to make good choices. There are practical problems, too. Many students need to reach parents about rides, after-school activities, or last-minute family changes. Taking phones away entirely would remove a simple and reliable way to handle those everyday situations.

Another advantage of Policy 1 is that it gives students a chance to practice responsible phone use. During free time, the school can guide us toward healthy habits: knowing when to put the phone down, respecting others, and managing distractions. These are real skills we will need long after graduation. A ban avoids the problem instead of teaching us how to handle it.

Of course, this policy would work best with clear rules and consequences. Phones could be required to stay on silent during lunch, certain areas could be off-limits, and students who break the rules could face fair consequences. With those guardrails in place, phones would not have to disrupt learning. Instead, they could become another tool students learn to use well.

In the end, allowing phones during free time is more practical and more educational than banning them completely. It respects students, keeps families connected, and helps us build the self-control we need in a digital world. I hope you will give Policy 1 serious consideration.

Summer projects should be student-designed. I know some people think teachers should design them so the work is more academic, but in my experience, when a teacher picks the project, most students just see it as another assignment to get through. When students get to choose what they work on, they actually learn more because they care about the topic.

One reason student-designed projects work better is that they let people use their own strengths. For example, my friend Maria is really into art. If a teacher assigned everyone to write a research paper over the summer, she might do a okay job, but she would be bored and probably copy a lot from the internet. Instead, she designed a project where she learned about different mural styles in our city and then painted a small mural on a wall in her garage. She had to research artists, plan a design, and write an artist statement. She learned more from that than she would from a generic paper because she was excited to see the final painting.

Another reason is that student-designed projects feel more connected to real life. Teachers can design good projects, but they often have to fit the whole class. When I was in seventh grade, we had to do a summer reading log with specific questions for one book. I liked the book, but the questions felt forced. The next summer, my teacher let us design our own project with approval. I chose to build a small raised garden bed and keep a journal about what I planted, what worked, and what failed. I had to read about soil, bugs, and watering schedules. That was real learning, and I still remember it. If a teacher had told me to do a garden project, maybe I would have liked it, but choosing it myself made me work harder.

Some people might say student-designed projects are too easy or that students will just pick something simple. That can happen, but the solution is not to take away choice. Schools can set rules for student-designed projects, like requiring a plan, a certain amount of time, and a final presentation or reflection. A teacher can approve the plan before summer starts. That way the project is still rigorous, but the student owns it.

In the end, summer is a break from regular school. If we have to do a project, it should not feel like a punishment. Letting students design their own summer projects teaches us to be responsible for our own learning, and that is a skill we will need in high school, college, and jobs. When we choose something we actually want to learn, we remember it long after summer ends.

Dear Principal,

When I think about the argument over community service, I picture two of my friends. Maya spends Tuesday afternoons helping third graders sound out words. Derek groans that he barely has time for homework and soccer. Both perspectives are real, yet I believe requiring service is the right call—not because every student will love it, but because it teaches something classrooms cannot.

A requirement does not have to be a burden. Our school already mandates physical education because movement matters. We require math and history because informed citizens need certain knowledge. Community service belongs in that same category. When students tutor younger children, they learn patience and how to explain ideas clearly. When they clean up litter in local parks, they see the direct result of their effort. These experiences shape character in ways a lecture never will. I have watched a quiet classmate become more confident after a semester reading to kindergartners. She had to find her voice, and the service gave her a reason.

Critics say service takes time away from what students need or want to do. I understand that pressure. Some students have jobs, care for siblings, or take demanding courses. But that is exactly why a well-designed requirement should include flexible options and a modest hour total. Ten or fifteen hours over a school year is not a life-destroying demand. It is roughly one afternoon every few weeks. In return, students discover interests and strengths they might never encounter. A friend who planned to study computer science spent a Saturday showing senior citizens how to video call their grandchildren. He complained beforehand, but afterward he talked about how grateful they were, and how he had never thought about technology as a tool for human connection.

There is also a practical benefit. Colleges and employers often look for evidence that a person can commit to something beyond themselves. More importantly, communities need young people. Elementary schools need reading tutors. Parks need cleanup crews. Food banks need volunteers to sort donations. If students are only encouraged, not required, to help, many will simply opt out. That is not because they are selfish; it is because teenagers are busy and sometimes need a nudge. The nudge can turn into a habit.

None of this means the requirement should be rigid or punitive. It should offer choices that match different skills and schedules. A student who is anxious around people might prefer organizing a supply drive. An athlete might coach a youth team. The point is not to make everyone the same kind of volunteer. The point is to make service a normal part of growing up.

Requiring community service will not solve every problem, but it tells students that their time and energy matter to others. That message is worth a few afternoons. I hope you will make it part of our school’s expectations.

Sincerely,  
[Student Name]

As the school considers revising its cell phone policy, it is essential to weigh the pros and cons of each potential approach. The two policies under consideration, allowing students to use phones during free times or banning them entirely, have distinct implications for our educational environment. After careful consideration, I firmly believe that Policy 1, which permits students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch periods and other free times, is the better choice.

First and foremost, allowing students to use their phones during free times acknowledges the reality of modern life. Most students have phones and use them regularly to communicate with friends and family, access information, and stay organized. By permitting phone use during lunch and other free periods, the school demonstrates an understanding of this reality and provides students with a sense of autonomy and responsibility. This approach also recognizes that phones can be valuable tools for learning and creativity, as students can use them to access educational apps, conduct research, and collaborate with peers on projects.

In contrast, a complete ban on phones at school, as proposed by Policy 2, may be overly restrictive and unrealistic. Such a policy could lead to frustration and resentment among students, who may feel that the school is not trusting them to use their phones responsibly. Moreover, a ban could also create logistical challenges for students who rely on their phones to stay in touch with parents or guardians, particularly in cases where students need to communicate about after-school activities, transportation, or personal matters.

Another significant advantage of Policy 1 is that it promotes responsible phone use and digital citizenship. By allowing students to use their phones during free times, the school can teach them about the importance of balancing screen time with other activities, respecting others' privacy and boundaries, and using technology in a way that is respectful and considerate of others. This approach can help students develop essential life skills, such as self-regulation, empathy, and critical thinking, which are vital for success in an increasingly digital world.

Finally, it is worth noting that Policy 1 can be implemented with clear guidelines and consequences to ensure that students use their phones responsibly. For example, the school could establish rules about phone use during lunch and other free times, such as requiring students to keep their phones on silent mode or to refrain from using them in certain areas of the school. By setting clear expectations and consequences, the school can minimize distractions and ensure that phone use does not disrupt the learning environment.

In conclusion, allowing students to bring phones to school and use them during free times is a more effective and realistic approach than banning them entirely. This policy acknowledges the importance of phones in modern life, promotes responsible phone use and digital citizenship, and provides students with a sense of autonomy and responsibility. I strongly believe that Policy 1 is the better choice for our school and urge you to consider its potential benefits for our educational community.

When schools assign summer work, they do so with a specific fear in mind: that months away from class will erase hard-won skills. To guard against that erosion, summer projects should be teacher-designed. This is not because students lack good ideas, but because teachers alone can ensure the work targets the exact knowledge and habits that need reinforcing. A student’s natural instinct is to choose something comfortable, even delightful; a teacher’s professional instinct is to choose something that stretches the learner just enough. If the goal is continued academic growth, the design must rest with someone who understands the curriculum, the standards, and the individual student’s gaps.

Consider a seventh grader who finished the year shaky on proportional reasoning. Left to design a summer project, she might bake cupcakes or build a model—activities with some math but no guarantee of proportional thinking. A teacher-designed project, however, could present a concrete challenge: plan a family meal for eight, then scale the recipe down for three and up for twenty, recording every ratio and explaining the logic. That same student may still enjoy the work, but now the pleasure is paired with deliberate practice. Another example: an English teacher who knows that incoming eighth graders struggle to support arguments with textual evidence might assign a summer reading journal with guided prompts, asking students to collect three quotes per chapter and explain what each reveals about a character. A student left to her own devices may read a graphic novel and write a one-sentence summary—fun, but not enough to build analysis skills.

Teacher-designed does not mean teacher-rigid. Within a well-built project there is still room for choice: pick from four approved novels, select a local ecosystem for an observation log, or choose between a written report and a short podcast. That choice preserves motivation without abandoning rigor. The teacher can also build in accessibility, ensuring every student has the materials and clear instructions, rather than assuming some families can buy supplies or supervise ambitious independent plans. Student-designed projects often look impressive but depend heavily on home resources, leaving less advantaged students stranded or embarrassed.

Ultimately, the summer project exists for a reason beyond keeping children busy. It is a bridge from one grade to the next, and a bridge needs an architect who knows both shores. Students bring the energy and curiosity; teachers bring the map. When teacher design and student choice are combined, summer work stops being a chore and becomes a genuine extension of the classroom.

The traditional summer assignment is familiar to nearly every student: a dog-eared packet of math worksheets or a uniform novel accompanied by a list of comprehension questions. Completed in a frantic rush during the final seventy-two hours of August, these exercises rarely inspire intellectual growth. If the genuine goal of summer projects is to counter the proverbial "summer slide" without extinguishing a student’s natural curiosity, the work must be designed by the students themselves.

Top-down mandates fundamentally misjudge what makes summer valuable. During the academic year, curricula are heavily prescribed; state standards, rigid bell schedules, and standardized assessments dictate nearly every hour of a child's day. Summer offers an irreplaceable vacuum. When educators fill that space with generic, teacher-crafted tasks, they reduce education to mere compliance. Conversely, allowing students to frame their own investigations transforms an imposition into an act of agency. A teenager who dreads assigned literary analysis might eagerly spend two months researching and writing the opening chapters of a historical novel. Another student indifferent to textbook chemistry might build a hydroponic garden on a back porch, charting water chemistry and plant yield with meticulous care. In both instances, deep learning occurs not in spite of personal interest, but because of it.

Beyond fostering genuine enthusiasm, self-directed initiatives nurture crucial executive functioning skills that conventional homework systematically ignores. Developing a project from scratch demands that learners grapple with logistical ambiguity: What is a realistic scope for eight weeks? What resources are required, and how will success be measured? When teachers provide the prompts, rubrics, and milestones, they assume the entire burden of organization, inadvertently shielding students from the productive friction of planning. Navigating that friction—identifying an authentic problem, designing a methodology, and adjusting course after inevitable false starts—mirrors how adults tackle creative and professional challenges.

Skeptics often worry that complete autonomy risks drifting into triviality, leaving disengaged students to propose low-effort hobbies. The remedy, however, is not to revert to prefabricated assignments, but to redefine the teacher’s role from taskmaster to advisor. Before the final bell of the school year rings, students can submit structured proposals outlining their central questions, methods, and final deliverables. Faculty need only act as sounding boards, ensuring the scope is sufficiently rigorous while leaving ownership of the inquiry entirely in the student’s hands.

Education should not merely be something that happens to students; it must be something they author. If schools wish to cultivate resilient, lifelong thinkers, they have to trust young people with their own intellectual agency. Entrusting students with the design of their summer projects signals that their private curiosities have merit,

Imagine a world where nobody has to worry about a drunk driver crossing the center line, a distracted teenager looking down at a text, or an exhausted commuter falling asleep at the wheel. According to the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," this vision might be closer to reality than many people realize. While this technology still faces genuine hurdles, the development of autonomous vehicles should continue because of their incredible potential to save lives, expand mobility, and make our transportation system far more efficient.

The most compelling argument in favor of driverless cars comes down to safety. As the article points out, human error is responsible for over 90 percent of traffic accidents, frequently stemming from texting, drowsiness, or impaired driving. These are not flaws in our roads or vehicle hardware; they are simply human weaknesses. Computers do not get tired, check social media, or drink before getting behind the wheel. Autonomous vehicles rely on a combination of laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors designed to track obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals continuously. If this equipment can eliminate even a fraction of the mistakes everyday drivers make, thousands of lives could be saved each year, and insurance costs would likely drop as a result.

Driverless cars also promise greater freedom for individuals who are currently left behind by our car-dependent society. Elderly and disabled individuals often cannot drive themselves, severely limiting their access to medical care, grocery stores, and social activities. Autonomous transit could give them their independence back. On a broader scale, Google cofounder Sergey Brin envisions driverless public transit systems that require only half the fuel and parking space of conventional cars. Embracing that kind of design could dramatically reduce urban pollution, ease gridlock, and repurpose massive parking lots into parks or housing.

Critics, however, raise valid concerns that cannot be ignored. The article notes that modern sensors still struggle in harsh weather like heavy rain, snow, and fog, as well as in unmarked construction zones. Systems can also be vulnerable to software glitches and cybersecurity attacks. Furthermore, semi-autonomous features present a unique hazard: when human drivers are expected to step in during an emergency, studies show they quickly zone out, resulting in dangerously slow reaction times. On top of that, the legal system has yet to decide whether an accident is the fault of the car owner, the software programmer, or the automaker.

While these risks are real, they are reasons to test and regulate the technology more carefully, not to abandon it. Sensor limitations and cybersecurity threats are engineering puzzles that can be solved with ongoing research. In fact, the problem of distracted backup drivers simply reinforces the need to move toward fully autonomous systems that do not depend on human intervention at all. As for legal liability, our court systems have successfully adapted to past breakthroughs like commercial aviation and the internet, and lawmakers can establish clear rules for autonomous vehicles as well.

Walking away from driverless cars means accepting a status quo where human error claims thousands of lives every day. Driverless cars offer a cleaner, more accessible, and far safer future. With responsible testing and updated laws, we can overcome the remaining obstacles and build a roadway system that protects everyone.

Dear Senator,

As our country continues to debate the best method for electing our president, I strongly believe that the Electoral College should be preserved. While some argue that it is undemocratic and outdated, I think it serves an important purpose in ensuring that our president is elected through a fair and representative process.

One of the main criticisms of the Electoral College is that it can lead to a situation where the winner of the popular vote does not win the presidency. This has happened twice in recent history, in 2000 and 2016, and it can seem unfair to some. However, as Judge Richard A. Posner points out, the Electoral College helps to preserve federalism and prevents candidates from winning solely by running up massive vote totals in densely populated urban areas. This means that candidates must build broad national coalitions and appeal to voters in all states, not just those in heavily populated areas.

Another argument against the Electoral College is that it leads to a focus on "swing states" and depresses voter turnout in safely Democratic or Republican states. According to Bradford Plumer, this is because of the winner-take-all rule in most states, where all electoral votes are awarded to the candidate who wins the state's popular vote. However, I think this criticism is overstated. While it is true that presidential campaigns often focus on swing states, this does not mean that voters in other states are ignored. In fact, the Electoral College gives smaller states a voice in the election process that they would not have if the president were elected solely by popular vote.

Some people argue that we should switch to a popular vote system, where the candidate with the most votes nationwide wins the presidency. However, I think this would lead to a number of problems. For one, it would mean that candidates could win the presidency by focusing solely on densely populated urban areas, ignoring the needs and concerns of voters in smaller states and rural areas. It would also lead to a situation where the outcome of the election is uncertain and potentially disputed, as we saw in the 2000 presidential election. In contrast, the Electoral College produces a clear and decisive winner quickly, avoiding the chaos of a nationwide recount.

In addition, the Electoral College helps to ensure that our president is elected through a fair and representative process. As the Office of the Federal Register explains, each state is allocated a certain number of electoral votes based on its population, with a total of 538 electoral votes available. This means that smaller states have a disproportionate number of electoral votes compared to their population, giving them a greater voice in the election process. This is an important check on the power of larger states and helps to ensure that the president is elected through a process that is fair and representative of all Americans.

In conclusion, while the Electoral College is not perfect, I believe that it serves an important purpose in our democracy. It helps to preserve federalism, ensures that candidates build broad national coalitions, and produces a clear and decisive winner quickly. I urge you to preserve the Electoral College and reject any attempts to switch to a popular vote system. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

Distance learning is something a lot of schools are starting to offer, and I think students would benefit from having it as an option. It shouldn't replace regular school for everyone, but being able to attend classes from home helps students in ways that a traditional classroom sometimes can't.

The biggest reason is that distance learning helps students who can't always make it to school. Some students get sick for long periods of time, have medical problems, or have to take care of family members. If they miss a lot of school, they fall behind and it becomes really hard to catch up. For example, if a student breaks a leg or needs surgery, they might be out for weeks. With video classes, they could still hear the lesson, ask questions, and turn in assignments. That is a lot better than coming back and having no idea what the class has been doing.

Another benefit is that some students just learn better at home. At school there are a lot of distractions, like people talking, noise in the hallway, or kids goofing off during class. Some students get anxious in big crowds or get bullied, and that makes it hard to focus on learning. At home they can work in a quiet space and go at a pace that works for them. I know a kid who was always stressed out at school, but when he did a few online classes his grades went up because he could actually concentrate on the lessons.

Distance learning can also give students more choices. A small school might not offer classes like Advanced Placement physics or a foreign language such as Japanese. With online classes, students could take those courses from a teacher somewhere else. This could help them get ready for college and explore things they're interested in. It also saves time and money because students don't have to travel far or move to a different school just to get the class they want.

Of course, there are some problems with learning from home, and I understand why some people disagree. Students have to be responsible and manage their own time, and not everybody is good at that. It can be tempting to turn off your camera, check your phone, or watch videos instead of paying attention. Students might also miss out on seeing their friends and joining clubs or sports, which are a big part of school. Some families also don't have good internet or a computer, which wouldn't be fair. But I think these problems can be solved. Schools could lend out laptops, require students to check in with teachers regularly, and let students go to school for activities even if they take classes from home.

Overall, I believe students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home as long as it is an option and not a requirement. It helps students who are sick, who struggle in a regular classroom, or who want classes their school doesn't offer. If schools give support and set clear rules, distance learning can help more students succeed. Everyone learns differently, so it makes sense for schools to give students more than one way to get an education.

Decisions shape the trajectory of human life, ranging from mundane daily choices to monumental forks in the road regarding career, health, and relationships. When confronted with difficult crossroads, people often seek guidance from others. While consulting a single trusted confidant can offer comfort, relying entirely on one viewpoint can be hazardous. Seeking multiple opinions significantly improves decision-making by illuminating cognitive blind spots, mitigating individual biases, and providing a comprehensive foundation of diverse expertise.

First and foremost, gathering varied perspectives serves as an essential safeguard against personal bias. Every person views the world through a lens colored by their own history, emotional inclinations, and risk tolerance. Consequently, advice from one individual inevitably carries those subjective filters. In the medical field, for instance, patients facing a severe diagnosis frequently seek a second or third opinion before undergoing invasive procedures. A surgeon may naturally favor an operative intervention, whereas an internist might recommend physical therapy or lifestyle modification. By consulting both, the patient uncovers alternatives that a single practitioner might downplay, ensuring that the chosen course of action is both deliberate and well-rounded.

Furthermore, soliciting diverse viewpoints provides a holistic view of multifaceted problems. Complex decisions rarely exist in a vacuum; they involve professional, financial, and emotional dimensions that no single person can fully evaluate. Consider an individual contemplating a major career transition to a distant city. Consulting a senior industry mentor offers insight into long-term professional advancement and salary benchmarks. However, discussing the move with a peer provides an unvarnished assessment of company culture and everyday work-life balance, while consulting a family member illuminates how relocation might affect personal relationships. By weaving these distinct threads of counsel together, the decision-maker constructs a three-dimensional view of the opportunity, avoiding the risk of solving one problem only to create another.

Finally, encountering differing opinions compels individuals to engage in active critical thinking rather than passive acceptance. When someone receives unanimous praise or uniform advice, they might advance without rigorously interrogating the plan. Conversely, when opinions conflict, the decision-maker is forced to evaluate the merits of each argument, test underlying assumptions, and identify which factors matter most to them. This comparative process clarifies personal values. The goal of seeking multiple opinions is not to let a majority vote dictate one’s life, but to gather raw material to forge an informed, autonomous conclusion.

Ultimately, wisdom rarely resides in an echo chamber. While gathering input from several people requires more time and effort, the dividends are undeniable. By neutralizing individual biases, illuminating the multifaceted nature of complex dilemmas, and fostering critical evaluation, consulting multiple voices transforms uncertainty into clarity. In a world full of unpredictable variables, seeking broad counsel remains one of the most reliable strategies for making choices that endure the test of time.

The rise of digital technology has revolutionized the way we approach education, and one of the most significant advancements is the introduction of distance learning. By allowing students to attend classes remotely via video conferencing and online platforms, institutions can cater to a wider range of learners. While concerns about the loss of physical interaction are valid, the benefits of distance learning far outweigh the drawbacks. This approach expands educational accessibility, accommodates diverse learning styles, and helps students develop essential self-directed skills that are crucial in today's digital workforce.

One of the primary advantages of distance learning is its flexibility. Traditional classrooms often follow a rigid schedule that can be overwhelming for some students and too slow for others. In contrast, remote learning environments enable students to create their own study spaces, free from distractions, and learn at their own pace. With access to recorded lectures and digital materials, students can review complex concepts as many times as they need to, pausing, fast-forwarding, or rewinding to grasp the material fully. For instance, a student struggling with calculus can revisit difficult topics, conduct additional research, and return to the discussion when they feel more confident, ultimately gaining a deeper understanding of the subject matter.

Moreover, distance learning breaks down significant barriers to quality education. Daily commutes can be time-consuming, exhausting, and expensive, taking a toll on students and their families. By attending classes from home, students can reclaim valuable time and energy, which can be invested in academic pursuits, extracurricular activities, or simply getting enough rest. This approach is particularly beneficial for students with unique challenges, such as chronic medical conditions, physical disabilities, or those living in remote areas with limited access to resources. For example, a student in a rural district can enroll in advanced courses or specialized electives offered by distant schools without having to relocate, thereby expanding their academic opportunities.

Some argue that online learning leads to social isolation, diminishing the importance of peer interaction in developmental growth. However, modern distance learning is not a solitary experience; it incorporates collaborative tools, virtual discussions, and digital forums that mirror the realities of the modern professional world. Since distance learning is offered as an option, rather than a replacement for traditional classrooms, students and families can choose the environment that best suits their needs. In fact, managing one's education online fosters personal responsibility, time management, and technological literacy – essential qualities that are highly valued in today's workforce.

As institutions continue to adopt distance learning, it is clear that this approach has the potential to revolutionize the way we learn. By providing students with the flexibility to learn at their own pace, breaking down barriers to quality education, and promoting self-directed learning, distance learning can help students thrive in an increasingly digital world. Ultimately, the benefits of distance learning make it an invaluable option for students, one that can help them succeed academically, personally, and professionally.

Dear Principal Johnson,

I am writing to share my thoughts on whether our school should require students to perform community service. Among my friends, opinions are split. Some spend their weekends tutoring elementary school kids or organizing park cleanups, and they talk about how rewarding that work feels. Others worry that another mandatory commitment would take away valuable time needed for homework, jobs, and family obligations. After weighing both perspectives, I believe our school should introduce a community service requirement, provided it remains reasonable and flexible.

The strongest argument for mandatory service is that it teaches life lessons a standard classroom simply cannot provide. For instance, a close friend of mine spends two afternoons a week helping second graders practice reading. She often mentions how the experience taught her patience, adaptability, and how to communicate ideas clearly. More than that, she developed genuine dependability because those kids counted on her to be there. Those are the exact qualities we need in college and future careers, where reliability matters just as much as test scores. Without a clear requirement, many students who could benefit from these eye-opening experiences might never take the initiative to try them.

A policy like this would also help students who want to give back but honestly do not know where to begin. It is easy for teenagers to feel overwhelmed by the logistics or assume they do not have useful skills to offer. If our school established clear expectations alongside a directory of approved organizations, getting involved would feel far less intimidating. Several classmates who volunteer regularly told me they only got started because a club advisor nudged them to attend a single event. Once they experienced the difference they could make firsthand, they chose to stick with it. Sometimes an initial push is all a student needs to discover a lasting passion.

Our local community also stands to gain immensely. When dozens of students show up for a Saturday cleanup, an entire neighborhood park can be cleared in a couple of hours instead of sitting neglected for months. Local after-school programs are constantly short-handed, and younger children thrive when they receive one-on-one attention from older role models. If every high schooler contributed even a modest amount of time each year, our school would collectively supply thousands of hours of meaningful support across our town.

I recognize that many students are already balancing heavy loads. Some work after school to help pay household bills, while others take care of younger siblings or compete in varsity sports. These realities are serious, and any graduation requirement must respect them. The school could keep the threshold manageable—perhaps ten hours per academic year—and allow students to earn credit over the summer, during weekends, or through school-organized service days. Furthermore, students with significant family caregiving duties or employment could be granted credit through relevant, approved service pathways. 

Some people argue that required service takes away the spirit of charity, but our school already requires subjects like physical education and government because we value well-rounded citizens. Service deserves that exact same status. While students may initially sign up to meet a requirement, many will walk away with genuine empathy and a broader perspective on the world around them.

Thank you for taking the time to consider student perspectives on this important decision. 

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

Imagine a highway where every car steers, brakes, and accelerates without human hands. It sounds futuristic, but that future is closer than many think. Google cofounder Sergey Brin envisions driverless public transportation using half the fuel and half the parking space. Automakers and tech companies are already testing autonomous vehicles with laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors. Although supporters claim these cars will save lives by eliminating human error, I believe the development of driverless cars should be slowed until the technology can handle real-world conditions and clear legal standards are established.

Supporters make a compelling point: human error causes over 90 percent of traffic accidents, often because of texting, drowsiness, or impaired driving. A computer never gets distracted or drunk, so autonomous vehicles could, in theory, reduce crashes, lower insurance costs, and offer new mobility to elderly and disabled passengers. Those are worthy goals. But the path from today’s prototypes to that safe future is filled with unresolved hazards.

Consider the technology itself. Current sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or unmarked construction zones—exactly the conditions where careful driving matters most. Software systems, like any computer program, remain vulnerable to glitches and cybersecurity threats. A hacked or malfunctioning car at highway speeds is not a minor inconvenience; it could turn a single vehicle into a deadly weapon.

The human factor is equally concerning. Semi-autonomous features require drivers to stay alert and take over in emergencies, yet studies show that passengers quickly lose focus when a computer is driving. Their reaction times slow, so the very moment a system fails or encounters an unexpected obstacle may be the moment the human is least prepared to act. This creates a dangerous middle ground—neither fully manual nor fully automatic—where responsibility is blurred and attention fades.

Finally, legal and ethical questions remain unanswered. When an accident inevitably occurs, it is unclear whether the vehicle owner, the software developer, or the automaker should be held legally responsible. Until these rules are clear, victims could face years of legal battles, and manufacturers may have little incentive to fix flaws quickly. A technology this disruptive should not be deployed widely while its failures have no clear accountability.

None of this means autonomous vehicles should be abandoned forever. But the current enthusiasm outpaces the technology’s readiness. We would be wise to wait until sensors can handle bad weather, software is secure, and laws assign responsibility. Saving lives is a noble goal—but rushing half-tested cars onto public roads could endanger more lives than it saves.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge you to support transitioning the United States presidential election system from the Electoral College to a national popular vote. While our current system has historical roots, it has increasingly compromised the core democratic principle of equal representation. To ensure that every citizen’s ballot carries identical weight, our nation must embrace a system where the presidency is decided directly by the American people.

According to the Office of the Federal Register, the Electoral College was conceived as a constitutional compromise balancing congressional selection of the executive against a direct citizen vote. Today, it allocates 538 electors based on each state’s congressional delegation, with 48 states utilizing a "winner-take-all" system to award their electors. While this structure was intended to balance competing interests, Bradford Plumer observes in "The Indefensible Electoral College" that it has led to fundamentally undemocratic outcomes. Most glaringly, the system allows a candidate to win the national popular vote yet still lose the presidency, as occurred in both 2000 and 2016. Furthermore, Plumer highlights how the winner-take-all allocation incentivizes campaigns to focus their attention almost entirely on a narrow set of swing states. Millions of voters living in predictably Republican or Democratic states are effectively ignored, which ultimately depresses voter turnout and fosters civic alienation.

Defenders of the Electoral College present compelling arguments for its retention. In "In Defense of the Electoral College," Judge Richard A. Posner contends that the institution is vital for preserving federalism. Posner argues that without it, candidates would run up large vote tallies in dense urban centers, whereas the current system forces candidates to build broad geographic coalitions across both large and small states. Additionally, Posner points out that the Electoral College provides decisive outcomes and confines chaotic recounts to individual states rather than triggering nationwide disputes. 

While these concerns regarding federalism and stability are significant, the reality of modern presidential politics undermines them. The Electoral College does not truly produce broad national coalitions; instead, it merely replaces urban dominance with swing-state favoritism. A candidate can ignore vast rural swaths of California and millions of urban residents in Texas simply because those states are not competitively balanced. Moreover, the risk of "faithless electors" defying their states' voters—an inherent flaw noted by Plumer—poses its own severe threat to institutional stability. Conflating federalism with presidential elections ignores that the Senate already protects state autonomy. In an executive election, the president represents the entire populace, not state governments.

Every American citizen deserves to know that their vote matters regardless of geographic boundaries. By supporting a transition to a direct popular vote, whether through constitutional amendment or interstate cooperation, you can help restore fundamental democratic fairness to our highest office. I respectfully ask that you champion this vital reform on behalf of all your constituents.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Constituent

Every year when June rolls around, most students are excited to finally relax, but that excitement usually gets ruined by summer homework. Schools say these projects keep our brains active so we do not lose what we learned, which makes sense in theory. However, the way schools usually do it—having teachers assign one big, identical project to every single person—does not really work. Summer projects should definitely be designed by students instead.

The biggest reason is motivation. When a teacher hands out a giant packet of math worksheets or tells everyone to read the exact same classic novel, almost nobody does it because they want to learn. In my experience, most kids just wait until the last three days before school starts, rush through the work while looking up summaries online, and end up hating the subject even more. On the other hand, if students get to choose their own project, they actually care about the result. For example, a student who likes computer science could spend the summer learning how to code a basic video game, or someone who plays music could record an original song. They are still practicing problem-solving, reading, and critical thinking, but they are doing it because it connects to their genuine interests.

In the real world, bosses do not hand out fill-in-the-blank worksheets; people have to set their own goals, manage their time, and figure out how to solve problems when things go wrong. Designing a summer project forces you to take that kind of responsibility. Last year, a friend of mine wanted to learn more about photography, so she spent her break taking portraits of local business owners in our town and writing short profiles about their shops. Students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home, provided distance learning is offered as an option rather than imposed as a replacement for the classroom. The flexibility it creates matters a great deal for students whose circumstances don't fit the standard school day, and the cost of offering it is small compared with what is gained.

Consider a student with a chronic illness. A teenager managing Crohn's disease or severe migraines may have good weeks and terrible ones. In a traditional system, a bad week means missed lessons, piles of makeup work, and a growing sense of being left behind. With a live video connection or recorded sessions, that same student can follow along from bed, ask a question by typing it into a chat window, and stay in step with classmates. The illness doesn't disappear, but it no longer dictates whether the student keeps up academically. The same logic applies to students recovering from surgery or injury, and to those with anxiety so acute that walking into a crowded building is itself an obstacle to learning.

Geography matters too. In rural areas, some students spend more than an hour each way on a bus. That is two hours a day that could go toward sleep, homework, or simply being a kid. Many small rural schools also cannot afford to staff courses like calculus, physics, or Mandarin, because only a handful of students would enroll. Online classes let those students take what a larger school would offer without moving. A girl in a remote Montana town can study advanced chemistry with a teacher three hundred miles away, and her options are no longer limited by her zip code.

Then there are students whose lives carry unusual demands: young athletes who travel for competitions, performers with rehearsal schedules, teens who work to help support their families. Rigid attendance rules often force them to choose between their commitments and their education. Distance learning lets them hold on to both. It also suits some students temperamentally. A quiet, easily distracted learner may do better in a calm home environment than in a noisy classroom, and being able to pause a recorded lecture and replay a difficult explanation is something no live classroom can match.

Critics are right to raise concerns. Learning at home takes self-discipline, and some students will drift without the structure of a physical school. Social development matters, too; friendships, clubs, and casual conversation in hallways teach things no lesson plan captures. Not every household has reliable internet or a quiet place to work, and the remote-learning struggles of the early 2020s showed how unevenly those resources are spread. These are real problems, but they argue for careful design rather than rejection. Schools can lend devices, provide hotspots, require regular check-ins with teachers, and let students combine home and in-person attendance. Because the arrangement is optional, students who would flounder at home can simply stay in the classroom.

Ultimately, education should adapt to the people it serves instead of forcing everyone through the same narrow door. Distance learning won't suit every student, and it shouldn't be forced on anyone. But for the sick, the isolated, the overextended, and the easily overwhelmed, the chance to learn from home can mean the difference between falling behind and succeeding. A school that offers that chance, with proper support, is simply taking its students' needs seriously.
