Dear Principal,

I am writing to argue against making a B average a requirement for students to participate in sports and other activities. I agree that schoolwork should come first, and students should try their best in every class. However, banning students with C averages from activities would probably hurt their grades and make school harder for many students instead of helping them improve.

First, sports and clubs give students a reason to stay connected to school. Some students may struggle in math, science, or English but feel successful on a team, in band, in drama club, or in student government. If they lose that part of school, they may feel like there is no place where they belong. Activities can help students build confidence, make friends, and learn responsibility. Those things can also make students more motivated to improve academically.

For example, a student with a C average might be having trouble because of one difficult class, not because they do not care about school. They might understand history and English well but have a hard time with algebra. If that student is told they cannot play soccer anymore, they could become discouraged and stop trying. On the other hand, being on a team can encourage them to attend school, finish assignments, and ask for help because they want to stay eligible.

Also, many activities already teach important skills that cannot always be learned from grades. Sports teach teamwork, discipline, leadership, and how to handle losing without giving up. Clubs teach students how to speak in public, plan events, solve problems, and work with people who have different ideas. These are skills students will need in jobs and adult life. A student with a C average is still capable of learning those skills and contributing to the school community.

A B average requirement could also be unfair to students with different situations. Some students have jobs after school to help their families. Others take care of younger siblings, have learning difficulties, or are dealing with problems at home. They may work very hard but still earn mostly Cs. It would not be right to assume that a C average means a student is lazy or does not deserve to participate.

Instead of requiring a B average, the school could create support for students whose grades are low. Students with below-average grades could be required to attend tutoring, meet with teachers, turn in missing work, or make an academic improvement plan. They could still participate in activities as long as they show effort and make progress. This would hold students responsible while also giving them help.

Activities should not be a reward only for students who already get high grades. They can be one of the reasons students keep trying in school. I hope you will choose a policy that supports students and helps them improve instead of taking away an important part of their school experience.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

The idea of distance learning has become increasingly common, with many schools now letting students attend classes from home through online platforms or video conferencing. Although critics point out that this model may lack face-to-face interaction and certain hands-on experiences, I believe students can benefit significantly from learning at home. Distance learning offers greater flexibility, broadens access to education, and can even improve academic outcomes.

First, learning from home gives students more control over their time. In a traditional classroom, students often have to follow a fixed schedule, which can be difficult for those juggling part-time jobs, family duties, or other responsibilities. When classes are available online, students can arrange their study time around their personal lives rather than the other way around. For example, a student who works in the evenings can attend classes during the day and stay on track academically. That kind of flexibility can reduce stress and support a healthier balance between school and life.

Another important benefit is accessibility. Students in rural or isolated areas frequently struggle to reach quality educational opportunities because of distance, limited transportation, or a lack of nearby schools. Distance learning helps close this gap by connecting students to courses and programs no matter where they live. A student in a small town, for instance, can take online classes offered by a university in a large city without moving or spending hours commuting. This expanded access can help level the playing field, giving more students the chance to pursue their goals regardless of their location.

Distance learning can also strengthen learning itself. Online platforms offer interactive tools, such as discussion boards, virtual group projects, video lectures, and simulations, that can keep students engaged and make difficult material easier to understand. Because students can pause, rewind, or revisit lessons, they can learn at a pace that works for them. Reviewing material on their own schedule often leads to better retention and a deeper understanding of the content.

Of course, distance learning may not fully replace the social connections and hands-on activities of a traditional classroom. Still, the advantages are hard to ignore. The flexibility, accessibility, and potential for stronger learning outcomes make attending classes from home a valuable option for many students. As technology continues to improve, distance learning will likely play an even larger role in education, offering students new ways to connect with material, teachers, and classmates while pursuing their academic goals.

Dear Principal [Name],

I am writing to share my thoughts as you consider changes to our school's cell phone policy. Between the two options being discussed, I strongly believe Policy 1 is the better route. Allowing students to carry their phones and use them during lunch and free periods—while keeping them turned off during class—strikes the right balance between protecting instruction and meeting the practical realities of daily life.

First and foremost, family communication and safety are major concerns. Parents often need to reach their kids about changing ride arrangements, doctor appointments, or family emergencies. Likewise, students need an immediate way to reach home if an after-school practice is canceled or if they start feeling unwell. Relying entirely on the main office is unrealistic; the office staff is already busy, and messages cannot always be delivered in time. In a more critical situation, such as severe weather or a campus lockdown, the ability to communicate directly gives both parents and students essential peace of mind. Policy 1 keeps these vital lines of contact open without turning classrooms into chaotic spaces.

Beyond safety, Policy 1 helps students build real-world responsibility. Once we graduate and enter college or the workforce, nobody will confiscate our devices; we will simply be expected to know when it is appropriate to use them. A policy that permits phones only during breaks gives us meaningful practice in developing that self-discipline. By contrast, an outright ban teaches little more than how to be sneaky. Determined students will inevitably hide phones in their pockets or slip away to the restrooms, forcing teachers and staff to waste valuable instructional time policing hallways. A fair, realistic rule is always much easier to enforce than one students view as overly restrictive.

It is true, as supporters of Policy 2 point out, that phones can be distracting. However, Policy 1 directly tackles that issue by requiring devices to be turned off and put away throughout class. When instruction is happening, the learning environment remains undisturbed. Lunch and study halls, on the other hand, are times for students to recharge, unwind, and socialize. Listening to music or catching up with a friend during a break helps students return to their next period refreshed. If someone breaks the rule, the school can handle it individually—perhaps by holding the phone in the office for the rest of the day—rather than punishing the entire student body for the actions of a few.

Finally, smartphones serve as everyday organizational tools. During free periods, students frequently check their digital planners, set homework reminders, or coordinate with classmates on group projects. A blanket ban strips away these conveniences and makes staying organized harder for many of us.

For all these reasons, Policy 1 offers a thoughtful compromise. It respects instructional time while preparing students to handle technology responsibly. I respectfully encourage you to choose Policy 1, supported by clear expectations and fair consequences. Thank you for taking the time to read my letter and for always working to improve our school.

Sincerely,

[Student Name]

Dear Principal Johnson,

I am writing to share my opinion on whether students should be required to perform community service. Some of my friends tutor elementary school children or clean up litter, and they believe helping others is deeply important. Other friends worry that a requirement would take time away from homework, jobs, and family responsibilities. After considering both sides, I believe our school should require community service, as long as the requirement is reasonable and flexible.

The strongest reason to require service is that it teaches students lessons a classroom cannot. My friend Maria tutors second graders in reading twice a month. She told me that at first she was only trying to earn volunteer hours, but she soon found herself looking forward to seeing the children improve. She has learned patience, communication, and responsibility. Many students never discover these strengths because they never have a reason to try. A requirement would give every student the chance to find out how rewarding service can be, rather than leaving that experience to the few who already volunteer.

A requirement would also benefit our community. Schools, parks, food banks, and libraries often struggle with too few helpers. If hundreds of students each contributed a modest number of hours, the effect would be significant. A single litter cleanup by a group of twenty students can transform a neighborhood park in an afternoon. Repeated across a whole school, such efforts would make our town cleaner, our younger students better educated, and our neighbors better supported. Students would also see that their actions have real, visible results.

In addition, community service can help students prepare for the future. Colleges and employers value experience that shows initiative and teamwork. Students who work with a community organization learn to show up on time, follow through on commitments, and cooperate with people of different ages and backgrounds. These skills are useful in any career. Students who might not have access to internships or other enrichment activities could gain valuable experience through a service program.

I understand the concerns of my friends who feel they are already too busy. Some students have part-time jobs, care for younger siblings, or have heavy course loads. A poorly designed requirement could add stress and make service feel like a punishment. For that reason, I suggest several safeguards. The number of required hours should be small, perhaps ten to twenty per year, and students should have the full year to complete them. They should be able to choose activities that match their interests and schedules, including weekend or summer options. Students who already help their families or hold jobs could receive credit for approved activities. With these provisions, the requirement would be manageable for nearly everyone.

Finally, a requirement does not have to take away from students' enthusiasm. Many people begin an activity because they are told to and then continue because they enjoy it. Just as students are required to take math and science so they can discover what they are capable of, they can be required to serve so they can discover the satisfaction of helping others.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge you to adopt a flexible community service requirement. It would strengthen our students' character, support our community, and prepare us for adult life. Thank you for considering my opinion.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

Requiring every student to join an extracurricular activity may sound like a good way to build school spirit, but I disagree with making it mandatory. Sports teams, clubs, student government, and school publications can offer valuable experiences. However, students have different responsibilities, interests, and personal circumstances. A school should encourage participation and make activities accessible, not turn them into another requirement that every student must fulfill.

For many students, extracurricular activities are already an important part of their education. A student who joins the debate team may become more confident speaking in public. Someone who works on the yearbook can learn photography, writing, design, and teamwork. Athletes often develop discipline because they must attend practices, manage their time, and support their teammates. These benefits are real, which is why schools should advertise clubs enthusiastically and provide a wide range of choices.

Still, a required activity could create serious problems for students with limited time outside school. Some teenagers work after school to help support their families or save money for college. Others are responsible for younger siblings while their parents are at work. A student who spends several hours each evening caring for a brother or sister is already demonstrating responsibility and leadership, even if that work does not appear on a club roster. Requiring that student to attend meetings or practices could add stress rather than provide an enriching experience.

Mandatory participation might also weaken the quality of activities. Clubs succeed when members genuinely want to be there. If students join only because they need to satisfy a rule, they may skip meetings, avoid assignments, or contribute very little. Imagine a student council filled with people who have no interest in planning events or representing classmates. The council would become less effective, and the students who truly care might have to do extra work. The same could happen on a sports team if students feel forced to participate but do not want to practice or compete.

In addition, not every student finds meaningful growth through organized school activities. Some students pursue interests independently, such as painting, coding, writing music, volunteering at a community center, or caring for animals. Others may be shy, dealing with anxiety, or still trying to find where they fit in. For them, being forced into a public group could make school feel less welcoming. Participation should be an opportunity to explore, not a punishment for being different.

A better policy would be to make extracurricular activities easier to join. Schools could hold club fairs, offer late buses, reduce or waive participation fees, and create short-term clubs for students who cannot commit all year. Teachers could also help students connect their hobbies to existing organizations or start new ones. These steps would increase involvement without ignoring the realities of students’ lives.

Extracurricular activities can be memorable and educational, but their value comes from choice and commitment. Schools should inspire students to participate, not require it from every student regardless of circumstance.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge your support for legislative efforts that would transition our presidential elections from the Electoral College to a system decided by the national popular vote. As our state’s representative, you bear a constitutional responsibility to ensure that the voices of your constituents are heard in Washington. Under our current framework, however, millions of American votes are routinely sidelined, weakening the core democratic premise of our republic.

The Electoral College was forged in the late eighteenth century as an uneasy compromise between a congressional appointment of the executive and a direct popular ballot, as documented by the Office of the Federal Register. Yet the mechanics established by this system—most notably the winner-take-all rule adopted by forty-eight states—have distorted modern governance. Because nearly all electoral votes are awarded entirely to whichever candidate wins a simple plurality within a state, campaigns direct their energy and resources toward a fleeting handful of swing states. As Bradford Plumer highlights in "The Indefensible Electoral College," this dynamic leaves voters in consistently conservative or liberal states largely ignored, depressing civic participation and voter turnout nationwide. More troubling still is the system’s capacity to produce a president who was rejected by the majority of the electorate, a fissure between democratic will and political power witnessed starkly in both 2000 and 2016. 

Defenders of the institution, such as Judge Richard A. Posner, offer serious considerations. Posner contends that the Electoral College bolsters federalism by compelling candidates to assemble broad geographical coalitions rather than simply driving up massive vote margins in dense metropolitan corridors. He further cautions that a direct popular vote would risk logistical turmoil, noting that the existing system confines potential recount disputes within state borders rather than inviting the chaos of a nationwide audit. 

These arguments, while grounded in institutional prudence, fail to account for how fundamentally disconnected the current process has become from ordinary citizens. Rather than fostering truly national coalitions, the Electoral College merely encourages politicians to cater to narrow demographics within a few battleground regions. A conservative voter in an overwhelmingly Democratic state or a progressive voter in an entrenched Republican bastion has virtually no stake in the contest. Furthermore, advanced administrative standards and unified recount statutes are far more achievable today than in the eighteenth century, meaning administrative convenience should no longer justify diluting the fundamental principle of "one person, one vote." 

Every citizen's ballot, regardless of geographic location, deserves identical weight in choosing the leader of our nation. By championing reforms such as the National Popular Vote interstate compact, you can help restore confidence in our electoral system and ensure that the presidency reflects the true will of the American people. Thank you for your service and your careful consideration of this vital issue.

Sincerely,  
A Concerned Constituent

Driverless cars could transform the way people travel, but they should be developed carefully instead of being rushed onto public roads. Autonomous vehicles might save lives, cut fuel use, and give independence to people who cannot drive. At the same time, the technology still has real weaknesses, and lawmakers have hard questions to answer about safety and responsibility. For these reasons, I believe society should support the continued development and testing of driverless cars, as long as strong safety standards are required.

The strongest argument for these vehicles is their potential to prevent accidents. The article explains that human error causes more than 90 percent of crashes, often because drivers are texting, tired, or impaired by alcohol or drugs. A computer does not get sleepy or reach for a phone. Autonomous cars use laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors to watch the road constantly, detecting obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals. If this technology proves reliable, it could prevent many crashes and save many lives. Fewer accidents might also mean lower insurance costs for families.

Driverless cars could also help people with limited mobility. Elderly and disabled passengers, along with others who cannot safely operate a car, might gain a new level of freedom. Rather than relying on relatives, buses, or expensive ride services, they could get to work, medical appointments, stores, and social events on their own. The article also mentions Sergey Brin's vision of driverless public transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. If that idea became reality, it could ease congestion, conserve resources, and improve the design of our cities.

Even so, the article makes clear that driverless cars are not ready to replace human drivers everywhere. Their sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, or fog, and unmarked construction zones may confuse them when road conditions change quickly. Software glitches and cybersecurity threats add to the concern. A car that fails because of a software error, or because a hacker takes control, could put passengers and other drivers in serious danger. Companies therefore need to test these vehicles in many different conditions before letting them operate without human supervision.

Semi-autonomous cars bring another problem: they can give drivers a false sense of security. These vehicles may expect a human to take over in an emergency, yet studies cited in the article show that people quickly lose focus once a computer is driving. A distracted driver may react too slowly to prevent a crash. There is also the unresolved question of legal responsibility. After an accident, should the vehicle owner, the automaker, or the software developer be blamed? Clear laws must answer this question before driverless cars become common.

In the end, driverless cars deserve continued development because they could reduce accidents, increase independence, and make transportation more efficient. However, these benefits should not blind us to the technology's present limits. Companies and governments need to solve the problems of bad weather, software security, driver attention, and legal responsibility. With careful testing and firm regulations, driverless cars may someday become a safe and valuable part of everyday life.

Dear Principal Thompson,

I am writing to share my thoughts on the proposal to require at least a B average for participation in sports and extracurricular activities. While I completely understand and respect that your goal is to promote academic excellence, I believe raising the threshold would end up doing more harm than good. I strongly encourage you to reconsider this change.

First, this rule would penalize the very students who need school activities the most. For a lot of students currently holding a C average, athletics, music, theater, and student clubs are the primary reason they stay excited about coming to school every morning. These programs give people a real sense of belonging, structure, and purpose. Stripping those opportunities away risks leaving these students feeling alienated from the school community. When a student feels disconnected, their motivation rarely improves; more often, attendance slips, disengagement grows, and some students give up on school entirely. 

It is also worth remembering that a C is not a failing grade. A C means that a student is passing and meeting standard curriculum expectations. Many students with average marks are working just as hard as their peers, but they may wrestle with learning difficulties, balance after-school jobs, or manage heavy family obligations at home. Barring them from the soccer field, the stage, or the school newspaper sends a discouraging message: that unless you are an academic high-achiever, you do not deserve to be part of school life. Every student deserves the chance to grow outside the classroom, not just those who test well.

Furthermore, extracurriculars teach essential life skills that classes alone cannot provide. In athletics and clubs, students learn discipline, accountability, collaboration, and time management. In fact, many students actually earn better grades while an activity is in season because the strict schedule forces them to organize their time wisely. If we eliminate those commitments, there is no guarantee that an athlete kept off the team will spend those extra afternoon hours studying. More likely, they will simply be unsupervised, disengaged, and less focused.

Finally, setting the bar at a B average would decimate participation numbers across the entire school. Smaller sports teams, performing arts groups, and niche clubs rely on broad participation to function. If a significant portion of the student body becomes ineligible overnight, programs might not have enough members to field rosters or stage productions. That outcome would damage our overall school culture and hurt even the students who do meet the academic cutoff.

Grades certainly matter, but there are far more constructive ways to help students succeed. Instead of excluding people, the school could maintain a C-average requirement while pairing struggling students with mandatory study tables, peer tutoring, or regular academic check-ins through their coaches and club sponsors. Interventions like these uplift students rather than locking them out.

Requiring a B average would cut off valuable opportunities for the students who benefit from them most without solving the root causes of their academic struggles. A supportive policy, rather than an exclusionary one, would serve our entire student body far better. Thank you for listening to our perspective on this decision.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

Cell phones have become essential tools for communication, navigation, employment, and emergency assistance. Because they are so common, many drivers believe they should be allowed to use them in limited ways while operating a vehicle, especially through hands-free technology. However, drivers should not use cell phones in any capacity while a vehicle is in motion unless there is a genuine emergency. Even brief phone use divides attention, increases the risk of crashes, and endangers not only the driver but also passengers, pedestrians, and other motorists.

The greatest danger of cell phone use is distraction. Safe driving requires visual, manual, and mental attention. A driver must watch traffic signals, monitor nearby vehicles, anticipate sudden hazards, and make quick decisions. Texting is particularly dangerous because it removes a driver’s eyes and hands from the road. Looking down for only a few seconds can cause a vehicle to travel the length of a football field without the driver fully seeing what is ahead. Even checking a notification, selecting a song, or entering an address into a navigation app can create enough distraction for a serious accident to occur.

Some people argue that hands-free calling is safe because the driver’s hands remain on the steering wheel. Although hands-free technology may reduce manual distraction, it does not eliminate cognitive distraction. A driver engaged in a conversation may focus on the other person’s words, emotions, or questions instead of the traffic environment. Unlike a passenger, a person on the phone cannot see road conditions and is unlikely to pause a conversation when traffic becomes complicated. As a result, a driver may react more slowly to a braking vehicle, a child entering the street, or a changing traffic light. The issue is not simply whether a phone is held in the hand; it is whether the phone competes for the driver’s attention.

There are practical alternatives that make a strict rule reasonable. Drivers can set their destination before beginning a trip, place their phones on silent mode, and pull into a safe parking area before making calls or responding to messages. Modern phones also offer driving modes that automatically silence notifications or send brief automatic replies. For people who depend on their phones for work or family responsibilities, these precautions may be inconvenient, but inconvenience is far less serious than causing an avoidable injury or death.

Emergency situations should remain an exception. A driver who witnesses a crash, faces a medical emergency, or needs immediate assistance should be able to contact emergency services when it is safe to do so. In ordinary circumstances, however, calls, messages, social media, and navigation adjustments can wait until the vehicle is stopped.

Ultimately, operating a vehicle is a responsibility that demands full attention. Because cell phones can distract drivers visually, physically, and mentally, their use while driving should be prohibited in all nonemergency situations. A phone call or message may feel urgent, but no communication is more important than protecting human life on the road.

As we consider the potential policy change that would require students to maintain at least a grade B average to participate in sports and other activities, it is essential to weigh the pros and cons of such a decision. While the intention behind this policy may be to encourage academic excellence, I strongly believe that it would be misguided and ultimately harmful to many students. In this letter, I will argue against requiring a minimum grade B average for participation in activities, citing the potential negative impact on student motivation, the importance of extracurricular activities in education, and the inequitable effects on students with varying learning abilities.

Firstly, implementing such a policy would likely have a discouraging effect on students who are currently struggling academically. Many students with a grade C average are already working hard to keep up with their schoolwork, and the added pressure of meeting a higher grade threshold to participate in activities they enjoy could lead to frustration and disillusionment. This could result in a decrease in motivation, as students may feel that their efforts are not being recognized or valued. Moreover, students who are passionate about sports or other activities may become disengaged from their academic pursuits altogether, leading to a decline in their overall academic performance. By setting an unattainable goal, we risk discouraging students from striving for excellence, rather than encouraging them to do so.

Furthermore, extracurricular activities play a vital role in providing students with essential life skills, such as teamwork, communication, and problem-solving. These activities also offer a much-needed break from academic pressures, allowing students to recharge and refocus. By denying students with a grade C average the opportunity to participate in these activities, we would be depriving them of a well-rounded education. Many students rely on sports and other activities as a way to develop their interests, build relationships, and explore their passions outside of the classroom. By restricting access to these activities based on academic performance, we would be limiting the opportunities for students to grow and develop as individuals.

Lastly, it is essential to consider the inequitable effects of such a policy on students with varying learning abilities. Some students may require additional support or accommodations to succeed academically, and a blanket policy requiring a minimum grade B average would unfairly penalize these students. Additionally, students from disadvantaged backgrounds may face unique challenges that impact their academic performance, such as limited access to resources or support outside of school. By implementing a policy that favors students who are already high achievers, we would be exacerbating existing inequalities and creating a more exclusive environment.

In conclusion, while the intention behind the proposed policy may be to promote academic excellence, I firmly believe that it would have unintended and far-reaching consequences. By restricting access to sports and other activities based on academic performance, we would be discouraging student motivation, limiting opportunities for growth and development, and perpetuating inequalities. Instead, I propose that we focus on providing additional support and resources to help students who are struggling academically, while also recognizing and valuing the diverse talents and interests that our students bring to the table. By doing so, we can create a more inclusive and supportive learning environment that allows all students to thrive and reach their full potential.

Dear Senator [Last Name],

I am writing to respectfully urge you to support transitioning our presidential election system from the Electoral College to a national popular vote. The presidency is the only office representing the entire nation, and each citizen's vote should carry equal weight. Because the current process falls short of that fundamental standard, I hope you will advocate for reform.

The most glaring flaw of the Electoral College is that it can overturn the will of the voters. As Bradford Plumer points out in "The Indefensible Electoral College," a candidate can win the national popular vote yet still lose the White House, just as occurred in 2000 and 2016. This disconnect stems directly from the system’s design. According to the Office of the Federal Register, each state’s allotment of electors equals its congressional delegation, and forty-eight states plus Washington, D.C., award all their electors through a winner-take-all rule. Under this framework, winning a state by a handful of votes yields the exact same outcome as winning it by millions, effectively discarding every ballot cast for the losing candidate in that state.

This arrangement also skews how presidential campaigns are conducted. Plumer notes that candidates spend almost all their time and resources targeting a few battleground states, largely ignoring solid "red" or "blue" states. Millions of voters in these overlooked areas—including our own state—rarely see candidate visits or campaign events, which inevitably depresses voter turnout. Under a national popular vote, every citizen's ballot would hold the same value, encouraging presidential hopefuls to compete for votes across the entire country.

Supporters of the status quo offer arguments that certainly merit consideration. In "In Defense of the Electoral College," Judge Richard Posner argues that the system protects federalism and prevents candidates from winning simply by racking up massive vote tallies in dense urban centers. He contends that it forces candidates to construct broad national coalitions. In practice, however, candidates already bypass most states, focusing narrowly on purple swing states rather than building genuine national support. A popular vote would actually incentivize reaching out to rural towns, suburbs, and cities alike, since every additional vote counts toward the final total regardless of geographic boundaries.

Posner also emphasizes that the Electoral College yields a prompt, decisive outcome and confines recounts to specific states instead of triggering nationwide chaos. While narrow margins can create uncertainty, the existing system is hardly immune to crisis; the 2000 election hung on Florida's recount for weeks. Clear statutory thresholds could manage national recounts just as effectively. Furthermore, as the Federal Register explains, the Electoral College was an eighteenth-century compromise between election by Congress and popular vote. Our modern democracy should not be bound to an outdated compromise, especially when Plumer highlights risks like "faithless electors" who can defy their state's popular choice.

Ultimately, this issue comes down to democratic fairness. Voters must be able to trust that the candidate who earns the most votes nationwide will lead the country. Replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote would ensure every citizen has an equal voice. I urge you to support state and federal efforts, such as interstate compacts or constitutional amendments, to make this vital reform a reality.

Thank you for your time and continued service to our state.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

Another reason is that forcing people to volunteer takes away the real meaning of community service. Right now, I have friends who genuinely love helping out. That does not really help the community, and it might make students resent volunteering instead of wanting to do it later in life.

The principal’s decision requiring every student to join at least one extracurricular activity has stirred a lot of debate among students, teachers, and parents. While some people believe this requirement will help students grow, I disagree. Making extracurricular participation mandatory could do more harm than good, especially for students whose needs and circumstances don’t fit the rule.

To begin with, forcing everyone into an activity ignores the fact that students have different interests and strengths. A musician who would rather spend time practicing piano might end up pushed into a sport they have no interest in. Instead of building confidence or leadership, the experience can become a chore. Students may simply go through the motions without real enthusiasm, which defeats the purpose of extracurricular involvement. When students are placed in activities that don’t match their goals, they lose the chance to explore what truly matters to them.

Mandatory activities can also take time away from schoolwork and other responsibilities. Many students already struggle to balance homework, studying, family duties, and even part-time jobs. Adding a required meeting, practice, or club session can make an already busy schedule overwhelming. A student who needs extra help in math, for example, may have less time to meet with a teacher because they must attend a mandatory activity instead. Rather than helping students become more engaged, the requirement can stretch them too thin and hurt their academic performance.

There is also the issue of stress. When participation is required, students may feel pressure to perform well even in activities where they lack experience or confidence. Someone who is not athletic but must join a sports team could feel embarrassed or inadequate. Instead of enjoying a low-pressure hobby, they may worry about letting teammates down or being judged. For students already dealing with anxiety or self-doubt, this added pressure can be damaging and may affect their mental health over time.

I understand that the principal wants students to be more involved and well-rounded. However, requiring everyone to participate in an extracurricular activity overlooks the fact that students are individuals with different interests, schedules, and comfort levels. A better approach would be to encourage students to find activities they genuinely enjoy and to make it easier for them to join when they are ready. Giving students the freedom to choose, rather than forcing them, creates a more positive environment where they can develop real motivation, confidence, and a sense of belonging.

Dear Senator [Last Name],

My name is [Your Name], and I am a student in your district. I am writing to ask you to support changing the way we elect the president from the Electoral College to a national popular vote. I know this is a big change, but I think it is the fairest way to make sure every citizen's vote counts the same.

The biggest problem with the Electoral College is that the person with the most votes can still lose. According to Bradford Plumer, this happened in 2000 and 2016. In both elections, the candidate more Americans voted for did not become president. That seems wrong to me. In school we learn that democracy means majority rule, but the Electoral College can go against that. If millions of people vote for one person and another person wins, many citizens will feel their vote did not matter.

Another problem is that campaigns only pay attention to a few places. The Office of the Federal Register explains that 48 states and Washington, D.C. use a "winner-take-all" system, so the candidate who wins a state by even a small amount gets all of its electoral votes. Plumer says this causes candidates to focus almost entirely on a handful of swing states. People in states that are safely Democratic or Republican hardly ever see candidates or ads, and that can make them less likely to vote since the result already seems decided. With a national popular vote, a vote in any state would be worth the same, and candidates would have a reason to try to reach voters everywhere.

I do understand the other side. Judge Richard Posner argues that the Electoral College protects federalism and forces candidates to build broad coalitions across both large and small states. He worries that without it, candidates would only try to win by running up huge vote totals in big cities. That is a fair concern, but I am not sure it is true. In a popular vote, a candidate would need votes from all over the country, including small towns and rural areas, because those votes add up too. Right now, a candidate can ignore most of the country as long as they win the right swing states, so the system does not really make candidates visit everyone anyway.

Posner also says the Electoral College gives a clear winner quickly and keeps recounts inside single states instead of one giant national recount. This is probably the best argument for keeping it. A national recount would be hard and expensive if an election were very close. However, a close national race is less likely than a close race in one state, and we could create clear national rules for recounts ahead of time. I think a possible recount is a small price to pay to make sure the winner is the person most Americans actually chose.

Finally, the Electoral College has other weaknesses. Plumer points out that "faithless electors" could vote against their state's popular choice. Even if that rarely happens, it shows the system has a risk that voters cannot control. The Federal Register says the Electoral College was created as a compromise by the Founding Fathers. A compromise from long ago does not have to be the best system for today.

For these reasons, I hope you will support a national popular vote for president. It would make every vote equal, encourage candidates to campaign everywhere, and remove the chance that the loser of the vote becomes president. Thank you for taking the time to read my letter.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

The decision by the principal to require all students to participate in at least one extracurricular activity has sparked a heated debate among students, teachers, and parents. While some argue that this mandate will have a positive impact on students' overall development, I strongly disagree with this decision. In my opinion, forcing students to participate in extracurricular activities can have negative consequences and may not be beneficial for every student.

First and foremost, requiring students to participate in extracurricular activities can be overly burdensome and may lead to undue stress. Many students already have heavy academic workloads, and adding an extracurricular activity to their schedule can be overwhelming. For instance, students who are struggling in their classes may find it challenging to balance their academic responsibilities with the demands of an extracurricular activity. This can lead to a decline in their academic performance, which can have long-term consequences on their future prospects. Furthermore, students who are not interested in sports or other traditional extracurricular activities may feel forced to participate in something they do not enjoy, which can lead to frustration and dissatisfaction.

Another significant concern is that this mandate may not account for students' individual interests and talents. While some students may excel in sports or student council, others may have different passions and strengths that are not recognized or valued by the school. For example, a student who is an avid artist or musician may not have opportunities to pursue their interests through traditional extracurricular activities. By requiring all students to participate in a predetermined set of activities, the school may be neglecting the diverse range of talents and interests that exist among its students. This can lead to a lack of motivation and engagement among students who do not feel that their interests are being recognized or supported.

In addition, this decision may also have unintended consequences, such as creating an uneven playing field. Students who come from affluent families may have an advantage in terms of access to resources and opportunities, which can give them an unfair edge in extracurricular activities. For instance, a student whose family can afford private coaching or equipment may have a greater chance of succeeding in sports than a student who does not have access to these resources. This can lead to a lack of diversity and representation in extracurricular activities, which can perpetuate existing social and economic inequalities.

In conclusion, while the intention behind the principal's decision may be to promote student development and engagement, I strongly believe that requiring all students to participate in extracurricular activities can have negative consequences. Instead of mandating participation, the school should focus on providing a range of opportunities and resources that cater to different interests and talents. By doing so, the school can create a more inclusive and supportive environment that allows students to thrive and develop their passions, without imposing undue stress or burdens. Ultimately, this approach will lead to a more positive and productive experience for all students, and will help to foster a sense of community and engagement that is essential for academic success.

Cell phones have become essential tools for communication, navigation, work, and emergency help. Because they are so common, many drivers believe they should be able to use them in limited ways behind the wheel, particularly with hands-free technology. Still, drivers should not use cell phones in any capacity while a vehicle is moving unless there is a genuine emergency. Even brief use divides attention, raises the risk of a crash, and endangers passengers, pedestrians, and other motorists as well as the driver.

The biggest danger of phone use is distraction. Safe driving takes visual, manual, and mental attention all at once. A driver has to watch traffic signals, keep track of nearby vehicles, anticipate sudden hazards, and make quick decisions. Texting is especially risky because it pulls both the eyes and the hands away from the road. Glancing down for just a few seconds can mean traveling the length of a football field without really seeing what lies ahead. Even small tasks, like checking a notification, choosing a song, or typing an address into a map app, can create enough distraction for a serious accident.

Some people argue that hands-free calling is safe because the driver's hands stay on the wheel. Hands-free technology may reduce manual distraction, but it does not remove cognitive distraction. A driver in a conversation is often absorbed in the other person's words, feelings, or questions rather than in the traffic around them. A passenger can see the road and naturally pause when conditions get tricky, but someone on the phone cannot, and the caller may keep talking regardless. That delay can slow a driver's reaction to a braking car, a child stepping into the street, or a light turning red. The real question is not whether the phone is in a driver's hand, but whether it competes for the driver's attention.

Practical alternatives also make a strict rule reasonable. Drivers can enter their destination before leaving, switch their phones to silent, and pull into a safe parking spot before making a call or answering a message. Many phones even have driving modes that silence notifications or send short automatic replies. For people who rely on their phones for work or family obligations, these steps may be inconvenient. But inconvenience is a small price compared with an avoidable injury or death.

Emergencies should remain an exception. A driver who sees a crash, suffers a medical problem, or needs immediate help should be able to contact emergency services as soon as it is safe. In ordinary situations, though, calls, texts, social media, and changes to navigation can wait until the car is stopped.

In the end, driving is a responsibility that demands a person's full attention. Because phones can distract drivers visually, physically, and mentally, using them while driving should be prohibited in all nonemergency situations. A call or message may feel urgent in the moment, but nothing it contains is more important than protecting lives on the road.

Driverless cars are coming, and I think we should keep developing them. The technology is not perfect yet, but the possible benefits are too big to ignore. If companies keep testing and improving these cars, they could make our roads safer and help a lot of people who can't drive.

The biggest reason I support driverless cars is safety. The article says human error causes over 90 percent of traffic accidents. A lot of that comes from things people choose to do, like texting while driving, or things they can't always control, like being drowsy. A computer doesn't get tired and it doesn't pick up a phone. If driverless cars have laser radar, cameras, GPS, and sensors that detect obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals, they could react to problems without the mistakes humans make. If that cuts down crashes even a little, it would save lives, and that matters more than almost anything else.

Another good reason is that these cars could help people who have a hard time getting around. The article mentions that driverless cars could give mobility to elderly or disabled passengers. Some people can't drive because of their age or a disability, so they depend on other people for rides. A driverless car could give them independence to go to the doctor, the store, or visit family on their own. I think that is a strong reason to keep working on this technology.

There are also money and environmental benefits. The article says Sergey Brin imagines driverless public transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. That would mean less pollution and less wasted space in cities. The article also says driverless cars could lower insurance costs, which would help families save money.

Of course, there are real problems, and I don't want to ignore them. The article explains that sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or unmarked construction zones. That is a big deal, because bad weather is when driving is most dangerous. The software could also have glitches or be hacked. Another worry is that semi-autonomous cars need a human to take over in an emergency, but studies show passengers lose focus quickly when a computer is driving. That means the person might not react fast enough when it counts. Finally, nobody knows who is legally responsible after a crash: the owner, the software developer, or the automaker.

These problems are serious, but I don't think they are reasons to stop developing the cars. They are reasons to keep working on them. Better sensors could be built to handle weather and construction zones, and better security could protect the software from hackers. The attention problem could be solved by moving toward fully driverless cars instead of ones that expect people to jump in at the last second. The legal question can be answered by lawmakers making clear rules before the cars are sold to everyone. These are problems we can fix, but human error causing over 90 percent of accidents is a problem we have right now.

In conclusion, I support the development of driverless cars. They could make roads safer, help elderly and disabled people, save fuel and parking space, and lower insurance costs. The risks in the article are real, but they can be worked on with more testing and good laws. If we wait for perfect technology, we keep losing lives to human mistakes in the meantime.

Dear Principal Davis,

I’m writing because I heard you’re deciding between two cell phone policies, and I think Policy 1 is the better one. That’s the policy where students can bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times, as long as they’re turned off during class.

First, phones help us stay in touch with our families. A lot of students get rides from parents, and plans change during the day. For example, last week my mom had to work late and texted me during lunch to tell me I should take the bus instead of waiting for her. If I didn’t have my phone, I would have been sitting outside for an hour or had to go to the office to get a message. The office is helpful, but it’s not always fast, especially during busy times. Emergencies don’t always happen before or after school.

Second, lunch and free time are supposed to be a break. Phones let us listen to music, play games, watch videos, or text friends. That might sound like it’s not important, but it helps us relax in the middle of a stressful day. Some students also use that time to check the school website or an app for homework and grades. If phones are banned completely, we lose a tool we actually use. It doesn’t hurt class time because Policy 1 already says phones have to be off during class.

Third, high school should be teaching us how to handle phones responsibly. In real life, we are going to have phones at work, at college, and at home. If school just says “no phones at all,” we never get practice learning when to put them away. Policy 1 gives a clear rule: off during class, okay during free time. If someone breaks that rule, the teacher can take the phone and there can be a consequence. That’s fair. It punishes the person who broke the rule instead of punishing everyone.

I understand the worry that phones can be distracting or cause drama. But that can happen at lunch with or without phones. The problem in class is already handled by Policy 1 because phones have to be turned off. Also, if the school bans phones completely, some students will still bring them and hide them. Then the school has a bigger problem because students are sneaking around instead of following a clear rule.

Policy 1 is fair, safe, and practical. It protects class time but gives students a little freedom during the parts of the day that belong to us. Please choose Policy 1.

Sincerely,
Alex Morgan

Distance learning can give students a valuable alternative to attending school in person every day. Although online classes cannot replace every benefit of a traditional classroom, students would benefit from having the option to learn from home in appropriate circumstances. Remote attendance can make education more accessible, allow students to work at a pace that suits them, and help schools continue instruction during disruptions.

First, learning from home can help students whose personal circumstances make regular attendance difficult. Some students live far from school and spend hours each day on buses or in cars. Others have temporary illnesses, disabilities, or anxiety that make a crowded school environment challenging. For these students, online classes can prevent absences from becoming a barrier to academic progress. A student recovering from surgery, for example, may be physically unable to walk through school hallways but still able to participate in a video lesson, complete assignments, and ask questions. Without remote access, that student might fall behind simply because of a health problem rather than a lack of ability or effort.

Distance learning can also give students greater control over their learning. In a classroom, a teacher must often move at one pace for an entire group. Online lessons, especially recorded ones, allow students to pause, replay, and review difficult material. A student struggling with algebra could watch an explanation of an equation several times before attempting homework. At the same time, a student who understands the material quickly may be able to complete work independently and move on to more challenging activities. This flexibility does not mean students should be left alone without guidance; teachers can still hold live discussions, offer feedback, and schedule individual meetings. However, technology can make instruction more responsive to different learning needs.

Another important advantage is that online learning helps schools remain prepared for emergencies. Severe weather, public health concerns, transportation failures, or other disruptions can close school buildings for days or weeks. If students and teachers already know how to use online platforms, learning does not have to stop completely. During a snowstorm, for instance, a teacher could conduct a brief video conference, post readings and assignments, and answer questions electronically. Students would maintain a routine instead of losing valuable instructional time.

Critics correctly point out that students need social interaction. School is not only a place to learn mathematics, science, and literature; it is also where young people develop friendships, communication skills, and a sense of community. In addition, some homes lack reliable internet access or a quiet place to study. For these reasons, distance learning should be an option rather than a requirement, and schools should provide devices, internet support, and regular opportunities for online students to connect with teachers and classmates.

Overall, students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home because it expands access to education and provides flexibility when traditional attendance is impossible. While in-person learning should remain important, a well-designed remote option can ensure that more students have a fair chance to succeed.

Extracurricular activities have long been recognized as vital components of a well-rounded education, offering students a chance to explore new interests, develop teamwork and leadership skills, and cultivate lifelong passions beyond the classroom. By participating in sports, working on the yearbook, or serving on the student council, many students discover hidden talents and form lasting connections with their peers. Recently, our principal announced a new policy requiring every student to participate in at least one extracurricular program. Although this initiative is well-intentioned, it overlooks the complexities of student life and may ultimately do more harm than good.

One major concern is that a blanket mandate disregards the significant responsibilities many students shoulder outside of school. For example, some students balance part-time jobs with their academic commitments, contributing to their family's finances or saving for college. Others take on caregiving roles, looking after younger siblings or assisting elderly relatives with daily tasks. By imposing a mandatory after-school commitment, these students are forced to make difficult choices between their essential domestic duties and compliance with the school's policy. This approach risks alienating and penalizing students who already manage a delicate balance of responsibilities, rather than fostering equity and inclusivity.

Moreover, requiring extracurricular engagement can exacerbate the risk of academic burnout and mental fatigue. The modern high school curriculum is demanding, with many students spending hours each evening on homework, study, and exam preparation. Downtime is not a luxury, but a necessity that allows adolescents to rest, recharge, and maintain their emotional well-being. By stripping away this flexibility, the school may inadvertently push students toward exhaustion. Rather than enjoying their chosen activities, overburdened teenagers may view them as yet another source of stress and obligation.

By acknowledging and respecting students' individual choices and priorities, the school can foster a more positive and supportive environment, where extracurricular activities truly enrich the educational experience.

By recognizing the diversity of students' lives and responsibilities, the school can work toward creating a more inclusive and supportive environment, where extracurricular activities complement and enhance the academic experience, rather than adding to the burden. Summer break is often caught between two competing instincts: the desire to give adolescents reprieve from structural exhaustion, and the fear that months of intellectual dormancy will unravel hard-won academic momentum. When schools respond by mandating summer assignments, the instinct is almost invariably to standardize them through teacher-designed packets, uniform reading logs, and prefabricated worksheets. Yet this impulse toward control ignores the primary asset that summer affords: uninterrupted, self-directed time. Summer projects yield far richer intellectual and personal dividends when they are designed by students rather than assigned by faculty.

The traditional, teacher-crafted assignment frequently triggers resentment because it mimics the coercive compliance of the academic term without any of its collaborative energy. A student handed forty pages of historical source analysis or a generic algebra review will often rush through the task in the final forty-eight hours of August, retaining little beyond a renewed dread of the classroom. By contrast, autonomy changes the psychological stakes of an assignment. When students are charged with conceptualizing their own projects, learning ceases to be a chore imposed from above and becomes an exercise in curiosity. A teenager intrigued by urban ecosystems might design a field study cataloging insect biodiversity in community gardens, while an aspiring engineer might spend July coding a rudimentary mobile application. Even if the technical scope of these endeavors is modest, the intellectual investment is genuine.

Crucially, designing an independent project forces students to develop executive functions that conventional classroom settings often insulate them from. School typically tells students what to read, when to submit it, and which rubric defines excellence. Designing one’s own summer project, however, requires wrestling with the ambiguous reality of real-world work. Students must define an inquiry question, establish feasible milestones, locate their own primary sources or raw materials, and self-regulate without the ticking clock of daily attendance. Learning how to scale an ambitious idea down to a manageable eight-week endeavor is a far more durable skill than memorizing pre-selected vocabulary words.

Critics of this student-led approach understandably worry about rigor and accountability. Without direct teacher oversight, won't some students pick trivial topics or coast by on minimal effort? This concern misidentifies where teacher expertise is most effectively applied. Teachers should not be syllabus-makers over the summer, but proposal evaluators before it begins. In May, students can submit detailed project proposals, outlining their objectives, methodologies, and proposed final deliverables. Instructors can offer constructive friction—pushing for greater depth, suggesting methodologies, or questioning feasibility—before giving approval. 

Ultimately, education fails if it leaves young people incapable of directing their own intellects once the bell rings. Summer is the rare window where the rigid architecture of bell schedules dissolves. Replacing that vacuum with teacher-designed drudgery wastes an invaluable opportunity; handing students the blueprint teaches them to build an intellectual life entirely their own.

Dear Principal,

I recently heard about the possible policy change that would require students to have at least a grade B average to participate in sports and other activities. I strongly disagree with this idea and I'd like to share my thoughts on why I think it's not a good idea.

First of all, I think this policy would be unfair to a lot of students who are really passionate about sports and activities, but might not be as strong in academics. Just because someone isn't a straight-A student doesn't mean they're not capable of excelling in other areas. For example, I have friends who are amazing athletes, but they struggle in certain subjects like math or English. If this policy were to go into effect, they would be forced to choose between their grades and the activities they love. This could lead to a lot of students becoming discouraged and feeling like they don't belong in our school.

Another reason I'm against this policy is that it would put too much pressure on students to prioritize grades over everything else. While good grades are important, they're not the only thing that matters in life. Extracurricular activities like sports, music, and art are essential for developing important skills like teamwork, communication, and creativity. By taking these opportunities away from students who don't have a B average, we would be depriving them of the chance to grow and develop as individuals.

Furthermore, I think this policy would have a negative impact on student morale and motivation. If students feel like they're not good enough to participate in activities because of their grades, they might start to feel like they're not good enough in general. This could lead to a decrease in self-esteem and a lack of motivation to even try in their classes. On the other hand, if students are allowed to participate in activities they enjoy, they might be more motivated to work hard and improve their grades so they can continue to do what they love.

I also think it's worth considering the fact that a lot of students who have a C average are still passing their classes and meeting the minimum requirements to graduate. They might not be the strongest students, but they're still learning and making progress. By denying them the opportunity to participate in activities, we would be sending the message that they're not worthy of being part of our school community.

In conclusion, I strongly believe that requiring a B average to participate in sports and activities is not a good idea. It would be unfair to students who are passionate about extracurricular activities, put too much pressure on students to prioritize grades, and have a negative impact on student morale and motivation. I think we should focus on finding ways to support students who are struggling academically, rather than taking away opportunities that could help them grow and develop as individuals. The widespread use of cell phones has become an integral part of daily life, with the majority of humans relying on these devices for communication, navigation, and entertainment. However, the question of whether drivers should be allowed to use cell phones while operating a vehicle has sparked a heated debate. While some argue that cell phone use is a necessary convenience for drivers, others claim that it poses a significant threat to road safety. In this essay, I will argue that drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

The primary concern with cell phone use while driving is the distraction it causes. When a driver is engaged in a phone call, texting, or browsing, their attention is diverted away from the road, increasing the risk of accidents. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), distracted driving was responsible for 3,166 deaths in the United States in 2017. The distraction caused by cell phone use is not limited to the physical act of holding the phone or typing; it also includes cognitive distraction, where the driver's mind is focused on the conversation or task at hand rather than the road. This cognitive distraction can be just as deadly as physical distraction, as it impairs the driver's ability to react to changing road conditions.

Another argument against cell phone use while driving is that it compromises reaction time. When a driver is engaged with their phone, they are less likely to notice and respond to hazards on the road, such as pedestrians, other vehicles, or road debris. Even hands-free phone use, which is often touted as a safer alternative, can still cause significant distraction and impair reaction time. Studies have shown that hands-free phone use can still divert a driver's attention away from the road, increasing the risk of accidents.

Furthermore, allowing cell phone use while driving sets a bad precedent and sends a mixed message to drivers. If drivers are permitted to use their phones while driving, it may be seen as an endorsement of distracted driving, which can lead to a culture of complacency and indifference to road safety. Conversely, banning cell phone use while driving sends a clear message that road safety is a top priority and that distracted driving will not be tolerated.

In conclusion, the risks associated with cell phone use while driving far outweigh any potential benefits. The distraction caused by cell phone use, whether physical or cognitive, can have deadly consequences, and compromising reaction time can lead to accidents. Rather than allowing cell phone use while driving, governments and regulatory agencies should prioritize road safety and implement strict laws and penalties to discourage distracted driving. By doing so, we can reduce the number of accidents and fatalities on our roads and create a safer driving environment for everyone. Ultimately, the safety of drivers, passengers, and pedestrians should take precedence over the convenience of cell phone use, and drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

Dear Principal Collins,

As our school administration considers whether to mandate community service for graduation, students across campus have engaged in passionate debates on the subject. Some of my peers spend their weekends tutoring elementary school children or clearing litter from our local parks, finding immense fulfillment in these efforts. Others, however, struggle to keep up with existing demands on their time. While I admire the intention behind promoting civic engagement, I believe that requiring all students to complete community service is counterproductive. Instead, our school should actively encourage and facilitate voluntary service.

First, a blanket mandate fails to account for the diverse and demanding responsibilities students already manage. Many high schoolers must balance challenging academic schedules, sports, and family commitments. More critically, an obligatory service requirement disproportionately harms students from lower-income backgrounds. Several of my classmates work part-time jobs after school not for disposable income, but to help their families pay rent and buy groceries; others must supervise younger siblings while their parents work evening shifts. Adding twenty or thirty mandatory hours of unpaid service would force these students to choose between fulfilling a graduation requirement and meeting fundamental family needs.

Furthermore, making service mandatory fundamentally changes its nature, often defeating the educational purpose it is meant to serve. The term "mandatory volunteerism" is an oxymoron. When students choose to mentor younger children or clean public spaces of their own volition, they approach the work with enthusiasm, empathy, and genuine dedication. Conversely, when individuals are compelled to participate under threat of academic penalty, the experience often transforms into a burdensome chore. Reluctant students are more likely to do the bare minimum simply to get their paperwork signed, which offers little real value to the community organizations hosting them and can foster long-term resentment toward civic involvement.

Rather than imposing a rigid mandate, our administration should focus on inspiring and facilitating voluntary involvement. The school could introduce a recognized service-learning elective, host community partner fairs on campus, or establish an honor cord for students who complete a designated number of service hours. Providing transportation for group volunteer projects on weekends would also eliminate accessibility barriers without penalizing those who cannot participate. 

Community service is an invaluable pursuit that has the potential to transform both the volunteer and the surrounding neighborhood. However, genuine altruism cannot be produced by administrative decree. By offering opportunities, resources, and recognition rather than ultimatums, our school can foster a culture of voluntary compassion that will endure long after we graduate. 

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

Whenever I have a big decision to make, my first instinct is usually to ask someone I trust, like my mom or my best friend. But if it is something really important, asking just one person is rarely enough. Everyone has their own way of looking at the world, and no single person knows everything. Getting advice from multiple people helps someone make a better choice because it exposes blind spots, balances out personal biases, and helps the person feel more confident in their final decision.

One big reason to get more than one opinion is that people have completely different types of experience. For instance, last spring I had to pick my schedule for the upcoming school year, and I could not decide whether to take an advanced science class or stick with the standard level. My school counselor looked at my grades and told me to take the advanced class because it would look great on college applications. However, when I talked to a senior who had actually taken the course, she told me that the lab reports took hours every weekend and the teacher gave very little extra help. Then I asked my parents, and they reminded me that I had already committed to playing soccer in the fall and might burn out. If I had only listened to my counselor, I would have walked into the semester completely unprepared for the workload. Hearing from several people gave me the full picture.

Another reason to seek multiple perspectives is that people have their own biases and emotions. When people give advice, they often project their own personalities onto your situation. For example, if you get into a serious disagreement with a close friend, one person might tell you to completely cut them off because they personally tend to hold grudges. Another friend might tell you to apologize immediately, even if you did nothing wrong, just to keep the peace. If you only listen to one of those friends, you might end up making things worse. By listening to both, you can see the two extremes, filter out the drama, and find a sensible middle

When you clean up a park with a group, you learn teamwork and responsibility. These skills matter for jobs later, and colleges also like to see that students care about more than just grades. The Case for Prohibiting All Cell Phone Use While Driving

Modern drivers face a nearly constant stream of distractions: an incoming text, a navigation alert, a phone call, or a social media notification. Because cell phones are so common, many people believe they can use them while driving without putting anyone at risk. However, being able to physically handle a phone does not mean it is safe to do so. Drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle because even brief, hands-free use can distract them enough to endanger passengers, pedestrians, and other drivers.

The clearest danger is manual and visual distraction. Texting, dialing a number, changing music, or even quickly checking a notification requires a driver to look away from the road. It may also require one hand to leave the steering wheel. At highway speeds, just a few seconds of looking down can cause a car to travel the length of a football field with little attention paid to what is ahead. During that time, a driver could miss a child entering a crosswalk, a vehicle stopping suddenly, debris in the road, or a changing traffic signal. Even if the driver looks away only briefly, the consequences can be severe.

Some people argue that hands-free technology solves this issue, but it does not remove the most important type of distraction: cognitive distraction. A driver may keep both hands on the wheel and their eyes facing forward while talking on the phone, yet their attention is still divided. Conversations require thinking, listening, responding, and sometimes dealing with emotional or stressful topics. As a result, the driver may see the road without fully processing what is happening. Research on inattention blindness suggests that people using hands-free phones can fail to notice hazards directly in front of them because their minds are focused elsewhere. Their reaction times may slow, and their awareness of the surrounding traffic may decrease. Voice-activated texting has a similar problem because composing and correcting a message demands attention that should be devoted to driving.

A complete ban would also be simpler and more effective than rules that only prohibit handheld phones. If hands-free use remains legal, it can be difficult for police officers to determine whether a driver is holding a phone or using a device through Bluetooth or voice commands. Different rules can also confuse drivers and encourage them to believe that certain kinds of phone use are harmless. A total ban would create a clear standard: if a vehicle is in motion, the phone should not be in use.

Critics may say that drivers need access to their phones in emergencies. However, in a genuine emergency, the safest option is to pull over before making a call or sending a message. Many vehicles also include built-in emergency systems that can be used when necessary. Emergency situations should not become an excuse for routine phone use behind the wheel.

Ultimately, no call, text, or notification is more important than a human life. The safest time to use a cell phone is after the driver has stopped the vehicle. To protect everyone on the road, drivers should be legally prohibited from using cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.
