Dear Senator [Last Name],

I am writing to urge you to support replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote for presidential elections. As one of your constituents, I believe that every citizen's ballot ought to carry equal weight, regardless of geographic boundaries. The framework we currently rely on falls well short of that standard.

The most glaring flaw in the Electoral College is its ability to overturn the clear choice of the public. As Bradford Plumer observes in "The Indefensible Electoral College," a candidate can win the national popular vote and still lose the White House, exactly as happened in 2000 and 2016. In any genuine democracy, the candidate who receives the most votes should win the election. When the opposite occurs, trust in our government erodes, leaving millions of citizens feeling as though their voices were entirely disregarded.

The existing system also fundamentally distorts how presidential campaigns are run. According to the Office of the Federal Register, forty-eight states and Washington, D.C. award their electors through a "winner-take-all" rule, granting every single electoral vote to whichever candidate wins the state. As Plumer explains, this setup prompts campaigns to direct almost all their time and money toward a narrow set of swing states, essentially abandoning voters in solidly red or blue areas. A Republican living in California or a Democrat in Texas has little hope of seeing a candidate visit and minimal incentive to even show up at the polls. By contrast, a national popular vote would value every ballot equally, encouraging candidates to reach out to communities nationwide.

Supporters of the status quo offer thoughtful counterarguments. In "In Defense of the Electoral College," Judge Richard A. Posner contends that the system safeguards federalism and obligates contenders to build broad coalitions spanning large and small states, preventing anyone from winning solely by running up numbers in dense cities. Yet under the current rules, candidates already ignore most of the country to pander to a handful of battleground states. Under a direct popular vote, candidates would have to seek votes everywhere—including small towns, suburbs, and rural counties—because every single ballot contributes to the nationwide total. Walking away from non-urban voters would mean throwing away millions of crucial votes.

Judge Posner also suggests that the Electoral College avoids the disruption of a nationwide recount by confining disputes to individual states. Administrative convenience, however, should not outweigh democratic fairness. In truth, the current system heightens recount risks by allowing the presidency to turn on razor-thin margins in a single state, as the nation experienced in Florida in 2000. Additionally, as Plumer points out, the persistent threat of "faithless electors" voting against their state's electorate injects an unnecessary, undemocratic risk into the process.

As the Federal Register outlines, the Founders designed the Electoral College as an eighteenth-century compromise between an election in Congress and a vote of the people. While that arrangement fit the political realities of its era, our country has evolved, and Americans today expect their ballots to determine the presidency directly. I respectfully ask that you advocate for a national popular vote, whether through a constitutional amendment or an interstate compact, so that our leadership truly reflects the will of the people.

Thank you for your time, consideration, and service to our state.

Sincerely,  
[Your Name]

When people face difficult decisions, they often turn to others for guidance. Although one trusted advisor can offer useful insight, seeking several opinions is usually a wiser approach. Consulting different people gives a decision-maker a broader range of perspectives, helps uncover blind spots, and limits the influence of any one person’s bias. By comparing viewpoints, someone can make a more informed and balanced choice.

One major benefit of asking for multiple opinions is that it expands a person’s perspective. Everyone brings different experiences, values, and knowledge to a situation. For example, a student deciding whether to study engineering or art may hear very different advice from a parent, a teacher, and a professional artist. A parent may emphasize financial security and steady employment. A teacher might focus on the student’s academic abilities, while an artist could stress the importance of creativity and personal fulfillment. None of these viewpoints is necessarily wrong, but no single one tells the entire story. Listening to all of them allows the student to consider both practical concerns and personal interests before making a decision.

Getting advice from several people can also reveal blind spots. When people are emotionally invested in a choice, they may overlook risks or ignore alternatives that do not match what they want to hear. Someone who is less involved can often see details more clearly. For instance, a person considering a new job might be excited about a higher salary and fail to think seriously about a long commute or an unhealthy work-life balance. One friend may point out the cost and stress of commuting, while another may mention that the company has a reputation for employee burnout. Without those outside observations, the person might accept the job and regret it later. In this way, multiple opinions can protect someone from narrow or overly hopeful thinking.

Another advantage is that seeking several views reduces the effect of individual bias. A single advisor may have personal preferences, limited experience, or even a conflict of interest. For example, a financial advisor who earns commission on certain products might recommend an investment that benefits the advisor more than the client. If the client speaks with another advisor or reads information from independent sources, they may notice important differences in the recommendations. Comparing advice makes it easier to recognize when someone is being overly subjective or motivated by self-interest.

Of course, too many opinions can sometimes be confusing, especially when people disagree. However, disagreement can be useful rather than harmful. Conflicting advice forces a person to think more carefully about what matters most to them. Instead of simply following one recommendation, they must examine the reasons behind each opinion and decide which arguments are strongest. This process can lead to a choice that feels more thoughtful and personally meaningful.

In the end, seeking multiple opinions is a valuable way to make better decisions. It gives people a fuller view of the situation, reveals possible risks, and reduces the danger of relying on one biased perspective. Even when advice conflicts, it encourages deeper reflection. By listening carefully to several voices, a person can make a choice that is both well-informed and genuinely their own.

Drivers Should Not Use Cell Phones While Driving

Cell phones have become so woven into daily life that many people feel uncomfortable being separated from them even for a few minutes. That habit does not disappear when a person gets behind the wheel. Yet driving demands constant attention, quick judgment, and coordinated physical response, and a phone competes for all three. Drivers should not be permitted to use handheld cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle, and even hands-free use should be strongly discouraged and limited to narrow exceptions such as navigation set before the trip begins.

The strongest argument for a ban is the danger distracted driving poses. Researchers generally describe three kinds of distraction: visual, manual, and cognitive. Texting combines all three. A driver who glances at a screen for just five seconds while traveling at highway speed covers roughly the length of a football field without looking at the road. In that time, traffic can stop, a pedestrian can step off a curb, or a car can drift into the lane. Studies of crash data consistently link phone use to a significantly higher risk of collisions, and the injuries and deaths that result are entirely preventable.

Some people argue that hands-free devices solve the problem. They reason that if both hands remain on the wheel, the driver is safe. However, the evidence suggests that cognitive distraction is as serious as manual distraction. A driver engaged in an intense phone conversation may look at the road without actually processing what is there. This phenomenon, sometimes called inattentional blindness, means the driver can miss red lights, brake lights, or hazards even while facing forward. Because the mind is occupied elsewhere, hands-free calls reduce the danger only partially. For this reason, a rule that simply requires hands-free technology offers a false sense of security.

Another objection is that a total ban infringes on personal freedom or ignores real needs, such as emergencies or work obligations. These concerns deserve consideration, but they do not outweigh public safety. Driving is a regulated activity precisely because one person's choices can seriously harm others. We already require seat belts, sobriety, and obedience to speed limits for the same reason. A driver's convenience does not justify risking the lives of passengers, other motorists, cyclists, and pedestrians who never agreed to share that risk. Moreover, genuine emergencies can be handled by pulling over safely before making a call. Almost no message is so urgent that it cannot wait a few minutes.

Enforcement is also a legitimate concern, since officers cannot always see what a driver is doing. Still, difficulty of enforcement is not a reason to abandon a good rule. Clear laws, meaningful fines, public awareness campaigns, and technology such as "do not disturb while driving" settings can all change behavior over time, just as they did with drunk driving and seat belt use. Social norms often follow the law, and a firm standard helps establish that answering a text behind the wheel is unacceptable.

In conclusion, the convenience of using a phone while driving is trivial compared with the human cost of a crash. Visual, manual, and cognitive distractions all threaten the focus that safe driving requires, and hands-free devices do not eliminate the risk. Society should prohibit cell phone use by drivers, allowing only minimal exceptions such as pre-set navigation or emergency calls made after stopping safely. Protecting lives is worth the small inconvenience of waiting until the car is parked.

Drivers Should Not Use Cell Phones While Driving

Cell phones have become so woven into daily life that many people feel uneasy when separated from them for even a few minutes. That constant connection, however, becomes dangerous when it follows a person into the driver's seat. Although a few narrow exceptions are reasonable, drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity that takes their attention, eyes, or hands away from the task of driving.

The strongest argument for restricting phone use is the danger it creates. Driving demands continuous attention to traffic, pedestrians, road conditions, and sudden hazards. Texting, scrolling, or dialing pulls a driver's focus in three ways at once: visually, because the eyes leave the road; manually, because a hand leaves the wheel; and cognitively, because the mind is occupied elsewhere. A driver traveling at highway speed who glances at a message for just five seconds covers roughly the length of a football field without looking at the road. Thousands of people die each year in crashes involving distracted drivers, and cell phones are among the leading causes. These deaths are preventable, and they often involve innocent passengers, cyclists, and pedestrians who made no choice to take the risk.

Some argue that hands-free calling solves the problem, but research suggests otherwise. Studies of driver performance show that cognitive distraction persists even when both hands are on the wheel and both eyes are on the road. A person engaged in an intense conversation reacts more slowly to brake lights and is more likely to miss important cues. Hands-free technology addresses only one form of distraction while leaving the mental one untouched. For this reason, a ban that merely requires a headset or speaker offers false reassurance.

Others contend that people should be free to manage their own risk, or that phones are necessary for work and emergencies. Personal freedom, however, ends where it endangers others. Driving is a shared activity on public roads, and society already limits behavior that threatens everyone's safety, such as drunk driving and running red lights. As for necessity, almost no message is so urgent that it cannot wait until a driver has pulled over. Emergencies are the clearest example of a legitimate exception: a driver who must call for help after an accident or witnesses a crime can park safely and make the call, or, if stopping is impossible, use a single voice command. Allowing narrow exceptions for emergency calls and for navigation set up before the trip begins is sensible, but these exceptions should not become loopholes for general use.

Enforcement and culture also matter. Laws that clearly prohibit handheld use, paired with meaningful fines and public education campaigns, have helped change attitudes in places where they have been adopted, much as seat belt laws and drunk driving campaigns did in earlier decades. Technology can help as well. Phones can automatically silence notifications while a vehicle is in motion, removing temptation before it arises.

In conclusion, the convenience of using a phone behind the wheel is not worth the lives it puts at risk. Because even hands-free use impairs attention, the safest policy is to prohibit nonessential phone use while driving and to permit only true emergencies and pre-set navigation. A message can always wait, but a life lost on the road cannot be returned. Drivers owe it to themselves and everyone around them to put the phone down and focus on the road.

When people face an important decision, they often ask more than one person for advice. First, multiple opinions provide access to a wider range of knowledge and experience. No single person understands every aspect of a complicated decision. A current student can describe daily campus life, and a financial aid counselor can explain scholarships, loans, and long-term costs. If the student listened only to a friend who chose a college because it had attractive dormitories, the student might overlook more important issues such as affordability or available programs.

Seeking several opinions can also help people recognize their own biases. People naturally tend to favor choices that feel familiar, exciting, or easy. A person considering buying a car, for instance, may be attracted to a stylish vehicle with impressive technology. However, a mechanic might point out that the model has expensive repair costs, while a family member may remind the buyer to consider fuel efficiency and insurance rates. These additional viewpoints do not necessarily prevent the buyer from choosing the preferred car, but they make the decision more realistic. The buyer can compare excitement with practical concerns instead of acting on impulse.

In addition, different opinions can reveal possible consequences that one person might not have considered. Imagine someone deciding whether to accept a new job in another city. A close friend may encourage the move because it offers higher pay and a chance for adventure. However, a mentor might ask whether the job provides opportunities for advancement, while a relative may raise questions about housing costs and being far from family. By listening carefully, the person can weigh both short-term benefits and long-term effects. The person seeking help must evaluate the sources and decide which opinions are relevant. It is usually best to ask people who have knowledge, honesty, and genuine concern rather than simply collecting as many answers as possible.

Ultimately, seeking multiple opinions improves decision-making because it broadens a person’s perspective, reduces the influence of bias, and prepares the person for possible outcomes. Important choices are rarely simple, and no one sees every part of a situation alone. By listening to several thoughtful voices and then making an independent judgment, people can choose more wisely and with greater confidence.

When teachers design these projects, they mostly feel like tedious busywork that kids put off until the last weekend of August. Summer projects should definitely be student-designed instead, because students learn a lot more when they actually care about what they are doing.

First of all, motivation is a huge issue during the summer. When a teacher picks a generic book for everyone to read or assigns a massive packet of practice problems, nobody is excited about it. For example, two summers ago, my class was assigned a massive history research packet on a topic we had already covered. Most of my friends just copied answers from each other or skimmed online summaries the night before school started. Nobody actually learned anything. On the other hand, if a student gets to design their own project, they will choose something that matches their hobbies or future goals. A student interested in computer science could build a simple website, while someone interested in art could create a portfolio of sketches. Another reason student-designed projects are better is that they teach real independence and life skills. In the real world, you do not always have a teacher handing you a detailed rubric with every single step laid out. Designing your own project forces you to ask yourself big questions: What do I want to accomplish? What materials do I need? How am I going to pace myself over two whole months? Learning how to set your own goals and manage your time without daily reminders is way more valuable than just filling out teacher-made worksheets.

If we're allowed to use our phones, we'll have to learn how to do so responsibly and without disrupting others. I agree with the principal's decision that every student should have to join at least one extracurricular activity. At first it might sound like one more thing adults are forcing on us, but I think it would actually make school better for most students, and even the ones who complain about it at the start.

The biggest reason is that activities help students meet people they would never talk to otherwise. In my school, most kids stay with the same friend group from class to class. If you're quiet or new, it can be really lonely. When I joined the yearbook committee last year, I ended up working with seniors and kids from other grades who I never would have met. We had to take pictures at games and plan the layout together, so we had to talk. By the end of the year, I had friends I would have never made in a regular classroom. If everyone had to join something, fewer people would feel left out.

Another reason is that activities teach skills that regular classes don't. In math or English, you mostly work by yourself and get a grade. In student council or a sports team, you have to work with others, meet deadlines, and solve problems when things go wrong. For example, when our student council planned the fall dance, the music was late and we had to figure out a backup plan fast. That taught me more about being responsible than any worksheet. These are the kinds of skills that employers and colleges look for, so having everyone practice them is a good thing.

Some people say a requirement is unfair because students already have too much homework or have jobs after school. That is a fair point, and I think the school should be flexible. The rule says "at least one" activity, so a student could choose something small like a club that meets once a week. The school could also count things like helping at a family business or taking care of siblings if a student really can't stay after school. A requirement doesn't have to be hard if the school offers lots of choices and works with students' schedules.

Other people argue that students who are forced to join won't care and will just be bored. I understand that, but I think many students just haven't found what they like yet. I never thought I would enjoy photography until I had to take pictures for the yearbook. If I hadn't been pushed into trying something, I would have gone home every day and played video games. A lot of kids probably don't join because they're nervous or think nobody will want them. A requirement gives them a reason to try, and once they're there, they might find something they love.

Finally, activities make students feel more connected to the school. When you're on a team or in a club, you want to go to school more, and you care about how the school looks. Students who are involved are less likely to skip class or get into trouble because they have somewhere to be and people counting on them. That would help the whole school, not just the individual students.

In conclusion, I support the principal's decision because extracurricular activities help students make friends, learn real-life skills, and feel like part of the school. As long as the school gives students plenty of options and is flexible for those with real conflicts, requiring one activity is a smart idea that would help almost everyone.

The idea of driverless cars has generated a great deal of debate. Some people see them as the next major step in transportation, while others worry about safety and legal responsibility. After reading “Driverless Cars Are Coming,” I support their development. Although the concerns are real, the potential to prevent crashes and help people who cannot drive makes the technology worth pursuing.

One of the strongest reasons to support driverless cars is their ability to reduce accidents. The article notes that human error causes more than 90 percent of traffic accidents, often from texting, drowsiness, or impaired driving. Unlike people, autonomous vehicles do not get distracted or tired. With laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors, they can spot obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals. Fewer crashes would mean fewer deaths and lower insurance costs. In addition, driverless cars could give elderly and disabled passengers a new level of independence.

Another benefit mentioned in the article is efficiency. Sergey Brin imagines a future of driverless public transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today’s cars. This could reduce our dependence on fossil fuels and ease parking problems in crowded cities. If fewer people needed to own cars, vehicles could be used more often instead of sitting idle, creating a more streamlined transportation system.

Of course, critics raise valid points. Sensors can have trouble in heavy rain, snow, or fog, and construction zones without clear markings can confuse them. Software glitches and cybersecurity threats also remain serious concerns. Some semi-autonomous systems still require drivers to stay alert and take over, but studies show that people quickly lose focus when a computer is driving. These issues, however, are not permanent barriers. With continued research and testing, sensors and software can improve. Clear laws and regulations can also address questions about who is responsible when an accident occurs—the owner, the software developer, or the automaker.

In conclusion, driverless cars could save lives, expand mobility, and reduce fuel use and parking needs. The safety and legal challenges deserve attention, but they should not stop progress. By supporting development and creating thoughtful regulations, we can work toward a transportation system that is safer, more efficient, and more accessible. Driverless cars may not be perfect yet, but they are a step in the right direction.

Proceed with Caution: Why Driverless Cars Are Not Yet Ready

The idea of driverless cars seems like something from the future: vehicles that can travel on their own, reduce accidents, and give independence to people who cannot drive. Although these benefits are appealing, the article “Driverless Cars Are Coming” shows that autonomous vehicles are not yet safe enough for widespread use. Driverless cars may eventually improve transportation, but their current sensor problems, cybersecurity risks, distracted human supervision, and unanswered legal questions make it too risky to rush them onto public roads.

Supporters of driverless cars have strong reasons to be hopeful. The article explains that human error causes more than 90 percent of traffic accidents. Texting, driving while tired, and impaired driving all lead to dangerous mistakes that a computer might avoid. Autonomous vehicles could reduce crashes, save lives, lower insurance costs, and help elderly or disabled people travel more easily. In addition, Sergey Brin imagines driverless public transportation that would use less fuel and require less parking space. These advantages could make communities safer and more efficient. However, those benefits depend on the technology working safely in all kinds of situations, and it is not ready to do that yet.

One of the biggest concerns is that driverless cars may not perform well in difficult driving conditions. According to the article, their sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, and unmarked construction zones. These are often the situations when drivers need the most reliable guidance. If a vehicle cannot clearly detect an obstacle, lane marking, or traffic signal, it could make a dangerous decision in only a few seconds. Roads are not always predictable or clearly marked, especially during bad weather or construction. A system that works well on a clear, sunny day may not be dependable when conditions become more complicated.

Technology failures also create serious safety concerns. The article states that autonomous software can be vulnerable to glitches and cybersecurity threats. A computer system may be able to avoid certain human mistakes, but it can also malfunction or be hacked. If one driver makes a poor choice, the danger is usually limited to that vehicle. However, a software flaw affecting many cars could put a large number of people at risk. Before driverless vehicles become common, companies must prove that their systems can resist hacking and respond safely when something goes wrong.

Semi-autonomous cars present another problem because they still depend on human drivers in emergencies. The article explains that people are expected to stay alert and take control when necessary. Yet studies show that passengers quickly lose focus when the computer is driving, causing slower reaction times. This creates a dangerous middle ground. Drivers may assume that the car can handle everything, but they may suddenly be expected to react in an emergency. By the time a distracted person understands what is happening, it could be too late to prevent a crash.

Finally, the legal questions surrounding driverless cars have not been settled. When an accident occurs, it is unclear whether responsibility belongs to the owner, the automaker, or the software developer. Without clear rules, victims may have difficulty receiving compensation, and companies may not be fully accountable for safety problems.

In conclusion, driverless cars offer important possibilities, including fewer accidents and greater freedom for people who cannot drive. Still, the risks are too serious to ignore. Until sensors work reliably in difficult conditions, software is protected from threats, drivers can safely respond to emergencies, and legal responsibility is clear, driverless cars should not be widely used. The future may include autonomous vehicles, but safety must come before speed.

Summer projects are meant to keep students learning during the break, but a poorly planned assignment can make learning feel like nothing more than a chore. The question of who should design these projects—teachers or students—matters because students are more engaged when they have ownership over their work. Schools should require summer projects that are mostly student-designed, while teachers provide clear expectations, structure, and support.

To begin with, student-designed projects can create real motivation. When students choose a subject they genuinely care about, they are more likely to work consistently and remember what they learn. For instance, a seventh grader who is interested in sharks could read scientific articles, examine population data, and make an infographic about shark conservation. That student would probably learn more from researching a favorite topic than from completing a generic packet assigned to everyone in the class. Having a choice can turn summer work from an obligation into an opportunity to explore curiosity.

Student-designed projects also make it easier to meet different learning needs. A single teacher-created assignment may be too difficult for some students and too simple for others. Students have different strengths, interests, and access to resources during the summer, so one project will not fit every person equally well. For example, a student who finds long essays challenging but loves basketball could track shooting percentages, create graphs showing improvement, and write short reflections about practice. This would still involve math, organization, and writing, but it would connect those skills to something meaningful. In the same way, a student interested in coding might create a simple app, while another student who enjoys cooking could test recipes and explain the science behind baking.

Allowing students to choose their topics does not mean that teachers have no role. Teachers can set academic goals without controlling every detail of the project. They might require students to include research, writing, data analysis, and a final presentation. They could also provide a rubric, deadlines, and check-ins before the summer begins. For example, a teacher could ask each student to submit a project proposal, keep a process journal, and present the results in the fall. Within that structure, one student might investigate local history, another might develop a small business plan, and another might study pollution in a nearby stream. All three projects could meet the same standards while allowing students to follow their own interests.

Some people may argue that teacher-designed projects are better because they guarantee rigor and make sure students review important standards. This concern is reasonable, especially because summer projects should still have academic value. However, teacher guidance does not have to mean teacher control. A strong rubric can ensure that every project includes serious learning, even if students choose different subjects and formats. In fact, students may work harder to meet high expectations when the project reflects their own goals.

Ultimately, summer learning should do more than fill students’ time. It should help them become independent, curious learners. Student-designed projects, supported by teacher-created guidelines, accomplish this better than assignments that are entirely teacher-designed. They encourage motivation, recognize individual differences, and teach students how to plan, manage time, and take responsibility for their education. When students return to school in the fall, they can bring back not only completed projects, but also confidence in their ability to learn on their own.

When it comes to summer projects, I think they should be student-designed. This might seem like it would lead to students slacking off and not doing any real learning, but I believe it's actually the opposite. When students get to choose their own project, they're more likely to pick something they're actually interested in, which means they'll be more motivated to learn.

For example, last year I had to do a science project over the summer, and my teacher assigned us a list of topics to choose from. I ended up choosing a project on renewable energy, but only because it seemed like the easiest one. I didn't really care about the topic, and as a result, I didn't put much effort into it. I just went through the motions and did the bare minimum to get it done. If I had been able to choose my own topic, I probably would have chosen something like robotics or coding, which are areas I'm really passionate about. I would have been way more invested in the project and would have learned a lot more.

Another reason student-designed projects are better is that they allow students to explore their own interests and strengths. When teachers assign projects, they often have to make sure everyone is doing something similar, so they can grade them fairly. This means that students who might be talented in a particular area don't get to showcase their skills. For instance, I have a friend who's really into art, but our school doesn't offer many art classes. If she could design her own summer project, she could focus on art and create something really amazing. This would not only be more enjoyable for her, but it would also give her a chance to develop her talents.

Some people might argue that student-designed projects would be too easy or that students wouldn't learn anything meaningful. But I don't think that's true. If students are given the freedom to choose their own project, they'll still have to meet certain requirements and standards. For example, they might have to write a report or create a presentation to share with the class. This would ensure that they're still learning and demonstrating their knowledge, even if they're doing it in a more self-directed way.

In addition, student-designed projects can help prepare students for the real world. In most careers, people don't have someone telling them exactly what to do all the time. They have to be able to take initiative and come up with their own ideas. By giving students the freedom to design their own summer projects, we're teaching them important skills like independence, creativity, and problem-solving.

Overall, I think summer projects should be student-designed. This would allow students to take ownership of their learning, explore their interests, and develop their strengths. It would also give them the freedom to be creative and come up with their own ideas, which is an essential skill for success in any field. By giving students more autonomy, we can help them stay engaged and motivated, even during the summer months.

I see it every day: people at red lights glancing at their laps, one hand on the wheel and the other holding a phone. I understand why people do it. A text feels quick, a call feels harmless, and changing a song seems automatic. But driving already asks for our eyes, hands, and attention all at once. Because of that, drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while the car is moving. Not texting, not talking on speakerphone, not even using a mounted phone for directions while tapping the screen.

The main reason is that our brains cannot actually multitask. When I first heard that in driver's ed, I thought it meant people just needed to try harder. But my instructor explained that your brain switches back and forth between tasks really fast, and each switch leaves a small gap. In a car going 55 miles per hour, a one-second gap means you have traveled about 80 feet without fully paying attention. That is the length of a basketball court. A lot can go wrong in that space: a kid runs into the street, a car brakes suddenly, or a light changes. Even a quick glance at a phone can turn into a crash.

Some people argue that hands-free phone calls are safe because your hands stay on the wheel. I used to think that made sense, but it does not hold up. The problem is not just your hands; it is your mind. When you are having a conversation, you are picturing the person, thinking about what they said, and planning what to say next. That is mental energy that should be going to scanning the road. A driver on a hands-free call can look right at a stop sign and still blow through it because their brain did not process what their eyes saw. My dad once missed our exit while talking to his boss on speakerphone, and that was just an annoying mistake. If it had been a pedestrian, it would have been much worse.

I also think "any capacity" should include using a phone for GPS. I know maps help people, but there is a difference between setting up directions before you start driving and poking at a screen while moving. If you need to change the route, pull over. It is not worth risking a life to save thirty seconds.

Some people might say banning all phone use is unrealistic because phones are part of life now. But we already accept strict rules for other dangerous things. You cannot drink and drive, and you cannot drive with your windshield covered in snow. Using a phone while driving should be treated the same way. A phone is not a right; it is a tool that can wait.

Driving is one of the most dangerous things most of us do every day. If we allow any phone use, we are basically saying that a text or a call is more important than someone's safety. It is not. Drivers should put the phone out of reach, set everything up before they start the car, and keep their attention on the road. Nothing on a screen is worth a life.

The rapid advancement of digital technology has fundamentally transformed how society communicates, works, and learns. In recent years, educational institutions have increasingly integrated virtual classrooms, enabling students to attend lectures and complete coursework from home. While traditional in-person schooling has long been the standard, offering distance learning as a viable option provides profound advantages. Students benefit substantially from virtual education because it accommodates diverse learning styles, fosters essential self-discipline, and broadens accessibility for individuals facing unique life circumstances.

First and foremost, distance learning provides an adaptable environment that supports individualized academic pacing. Traditional classrooms inevitably cater to the median student, often leaving struggling learners overwhelmed and advanced learners disengaged. At home, students can often revisit recorded lectures, pause complex explanations, and manage their study hours during periods of peak cognitive focus. Furthermore, learners with neurodivergent profiles or sensory processing sensitivities often find conventional school settings noisy, crowded, and anxiety-inducing. A controlled home environment allows these students to eliminate external distractions, manage their own physical comfort, and ultimately concentrate more effectively on their academic growth.

In addition to academic customization, learning from home cultivates crucial life skills, notably independence and digital literacy. Without the physical oversight of a teacher monitoring every minute of the day, remote students must learn to organize their schedules, meet deadlines, and navigate independent research. These capabilities mirror the demands of modern universities and the increasingly remote professional landscape. By utilizing video conferencing, digital collaboration tools, and online submission portals, students acquire proficiency in technologies that dominate contemporary workplaces. Consequently, distance education prepares students for future career success far more dynamically than traditional lecture-and-worksheet paradigms.

Opponents of distance education frequently argue that learning from home diminishes social interaction and limits spontaneous peer collaboration. While interpersonal socialization is undeniably an important component of childhood and adolescent development, offering distance learning as an *option* does not mean eliminating physical schools entirely. Rather, it serves as an indispensable alternative for students who are marginalized by conventional settings. For instance, students with chronic illnesses, teenagers pursuing rigorous athletic or artistic training, or families residing in remote rural regions gain access to robust academic programs that would otherwise be geographically or physically inaccessible. Furthermore, modern digital platforms integrate breakout rooms, discussion boards, and collaborative virtual projects, ensuring that peer engagement remains an active component of the virtual classroom.

In conclusion, permitting students to attend classes from home offers undeniable educational and personal benefits. By offering flexible learning conditions, nurturing autonomous time management, and providing equitable access to diverse demographics, distance learning modernizes education to fit the needs of a changing world. Rather than restricting students to a uniform, physical setting, educational institutions should embrace remote learning as an empowering choice that helps every student realize their full intellectual potential.

Dear Principal Davis,

As our school weighs the pros and cons of implementing a mandatory community service requirement for graduation, I wanted to share my thoughts on this important issue. Many of my friends and classmates are already dedicated to giving back to the community, whether it's through tutoring elementary school children or organizing park cleanups. They often speak about the sense of fulfillment and purpose they derive from these experiences. However, I've also seen how demanding academic schedules, part-time jobs, and family responsibilities can leave some students struggling to keep up. While I appreciate the value of cultivating civic responsibility, I firmly believe that requiring community service would be a misguided approach. Instead, our school should focus on encouraging and supporting voluntary service.

The primary concern I have with a mandatory service requirement is that it fails to account for the diverse realities and challenges that students face outside the classroom. For many teenagers, extracurricular activities aren't just a hobby or a way to pass the time; they're a necessity. Some students work part-time jobs to help support their families, while others care for younger siblings or devote long hours to studying in order to qualify for college scholarships. Adding a fixed hourly requirement for community service to an already packed schedule can be overwhelming, leading to stress, sleep deprivation, and decreased academic performance. By acknowledging and respecting these varying commitments, we can create a more inclusive and supportive environment that allows students to engage in community service in a way that's meaningful and sustainable for them.

Moreover, the idea of "mandatory volunteering" seems inherently contradictory. When we're forced to participate in community service, doesn't that undermine the very spirit of volunteerism? Doesn't it become just another checkbox on a list of graduation requirements, rather than a genuine expression of our desire to make a positive impact? By keeping community service optional, we can ensure that students are motivated by a genuine desire to help others, rather than simply fulfilling a requirement. This approach also allows students to explore different types of service and find the activities that truly resonate with them, leading to a more profound and lasting sense of engagement.

In addition, our school can play a vital role in facilitating and supporting community service, even if it's not mandatory. We could provide resources and guidance to help students find service opportunities that align with their interests and schedules. We could also recognize and celebrate the contributions of students who do choose to participate in community service, whether through special events, awards, or simply acknowledging their efforts in school publications. By taking a more nuanced and supportive approach, we can foster a culture of civic responsibility and empathy that extends far beyond the confines of a mandatory requirement.

Ultimately, I believe that our school should prioritize flexibility and autonomy when it comes to community service. By trusting students to make their own choices and providing the support and resources they need, we can create a more vibrant and engaged community that's driven by a genuine desire to make a difference.

Drivers should not be able to use handheld cell phones while operating a vehicle, and the law should come close to an absolute ban on any use that takes eyes, hands, or attention away from the road. The phrase "in any capacity" deserves some care, though. A narrow exception for hands-free navigation and emergency calls is defensible. Texting, scrolling, and holding a phone to one's ear are not.

Start with what driving actually demands. It is not a single skill but a constant juggling of perception, prediction, and quick physical response. A car traveling at 55 miles per hour covers about 80 feet every second. Glance at a text for five seconds and you have crossed more than a football field essentially blind. Nothing about a notification is urgent enough to justify that gamble, yet millions of people take it daily because the phone is within reach and the habit feels harmless. Crash data tells a grimmer story: the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration attributes thousands of deaths each year to distracted driving, and researchers widely suspect the true figure is higher because drivers rarely admit to phone use after a collision.

Some defenders of phone use argue that talking on a hands-free device is no different from chatting with a passenger. The research does not support this comfortable idea. A passenger shares the road with you; they notice the truck merging, and they stop talking when traffic gets tense. A person on the phone has no such awareness. Studies using driving simulators have found that even hands-free conversation pulls cognitive resources away from the visual task, producing slower reactions and more missed cues. The danger lies not only in where your hands are but in where your mind has gone. For that reason, I think a total ban on handheld use is the minimum, and lawmakers should be honest that hands-free calling carries real, if smaller, risks.

There are legitimate counterpoints. Phones now serve as maps, music players, and lifelines. A driver stranded on a dark highway or witnessing a crash should be able to call for help, and navigation apps have arguably prevented as many wrong turns and panicked lane changes as they have caused distractions. A rule that forbids everything would be both unenforceable and unreasonable. The sensible approach is to permit a phone mounted on the dashboard, set up before the trip begins, and operated by voice or a single tap. Emergency calls, ideally made after pulling over, should always remain acceptable.

Enforcement matters as much as the rule itself. Laws that carry only small fines have done little to change behavior, because the odds of getting caught feel remote. Stronger penalties, including license points and higher fines for repeat offenders, send a clearer signal. Technology can help too. Phones already can detect when they are moving at driving speed, and automatic do-not-disturb settings could silence most notifications by default, leaving drivers to opt out rather than opt in.

Ultimately this is a question of responsibility to other people. A driver who texts is not only risking a personal injury; they are endangering pedestrians, cyclists, and families in other cars who never agreed to share that risk. Freedom to use one's phone ends where it threatens someone else's life. Society has accepted this logic with drunk driving, and the same reasoning applies here. The message on the screen can wait. The person crossing the street cannot.

Cell phones have become such a constant part of everyday life that being separated from them, even briefly, makes a lot of people anxious. Yet that constant urge to stay connected turns deadly the second someone gets behind the wheel. While a few narrow exceptions make sense, drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones while operating a vehicle in any way that pulls their eyes, hands, or attention away from the road.

The primary reason to restrict phone use while driving is simple: the danger is immense. Operating a vehicle requires ongoing awareness of surrounding traffic, pedestrians, changing weather, and sudden obstacles. When a driver texts, scrolls, or dials, their attention is compromised on three distinct levels. It is visual because their eyes leave the road, manual because at least one hand leaves the steering wheel, and cognitive because their mind is focused on the screen rather than their surroundings. At highway speeds, looking down at a text for just five seconds means traveling the entire length of a football field essentially blindfolded. Thousands of people lose their lives each year in crashes caused by distracted driving, with smartphones frequently at the center of these incidents. Most of these tragedies are entirely preventable, and they often claim the lives of pedestrians, cyclists, and passengers who did nothing wrong.

Many drivers assume that hands-free setups eliminate this hazard, but research paints a different picture. Studies show that mental distraction remains high even when both hands stay on the wheel and the driver looks straight ahead. Carrying on an involved phone conversation narrows a person’s field of vision and slows their reaction time when someone ahead taps the brakes. Because hands-free features address only the physical aspect of distraction while ignoring the mental strain, laws that merely ban handheld devices give motorists a false sense of security.

Some might argue that adults should be allowed to manage their own risks, or that their jobs demand constant availability. However, individual freedom stops where it puts innocent people in harm's way. Driving is a shared responsibility on public roads, which is why society already regulates behaviors like speeding and driving under the influence. As for work-related calls, almost no message is urgent enough to justify risking a collision. True emergencies—such as needing to report an accident or call an ambulance—are the only reasonable exceptions, and even then, motorists should pull over safely whenever possible. Setting a GPS route before putting the car in gear is similarly acceptable, provided the driver does not manipulate the screen while moving.

Shifting public habits takes both legislation and technology. Just as seatbelt laws and anti-drunk-driving campaigns gradually changed public behavior decades ago, clear prohibitions backed by realistic fines can reshape social norms around texting and driving. Built-in smartphone settings, like automated driving modes that silence notifications on the move, can also remove temptation before it starts.

Ultimately, no text message or phone call is worth a human life. Because even hands-free devices sap critical focus, the safest standard is to ban nonessential phone use behind the wheel altogether. A notification can always wait, but a life taken in a split second can never be brought back.

I think students would really benefit from being able to attend classes from home. There are a lot of reasons why this could be a good thing. For one, some students have a hard time getting to school in the morning. Maybe they live far away, or their parents have to work early and can't drive them. If they could just attend classes from home, that would solve the problem. They could just wake up, have some breakfast, and then log in to their classes online. It would be so much easier for them.

Another reason why attending classes from home could be beneficial is that it would be great for students who get sick easily. My friend Emily is like that. She's always getting colds and fevers, and she has to miss a lot of school. If she could just attend classes from home, she wouldn't fall behind as much. She could still do her schoolwork and participate in class discussions, even if she's not feeling well enough to go to school in person. That way, she wouldn't have to worry about missing out on important lessons or getting behind on her homework.

Attending classes from home could also be helpful for students who have other commitments that they need to take care of during the day. For example, maybe they have to take care of a family member or work a part-time job. If they could just attend classes online, they could do that and still get their schoolwork done. It would be a lot more flexible for them. My brother has to work on weekends, but sometimes he has to work on weekdays too. If he could attend classes from home, he could do his schoolwork and still go to work when he needs to.

Some people might say that attending classes from home would be bad because students would miss out on social interactions with their friends and teachers. But I don't think that's necessarily true. With video conferencing, students could still see and talk to their friends and teachers, even if they're not in the same room. It's not the same as being there in person, but it's still better than nothing. And besides, students could still go to school sometimes, like for special events or when they need extra help from a teacher. It wouldn't have to be all or nothing.

In addition, attending classes from home could be better for students who get distracted easily in a traditional classroom setting. Some students just can't focus when there are other people talking and making noise around them. If they could attend classes from home, they could work in a quieter environment and maybe even get more done. My sister is like that. She gets really distracted when people are talking loudly, so she often does her homework in her room with her headphones on. I believe students should be required to complete some community service before graduating, although the requirement should be flexible enough to respect students’ schedules and interests. School is not only a place to learn math, history, and science. It is also a place where young people learn how their actions affect others. Community service gives students a chance to practice responsibility in a way that classrooms alone cannot.

Many students do not realize how much help is needed close to home. A student who tutors an elementary school child may discover that spending one hour a week practicing multiplication or reading a story can make a real difference. The younger child may become more confident, while the tutor learns patience and communication skills. Similarly, students who clean up a park or neighborhood may begin to care more about littering when they see how much trash collects in public spaces. These experiences make community problems feel personal instead of distant.

Required service could also help students find strengths and interests they did not know they had. Not everyone enjoys the same kind of volunteer work. One student might like helping at an animal shelter, while another might prefer organizing canned food donations, visiting senior citizens, coaching younger athletes, or assisting at a library. If the school allows a wide variety of approved activities, students can choose work that fits their abilities. A quiet student who is uncomfortable speaking to groups could sort donations, while a student interested in medicine could volunteer at a health fair. The requirement would not be forcing everyone into one activity; it would be encouraging everyone to contribute in some meaningful way.

I understand why some students worry that community service will take time away from homework, jobs, sports, or family responsibilities. That concern is reasonable. For this reason, the school should not demand an unrealistic number of hours. A modest requirement spread over several years would be manageable. Students should also be allowed to count service they already perform, such as helping at a church event, caring for community gardens, or volunteering through a team or club. In special circumstances, such as having a job to support one’s family, students could receive alternative options or adjusted deadlines.

Community service should not become just another box to check for graduation. Teachers and counselors could ask students to briefly reflect on what they learned after completing their hours. Even a short reflection could help students connect their work to larger lessons about citizenship, empathy, and leadership.

Requiring community service would send the message that being educated means more than preparing for a career. It means recognizing that we belong to a community and have the ability to improve it. With reasonable expectations and flexible choices, this requirement would benefit both students and the people they serve.

Cell phones have become essential tools for communication, navigation, work, and emergency assistance. Because they are so common, many drivers believe they can safely make calls, follow directions, or send quick messages while behind the wheel. However, drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle. Even seemingly harmless phone use divides a driver’s attention, slows reaction time, and creates unnecessary risks for passengers, pedestrians, and other motorists.

The central problem with cell phone use is distraction. Safe driving requires constant attention to changing conditions: traffic lights, road signs, nearby vehicles, weather, cyclists, and people crossing the street. A driver may need to brake or steer suddenly with little warning. Looking down at a screen for only a few seconds can mean traveling the length of a football field without fully watching the road. Texting is especially dangerous because it requires visual, manual, and mental attention at the same time. Yet voice calls and hands-free devices can also be unsafe because a conversation distracts the driver mentally. A person focused on a phone call may look at the road but fail to notice important information, such as a car braking ahead or a child approaching a crosswalk.

Some people argue that hands-free technology should be allowed because it lets drivers keep both hands on the wheel. Although hands-free devices reduce the need to physically hold a phone, they do not eliminate cognitive distraction. The human brain cannot fully concentrate on a serious conversation and complex driving conditions simultaneously. In fact, drivers talking through speakers may become overly confident because they feel safer than they actually are. Navigation apps can be useful, but directions should be entered before the vehicle begins moving. If a driver needs to change a destination, answer a call, or read a message, the responsible choice is to pull over somewhere safe.

A broad restriction on phone use would also encourage a clearer social expectation. Laws that permit some forms of phone use while banning others can be difficult to enforce and may confuse drivers. A simple rule—do not use a phone while the vehicle is in operation—would be easier to understand. It would also help change behavior over time, much as seat belt laws and restrictions on drunk driving have made safety practices more widely accepted. Drivers should prepare before leaving, silence nonessential notifications, and use “do not disturb” settings to reduce temptation.

There should, of course, be practical consideration for emergencies. If a driver faces an urgent situation, such as witnessing a crash or experiencing a medical emergency, contacting emergency services may be necessary. Whenever possible, however, the driver should first stop the vehicle in a safe location. The goal is not to deny people access to help, but to prevent routine convenience from becoming a deadly distraction.

Ultimately, operating a vehicle is a serious responsibility, not an activity that should be combined with constant digital communication. Because even brief cell phone use can impair attention and endanger lives, drivers should not use phones in any capacity while actively driving. The few minutes saved by answering a message or taking a call are never worth the possible cost of a preventable crash.

The widespread use of cell phones has made them a constant presence in daily life. Many people depend on them for communication, directions, and entertainment. But when someone gets behind the wheel, the question of whether drivers should be allowed to use cell phones at all becomes urgent. Although cell phones offer convenience, I believe drivers should not be permitted to use them in any capacity while operating a vehicle. The dangers of distracted driving are simply too serious to ignore.

One of the strongest reasons for a complete ban is the sharp increase in accident risk. Studies have consistently shown that texting, browsing, or even talking on a phone can pull a driver’s attention away from the road. This leads to slower reaction times, less awareness of surrounding traffic, and weaker control of the vehicle. The results can be catastrophic, including crashes, injuries, and deaths. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has identified distracted driving as a leading cause of accidents, with thousands of lives lost or damaged every year. Allowing any phone use behind the wheel puts drivers, passengers, pedestrians, and other motorists in danger.

Some people argue that hands-free devices or voice-activated systems offer a safe compromise. However, this view overlooks the mental distraction involved. Even when a driver’s hands are on the wheel and eyes are on the road, a conversation still demands cognitive attention. Research from the American Automobile Association indicates that drivers using hands-free technology still experience reduced reaction times and a higher crash risk. A phone call, whether handheld or not, can make it harder to notice sudden hazards or respond quickly to changing conditions.

Permitting any cell phone use while driving also risks normalizing distracted behavior more broadly. If drivers feel that glancing at a screen or taking a call is acceptable, they may become more comfortable with other distractions, such as eating, adjusting a playlist, or reaching for items in the car. Over time, this can make distracted driving seem ordinary rather than dangerous, weakening the message that full attention belongs on the road.

In the end, the risks of using a cell phone while driving far outweigh any convenience it might provide. A complete prohibition would encourage drivers to keep their focus where it belongs and help reduce accidents, injuries, and deaths. By treating undistracted driving as the standard, we can create safer roads and protect everyone who uses them.

Why Seeking Multiple Opinions Leads to Better Choices

When facing an important decision, most people instinctively turn to someone they trust. A single trusted voice can be comforting, but it is rarely enough. Seeking multiple opinions helps a person make a better choice because it exposes blind spots, reveals a wider range of options, and makes it easier to separate good advice from personal bias.

The first benefit of consulting several people is that every adviser has limited experience. No one sees a problem from every angle. Consider a high school senior deciding between a large state university and a small private college. A parent might emphasize cost and job prospects, since those are the concerns of someone who will help pay the bills. A school counselor might focus on academic fit and graduation rates. A recent graduate might describe campus culture, class sizes, and how helpful professors actually were. Each perspective is accurate but incomplete. Only by hearing all three can the student weigh financial, academic, and social factors together rather than letting one dominate the decision.

Second, multiple opinions can introduce options a person has not considered. Someone struggling with a job offer might assume the choice is simply to accept or decline. A mentor might suggest negotiating the salary, while a friend in the same industry might point out that asking for a later start date could allow time to finish a certification. Because different people draw on different networks and experiences, they generate different solutions. A single adviser tends to answer the question as it was asked, while a group often reframes the question itself.

Third, hearing several viewpoints helps a person detect bias. Every adviser has motives, whether conscious or not. A salesperson recommending a particular laptop may earn a commission. A relative urging someone to stay in their hometown may be motivated by a wish not to lose them. A friend who dislikes risk may discourage a business idea simply because the friend would never take such a chance. When only one opinion is available, these influences are hard to see. When three or four people are compared, patterns emerge. If most advisers raise the same concern, it is probably valid; if only one person holds a strong view, the person can ask whether that view reflects the situation or the adviser's own preferences.

Critics might argue that too many opinions create confusion. Conflicting advice can leave a person anxious and indecisive, and trying to please everyone can lead to a weak compromise. This risk is real, but it is manageable. The goal is not to follow the majority vote; it is to gather information and then think independently. A sensible approach is to consult a small number of people with different backgrounds, ask each to explain their reasoning, and then weigh those reasons against one's own values and goals. Disagreement among advisers is not a flaw in the process. It often shows exactly where the hardest trade-offs lie.

In the end, seeking multiple opinions strengthens decision-making because it broadens perspective, expands possibilities, and exposes hidden bias. A single piece of advice may be wise, but there is no easy way to know that without comparison. By listening to several thoughtful people and then making the final judgment themselves, individuals are more likely to choose in a way that is informed, balanced, and genuinely their own.

Dear Principal Smith,

I am writing to express my concern about the proposed policy requiring students to maintain at least a B average to participate in sports and other activities. I understand that the goal is to encourage academic success, but I believe this change would hurt many students and our school community more than it would help.

First, a C average represents satisfactory academic progress, not failure. Many students work hard and still earn Cs, especially when they are taking challenging courses. A student may be an excellent writer but struggle with algebra, or a talented musician who finds chemistry difficult. Requiring a B average would punish students for not being exceptional in every subject. Since a C is a passing grade, students who earn one are still meeting important academic expectations.

Also, extracurricular activities often help students improve in school. Sports, clubs, and arts programs give students structure, adult mentors, and a reason to come to school each day. Many students complete homework, attend tutoring, or ask teachers for extra help because they want to remain on a team or continue participating in a club. If the required average is raised to a B, some students with C averages may feel that the goal is impossible and give up instead of trying harder.

Activities also teach important skills that cannot always be learned in a classroom. On a sports team, students learn cooperation, responsibility, time management, and how to handle success and disappointment. In clubs, band, theater, and student government, students develop leadership skills and confidence. These experiences can help students become more organized and motivated in their academic work. Removing them from activities could take away one of the main reasons some students stay connected to school.

In addition, a B-average requirement could unfairly affect students who have responsibilities outside of school. Some students work part-time jobs, care for younger siblings, or deal with family problems while trying to keep up with classes. They may earn Cs not because they do not care about school, but because they are balancing many demands. Preventing them from participating in activities would make school feel less welcoming at a time when they may need support the most.

Instead of requiring a B average, the school could continue to require passing grades and offer extra academic support to students who are struggling. Study halls, tutoring sessions, progress checks, or meetings with teachers and coaches could encourage improvement without excluding students from activities. This approach would hold students accountable while still giving them the motivation and support they need.

I believe our school should encourage students to improve, not take away the programs that may help them succeed. For these reasons, I respectfully ask you not to require a B average for participation in sports and other activities.

Sincerely,  
[Student Name]

I agree that students should be required to participate in at least one extracurricular activity, as long as the school offers many different choices and makes reasonable exceptions for students with serious family or work responsibilities. Extracurricular activities are not just something to put on a college application. They can help students make friends, learn responsibility, and discover interests they might never find in regular classes.

First, activities give students a chance to feel connected to school. Not every student enjoys sitting in a classroom all day, and some students may feel like they do not really belong anywhere. Joining a team or club can change that. For example, a student who is quiet in English class might feel more comfortable joining the yearbook staff because they enjoy taking pictures or designing pages. They could meet other students with similar interests and become more confident over time. When students feel connected to their school, they may be more likely to attend regularly and care about their grades.

Extracurricular activities also teach skills that are hard to learn from textbooks. Sports can teach teamwork, discipline, and how to handle losing without giving up. Student council can teach leadership and public speaking. Drama club can help students become less nervous about presenting in front of people. Even a gardening club or chess club can teach patience and planning. These skills matter later in jobs and in everyday life. A person will probably have to work with others, solve problems, and manage their time no matter what career they choose.

Another reason to require one activity is that students may discover a talent they did not know they had. Some students would never sign up on their own because they are shy, busy, or worried that they will not be good at it. However, if they are encouraged to choose something, they may end up enjoying it. My cousin joined the robotics club only because his friends needed another member. At first, he did not know much about building robots, but he learned how to code and became one of the leaders of the group. Now he wants to study engineering after high school. If he had never joined, he might not have found that interest.

Of course, the requirement should not be unfair. Schools should not force every student to play a sport or stay after school every day. There should be options such as tutoring younger students, joining an online club, helping with school events, or participating in a lunchtime activity. Students who have jobs, care for siblings, or have transportation problems should be able to work with the school to find an option that fits their situation.

Overall, requiring one extracurricular activity would be a positive decision. It would push students to try new things, build useful skills, and become part of a community. School should be about more than passing classes, and activities can help make high school a more meaningful experience.

Dear Principal Reynolds,

As you weigh the school’s future policy regarding personal electronics, I appreciate the opportunity to share a student perspective. While I recognize the temptation to cut through classroom distractions with an absolute ban, I strongly urge you to adopt Policy 1, permitting students to keep their phones turned off during instructional time while allowing their use during lunch and designated free periods. 

A total prohibition on mobile devices ignores the logistical realities modern families navigate daily. Many of us balance shifting family responsibilities, part-time jobs, and unpredictable extracurricular schedules. A parent who works odd hours cannot always rely on an overburdened front office to relay a time-sensitive update about transportation, younger siblings, or a doctor’s appointment. Being able to check a single text message during the twenty-five minutes of lunch provides families peace of mind without disrupting an ongoing lesson. 

Beyond convenience, complete bans rarely produce the serene, focused environment administrators envision. Instead, they transform faculty into surveillance monitors and students into clandestine rule-breakers. When devices are banned from campus outright, students still bring them; they simply hide them in sleeves, behind bags, and inside bathroom stalls. Staff members end up expending substantial emotional energy and instructional time writing disciplinary referrals for benign infractions. By contrast, a policy that clearly demarcates acceptable zones of use treats students with dignity. It establishes an enforceable boundary: classrooms are spaces for academic engagement, while the cafeteria is a space for personal autonomy.

Perhaps most importantly, high school ought to prepare us for the world we will enter after graduation. In college lecture halls and professional workplaces, no one will confiscate our phones at the door. Success in those settings demands self-regulation—the discipline to silence a screen when attention is required elsewhere. Policy 2 attempts to solve the problem of distraction by removing temptation entirely, but insulation does not foster maturity. If the school desires to graduate responsible young adults, it must afford us the opportunity to practice restraint. Letting students switch off their devices before the bell rings and switch them back on when dismissal sounds is a small, daily exercise in personal accountability.

There is no doubt that smartphones can erode attention if left unchecked. A firm classroom ban, paired with clear consequences for devices seen or heard during instructional minutes, directly targets that problem without imposing an artificial blackout on the rest of the day. Policy 1 strikes the balanced, pragmatic middle ground our school community needs. 

Thank you for your time, your consideration, and your dedication to cultivating an environment where we can learn not just academic subjects, but the habits of responsible adulthood.

Sincerely,

Morgan Taylor

Every year, thousands of lives are cut short on the road because of mistakes a computer would never make. In the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," the author weighs the exciting promise of autonomous vehicles against their very real safety and legal challenges. While the technology is far from perfect right now, the potential to save lives, restore personal independence, and cut down on waste makes continuing the development of driverless cars the right choice for our future.

The most compelling argument in favor of autonomous vehicles comes down to safety. The article points out that human error causes more than 90 percent of traffic accidents, with drivers frequently distracted by texting, impaired by alcohol, or falling asleep at the wheel. Machines, on the other hand, do not get exhausted or look away to check a phone. By relying on laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors, autonomous cars can constantly track obstacles, lane markers, and traffic signals from every angle. If this technology can eliminate even a fraction of the mistakes human drivers make every day, countless lives will be saved. As an added benefit for everyday families, fewer collisions would also mean lower insurance costs.

Beyond safety, driverless cars could offer life-changing freedom to people who are currently cut off from basic transportation. The author notes that autonomous vehicles could provide reliable mobility for elderly or disabled individuals who are unable to drive themselves safely. For someone who has had to give up their keys, an automated car means being able to run errands, visit friends, and make it to doctor appointments without having to wait on a family member or ride service. That regained sense of independence is a meaningful human benefit that justifies our continued investment.

There are also massive environmental and urban benefits to consider. Google cofounder Sergey Brin envisions a future centered on driverless public transportation that requires only half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. In cities that are already choking on traffic and dedicating huge amounts of valuable real estate to parking lots, that kind of efficiency would be a major upgrade.

Critics of the technology certainly raise fair points that cannot be ignored. Today's sensors can still struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, and unmarked construction zones, while software systems always carry some risk of glitches or hacking. The article also mentions that drivers in semi-autonomous cars tend to tune out, which slows down their reaction time when an emergency forces them to grab the wheel. On top of that, lawmakers still have not settled the legal question of whether an owner, software engineer, or automaker should be blamed when a crash does occur. 

Yet these concerns are growing pains of an emerging technology, not reasons to abandon it altogether. Sensor hardware can be improved through rigorous testing in bad weather, cybersecurity can be strengthened, and clear regulations can establish accountability just as the legal system has done for past innovations. 

Turning our backs on driverless technology would simply mean accepting a status quo where human error continues to take lives daily. By testing carefully and writing smart laws, we can overcome these early hurdles and build a safer, more accessible transportation system.
