Dear Principal,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed policy change that would require students to have at least a grade B average to participate in sports or other activities. While I understand the intention behind this policy, which is to promote academic excellence and encourage students to work harder, I firmly believe that it would have a negative impact on our school community and would not achieve its intended goals.

First and foremost, this policy would unfairly penalize students who may not be naturally gifted academically but have other talents and strengths that make them valuable members of our school teams and clubs. Many students with a grade C average are still diligent and hardworking, and their grades do not necessarily reflect their full potential or dedication. By barring them from participating in activities, we would be denying them the opportunity to develop their skills, build their confidence, and form meaningful relationships with their peers. This would not only be demotivating but also damaging to their self-esteem and overall well-being.

Another reason why I oppose this policy is that it would create an unfair and elitist system, where only students who are academically gifted are allowed to participate in activities. This would lead to a divide between students who are deemed "worthy" of participating and those who are not, creating a toxic and exclusive environment. Our school should be a place where all students feel welcome, included, and supported, regardless of their academic abilities. By implementing this policy, we would be sending a message that only certain students are valued and deserving of opportunities, which would be detrimental to our school's diversity and inclusivity.

Furthermore, this policy would also neglect the fact that many students participate in activities not just for personal enjoyment but also as a way to develop important life skills such as teamwork, communication, and time management. These skills are essential for success in all areas of life, and by denying students the opportunity to participate in activities, we would be depriving them of the chance to develop these skills. Additionally, many students use activities as a way to relieve stress and improve their mental health, which is essential for their overall well-being. By taking away this outlet, we would be putting their mental health at risk.

In conclusion, while I understand the desire to promote academic excellence, I strongly believe that requiring a grade B average to participate in activities is not the right approach. It would unfairly penalize students who are not academically gifted, create an elitist system, and neglect the importance of activities in developing essential life skills and promoting mental health. Instead, I propose that we focus on providing additional support and resources to students who are struggling academically, such as tutoring and mentoring programs, to help them improve their grades and reach their full potential. This approach would be more inclusive, supportive, and beneficial to our school community as a whole.

Summer break gives students a rare stretch of unstructured time, and schools are right to want that time to include some learning. But the question of who designs the summer project matters a great deal. Although teacher-designed projects offer consistency, student-designed projects are the better choice because they build motivation, ownership, and real-world skills that a teacher-assigned worksheet packet rarely can.

The strongest argument for student-designed projects is motivation. During the school year, students already complete hundreds of assignments chosen by someone else. By summer, many are tired of tasks that feel like obligations. A project they invent themselves is far more likely to be finished, and finished well. A student who loves baseball, for example, might analyze batting statistics to determine whether a team's strategy actually leads to wins. Another who enjoys cooking might research the chemistry of baking and produce a small recipe book with tested results. Neither student needs to be nagged to work on something they care about, and the learning that results is deeper because curiosity drives it.

Student-designed projects also teach skills that teacher-designed ones usually skip. Planning a project from scratch requires a student to define a question, set a timeline, gather resources, and adjust when something goes wrong. These are the same abilities that colleges and employers say they want: initiative, time management, and problem-solving. When a teacher hands over a detailed assignment, the student practices following directions, which is useful but only one part of learning. When a student must decide what to make and how to make it, she practices managing her own learning, which is exactly what summer demands, since no teacher is nearby to supervise.

Critics argue that students may choose projects that are too easy or poorly focused, and that teacher-designed assignments ensure academic rigor and equity. This concern is reasonable, but it can be solved without taking away student choice. Schools can require a short proposal in June that the teacher approves, along with clear criteria: the project must involve research, produce a tangible product, and include a written reflection. A teacher can then ask a student to narrow a vague idea or push a too-simple one further. A student who proposes "reading about space," for instance, might be guided toward building a scale model of the solar system and explaining the measurements behind it. This arrangement keeps standards high while preserving the student's authorship.

Another objection is that students without strong support at home may struggle to design anything at all. Here, too, structure helps. Teachers can offer a menu of sample topics, brainstorming sessions before school ends, and optional check-ins during the summer. Students who need more guidance can choose from teacher-suggested ideas and adapt them, so the model remains flexible rather than rigid.

Finally, student-designed projects make the end of summer more meaningful. When classes resume, students can present what they made, and classmates see a wide range of interests and talents. A presentation on building a working rain barrel or writing a short story collection is more engaging than twenty identical reports on the same assigned topic. Such sharing builds community and shows students that learning is not confined to classrooms.

In the end, the goal of summer projects is not simply to keep students busy but to keep them curious. Teacher guidance remains valuable, particularly in approving proposals and setting standards, but the central ideas should come from students themselves. By letting them design their own projects, schools encourage responsibility, creativity, and a lasting habit of learning that extends well beyond summer.

Some students might think distance learning is just a backup plan for snow days, but I believe students would really benefit from being able to attend classes from home. I am not saying every school should be online all the time, but having the option would make school more flexible, less stressful, and easier for many different kinds of students.

One big benefit is saving time and energy. At my school, some kids ride the bus for over an hour each way. By the time they get home, they are too tired to do homework or study. If they could attend classes from home some days, they could get more sleep, eat a proper breakfast, and not have to rush. Last year our school had a few remote days because the heating system broke. I woke up right before class started, still learned the material, and then did my homework right away instead of collapsing on the couch after the bus ride. That showed me how much the commute can drain you.

Another reason is that online learning lets students go at their own pace. In a regular classroom, the teacher usually explains something once. If you miss it, too bad. But with distance learning, many teachers record lessons or post slides online. You can pause, rewind, and rewatch until you understand. My friend has a hard time keeping up with notes in class. During remote learning, he used captions and paused the videos. His history grade actually went up because he could listen to the lectures more than once. In a normal classroom, he would not get that chance.

Home can also be less stressful for some students. Kids who deal with anxiety, bullying, or noisy classrooms can focus better at home sometimes. I know a girl who barely raised her hand in class because she was nervous. When we had online discussions, she typed in the chat a lot more and shared good ideas. She said she felt safer speaking that way. I understand that not everyone has a quiet home, but having the option is still better than forcing everyone into the same setting.

Distance learning is not perfect. It is easy to get distracted by your phone, your bed, or your siblings. Some students do not have good internet or an adult at home to help. But those are problems schools can work on, like offering loaner hotspots or optional online days. Just because something has downsides does not mean students would not benefit from it.

In conclusion, I think students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home as an option. It saves time, lets students learn at their own speed, and helps kids who struggle in a traditional classroom. It should not replace school completely, but giving students the choice could make education work better for more people.

The rise of distance learning has sparked a lively debate about its potential benefits and drawbacks for students. While some argue that attending classes from home can be detrimental to a student's educational experience, I firmly believe that it can be a highly beneficial option for many learners. By providing students with the flexibility to attend classes remotely, schools can cater to a diverse range of needs and learning styles, ultimately leading to improved academic outcomes.

For one, distance learning can be a game-changer for students with physical or mental health issues that make it difficult for them to attend traditional brick-and-mortar schools. By allowing these students to participate in classes from the comfort of their own homes, schools can ensure that they receive the education they deserve without having to compromise their well-being. Moreover, distance learning can also be a boon for students who live in remote or rural areas where access to quality educational institutions may be limited. With the help of online or video conferencing tools, these students can now access a wide range of courses and educational resources that may not have been available to them otherwise.

Another significant advantage of distance learning is that it allows students to learn at their own pace. In a traditional classroom setting, teachers often have to cater to the needs of a large group of students, which can be challenging, especially for those who may need extra support or time to grasp certain concepts. With distance learning, students can review course materials, watch video lectures, and complete assignments on their own schedule, which can be particularly helpful for those who may need to balance school with work or other responsibilities. Additionally, distance learning can also help to reduce distractions and minimize the pressure to conform to social norms, allowing students to focus more intently on their studies.

Of course, some may argue that distance learning lacks the social interaction and human connection that is essential for a well-rounded educational experience. While it is true that online learning may not provide the same level of face-to-face interaction as traditional classroom learning, many schools are now using innovative technologies to create virtual learning environments that mimic the social dynamics of a physical classroom. For example, video conferencing tools can enable students to participate in virtual discussions, collaborate on group projects, and even interact with teachers and peers in real-time. Furthermore, many online learning platforms also provide students with access to online communities and forums where they can connect with fellow learners, ask questions, and share resources.

In conclusion, attending classes from home can be a highly beneficial option for many students. By providing flexibility, accessibility, and personalized learning experiences, distance learning can help to improve academic outcomes, increase student engagement, and reduce barriers to education. While there may be some challenges associated with online learning, many schools are now using innovative technologies to create virtual learning environments that are engaging, interactive, and effective. As the educational landscape continues to evolve, it is likely that distance learning will play an increasingly important role in shaping the future of education.

Dear Senator,

I am writing as a constituent to ask you to oppose any move to replace the Electoral College with a direct national popular vote. I understand why some people are frustrated with the current system, but I believe it still serves important purposes and should be kept.

The Electoral College was designed by the Founding Fathers as a compromise between letting Congress pick the president and letting a simple majority of voters decide. According to the Office of the Federal Register, it is a process, not a place, made up of 538 electors, and a candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win. Every state gets at least three electors because each state has two senators and at least one House member. That means small states have a slightly larger voice than their population alone would give them. Judge Richard Posner argues this is a key benefit: it forces candidates to build support across large and small states, not just pile up huge vote totals in a few densely populated cities or in one region. If we switched to a popular vote, a candidate could win by focusing almost entirely on urban centers and ignoring rural voters and smaller states altogether.

Another advantage is that the Electoral College keeps recounts manageable. Posner points out that a close national popular vote would require recounting ballots in all fifty states, which could create chaos and long delays. With the Electoral College, any disputed recount is confined to individual states. We saw this in Florida in 2000: the legal fight was messy, but it did not force a recount of every vote in the country. That is a real practical benefit.

I know there are strong arguments on the other side. Bradford Plumer notes that the winner-take-all rule used by 48 states and Washington, D.C., causes candidates to ignore safe Democratic or Republican states and focus almost entirely on a handful of swing states. That can depress voter turnout in places like California or Texas, where people may feel their vote does not matter. Plumer also points out that a candidate can lose the national popular vote and still win the presidency, as happened in 2000 and 2016. Those are legitimate concerns, and I do not dismiss them.

However, a national popular vote would not fix the problem of ignored voters; it would just shift it. Candidates would spend their time in large metropolitan areas and heavily populated states, while voters in rural communities and small states would be even less relevant than they are now. The Electoral College, for all its flaws, forces candidates to pay attention to a wider range of the country. Plumer also mentions the possibility of “faithless electors,” but those cases are extremely rare and have never changed the outcome of a modern presidential election.

In short, the Electoral College is not perfect, but it balances regional interests, prevents a purely urban-focused campaign strategy, and keeps disputed elections from turning into nationwide recounts. I hope you will support keeping this system rather than moving to a direct popular vote.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

The debate over whether summer projects should be teacher-designed or student-designed has sparked intense discussion among educators. While some argue that teacher-designed projects provide structure and continuity with the academic year, I firmly believe that student-designed projects offer numerous benefits that outweigh the advantages of the former approach. By allowing students to take the reins and design their own projects, educators can foster a sense of autonomy, creativity, and motivation that is essential for deep learning.

When students are given the freedom to choose their own projects, they are more likely to pursue topics that genuinely interest them, leading to a higher level of engagement and enthusiasm. For instance, a student passionate about environmental conservation might design a project that involves conducting a neighborhood waste audit, proposing sustainable practices to local businesses, and creating a social media campaign to raise awareness about the importance of recycling. This type of project not only allows students to explore their interests but also enables them to develop a range of skills, from research and critical thinking to communication and problem-solving. In contrast, teacher-designed projects can sometimes feel forced or contrived, leading to a lackluster response from students.

Another significant advantage of student-designed projects is that they promote self-directed learning and time management skills. When students are responsible for designing and executing their own projects, they must prioritize tasks, set deadlines, and allocate their time effectively to meet their goals. This process helps students develop a sense of agency and accountability, as they are solely responsible for the success or failure of their project. Moreover, student-designed projects can also facilitate the development of essential life skills, such as goal-setting, self-assessment, and self-reflection. As students work on their projects, they are encouraged to reflect on their progress, identify areas for improvement, and adjust their approach as needed – all critical skills that will serve them well in their future academic and professional pursuits.

Some might argue that student-designed projects lack the structure and guidance that teacher-designed projects provide, potentially leading to a lack of coherence or rigor. However, this concern can be mitigated by providing students with clear expectations, guidelines, and support throughout the project development process. Teachers can offer workshops, one-on-one consultations, and online resources to help students brainstorm ideas, refine their proposals, and troubleshoot challenges that arise during the project implementation phase. By striking a balance between autonomy and guidance, educators can ensure that student-designed projects are both meaningful and academically sound.

In conclusion, student-designed summer projects offer a unique opportunity for students to take ownership of their learning, pursue their passions, and develop essential skills that will benefit them throughout their lives. By giving students the freedom to design their own projects, educators can foster a love of learning that extends beyond the classroom walls and into the broader community. As we strive to create a more engaging, effective, and student-centered education system, it is essential that we prioritize student autonomy and agency in the learning process – and student-designed summer projects are an excellent place to start.

When people ask for advice, they sometimes talk to more than one person. I think this is a smart move because one person can only see a problem from their own angle. Getting several opinions is like looking at a picture from different sides; you notice things you might have missed otherwise.

For example, last spring I was trying to decide whether to sign up for honors biology or stay in regular biology. I first asked my best friend. She said honors was too much homework and told me not to do it because she wanted us to have lunch together and not stress about tests. That was one opinion, but it was mostly based on her feelings. Then I asked my older cousin, who already took the class. She told me honors biology was hard but manageable if I stayed organized, and it would help me later if I wanted to take AP science. Finally, I asked my science teacher from the year before. He said I had strong lab skills and should challenge myself, but he also warned me not to take honors if I was already overwhelmed by my math class. Each person gave me a different piece of the puzzle. My friend cared about my free time, my cousin knew the actual workload, and my teacher knew my academic skills. If I had only asked my friend, I might have missed a good opportunity. If I had only asked my cousin, I might not have thought about how my schedule fit together.

Another time, my family had to choose between two used cars. My dad asked a mechanic, a neighbor who owned the same model, and my uncle who drives a lot for work. The mechanic noticed one car had a small oil leak. The neighbor said the other car’s back seat was uncomfortable for kids on long trips. My uncle pointed out that the first car had cheaper insurance for a new driver like my older sister. Alone, none of them had the whole answer. Together, they helped my dad pick the car that was safest and cheapest in the long run.

Seeking multiple opinions also helps you catch bad advice. Sometimes a person gives advice based on what worked for them, but their situation may be totally different from yours. If you hear the same warning from two or three people, you can take it more seriously. If you hear different suggestions, you can compare them and see which one fits your life best.

Of course, asking too many people can get confusing. But if you choose a few people who know different things, like a friend, a family member, and someone with experience, you get a more complete picture. In the end, the choice is still yours, but you can make it with more confidence because you understand the pros and cons from more than one point of view.

The widespread adoption of smartphones has revolutionized daily life, but their use behind the wheel poses a significant threat to public safety. Driving requires unwavering attention, yet many motorists divide their focus between the road and their digital screens. The risks associated with mobile device interaction while driving are substantial, leading to the conclusion that drivers should be prohibited from using cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

One argument often made in favor of limited phone use while driving is the notion that hands-free interfaces, such as Bluetooth headsets or integrated dashboard displays, mitigate the risks. However, research in neuroscience and psychology reveals that the primary hazard of mobile technology is cognitive, rather than physical. Engaging in voice conversations or processing audio prompts can induce "inattention blindness," a state in which the brain filters out vital visual information due to its preoccupation with the remote dialogue. As a result, reaction times are significantly impaired, comparable to those of drivers under the influence. This phenomenon underscores the dangers of relying on hands-free systems as a solution, as it creates a false sense of security.

The staggering human and economic costs of distracted driving further support a comprehensive ban on cell phone use while driving. Thousands of preventable fatalities and hundreds of thousands of severe injuries occur annually due to drivers diverting their attention from the road for mere seconds. At highway speeds, a fleeting glance at a notification or adjustment of a digital map can blind a driver for the length of an entire football field. The operation of an automobile is a complex task that demands an unwavering commitment to safety, not just for the driver, but also for passengers, pedestrians, and fellow commuters. By permitting casual phone use, we trivialize this responsibility and prioritize personal convenience over human life.

Some argue that mobile devices provide essential functions, such as turn-by-turn navigation and emergency assistance, which necessitate their use while driving. However, these capabilities do not require interaction with a phone while in motion. Route planning, GPS programming, and audio selections can be easily established before the vehicle is set in motion. In the event of a genuine emergency, the need for immediate assistance can be balanced against the risks of phone use, and alternative solutions, such as pulling over to a safe location, can be employed. Ultimately, the preservation of human life and the prevention of catastrophic accidents must take precedence over the convenience of phone use while driving.

In conclusion, the use of cell phones while driving poses a significant threat to public safety, and the risks associated with this behavior far outweigh any potential benefits. By prohibiting the use of cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle, we can reduce the incidence of distracted driving and create a safer environment for all road users. This measure is not only a moral imperative but also a necessary step towards mitigating the devastating consequences of distracted driving. By prioritizing safety and responsible driving practices, we can work towards a future where the risks associated with cell phone use while driving are significantly reduced.

Dear Principal,

I recently heard about the possible new policy that would require students to have at least a grade B average to participate in sports and other activities. As a student who is actively involved in the school soccer team, I have to say that I'm really concerned about this idea. I understand that the goal is to encourage students to work harder and achieve better grades, but I don't think this policy would be fair or effective.

First of all, many students, like my friends and me, have a grade C average, which isn't bad. We're still passing our classes and learning the material, but we might not be naturally good at academics or we might have other things going on that make it harder for us to get straight A's or B's. By not allowing us to participate in activities, you'd be taking away something that we really enjoy and that helps us stay motivated and connected to the school. Plus, being part of a team or club teaches us important skills like teamwork, communication, and time management, which are just as valuable as getting good grades.

Another problem with this policy is that it would unfairly punish students who are struggling in certain subjects. For example, I know someone who is really bad at math, but she's amazing at art and is actually considering a career in graphic design. If she can't participate in the art club because her math grade is bringing down her average, that's not only unfair to her, but it's also wasting her talent and potential. We should be encouraging students to explore their strengths and interests, not limiting them because of one or two weak subjects.

I also think that this policy could lead to students feeling really discouraged and disconnected from the school. If they're not allowed to participate in activities, they might feel like there's no point in even trying to improve their grades. They might start to feel like they're not good enough or that they don't belong here, which could lead to more problems like absenteeism, behavioral issues, and lower self-esteem.

Instead of requiring a minimum grade average, maybe we could find other ways to support students who are struggling academically. We could offer more tutoring or mentoring programs, or provide more resources to help students stay organized and manage their time effectively. That way, students who are struggling would get the help they need, and students who are doing well would still be able to participate in activities and enjoy the benefits that come with being part of a team or club.

In conclusion, while I understand the intention behind the proposed policy, I strongly believe that it would be unfair and ineffective. I think we should focus on finding ways to support students who are struggling, rather than punishing them for not meeting a certain standard. I hope you'll consider our perspectives and find a solution that works for everyone.

Dear Principal Martinez,

I am writing this letter to share my thoughts on the two cell phone policies you are considering for our school. I know that phones can sometimes be a distraction during the school day, but I strongly believe that Policy 1 is the better choice for our school community. Letting students have their phones during lunch and other free times, while requiring them to be turned off in class, is a much fairer and more realistic rule than banning them completely.

First of all, having access to our phones makes dealing with after-school logistics much easier for both students and parents. A lot of us have busy schedules after the final bell rings, including sports practices, club meetings, part-time jobs, or babysitting younger siblings. Practice times get changed at the last minute because of bad weather, or parents get stuck late at work and need to adjust who is picking us up. If we are allowed to check our phones quickly during lunch or right after school ends, we can coordinate our rides and keep our families updated. If phones are banned completely, the front office would be flooded with phone calls all afternoon from parents trying to get messages to their kids.

Another important reason is student safety. Many students walk to school, ride city buses, or wait at bus stops early in the morning and late in the afternoon. Parents want their kids to carry a phone in their backpacks for safety reasons in case something happens on the way to or from campus. If Policy 2 were put in place, students would either have to leave their phones at home and feel unsafe traveling, or they would bring them anyway and constantly risk getting in trouble.

Most importantly, Policy 1 teaches us responsibility instead of just punishing everyone. When we graduate and go to college or get jobs, nobody is going to take our phones away at the door. We have to learn when it is appropriate to use them and when we need to focus. Under Policy 1, the rule is simple and clear: when the bell rings for class, your phone is off and put away. During lunch, when we are already taking a break, eating, and hanging out with friends, using our phones to listen to music or check a message does not hurt anyone's education. 

A total ban under Policy 2 would just make teachers and administrators spend their whole day acting like security guards, searching bags and confiscating phones from good students who just forgot to leave them at home. Policy 1 is a fair compromise that respects students while still keeping the focus on learning where it belongs.

Seeking advice from more than one person can lead to better decisions because each person notices different risks, values different outcomes, and brings different experiences to the situation. A single opinion may be thoughtful, but it is still limited by one person’s perspective. Hearing several viewpoints does not mean blindly following the majority. Instead, it gives someone more information to weigh before deciding what fits their own needs.

For example, imagine a high school senior choosing between attending a nearby college with a scholarship and a more expensive university farther from home. A parent might focus on financial stability and point out that graduating with less debt can create more freedom after college. A teacher may know which school has the stronger program in the student’s intended major. A recent graduate could describe less obvious parts of campus life, such as whether internships are accessible or whether students can easily get help from professors. Meanwhile, a friend might raise an emotional concern: the student may thrive more at a school where they feel excited and independent. None of these opinions alone settles the question, but together they create a fuller picture.

Multiple opinions can also expose assumptions that a person has not questioned. Someone considering a new job might initially focus only on the salary. A colleague could remind them to ask about advancement opportunities, while a family member might mention the long commute or the effect of frequent travel on personal life. An experienced mentor may advise looking at the company’s stability, management style, and benefits rather than accepting a high salary as proof that the job is better. After hearing these ideas, the person may realize that a slightly lower-paying position offers more predictable hours, better health insurance, and a healthier work environment. That choice could be more valuable in the long run.

Different opinions are especially useful when a decision involves unfamiliar information. A person buying their first car, for instance, may be impressed by a vehicle’s appearance or technology features. A mechanic could identify maintenance concerns, an insurance agent could explain the cost of coverage, and an owner of the same model could discuss fuel economy and reliability over time. By comparing these perspectives, the buyer is less likely to make an expensive decision based on a brief test drive or an advertisement.

Of course, asking many people for advice can become confusing if every voice is treated as equally reliable. The quality of the advice matters. It is wise to consider whether a person has relevant knowledge, whether they understand the situation, and whether they may have a personal bias. A friend who loves taking risks may encourage a decision that is exciting but unsuitable for someone with different responsibilities. In the end, the person making the choice must decide for themselves.

Still, collecting several thoughtful opinions is a practical way to make wiser choices. It broadens understanding, reveals overlooked consequences, and helps people distinguish between a quick impulse and a well-considered decision.

When people have an important decision to make, it can be helpful to ask more than one person for advice. One person might notice something that another person misses. Also, different people have different experiences, so they may give advice from different points of view. Listening to multiple opinions does not mean a person has to follow all of them. It means they have more information before making their own choice.

For example, imagine a student trying to decide which classes to take next year. They might ask a friend, a parent, and a teacher. A friend could explain which classes are interesting or which teachers give a lot of homework. A parent might think about college requirements or whether the student is taking on too much at once. A teacher may know the student’s strengths and could suggest a class that matches their skills. If the student only asked one friend, they might choose a class just because their friend is in it. By hearing several opinions, the student can make a choice based on what is actually best for them.

Multiple opinions can also protect people from making rushed or emotional decisions. Sometimes when people are upset, excited, or stressed, they do not think clearly. For instance, if someone gets into an argument with a close friend, they may feel like ending the friendship right away. If they talk only to someone who is also angry at that friend, the advice might make the situation worse. However, another person might remind them to calm down, talk honestly, and consider the other friend’s side. Hearing that different view could keep them from making a decision they regret later.

Another reason different opinions help is that people have different kinds of knowledge. If someone is buying their first car, they might ask a parent about cost, a mechanic about reliability, and a friend who recently bought a car about insurance and gas money. Each person knows something useful. The parent may warn them not to spend all their savings, while the mechanic may point out that a cheap car could have expensive problems. The friend might explain that monthly costs can add up faster than expected. Together, those opinions give the buyer a more realistic picture.

Of course, getting advice from many people can sometimes be confusing. People may disagree, and the person making the decision may feel pulled in different directions. Still, disagreement can be useful because it makes someone think more carefully. They can compare the reasons behind each opinion instead of simply doing what the first person says.

In the end, the final decision belongs to the person who asked for advice. However, seeking multiple opinions can help them see more choices, avoid mistakes, and understand possible consequences. It is like looking at a problem from different angles before deciding which direction to go.

Dear Principal Johnson,

I am writing to share my opinion about the cell phone policy. I believe Policy 1 is the better choice, which would let students bring phones to school and use them at lunch and during free times, as long as they are turned off in class. I think this policy is fair and it solves more problems than it creates.

First, phones are a safety tool. If there is an emergency, like a fire, a lockdown, or someone getting hurt, students and parents would want to be able to reach each other. Even on a normal day, plans change. Sometimes a bus gets canceled or practice ends early, and a student needs to call a parent for a ride. Right now we have to ask to use the office phone, and that can take a long time, especially if the office is busy. If students had their own phones during free times, they could just send a quick text and get it done. Banning phones completely would take that option away, and I don't think that is worth it.

Second, Policy 1 teaches responsibility. Students are going to have phones for the rest of their lives, and they will need to know when it is okay to use them and when it is not. At a job, for example, you can't be on your phone while a customer is talking to you. If we are only allowed to use them at lunch, we learn to wait and focus during class. If the school bans phones totally, we never get to practice that. I think students will act more mature if they are trusted with a rule that has limits.

Third, a total ban would be hard to enforce. Lots of students would probably still sneak their phones in, and teachers would spend time looking for them and taking them away instead of teaching. That would cause more arguments between students and staff. With Policy 1, the rule is simple: phones off in class. It is a lot easier to follow because students get something in return. When people feel a rule is reasonable, they are more likely to follow it.

I understand the worries about Policy 1. Some people think phones will distract students or lead to cheating or cyberbullying. Those are real concerns. But I think the rule about turning phones off during class helps with distractions and cheating, since phones would not be out during tests or lessons. If a teacher sees a phone on during class, there can be a clear consequence, like the phone being held until the end of the day. For bullying, that can happen outside of school too, so banning phones at school does not really stop it. It would be better to have the school deal with it when it happens.

Also, lunch and free time are supposed to be a break. Students are in class for hours, and being able to check messages, listen to music, or talk to family can help us relax. I think a lot of students would come back to class in a better mood and ready to work. Some students might also use their phones to look up homework or check their grades, which is helpful.

For these reasons, I hope you choose Policy 1. It keeps students safe, teaches us responsibility, and is easier to enforce than a full ban. Thank you for taking the time to read my letter and for thinking about what students need.

Sincerely,
A concerned student

Dear Senator [Last Name],

I am writing to urge you to support moving the United States from the Electoral College to election of the president by national popular vote. As a constituent who cares about equal representation, I believe every citizen's vote should carry the same weight, no matter which state that citizen lives in. The current system fails that basic democratic test.

The most troubling flaw in the Electoral College is that it can override the will of the voters. As Bradford Plumer points out in "The Indefensible Electoral College," a candidate can win the national popular vote and still lose the presidency, as happened in 2000 and 2016. In a democracy, the candidate with the most votes should win. When the system produces the opposite result, public confidence in the legitimacy of elections suffers, and millions of citizens conclude that their ballots did not count.

A second problem is how the system shapes campaigns. According to the Office of the Federal Register, forty-eight states and Washington, D.C. use a "winner-take-all" system, giving all of a state's electoral votes to whoever wins that state's popular vote. Plumer explains the consequence: candidates focus almost entirely on a handful of swing states and ignore voters in states that are reliably Democratic or Republican. A Republican voter in California or a Democratic voter in Texas has little reason to expect a campaign visit, and may have little reason to vote at all. This depresses turnout and leaves much of the country out of the national conversation. Under a popular vote, a vote in any state would be worth the same, and candidates would have an incentive to seek support everywhere.

I recognize the arguments on the other side. Judge Richard Posner defends the Electoral College on the grounds that it preserves federalism and forces candidates to build broad coalitions across both large and small states rather than running up huge totals in densely populated urban areas. This concern deserves a serious response. However, the current system does not actually require candidates to appeal to the whole country; it requires them to appeal to a few closely divided states. A popular vote would reward candidates for winning votes in rural, suburban, and urban communities alike, since every vote in every place would add to the same national total. A candidate who ignored small towns would be giving up millions of votes.

Posner also argues that the Electoral College produces a clear winner quickly and confines recounts to individual states, avoiding a chaotic nationwide recount. That is a legitimate administrative worry, but it is not a reason to preserve an undemocratic outcome. Close elections can be handled through clear, uniform recount standards, and a national margin of millions of votes would rarely come close to requiring a recount. In fact, the present system makes recounts more dangerous, because the entire presidency can hinge on a few hundred or few thousand votes in a single state, as it did in Florida in 2000. Finally, the possibility of "faithless electors" voting against their state's popular choice, which Plumer notes, adds an unnecessary risk of an outcome that defies the voters.

The Founders created the Electoral College, as the Federal Register describes, as a compromise between election by Congress and election by popular vote. That compromise made sense in its time, but today Americans expect to choose their leaders directly. I respectfully ask you to support a national popular vote, whether through a constitutional amendment or through your state's participation in an interstate compact. Doing so would ensure that every citizen's vote counts equally and that the person elected president is the person the people actually chose.

Thank you for your time and service.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

I disagree with the principal’s decision to require every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. Sports, yearbook, student council, and other activities can make school more enjoyable and help students develop important skills. However, requiring everyone to join overlooks the importance of choice, creates problems for students with responsibilities outside school, and may even lower the quality of the activities. Extracurriculars should be strongly encouraged and made available to all students, but they should not be mandatory.

First, voluntary participation is a major part of what makes extracurricular activities valuable. Students usually join clubs and teams because they are interested in them. An aspiring photographer may want to work on the yearbook, a basketball fan may try out for the team, and a student who enjoys organizing events may run for student council. Because these students chose to participate, they are more likely to work hard, attend meetings, and contribute ideas.

If participation becomes a requirement, though, it may feel like just another assignment. For example, a student forced to join student council even though he or she does not enjoy planning school events may sit quietly during meetings or complete tasks with little effort. That student is not necessarily lazy; he or she simply may have no interest in that activity. The same club that inspires one student could become stressful or frustrating for another. Allowing students to choose gives activities more energy because the members actually want to be there.

Another problem is that not every student has the same amount of free time after school. Some students have part-time jobs to help their families. Others care for younger siblings, attend appointments, or need extra time to complete difficult schoolwork. A student who works several evenings each week may not be able to attend regular practices or meetings. Requiring that student to join an activity could create unnecessary pressure and force him or her to choose between school rules and family responsibilities.

For instance, a student who has to pick up a younger brother from elementary school cannot always stay late for debate club or soccer practice. It would be unfair to punish that student for circumstances beyond his or her control. Schools should recognize that learning also happens through work, family responsibilities, and personal challenges. Not every meaningful experience takes place in a school club.

Mandatory participation could also weaken extracurricular programs. Clubs and teams often depend on members who are dependable and motivated. If students join only because they must, advisers and team leaders may spend more time reminding people to attend or finish assignments. The yearbook staff could have members who miss deadlines, and a sports team could have players who do not practice seriously. Rather than improving activities, forced participation might make them harder to manage.

Instead of requiring every student to join, the school could offer an activity fair, advertise clubs more clearly, and provide transportation for students who need it. Teachers could also help students find activities that match their interests. These steps would encourage participation without treating every student’s schedule and situation as the same.

Extracurricular activities are most meaningful when students choose them for themselves. The principal should support and promote them, but participation should remain voluntary.

Summer projects should be mostly student-designed because students are more likely to care about and actually learn from a project they choose themselves. Teachers can still give guidelines and check that the project is challenging enough, but they should not decide every topic. Summer is supposed to be a break from the normal school schedule, so projects should give students some freedom while still keeping their minds active.

One reason student-designed projects are better is that students have different interests. A teacher-designed project might be useful for some people but boring or frustrating for others. For example, a teacher might assign every student to read the same historical novel and write a report. Some students may enjoy reading it, but another student might be more interested in science, art, sports, or technology. If that student could design a project, they might research how basketball shoes are made, build a simple website, or learn about the environmental effects of fast fashion. They would still be reading, writing, researching, and problem-solving, but they would probably put in more effort because the topic matters to them.

Student-designed projects can also teach responsibility. In school, teachers often tell students exactly what to do, when to do it, and how many pages it should be. In real life, people have to make plans for themselves. A summer project could help students practice setting goals, organizing time, and solving problems when something does not work. For instance, a student who wants to grow vegetables in a backyard garden would have to research which plants grow well in the summer, remember to water them, and keep track of what happens. Even if some plants die, the student can explain what went wrong and what they would change next time. That is still learning.

Another benefit is that student projects can connect school to the community. A student might interview a grandparent about family history, volunteer at an animal shelter and write reflections, or create a map of local parks and trails. These projects can teach skills that do not always fit into a regular class period. They can also make students notice things outside of school that they normally ignore.

However, student-designed does not mean students should be left with no help. Some students may not know what kind of project to choose, or they may choose something too easy, like watching movies all summer. Teachers should provide a list of possible ideas, requirements, and a simple rubric. For example, every project could need a question, research or practice, proof of progress, and a final presentation or reflection. That way, students have choices but still have clear expectations.

Overall, summer projects should be student-designed with teacher guidance. When students choose meaningful topics, they are more motivated, more independent, and more likely to remember what they learned.

Dear Senator [Last Name],

I am writing to urge you to support replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote for president. Although the Electoral College was created as a compromise, it now conflicts with the democratic principle that every citizen’s vote should carry equal weight.

According to the Office of the Federal Register, the Founding Fathers established the Electoral College as a compromise between election by Congress and direct election by qualified citizens. The system includes 538 electors, and a candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win. In most states, however, electors are awarded through a winner-take-all system: the candidate who wins a state’s popular vote receives all of that state’s electoral votes. This arrangement can allow a candidate to become president even after receiving fewer votes nationwide. As Bradford Plumer explains, this occurred in both 2000 and 2016. When the candidate preferred by the most voters can still lose, many Americans understandably question whether the system is fair.

The winner-take-all approach also changes how candidates campaign. Plumer points out that presidential candidates concentrate heavily on a small number of competitive swing states while paying far less attention to states that are considered safely Democratic or safely Republican. As a result, voters in many parts of the country may feel ignored because campaigns rarely visit, advertise, or address the concerns of their communities. This can discourage participation. Under a national popular vote, every vote would matter equally, whether it came from a large state such as California or a smaller state such as Wyoming. Candidates would have a reason to seek votes in every state rather than focusing mainly on a few battlegrounds.

Supporters of the Electoral College raise important concerns. Judge Richard A. Posner argues that it protects federalism and keeps candidates from winning simply by piling up votes in densely populated cities or one region of the country. He believes the system encourages candidates to form broad coalitions among large and small states. However, the current system does not always create that broad appeal. Instead, it can reward candidates for concentrating their efforts on a narrow group of closely divided states. A national popular vote would encourage candidates to reach out to voters everywhere, since gaining additional votes in any community could help determine the final result.

Posner also argues that the Electoral College usually produces a quick and decisive outcome and prevents the difficulty of conducting a nationwide recount. It is true that recounts limited to one state may be easier to manage than recounts across the country. Still, the 2000 election demonstrated that a recount in a single decisive state can create a major national dispute. Clear national standards and careful election administration could help make a popular-vote system fair and reliable.

The Electoral College may have served as a compromise at the nation’s founding, but it no longer serves voters well. It can allow the popular-vote loser to become president, reduces attention to voters in noncompetitive states, and limits campaigns to a small part of the electorate. I respectfully ask you to support a constitutional amendment establishing a national popular vote so that the president is chosen directly by the people.

Sincerely,  
[Your Name]

Driverless cars may sound like science fiction, but they are already being tested on public roads. The question is no longer whether the technology can exist, but whether we should keep pushing it forward. Despite real obstacles, the development of driverless cars deserves continued support, because the potential to save lives and widen access to transportation is too significant to abandon.

The strongest argument comes from the numbers. According to the article, human error causes over 90 percent of traffic accidents, and the usual culprits are painfully familiar: texting, drowsiness, and impaired driving. A computer does not glance at a phone or nod off after a long shift. Sensors such as laser radar, cameras, and GPS can monitor the road continuously, detecting obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals without ever losing interest. If machines can remove even a portion of that 90 percent, the result would be thousands of people who get home safely instead of ending up in hospitals or worse. Lower insurance costs would follow naturally, a welcome side effect for ordinary families.

Safety is not the only benefit. Elderly and disabled people often depend on relatives, expensive services, or limited public transit to get around. A driverless car could give them independence they have been denied, allowing a person who can no longer drive to visit a doctor, shop for groceries, or see friends on their own schedule. Sergey Brin's larger vision pushes this even further: a network of driverless public transportation using half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. Imagine cities where lots of pavement given over to parked vehicles could become parks or housing.

Still, the critics make fair points, and they should not be brushed aside. Current sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, and unmarked construction zones, which are exactly the conditions that challenge human drivers too. Software can glitch, and it can be hacked. Semi-autonomous systems raise a subtler problem, since they expect a human to stay alert and grab the wheel in an emergency, yet studies show that people quickly lose focus once a computer is driving. Then there is the legal puzzle of who is responsible after a crash: the owner, the software developer, or the automaker?

These problems are serious, but they are problems of development, not reasons to stop developing. Weather limitations can be addressed with better sensors and more testing. Cybersecurity is a challenge that every connected technology faces, and engineers can strengthen defenses over time. The attention-span problem actually argues for pursuing fully autonomous vehicles rather than half-measures, since a car that never needs a human backup removes the dangerous handoff entirely. As for liability, courts and lawmakers have settled new questions before, from airplanes to the internet. Unresolved law is a reason to write better law, not to halt progress.

Abandoning the technology would also carry a cost. Every year that passes with human drivers alone is another year of preventable crashes caused by distraction and exhaustion. Caution is wise, and strict testing standards should be required before these cars become common. But caution is different from retreat.

Driverless cars are not perfect, and the article is honest about their flaws. Yet the flaws look fixable, while the promise of fewer deaths, greater independence, and more efficient cities is concrete. For those reasons, society should continue developing driverless cars, carefully and with firm rules, but without losing sight of how much good they could do.

The increasing ubiquity of cell phones has introduced an unprecedented challenge to road safety. While these devices offer convenience and connectivity, their presence in the hands—and minds—of drivers poses a clear and present danger. Although many argue for limited or hands-free use, the evidence overwhelmingly supports a strict prohibition: drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

The most obvious danger of cell phone use while driving is physical distraction. Texting, dialing, or even glancing at a notification requires a driver to remove at least one hand from the wheel and, more importantly, their eyes from the road. At highway speeds, a vehicle can travel the length of a football field in just a few seconds. During that time, a driver looking at a screen is effectively driving blind. This visual and manual impairment is not a minor lapse in judgment; it is a complete abandonment of the primary task of controlling a two-ton machine. Unlike adjusting a radio or taking a sip of coffee, cell phone interactions demand sustained, focused attention that directly competes with driving.

However, the danger extends far beyond the physical act of holding a phone. Even hands-free devices, which are often promoted as safe alternatives, create a severe cognitive distraction. The human brain is not designed to perform two complex tasks simultaneously; it rapidly switches attention between them. A conversation requires the driver to visualize the person on the other end, process their words, and formulate responses. This mental workload dramatically reduces the driver’s situational awareness. Studies have shown that drivers engaged in phone conversations, even with both hands on the wheel, suffer from "inattention blindness," failing to process critical visual cues such as red lights, pedestrians, and sudden braking by other vehicles. They may be looking at the road, but they are not truly seeing it. Therefore, the problem is not merely the device, but the divided attention it demands.

Furthermore, permitting any cell phone use creates a legal and social gray area that is impossible to enforce effectively. If hands-free use is allowed, law enforcement officers must somehow determine whether a driver was merely talking or was distracted by a complex conversation at the moment of a crash. A total ban provides a clear, unambiguous standard. It sends a powerful message that driving requires one’s full, undivided attention. The convenience of a phone call or a voice-dictated text message is simply not worth the risk of a fatal collision.

In conclusion, the argument for allowing any cell phone use while driving fails under scrutiny. The physical distraction of handling a device and the profound cognitive impairment caused by phone conversations, even hands-free ones, make driving unsafe. A vehicle is not an extension of one’s living room or office; it is a potentially lethal instrument that demands complete focus. To protect all road users, the only rational and responsible policy is a total ban on all cell phone use by drivers. The call can wait; a life may not.

As the principal considers revising the school's cell phone policy, it is essential to weigh the pros and cons of each potential approach. After careful consideration, I firmly believe that Policy 1, which allows students to bring phones to school and use them during designated free periods, is the better option. This policy strikes a balance between acknowledging the importance of mobile devices in modern life and minimizing potential distractions during class time.

One of the primary reasons Policy 1 is preferable is that it recognizes the reality of teenagers' lives. Many students rely on their phones to stay in touch with family members, particularly in cases of emergency or after-school pickup arrangements. By allowing students to have their phones at school, albeit with restrictions, the policy acknowledges this necessity while also teaching students about responsible phone use. Furthermore, permitting phone use during lunch and other free times enables students to stay connected with friends and family, which can help reduce feelings of isolation and improve overall well-being.

Another significant advantage of Policy 1 is that it promotes autonomy and trust among students. By allowing students to use their phones during designated times, the school demonstrates that it trusts them to make responsible choices. This can have a positive impact on student behavior, as students are more likely to respect the rules and boundaries when they feel that their rights and needs are being considered. In contrast, a blanket ban on phones, as proposed in Policy 2, may be perceived as overly restrictive and lead to resentment among students.

In addition to these benefits, Policy 1 can also enhance student safety. In the event of an emergency, students with phones can quickly contact authorities or family members for help. This is particularly important for students who walk or bike to school, as they may be more vulnerable to potential dangers. By allowing students to have their phones at school, the policy can provide an added layer of protection and reassurance for both students and parents.

On the other hand, Policy 2, which prohibits phones altogether, may be overly restrictive and ineffective. Such a policy may lead to students finding ways to sneak their phones into school, which could create more problems than it solves. Moreover, a total ban on phones may not address the underlying issues of distraction and addiction, which require education and guidance rather than simply removing the device.

In conclusion, Policy 1 is the better option for our school's cell phone policy. By allowing students to bring phones to school and use them during designated free periods, the policy promotes autonomy, trust, and responsible phone use. It also acknowledges the importance of mobile devices in modern life, enhances student safety, and provides a more effective and realistic approach to managing phone use. Lunch and breaks are when students can relax, talk with friends, listen to music, check messages, or sort out their schedules. Dear Senator,

My name is Jordan Ellis, and I am a high school student in your district. I am writing to ask you to support changing the way we elect the president from the Electoral College to a national popular vote. After reading about how the system works, I think it is unfair to voters and does not match what we are taught about democracy.

First, the Electoral College lets a person lose the popular vote and still become president. According to Bradford Plumer, this happened in 2000 and 2016. That means more Americans picked one candidate, but the other candidate got the job. In school we learn that every vote should count the same, but this system does not do that. The Office of the Federal Register explains that a candidate needs 270 of the 538 electoral votes to win, so the race is really about those electors and not the total number of people who voted.

Second, the winner-take-all rule makes many voters feel ignored. The Federal Register says that forty-eight states and Washington, D.C. give all their electoral votes to whoever wins the state. Plumer points out that because of this, campaigns spend almost all their time in a few swing states and mostly skip states that are safely Democratic or Republican. If I lived in a state that always votes one way, my vote might feel pointless, and that could be why some people do not bother to vote. A national popular vote would give candidates a reason to care about voters everywhere, because every vote would add to the same total.

I know there are good arguments on the other side. Judge Richard Posner argues that the Electoral College protects federalism and forces candidates to build broad coalitions across big and small states. He worries that without it, candidates could just run up huge numbers in big cities or one region. I understand this concern, but I do not think it is very convincing. In a popular vote, a candidate would still need millions of voters from many places to win, and each voter in a small town would count just as much as a voter in a city. Right now, candidates already ignore many small and large states if they are not competitive, so the system does not really make them visit everyone.

Posner also says the Electoral College gives a clear winner quickly and keeps recounts inside one state instead of the whole country. That is a fair point, because a national recount could be a big mess. However, close races could be handled with clear national rules for recounts, and we already have a way to count votes state by state. I think fairness to voters is more important than avoiding some extra work. Also, Plumer mentions that faithless electors could vote against their state's choice, which shows the Electoral College adds another risk that a popular vote would not have.

In conclusion, a national popular vote would make sure the person with the most votes wins, give every voter equal importance, and encourage campaigns to talk to the whole country. I hope you will support efforts to change to this system, whether through a constitutional amendment or another approach. Thank you for taking the time to read my letter and for listening to young people in your district.

Sincerely,
Jordan Ellis

For generations, the onset of summer vacation has been shadowed by a familiar dread: the manila envelope stuffed with repetitive math drills, the rigid reading list of nineteenth-century classics, or the prescriptive science packet. Schools assign this work with good intentions, hoping to prevent the notorious "summer slide." Yet when projects are exclusively designed by teachers, they frequently achieve the opposite of their intended purpose, reducing learning to an exercise in compliance rather than curiosity. To keep students intellectually vibrant over the break, schools should entrust them with designing their own summer projects.

The chief flaw of teacher-designed summer work lies in its uniformity. In a classroom, a shared curriculum provides structure and facilitates group discussion. Over a ten-week summer break, however, that same standardization feels detached and arbitrary. When thirty students are forced to construct the exact same papier-mâché cell model or write identical chapter summaries, the task becomes a chore to be completed hastily in the final days of August. Worse, it reinforces the damaging notion that education is something passively received—an external imposition—rather than an active pursuit driven by personal interest.

By contrast, self-designed projects ignite intrinsic motivation. Summer offers a rare gift that the standard academic calendar systematically denies: time for self-directed exploration. When granted the freedom to frame their own inquiry, students often tackle challenges far more ambitious than anything a syllabus would dare demand. A student fascinated by urban planning might spend July cataloging pedestrian hazards in their neighborhood and drafting a proposed park redesign. Another, drawn to mechanics, might rebuild a discarded lawnmower engine, logging their diagnostic process and setbacks in an engineering journal. A young writer might set out to draft the opening chapters of a fantasy novel, wrestling directly with pacing and voice. In each case, the educational return is immense precisely because the student owns the labor.

This autonomy also teaches crucial executive functioning skills that teacher-designed tasks actively bypass. Choosing what to study forces a student to define scope, set realistic deadlines, locate unconventional resources, and pivot when an initial idea falters. In the adult world, professional success rarely looks like filling out an assigned rubric; it looks like identifying a problem, formulating an approach, and sustaining the stamina to see it through. Teachers do not need to abdicate their role entirely in this model. Before the final bell rings in June, educators can review student proposals, helping them refine their goals to ensure genuine academic rigor.

Summer should not merely be an extension of the school term by other means. If the goal of education is to cultivate lifelong learners, schools must be brave enough to step back and let students steer. Entrusting them to design their own summer projects transforms a season of passive drudgery into a laboratory for authentic independence.

While these devices facilitate unprecedented communication and efficiency, their integration into the driver's seat poses a profound threat to public safety. Schools operate at their best when they nurture curiosity, not when they impose conformity. While our principal’s recent decree requiring every student to join an extracurricular activity stems from an admirable desire to build school spirit and foster well-rounded individuals, it fundamentally misinterprets both the purpose of these programs and the lived realities of the student body. Mandating after-school participation transforms genuine passions into institutional chores, ultimately doing more harm than good.

The most glaring flaw in this policy is its blind spot toward students' personal lives outside the classroom. The final school bell does not ring in an afternoon of leisure for everyone. Many teenagers head directly from their final class to part-time jobs that help their families pay rent or buy groceries. Others rush home to care for younger siblings while parents work late, or spend hours managing chronic health conditions and demanding domestic duties. Imposing an arbitrary obligation on students who are already stretched thin is not an act of enrichment; it is an act of exclusion that unfairly penalizes those carrying adult responsibilities.

Equally concerning is what happens to the clubs and teams themselves when participation is coerced. Extracurriculars thrive on voluntary enthusiasm. When someone auditions for the school play, joins the track team, or signs up for the debate club, they do so out of curiosity, ambition, or raw excitement. Fill those rosters with peers who are merely punching an administrative time card, and the dynamic quickly collapses. Reluctant players lower the morale of dedicated teammates, and unmotivated committee members stall collaborative projects. Passion cannot be assigned by fiat, and forcing it onto an uninterested student breeds cynicism rather than camaraderie.

Furthermore, we live in an era where adolescent burnout has reached alarming levels. Caught between rigorous coursework, standardized testing, and the looming anxieties of college admissions, young people desperately need unscripted time. A student who spends their afternoon reading quietly, drawing in a personal sketchbook, or simply decompressing with family is not wasting their hours—they are preserving their mental health. Denying them the agency to choose how they recharge sends a damaging message: that personal downtime has no value unless it can be cataloged on a high school transcript.

Instead of resorting to mandates, the administration should focus on access and invitation. The school could expand the variety of offerings, ensure meeting times accommodate varied schedules, and eliminate prohibitive fees for uniforms or equipment. If the school creates an environment where extracurriculars are genuinely engaging, students will show up willingly. Forcing their hand only turns vibrant communities into mandatory study halls, hollowing out the very spirit the policy hopes to cultivate.

Dear Principal,

I respectfully urge you not to require students to maintain a B average before they can participate in sports, clubs, music, theater, and other school activities. Academic achievement matters, and students should be encouraged to improve their grades. However, banning students with C averages from activities would probably hurt the very students who need school support the most.

Activities give many students a reason to come to school, stay focused, and feel connected to their classmates. A student who struggles in algebra might still be a dedicated soccer player, a talented drummer, or an important member of the debate team. Through those activities, that student learns discipline, teamwork, responsibility, and time management. Those skills can also improve performance in the classroom. If participation is taken away, the student may lose motivation instead of suddenly earning higher grades.

Sports are a good example. Athletes often have to attend practices, follow training schedules, and work closely with coaches. A coach may notice when a player is falling behind academically and encourage that student to attend tutoring or finish missing assignments. Without the team, that connection could disappear. The same is true for band directors, club advisers, and theater teachers. These adults often become mentors who help students believe they can succeed.

A B average is also not the best way to measure effort or progress. A student taking advanced classes may work extremely hard and still earn a C in a difficult subject. Another student may have family responsibilities, a job after school, or challenges with reading that make high grades harder to reach. It would be unfair to treat every C average as proof that a student is not trying. Grades are important, but they do not show the whole person.

Instead of an automatic ban, our school could create a policy that connects activities with academic help. Students below a B average could be required to attend tutoring, meet regularly with a teacher, complete a study plan, or show improvement over time. This approach would keep expectations high while giving students practical support. It would also teach accountability: students would understand that participation comes with responsibilities, but they would not be excluded from the school community.

Activities can even lead to future opportunities. Students may earn scholarships, discover careers, build friendships, and develop confidence through them. Denying participation to students with C averages could close doors when school should be opening them.

Our school should encourage students to improve academically without taking away the places where they feel successful and supported. Please consider a policy based on academic assistance and progress rather than a strict B-average requirement. That would be both challenging and fair.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student
