Every day, millions of drivers step behind the wheel, trusting their own instincts and those of strangers hurtling past them at highway speeds. Yet modern transportation remains profoundly dangerous, plagued by distraction, fatigue, and poor judgment. In the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," the author outlines the debate surrounding autonomous vehicles, charting a course between remarkable safety innovations and formidable technical hurdles. Despite legitimate concerns regarding sensor limitations and legal accountability, society must vigorously pursue the development of driverless cars. The staggering human cost of human-driven transport demands that we replace human fallibility with algorithmic precision.

The most compelling justification for autonomous technology lies in the grim mathematics of road safety. Human error currently accounts for over ninety percent of all vehicular crashes. Drivers text, nod off during late commutes, and drive while impaired, turning two-ton machines into lethal hazards. Autonomous systems do not experience exhaustion, nor do they glance away to check a smartphone. Equipped with laser radar, cameras, computer sensors, and GPS, these vehicles perceive their surroundings with continuous 360-degree awareness. By systematically removing reckless behaviors from the roadway, widespread autonomous adoption can prevent catastrophic crashes, save countless lives, and drastically reduce consumer insurance rates.

Beyond saving lives, autonomous vehicles promise to transform urban living and broaden individual freedom. For the elderly and individuals with disabilities, personal transit is often out of reach; self-driving cars offer these marginalized populations newfound independence. Furthermore, the ecological and structural footprint of personal transit could shrink dramatically. Tech innovators like Google cofounder Sergey Brin envision a future defined by autonomous public transit networks that consume half the fuel and occupy half the parking real estate required today. Reclaiming vast swathes of asphalt parking lots for green spaces and housing would fundamentally revitalize modern cities.

Skeptics legitimately point to existing vulnerabilities, noting that current sensors falter in heavy rain, snow, fog, and confusing construction zones. They worry about software glitches, cybersecurity breaches, and the dangerous lapse in attention that occurs when human passengers must suddenly assume control of semi-autonomous cars. Others wonder who assumes legal liability—the car's owner, the software engineer, or the manufacturer—when a collision inevitably happens. 

These reservations describe a technology in its adolescence, not an inherently flawed ambition. Halting development leaves society tethered to the very human errors that kill tens of thousands each year. The appropriate remedy for sensor blindness in severe weather or vulnerabilities in code is more rigorous testing and engineering refinement, not abandonment. Similarly, questions of legal liability and insurance can be answered through proactive legislation, just as legal frameworks evolved to accommodate commercial aviation and maritime shipping.

Transitioning toward fully autonomous transit will not happen overnight, nor will it be free of growing pains. Still, the alternative—preserving an outdated status quo rooted in human error, heavy emissions, and limited accessibility—is indefensible. By funding and perfecting the development of driverless cars, we take a necessary step toward an equitable, sustainable, and fundamentally safer future.

Dear Senator,

I urge you to support changing presidential elections to a national popular vote. The Electoral College was created as a constitutional compromise, but a system designed more than two centuries ago should be reconsidered when it can produce a president rejected by a majority of voters. Every citizen’s vote should carry equal weight, regardless of the state in which that citizen lives.

The current system allows a candidate to win the presidency without winning the national popular vote. As Bradford Plumer explains in “The Indefensible Electoral College,” this occurred in both 2000 and 2016. Such outcomes undermine public confidence because voters reasonably expect the candidate supported by the most Americans to win. Under the Electoral College, however, the key goal is not earning the most votes nationwide; it is obtaining at least 270 of the 538 electoral votes. Since each state receives electors based on its members of Congress, including two electors for its senators, voters in less-populated states have more influence per person than voters in larger states.

Moreover, the winner-take-all system used by forty-eight states and Washington, D.C. causes campaigns to focus on only a few competitive states. The Office of the Federal Register confirms that most states award all their electoral votes to the candidate who wins the state’s popular vote. Consequently, a candidate who earns 49 percent of a state’s vote usually receives no electoral votes from that state, while the winner receives all of them. Plumer argues that campaigns therefore concentrate on “swing states” and often ignore voters in states that are safely Democratic or Republican. A voter in a noncompetitive state should not be treated as less important simply because the outcome there is predictable. A national popular vote would give candidates a reason to seek votes everywhere: in rural communities, suburbs, small towns, and major cities in every state.

Supporters of the Electoral College raise serious concerns. Judge Richard A. Posner argues that the system protects federalism and encourages candidates to form broad coalitions rather than winning only by gaining huge margins in cities or one region. He also notes that state-based elections can make recounts easier to manage because disputes may be limited to one state rather than spread across the country. These are important advantages to consider.

However, a popular-vote system would not require candidates to ignore rural or small-state voters. Every additional vote would matter equally, so candidates would have an incentive to campaign in all regions instead of concentrating their attention on a few battleground states. Under the present system, many rural voters in reliably partisan states are ignored just as surely as urban voters are. In addition, close elections already can require recounts under the Electoral College, as demonstrated by the disputed 2000 election. Clear national standards for ballots, recounts, and election administration could reduce confusion while preserving the principle of equal representation.

The Electoral College was a compromise between congressional selection and direct popular election, according to the Federal Register. Compromises may be necessary at times, but they should not permanently prevent equal political participation. Presidential elections should reflect the choice of the greatest number of Americans. I respectfully ask you to support efforts that move the nation toward election of the president by national popular vote.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Constituent

When a winter storm shut down our district for a week, my biology teacher moved our frog dissection lesson online. Instead of losing five days of instruction, we watched a high-resolution video, labeled digital diagrams, and discussed questions in a live chat. That experience convinced me that distance learning can be more than a backup plan; it can offer real advantages. Students benefit from attending classes from home because it gives them control over pace and environment, and it removes barriers that often make traditional school inefficient.

A major advantage is flexibility. In a classroom, a teacher must move at a speed that suits the middle of the room. At home, a student can pause a recorded lecture to take notes, rewatch a confusing math explanation, or speed through material she already understands. My friend with dyslexia, for instance, uses captions and replays audio passages as many times as necessary, which would be impossible in a live classroom. This kind of self-pacing turns passive listening into active learning.

Comfort and reduced stress also matter. Not every student thrives in a crowded, noisy building. For students with social anxiety, chronic illness, or sensory sensitivities, home can be a calmer setting where they can actually concentrate. A student recovering from surgery or managing a condition like Crohn's disease can keep up with assignments without the exhaustion of navigating hallways or enduring discomfort. Even for ordinary students, the extra hour saved from a long bus ride can mean more sleep, a real breakfast, or time to review notes before class.

There are, of course, concerns about isolation and screen fatigue. But these are challenges of poor implementation, not reasons to reject the option entirely. Schools can schedule small in-person labs, group projects, or hybrid check-ins so students still connect socially. Teachers can design shorter online sessions with frequent breaks instead of recreating a seven-hour school day on camera.

Distance learning can also widen access to specialized courses. A rural school with only one Spanish teacher might not offer Mandarin or advanced physics. Through video conferencing, a student could join a class taught miles away or hear a guest speaker from another country without a field trip budget. When a blizzard, a pandemic, or a family move interrupts attendance, learning does not have to stop.

That said, distance learning works best when students have reliable internet, a quiet place to work, and some self-discipline. Schools should provide devices and hotspots, and parents or mentors should help younger children stay on track. With these supports, the benefits are clear. Attending classes from home is not a lesser version of school; it is a different, often better, way for many students to learn.

I am a student in your district, and I believe we should change the way we elect the president to a national popular vote. The current Electoral College system is unfair and makes many voters feel like their votes don’t really count.

According to the Office of the Federal Register, the Electoral College is not a place but a process set up as a compromise. It has 538 electors, and a candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win. Each state gets electors equal to its members in Congress. Most importantly, 48 states use a winner-take-all system, so a candidate who wins a state by even a tiny margin gets all of that state’s electoral votes. This creates a serious problem: a candidate can lose the national popular vote and still become president. Bradford Plumer points out that this happened in 2000 and 2016. That doesn’t seem democratic. The person who gets fewer votes should not win the White House.

The winner-take-all rule also makes candidates ignore most of the country. Because so many states are reliably red or blue, presidential campaigns spend almost all their time in a handful of swing states. Voters in safe states are less likely to be contacted, and some people don’t bother voting because they think their vote won’t change the outcome. There is also the rare problem of faithless electors, who can vote against their state’s popular choice. If we used a national popular vote, every vote would count equally no matter where you live. A Republican in California and a Democrat in Mississippi would still matter.

Dear Principal Williams,

I am writing to share my views on the proposed policy that would require students to maintain at least a B average to participate in sports and other activities. I understand that the goal is to encourage academic success, and I respect that purpose. However, I believe this policy would hurt many students, including those it is meant to help, and I urge you to reconsider it.

First, activities often give students the very motivation they need to do well in class. Many students with a C average are not struggling because they lack ability; they struggle because they feel disconnected from school. For these students, a team, a club, or a band may be the main reason they show up every day and stay out of trouble. If we take away the activity, we remove their incentive to try. A student who loses soccer may not suddenly study more. Instead, he may lose his sense of belonging and his grades may fall even further.

Second, a B requirement would exclude a very large number of students. Since many students currently have a C average, this policy would empty rosters and cancel clubs. Teams might not have enough players to compete, and the school play or the yearbook staff might not have enough members to function. Activities build school spirit and community, and everyone benefits when they thrive, including students who earn straight A's. Penalizing so many students would weaken the school as a whole.

Third, activities teach skills that grades do not measure. Athletes learn teamwork, discipline, and perseverance. Students in drama, student government, or newspaper learn communication and leadership. Colleges and employers value these abilities, and students who never develop them because of a grade cutoff will be less prepared for life after high school. A C is a passing grade, and a student earning it is meeting the school's standards. It seems unfair to say that such a student is not good enough to take part in school life.

Fourth, the policy ignores the fact that students face different challenges. Some have jobs, care for younger siblings, or have learning differences that make earning a B much harder. These students may work just as hard as a student who earns A's easily. A strict B requirement would punish circumstances rather than effort.

I do agree that grades matter, and there are better ways to encourage them. The school could offer free tutoring or a supervised study hall for students whose grades are slipping. Instead of a B average, the policy could set a minimum of a C average, or it could place students on academic probation for a grading period and give them support before removing them from an activity. Coaches and advisers could also check in with teachers regularly. These approaches would hold students accountable while keeping them connected to the school.

In conclusion, requiring a B average would reduce motivation, shrink participation, limit valuable learning, and unfairly burden students facing real obstacles. A policy built on support and improvement would serve our school better than one built on exclusion. Thank you for taking the time to consider the students' perspective. I hope you will choose a solution that helps all of us succeed both in the classroom and beyond it.

Respectfully,

A Concerned Student

Cell phones have become practically inseparable from daily life. People rely on them for everything from work emails and turn-by-turn navigation to streaming music and staying in touch with family. Because these devices are such a constant presence, it is easy to assume using them behind the wheel is harmless. However, driving is inherently dangerous and demands an individual's undivided focus. For that reason, drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while a vehicle is in motion.

The primary reason to restrict phone use on the road is the sheer level of distraction it causes. Safe driving requires visual, manual, and cognitive attention all working together. Texting is particularly dangerous because it compromises all three at once: a driver takes their eyes off the road, removes a hand from the wheel, and directs their thoughts to a screen. Research shows that looking down at a text for just a few seconds at highway speeds is equivalent to driving the length of an entire football field blindfolded. In that brief window, a car ahead can brake unexpectedly, a pedestrian can step off the curb, or the vehicle can drift into oncoming traffic. Thousands of fatal crashes each year stem directly from distracted driving, making these tragedies entirely avoidable.

Many people assume that using hands-free features solves this problem, but the evidence says otherwise. While voice commands and Bluetooth headsets eliminate the need to physically hold a phone, they do not remove the mental distraction. Studies on driver reaction times show that carrying on a conversation still diverts vital cognitive bandwidth away from the road. Drivers on the phone frequently suffer from "inattention blindness," meaning they look directly at hazards, brake lights, or road signs without actually processing them. Even if both hands remain on the wheel, a driver whose mind is immersed in a conversation cannot react as quickly to sudden changes in traffic. 

Some critics argue that an outright ban infringes on personal choice, believing individuals should decide for themselves when it is safe to check a notification. Yet driving is not a private activity carried out in isolation; it takes place in a shared public space. A distracted driver puts passengers, pedestrians, cyclists, and other motorists at risk without their consent. Society already accepts necessary limits on personal freedom to preserve public safety, such as enforcing speed limits, penalizing drunk driving, and requiring seatbelts. Restricting phone use falls squarely under the same protective logic. Personal convenience simply should not take priority over someone else's safety.

Naturally, there are moments when a phone is genuinely needed, such as in an emergency. Sensible policies can easily account for this. If a driver needs to call 911 or report a road hazard, they can pull over to a safe shoulder or parking lot. Navigation routes can be set before shifting out of park, and non-urgent calls and texts can wait until the trip is over. Almost any practical need can be managed without touching a device while cruising down the road.

Ultimately, the convenience of staying constantly connected does not justify the immense risks of distracted driving. Whether typing out a message or talking through a headset, using a phone pulls a driver’s focus away from their most critical task: operating several tons of metal safely. Stricter laws, consistent enforcement, and a real cultural shift are needed to make distracted driving as unacceptable as drunk driving. No text or call is worth a human life.

Distance learning has moved from a niche option to a common feature of modern education. While nothing can fully replace the energy of a physical classroom, I believe students benefit substantially when schools give them the choice to attend classes from home. Flexibility, accessibility, and personalized learning make this option a valuable addition to any school system.

The strongest argument for distance learning is flexibility. Students do not all live the same lives. Some are competitive athletes who travel for tournaments, some care for sick relatives, and others have part-time jobs that help support their families. For these students, a rigid schedule in a building can mean falling behind or dropping out. With online classes or video conferencing, a student who is traveling can still join a lesson, and a student who must work in the afternoon can review recorded lectures at night. Flexibility keeps these students connected to their education rather than forcing them to choose between school and their responsibilities.

Distance learning also improves access, especially for students who face physical or medical barriers. A student recovering from surgery, living with a chronic illness, or managing a disability that makes commuting difficult can continue learning without interruption. Students in rural areas, who may live an hour or more from the nearest school, benefit as well. Online courses can even give them opportunities their local schools cannot provide, such as advanced physics, a foreign language, or college-level classes. Without distance learning, these students would simply go without.

In addition, some students learn better at home. A crowded classroom can be distracting or stressful, and students who struggle with anxiety or who are bullied may find it hard to concentrate at school. At home, they can work in a calmer environment and move at a comfortable pace, pausing a recorded lesson to take notes or replaying a difficult explanation. Such control can build independence and time-management skills that will be useful in college and in the workplace, where self-directed work is increasingly common.

Critics argue that distance learning isolates students and reduces the social interaction that is essential to development. They also point out that some students lack self-discipline or reliable internet access, which can lead to poor performance. These concerns are legitimate, but they are arguments for careful implementation rather than for rejecting the option altogether. Schools can require regular video participation, schedule virtual group projects, and invite remote students to attend clubs, sports, or occasional in-person events. They can also lend laptops and provide internet hotspots to families who need them. Because distance learning would be an option rather than a requirement, students who thrive in traditional classrooms could still choose to attend in person.

In conclusion, allowing students to attend classes from home offers real advantages. It gives busy and struggling students flexibility, extends education to those who cannot easily reach a school, and lets some learners work in the environment that suits them best. The drawbacks, such as isolation and unequal access to technology, can be reduced with thoughtful support. Schools that offer distance learning as a choice are not abandoning the traditional classroom; they are widening the path to success for all of their students.

As outlined in the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," a heated debate surrounds the development of these vehicles, pitting their potential benefits against legitimate concerns about safety and regulation. Although critics rightfully point out the limitations of current sensor technology and the lack of clear answers to pressing legal questions, the ongoing advancement of autonomous vehicles is a crucial step forward. We should be actively supporting the development of driverless cars, as they promise to revolutionize the way we think about transportation, making our roads safer, our environment cleaner, and our lives more convenient.

One of the most significant advantages of driverless cars is their potential to greatly reduce the number of traffic accidents. The article highlights that human error is responsible for over 90 percent of traffic crashes, often caused by texting, drowsiness, or impaired driving. In contrast, autonomous vehicles utilize a suite of advanced technologies, including laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors, to continuously monitor their surroundings and make safe decisions. By taking the fallible human element out of the equation, self-driving technology can dramatically lower crash rates, reduce insurance costs, and prevent thousands of senseless tragedies every year. This is not merely a theoretical benefit; the data suggests that widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles could save countless lives and reduce the economic burden of accidents on our healthcare system.

Beyond the critical issue of safety, autonomous transportation also offers a range of social and environmental benefits. For individuals who are unable to operate traditional vehicles, whether due to age, disability, or other factors, driverless cars promise a new level of independence and mobility. Imagine being able to attend social events, visit loved ones, or simply go for a drive without having to rely on others for transportation. Furthermore, a fleet of autonomous vehicles could be designed to optimize fuel efficiency, reducing our reliance on fossil fuels and decreasing congestion on our roads. As Google cofounder Sergey Brin envisions, a future of driverless public transportation could use half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars, making our cities more livable and sustainable.

While there are undoubtedly challenges to be addressed, including the need for clearer regulations and more robust safety protocols, these obstacles should not deter us from pursuing the development of autonomous vehicles. Instead, they should serve as a catalyst for innovation and collaboration, driving us to create solutions that balance the benefits of driverless technology with the need for safety and accountability. By working together to overcome these hurdles, we can unlock the full potential of autonomous vehicles and create a transportation system that is safer, more efficient, and more equitable for all. Ultimately, the benefits of driverless cars far outweigh the costs, and it is our responsibility to ensure that this technology is developed and implemented in a way that prioritizes the well-being of individuals and the environment.

I agree with the principal's decision to require every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. Although some students may initially resist the idea, the requirement would benefit individual students and the school as a whole. Extracurricular activities build important life skills, help students form connections, and give young people a chance to discover interests they might never find in a classroom.

First, extracurricular activities teach skills that textbooks cannot. A student who works on the yearbook, for example, learns to meet deadlines, collaborate with a team, and take responsibility for a finished product. A member of the student council practices public speaking, negotiation, and leadership by planning events and representing classmates' concerns. Even athletes learn discipline and perseverance as they train through fatigue and recover from losses. These abilities are exactly what colleges and employers look for, yet many students never develop them if their only commitments are classes and homework. A requirement ensures that every student, not just those who already feel confident, has the chance to grow in these ways.

Second, extracurricular activities help students build friendships and a sense of belonging. In a large school, it is easy for a quiet or new student to feel invisible. Walking through the halls without a group can be isolating, and that isolation often affects both happiness and grades. Joining a drama club or a running team places students alongside peers who share a common goal. Working toward a school play or a championship creates bonds that cross the usual social lines between grades and cliques. Students who feel connected to their school are more likely to attend regularly, behave well, and care about their performance. By requiring participation, the principal would be helping to make sure no student is left on the sidelines.

Third, a requirement can lead students to discover talents and passions they did not know they had. Many teenagers stick to what is familiar because they fear failure or embarrassment. A student who has never considered art might try the school mural project and realize he loves it. Another who believes she is "not athletic" might join the swim team and find a sport she enjoys for life. Without a push, these discoveries might never happen. Since students may choose from a wide range of options, from robotics to choir to community service, the requirement does not force anyone into something they dislike. It simply asks them to step outside their routine.

Critics may argue that students are already overloaded with schoolwork and that some have jobs or family responsibilities after school. This concern is valid, but it can be addressed with flexibility. The school could offer activities that meet during lunch or only once a week, and it could allow work or caregiving responsibilities to count in special cases. Others may say that forced participation produces unmotivated students. However, many people begin an activity reluctantly and end up enjoying it once they experience success and friendship. A small initial nudge can lead to genuine commitment.

In conclusion, requiring each student to join at least one extracurricular activity is a wise policy. It develops teamwork and leadership, strengthens friendships and school spirit, and encourages students to explore new interests. With reasonable flexibility for those with special circumstances, the policy would enrich students' education far beyond the classroom. For these reasons, I fully support the principal's decision.

By consulting both, the individual gains a balanced portrait of both the genuine hazards and the viable opportunities.

In this way, multiple perspectives uncover vital considerations that would otherwise remain hidden.

Finally, synthesizing multiple perspectives transforms the decision-maker from a passive follower into an active evaluator. When given only one piece of advice, a person is often tempted to obey it uncritically out of convenience. However, when presented with competing viewpoints, the individual is forced to examine the underlying reasoning of each argument. They must analyze why one mentor recommends patience while another urges immediate action. This comparative process sharpens critical thinking, empowering the decision-maker to extract the most valid elements from each suggestion and tailor a bespoke solution that aligns with their personal values and objectives.

Dear Principal,

I am writing to share my perspective regarding the proposed policy change that would require students to maintain at least a B average to participate in sports and extracurricular activities. While I deeply appreciate your dedication to fostering academic excellence throughout our school, I strongly urge you not to implement this policy. Barring students with a C average from activities would inadvertently harm the very students who need these programs the most.

First and foremost, extracurricular activities provide the primary motivation for many students to stay engaged in school. For individuals who struggle with core academics, athletics, music, theater, and clubs serve as a daily anchor. These programs require participants to attend classes, respect school rules, and maintain passing marks. When the bar is set at a C average, it represents a realistic and attainable baseline for students who find academics challenging. If the threshold is abruptly raised to a B average, many students who work diligently just to earn a C may feel that eligibility is out of reach. Disheartened, they may disengage from their coursework entirely, leading to higher rates of absenteeism and potential dropouts.

Furthermore, extracurricular activities are not merely privileges; they are vital educational spaces where students develop essential life skills. On the athletic field or in the debate hall, students learn teamwork, leadership, resilience, time management, and emotional discipline. Denying these developmental opportunities to students who have satisfactory academic standing—which a C average fundamentally represents—deprives them of well-rounded growth. Moreover, physical activities and creative arts offer essential stress relief and promote mental health. Removing these outlets from students who are already working hard academically could increase their anxiety and lower their overall well-being.

Finally, an elevated grade requirement can lead to unintended negative consequences for classroom culture. To maintain a B average, students might shy away from challenging honors or Advanced Placement courses in favor of easier classes where a high mark is guaranteed. Alternatively, students who face learning disabilities, language barriers, or demanding family responsibilities outside of school would be disproportionately penalized, despite putting forth their best effort. 

Instead of excluding students with a C average, our school should implement targeted support systems, such as mandatory study halls or peer tutoring sessions for student-athletes and club members. This approach would hold students accountable while actively providing the resources they need to improve.

Extracurricular activities are one of the most effective tools our school has to build character, community, and scholastic discipline. By maintaining the current eligibility standard and pairing it with academic support, we can encourage students to strive for higher achievement without taking away the activities that give their high school experience meaning. Thank you for your time, consideration, and continued commitment to our student body.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

Dear Senator,

I urge you to support changing presidential elections to a national popular vote. The Electoral College may have been created as a constitutional compromise, but the problems it creates today outweigh its historical purpose. Every citizen’s vote should carry equal weight in choosing the nation’s highest office.

The Office of the Federal Register explains that the Electoral College gives each state electors equal to its number of representatives and senators, for a total of 538 electors. A candidate needs 270 electoral votes to become president. In almost every state, however, the winner of the state’s popular vote receives all of its electoral votes. This winner-take-all system means that millions of votes do not affect the final outcome. A Republican in California or a Democrat in Texas may vote faithfully in every election, yet campaigns often treat those voters as politically irrelevant because the state’s electoral result is considered certain.

Bradford Plumer points out that this arrangement allows a candidate to win the presidency without winning the most votes nationwide. That occurred in both 2000 and 2016. Even if the Electoral College follows the constitutional rules, such outcomes weaken public confidence in democracy. It is difficult to explain why a candidate supported by fewer Americans should receive the office that represents all Americans. A national popular vote would establish a straightforward principle: the candidate with the most votes wins.

Replacing the Electoral College would also encourage candidates to seek support everywhere. Under the current system, campaigns concentrate their advertising, visits, and policy promises on a small number of closely divided “swing states.” Voters in states that reliably support one party are often ignored. A popular-vote system would give candidates a reason to campaign for additional votes in every community, whether urban, rural, Republican, Democratic, or independent. One additional voter in our state should matter just as much as one additional voter in any other state.

Supporters of the Electoral College, including Judge Richard A. Posner, argue that it protects federalism and prevents candidates from winning only by piling up votes in large cities or one region. They also contend that it produces decisive results and limits recount disputes to individual states. These are serious concerns. Yet candidates already must appeal to diverse voters to win a national majority or plurality. Cities alone do not contain enough voters to elect a president; neither does any single region. A popular-vote system would reward candidates who can persuade people across the country rather than those who can narrowly win a few strategically important states.

Concerns about recounts are also manageable. Modern election procedures can include clear national standards, audits, and recount thresholds, just as states already use rules to resolve close contests. We should not preserve an unequal system merely because changing it would require careful planning.

The Electoral College was designed for a different era and has become less representative over time. I respectfully ask you to support efforts, including the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact and constitutional reform, that move our country toward electing presidents by the vote of the people. Democracy is strongest when every ballot has the same value.

I think students would benefit from having the option to attend classes from home, especially when they have a good reason for it. Distance learning should not completely replace regular school, because students need face-to-face interaction, but it can be a useful choice for students who are sick, have family responsibilities, or learn better in a quieter environment.

One important benefit is that students would not have to miss as much school when they are ill. For example, if a student has a bad cold or is recovering from an injury, going to school might be difficult or could spread germs to other people. However, if that student could join class through video conferencing, they could still listen to lessons, take notes, and ask questions. They would not fall behind as easily. This could also help students who have long-term medical conditions and have to miss school more often than others.

Learning from home could also help students with busy or unusual situations. Some students help take care of younger siblings after school, travel for sports or performances, or have appointments that make it hard to attend every class in person. If the school had an online option, those students could keep up with assignments instead of feeling stressed about missing important lessons. It would make education more flexible without lowering expectations.

Another advantage is that some students concentrate better at home. Classrooms can be noisy, and students may get distracted by friends talking or other things happening around them. At home, a student could create a calm workspace and focus more carefully on the lesson. Online classes may also make it easier for quieter students to participate. For instance, a student who is nervous about raising their hand in a crowded classroom might feel more comfortable typing a question in a chat or speaking through a microphone.

However, attending from home should be an option, not something every student is forced to do. In-person school gives students chances to make friends, work in groups, join clubs, and talk directly with teachers. It can also be harder to stay motivated at home. A student might be tempted to look at social media, play games, or sleep during class if no adult is nearby. Schools would need rules, such as requiring cameras when possible, checking attendance, and making sure online students participate.

There is also the problem that not every student has strong internet or a quiet place to work. Schools should provide laptops, internet support, or spaces where students can connect if they need them. Otherwise, distance learning could be unfair to students with fewer resources.

Overall, students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home because it gives them more flexibility and helps them continue learning during difficult situations. Traditional school should still be the main choice for most students, but having a distance-learning option could make school more supportive and accessible for everyone.

Seeking advice from multiple individuals can significantly enhance the decision-making process, ultimately leading to more informed and better choices. This approach allows individuals to gather a diverse range of perspectives, each bringing unique insights and experiences to the table. For instance, when contemplating a career change, consulting with both a career counselor and a professional in the desired field can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the opportunities and challenges involved. The career counselor may offer valuable guidance on resume building, interview techniques, and job market trends, while the professional can share firsthand experiences, industry-specific knowledge, and potential pitfalls to avoid.

Moreover, seeking multiple opinions can help individuals identify potential biases and limitations in their own thinking. When we are faced with a difficult decision, our own emotions, experiences, and assumptions can sometimes cloud our judgment, leading to a narrow or skewed perspective. By consulting with others, we can gain a more nuanced understanding of the situation, as different advisors may highlight aspects we had not considered or provide alternative solutions we had not thought of. For example, a person considering whether to relocate to a new city for a job opportunity might talk to a friend who has made a similar move, a financial advisor to discuss the economic implications, and a family member to explore the potential impact on personal relationships. Each of these advisors can offer distinct viewpoints, enabling the individual to weigh the pros and cons more effectively and make a decision that balances career aspirations with personal well-being.

The process of seeking multiple opinions also fosters critical thinking and evaluation skills. As individuals gather advice from various sources, they must synthesize the information, comparing and contrasting different viewpoints, and assessing the credibility and relevance of each. This analytical process helps in identifying common themes, areas of agreement, and points of contention, which can, in turn, inform a more thoughtful and well-rounded decision. Furthermore, discussing one's plans and ideas with multiple advisors can encourage a deeper reflection on one's own goals, values, and priorities, leading to a clearer sense of direction and purpose. In the context of educational choices, for example, speaking with both academic advisors and professionals in the desired field can help students clarify their career aspirations, understand the prerequisites and challenges involved, and select a course of study that aligns with their strengths and interests.

Summer projects should be primarily student-designed because students are more likely to learn deeply when they can connect academic skills to their own interests. Although teachers should provide clear expectations, deadlines, and support, allowing students to choose the topic and format of a summer project encourages independence, creativity, and genuine curiosity. A project that feels personally meaningful is more likely to keep a student learning during a break than one that feels like an extra worksheet packet.

First, student-designed projects increase motivation. During the school year, students complete many assignments chosen by teachers, often with limited opportunities to explore subjects they care about most. Summer provides a chance for students to pursue those interests while still practicing important academic skills. For example, a student interested in animals could create a research project about local bird species, keeping a journal of observations and making graphs that show how often different birds appear. This project would involve science, writing, and mathematics, but it would not feel like ordinary homework. Because the student selected the topic, he or she would be more willing to spend time reading, observing, and revising the work.

Student-designed projects also teach responsibility. In adulthood, people often have to identify problems, set goals, and organize their own work rather than wait for instructions. A summer project can help students practice these habits. A student who decides to design a small vegetable garden, for instance, must research what plants grow well in the local climate, create a budget for seeds, plan a watering schedule, and document results. Even if some plants fail to grow, the student learns from the experience. Teacher-designed assignments may provide more structure, but they do not always require students to make meaningful decisions. Designing a project teaches students how to manage time and adapt when plans change.

In addition, students have different backgrounds and access to different opportunities during the summer. A teacher-designed project may assume that every family can visit museums, buy supplies, travel, or use reliable technology. Student-designed projects can be more flexible. One student might interview a grandparent about family history, while another might write short stories, learn several recipes, or investigate the history of a neighborhood. These projects can be completed with materials and experiences already available to the student. Giving students choices makes summer learning more equitable.

Of course, student-designed does not mean completely unstructured. Teachers should establish academic standards so that projects remain meaningful. They could require students to submit a proposal before summer begins, keep a weekly progress record, and present their work when school resumes. Teachers could also offer a list of possible project categories for students who need ideas. This approach combines student freedom with guidance and accountability.

Ultimately, summer projects should be student-designed because choice makes learning more engaging, practical, and inclusive. When students pursue questions that matter to them, they are more likely to continue learning beyond the classroom. With thoughtful teacher support, student-designed projects can turn summer break into an opportunity for both academic growth and personal discovery.

Seeking multiple opinions when faced with a decision can be incredibly beneficial, as it allows individuals to gather a wide range of perspectives and insights that might not have been considered otherwise. For instance, when someone is trying to decide on a career path, they may talk to a guidance counselor, a family member, and a professional in their desired field. Each of these people can offer unique advice based on their own experiences and expertise, which can help the individual make a more informed decision. The guidance counselor may be able to provide information about the job market and required skills, while the family member can offer a more personal perspective on what might be a good fit. Meanwhile, the professional in the field can share firsthand knowledge about what to expect and the realities of the job.

One of the primary advantages of seeking multiple opinions is that it can help individuals identify potential pitfalls and avoid making mistakes. When only one person's advice is considered, there is a risk of being misled or missing crucial information. By talking to multiple people, individuals can get a more well-rounded view of the situation and make a more informed decision. For example, if someone is considering buying a new car, they may talk to a friend who recently purchased a similar vehicle, a mechanic, and a financial advisor. The friend can provide information about their personal experience with the car, the mechanic can offer insights into the car's reliability and maintenance needs, and the financial advisor can help the individual determine whether the purchase is affordable and makes sense financially.

In addition to providing a more comprehensive understanding of the situation, seeking multiple opinions can also help individuals develop their critical thinking skills. When considering different perspectives, individuals are forced to weigh the pros and cons of each option and think carefully about what is most important to them. This process can help individuals clarify their own thoughts and feelings, and make a decision that is more in line with their goals and values. Furthermore, seeking multiple opinions can also provide a sense of validation and confidence in one's decision. When multiple people offer similar advice or endorse a particular choice, it can be reassuring and help individuals feel more certain that they are making the right decision.

Ultimately, seeking multiple opinions is an important part of the decision-making process, as it allows individuals to gather a wide range of perspectives and insights, identify potential pitfalls, and develop their critical thinking skills. By talking to multiple people and considering different viewpoints, individuals can make more informed decisions that are tailored to their unique needs and circumstances. Whether it's a major life decision, such as choosing a career or buying a house, or a smaller decision, such as what to eat for dinner or which movie to see, seeking multiple opinions can be a valuable tool for making the best choice possible.

I strongly disagree with the principal's decision that all students must participate in at least one extracurricular activity. While I think extracurricular activities can be really beneficial, I don't think it's fair to force every single student to join one. For one thing, some students are already really busy with schoolwork and other responsibilities. My friend Emily, for example, has to take care of her younger brother after school every day because her mom works late. She's already struggling to keep up with her homework, so adding an extracurricular activity on top of that would be really overwhelming for her.

Another reason I disagree with this decision is that not every student is interested in the same things. Some people might love playing sports, while others might hate it. My brother, for instance, is super into music and loves playing the guitar, but he's really bad at sports. If he was forced to join a sports team, he would probably be miserable and might even get discouraged from doing anything extracurricular at all. On the other hand, if he could join a music club or start a guitar group, he would probably love it and be really motivated to participate.

Furthermore, requiring every student to participate in an extracurricular activity could lead to some students just going through the motions. If someone is only joining a club or team because they have to, they're not going to be very enthusiastic or dedicated. This could bring down the overall morale of the group and make it less enjoyable for the people who are actually passionate about it. For example, if someone who doesn't like writing is forced to join the school newspaper, they might not put in much effort or contribute very much to the team. This could be frustrating for the other members of the newspaper staff who are really committed to producing a great paper.

I also think that this decision could be really stressful for some students. There are already so many pressures and expectations in high school, from grades to college applications to social media. Adding another requirement on top of all that could be really overwhelming for some people. I know someone who's already dealing with anxiety and depression, and I think this would just make things worse for them. They need to be able to focus on their mental health and well-being, not on fulfilling some extracurricular requirement.

I do think that extracurricular activities can be really valuable, though. They can help you develop new skills, make friends, and learn important things like teamwork and time management. But I think students should be able to choose whether or not to participate, and what activities they want to join. This way, everyone can find something that they're really interested in and passionate about, and they'll be more likely to stick with it and get something out of it. By giving students the freedom to choose, we can make sure that everyone has a positive and rewarding experience, rather than just going through the motions to fulfill a requirement.

By allowing students to use their phones during free times, the school is recognizing the importance of these devices in their daily lives. Additionally, this policy shows trust in students' ability to use their phones responsibly, which can help foster a sense of maturity and self-discipline. When students are given the freedom to make choices, they are more likely to take ownership of their actions and behave responsibly.

On the other hand, Policy 2, which prohibits phones altogether, may be overly restrictive and unrealistic. In today's digital age, phones are an integral part of daily life, and banning them entirely may cause more harm than good. For example, students may need to contact their parents or guardians in case of an emergency, and not having access to a phone could be a significant inconvenience. Furthermore, a complete ban on phones may lead to students finding ways to circumvent the rule, which could result in more problems than it solves. When my cousin Dana was deciding between two college offers, she called her mother first. Her mother said to take the cheaper state school and graduate without debt. Then she called her old chemistry teacher, who urged her toward the private college with its smaller labs and research placements. Dana hung up the second call more confused than before, but within a week she understood something she hadn't at the start: the disagreement itself was the most useful information she had gathered.

Any single adviser sees a decision through a narrow window. A parent tends to notice financial risk, because parents often carry the memory of bills and the instinct to protect. A teacher notices opportunity, since teachers spend their days watching what a good program can do for a student. Neither is wrong. Each is simply reporting from where they stand. Talk to only one of them and you inherit their blind spots along with their wisdom. Talk to both and you begin to see the shape of the whole problem, including the tradeoffs that no single person thought to mention.

Multiple opinions also expose bias, which is often invisible to the person holding it. A car salesman who recommends the extended warranty may sincerely believe it's worthwhile, yet he earns a commission when you agree. A friend who tells you not to move across the country may be thinking, quietly, about how much she will miss you. When three or four people point in the same direction despite different motives, that agreement carries weight. When one voice stands alone against the rest, it invites a closer look at why. Without comparison, there is no way to tell sound judgment from self-interest.

There is a practical side, too. Medicine offers the clearest case. A patient told she needs major surgery will often get a second opinion, and sometimes the second surgeon proposes physical therapy or a less invasive procedure. Even when the second doctor confirms the first diagnosis, the patient proceeds with a steadier mind, no longer wondering whether a cheaper or safer path was overlooked. Confidence that comes from checking is sturdier than confidence that comes from hope.

Of course, collecting opinions can go badly. Ask too many people and the result is noise, a chorus of conflicting suggestions that leaves you paralyzed. Some people use advice-seeking as a way to delay choosing, or to shop around until someone says what they already wanted to hear. The habit works best when it is deliberate: a few people, chosen because they know different things, asked specific questions. Asking "What would you worry about here?" tends to yield more than "What should I do?"

In the end, Dana chose the state school, but not because her mother won the argument. The teacher's advice had made her realize she wanted research experience, so she applied to a summer lab program at the university and secured a spot. She got the affordability and the opportunity, a combination she would never have imagined if she had listened to only one voice.

That, finally, is the case for hearing from more than one person. Advice doesn't hand you an answer so much as widen the range of answers you can see. The decision remains yours, but it becomes a better-informed one, built from several perspectives rather than a single point of view.

The arrival of driverless cars is often described as an inevitable step toward a safer, more efficient future. Proponents point to a world with fewer accidents, lower insurance costs, and greater independence for people who cannot drive. While that vision is attractive, I believe the current push to develop and deploy autonomous vehicles is premature. The technology is not yet reliable enough in real-world conditions, and the unresolved legal and human factors make widespread use a dangerous gamble.

Supporters of driverless cars rightly note that human error causes over 90 percent of traffic accidents, often because drivers are texting, drowsy, or impaired. Removing that element could, in theory, save thousands of lives. Autonomous vehicles use laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors to detect obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals, and Sergey Brin imagines a system that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today’s cars. Those benefits are real, but they rest on the assumption that the technology will work almost flawlessly. It does not.

The article itself highlights serious weaknesses. Current sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or unmarked construction zones—exactly the kinds of conditions where a human driver’s judgment is often most valuable. Software systems are also vulnerable to glitches and cybersecurity threats, meaning a car could fail unexpectedly or even be hacked. A vehicle that performs beautifully on a clear, well-marked highway may become unreliable the moment weather turns or road markings fade. Until these systems can handle the messy unpredictability of everyday driving, putting them in control of thousands of pounds of moving metal is reckless.

Even the supposed middle ground—semi-autonomous cars that require a human to stay alert and take over in emergencies—creates its own dangers. Studies mentioned in the article show that passengers quickly lose focus when a computer is doing the driving, which slows their reaction times. A driver who has been reading or looking at a phone for an hour cannot suddenly snap back to attention in the split second before a crash. This halfway approach may be more dangerous than either fully manual or fully autonomous driving.

Finally, the legal and ethical questions are far from settled. When an accident inevitably occurs, who is responsible? The vehicle owner, the software developer, or the automaker? Without clear accountability, victims may be left without fair recourse, and companies may avoid taking full responsibility for their products. This uncertainty alone is reason to slow down.

Driverless cars may eventually transform transportation for the better, but not yet. The promise of fewer accidents and greater mobility cannot justify rushing past unresolved safety, security, and legal problems. We should continue researching the technology, but we should not allow it onto public roads on a large scale until it can handle bad weather, resist cyberattacks, and come with clear rules about responsibility. Safety must come before speed.

Driverless cars should continue to be developed because they could make transportation safer, more efficient, and more accessible. The technology still has real weaknesses, but the possible benefits are too important to ignore. Rather than giving up on autonomous vehicles because of today's problems, companies and governments should keep improving the technology and set clear safety and legal rules before these cars become common.

The best reason to support driverless cars is that they could save lives. The article states that human error causes more than 90 percent of traffic accidents, and it points to habits like texting, drowsiness, and impaired driving. A driverless car never gets tired, checks a phone, or drinks alcohol. It relies on laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors to detect obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals. If these systems are designed and tested with care, they could prevent many crashes that result from careless human choices. Fewer accidents would also mean lower insurance costs and less of the emotional and financial pain that families suffer after a collision.

Autonomous vehicles could also change daily life for people who have trouble driving. Elderly people and people with disabilities often have to depend on relatives, public transportation, or costly ride services. A driverless car could give them much more independence, allowing them to get to work, medical appointments, stores, or social events without asking someone else for a ride. For these people, the technology would be more than a convenience. It would offer freedom and opportunity.

The article also describes Google cofounder Sergey Brin's vision of driverless public transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. If fewer people needed to own their own vehicles, towns and cities might see less congestion and fewer huge parking lots. Burning less fuel would help the environment as well. A shared, automated system could leave cities cleaner and easier to get around in.

Still, critics raise serious concerns, and they deserve to be taken seriously. Sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or construction zones where markings are unclear, and software can suffer from glitches or cyberattacks. These problems show why driverless cars should not be pushed onto the road before they are ready. Semi-autonomous systems worry me most, since people tend to lose focus once a computer is driving, even though they may suddenly need to take over in an emergency. Developers should therefore build vehicles that can handle difficult conditions and that clearly signal when a human must step in. Lawmakers, meanwhile, need to decide who is responsible when a crash happens: the owner, the automaker, or the software developer.

Driverless cars are not perfect, but human drivers are not perfect either. Since human mistakes cause so many crashes, autonomous technology could protect lives and open up transportation to millions of people who lack it now. With careful testing, strong cybersecurity, and clear legal standards, driverless cars can become a safer and more useful part of our future.

Dear Principal Harris,

I understand that you are thinking about requiring a B average for students who want to play sports or join other activities, and I appreciate the chance to share a student's view. I am against the change. The policy is meant to help us, but I believe it would do the opposite for many of the students it targets.

Start with the number of students affected. A great many of us have a C average. A C is not a failing grade; it means a student is understanding most of the material and passing. Under the new rule, all of those students would suddenly be told they are not good enough to join the soccer team, the drama club, or the band. That is a harsh message to send to people who are working and passing their classes.

I also worry about what activities actually do for us. For some students, practice after school is the reason they get up and come to class at all. A boy who loves basketball may sit through math because he knows the gym is waiting at three o'clock. Take that away, and you may remove the one thing keeping him connected to school. Instead of studying more, he might go home to an empty house, drift away from his friends, or simply stop trying. Motivation does not usually improve when we lose something we love.

Activities teach skills that no textbook can. On a team, I have learned how to manage my time, how to handle losing, and how to depend on other people. Students in the school newspaper learn deadlines, and students in the orchestra learn discipline. These lessons matter just as much as a letter on a report card, and a C student deserves them as much as an A student does.

There is also the matter of fairness. Some students earn lower grades because they have a learning disability, because they are learning English, or because they work part-time or care for younger siblings at home. A B average is simply harder for them to reach, no matter how hard they try. Such a rule would punish circumstances, not effort.

I do agree that grades are important, and I would not want students to ignore their classes for the sake of sports. So I would like to suggest some alternatives. The school could offer free tutoring or a supervised study hall before practices. Students with a D or an F could be placed on a probation period, with a chance to improve before losing their place. Coaches and advisors could also check in on grades each month. These steps would encourage better work without shutting students out.

A school should be a place that opens doors, not one that closes them on the students who already struggle most. I hope you will keep the current standard, or at least try supportive approaches first. Thank you for listening to our opinions and for caring about our success.

Sincerely,
A concerned student

Distance learning has moved from a rare experiment to a common feature of modern education, and the question of whether students benefit from attending classes at home deserves a careful answer. While in-person schooling offers real advantages, I believe schools should offer distance learning as an option, because it expands access, accommodates individual circumstances, and teaches skills students will need in the future.

The strongest argument for distance learning is access. Not every student can attend a traditional classroom reliably. A student recovering from a serious illness, living with a chronic condition, or dealing with a long-term injury may miss weeks or months of instruction. Without a remote option, that student falls behind and may never fully catch up. With video conferencing, the same student can follow lessons live, submit assignments, and remain connected to teachers and classmates. The same is true for students in rural areas who face long bus rides, or for young athletes and performers whose training and travel schedules conflict with school hours. For these students, distance learning is not a convenience but the difference between continuing their education and losing ground.

Distance learning also allows for flexibility that can improve learning for some students. Not everyone thrives in a crowded classroom. Students who are easily distracted by noise, who experience social anxiety, or who are targets of bullying may find that a quiet home environment helps them concentrate and participate more confidently. Online discussion boards, for example, give shy students a chance to share ideas they might never voice aloud in class. In addition, recorded lessons allow students to pause, rewind, and review difficult material at their own pace, something a live classroom rarely permits. A student who struggles with a algebra concept can watch the explanation three times without feeling embarrassed.

Finally, learning from home builds skills that matter beyond school. Remote work and online collaboration are now routine in many careers. Students who attend class virtually practice time management, self-discipline, written communication, and comfort with digital tools. These habits prepare them for college courses, many of which now include online components, and for workplaces where independence is valued.

Critics raise legitimate concerns. Some argue that students lose social interaction and the sense of community that school provides. Others point out that students without reliable internet or a quiet workspace are disadvantaged, and that younger children often need adult supervision to stay on task. These problems are real, but they argue for careful design rather than rejection. Because distance learning would be an option and not a requirement, students who need face-to-face interaction can remain in school. Schools can also lend laptops, provide internet hotspots, and require regular check-ins, live sessions, and occasional in-person activities to keep remote students engaged. Many districts did exactly this during the pandemic and learned which supports work best.

In conclusion, students can benefit significantly from attending classes at home when the option is thoughtfully offered. Distance learning keeps education available to students who cannot attend in person, gives others a learning environment that suits them better, and develops skills useful in a digital world. Traditional classrooms will remain essential for many learners, but schools serve students best when they provide more than one path to success.

Driverless cars are no longer just something from a movie. Companies like Google are already testing them on real roads. The article "Driverless Cars Are Coming" shows both good and bad sides of this technology. After thinking about both, I believe we should keep developing driverless cars, but we should be careful and not rush them onto the road before they are ready.

The biggest reason to support driverless cars is safety. The article says human error causes over 90 percent of traffic accidents. That is a huge number. A lot of these crashes happen because people are texting, falling asleep, or driving while impaired. A computer does not get tired and it does not check its phone. If driverless cars can take away even part of that 90 percent, they could save a lot of lives. I think that alone is worth continuing the research.

Another good point is that these cars could help people who can't drive now. The article mentions that elderly or disabled passengers could get more mobility. My grandfather stopped driving a few years ago because his eyesight got bad, and he has to ask other people for rides. A car that drives itself would let him go to the store or the doctor whenever he wanted. There are also other benefits, like lower insurance costs. Sergey Brin even imagines driverless public transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. That would be better for the environment and for crowded cities.

Still, the article brings up problems that can't be ignored. The sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or in construction zones that don't have clear markings. That is a big deal because bad weather and construction happen all the time. A car that only works in perfect conditions isn't very useful, and it could be dangerous. The software can also have glitches or be hacked, which is scary when the computer controls a moving car.

Another problem is with semi-autonomous cars, which need a human to take over in an emergency. The article says studies show people lose focus quickly when a computer is driving, so their reaction times get slower. This means the car might hand control back to a driver who isn't paying attention. Also, nobody knows who is legally responsible after a crash. It could be the owner, the software developer, or the automaker. Until that is figured out, accidents could turn into long arguments instead of fair solutions.

Even with these problems, I think they are things that can be fixed with more work, and that is why development should continue. Sensors can be improved, software can be tested more, and lawmakers can write new rules about responsibility. None of these problems means the idea is bad. They just mean it is not finished yet. If we stopped developing the cars, we would also be giving up the chance to prevent so many crashes caused by human mistakes.

In conclusion, driverless cars should keep being developed. They could make roads safer, help elderly and disabled people, and save fuel and space. The problems with weather, hacking, distracted drivers, and legal responsibility are serious, so companies need to keep testing and the government needs to make clear laws. If we take it slowly and fix these issues first, driverless cars could really improve the future.

When people are faced with a tough decision, it's common for them to ask for advice from someone they trust. However, seeking advice from just one person might not be enough. Talking to multiple people can be really helpful in making a better choice. This is because different people can offer unique perspectives, experiences, and insights that can help you consider various aspects of the decision.

For instance, let's say you're trying to decide which college to attend. If you ask your parents for advice, they might focus on the practical aspects, such as the cost of tuition, the location, and the job prospects after graduation. They might also have some personal biases, like wanting you to stay close to home. On the other hand, if you ask your school counselor for advice, they might be more aware of the academic programs and resources available at each college. They might also know more about the social scene and extracurricular activities, which could be important to you. By talking to both your parents and your school counselor, you can get a more well-rounded view of the options and make a more informed decision.

Another reason why seeking multiple opinions can be helpful is that it can help you identify potential pitfalls or downsides that you might not have considered. For example, let's say you're thinking about quitting your part-time job to focus on your studies. If you ask your friends for advice, they might tell you to go for it, that you deserve a break and that your studies are more important. However, if you also talk to your boss or a mentor, they might warn you about the potential consequences of quitting, such as losing a valuable reference or struggling to find a new job later on. By considering both perspectives, you can weigh the pros and cons more carefully and make a decision that's right for you.

Seeking multiple opinions can also help you avoid groupthink or biased advice. If you only ask people who think the same way as you, you might not get a realistic view of the situation. For instance, if you're thinking about joining a sports team, and you only ask your friends who are already on the team, they might all encourage you to join without considering the potential downsides, such as the time commitment or the risk of injury. However, if you also talk to someone who's not on the team, or who's had a different experience, they might offer a more balanced view and help you consider aspects that you hadn't thought of before.

Additionally, seeking multiple opinions can help you develop your critical thinking skills. When you hear different perspectives and opinions, you have to evaluate and compare them, thinking about which ones make the most sense and why. This process can help you clarify your own thoughts and feelings, and make a decision that's more in line with your values and goals. It's like doing research for a school project, where you have to consider multiple sources and evaluate the evidence before drawing a conclusion.

In conclusion, seeking multiple opinions can be really helpful when you're faced with a tough decision. By talking to different people, you can get a more well-rounded view of the options, identify potential pitfalls, avoid groupthink, and develop your critical thinking skills. It's not about following everyone's advice, but about considering different perspectives and making a decision that's right for you. So, next time you're unsure about what to do, don't be afraid to ask for advice from multiple people – it could make all the difference in making a better choice.

Dear Senator,

I urge you to support changing presidential elections to a national popular vote. Although the Electoral College was created as a constitutional compromise, it no longer ensures that every citizen’s vote carries equal weight. A president should be the candidate chosen by the greatest number of American voters, not the candidate who wins the right combination of states.

The Office of the Federal Register explains that the Electoral College assigns each state electors equal to its members of Congress: its House members plus two senators. Since every state receives two electors for its senators regardless of population, voters in smaller states have more influence per person than voters in larger states. In addition, forty-eight states use a winner-take-all system. Once a candidate wins a state by even a tiny margin, that candidate receives all of its electoral votes. Millions of votes for the other candidate then have no effect on the state’s electoral outcome.

This system can produce results that conflict with the will of the national electorate. Bradford Plumer notes that candidates who won the popular vote nevertheless lost the presidency in 2000 and 2016. Such outcomes damage public confidence because citizens reasonably expect the candidate with the most votes to win. Under a national popular-vote system, every ballot would count equally, whether it came from a rural community, a large city, or a state that usually votes strongly for one party.

The current system also distorts presidential campaigns. Because most states are considered safely Democratic or Republican, candidates concentrate their time, advertising, and promises on a small number of competitive “swing states.” Plumer argues that this leaves voters in other states ignored and can reduce turnout. For example, a voter in a reliably Republican or Democratic state may feel that a presidential vote does not matter because the statewide result is already expected. A popular vote would give candidates a reason to seek support everywhere. A Republican vote in California and a Democratic vote in Texas would matter just as much as any other vote.

Supporters of the Electoral College, including Judge Richard A. Posner, argue that it protects federalism and forces candidates to build broad coalitions rather than merely accumulating votes in populous cities or one region. They also argue that it provides quick, decisive outcomes and limits recount disputes to individual states. These are important concerns. However, a national popular vote would still require candidates to appeal to voters across the country. Large cities alone could not elect a president, because even the largest urban areas contain only a fraction of the nation’s voters. Candidates would need support from suburban, rural, and small-town communities as well. Furthermore, clear election rules, audits, and recount procedures could address close national results without accepting a system in which the popular-vote winner can lose.

The Electoral College may have reflected an earlier compromise, but democracy should rest on the principle of political equality. Please support reforms that move the United States toward electing its president by the national popular vote. Every citizen’s vote should count equally, and the candidate with the most votes should lead the nation.
