Dear Principal Martinez,

I’m writing about the idea of requiring all students to perform community service. I know some of my friends already do it because they think helping is important, but others say it takes too much time away from homework, jobs, or sports. I think we should require community service, but in a way that doesn’t overload students.

First, community service shows you a part of the world you don’t see in school. Last fall my friend Sara tutored a third grader in reading. She said it was frustrating at first because he didn’t want to sound out words. But after a few weeks he read a whole page by himself, and she felt like she actually made a difference. If it were optional, she might not have tried it. A requirement would push more students like her to discover they can help.

Also, some problems around our town are too big for adults to handle alone. A group from our school cleaned up litter at the park near the creek. After one Saturday, they filled twelve trash bags. The park looked cleaner, and little kids could play without broken glass. If only volunteers showed up, there might be three people instead of fifteen. A requirement makes sure enough hands show up.

I get the other side. Students have homework, part-time jobs, and practice. My friend Marcus works at a grocery store after school and says he can’t give up his Saturday. That’s real. But the school could set a low number of hours, like twenty or thirty hours per year, and let students choose when to do it. That’s about one afternoon a month. It’s not nothing, but it’s not impossible. We could also count things students already do, like helping at a food pantry or coaching a youth team.

Some people say forced service isn’t really service because your heart isn’t in it. I used to think that too. But last winter my mom made me help at the food pantry. I went in annoyed. After sorting cans and packing boxes for two hours, I started talking to the volunteers. They told me how many families come each week. I left tired, but I understood why it mattered. I wouldn’t have gone on my own, so I’m kind of glad I was pushed.

I’m not saying we need a huge requirement. But a small one would help the community and teach students that we can be part of fixing problems instead of just walking past them. Thank you for listening.

Sincerely,
[Student Name]

Dear Principal [Last Name],

I am writing to share my view on the school's cell phone policy. After considering both options, I believe Policy 1, which allows students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times as long as they are turned off during class, is the better choice. It protects the learning environment while recognizing the real role phones play in students' lives.

The strongest reason to choose Policy 1 is safety and communication. Families depend on being able to reach their children, especially in emergencies. If there is a medical problem, a severe weather event, or a threatening situation, a phone allows a student to contact a parent or call for help immediately. Even in ordinary situations, phones are practical. A student who misses the bus, stays late for a club, or has a change in pickup plans can let a parent know quickly instead of searching for a office phone. A total ban would remove this safety net for every student, and many parents would worry about that.

Policy 1 also teaches responsibility. Students will have phones in college, at work, and throughout adult life, and they will need to know when using them is appropriate. A rule that allows phones at lunch but requires them to be off in class asks students to practice self-control and respect for others. Banning phones completely avoids that lesson instead of teaching it. When students follow the rules and see that privileges depend on responsible behavior, they build habits that will serve them long after graduation.

Some people argue that phones are distracting, lead to cheating, and encourage cyberbullying, and these concerns are serious. However, Policy 1 already addresses the biggest problem, which is distraction during class. Because phones must be turned off during lessons, teachers can enforce clear consequences, such as confiscating a phone for the period or contacting parents after repeated violations. As for cheating, teachers can require phones to be put away during tests, and the same rule applies to calculators or notes. Cyberbullying also does not stop when phones are banned at school; it happens at home and on weekends. A better solution is to teach digital citizenship and to give students trusted adults to go to when problems arise.

Finally, allowing phones during free time can improve student well-being. Lunch and breaks are the moments when students relax. Some use their phones to listen to music, call a family member, or keep in touch with friends, which can reduce stress during a long day. Others may use them to check assignments, photograph notes from the board, or look up information for a project. A complete ban would treat all of these uses as problems, even though many are harmless or helpful. It would also likely create resentment, and students who feel a rule is unfair are more likely to hide phones and break it.

In conclusion, Policy 1 offers the best balance. It keeps classrooms focused, gives families peace of mind, and teaches students responsible technology habits. Policy 2 may seem simpler, but it would remove useful safety and learning tools and fail to prepare students for the world they will enter. I respectfully ask you to adopt Policy 1 and to support it with clear rules and consistent consequences. Thank you for taking the time to consider my opinion.

Sincerely,

I strongly agree with the principal’s decision to require every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. While a mandate like this will inevitably meet some resistance, the truth is that high school should be about more than just sitting at a desk and taking tests. Joining an activity outside the classroom builds practical life skills, connects students to their school community, and pushes young people to discover passions they never knew existed.

To begin with, clubs and teams teach lessons that textbooks simply cannot provide. A student working on the yearbook staff learns how to manage tight deadlines, coordinate with peers, and take ownership of a major project. Serving on the student council offers hands-on experience with public speaking, diplomacy, and organizing school-wide events. Even athletics, which many view as just games, instill resilience and self-discipline when players have to shake off a tough loss or push through exhausting practices. These are precisely the qualities that future employers and colleges search for, yet students who do nothing more than commute between home and class rarely have the chance to develop them. 

Beyond practical skills, extracurriculars foster a real sense of belonging. In any large school, feeling invisible is a genuine risk. Wandering crowded hallways without an anchor can make anyone feel disconnected, and that isolation usually drags down both mental health and academic performance. When a student signs up for the drama club, the cross-country team, or the debate squad, they immediately gain a group of peers working toward a shared objective. Rehearsing for opening night or training for a meet breaks down the usual barriers between grade levels and social circles. Students who feel tied to a community are far more likely to show up every day, stay out of trouble, and actually care about how they do in school.

Mandating participation also provides the gentle push many students need to try something unfamiliar. Most teenagers stay in their comfort zones because they dread failing or looking awkward in front of others. A teenager who has never picked up a paintbrush might join the mural crew and realize they have an eye for design, while someone who insists they are not the athletic type could join the swim team and find a healthy outlet for life. Because our school offers dozens of choices—from robotics and choir to volunteer groups—nobody is being forced into an activity they hate. They are simply being asked to explore.

Critics might point out that students are already stressed with homework, part-time jobs, or family duties. These are reasonable concerns, but they can be solved with smart, compassionate policies. The administration could schedule clubs during lunch periods or provide options that meet only once a week, while also recognizing outside commitments like caregiving or employment as fulfilling the requirement. As for the worry that required students will be unmotivated, people often start an activity reluctantly only to find they love it once they make friends and see progress. 

Ultimately, this policy treats high school as a complete experience rather than a checklist of academic credits. By nudging everyone to get involved, the school will help students build character, forge lasting friendships, and find their place in the building. The principal is making the right call.

Students would benefit from having the option to attend classes from home, although distance learning should not completely replace traditional schooling. For many students, being physically present in a classroom provides structure, social interaction, and direct support from teachers. Still, an online option can make education more accessible and flexible, especially for students whose circumstances make daily attendance difficult.

One major advantage is that remote learning can help students who are ill, recovering from an injury, or managing a chronic medical condition. Missing several weeks of school can be stressful because students often return to find that their classmates have moved ahead. If they can join lessons through video conferencing, they can continue hearing explanations, participating in discussions, and completing assignments with the class. This is often more effective than simply reading missed material alone after returning to school.

Distance learning can also benefit students with demanding responsibilities outside school. For example, a student who lives far from campus may spend hours each day traveling on buses or in a car. Attending some classes from home could give that student more time to study, sleep, or participate in family responsibilities. Students who compete seriously in athletics, perform in music, or care for younger siblings might also find that an occasional remote option helps them balance school with the rest of their lives.

In addition, some students learn better in a quieter and more controlled environment. A crowded classroom can be distracting for students who struggle to concentrate, while online tools may allow them to replay a recorded lesson, review written instructions, or ask questions through chat. These features do not make school easier in an unfair way; rather, they give students different paths to understand the same material.

However, learning from home has clear disadvantages if it becomes the normal arrangement. Students can feel isolated when they rarely interact face-to-face with classmates. School is not only a place to memorize information; it is also where young people learn to cooperate, communicate, solve disagreements, and form friendships. Furthermore, not every home has reliable internet, a quiet study space, or an adult who can help when technology fails. Some students may also find it difficult to remain motivated without the routine of entering a classroom each morning.

For these reasons, schools should treat distance learning as a flexible option rather than a universal solution. They could allow students to attend remotely during illness, family emergencies, severe weather, or other special situations. Teachers should also make sure that remote students can participate actively instead of merely watching a screen. When used thoughtfully, learning from home can prevent students from falling behind and give them greater control over their education without taking away the valuable experiences that occur in a real school community.

As you consider whether to require community service for all students, I want to offer my strong support for making it part of our school curriculum. Community service does more than help the community; it also gives students real-life skills and experiences that classrooms alone cannot provide. A requirement would help us develop responsibility, empathy, and compassion that will stay with us long after graduation.

Some students worry that service hours will cut into academics or personal interests. I understand that concern, but I see community service as a complement rather than a burden. When students tutor younger children, for example, they practice communication, patience, and leadership—abilities that matter in almost any career. Service also lets students apply what they learn in school to real-world situations. Instead of taking time away from learning, it can make learning more meaningful.

Mandatory community service can also bring students from different backgrounds together. Working side by side on a project, whether it is serving meals at a soup kitchen or sorting donations at a food bank, helps us understand challenges that other families face. Those experiences build empathy and can break down social barriers within our own school. In the end, we become a more inclusive and supportive community, not just a collection of students who rarely interact outside class.

There are practical benefits as well. Colleges and employers often look for a record of volunteer work, so students who complete service hours may have an advantage in applications and interviews. Service projects also create chances to meet professionals and community organizations, which can help students explore interests and build confidence in their future direction. A school requirement would ensure that every student, not just those with free time or family connections, can access these opportunities.

I know that adding a requirement may feel like one more obligation in an already busy schedule. But I believe the benefits outweigh the inconvenience. Community service teaches responsibility, connects us to people we might otherwise never meet, and prepares us for life after high school. By making it mandatory, our school would show that helping others is not just an optional activity but a core part of what it means to be educated. I hope you will consider this perspective as you make your decision.

When it comes to summer projects, I believe that they should be student-designed. This approach allows students to take ownership of their learning and pursue topics that genuinely interest them. When teachers design the projects, they might not always align with the students' passions or strengths, which can lead to a lack of motivation and engagement.

On the other hand, when students are given the freedom to design their own projects, they are more likely to be invested in the outcome. For instance, a student who loves photography can create a project that involves taking pictures of local wildlife or landmarks, while a student who is passionate about environmental issues can design a project that focuses on reducing waste in their community. This autonomy allows students to explore their interests in-depth and develop a sense of purpose, which is essential for meaningful learning.

Another benefit of student-designed projects is that they can help students develop essential skills such as time management, critical thinking, and problem-solving. When students are in charge of their own projects, they have to plan, organize, and execute their ideas, which requires a lot of responsibility and self-discipline. For example, a student who wants to create a documentary about a social issue has to research, interview people, and edit the footage, all while meeting a deadline. This process helps students develop a sense of responsibility and accountability, which is crucial for success in academics and beyond.

Moreover, student-designed projects can also help students develop a growth mindset. When students are given the freedom to design their own projects, they are more likely to take risks and try new things, which can lead to unexpected discoveries and learning opportunities. For instance, a student who wants to create a mobile app might encounter obstacles and setbacks, but they will also learn to persevere and adapt, which is an essential skill for success in today's fast-paced and ever-changing world.

In contrast, teacher-designed projects can sometimes feel rigid and formulaic, which can stifle creativity and innovation. When teachers dictate the parameters of the project, students might feel like they are just going through the motions, rather than truly engaging with the material. This can lead to a lack of enthusiasm and motivation, which can negatively impact the learning experience.

Of course, some might argue that student-designed projects can be chaotic and disorganized, and that teachers need to provide guidance and structure to ensure that students stay on track. However, this can be addressed by providing students with general guidelines and expectations, while still giving them the freedom to design their own projects. For example, teachers can provide a list of possible topics or themes, and then let students choose the one that interests them the most. This way, students still have the autonomy to pursue their passions, while also receiving the support and guidance they need to succeed.

In conclusion, I firmly believe that summer projects should be student-designed. This approach allows students to take ownership of their learning, develop essential skills, and cultivate a growth mindset. By giving students the freedom to design their own projects, we can help them develop a love of learning that extends beyond the classroom, and prepares them for success in all aspects of life.

The concept of distance learning has gained significant traction in recent years, with many schools now offering students the option to attend classes from the comfort of their own homes. This innovative approach to education has sparked a heated debate about its potential benefits and drawbacks. In my opinion, students would greatly benefit from being able to attend classes from home, and I firmly believe that this option should be widely adopted.

First and foremost, attending classes from home would provide students with greater flexibility and autonomy. For instance, students who have to balance school with part-time jobs or family responsibilities would be able to manage their time more effectively. They could attend classes at times that suit them best, without having to worry about commuting to campus or adhering to a rigid schedule. This flexibility would be particularly beneficial for students who live in remote areas or have mobility issues, as it would enable them to access education that might otherwise be out of reach. For example, a student living in a rural area could attend classes at a university located hundreds of miles away, without having to relocate or incur significant transportation costs.

Another significant advantage of distance learning is that it would allow students to learn in an environment that is comfortable and familiar to them. Many students struggle to concentrate in traditional classroom settings, where distractions and disruptions can be plentiful. In contrast, attending classes from home would enable students to create a dedicated learning space that is tailored to their individual needs and learning style. This could lead to improved focus, increased productivity, and better academic outcomes. Furthermore, students who are introverted or have anxiety issues may find that attending classes from home helps to reduce their stress levels and boost their confidence.

In addition to these benefits, distance learning would also provide students with access to a wider range of educational resources and courses. With the advent of online and video conferencing technologies, students could participate in classes and workshops that are taught by experts from all over the world. This would not only broaden their horizons and expose them to new ideas and perspectives but also enable them to develop a more nuanced understanding of global issues and trends. For example, a student interested in international business could attend online lectures and seminars taught by professors from leading universities in Europe, Asia, or the Americas.

Finally, it is worth noting that distance learning would also have a positive impact on the environment. By reducing the need for commuting and transportation, students would be able to minimize their carbon footprint and contribute to a more sustainable future. This is a critical consideration, given the pressing concerns about climate change and environmental degradation that we face today.

In conclusion, attending classes from home would be a highly beneficial option for students, offering them greater flexibility, autonomy, and access to educational resources. By providing students with the ability to learn in a comfortable and familiar environment, distance learning would help to improve academic outcomes, reduce stress levels, and promote sustainable living. As technology continues to evolve and improve, I firmly believe that distance learning will become an increasingly important part of our educational landscape, and I strongly advocate for its widespread adoption.

The Road Demands Undivided Attention

In an age when cell phones are ubiquitous, the temptation to check a message or answer a call while driving is nearly universal. Yet the very device that connects us also endangers us. Although some argue that hands-free technology makes phone use safe behind the wheel, the evidence shows otherwise. Drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle because even hands-free conversations create dangerous cognitive distractions that undermine road safety.

The central problem is not merely where a driver’s hands are, but where the driver’s mind is. Driving demands continuous visual scanning, rapid judgment, and motor coordination. A phone conversation, even when the device is mounted and the driver’s eyes are on the road, diverts mental resources away from these tasks. Research on “inattention blindness” shows that drivers engaged in phone conversations may look at the road but fail to process critical hazards, such as a pedestrian entering a crosswalk or a car braking suddenly. Because hands-free calls remove only manual and visual distraction, not the cognitive load, they create a false sense of security without addressing the core danger.

Crash statistics reinforce this conclusion. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has repeatedly identified distracted driving as a leading cause of traffic fatalities, and studies estimate that texting while driving can increase crash risk by more than twenty times. More importantly, meta-analyses comparing handheld and hands-free phone use find no significant safety advantage for hands-free devices. In fact, a driver talking on a hands-free phone may exhibit slower reaction times comparable to a driver with a blood alcohol concentration at the legal limit. If a behavior produces impairment similar to drunk driving, permitting it in any form is difficult to justify.

Defenders of phone use often cite emergencies, navigation, or work obligations. These concerns are real, but they do not require drivers to use phones while the vehicle is in motion. A driver can pull over to make a call, set navigation before departing, or enable a “do not disturb while driving” mode that automatically replies to messages. Modern smartphones can route urgent calls through voice assistants, but even these interactions should be minimized and, ideally, limited to parked vehicles. The minor inconvenience of waiting to communicate is a reasonable price for preventing fatal collisions.

In conclusion, cell phones are valuable tools, but they have no place in the hands or minds of an active driver. Because cognitive distraction persists even with hands-free technology, and because the crash risk is severe, the only responsible policy is a complete ban on cell phone use while driving. Laws should reflect what traffic safety research has long demonstrated: when a car is moving, the driver’s attention belongs to the road, not to the phone.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge you to support changing presidential elections to a national popular vote. The Electoral College may have been created as a compromise, but today it can produce results that do not reflect what most voters chose. For a democracy to feel fair, the candidate with the most votes nationwide should become president.

According to the Office of the Federal Register, the Electoral College has 538 electors, and a candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win. Each state receives electors based on its number of representatives and senators. This system means that citizens’ votes do not all have the same effect. In 48 states and Washington, D.C., the winner of the state popular vote receives all of that state’s electoral votes. If a candidate loses a state by a very small amount, the votes for that candidate usually do not help at all in the final Electoral College count.

This problem is especially clear when a candidate wins the popular vote but loses the presidency. Bradford Plumer points out that this happened in both 2000 and 2016. Even if people disagree about the candidates in those elections, it is hard to defend a system where more Americans vote for one candidate but another candidate becomes president. A popular-vote system would make every vote count equally, whether it came from a small town, a large city, or a state that usually votes strongly for one party.

The winner-take-all system also causes campaigns to focus on only a few “swing states.” Plumer explains that candidates spend most of their time and money trying to win closely divided states while ignoring voters in states considered safely Republican or safely Democratic. For example, a voter in a state that is expected to go strongly for one party may feel that there is little reason to vote because the outcome is already assumed. Under a national popular vote, candidates would have a reason to seek votes everywhere. A Republican vote in California and a Democratic vote in Texas would matter just as much as a vote in a swing state.

Supporters of the Electoral College, including Judge Richard A. Posner, argue that it protects federalism and forces candidates to build broad coalitions instead of just gaining huge totals in cities. They also argue that a national popular vote could lead to a difficult nationwide recount. These concerns deserve consideration. However, candidates already have an incentive to reach many different kinds of voters if every individual vote matters. Winning a national majority would require support from rural, suburban, and urban areas across many regions. Also, modern election systems can recount close elections when needed. It is not a good reason to keep an unfair system simply because a recount might be complicated.

The Electoral College was an important historical compromise, but it should not be treated as perfect forever. Our country should choose its president based on the will of the greatest number of voters. I ask you to support efforts, such as the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact or a constitutional amendment, that would move the United States toward electing presidents by popular vote.

Sincerely,  
A Concerned Student

Dear Principal,

I am writing to express my strong support for requiring all students to complete community service. Although some students may worry that volunteering would take time away from schoolwork, jobs, or hobbies, I believe its benefits are greater than its costs. Community service should be a graduation requirement because it builds responsibility, teaches useful skills, and strengthens both students and the community.

To begin with, service helps students become more empathetic and responsible. When students work with people whose lives are different from their own, they learn to look beyond their personal concerns. For example, one of my friends tutored elementary school students after school. At first, she signed up mainly because she needed volunteer hours. After several weeks, however, she became truly invested in helping one struggling reader. She learned to be patient, to offer encouragement, and to celebrate small improvements. When the child finally read an entire book aloud, my friend felt proud of what they had accomplished together. That kind of growth may not appear on a test, but it is still an important part of education. Requiring service would give every student a chance to gain that experience.

Community service also develops practical skills that students will need in college, careers, and everyday life. Students who organize food drives, clean up litter, or help at senior centers practice communication, teamwork, and problem-solving. For instance, a group planning a park cleanup has to choose a date, divide responsibilities, gather supplies, and possibly coordinate with local officials. These are the same kinds of skills that employers and colleges value. Volunteering can also teach students how to manage their time. Some people say service would make students’ schedules too busy, but learning to balance commitments is an important lesson in itself.

In addition, a school-wide service requirement could make a real difference in our community. A few volunteers can help, but if every student participates, the results could be much greater. More children could receive tutoring, more public spaces could be cleaned, and more local organizations could get the support they need. Students might help at food pantries, visit seniors who are lonely, or work on community gardens. Service projects could also bring together students from different grades and social groups. Working side by side toward a common goal can break down cliques and create more school spirit. Our community would see that our school is not only a place where students learn facts, but also a place where young people learn to care for others.

Of course, some students have demanding schedules, family responsibilities, or after-school jobs. For that reason, the requirement should be flexible. Students could complete a reasonable number of hours over several years, choose projects connected to their interests, or take part in service opportunities offered during school hours. With planning and choices, community service would be manageable rather than overwhelming.

For these reasons, I urge you to require community service for all students. It would help us become more responsible and compassionate, teach skills we will use throughout our lives, and improve the community we share. I hope you will seriously consider this proposal.

Sincerely,  

A Student

I agree with the principal's decision, though with one condition: the requirement has to be flexible enough that every student can find something that fits. Done well, a rule like this doesn't add a burden to school life. It opens a door that many students would otherwise never walk through.

Consider how easily a teenager can drift through high school without belonging to anything. A student arrives in the morning, sits through six or seven classes, goes home, and repeats the cycle. Classmates become faces in the same rows of desks. Without a shared project, there's little reason to speak to the quiet kid in the back of chemistry or the sophomore who just transferred. An extracurricular changes that. A student working on the yearbook has to negotiate page layouts with people from other grades, chase down photographs, and meet deadlines together. Friendships form almost as a byproduct, because people who struggle toward the same goal tend to end up knowing each other.

Skills grow in these settings, too, and they're skills that textbooks handle poorly. Serving on student council means learning to run a meeting, argue a position without insulting anyone, and accept it when the vote goes the other way. Playing on a soccer team teaches a person to show up on cold afternoons, take correction from a coach, and recover from a bad loss. Colleges and employers notice this. Admissions officers look for evidence that an applicant has committed to something over time, and a supervisor hiring a first-time worker will often care more about reliability and teamwork than about a particular grade in algebra.

Some will object that students are already overloaded. Homework, part-time jobs, and family responsibilities fill many schedules, and adding a requirement might seem unfair. That's a reasonable worry, but it's an argument for designing the policy carefully, not for scrapping it. The requirement is for just one activity, and the range of choices can be wide: a robotics club that meets once a week, a recycling committee, the school play's stage crew, a tutoring program. A student who works after school might count a service project on weekends. Flexibility keeps the rule from turning into a punishment.

There's also a quieter benefit. Many teenagers don't know what they like because they've never tried anything. A boy who assumes he's not athletic might discover he loves running cross-country, where he competes mostly against his own times. A girl who thinks she hates public speaking might find, in the debate club, that she's good at it. If participation were purely voluntary, these students would likely stay home, never learning what they missed. A gentle push can reveal talents that no classroom assignment ever would.

Finally, schools with active student life tend to feel different. Hallways are livelier, attendance often improves, and students who feel connected to a team or club are less likely to disengage or drop out. When almost everyone has a stake in something, school stops being merely a place to endure and becomes a place where people have reasons to be.

For these reasons, I support the principal's decision. The requirement asks little, only that each student give a small portion of the week to something beyond the classroom, but it can return a great deal: friends, confidence, practical skills, and perhaps a passion that lasts well beyond graduation. A school should want that for every student, not only for those who already seek it out.

The intention behind mandatory extracurricular activities is easy to admire. Administrators want vibrant campuses, engaged teenagers, and graduates who offer colleges more than just a transcript of grades. Yet transforming clubs, athletics, and arts programs from voluntary pursuits into compulsory requirements is a mistake. When schools mandate passion, they inevitably drain it of its value, turning what should be an outlet into just another chore.

The most glaring flaw in this policy lies in the assumption that every student’s after-school hours are genuinely free. High schoolers do not live in identical circumstances. One student might need to catch an early bus to care for younger siblings until a parent finishes a late shift. Another might work twenty hours a week at a grocery store to help pay household bills or save for tuition. For these teenagers, staying on campus until five o'clock for track practice or yearbook layout is not merely an inconvenience; it represents an impossible conflict. Penalizing them because their real-world responsibilities clash with school-sponsored activities is fundamentally unfair.

Beyond practical logistics, the mandate overlooks the reality of academic burnout. The modern school day is rigorous, frequently followed by hours of homework, exam preparation, and family duties. Some students simply need solitude to recharge. For an introverted teenager, an hour spent reading alone, practicing an instrument at home, or decompressing without social evaluation is far more restorative than forced camaraderie in the debate hall. Coercing students into structured socialization assumes that healthy personal development only happens in adult-supervised group settings.

Furthermore, conscripting students into activities damages the culture of those groups for everyone involved. An extracurricular organization thrives on the shared enthusiasm of people who actively chose to walk through the door. When a student council meeting or drama rehearsal is populated by teenagers who are merely checking a box to fulfill an administrative decree, the dynamic shifts. Projects stall, morale dips among dedicated members, and faculty advisors spend their afternoons managing disengaged bystanders rather than mentoring committed participants. Quality suffers when compliance replaces curiosity.

Schools should certainly foster involvement, but through inspiration and accessibility rather than coercion. If participation numbers are low, the productive response is to investigate the underlying barriers. Administrators could offer late activity buses, eliminate participation fees, or encourage students to charter clubs around niche interests like coding, community gardening, or graphic design. An extracurricular pursuit is meant to help young people discover who they are on their own terms. That discovery loses all meaning when it is made under administrative order.

Dear Principal,

I respectfully disagree with the idea that students should need at least a B average to participate in sports and other activities. I understand that the school wants students to take academics seriously, and I agree that grades matter. However, banning students with C averages from activities would probably make their school performance worse instead of better.

For many students, sports, band, drama, clubs, and other activities are the reasons they stay connected to school. A student who struggles in math or English might still feel successful on a basketball team, in the marching band, or as part of the debate club. Those activities give students confidence and a group of friends who encourage them. If students lose that support because of one average, they may feel like school is only a place where they are failing.

Activities also teach important skills that do not always show up on a report card. On a team, students learn responsibility, cooperation, time management, and how to handle pressure. If someone knows they have practice after school, they may be more likely to finish homework during study hall or ask a teacher for help before practice. Personally, I know students who work harder because they want to remain eligible for their teams or clubs. Taking activities away could remove one of their biggest motivations.

A B average is also not always a fair way to judge effort. Some students have difficult classes, learning differences, family responsibilities, jobs, or problems at home. A student with a C average may be working extremely hard and improving. For example, a student who raises a failing math grade to a C has made important progress, even if their overall average is not yet a B. Under the proposed policy, that student could still lose the activity that was helping them stay motivated.

Instead of requiring a B average, the school could use a more supportive policy. Drivers Should Not Use Cell Phones While Driving

Cell phones have become so woven into daily life that many people feel uneasy when separated from them for even a few minutes. That constant connection, however, becomes dangerous when a person is behind the wheel. Although a small number of hands-free uses may be reasonable, drivers should not be permitted to use cell phones in any capacity that requires visual, manual, or significant mental attention while operating a vehicle.

The strongest argument against phone use while driving is the danger it creates. Driving demands continuous attention to changing conditions: traffic signals, pedestrians, merging vehicles, and sudden hazards. Using a phone to text, scroll, or dial pulls attention away from these tasks. Researchers often describe three kinds of distraction: visual, manual, and cognitive. Texting combines all three, which makes it especially hazardous. A driver traveling at highway speed who glances at a screen for only five seconds can cover the length of a football field without watching the road. In that time, a car ahead can brake, a lane can close, or a child can run into the street.

Some people argue that hands-free calling solves the problem. It does reduce the manual burden, but it does not remove the cognitive one. A driver absorbed in a stressful conversation may look at the road without actually registering what is happening on it. This is sometimes called inattentional blindness, and studies of driving performance have found slower reaction times and more missed cues among drivers on hands-free calls. The belief that hands-free use is safe may even encourage drivers to talk longer and more often, increasing their exposure to risk.

Others contend that banning phone use infringes on personal freedom or is impractical to enforce. Yet society already limits individual freedom when behavior endangers others. We prohibit drunk driving, require seat belts, and enforce speed limits because the consequences of carelessness fall on innocent people, not only on the driver. A distracted driver who causes a crash can injure passengers, cyclists, and strangers who never agreed to share that risk. Enforcement is admittedly difficult, but difficulty is not a reason to abandon a rule. Clear laws, meaningful fines, and public education campaigns have changed attitudes toward seat belts and drunk driving, and they can do the same here. Technology can also help, since phones can automatically enter a driving mode that silences notifications and blocks texting when the vehicle is in motion.

A reasonable policy would still allow narrow exceptions. Navigation apps that give spoken directions, or a single-touch emergency call to report an accident or medical crisis, serve safety rather than undermine it. Setting the destination before departure, mounting the phone in a fixed position, and relying on voice prompts can keep these uses from becoming distractions. The guiding principle should be that any phone function used while driving must not require the driver to look away from the road or engage in a demanding exchange.

In conclusion, the convenience of staying connected does not outweigh the risk of injury and death on the road. Texting, browsing, and even extended phone conversations impair a driver's ability to respond to danger, and the harm extends well beyond the person holding the phone. Drivers should therefore be prohibited from using cell phones while operating a vehicle, apart from limited, safety-oriented functions. No message or call is so urgent that it cannot wait until the car is parked.

Dear Principal Johnson,

I am writing to share my perspective on the proposal to require a B average for participation in sports and extracurricular activities. While I recognize that this initiative comes from a genuine desire to raise academic achievement, I worry that setting the threshold so high will ultimately backfire—particularly for the many students who currently maintain a C average. For their sake and for the health of our school community, I urge you not to adopt this policy.

For a great number of students, extracurriculars are not just an extra privilege; they are the primary anchor keeping them invested in school. Whether it is stepping onto the soccer field, rehearsing with the marching band, or participating in a debate, these activities provide purpose and belonging. When students feel tied to a team or an ensemble, they have an immediate, tangible reason to show up every day, stay out of trouble, and keep up with their classwork. If we bar students with a C average from the very programs that keep them tethered to school, they will not automatically channel their energy into studying. More likely, they will feel alienated and stop trying altogether.

We also have to acknowledge that a C average reflects solid, passing work. Academics do not come easily to everyone, and for many hardworking students, a C in a challenging course like chemistry or algebra represents late nights and genuine perseverance. Furthermore, many students juggle heavy responsibilities outside the building, from working part-time shifts to help support their households to caring for younger siblings. A student might not be an honor roll scholar, but they might be an exceptional team captain, a dedicated artist, or an inspiring leader. By barring these students from participating, we risk sending the disheartening message that only high academic achievers deserve to contribute to our school's culture.

Just as importantly, athletics and clubs provide an education that cannot be tested on paper. Being part of a team cultivates discipline, accountability, resilience, and the ability to work with people from all walks of life. Juggling rehearsals or game schedules alongside homework also forces students to develop real-world time management. Stripping these opportunities away from students who are already struggling would deprive them of the very experiences that help them mature into capable, confident young adults.

If our goal is truly to help students raise their grades, there are far more supportive ways to achieve it than simple exclusion. The school could establish mandatory study halls or peer tutoring sessions tied to team practices. Coaches and faculty advisors could track progress weekly, placing students on an academic probation period if their grades begin to slip rather than benching them immediately. An approach centered on guidance and accountability would motivate students to pull their grades up without pushing them out of the activities they love.

A B-average mandate might seem like a quick way to demand excellence, but in reality, it would shut out students who need our support the most. I respectfully ask that you maintain the current standard and look toward constructive alternatives that uplift our entire student body. Thank you for listening to our voices and considering our perspective on this important issue.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

The dream of stepping into an automobile, turning away from the windshield, and letting an algorithm handle the morning commute has moved rapidly from science fiction into engineering reality. Industry advocates promise an era of unprecedented convenience and safety, picturing cities freed from gridlock and parking shortages. Yet, as the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming" reveals, the path toward full autonomy is fraught with significant technical vulnerabilities, human behavioral obstacles, and unresolved legal dilemmas. Until these foundational flaws are thoroughly resolved, aggressive development and deployment of autonomous vehicles should be halted.

Foremost among these concerns is the unreliability of autonomous navigation systems in everyday driving conditions. Autonomous vehicles rely on a fragile network of cameras, GPS, laser radar, and computer sensors to interpret lane markings and traffic signals. However, as critics in the article point out, these systems frequently falter during adverse weather—such as heavy rain, snow, or dense fog—and when navigating dynamic, unmarked construction zones. Driving safely cannot be an enterprise reserved strictly for clear, sunny skies. When the ambient environment blinds a vehicle's primary perceptual tools, the likelihood of catastrophic failure spikes dramatically. Compounding this physical limitation is the ever-present threat of software glitches and cybersecurity breaches, which could compromise entire fleets at the expense of public safety.

Equally troubling is the paradoxical demand placed on human operators during this transitional era. Many vehicles are designed as semi-autonomous, meaning a human driver must remain vigilant and ready to take the wheel in emergencies. In practice, this design creates a dangerous cognitive trap. According to the article, studies indicate that passengers rapidly lose focus once a computer assumes control, which severely delays their reaction times when immediate intervention is needed. Human beings simply do not function well as passive monitors waiting to avert sudden disasters. Expecting a distracted driver to instantly assess and correct an algorithmic failure in split-second conditions is an inherently flawed safety model.

Beyond the mechanical and behavioral complications lies a legal vacuum that society has yet to address. When an autonomous car inevitably crashes, who shoulders the blame? Current liability frameworks are entirely unprepared to distinguish whether fault lies with the vehicle’s owner, the software programmer, or the manufacturing firm. Entrusting life-and-death choices to software without a clear ethical consensus or legal framework for restitution invites chaotic legal battles and leaves victims unprotected.

The prospect of reducing the tragic toll of human error on our roadways is unquestionably attractive, but good intentions cannot substitute for dependable technology. The persistent sensor failures, the hazards of delayed human takeover, and the absence of clear liability standards all underscore the premature nature of autonomous transport. Until innovators can guarantee systems that perform reliably in all real-world conditions and policymakers establish robust legal guardrails, the race to eliminate the human driver remains an unacceptable gamble with public safety.

Summer projects should be student-designed, though within a framework that teachers set up and check along the way. The point of a summer assignment is to keep a young mind working while school is out, and nothing keeps a mind working like a question the student actually wants answered.

Consider what a typical teacher-designed project looks like: a packet of math problems, a required novel with a worksheet, a five-paragraph essay due the first day of class. These assignments are not worthless, but they tend to be done in a frantic weekend in late August. Students know the work is a formality, and many treat it that way. Some copy from friends. Others learn nothing beyond the fact that summer, too, belongs to school. The assignment preserves the form of learning while draining it of the curiosity that makes learning stick.

Now picture a student who loves baseball designing a statistics project. She tracks a local team's batting averages across June and July, builds a spreadsheet, and tests whether the team really hits better at home. Or a boy who has always sketched cars decides to research how engine design changed over fifty years and builds a small illustrated timeline. Neither project would appear on a standard syllabus, yet each demands real skills: forming a question, gathering data, organizing information, drawing conclusions, explaining findings. Those are the very abilities teachers want to see strengthened. The difference is that the student supplies the motivation herself, so the work happens over weeks rather than in one last-minute scramble.

Critics reasonably worry that students will choose something easy, or nothing at all. That risk is real, but it can be managed without handing the whole design back to teachers. A school might ask each student to submit a short proposal in June explaining the question, the plan, and the finished product. The teacher can approve it, push for more rigor, or suggest a narrower focus. A check-in email in mid-July keeps the student honest. In this arrangement the teacher acts as an editor and coach, which is arguably a better use of expertise than writing yet another worksheet.

There is also a fairness argument. Teacher-assigned reading lists and problem sets quietly assume every family has the same resources: a library card, a quiet room, a parent who is home. A self-designed project can be built from what a student already has access to. One teenager might interview a grandparent about immigrating to the country; another might teach herself basic coding on a free website. Both are learning, and neither is penalized for lacking a particular textbook or a well-stocked bookshelf.

Finally, designing a project is itself an education. Deciding what to study, estimating how long it will take, and adjusting when a plan falls apart are skills adults use constantly and schools rarely teach directly. A student who has managed a six-week project of her own will return in September with more than subject knowledge. She will have practiced running her own learning, which is the best preparation for any classroom.

Summer should not be a blank space between school years, but it also should not be a miniature version of the school year. Letting students design their projects, with teachers guiding and approving, honors both goals. It keeps them learning, and it reminds them that learning can be something they choose.

After considering both options, I believe Policy 1, which allows students to carry phones and use them during lunch and other free times as long as they are turned off during class, is the better choice. Parents and guardians often need to reach their children quickly, whether because of a change in pickup plans, a medical appointment, or a family emergency. Students also need a way to contact home if they feel sick or get stranded after an activity. A total ban would force everyone to rely on the front office, which is often busy and cannot relay every message right away. In a more serious emergency, such as a lockdown or severe weather, students and parents would feel much safer knowing they could be in touch. Policy 1 keeps that option open without allowing it to disrupt learning, since phones must be off during class.

Policy 1 also teaches self-control, a skill students will need long after graduation. In college and in the workplace, no one will take away their phones; they will be expected to manage them appropriately. A school that allows phones in limited settings gives students daily practice in knowing when to use technology and when to put it away. A complete ban teaches nothing except how to hide a phone. Students who are determined to use their phones will sneak them into pockets and bathrooms, and teachers will spend valuable time hunting for violations. A clear, reasonable rule that students see as fair is much easier to enforce than one they see as excessive.

Some people argue that Policy 2 is better because phones are distracting, and I agree that phones can interfere with learning. However, Policy 1 already addresses this problem by requiring phones to be turned off during class. The focus of the classroom stays intact. Lunch and free periods are students' time to relax, talk with friends, and recharge. Using a phone to listen to music, check messages, or call a parent during these breaks is harmless, and it may even help students return to class refreshed. If misuse occurs, the school can apply consequences, such as having the phone held in the office for the first offense and requiring a parent to pick it up after repeat offenses. That approach holds individual students accountable without punishing everyone.

Finally, phones are also useful educational tools. Students can photograph assignments written on the board, set homework reminders, and look up information for projects during free periods. Many students rely on their phones for calendars and for contacting group members. A total ban removes these conveniences and may disadvantage students who do not have other easy ways to stay organized.

In conclusion, Policy 1 offers the best balance. It keeps classrooms focused, supports student safety, reduces conflict over enforcement, and helps students develop responsibility. Policy 2 may appear simpler, but it ignores real needs and invites rule-breaking. I respectfully urge you to adopt Policy 1 and to pair it with clear expectations and fair consequences. To address the issue of summer learning loss, many schools require students to complete academic projects during their break. While the intention behind these assignments is commendable, the way they are executed can significantly impact their effectiveness. Rigid, teacher-designed assignments often reduce summer learning to a mere compliance exercise, stripping it of any real value or engagement. Instead, schools should adopt a more student-centered approach, allowing students to design their own summer projects. This approach fosters intrinsic motivation, helps develop essential executive functioning skills, and enables students to engage deeply with subjects that genuinely interest them.

When students are given the autonomy to choose their own projects, they are more likely to be motivated by a desire to learn, rather than simply fulfill a requirement. Traditional, teacher-assigned tasks, such as uniform packets of worksheets or prescribed reading lists, can be uninspiring and even resented by students. In contrast, student-designed projects can be tailored to individual interests and passions. For example, a student interested in programming might create a functional mobile application, while an artistically inclined student might write and illustrate a graphic novel exploring historical events. By allowing students to pursue their own interests, schools can transform the summer assignment from a chore into a meaningful learning experience.

Moreover, designing and executing an independent project helps students develop critical life skills, such as self-direction, time management, and problem-solving. In a classroom setting, teachers typically provide guidance and structure, but when students work on their own projects, they must take on these responsibilities themselves. They must articulate clear research questions, establish realistic timelines, acquire necessary resources, and navigate unexpected obstacles. These skills are essential for success in higher education and the modern workforce, where individuals are valued for their ability to think critically, solve complex problems, and work independently.

Some may argue that teacher-designed projects are necessary to ensure academic rigor and continuity. However, this does not have to be a trade-off. Educators can provide a structured framework, including clear rubrics and expectations, while still allowing students to design their own projects. By requiring students to submit project proposals before the academic year ends, teachers can review their ideas and provide feedback on academic merit and scope. This approach strikes a balance between giving students the freedom to pursue their interests and maintaining high academic standards.

Ultimately, the goal of education should be to cultivate curious, autonomous, and lifelong learners. Teacher-prescribed summer homework can often have the opposite effect, stifling curiosity and creativity. By empowering students to design their own summer projects, schools can ensure that the break remains productive, intellectually stimulating, and personally transformative. This approach honors students' unique interests and prepares them for the demands of the future, where they will be expected to think critically, work independently, and pursue their own goals and passions. By giving students the reins over their learning, schools can help them develop into motivated, self-directed, and engaged learners.

If a teacher assigns a project like "write a five-page report on a historical event," a lot of kids will just put it off until the last week of August and rush through it. I know because I've done it. But if I got to choose my own topic, I would probably be more excited. For example, I love cooking, so I could make a project about how different cultures use spices, try out a few recipes, and write about what I learned. That would feel like something I wanted to do, not something I had to do.

Second, student-designed projects teach skills that teacher-designed ones usually don't. When a teacher makes the project, the student just follows the directions. When the student designs it, they have to plan, set goals, and manage their time. Those are real-life skills. If someone decides to build a small garden and track how fast different plants grow, they have to figure out what supplies they need, how often to water, and how to record the results. Nobody is telling them every step, so they have to think for themselves. That is a lot closer to what adults do at work or in college.

Some people would say that teacher-designed projects are better because they make sure everyone learns the same material. That is a fair point, especially for subjects like math, where students might forget things over the summer. A teacher might worry that a student who designs their own project will pick something too easy or not related to school at all. But this problem can be fixed. Teachers could give a list of requirements, like the project has to connect to at least one school subject, include some writing or reflection, and be approved before summer starts. That way students still have freedom, but they can't just do nothing. A student who wants to improve at math could design a project about budgeting for a trip or tracking sports statistics, which still uses math skills.

Another good thing about student-designed projects is that they let students show their individual strengths. In a class of thirty kids, everyone is good at different things. One student might like art, another might like science, and another might like writing. A single teacher-made assignment can't fit everybody. Letting students design their own lets the artist make a comic about the water cycle while the writer makes a short story about a historical figure. Everyone is still learning, but in a way that fits them.

Finally, student-designed projects make for better presentations in the fall. If everyone did the same assignment, the class would hear the same thing thirty times, which gets boring fast. If every project is different, students would actually want to listen and learn from each other.

In conclusion, summer projects should be designed by students with teacher approval and basic requirements. This keeps students motivated, teaches them responsibility, and still makes sure they keep learning during the break. If schools want kids to take summer learning seriously, they should let kids have some control over it.

When you have a big decision to make, it can be tempting to just ask one person and go with whatever they say. But I think talking to more than one person usually leads to a better choice, because everyone sees things a little differently and no single person knows everything.

One reason is that different people have different experiences. For example, last year I was trying to decide whether to join the school band or try out for the soccer team, since the practices were at the same time. My dad told me to do soccer because he played when he was young and said it taught him teamwork. If I had only listened to him, I probably would have picked soccer right away. But then I talked to my older cousin, who was in band all through high school. She told me band gave her a lot of friends and that she got to travel for competitions. Hearing both sides made me realize that I had been thinking about it too simply. Each person was giving me advice based on what happened to them, so I needed both to get the whole picture.

Another reason is that people can notice things you miss. When you are close to a problem, you sometimes get stuck on one detail. My friend Marcus was deciding whether to take an advanced math class. He was nervous because he got a B in the last one. His teacher told him he had the skills but just needed to study more consistently. His mom said she was worried about the workload because he already has a lot of homework. Those were two different points, and neither one was wrong. Marcus ended up taking the class but talked to his teacher about getting extra help. If he had only heard one opinion, he might have either quit out of fear or jumped in without a plan.

Getting more than one opinion can also protect you from bias. Sometimes people give advice that is really about what they want, not what is best for you. A salesperson at a store might say a certain phone is the best one because they get paid more for selling it. Even people who care about us can be biased. A parent might want you to stay close to home for college because they will miss you. A friend might tell you to do something because they want you to come along. When you ask several people, it is easier to spot which parts of the advice are actually helpful and which parts are just personal preference.

Finally, hearing different opinions helps you figure out what you really think. Sometimes when people disagree, it makes you ask yourself questions you had not thought about. When my cousin and my dad gave me opposite advice, I had to stop and ask what I cared about most. I realized I liked music more than I wanted to admit, and that helped me decide. In the end, the choice was still mine, but I felt more confident because I understood the reasons behind it.

Of course, there can be a downside if you ask too many people. You might get confused or never make up your mind. I think the best way is to ask a few people you trust who have different viewpoints, then think carefully about what they said. Overall, getting multiple opinions gives you more information, helps you avoid bias, and makes your final decision feel more like your own.

Every June, backpacks empty and library books gather dust. Schools hoping to prevent the “summer slide” sometimes mail home thick packets or assign identical book reports. Yet many students dread these tasks, completing them hastily in August or not at all. If the goal is continued learning, the project should be shaped by the student, not dictated by the teacher.

Student-designed projects tap into intrinsic motivation. A seventh grader who spends July building a skateboard ramp is solving geometry problems: measuring angles, calculating weight distribution, and adjusting slope. That same student might resent a worksheet on angles. When learners choose a question or project that matters to them, the work stops feeling like an obligation and starts feeling like an exploration. A high school junior with a passion for photography could document neighborhood changes over the summer, writing captions and researching local history. Another might test water quality at a nearby creek after heavy rains. These projects require reading, math, writing, and scientific thinking, yet they arise from genuine curiosity.

By contrast, teacher-designed summer assignments assume one size fits all. A required novel may be perfect for some and torture for others. A math packet may review skills a student already mastered or move too quickly through concepts that need more support. During the school year, teachers adjust instruction based on daily observations. Over the summer, that adjustment disappears. The result is often busywork completed by parents, copied from friends, or left until the last weekend before school resumes. Worse, such assignments can teach students that learning is something done only to satisfy a teacher.

Skeptics might argue that without a teacher’s design, students will choose easy projects or do nothing. That risk is real, but the solution is not to remove choice. Schools can provide a framework: every student submits a proposal in June, identifies the question or product, lists the skills they will practice, and agrees to share evidence in August. A teacher can approve the plan or ask for more rigor. In this model, the student designs the content while the school sets expectations for depth and accountability. A fourth grader who wants to learn about baking might keep a measurement journal, test recipes, and present a cost analysis of ingredients. A tenth grader might read three books by authors from different continents and write a comparative essay. The choices are nearly endless, but the learning remains serious.

Summer is a rare stretch of time when students can follow a question without bells interrupting their thoughts. Teacher-designed projects often waste that freedom. Student-designed projects, supported by clear guidelines, teach the most important lesson of all: that learning can be self-directed and satisfying long after the final bell rings.

When facing an important decision, people often benefit from asking more than one person for advice. Although making a choice independently can build confidence, relying on only one opinion may limit a person’s understanding of the situation. Different people notice different risks, offer different experiences, and may challenge assumptions that the decision-maker has not questioned. By seeking multiple opinions, a person can gather useful information, compare viewpoints, and ultimately make a more thoughtful choice.

First, multiple opinions can reveal options that a person or a single adviser might overlook. For example, a high school student deciding where to apply to college might initially focus only on a famous university because a friend recommends it. However, a teacher may point out that another school has a stronger program in the student’s intended field, while a parent may remind the student to consider tuition costs and financial aid. A counselor might also suggest looking at class sizes, internship opportunities, and distance from home. None of these perspectives is necessarily more important than the others, but together they give the student a fuller picture. Instead of choosing based only on reputation, the student can select a college that fits academic goals, finances, and personal needs.

Seeking several opinions also helps people recognize possible problems before they commit to a decision. This is especially important in situations involving money, health, or safety. Suppose someone is considering buying a used car. A family member might think the car looks attractive and affordable, while a mechanic may notice signs of engine trouble. Another friend who recently bought a similar model could warn about expensive repairs or poor fuel efficiency. If the buyer listens only to the first positive opinion, that person may end up with a costly mistake. By hearing different viewpoints and checking the car carefully, the buyer can decide whether to negotiate a lower price, choose another vehicle, or avoid the purchase entirely.

In addition, listening to others can make a person examine personal biases. People sometimes prefer advice that confirms what they already want to do. A student may want to quit a demanding activity because it feels difficult, or an employee may want to accept a new job simply because the salary is higher. Talking to several trusted people can provide a useful balance. One person may encourage the student to persevere, while another may ask whether the activity is harming school performance or mental health. Similarly, a mentor may remind the employee to consider work-life balance, job security, and opportunities for growth rather than focusing only on income. These questions can lead to a more honest evaluation of the decision.

Of course, gathering advice does not mean that a person must follow every suggestion. Too many opinions can become confusing, and the final choice should reflect the individual’s own values and circumstances. Still, hearing several perspectives provides information that one person alone may not have. By comparing advice, identifying risks, and considering alternatives, people are more likely to make decisions that are informed, practical, and personally meaningful.

Students would benefit from having the option to attend classes from home, although it should not completely replace going to school in person. Distance learning can help students who are sick, have family responsibilities, live far from school, or learn better in a quieter environment. At the same time, schools should make sure online students still have ways to participate and get help from teachers.

One important benefit is that students would not have to miss as much school because of health problems. For example, if a student has a cold, a broken leg, or a condition that makes it hard to travel, they could still join class through video conferencing. They would be able to hear the lesson, ask questions, and turn in assignments instead of falling behind for several days or weeks. This could also keep other students healthier because someone who is contagious would not need to come into the classroom.

Attending from home could also help students who have difficult schedules. Some students have to help take care of younger siblings after school, work part-time jobs, or travel long distances on a bus. If schools offered some online options, these students might have more flexibility. For instance, a student who has an early medical appointment could attend the first part of class online rather than missing the whole day. This does not mean school should become easier, but it could make education more possible for students with real responsibilities.

Another reason is that some students focus better at home. Classrooms can be noisy and distracting, especially for students who struggle with anxiety or attention problems. At home, a student may be able to sit in a quiet room, use headphones, and take notes without being surrounded by conversations and distractions. They can also replay recorded lessons if they did not understand something the first time. In a regular classroom, if a student misses one explanation, they may be too embarrassed to ask the teacher to repeat it.

However, learning from home is not perfect. Students can feel lonely, get distracted by games or social media, and have less chance to make friends. School is not only about math, science, and English. It is also where students learn to work with others, speak in groups, and be part of a community. Because of this, I do not think every student should be required to learn from home. In-person classes are still important.

Overall, students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home as an option. It could help students stay caught up when they are sick, manage complicated schedules, and learn in an environment where they can focus. Schools should offer it carefully, with clear expectations for attendance and participation. Giving students more than one way to learn would make school more fair and flexible for different situations.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge you to oppose replacing the Electoral College with a direct national popular vote for president. While concerns about the current system deserve attention, the Electoral College remains a carefully designed safeguard of federalism and national stability.

The Electoral College was established in the Constitution as a compromise between letting Congress choose the president and relying solely on a nationwide popular tally. Each state receives as many electors as it has members in Congress, meaning even the smallest states are guaranteed at least three electoral votes. A candidate must assemble a broad coalition of states to reach the required 270 electoral votes, rather than simply running up overwhelming margins in a few densely populated regions. As Judge Richard Posner notes, this structure forces candidates to appeal to voters in diverse areas, from large coastal cities to rural farming communities, and it prevents any single region from dominating presidential elections. Removing this balance would tilt campaigns almost entirely toward major urban centers, leaving much of the country unheard.

I recognize that critics raise important objections. Two recent presidents won the Electoral College while losing the national popular vote, and in winner-take-all states, millions of voters in safe red or blue states can feel ignored. The focus on a handful of swing states is real, and so is the theoretical risk of faithless electors. These flaws deserve serious discussion. However, the proposed alternative carries its own dangers. A direct popular vote would likely trigger a nationwide recount in any close election, with every precinct in all fifty states potentially contested. The Electoral College, by contrast, confines recounts to individual states and typically produces a clear, decisive winner without prolonged national uncertainty.

The winner-take-all approach used by forty-eight states has shortcomings, but the system’s core purpose is not simply to mirror the popular vote; it is to require a geographically broad mandate. That is a feature, not a bug. Presidential candidates should have to win not only many votes but many different kinds of communities across the country.

I ask you to defend the Electoral College against calls for its abolition. Rather than abandoning this constitutional compromise, we should address its flaws through measured reforms, such as encouraging states to allocate electors proportionally as Maine and Nebraska already do. Preserving the Electoral College protects the interests of small states, promotes national coalition-building, and ensures that presidential elections remain stable and representative of our federal union.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]

In an emergency, a student can quickly contact a parent or guardian, which is especially valuable during after-school activities or unexpected situations.
