When people face an important decision, they often turn to family members, friends, teachers, or professionals for advice. Although one trusted opinion can be helpful, seeking multiple opinions usually leads to better choices. Different people notice different risks, offer different experiences, and help a person examine whether a decision truly matches his or her goals. By listening to several perspectives instead of relying on only one, people can make decisions that are more informed and balanced.

First, different advisers can provide information that one person may not know. For example, a student deciding which college to attend might ask a parent, a guidance counselor, an older sibling, and a recent graduate. A parent may focus on tuition costs and safety, while a counselor may know about academic programs and scholarships. A sibling who has attended college may explain practical issues such as dorm life, transportation, or workload. None of these opinions alone gives the complete picture. However, together they can help the student compare schools more carefully and avoid making a choice based only on a campus visit or a ranking.

Multiple opinions can also protect people from biased or emotional decisions. Everyone has personal preferences, and even well-meaning advisers may encourage choices that reflect their own values more than the decision-maker’s needs. For instance, a friend might urge someone to accept a job because it pays well, while a mentor might point out that the job offers little opportunity for growth. Another person may remind the job seeker to consider the daily commute, work environment, and effect on family life. Hearing these contrasting views can reveal questions that the person had not considered. Instead of simply choosing the highest salary, the job seeker can weigh income against long-term happiness and career development.

In addition, asking several people for advice encourages careful thinking. When someone hears the same concern from more than one source, that concern may deserve serious attention. If several mechanics independently say that an older car will require expensive repairs, the owner may realize that keeping the car is not the best financial choice. On the other hand, if only one person strongly objects to a decision while others provide convincing evidence in favor of it, the decision-maker can evaluate whether that objection is based on facts or personal preference. Multiple opinions do not mean that a person must follow the majority; rather, they provide evidence that can be compared and judged.

Of course, receiving too much advice can sometimes be confusing. People may hear conflicting recommendations and feel pressured to please everyone. For this reason, they should choose advisers who are knowledgeable, honest, and familiar with the situation. They should also remember that the final decision belongs to them. Advice is most useful when it helps clarify personal priorities rather than replace independent judgment.

Ultimately, seeking multiple opinions improves decision-making because it broadens a person’s understanding, reduces the influence of bias, and encourages thoughtful evaluation. Whether someone is choosing a school, a job, a car, or another important path, listening to several informed perspectives can reveal options and consequences that might otherwise be overlooked.

Dear Principal Williams,

I know how difficult it must be to revisit our cell phone policy, and I appreciate that you are weighing both sides carefully. While I understand the appeal of a complete ban, I believe Policy 1—allowing students to bring phones but requiring them to be off during class—is the better choice for our school community. It balances safety, responsibility, and the realities of modern student life.

One of the strongest arguments for Policy 1 is safety. Many students walk home, wait for buses, or travel to after-school jobs and activities. Having a phone gives us a direct line to parents if plans change or an emergency arises. A school day does not end at the final bell, and the walk to a car or the ride on public transit can be exactly when a phone is most needed. If phones are banned entirely, students either leave them at home—losing that safety net—or hide them in backpacks, which creates unnecessary stress and rule-breaking.

Beyond safety, allowing phones during lunch and free periods teaches us how to manage our own attention. High school is supposed to prepare us for college and the workplace, where no one confiscates a phone at the door. We need practice making good choices: putting the device away when it is time to focus, using it briefly to decompress, and then returning to our responsibilities. A complete ban removes that learning opportunity. If we never get to practice self-regulation in a structured environment, we are more likely to struggle with it later when the rules disappear.

There is also the simple reality that our phones are how many of us connect socially. Lunch is often the only unstructured time in a long academic day. For some students, texting a friend in another lunch period, sharing a funny video, or checking a group chat is a way to relax before the next class. For students who feel isolated in the cafeteria, a phone can be a lifeline to a supportive community. Banning phones completely would not make those students suddenly join a club or make new friends; it would simply remove one of the few tools they have to feel less alone.

I understand the concern that phones can be distracting, and I agree that they should not be used during instruction. Policy 1 already addresses that by requiring phones to be turned off in class. Teachers can enforce that rule consistently, and the consequence for violating it can be clear and firm. But punishing everyone by banning phones entirely punishes the students who follow the rules and ignores the legitimate reasons students need their devices outside of class.

A school should be a place where we learn responsibility, not just where we are protected from temptation. Policy 1 gives us clear boundaries while still treating us as young adults capable of making good decisions. I urge you to adopt it.

Sincerely,

Alex Chen  
Student, Grade 11

The traditional image of school—rows of desks, a teacher at the front of the room, and a bell marking each period—has changed considerably. Many schools now offer distance learning, which allows students to attend classes from home through online platforms or video conferencing. Although some people worry that remote learning can limit social interaction, I believe students benefit from having it as an option. It provides flexibility, allows for more individualized learning, and gives students access to opportunities that may not be available in a traditional classroom.

One important advantage of attending class from home is flexibility. Regular school schedules require students to learn at the same place and time every day, but not every student has the same needs or circumstances. For instance, a student who has a health condition, helps care for a younger sibling, or trains seriously for athletics or the arts may find it difficult to follow a strict school-day schedule. With distance learning, students can join live lessons when they are able or watch recorded lessons later. This can reduce stress and make it easier for them to balance school with other responsibilities.

Distance learning can also help students learn at a pace that works for them. In a regular classroom, teachers usually have to teach at a speed that fits most of the class. As a result, some students may become bored because the material is too easy, while others may fall behind because they need more time. Online lessons can give students more control. A student who struggles with algebra, for example, can pause a video, replay an explanation, and take extra time before finishing an assignment. At the same time, a student who is strong in reading can move ahead by exploring more challenging books or articles instead of waiting for everyone else to finish.

Another major benefit is that online learning can expand access to classes and resources. Students at small or rural schools may not have advanced placement courses, specialized electives, or world language classes because their schools cannot hire teachers for every subject. Through distance learning, however, a student in a remote community could take calculus with a qualified teacher from another city. Remote instruction can also be especially helpful for students with chronic illnesses. Rather than missing weeks of school and falling behind, they can stay connected to teachers and classmates through video conferencing. In situations like these, distance learning is more than a convenience; it can be essential to a student’s education.

Of course, learning from home has challenges. Some students may feel isolated, and others may have trouble staying focused without the structure of a classroom. These concerns are reasonable, but they do not mean schools should reject distance learning altogether. Since it is an option rather than a requirement, students can still participate in clubs, sports, school events, and occasional in-person activities. Schools can also provide schedules, check-ins, and group projects to help students stay motivated and connected.

Overall, students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home. The flexibility, personalized pacing, and wider access to courses can help many students succeed when a traditional classroom does not fully meet their needs. Distance learning should not replace in-person school for everyone, but it is a valuable option that can make education more accessible and effective.

I agree with the principal’s decision to require every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. Some people may think that clubs and teams should be completely optional, but I believe involvement outside the classroom helps students grow academically, socially, and personally. Extracurricular activities are not just extra things to do after school. They teach important lessons that students may not learn from textbooks alone.

One major benefit is that activities teach teamwork and responsibility. Whether students join a sports team, work on the yearbook, or serve on student council, they have to cooperate with others to reach a common goal. For example, a basketball player soon learns that scoring points is not enough. Winning requires communication, passing, practice, and trust between teammates. In the same way, students on the yearbook staff must share assignments, meet deadlines, and help solve problems when something goes wrong. These are useful skills for college, jobs, and everyday life.

Extracurricular activities can also help students discover talents they did not know they had. A shy student might join drama club and realize that performing on stage is exciting. Someone who signs up for debate because a friend encourages them might become a confident speaker. Student council can help students learn how to plan events, manage money, and speak in front of large groups. If participation remains completely voluntary, many students may never take a chance on something unfamiliar. Requiring one activity could give them the push they need to find a new interest or strength.

Another advantage is that activities often improve time-management skills. Students with soccer practice, robotics meetings, or band rehearsals have to plan their afternoons carefully. They may use study hall more wisely, finish homework before practice, and avoid putting assignments off until the last minute. Being busy does not automatically make someone a better student, but it can encourage students to become more organized. In many schools, students who are involved in activities also have better attendance and stronger grades because they feel more connected to school.

Of course, some people argue that mandatory participation could cause stress or force students into activities they dislike. This is a reasonable concern, especially for students with family responsibilities or jobs after school. However, the requirement could be flexible. Schools could offer many different choices, including art, music, service clubs, academic competitions, and activities that meet during lunch or before school. Students would not all have to play a sport or stay late every day. They could choose an activity that fits their interests and schedules.

Requiring participation is not meant to punish students or take away their freedom. Instead, it gives every student a chance to be part of the school community. It may especially help students who are shy, new to the school, or do not have much encouragement at home. Through one club, team, or organization, they can make friends, develop skills, and feel that they belong.

For these reasons, I support the principal’s decision. Extracurricular activities build confidence, responsibility, teamwork, and time-management skills. Although the requirement may seem restrictive at first, its benefits are much greater than its drawbacks. By encouraging every student to get involved, the school is opening doors to friendship, growth, and future success.

When individuals are faced with a difficult decision, it is not uncommon for them to seek advice from multiple sources. This approach can be incredibly beneficial, as seeking multiple opinions can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the situation and ultimately lead to a better choice. By consulting with various people, individuals can gain access to a diverse range of perspectives, experiences, and expertise, which can help to inform and refine their decision-making process.

One of the primary reasons why seeking multiple opinions is helpful is that it allows individuals to consider different viewpoints and evaluate the pros and cons of a particular decision. For instance, when deciding on a career path, a person may speak with a career counselor, a mentor in their desired field, and a friend who has experience in a related industry. Each of these individuals can offer unique insights and advice, highlighting potential benefits and drawbacks that the person may not have considered otherwise. By weighing the different opinions and perspectives, the individual can make a more informed decision that takes into account multiple factors and potential outcomes.

Another advantage of seeking multiple opinions is that it can help individuals to identify and mitigate potential biases and blind spots. When people receive advice from only one person, they may be influenced by that person's biases and assumptions, which can lead to a narrow or misguided perspective. By consulting with multiple people, individuals can gain a more nuanced understanding of the situation and avoid being swayed by a single, potentially flawed, point of view. For example, when considering a major purchase, such as a house or a car, a person may seek advice from a financial advisor, a real estate agent, and a friend who has recently made a similar purchase. By considering the different opinions and perspectives, the individual can gain a more balanced understanding of the situation and make a decision that is based on a thorough evaluation of the facts.

Furthermore, seeking multiple opinions can also provide individuals with a sense of validation and confidence in their decision. When people receive consistent advice or feedback from multiple sources, they can feel more assured that they are making the right choice. On the other hand, when individuals receive conflicting opinions, they can use this as an opportunity to re-evaluate their decision and consider alternative perspectives. For instance, when deciding on a medical treatment, a person may consult with multiple doctors, each with their own area of expertise. By considering the different opinions and recommendations, the individual can make a more informed decision that takes into account the latest research and medical advancements.

In conclusion, seeking multiple opinions can be a highly effective way to make a better choice. By consulting with various people, individuals can gain access to a diverse range of perspectives, experiences, and expertise, which can help to inform and refine their decision-making process. Whether it's considering different career paths, making a major purchase, or evaluating medical treatment options, seeking multiple opinions can provide individuals with a more comprehensive understanding of the situation and ultimately lead to a more informed and confident decision. Ultimately, by seeking out multiple opinions and considering different perspectives, individuals can make choices that are more thoughtful, deliberate, and effective.

I agree with the principal’s decision to require every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. Some people may argue that mandatory involvement creates stress or pushes students into activities they do not enjoy. However, the advantages are much greater than the drawbacks. Extracurricular activities teach responsibility, create meaningful friendships, and help students discover abilities that may not appear in a regular classroom.

To begin with, activities outside the classroom help students become more responsible and manage their time better. Whether students join a sports team, work on the yearbook, or serve on student council, they have to balance meetings, practices, deadlines, and homework. This can be challenging at first, but it encourages students to plan ahead. For example, a student with soccer practice three afternoons each week cannot wait until the night before an essay is due to begin writing it. That student may start using a planner, setting priorities, and finishing assignments earlier. These skills are useful far beyond high school because college, jobs, and adult life all require people to manage busy schedules.

Extracurricular activities also give students a stronger sense of belonging. In many classes, students spend most of their time listening to a teacher or working independently. Clubs and teams, on the other hand, give them more chances to cooperate with others. Students on the yearbook staff may interview classmates, take photographs at school events, and work together to meet publication deadlines. Student council members learn how to share ideas, listen to opposing opinions, and speak in front of groups. Athletes must communicate with teammates and support one another during games.

For students who are shy or new to a school, even one activity can make a major difference. A club can feel like a smaller community within a large building. In addition, extracurricular activities allow students to explore interests and talents that traditional classes may not reveal. For instance, a student who joins the school newspaper might discover a love of writing and decide to study journalism in college. Without the requirement, that student might never take the first step.

Critics are right that students already have busy schedules, and activities should not become another source of pressure. Still, this concern can be addressed if schools offer many choices. Students should not all be forced into sports or one particular club. Schools can provide options such as art clubs, academic teams, volunteer groups, music programs, athletics, and student government. With enough variety, most students can find an activity that fits both their interests and their schedule.

Overall, requiring students to join at least one extracurricular activity is a smart decision. It teaches responsibility, builds friendships, strengthens the school community, and helps students uncover new interests. Extracurricular activities are not simply optional extras; they are an important part of a complete education.

The Road Ahead: Why Driverless Cars Deserve Development

Every year, countless lives are lost on roads because of mistakes that a machine might never make. In "Driverless Cars Are Coming," the author weighs the promise of autonomous vehicles against their real risks. Although the technology faces serious obstacles, the potential to save lives, expand independence, and reduce waste makes continued development of driverless cars the right choice.

The strongest argument for these vehicles is safety. According to the article, human error causes over 90 percent of traffic accidents, often because drivers are texting, drowsy, or impaired. A computer does not get tired, drink alcohol, or glance at a phone. Driverless cars rely on laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors to detect obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals, giving them constant awareness of their surroundings. If these systems can eliminate even a portion of the crashes caused by human failings, thousands of injuries and deaths could be prevented each year. Fewer crashes would also lower insurance costs, benefiting ordinary families.

Driverless cars also offer a level of freedom that many people currently lack. The article notes that autonomous vehicles could provide mobility for elderly or disabled passengers who cannot safely drive. For someone who has lost the ability to drive, a self-driving car could mean attending medical appointments, visiting friends, and shopping without depending on others. That independence is a powerful human benefit that justifies research and investment.

Furthermore, Google cofounder Sergey Brin envisions a future of driverless public transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. In a world where cities struggle with congestion, pollution, and crowded parking lots, such efficiency would be transformative. If fewer people need to own cars, communities could reclaim land now devoted to parking and reduce energy consumption.

Critics raise legitimate concerns, and they should not be dismissed. Current sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or unmarked construction zones, and software remains vulnerable to glitches and cybersecurity threats. The article also warns that passengers in semi-autonomous cars quickly lose focus, slowing their reaction times when they must take over in an emergency. Finally, it is unclear who should be legally responsible after an accident: the owner, the software developer, or the automaker. These problems are serious, but they are challenges of an unfinished technology, not reasons to abandon it. Weather limitations can be addressed through better sensors and testing. Security flaws can be reduced through rigorous standards. The problem of distracted semi-autonomous drivers suggests that developers should aim for fully autonomous systems that do not depend on human backup. And legal questions are exactly the kind that lawmakers and courts can resolve through new regulations, just as they adapted to earlier inventions like the automobile itself.

Stopping development now would also mean accepting the dangers of the current system, in which human error continues to kill people every day. Responsible development, with thorough testing and clear laws, allows society to address the weaknesses while moving toward the benefits.

In conclusion, driverless cars present real technical, ethical, and legal challenges, but their potential advantages outweigh these concerns. They could dramatically reduce crashes, help elderly and disabled people live independently, and make transportation more efficient. Rather than turning back, we should proceed carefully, solve the remaining problems, and work toward a safer future on the road.

Dear Principal,

I believe the school should adopt Policy 1, which allows students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times, while requiring them to be turned off during class. This policy recognizes that phones are an important part of modern life without allowing them to interfere with learning. A complete ban would be difficult to enforce, inconvenient for families, and less fair to responsible students.

First, phones can improve student safety and communication. Many students ride buses, walk home, participate in after-school activities, or have changing transportation plans. If a practice is canceled, a parent is running late, or an emergency occurs, students should be able to contact their families quickly. Although the school office can help in some situations, it may not always be available immediately, especially after school. Allowing phones to remain in students’ backpacks during class gives families peace of mind while still protecting instructional time.

Second, Policy 1 helps students learn responsibility. In the real world, people must manage distractions at work, in college, and in public places. Students should practice making responsible choices rather than having every possible distraction removed. A policy that requires phones to be off during class teaches students that there is an appropriate time for technology and an appropriate time to focus. If a student breaks the rule by using a phone in class, the school can apply a clear consequence, such as temporarily confiscating the device or contacting a parent. This approach holds students accountable for their behavior without punishing everyone for the mistakes of a few.

In addition, phones can be useful during free time. Students may use them to check schedules, communicate with parents, listen to music with headphones, read, or organize assignments. Some students also use phones to look up information for schoolwork or access digital planners. Lunch and other breaks are meant to give students time to relax and manage personal needs. Responsible phone use during these periods would not reduce class learning because it would occur outside instructional time.

Supporters of a total ban may argue that phones cause distractions, cyberbullying, or rule violations. These concerns are real, but banning phones completely will not eliminate them. Students may still find ways to bring phones secretly, making enforcement more difficult and creating unnecessary conflict between students and staff. A better solution is to establish clear expectations: phones must be silent and put away during class, may not be used to photograph or record others without permission, and may be used only during designated free periods. Clear rules and consistent consequences can address misuse more effectively than an unrealistic ban.

For these reasons, Policy 1 is the better choice. It protects class time, supports safety, and teaches students responsibility. By allowing phones only during lunch and other free times, the school can balance the benefits of technology with the need for a focused learning environment.

Summer projects should be student-designed, though within a framework that teachers set. The purpose of a summer assignment is to keep a young mind working while the structure of school is absent, and nothing sustains effort in that vacuum as reliably as genuine interest. A teacher can hand out a worksheet packet or a required reading list, but no teacher can make a fifteen-year-old care in July. A student who has chosen the question to pursue is far more likely to keep going when the beach, a part-time job, or a video game offers easier pleasures.

Consider the typical teacher-designed project. Every student in a ninth-grade biology class receives the same prompt: build a poster on a cell organelle, or read a single novel and answer ten questions. Some students find this tolerable. Many finish it on the last weekend of August, copying from the internet in a rush, and retain almost nothing by October. The assignment measures compliance rather than learning. It also treats a room of very different people as one, ignoring the girl who already knows the material cold and the boy who never quite understood last year's unit.

Now imagine the same biology class under a different arrangement. A student who spends her weekends at a dog shelter proposes to track how diet changes affect the energy and coat condition of the animals there. Another, who loves baseball, wants to analyze whether pitch velocity declines over a season and why. A third, hesitant and unsure, decides to teach herself basic coding by building a small program that sorts her family's recipes. None of these ideas appears on a standard syllabus, yet each requires research, planning, written reflection, and sustained effort. They also reveal something a uniform assignment never could: how a student thinks when no one is dictating the terms.

Critics have a fair point, though. Left entirely alone, some students will choose projects that are too easy, too vague, or too ambitious to finish. Others, especially those without much guidance at home, may not know where to begin. Total freedom can quietly favor the already confident. That is why teachers still matter. They should set the boundaries: a required length of work, a proposal due before school lets out, a few check-ins by email, and clear criteria for what a finished project must show. A teacher might say, "Pick any topic connected to our science curriculum, show me your method, and present your findings in September." This keeps standards intact while leaving the real decision, what to explore, in the student's hands.

The proposal stage itself teaches a valuable skill. Deciding what is worth studying, and how to study it, is much of what real researchers, engineers, and writers do. Students rarely get to practice it, because school usually supplies the questions ahead of time. A summer project is one of the few chances to reverse that, since the stakes are low and the calendar is long.

There is also the matter of what students carry back into the classroom. A teacher-designed project returns as a stack of near-identical papers, graded and forgotten. Student-designed projects return as varied, sometimes surprising presentations that classmates actually want to hear. That exchange of curiosity can set a stronger tone for the new year than any review unit.

Summer learning should feel like something a student chose, not something done to them. Teachers should supply the guardrails, and students should pick the road.

Dear Principal,

I believe students should be required to perform community service, as long as the requirement is reasonable and flexible. A small amount of service each year would help students understand the needs of others, strengthen our school's relationship with the community, and teach skills that are hard to learn in a classroom.

To begin with, community service reminds students that they belong to something larger than their own schedules. It is easy to get caught up in homework, sports, jobs, and friends, but many people nearby need help. Elementary students may need tutors, elderly residents may need someone to carry their groceries, and local parks always need volunteers to pick up litter. When students take part in these activities, they see problems firsthand instead of just hearing about them. A student who spends an afternoon tutoring a younger child, for example, may realize how much patience and encouragement can build that child's confidence. That kind of experience can make an older student more caring and responsible.

Service can also benefit the town and improve our school's reputation. If students organize a neighborhood cleanup, collect food for a shelter, or volunteer at the library, community members will see the school making a positive contribution. In return, local organizations may be more willing to support school events, internships, or scholarships. Service does not have to mean one enormous project, either. Several small efforts, like cleaning a playground or helping at a community garden, can still make a visible difference.

Required service also teaches practical life skills. Students learn to talk with people of different ages, work as a team, solve unexpected problems, and manage their time, all of which colleges and employers value. Someone helping at an animal shelter might learn to follow directions carefully and cooperate with other volunteers. A student who tutors children might grow more comfortable speaking in front of a group. These lessons stick because they come from real responsibility.

I understand that some students worry service would take time away from schoolwork, family obligations, or paying jobs. That is a fair concern, and it is the reason the requirement should not be excessive. The school could ask for a manageable number of hours each semester and offer plenty of choices, such as weekend projects, service on campus, or opportunities close to home. Students with heavy work or family duties could request alternatives or extensions. A flexible program would make service possible without placing an unfair burden on anyone.

Requiring community service does not mean asking students to give up everything they enjoy. It means encouraging each of us to spend a small part of our time helping others and improving the place where we live. With a fair and flexible requirement, our school can help students become not only better learners but also more thoughtful and responsible citizens.

Sincerely,  
A Concerned Student

Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge you to support electing the president by national popular vote. The Electoral College began as a constitutional compromise, but today it does not give every citizen's vote equal weight. The president should be the candidate chosen by the most American voters, not the one who assembles the right combination of states.

According to the Office of the Federal Register, each state receives a number of electors equal to its House members plus its two senators. Because every state gets those two senatorial electors no matter how many people live there, a voter in a small state has more influence than a voter in a large one. The winner-take-all rule, used by forty-eight states, adds to the problem. A candidate who carries a state by a razor-thin margin still collects all of its electoral votes, and the millions of ballots cast for the runner-up do nothing to change the state's outcome.

This system can also produce results that contradict the will of the national electorate. Bradford Plumer points out that candidates won the popular vote but lost the presidency in both 2000 and 2016. Outcomes like these erode public trust, since most citizens reasonably expect the candidate with the most votes to win. A national popular vote would count every ballot the same, whether it was cast in a rural town, a big city, or a state that reliably favors one party.

The current system also shapes how campaigns are run. Since most states are safely Democratic or Republican, candidates spend their time, money, and promises on a handful of competitive "swing states." Plumer argues that this leaves voters elsewhere ignored and may depress turnout. A person in a dependably red or blue state can easily conclude that a presidential vote hardly matters when the statewide result seems settled. Under a popular vote, candidates would have a reason to look for support everywhere, and a Republican vote in California or a Democratic vote in Texas would be worth as much as any other.

Defenders of the Electoral College, such as Judge Richard A. Posner, contend that it protects federalism and forces candidates to build broad coalitions instead of piling up votes in crowded cities or a single region. They also say it delivers a quick, clear winner and confines recounts to individual states. These are serious points, and I do not dismiss them. Still, a national popular vote would continue to reward candidates who appeal to voters across the country. Even the largest cities hold only a fraction of the population, so no candidate could win by relying on urban areas alone. Suburban, rural, and small-town voters would remain essential. As for recounts, clear rules, audits, and well-planned recount procedures could handle a close national result without keeping a system in which the popular-vote winner can lose.

The Electoral College may have suited the needs of an earlier era, but a modern democracy should be built on political equality. I hope you will support reforms that move the United States toward choosing its president by national popular vote. Every citizen's vote should count equally, and the candidate who earns the most votes should lead the country.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Constituent

My principal recently announced that every student must take part in at least one extracurricular activity, such as a sport, yearbook, or student council. The idea has sparked debate among students, teachers, and parents. Although some people believe this requirement will help students grow, I disagree. Requiring extracurricular participation may do more harm than good, and it does not fit every student.

To begin with, adding an extracurricular activity to an already full schedule can create unnecessary stress. Many students already juggle demanding classes, homework, and test preparation, so squeezing in another commitment can feel overwhelming. For example, a student who is struggling in math or science may have trouble balancing extra practice or tutoring with the time required by a club or team. As a result, their grades could slip, which might hurt their future opportunities. Additionally, not every student enjoys traditional options like sports or student government. Forcing them into activities they do not care about can lead to frustration and resentment rather than personal growth.

Another problem is that the requirement may overlook students' individual interests and talents. Some students thrive in athletics or leadership roles, but others are passionate about art, music, coding, or independent projects that do not fit neatly into the school's existing extracurricular menu. A talented painter, for instance, may have few chances to explore that interest if the school only promotes conventional clubs and teams. When students are pushed toward a narrow set of activities, the school may accidentally ignore the wide range of abilities and passions in its own hallways. This can leave students feeling unmotivated and disconnected because their strengths are not recognized or supported.

The mandate could also create an uneven playing field. Students from wealthier families often have better access to private coaching, equipment, transportation, and other resources, which can give them a clear advantage in competitive activities. A student who cannot afford specialty gear or extra training might be less likely to succeed in sports, even if they work hard. In this way, requiring everyone to participate may deepen existing social and economic inequalities instead of reducing them.

In conclusion, I understand that the principal wants to encourage student development and school spirit. However, making extracurricular activities mandatory can add stress, ignore individual interests, and widen gaps between students. Rather than forcing participation, the school should offer a wider variety of activities and make them more accessible to all students. This approach would create a more inclusive environment where students can pursue what they genuinely enjoy, without unnecessary pressure. Ultimately, students are more likely to grow and feel connected to their school when they choose activities that match their own goals and passions.

Dear Senator,

As our country continues to debate the best way to elect our president, I wanted to take a moment to share my thoughts on the Electoral College. After researching the topic and considering different perspectives, I believe that the Electoral College should be kept in place. While some argue that it is undemocratic and outdated, I think it plays a crucial role in preserving federalism and ensuring that our president is elected through a broad national coalition.

One of the main criticisms of the Electoral College is that it can lead to a situation where the winner of the popular vote does not win the presidency. This happened in 2000 and 2016, and it can be frustrating for voters who feel that their voices are not being heard. However, as Judge Richard A. Posner points out, the Electoral College prevents candidates from winning solely by running up massive vote totals in densely populated urban areas or single regions. This means that candidates must build a broad coalition of support across multiple states, rather than just focusing on one area. I think this is an important aspect of our electoral system, as it ensures that our president is elected through a national campaign, rather than just a regional one.

Another argument against the Electoral College is that it can lead to "faithless electors" who vote against their state's popular choice. While this is a theoretical possibility, I do not think it is a strong enough reason to abolish the Electoral College. As the Office of the Federal Register notes, the Electoral College is a process, not a place, and it has been established in the Constitution as a compromise between election of the president by Congress and election by popular vote. I think it is unlikely that faithless electors would be able to significantly alter the outcome of an election, and I do not think it is a reason to get rid of the entire system.

On the other hand, I think the benefits of the Electoral College far outweigh its drawbacks. For example, it produces a clear, decisive winner quickly, and avoids the chaos of a nationwide popular-vote recount. As Judge Posner notes, any disputed vote recounts would be confined to individual states, rather than having to be conducted nationwide. This makes the electoral process much more efficient and reliable. Additionally, the Electoral College ensures that smaller states have a voice in the election process, rather than being overshadowed by larger states with more population.

Some argue that the Electoral College is undemocratic because it can lead to a situation where a candidate wins the presidency without winning the popular vote. However, I think this argument is based on a flawed assumption that the popular vote is the only measure of a candidate's legitimacy. As Bradford Plumer notes, the winner-take-all system in most states can lead to a situation where voters in safely Democratic or Republican states feel like their votes do not matter. However, I think this is a problem with the way we allocate electoral votes, rather than a problem with the Electoral College itself. Perhaps we could consider allocating electoral votes proportionally, like Maine and Nebraska do, to give voters in all states a greater sense of engagement and participation in the electoral process.

In conclusion, while I understand the criticisms of the Electoral College, I believe that it plays a vital role in our electoral system. It preserves federalism, ensures that our president is elected through a broad national coalition, and produces a clear, decisive winner quickly. Rather than abolishing the Electoral College, I think we should consider reforms that would make it more representative and inclusive of all voters. Thank you for taking the time to consider my thoughts on this important issue.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

After thinking about the two proposed cell phone policies, I believe Policy 1 is the stronger choice. Allowing students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and free periods strikes a fair balance: it gives us a chance to stay connected without letting phones disrupt class.

One reason I support Policy 1 is that it reflects how many of us already manage our daily lives. Students use their phones to check in with parents, coordinate schedules, and look up information. When we can use them during lunch or free time, we stay organized while still keeping class time focused. This policy also shows trust in students, and being trusted often makes people more likely to act responsibly.

Policy 1 is also better preparation for the future. In college and most jobs, people are expected to handle their own phone use without strict bans. They have to learn when it is appropriate to check a message and when they need to concentrate. Giving students practice with that balance now helps develop self-regulation, time management, and good judgment. On the other hand, completely banning phones, as Policy 2 does, might not teach those skills.

Another important point is safety and well-being. Having a phone available lets students contact a parent or guardian quickly in an emergency. During free periods, phones can also help students who feel anxious or left out connect with a friend or family member for support. That access can make school feel a little less isolating for some students.

I understand the concern that phones might become a distraction. However, this can be handled with clear rules and consistent consequences. Teachers can remind students to turn phones off or put them away during class, and students who misuse the privilege can lose it. By setting expectations and following through, the school can reduce distractions while still allowing the benefits of phone use.

Summer projects should be primarily student-designed, with teachers offering guidance and clear academic expectations. A break from school does not have to mean a break from learning, but students are more likely to learn deeply when they have some control over what they investigate. Instead of assigning every student the same packet of reading questions or research report, schools should let students build projects around their interests, communities, and goals.

Choice makes a major difference in motivation. A student who is fascinated by animals may be willing to spend weeks observing birds in a local park, keeping a journal of migration patterns, and researching habitat loss. Another student might prefer to interview grandparents about family history, create a short documentary, or design a budget for a small business idea. Each project can develop important skills such as research, writing, organization, and problem-solving, yet the work feels less like an extension of homework. During summer, when students have fewer schedules and deadlines, curiosity can become a stronger teacher than pressure.

Student-designed projects also recognize that young people do not all have the same summer experiences. One student may travel, attend camp, or have access to museums and libraries. Another may work a part-time job, care for siblings, or remain close to home. A teacher-designed assignment can accidentally assume that every family has the same resources. For example, requiring a visit to several historical sites may be easy for a student with transportation and money but difficult for someone whose parents work long hours. If students can design their own projects, they can choose realistic topics and materials. A student working at a grocery store could study food waste or track pricing changes, turning an ordinary responsibility into a meaningful investigation.

This approach does not mean teachers should simply tell students, “Do anything you want.” Complete freedom can be confusing, especially for students who have not yet learned how to plan a long-term project. Teachers should provide a structure: a proposal due before summer, a list of possible formats, checkpoints, and a rubric that emphasizes effort, reflection, evidence, and presentation. They might require students to ask a question, use at least two reliable sources, create a final product, and explain what they learned. Such guidelines preserve academic value without forcing every student into the same topic.

Teacher-designed projects can be useful when a class needs to practice a particular skill, such as reading a shared novel before an advanced course. However, these assignments should be limited and flexible. A long uniform project often becomes a task to finish quickly rather than an opportunity to grow. Students may search for answers online, copy a summary, or wait until the last days of August because the assignment has no personal meaning.

The best summer learning connects school to real life. When students design projects with teacher support, they practice independence while discovering that learning can happen in gardens, workplaces, kitchens, libraries, and neighborhoods. That lesson may last much longer than any worksheet completed over vacation.

Drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle because driving requires full attention. Cell phones are useful for communication, directions, music, and emergencies, but none of those uses are more important than keeping people safe on the road. Even when a driver thinks they are only looking away for a second, that second can be enough time to miss a stopped car, a pedestrian, or a changing traffic light.

Many people believe hands-free phones are safe because the driver is not holding the phone. However, the biggest problem is not only having one hand off the wheel. It is also mental distraction. When someone is talking on the phone, listening to a complicated message, or trying to follow a GPS instruction, their mind is partly focused somewhere else. They may still have both eyes on the road, but they may react more slowly because they are thinking about the conversation instead of what is happening around them. Driving is not something people should do halfway.

Texting is especially dangerous because it takes a driver’s eyes, hands, and attention away from driving at the same time. A car can travel a long distance in only a few seconds. If a driver looks down to answer “okay” or check a notification, the car could move across an intersection or toward another vehicle without the driver noticing. This can hurt not only the driver, but also passengers, cyclists, pedestrians, and other families on the road.

Some people argue that phones are needed for GPS. Maps can be helpful, especially when someone is driving somewhere unfamiliar. Still, drivers can set up directions before they start the car. They can also pull over safely if they need to change the destination or look at the map. The same idea applies to changing music, checking a message, or making a call. None of those things need to happen while the vehicle is moving. Waiting a few minutes is a small inconvenience compared to causing a crash.

Emergency situations are the one major exception people might bring up. If someone sees an accident or has a medical emergency, calling for help is important. However, if possible, the driver should pull over first or ask a passenger to make the call. In a serious emergency, a driver still needs to control the vehicle safely instead of creating another dangerous situation.

Overall, drivers should keep their cell phones away while operating a vehicle. Phones are a normal part of everyday life, but they should not control someone’s attention behind the wheel. A text, call, song, or notification can always wait until the car is parked. Safety should come before convenience because one distracted moment can change someone’s life forever.

Driverless cars should continue to be developed because they could make transportation safer, more efficient, and more accessible. Autonomous vehicles still face real technological and legal problems, but the potential benefits are too important to ignore. Instead of giving up on the idea because of today's risks, companies and governments should test and regulate these cars carefully until they are ready for everyday use.

The best reason to support driverless cars is that they could save lives. The article points out that human error causes more than 90 percent of traffic accidents. People text while driving, nod off at the wheel, speed, or get behind the wheel after drinking. A computer never gets sleepy, checks a phone, or decides it is fine to drive after a few drinks. Driverless cars rely on laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors to spot obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals. With enough improvement and testing, these systems could react more consistently than many human drivers. Fewer crashes would mean fewer injuries and deaths, and it could also bring lower insurance costs for families.

These vehicles could also help people who have trouble driving on their own. Elderly people may have to stop driving when their vision declines or their reaction times slow down. People with disabilities often face transportation barriers that limit their independence. A dependable driverless car could let them get to work, doctor's appointments, stores, or a friend's house without having to ask someone else for a ride. For many of these people, that kind of freedom would noticeably improve daily life.

Driverless transportation might also cut down on fuel use and parking space. Google cofounder Sergey Brin imagines a future where driverless public transportation uses half the fuel and half the parking space that today's cars require. If fewer people felt the need to own a car, communities could turn parking lots into parks, housing, or businesses. Shared autonomous vehicles could also reduce the waste of cars that sit idle for most of the day.

Critics make a fair point that the technology is not ready to run without limits. The article notes that sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, and construction zones where lane markings are missing. Software can have glitches, and connected vehicles may be open to cybersecurity threats. It is also unclear who should be legally responsible when a driverless car is involved in an accident: the owner, the software developer, or the automaker. Still, these problems call for careful development rather than a complete rejection of the technology. Governments can demand strict safety testing, strong cybersecurity protections, and clear rules about responsibility. They can also introduce the cars gradually, starting in places where conditions are safest.

In the end, driverless cars deserve continued development because they could reduce accidents caused by people, give elderly and disabled passengers more independence, and create a more efficient transportation system. The dangers described in the article are serious, but testing, regulation, and steady improvement can address them. With responsible planning, driverless cars could become a valuable tool for making roads safer and transportation available to more people.

Why Seeking Multiple Opinions Leads to Better Choices

When facing an important decision, most people instinctively turn to someone they trust. A single trusted voice can be comforting, but it is rarely enough. Seeking several opinions helps a person make a better choice because it exposes blind spots, balances individual bias, and supplies a wider range of knowledge. The extra effort is a small price for a decision that may shape years of someone's life.

First, every advisor has blind spots, and different advisors have different ones. Consider a high school senior deciding between a large state university and a small private college. A parent might emphasize cost and job prospects, since those are natural concerns for someone who will help pay the bills. A school counselor might point out graduation rates and how well each school supports students in the student's intended major. A recent graduate of one of the schools could describe daily life, from class sizes to how easy it is to meet professors. No single person would raise all of these factors. Together, they give the student a fuller picture than any one conversation could.

Second, multiple opinions help balance personal bias. Advisors are shaped by their own experiences, preferences, and sometimes self-interest. A friend who dropped out of college and succeeded in business may downplay the value of a degree. A relative who struggled without one may insist it is essential. Neither is lying; both are drawing on the stories they know best. When a person hears both, the extremes tend to offset each other, and the decision-maker can look for the points on which the advisors agree. Self-interest matters too. A car salesperson recommending a particular model or a friend who does not want a roommate to move away may not give fully objective advice. Hearing from people with no stake in the outcome helps reveal when someone's advice is quietly serving their own needs.

Third, different people bring different kinds of expertise, and some decisions require several. Medicine offers a clear example. A patient diagnosed with a serious condition who gets a second opinion may learn about a less invasive treatment the first doctor did not mention, or may have the original diagnosis confirmed and proceed with greater confidence. Either result is valuable. In the first case, the patient avoids an unnecessary risk. In the second, the patient gains certainty and can commit to the plan without lingering doubt. Similarly, someone deciding whether to buy a house benefits from talking to a financial advisor about affordability, an inspector about the property's condition, and neighbors about the community. Each person answers a different question that the buyer might not have thought to ask.

Some might argue that too many opinions create confusion, and that is a fair concern. If advice conflicts, a person can feel more uncertain than before. But conflict is itself useful information. It signals that the decision involves real trade-offs, and it pushes the person to clarify his or her own priorities. The goal is not to follow the majority or to collect votes, but to gather perspectives and then weigh them thoughtfully. The final decision should still belong to the person who will live with it.

In conclusion, seeking multiple opinions strengthens decision-making by revealing blind spots, offsetting bias, and drawing on varied expertise. Whether choosing a school, a medical treatment, or a home, a person who listens widely is better prepared to see the whole situation. Good advice is valuable, but diverse advice, carefully considered, is far more likely to lead to a choice a person can trust.

Two afternoons a week at a robotics meeting or a rehearsal for the fall play gives the day a shape, and it gives students a reason to show up that has nothing to do with grades.

The strongest argument, I think, is what students learn in these settings that a classroom rarely teaches. In math class, you're graded alone. On the yearbook staff, if one person misses a deadline, forty pages stall, and everyone feels it. That kind of shared responsibility is hard to simulate in a lecture. A student who has to chase down photographs, negotiate layouts with a bossy co-editor, and finish by a printer's cutoff learns more about patience and accountability than a worksheet could ever deliver. The same goes for the soccer player who has to trust a teammate to cover the left side of the field.

Then there's the matter of belonging. Every school has students who slip through unnoticed: the quiet freshman who eats lunch at the edge of the cafeteria, the transfer who hasn't found anyone yet. Left to themselves, some of these kids never join anything, because walking into a room full of strangers is frightening. A requirement removes the burden of choosing to be brave. Once they're in the room, friendships tend to form almost automatically, because people who build a set or march in formation together have something to talk about. I have seen a shy classmate of mine become the loudest voice on the debate team within a semester, and I doubt she would have signed up voluntarily.

Critics will say that forcing participation defeats the purpose, since an activity chosen under pressure won't be enjoyed. There's some truth in that, and it's why the variety matters. If the only options were football and chorus, the policy would fail. But a school that also offers chess club, community gardening, a tutoring program, a film society, and a service group can match nearly any temperament. Students who resent the rule at first often discover they like the activity anyway; plenty of people only learn what they enjoy by trying it.

Others worry about time, especially for students who work after school or care for younger siblings. That concern is legitimate, and the policy should account for it. Flexible options, such as lunchtime clubs, weekend volunteering, or credit for a job or family responsibilities, would keep the rule fair without gutting its purpose.

Ultimately, school is supposed to prepare young people for more than tests. It should help them figure out what they're good at, who they enjoy working with, and what they might care about for the rest of their lives. A required activity, offered with real variety and reasonable flexibility, nudges every student toward those discoveries. A small push now seems a fair price for the confidence, friendships, and skills that follow.

The debate surrounding summer projects has sparked intense discussion among educators, with some advocating for teacher-designed assignments and others championing student-designed initiatives. While both approaches have their merits, I firmly believe that student-designed summer projects are more effective in fostering a love of learning and promoting academic growth. When students are given the autonomy to design their own projects, they are more likely to be invested in the learning process, as they are able to explore topics that genuinely interest them.

This approach allows students to take ownership of their learning, which is essential for developing a sense of agency and motivation. For instance, a student who is passionate about environmental conservation might design a project that involves researching and implementing sustainable practices in their community. This kind of project not only deepens their understanding of the subject matter but also enables them to make a tangible impact, thereby cultivating a sense of purpose and fulfillment. In contrast, teacher-designed projects can sometimes feel arbitrary or disconnected from students' lives, leading to a lack of engagement and enthusiasm.

Moreover, student-designed projects encourage creativity, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills, all of which are essential for success in the 21st century. When students are given the freedom to design their own projects, they must navigate complex challenges, think outside the box, and develop innovative solutions. For example, a student who wants to explore the intersection of art and technology might design a project that involves creating digital art installations or developing a mobile app that showcases local artists' work. This kind of project requires students to think creatively, collaborate with others, and adapt to new technologies, all of which are vital skills in today's fast-paced, interconnected world.

Another significant advantage of student-designed projects is that they allow for more nuanced and personalized learning experiences. Every student has unique strengths, weaknesses, and learning styles, and teacher-designed projects can sometimes fail to account for these differences. By giving students the autonomy to design their own projects, educators can cater to diverse learning needs and abilities, ensuring that each student is able to learn and grow at their own pace. For instance, a student who struggles with traditional classroom assignments might thrive when given the opportunity to design a project that incorporates hands-on learning, visual arts, or community engagement.

While some might argue that student-designed projects lack structure and accountability, I would counter that these concerns can be mitigated through careful guidance and mentorship. Teachers can provide students with clear guidelines, resources, and support, helping them to develop a clear plan, set achievable goals, and track their progress. Regular check-ins and feedback sessions can also help to ensure that students stay on track and produce high-quality work. Ultimately, the benefits of student-designed summer projects far outweigh the potential drawbacks, as they offer students a unique opportunity to take ownership of their learning, cultivate essential skills, and explore their passions in a meaningful and impactful way. By embracing this approach, educators can help students develop a love of learning that extends far beyond the classroom, preparing them for success in an increasingly complex and rapidly changing world.

I am writing because I heard about the possible change that would require students to have at least a B average to play sports or join clubs. I strongly disagree with this policy, and I want to explain why from a student’s point of view.

First, a C average is not failing. It means a student is passing all their classes and understands the material, just maybe not perfectly. If someone is doing okay but not great, should we really take away the one thing that might be helping them stay focused? I know students who work really hard just to keep a C in math or science. They’re not lazy; they’re trying. If they can’t play basketball or be in the band, some of them will probably stop trying altogether because they’ll feel like school has nothing for them.

Second, activities teach things you can’t learn from a textbook. Being on a team or in a club teaches responsibility, showing up on time, working with people you don’t always like, and handling losing or making mistakes. Those are exactly the skills that can help someone improve in class. If we only let B-average students participate, we’re saying those lessons are a reward instead of a tool. That seems backwards.

Another problem is that grades aren’t always a fair measure of effort or ability. Some students have learning disabilities, anxiety, or family situations that make a B really hard even when they’re doing their best. A friend of mine has dyslexia and works twice as long on homework as I do, but she still gets C’s in English. She’s also one of the most dedicated members of the drama club. Taking that away from her wouldn’t make her a better reader; it would just take away the one place where she feels confident.

I also think this policy could hurt the activities themselves. If you cut out everyone with a C average, you might lose some of your best athletes, musicians, and leaders. A student who is average in class might be an amazing point guard or a great stage manager. The school would be weaker without them.

Instead of a strict B cutoff, maybe the school could require students with C’s to attend tutoring or a study hall a few times a week while still letting them participate. That way, they get support without losing the activity that keeps them motivated. Or there could be a probation period where students need to show improvement, not perfection.

Please consider the students who are trying hard but just can’t hit a B in every class. We shouldn’t be pushed out of the things that make school worth coming to.

Sincerely,
[Student name]

Driverless Cars: A Future Worth Pursuing

Imagine a world where no one dies because a driver was texting, falling asleep, or drunk behind the wheel. Driverless cars promise that kind of future, and although they come with real challenges, the technology should continue to be developed. According to the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," autonomous vehicles could save lives, reduce waste, and expand freedom for people who currently cannot drive. The problems the article raises are serious, but they are problems to be solved through further development, not reasons to stop.

The strongest argument for driverless cars is safety. The article notes that human error causes over 90 percent of traffic accidents, often because of texting, drowsiness, or impaired driving. These are failures of attention and judgment that a computer does not share. A car equipped with laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors can monitor obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals constantly, without getting tired or distracted. If such vehicles replace even a portion of human drivers, the number of crashes could drop dramatically, saving lives and lowering insurance costs for everyone.

Driverless cars also offer benefits beyond safety. The article describes Google cofounder Sergey Brin's vision of driverless public transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. In crowded cities, where parking lots consume valuable land, and where fuel use contributes to pollution, that kind of efficiency would be a major improvement. In addition, autonomous vehicles could provide mobility for elderly or disabled passengers who now depend on others to get around. For these people, a driverless car means independence, which is a benefit that cannot be measured only in dollars.

Critics raise legitimate concerns, and the article presents them fairly. Current sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or unmarked construction zones. Software can be vulnerable to glitches and cybersecurity threats. Semi-autonomous systems also require human drivers to stay alert, yet studies show that people lose focus quickly once a computer is driving. Finally, it is unclear who should be legally responsible after an accident: the owner, the software developer, or the automaker.

However, each of these concerns points to work that remains to be done rather than to a flaw that cannot be fixed. Sensor limitations in bad weather are technical problems, and technology tends to improve with testing and investment. Halting development would only delay those improvements. The concern about distracted human backups actually supports moving toward fully autonomous systems, since the danger comes from asking humans to monitor a machine, not from the machine itself. Cybersecurity risks already exist in many technologies we rely on, such as banking and air travel, and we manage them through constant updates and strong regulation. The legal questions, though difficult, can be settled by lawmakers who create clear rules for liability, just as laws adapted to earlier inventions like the automobile itself.

Continuing development is also the only way to find these problems before the cars are widely used. Testing under careful supervision allows engineers to discover weaknesses in rain, snow, and construction zones and to correct them. Abandoning the technology now would leave us with the known dangers of human driving, which already cause the overwhelming majority of crashes.

In conclusion, driverless cars should be developed. Their potential to prevent accidents, save fuel and space, and give independence to elderly and disabled people outweighs the obstacles described in the article. Those obstacles are real, and they demand caution, strong safety standards, and thoughtful laws. But they are challenges to overcome, not reasons to give up on a technology that could make our roads safer and our lives easier.

Almost everywhere you look today, people have their phones out. We use them for everything: texting friends, listening to music, checking grades, and scrolling through social media. Because smartphones are such a big part of daily life, it feels natural to check them whenever a notification pings. However, when a person gets behind the wheel of a car, the phone should be put away completely. Drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle because driving requires total attention, and any distraction can easily cause a fatal crash.

The most obvious reason cell phones should be banned while driving is the physical distraction. When drivers look down at a screen to read a text or skip a song, their eyes are not on the road. Teachers and driving instructors often mention that looking at your phone for just five seconds while going 55 miles per hour is like driving the entire length of a football field with your eyes closed. That is a terrifying thought. I see this happen all the time when I am riding in the car with my parents or walking across the street near my school. You will see someone drift into another lane or sit through a green light because their head is tilted down toward their lap. If a kid ran into the road or a car stopped suddenly, a distracted driver would not have time to react.

Some people might argue that hands-free features make it okay to talk on the phone, but that is still dangerous. Even if a driver's hands are on the steering wheel, their mind is somewhere else. Cognitive distraction is a real problem. When you are deep in a phone conversation, your brain is picturing the person you are talking to and processing what they are saying, instead of scanning the road for hazards. It is different from talking to a passenger because a passenger can see traffic and will naturally stop talking if things get intense or dangerous. A person on the other end of a phone call has no idea what is happening on the road.

People also argue that they need their phones for navigation.

That is a small change, but it shows that service can change how we see our own neighborhood.

That is why I think the school should require a small number of hours, like fifteen or twenty per year, and let students choose how to complete them. They could tutor, clean up litter, help at an animal shelter, or assist teachers after school. If students can pick something they care about, it feels less like a punishment. I am writing to share my opinion about the cell phone policy. I think Policy 1 is the better choice. Students should be allowed to bring phones to school and use them at lunch and during free times, as long as the phones are turned off during class. I believe this policy is fair, realistic, and safer for students.

First, phones are important for safety and emergencies. If something happens at school or on the way home, students need a way to reach their parents quickly. For example, if a bus is late or a practice gets canceled, a student can call or text a parent instead of waiting around with no way to get a ride. Some students also have medical problems, and their families want to be able to contact them. If phones are banned completely, students would have to go to the office and ask to use the school phone, which takes time and could be a big problem in a real emergency.

Second, Policy 1 still protects class time. The main worry about phones is that they distract students from learning, and I understand that. Nobody wants to be texting while the teacher is explaining something. But Policy 1 already says phones have to be turned off during class. That solves most of the problem. If a student breaks the rule, the teacher can take the phone and the student can get a consequence. This teaches students to follow rules and make good choices instead of just removing the temptation completely.

Third, a total ban would be really hard to enforce. Many students would still sneak their phones in, and teachers would spend a lot of time looking for them instead of teaching. That could make students and teachers frustrated with each other. When a rule is too strict, people look for ways around it. With Policy 1, students get something they want, so they are more likely to respect the rules about class time. It feels like a trade: we get our phones at lunch, and we keep them off when it matters.

Another reason is that lunch and free time are supposed to be a break. After sitting through several classes, students need time to relax. Some people listen to music, talk to friends, or call home.
