The widespread use of cell phones has become an integral part of daily life, with many individuals relying on them for communication, navigation, and entertainment. However, the use of cell phones while operating a vehicle has sparked a heated debate about safety and responsibility. As the majority of humans own and operate cell phones, the question arises whether drivers should be allowed to use them in any capacity while driving. In this essay, I will argue that drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle, as the risks associated with distracted driving far outweigh any potential benefits.

One of the primary concerns with using cell phones while driving is the significant increase in the risk of accidents. According to numerous studies, texting, browsing, or talking on a cell phone while driving can distract the driver, leading to a delayed reaction time, reduced situational awareness, and decreased control over the vehicle. This can result in devastating consequences, including collisions, injuries, and fatalities. In fact, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) reports that distracted driving is a leading cause of accidents, resulting in thousands of deaths and injuries each year. By allowing drivers to use cell phones, we are effectively putting the lives of not only the driver but also their passengers, pedestrians, and other road users at risk.

Furthermore, the argument that hands-free devices or voice-activated systems are safer alternatives is misguided. While these technologies may reduce the physical distraction of holding a phone or typing a text, they still engage the driver's cognitive attention, diverting it away from the road. A study by the American Automobile Association (AAA) found that even with hands-free devices, drivers can experience a significant decline in reaction time and increase in crash risk. Moreover, the cognitive load of conversation, whether hands-free or not, can still impair a driver's ability to respond to unexpected events or changing road conditions.

Another argument against allowing cell phone use while driving is that it sets a bad precedent for responsible driving habits. If drivers are permitted to use their phones, even in limited capacities, it may create a culture of complacency, where drivers feel that it is acceptable to engage in other distracting activities, such as eating, grooming, or reading, while behind the wheel. This can lead to a normalization of distracted driving, further increasing the risk of accidents and undermining efforts to promote safe driving practices.

In conclusion, the use of cell phones while operating a vehicle poses a significant threat to road safety, and drivers should not be allowed to use them in any capacity while driving. The risks associated with distracted driving, including accidents, injuries, and fatalities, far outweigh any potential benefits of cell phone use. Instead, drivers should focus on the road, following safe driving practices and minimizing distractions to ensure the safety of themselves and others. By prohibiting cell phone use while driving, we can promote a culture of responsible driving, reduce the number of accidents, and save lives. Ultimately, the safety of our roads and the well-being of our communities depend on it.

Extracurricular activities can enrich a student's education, but schools should not require every student to join one. Sports teams, clubs, student government, and yearbook staffs offer real chances to make friends, build leadership skills, and grow as a person. Still, a mandatory rule ignores the very different responsibilities, interests, and needs of individual students. Schools should strongly encourage involvement, but students and families should be able to decide what is realistic and meaningful for them.

To begin with, many students already have serious obligations outside of school. Some work after classes to help support their families or save for college. Others look after younger siblings while their parents are at work. A student who spends several hours each evening babysitting may simply have no time for soccer practice, debate meetings, or play rehearsals. Forcing that student to join an activity would add stress instead of enjoyment. Rather than learning responsibility through a club, the student would be stuck choosing between family duties and a school rule.

Students also get the most out of activities when they pick them freely. A student who loves writing may thrive on the school newspaper, and another may feel proud to play in the band. Both put in more effort because the activity fits their interests. By contrast, a student pushed into a club just to satisfy a requirement may show up to meetings, say nothing, and contribute very little, which can make the experience worse for everyone else. Someone who dislikes public speaking, for example, might join student council only because it is convenient, and then feel no motivation to plan events or represent classmates. Required participation can turn something meant to build enthusiasm into one more assignment to finish.

Time is another concern. High school classes are already demanding, particularly for students in advanced courses or those preparing for major exams. If every student must squeeze an official activity into a packed schedule, some will lose sleep or see their grades slip. Free time is not wasted time. Students can use it to read, exercise, make art, help care for relatives, or follow interests the school does not offer. These pursuits can teach discipline and creativity just as well, even if they never appear on a club roster.

Instead of requiring participation, schools should make activities easier to reach and more appealing. They could offer a wider range of clubs, provide late buses for students who lack transportation, and recognize students who serve their communities outside school. Teachers can also explain the benefits of getting involved and help shy or undecided students find something they might enjoy. These steps would raise participation without punishing students whose circumstances are different.

Extracurricular activities are valuable, but they should remain opportunities rather than obligations. Students learn responsibility in many ways, both inside and outside the school building. If schools encourage involvement while respecting personal choices and family responsibilities, they can build a community where students take part because they want to, not because they have to.

Dear Senator,

As the debate surrounding the Electoral College continues to gain momentum, I am writing to express my support for preserving this fundamental aspect of our democratic process. While some argue that the Electoral College is undemocratic and outdated, I firmly believe that it plays a crucial role in ensuring that our president is elected through a fair and representative process. The Founding Fathers established the Electoral College as a compromise between election of the President by a vote in Congress and election of the President by a popular vote of qualified citizens, and it has been a cornerstone of our electoral system ever since.

One of the primary concerns raised by critics of the Electoral College is that it can lead to a situation where a candidate wins the national popular vote but loses the presidency, as happened in 2000 and 2016. However, this argument overlooks the fact that the Electoral College is designed to ensure that candidates build broad national coalitions, rather than simply focusing on densely populated urban areas or single regions. As Judge Richard A. Posner argues, the Electoral College preserves federalism and prevents candidates from winning solely by running up massive vote totals in specific areas. This encourages candidates to engage with voters across the country, rather than simply targeting specific demographics or regions.

Another criticism of the Electoral College is that it leads to a focus on "swing states" at the expense of voters in safely Democratic or Republican states. While it is true that presidential campaigns often focus on a handful of key states, this does not necessarily mean that voters in other states are being ignored. In fact, the Electoral College system ensures that candidates must build support across a range of states, rather than simply relying on a single region or demographic. Additionally, the fact that 48 states and Washington, D.C. use a "winner-take-all" system, while Maine and Nebraska allocate electors proportionally, adds a layer of complexity to the electoral process that helps to prevent any one state or region from dominating the outcome.

Some argue that the Electoral College is undemocratic because it can lead to a situation where "faithless electors" vote against their state's popular choice. However, this argument is based on a flawed assumption that the Electoral College is somehow less democratic than a popular vote system. In reality, the Electoral College is a carefully designed system that takes into account the unique characteristics and interests of each state. While it is true that "faithless electors" can theoretically vote against their state's popular choice, this is an extremely rare occurrence and is not a sufficient reason to abandon the Electoral College altogether.

In contrast to a popular vote system, which could lead to a candidate winning the presidency solely by running up massive vote totals in densely populated urban areas, the Electoral College ensures that candidates must build support across a range of states and regions. This helps to prevent the kind of regional or demographic polarization that can occur in a popular vote system, and ensures that our president is elected through a fair and representative process. As the Office of the Federal Register notes, the Electoral College consists of 538 electors, with a majority of 270 electoral votes required to elect the President. This system ensures that candidates must build broad support across the country, rather than simply relying on a single region or demographic.

In conclusion, while the Electoral College may have its flaws, I firmly believe that it is a vital component of our democratic process. Rather than abandoning the Electoral College in favor of a popular vote system, we should be working to improve and refine the existing system to ensure that it continues to serve the interests of all Americans. I urge you to consider the importance of preserving the Electoral College and to work towards finding solutions that will strengthen and improve our electoral process, rather than abandoning it altogether. By doing so, we can ensure that our democratic system remains fair, representative, and truly reflective of the will of the American people.

In the modern era, the smartphone has transformed from a luxury into a ubiquitous extension of human activity. It serves as a personal assistant, entertainment hub, and primary communication channel. However, as these devices have integrated into daily routines, they have increasingly encroached upon environments where intense focus is paramount. Operating a motor vehicle demands an individual’s undivided attention, quick reflexes, and constant situational awareness. Because of the profound risks posed by divided attention, drivers should be categorically prohibited from using cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

The most evident danger of mobile phone use behind the wheel is manual and visual distraction. Activities such as texting, selecting music, or holding a phone to talk require drivers to physically take their hands off the steering wheel and their eyes off the road. At highway speeds, taking one’s eyes off the road for merely four or five seconds is equivalent to driving the entire length of a football field blindfolded. In that brief window, pedestrian movements, sudden braking from a leading vehicle, or unexpected debris can transform an ordinary commute into a fatal collision. Empirical safety data consistently demonstrates that manual phone use dramatically elevates crash risks, making strict bans on handheld operation an obvious public safety imperative.

Nevertheless, an effective policy must extend beyond handheld devices to forbid hands-free use as well. Many motorists mistakenly assume that Bluetooth headsets, dashboard integrations, and voice-to-text systems eliminate the risks of mobile communication. Scientific research into cognitive psychology reveals that this is a dangerous misconception. The human brain does not possess the capacity to efficiently multitask two complex, high-demand processes simultaneously. Engaging in a phone conversation imposes a heavy cognitive load that competes directly with the mental resources needed to monitor traffic patterns and anticipate hazards. This phenomenon, known as inattentional blindness, causes drivers to look directly at obstacles without cognitively registering them. Unlike a passenger, who intuitively pauses conversation during challenging driving maneuvers or heavy traffic, a remote caller remains oblivious to the road conditions, continually drawing the driver’s cognitive focus away from safe operation.

Critics of total prohibition often argue that mobile connectivity is essential for modern logistics, particularly regarding real-time navigation. While navigation applications undoubtedly provide value, this utility does not justify interactive use while driving. Route mapping can and should be configured before a journey begins, allowing audio directions to guide the trip without necessitating manual adjustments or persistent visual monitoring. Furthermore, should an urgent call or message arise, the responsible recourse is simply to pull over in a safe parking area before engaging with the device. Personal convenience must never take precedence over collective roadway safety.

Operating a motor vehicle is not an isolated individual privilege; it is a shared public responsibility that carries inherent life-or-death consequences. Both handheld and hands-free cellular use degrade human reaction times and impair spatial judgment to a degree comparable to driving under the influence of alcohol. To preserve human life and establish a definitive, unambiguous standard of safety, society must adopt a zero-tolerance approach. Drivers should not be permitted to use cell phones in any capacity while their vehicles are in motion.

When facing a difficult choice, most people instinctively turn to someone they trust. While talking to a single person can be reassuring, relying entirely on one perspective has its drawbacks. Seeking advice from several people usually leads to better choices because it uncovers blind spots, reveals possibilities that might otherwise be overlooked, and helps a person recognize hidden bias.

To begin with, every adviser views a situation through the lens of their own background. No single person sees every side of a problem. Take a high school senior deciding between a large state university and a small private college. A parent will naturally focus on tuition, financial aid, and career prospects, since they are often helping pay the bills. A guidance counselor, on the other hand, might point toward graduation rates, program rankings, and academic support. Meanwhile, a recent graduate from one of those schools can share what the campus culture and daily student life are actually like. Each person offers a piece of the truth, but none of them provides the whole picture. Only by gathering all three viewpoints can the student balance financial, academic, and social realities instead of letting one factor dictate the outcome.

In addition, consulting more than one person often introduces options that never crossed the decision-maker's mind. Someone considering a job offer might see the situation as a simple binary: accept the position or turn it down. Yet if they talk to an experienced mentor, that mentor might recommend negotiating the salary or benefits. A friend working in the same field might suggest asking for a deferred start date so the applicant can complete a credential first. While one adviser often just answers the specific question they are asked, speaking to several people tends to reframe the problem entirely, opening doors to creative compromises.

Hearing different opinions also makes it far easier to spot personal bias. Everyone carries preferences, whether they realize it or not. A salesperson recommending a piece of technology might be thinking about a commission. A family member encouraging someone to stay close to home may simply be afraid of missing them, and a cautious friend might discourage an entrepreneurial idea purely out of their own fear of failure. When an individual only listens to one voice, these motives are difficult to detect. When three or four opinions are laid side by side, patterns become obvious. If almost everyone raises the same red flag, it is probably worth taking seriously; if only one person objects, that hesitation might just reflect personal preference rather than practical reality.

Some might argue that gathering too many opinions causes unnecessary confusion and leaves a person paralyzed. This is a fair concern, but the goal of asking around is not to run a popularity contest or let a committee decide. Rather, the point is to collect enough information to think critically for oneself. Disagreement among advisers is actually useful because it highlights where the most significant trade-offs lie.

Ultimately, getting advice from multiple sources strengthens judgment by broadening perspective, creating new alternatives, and checking against bias. While any single person can offer good counsel, comparing several views ensures that the final decision is well-informed, balanced, and truly one's own.

Dear Senator,

I urge you to support changing presidential elections to a national popular vote, whether through a constitutional amendment or by joining efforts that ensure the candidate with the most votes becomes President. The Electoral College may have been a reasonable compromise at the nation’s founding, but its present operation gives unequal weight to citizens’ votes and leaves too many Americans outside the real campaign for the presidency.

The Federal Register explains that the Electoral College was created as a compromise between election by Congress and direct election by qualified citizens. Today, it has 538 electors, and a candidate needs 270 to win. Each state receives electors equal to its number of representatives and senators. This arrangement means that voters are not simply participating in one national election; they are participating in separate state contests whose results are usually converted into electoral votes. In forty-eight states and Washington, D.C., the winner of the state’s popular vote receives every electoral vote. That winner-take-all rule is the central problem.

As Bradford Plumer notes, a candidate can win the national popular vote but lose the presidency, as occurred in 2000 and 2016. In such cases, the candidate preferred by more voters nationwide does not take office. A democracy should not allow the outcome of its most important election to contradict the choice of the greatest number of citizens. Every eligible voter should have an equal stake in choosing the President, whether that voter lives in a rural county, a small state, a large state, or a major city.

The current system also distorts campaigning. Because most states are predictably Democratic or Republican, candidates focus their attention, advertising, and policy promises on a small group of competitive “swing states.” Plumer argues that voters in safely partisan states are often ignored, which can reduce turnout. A Republican voter in a strongly Democratic state and a Democratic voter in a strongly Republican state may reasonably feel that a presidential campaign has little reason to listen to them. Under a national popular vote, however, every additional vote would matter. Candidates would have an incentive to seek support everywhere, including communities that are now treated as politically settled.

Supporters of the Electoral College raise serious concerns. Judge Richard A. Posner argues that it protects federalism, prevents candidates from relying only on large urban areas, and encourages broad coalitions across regions and states. He also observes that state-by-state results can produce a quick resolution and limit recount disputes to a single state rather than the entire country. Those benefits deserve consideration. Yet candidates already have strong practical reasons to appeal broadly: no candidate can win a national popular vote by depending only on one city or region. Millions of voters live outside urban centers, and their votes would count just as much as anyone else’s. Broad coalitions should be built by persuading more people, not by targeting a few closely divided states.

Concerns about recounts should not outweigh equal representation. Nationwide election standards, improved ballot procedures, and transparent auditing can reduce uncertainty. More importantly, recounts are rare; the possibility of a close election should not justify a system that can regularly disregard the national majority.

Please support reforms that make the presidential election reflect the popular will. The President represents the entire nation, and every citizen’s vote should carry the same power in choosing that office.

Dear Principal [Last Name],

I am writing to share my view on the school's cell phone policy. After considering both options, I believe Policy 1, which allows students to use phones during lunch and free time as long as they are turned off during class, is the better choice. It protects the learning environment while recognizing the practical role phones play in students' lives.

The strongest reason to support Policy 1 is safety and communication. Students often need to reach their parents about last-minute changes: a canceled practice, a late ride, or a medical appointment. Without phones, students must rely on the front office, which can be slow and can overwhelm staff. In a genuine emergency, such as a medical problem or a threat to campus safety, the ability to contact family quickly could matter enormously. A total ban would remove that option for the very hours when students are away from home most of the day. Under Policy 1, students keep that lifeline, and the rule that phones be off during class prevents the safety benefit from becoming a distraction.

Policy 1 is also more realistic and easier to enforce. A complete ban sounds simple, but in practice it would require teachers and administrators to search for hidden phones, confiscate devices, and handle constant disputes. Many students would carry phones secretly, and teachers would spend valuable time policing rather than teaching. A policy that gives students a reasonable time to use their phones removes much of the temptation to break the rules. When students know they can check messages at lunch, they are far less likely to sneak a look during math class. Rules that people see as fair tend to be followed more willingly than rules they see as excessive.

In addition, Policy 1 helps students learn responsibility. Phones are not going away; students will be expected to manage them in college and in the workplace. Learning when it is appropriate to use a device and when to put it away is a skill that can only be practiced, not avoided. A school should prepare students for the world they will enter, and that includes teaching self-control and respect for others' time. By trusting students to follow clear limits, the school treats them as maturing young adults and gives them a chance to meet that expectation.

Some people argue that phones will still distract students and that a total ban is the only way to protect learning. This concern is understandable, and I agree that phones in class can harm focus. However, Policy 1 already addresses this by requiring phones to be turned off during instruction. Consequences for breaking this rule, such as having the phone held until the end of the day, can be clear and consistent. This keeps classrooms focused without taking away every benefit of phones. Furthermore, lunch is meant to be a break, and allowing students to relax, talk to friends, or check in with family can help them return to class refreshed.

In conclusion, Policy 1 offers the best balance. It keeps students connected in case of emergencies, is far easier to enforce than a total ban, and teaches responsibility while still protecting class time. I respectfully encourage you to adopt this policy. Thank you for taking the time to consider a student's perspective on this important decision.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]

The development of driverless cars has sparked intense debate in recent years, with proponents arguing that they will revolutionize transportation and opponents raising concerns about safety and liability. After careful consideration of the arguments presented in the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," I firmly believe that the development of driverless cars should be supported. The potential benefits of driverless cars, including a significant reduction in traffic accidents and increased mobility for the elderly and disabled, outweigh the concerns surrounding their implementation.

One of the most compelling arguments in favor of driverless cars is their potential to greatly reduce the number of traffic accidents on our roads. According to the article, human error is responsible for over 90 percent of traffic accidents, often due to distractions such as texting or drowsiness. Driverless cars, equipped with laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors, are able to detect obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals, making them far less prone to error than human drivers. This reduction in accidents would not only save lives but also lower insurance costs, making transportation more affordable for everyone. Furthermore, the increased mobility provided by driverless cars would be a game-changer for elderly or disabled passengers who are currently unable to drive themselves.

Another significant advantage of driverless cars is their potential to increase fuel efficiency and reduce parking space requirements. As Google cofounder Sergey Brin envisions, a future of driverless public transportation could use half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. This would not only reduce our reliance on fossil fuels but also help to alleviate the parking shortages that plague many cities. Additionally, the reduced need for personal vehicle ownership could lead to a more streamlined and efficient transportation system, with cars being used more frequently and effectively.

While critics and safety experts raise valid concerns about the limitations of current sensor technology and the potential for software glitches or cybersecurity threats, these issues can be addressed through continued research and development. As the technology improves, the risks associated with driverless cars will decrease, and the benefits will become even more pronounced. Furthermore, the legal and ethical questions surrounding liability in the event of an accident can be resolved through careful consideration and regulation. It is not unreasonable to expect that vehicle owners, software developers, and automakers will work together to establish clear guidelines and protocols for ensuring public safety.

In conclusion, the development of driverless cars has the potential to revolutionize transportation, saving lives, increasing mobility, and reducing our environmental impact. While there are valid concerns surrounding their implementation, these can be addressed through continued research and development, as well as careful consideration of the legal and ethical implications. As we move forward, it is essential that we support the development of driverless cars, working to create a safer, more efficient, and more sustainable transportation system for all. By doing so, we can create a future where driverless cars are not only a reality but also a cornerstone of our transportation infrastructure.

Dear Principal,

I am writing to share my perspective regarding the proposed policy that would require students to maintain at least a grade B average to participate in sports and extracurricular activities. While I recognize that this initiative stems from a genuine desire to elevate academic achievement across our school, I strongly urge you to reconsider. Barring students with a C average from after-school programs will ultimately undermine their academic motivation, strip them of vital developmental outlets, and damage our school’s sense of community.

First, extracurricular activities often serve as the primary motivator for students to stay engaged in school. For many who find traditional academics challenging, being part of an athletic team, the drama club, or the band provides a powerful incentive to attend classes and keep their grades up. Under the current policy, maintaining a C average—which represents satisfactory, passing work—serves as an attainable baseline that keeps these students accountable. If the threshold is raised to a B average, many students who work diligently just to earn a C may feel the goal is entirely out of reach. Faced with an impossible standard, they are more likely to give up on their studies entirely rather than push harder, leading to higher rates of disengagement and potential dropouts.

Furthermore, participation in clubs and sports provides essential benefits that directly support academic success and emotional well-being. Extracurriculars teach critical life skills that cannot always be learned in a traditional classroom, including leadership, discipline, time management, and resilience. For students experiencing academic or personal stress, these activities provide a constructive, healthy outlet and a supportive network of peers and mentors. Denying these positive influences to students simply because their grades are average isolates them during the hours when they most need positive supervision and structured engagement.

Finally, an outright ban punishes students who could benefit from targeted support instead. A grade C average indicates that a student is passing, even if there is room for improvement. Rather than excluding these students, the administration could implement a system of academic assistance. For example, the school could introduce mandatory study tables, peer tutoring, or regular check-ins for student-athletes and club members who hold a C average. Such a framework would address academic deficiencies constructively while allowing students to retain the activities that enrich their high school experience.

In conclusion, while high academic expectations are essential, raising the eligibility requirement to a B average risks alienating a significant portion of our student body. Extracurricular activities should be utilized as tools to inspire and support struggling students, not as privileges reserved exclusively for high achievers. I respectfully ask that you maintain the current grade C threshold and instead invest in supportive measures that help all students reach their full academic and personal potential.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

Dear Principal,

I believe students should be required to perform a reasonable amount of community service each year. School is meant to prepare us for more than tests and careers; it should also teach us how to participate responsibly in the communities where we live. A service requirement would give every student the chance to see that their time and skills can make a real difference.

Many students already volunteer because they understand this value. Tutoring younger children, for example, can help an elementary student become more confident about reading or math. The tutor may only spend an hour each week explaining fractions or listening to a child read, but that attention can change how the younger student feels about school. At the same time, the high school student learns patience, communication, and leadership. Those lessons are difficult to gain from a textbook.

Community service can also improve the places we share. When students clean up parks, collect food for local shelters, or help at a community garden, the results are visible. A cleaner playground encourages families to use it. A food drive can help people who are struggling to afford groceries. Projects like these remind students that problems in a community are not always someone else’s responsibility. If everyone assumes another person will help, nothing gets done.

Some students may argue that required service takes time away from homework, sports, jobs, or family responsibilities. This is a fair concern. A requirement should not be so large that it overwhelms students who already have busy schedules. However, the school could set a manageable goal, such as ten or fifteen hours per semester, and offer flexible options. Students could volunteer on weekends, during school-sponsored service days, or through projects connected to clubs and classes. Those with jobs or significant responsibilities at home could be given alternative arrangements. Requiring service does not have to mean ignoring students’ individual circumstances.

A requirement may also encourage students to try service they would not choose on their own. At first, someone might volunteer only because it is required. After helping at an animal shelter, assisting at a senior center, or mentoring a younger student, that person may discover an interest they did not know they had. Even if students do not continue volunteering afterward, they will still have experienced the importance of contributing to others.

Community service should be treated as an important part of education, not as punishment or a meaningless box to check. If the school provides choices, guidance, and reasonable expectations, every student can find a way to help. I hope you will require community service because it would strengthen both our students and our community.

Sincerely,  
A Concerned Student

Should Drivers Be Allowed to Use Cell Phones While Driving?

Almost everybody has a cell phone now, and most people check theirs all the time. It is easy to see why some drivers think they can use their phones in the car too. But I believe drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while they are operating a vehicle, with the possible exception of a phone that is already set up to work completely hands-free, like a GPS. Driving takes a lot of attention, and phones take that attention away.

The biggest reason is safety. When you drive, you have to watch the road, check your mirrors, and react to things like brake lights or a kid running into the street. Looking at a phone for even a few seconds is dangerous. I once read that if you look at a text for about five seconds while going 55 miles per hour, you travel the length of a football field without looking at the road. That is a scary thought. A lot can happen in that distance, and you would not be able to stop in time.

Some people say that talking on the phone is fine as long as you are not texting. But studies have shown that the problem is not just your hands, it is your brain. Even if your eyes are on the road, your mind can be focused on the conversation instead of the traffic. This is called distracted thinking, and it can make your reaction time slower. So even a hands-free call can still be risky, which is why I think phone use should be limited as much as possible.

Another argument people make is that they might need their phone for emergencies or directions. I understand that, and I think those are reasonable situations. However, there are safe ways to handle them. A driver can pull over to a safe spot to make an emergency call or fix their directions. They can also put the GPS in before they start driving. If something is really urgent, taking a minute to park is better than risking a crash. Most texts and calls can wait until you get where you are going.

Some people also say a law like this would be hard to enforce, since police cannot always see inside a car. That may be true, but hard to enforce does not mean it is a bad rule. Seat belt laws were also hard to enforce at first, and now most people wear them automatically. Laws change habits over time. If people know there is a fine or a ticket, they will probably think twice before picking up the phone. Also, schools and parents can teach teens about the dangers so they develop good habits early, since new drivers are especially likely to get distracted.

The last reason is that a crash does not only hurt the driver. It can hurt passengers, other drivers, and pedestrians who did nothing wrong. Using your phone is a choice, and it is not fair to put other people in danger because you wanted to answer a message. Nothing on a phone is worth someone's life.

In conclusion, drivers should not use cell phones while driving. The risks are too serious, and there are easy alternatives like pulling over or waiting until the trip is done. Phones are useful, but driving safely has to come first.

Dear Principal [Name],

I am writing to share my thoughts on the cell phone policy you are currently reviewing and to respectfully encourage you to choose Policy 1. Permitting students to carry their phones and use them during lunch and passing periods—while strictly keeping them powered off during class—strikes the right balance between maintaining an orderly learning environment and addressing the everyday realities students face.

To begin with, having access to a phone during free periods solves significant practical and family challenges. Many students juggle complicated schedules involving working parents, younger siblings who need rides, or extracurricular commitments that shift at the last minute. Being able to send a quick text during lunch to confirm a ride home or handle an urgent family matter is far more practical than having dozens of students line up in the main office to use a landline. In unexpected situations or minor emergencies, direct contact with family provides genuine peace of mind. A total ban penalizes the entire student body for issues caused by only a few.

Furthermore, Policy 1 protects instructional time just as effectively as a total ban, without creating unnecessary friction between teachers and students. The main argument for an outright ban is preventing distraction, which is completely understandable. However, requiring phones to be silenced and tucked away during class targets the distraction directly where it matters most. When a school enforces a complete prohibition, it rarely stops students from bringing their devices; instead, it turns hallways and classrooms into a game of hide-and-seek. Staff end up spending valuable energy policing backpacks and pockets. A policy that students recognize as reasonable is far more likely to earn their cooperation and compliance.

Beyond logistics, allowing phones during down time offers an important opportunity to develop digital maturity. After high school, nobody will confiscate our devices; we will be expected to know when to put them away during college lectures, staff meetings, and professional tasks. Banning phones entirely simply delays that learning process. Allowing students to use their phones during their own time, while demanding their full attention the moment the bell rings, reinforces the self-discipline we will actually need in the real world. 

Finally, breaks during the school day serve a purpose. For many students, listening to music at lunch, coordinating a group project, or checking an assignment deadline helps them decompress and prepare for the rest of the day. If there is concern that screens might discourage face-to-face interaction in the cafeteria, the school could easily designate certain tables as phone-free zones, giving students choices that fit their personal preferences.

While concerns about social media drama or inappropriate usage are valid, a campus ban does not solve those problems—it merely pushes them to the bus ride home or into the evening. Clear behavioral standards and accountability are much more effective tools for dealing with misuse than an across-the-board restriction.

For these reasons, I believe Policy 1 is the smarter, more practical path forward. It keeps our classrooms focused on academics while treating students with the trust and respect that foster personal responsibility. Thank you very much for your time and for considering the student perspective.

Sincerely,

Dear Senator,

As I consider the electoral process that determines the President of the United States, I strongly believe that it is time to transition from the Electoral College to a direct national popular vote. The current system, established as a compromise in the Constitution, has become outdated and undermines the fundamental principle of democracy: that every citizen's vote should carry equal weight. I urge you to support this reform, which would ensure that the voices of all Americans are heard equally in the presidential election.

Proponents of the Electoral College, such as Judge Richard A. Posner, argue that it preserves federalism and encourages national cohesion by compelling candidates to build broad coalitions across both large and small states. This argument suggests that the Electoral College prevents candidates from winning solely by accumulating votes in densely populated urban areas, thereby promoting a more nuanced understanding of the nation's diverse needs. Additionally, supporters point out that the Electoral College provides a clear and decisive winner, avoiding the potential chaos of a nationwide recount by limiting disputes to individual states.

However, a closer examination of modern presidential campaigns reveals that the Electoral College falls short of its intended goals. In reality, the "winner-take-all" system used by most states leads to a phenomenon where candidates focus almost exclusively on a handful of swing states, as noted by Bradford Plumer. This strategy ignores the concerns and votes of millions of Americans living in states that are safely Democratic or Republican, ultimately depressing voter turnout and fostering political disillusionment nationwide. The voices of rural voters in California or urban conservatives in Texas are effectively silenced, undermining the very federalism that the Electoral College is supposed to preserve.

Moreover, the Electoral College has created instances where the winner of the presidential election did not receive the most popular votes, as seen in the 2000 and 2016 elections. This discrepancy can lead to a crisis of democratic legitimacy, where the elected president lacks the support of the majority of the American people. Such outcomes erode trust in the electoral process and can have far-reaching consequences for the country's stability and cohesion.

In light of these concerns, I firmly believe that adopting a national popular vote system would better serve the democratic principles of our nation. By making every vote count equally, we can encourage candidates to engage with voters across the country, rather than focusing solely on swing states. This reform would also help to restore faith in the electoral process, ensuring that the president is elected through a system that truly reflects the will of the American people. I urge you to consider the merits of this proposal and work towards creating a more inclusive and representative democracy.

The widespread use of cell phones has created a serious challenge for road safety. These devices provide convenience, entertainment, and instant communication, but they can also become dangerous when used behind the wheel. Although some people argue that limited or hands-free phone use should be allowed, the evidence supports a stricter approach: drivers should not use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

The most immediate risk is physical distraction. Texting, dialing, checking a notification, or scrolling through an app requires drivers to take their eyes off the road and often remove a hand from the steering wheel. At highway speeds, a car can travel the length of a football field in only a few seconds. If a driver looks down at a phone during that time, the vehicle is essentially moving without guidance. Even a brief glance can be enough to miss a stopped car, a pedestrian entering a crosswalk, or a traffic light changing. Driving requires constant awareness, and a phone screen takes attention away from that responsibility.

Some people believe hands-free technology solves this problem because it allows drivers to keep both hands on the wheel. However, the danger of phone use is not limited to holding the device. Conversations, voice messages, and voice-to-text features create cognitive distraction. A driver may be looking straight ahead, but their mind is focused on listening, responding, or thinking about what to say next. Human beings cannot fully concentrate on two demanding tasks at once. Instead, the brain switches back and forth between them, leaving gaps in attention.

This divided attention can lead to what researchers call “inattention blindness.” Drivers using phones may see the road in front of them without fully processing what is happening. They can miss red lights, road signs, sudden braking, bicyclists, or pedestrians. A hands-free conversation may seem harmless because the driver’s hands and eyes appear to be where they should be, but the driver is still mentally less prepared to react. In a situation where seconds matter, that loss of focus can have tragic consequences.

Allowing some types of phone use also creates legal and social confusion. If hands-free calling or voice commands are permitted, it becomes difficult for law enforcement to determine whether a driver was simply speaking or was dangerously distracted. A total ban would create a clearer standard for everyone. It would also reinforce the idea that driving is not a time for multitasking. A vehicle is a powerful machine, and operating one safely requires full attention.

Of course, many drivers depend on their phones for directions, work, or emergencies. However, these needs can usually be handled before a trip begins or after the driver pulls over safely. Navigation can be set up in advance, messages can wait, and calls can be returned later. No conversation or notification is worth risking another person’s life.

Ultimately, drivers should not be able to use cell phones while operating a vehicle, whether the phone is held in the hand or used through hands-free technology. Physical distraction and mental distraction both reduce a driver’s ability to respond to danger. The safest and most responsible policy is a complete ban on cell phone use while driving. The call can wait, but a life may not.

I disagree with the decision to require every student to participate in an extracurricular activity. Activities like sports, yearbook, drama, and student council can be great experiences, but forcing students to join them could make school more stressful instead of more meaningful. Schools should strongly encourage students to participate, but they should also respect that students have different responsibilities and interests outside of school.

For many students, extracurricular activities are a chance to make friends and discover talents. For example, a shy student might join the yearbook staff and become more comfortable talking to people while interviewing students. Someone who enjoys basketball might learn teamwork and discipline by being on the team. These are important benefits. However, they happen best when students actually want to be there. If someone is forced to join the debate club just to meet a requirement, that person may not participate seriously. They might sit through meetings, do the minimum amount of work, and make the experience harder for the students who care about the club.

Also, not every student has extra time after school. Some students have jobs to help their families pay bills or save for college. Others take care of younger brothers or sisters while their parents work. A student might need to go home right after school to babysit, cook dinner, or help a family member. It would not be fair to punish that student for not joining a club or sport. Even if the school offers activities during lunch or before school, those times may still not work for everyone because of transportation, homework, or other responsibilities.

Another problem is that students already have a lot of pressure. They have classes, tests, homework, projects, and sometimes advanced courses. Adding a required activity could make students feel like they are always being judged on how busy they are. Some students need time to relax, read, exercise on their own, or focus on their mental health. Free time is not always wasted time. A student who spends afternoons drawing, practicing guitar, or learning computer coding at home may be developing real skills, even if those skills are not part of an official school club.

Instead of making extracurricular activities mandatory, the school could make them easier and more welcoming to join. It could hold an activity fair at the beginning of the year, let students try clubs for a few weeks before committing, and provide late buses for students who need transportation. Teachers could also tell students about less obvious choices, such as tutoring, robotics, volunteering, or helping with school events. This would give students opportunities without taking away their choices.

Extracurricular activities are valuable, but they should be opportunities, not requirements. Students are more likely to learn responsibility, teamwork, and confidence when they choose an activity that fits their lives.

I agree with the principal's decision to require every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. While some students may initially resist the idea, the benefits of involvement outside the classroom are significant. Extracurricular activities build important life skills, help students form connections, and encourage them to discover interests they might never have found otherwise.

First, extracurricular activities teach skills that textbooks cannot. A student who joins the yearbook staff, for example, learns to meet deadlines, collaborate with others, and take responsibility for a finished product. A member of the student council practices public speaking, negotiation, and leadership. Even playing on a sports team requires discipline, time management, and the ability to handle both victory and defeat gracefully. These abilities matter in college and in the workplace, where employers look for people who can cooperate, communicate, and manage their time. Requiring participation ensures that every student, not just those who already seek out opportunities, has the chance to develop these strengths.

Second, extracurricular activities help students feel connected to their school. Many students move through the day attending classes and going home without ever getting to know anyone beyond their immediate friends. This can leave them feeling isolated or invisible. When a shy new student joins the drama club or the school band, he or she meets classmates with shared interests and works toward a common goal. Research and common experience both suggest that students who feel a sense of belonging are more motivated, attend school more regularly, and are less likely to engage in risky behavior. A school-wide requirement would help make sure no student is left on the sidelines.

Third, a requirement pushes students to try new things. Left to their own choices, many teenagers stick with what is familiar or spend free hours on screens. A student who has never considered art might join the mural club to fulfill the requirement and discover a real talent. Another might try cross-country running and find a lifelong passion for fitness. Without that gentle push, these discoveries might never happen. Because the policy allows students to choose from a wide range of activities, such as sports, yearbook, student council, or clubs, they still have freedom to pick something that suits their personality.

Critics argue that some students already have heavy workloads, jobs, or family responsibilities, and that adding a requirement would overburden them. This is a fair concern, but it can be addressed rather than used to reject the policy. The school could offer flexible options, such as clubs that meet during lunch or once a week, and could count community service or supervised work experience. Requiring only one activity, rather than several, keeps the commitment manageable. Moreover, research on student achievement often shows that participation in activities can improve grades, since students learn to organize their time more effectively.

In conclusion, the principal's decision is a wise one. Extracurricular activities develop practical skills, create a sense of community, and open doors to new interests. With reasonable flexibility for students who have special circumstances, the requirement can benefit everyone. A school should educate the whole person, not just the test-taker, and this policy is a meaningful step toward that goal.

Dear Principal Henderson,

I am writing to share my thoughts on the proposal to make community service a requirement for all students. I know this idea comes from a good place because helping our town is important, but after talking about it with my classmates, I believe requiring service hours would do more harm than good. Instead of making it mandatory, the school should continue to encourage it as an optional choice.

Right now, a lot of my friends already volunteer. One of my friends spends two afternoons every week tutoring younger kids at the elementary school, and another joins weekend park cleanups to pick up litter along the river. They really enjoy doing it because it is their own choice, and they genuinely care about the impact they are making. However, if you force every single student to participate, community service turns into just another chore on a checklist. When people are forced to be somewhere they do not want to be, they usually do not bring a positive attitude. Instead of learning compassion, students might just rush through their tasks or do the bare minimum just to get their paper signed. That does not actually help the organizations we are supposed to be supporting.

Another major issue is the amount of time students actually have outside of school. Many students already have serious responsibilities that take up most of their free hours. For instance, some of my classmates work part-time jobs at grocery stores or restaurants to help their families pay bills or to save up for college. Other students have to take the bus straight home every day to watch their younger siblings until their parents get home from late work shifts. When you add heavy homework loads, studying for exams, and extracurricular activities like sports or band, a lot of students are already overwhelmed and staying up late. Adding mandatory volunteer hours would create unnecessary stress and could end up hurting people's grades or mental health. 

Rather than forcing everyone, I think the school could do more to support students who want to volunteer or who just need an easy way to get started. For example, the school could organize weekend volunteer events, invite local charities to set up tables during lunch, or offer elective credit or special recognition at graduation for students who complete a certain number of hours. 

Helping our community is a great goal, but volunteering means doing something willingly. Giving students the encouragement and resources to get involved on their own will build much more genuine empathy than forcing them to do it. Thank you for taking the time to read my letter and for considering the student perspective on this issue.

Sincerely,

Alex Rivera  
Grade 11 Student

Driverless cars should continue to be developed because they have the potential to make transportation safer, more efficient, and more accessible. Although the technology still has important weaknesses, the possible benefits are too significant to ignore. Instead of abandoning autonomous vehicles because of current concerns, companies and governments should improve the technology and create clear safety and legal rules before these cars become widely used.

The strongest argument for driverless cars is that they could save lives. According to the article, human error causes more than 90 percent of traffic accidents. Drivers may text while driving, become drowsy, or get behind the wheel while impaired. A driverless vehicle does not become tired, distracted by a phone, or affected by alcohol. Autonomous cars use laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors to identify obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals. If these systems are designed and tested carefully, they could prevent many crashes caused by careless or dangerous human decisions. Fewer accidents would also lower insurance costs and reduce the emotional and financial harm suffered by families after collisions.

Driverless cars could also improve life for people who cannot easily drive themselves. Elderly people, people with disabilities, and others who are unable to drive safely often must depend on relatives, public transportation, or expensive ride services. Autonomous vehicles could give these individuals greater independence. They could travel to work, medical appointments, stores, or social events without needing someone else to drive them. In this way, driverless cars would not merely be a convenience; they could provide freedom and opportunity to many people.

In addition, the article explains that Google cofounder Sergey Brin imagines driverless public transportation using half the fuel and half the parking space of today’s cars. If fewer people need to own personal vehicles, communities could have less traffic congestion and fewer large parking lots. Reducing fuel use would also benefit the environment. A transportation system that is shared, efficient, and automated could make cities cleaner and easier to navigate.

Critics are right to point out serious risks. Sensors may have trouble in heavy rain, snow, fog, or construction zones with unclear markings. Software can also have glitches or become vulnerable to cybersecurity threats. These concerns show that driverless cars should not be rushed onto roads before they are ready. Semi-autonomous systems are especially concerning because people may stop paying attention while the computer drives, even though they may need to take control during an emergency. Developers should therefore focus on building systems that can operate safely in difficult conditions and clearly communicate when human control is necessary. Laws must also determine whether the owner, automaker, or software developer is responsible when an accident occurs.

Driverless cars are not yet perfect, but neither are human drivers. Because human mistakes cause so many crashes, autonomous technology could protect lives and expand transportation options for millions of people. With careful testing, strong cybersecurity, and clear legal standards, driverless cars should be developed as a safer and more useful future for transportation.

Dear Principal,

I believe students should be required to perform community service, as long as the requirement is reasonable and gives them different ways to take part. Service helps students understand the needs of other people, strengthens the relationship between our school and the community, and teaches responsibility in ways a classroom sometimes cannot.

To begin with, volunteering shows students that their actions can make a real difference. It is easy for teenagers to think only about homework, sports, friends, and their own goals. Those things matter, but we also benefit from seeing the challenges that people outside our usual circles face. A student who tutors an elementary school child, for instance, may realize how hard reading can be for someone who gets little help at home. Even one hour a week of practice can build that child's confidence and skills. Meanwhile, the tutor learns patience, communication, and empathy.

Service can also improve the places where we live. When students pick up litter in parks, collect food for local families, visit senior citizens, or help at an animal shelter, they make the neighborhood cleaner and more welcoming. These jobs may seem small, but many small efforts add up. A group that spends one afternoon cleaning a playground can make it a healthier place for younger kids to play. Those students might also think twice before littering themselves, since they will have seen how much work it takes to clean up.

Some people say a requirement would take time away from studying, jobs, family duties, or activities students enjoy. That is a fair concern, but a service requirement does not have to be excessive. The school could ask for a limited number of hours each year, perhaps ten or fifteen, and allow students to earn them on weekends, at school-sponsored events, or during breaks. Students should also be able to choose from many kinds of service. Someone with limited transportation could help run a school donation drive, while another student might volunteer at the library or coach younger athletes. Flexible choices would make the program fairer and more meaningful.

Finally, a requirement would encourage students who might never volunteer on their own to give service a chance. Not everyone will enjoy it right away, but many of us might discover new interests or talents. A student who helps at a food pantry could become passionate about fighting hunger, and one who assists younger children might start thinking about teaching as a career. Even if some students do not keep volunteering after graduation, they will have learned that being a good citizen means contributing to others.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

Few technologies have woven themselves into the fabric of daily human existence as thoroughly as the smartphone. It serves as a wallet, an office, an entertainer, and an intimate lifeline. Yet this attachment breeds a dangerous complacency the moment an individual slides behind the steering wheel. Navigating a two-ton machine through dynamic environments demands continuous, undivided attention—a requirement fundamentally at odds with the persistent interruptions of mobile devices. Because any engagement with a phone severely impairs human performance, drivers should be barred from using them in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

Public policy has long treated hands-free technology as a reasonable compromise. Laws frequently penalize drivers for holding a phone to their ear or typing out a text while allowing them to converse freely through Bluetooth speakers or dashboard interfaces. This distinction is scientifically hollow. Cognitive research consistently demonstrates that the human brain cannot genuinely execute simultaneous high-order tasks. Instead, it toggles rapidly between them, creating an illusion of competence. When drivers are engaged in conversation, their visual fields narrow and their reaction times degrade to levels comparable to mild intoxication. They may look directly at a braking vehicle or a crossing pedestrian without mentally processing the hazard, a phenomenon known as inattention blindness. The danger does not lie merely in where drivers place their hands; it resides in where they place their minds.

Physical interaction with a device amplifies this peril exponentially. Glancing down to check a notification for just four seconds at highway speed is the functional equivalent of driving the length of a football field blindfolded. Modern software is deliberately engineered to exploit human psychology, leveraging variable rewards and urgent pings that make sustained self-control exceedingly difficult. While digital navigation offers genuine utility, that benefit does not justify active fiddling while in motion. Route planning belongs strictly to the moments before the transmission leaves park.

Resistance to an absolute prohibition typically centers on convenience or the demands of professional responsiveness. Yet driving is a licensed privilege contingent upon public safety, not an unassailable right. Society has repeatedly recalibrated its boundaries when prevailing habits proved lethal, as seen in the historical shifts surrounding seatbelt mandates and drunk driving enforcement. Interacting with a phone behind the wheel warrants the same social stigma and uncompromising legal boundary.

The development of driverless cars is a topic that has sparked intense debate in recent years. While some people believe that these cars will revolutionize the way we travel, others are concerned about the potential risks and challenges they pose. In my opinion, the development of driverless cars is a good idea, despite some drawbacks. The benefits of driverless cars, including reduced traffic accidents and increased mobility for certain groups, outweigh the potential risks.

One of the main advantages of driverless cars is that they could dramatically reduce the number of traffic accidents on the road. As the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming" points out, human error is responsible for over 90 percent of traffic accidents, often due to texting, drowsiness, or impaired driving. Driverless cars, on the other hand, are equipped with advanced sensors and computer systems that can detect obstacles and traffic signals, making them much safer than human-driven cars. For example, the article mentions that Google cofounder Sergey Brin envisions a future of driverless public transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. This not only reduces the risk of accidents but also helps to reduce our carbon footprint.

Another benefit of driverless cars is that they can provide mobility for elderly or disabled passengers who may not be able to drive themselves. This could be a game-changer for people who rely on others for transportation, giving them the freedom and independence to go where they want, when they want. Additionally, driverless cars could also reduce insurance costs, as the risk of accidents decreases. The Case for Distance Learning

As technology continues to shape everyday life, education has begun to extend beyond the traditional classroom. Distance learning allows students to attend classes from home through online platforms or video conferencing, and it has become a more common option in many schools. Although some people worry that learning from home can be isolating or less rigorous, students would benefit from having this choice. Distance learning provides flexibility, increases access to courses, and helps students build the independence and technology skills they will need later in life.

One major advantage of distance learning is that it gives students more flexibility. In a regular classroom, everyone is expected to follow the same schedule and move through lessons at roughly the same pace. However, students do not all learn in the same way or understand new material equally quickly. Online classes can allow students to review recorded lessons, pause during confusing sections, or spend more time practicing difficult skills. For example, a student having trouble with quadratic equations in algebra could replay a lesson several times before completing an assignment. Meanwhile, a student who understands the topic quickly may be able to move ahead without becoming bored. This kind of flexibility can make learning less frustrating and more productive.

Distance learning can also make education available to students who face barriers to attending school in person. Students with chronic illnesses, physical disabilities, or transportation problems may find it difficult to travel to school every day. Being able to participate from home would allow them to continue learning without dealing with those obstacles. In addition, online classes can connect students in rural or underfunded areas with courses that their local schools cannot offer. For instance, a student in a small town might be able to take Japanese, computer science, or an advanced placement course through video conferencing with a teacher in another district. Instead of being limited by where they live, students could have access to a wider range of opportunities.

Another benefit is that learning from home can help students become more responsible and self-directed. In a physical classroom, teachers can closely monitor students and remind them about assignments. Online learners must often manage their own schedules, meet deadlines, and speak up when they need help. These responsibilities can strengthen self-discipline and time-management skills, which are important in college and many jobs. Students also gain experience using online learning platforms, participating in video discussions, and submitting assignments electronically. Since technology is now a major part of both education and the workplace, these digital skills are valuable.

Of course, distance learning is not perfect. Students may miss daily face-to-face interaction with classmates, and certain subjects, such as science labs, art, or performing arts, can be harder to teach online. Still, these concerns do not mean that schools should reject distance learning completely. Hybrid programs could combine online instruction with in-person labs, clubs, group projects, or occasional class meetings. The purpose is not to replace traditional schools, but to provide another option for students whose needs may be different.

Overall, students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home. Greater flexibility, wider access to courses, and stronger independent learning skills outweigh the possible disadvantages when programs are designed carefully. Distance learning should be viewed not as a replacement for the classroom, but as a useful tool that can help more students succeed.
