The vision is seductive. Sergey Brin imagines a future in which no one buys a car because driverless public transportation uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today’s vehicles. In “Driverless Cars Are Coming,” supporters point out that human error causes over 90 percent of traffic accidents, often because of texting, drowsiness, or impaired driving. Under the right conditions, autonomous cars could reduce crashes, lower insurance costs, and offer new freedom to elderly or disabled passengers. Yet for all that promise, the article also exposes serious unresolved problems. I believe the development and widespread deployment of driverless cars should be slowed until the technology and legal systems catch up with the dream.

One major difficulty is that the sensors and software are not reliable in exactly the situations where careful driving matters most. The article notes that current systems can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or unmarked construction zones. A human driver may slow down, squint through a storm, or follow a construction worker’s hand signals. An autonomous car, however, may simply fail to understand what its cameras and laser radar are seeing. That is a dangerous mismatch. We would be handing control to machines that perform well on a clear, well-marked highway but falter precisely when roads become unpredictable.

Even more troubling is the human factor. Many of today’s vehicles are only semi-autonomous, meaning a person must remain alert and ready to take over in an emergency. But studies cited in the article show that passengers quickly lose focus when a computer is driving, and their reaction times slow. This creates a frightening middle ground: the car seems to be in control, so the driver relaxes, but the car may suddenly demand urgent human intervention. At the same time, software glitches and cybersecurity threats leave entire fleets vulnerable to failures or attacks that no individual driver can prevent.

Finally, the legal and ethical questions are far from settled. The article asks a crucial question: when an accident occurs, is the vehicle owner, the software developer, or the automaker responsible? Without a clear answer, victims of crashes could be trapped in lengthy legal battles while companies point fingers at one another. That uncertainty is not a minor detail; it affects whether people can trust the technology enough to share the road with it.

Driverless cars may eventually save lives and transform transportation. But the article’s evidence suggests that the technology is not yet ready for the messy, unpredictable real world. Until sensors can handle bad weather and construction zones, until human attention is better understood, and until liability is clearly defined, we should proceed with caution rather than speed toward a driverless future.

Dear Senator,

Every four years, Americans gather at polling stations under the impression that they are casting ballots directly for the next leader of the free world. In reality, our votes filter through an eighteenth-century mechanism that increasingly strains the democratic fabric of our republic. As one of your constituents, I write to urge your support for replacing the Electoral College with a direct national popular vote. 

Originally devised as a compromise between congressional selection and direct citizen suffrage, the Electoral College assigns each state electors based on its congressional delegation. While this system may have suited an infant nation of disparate colonies, modern practice has revealed deep flaws. Chief among these is the stark injustice highlighted by critic Bradford Plumer: the system permits a candidate to win the national popular vote yet lose the presidency. When millions more citizens choose one candidate only to see another inaugurated—as occurred in both 2000 and 2016—the very principle of consent of the governed is compromised. 

Furthermore, the winner-take-all model adopted by forty-eight states and Washington, D.C., distorts our national campaigns. Candidates routinely bypass vast swathes of the country to focus their time, money, and policy promises on a small cluster of swing states. Millions of conservative voters in California and liberal voters in Texas are effectively disenfranchised because their individual ballots carry no marginal weight in tipping the state total. This geographic lottery depresses voter enthusiasm and leaves the vast majority of Americans completely ignored during presidential cycles. 

Supporters of the status quo, such as Judge Richard A. Posner, offer compelling arguments in its defense. Posner suggests that the Electoral College preserves federalism by preventing urban centers from dominating the national agenda, compelling candidates to build diverse geographic coalitions. He also notes that it insulates the country from the chaos of a nationwide recount, keeping electoral disputes contained within individual state borders. 

These concerns, while serious, misunderstand both modern demography and true coalition building. Under a direct popular vote, no city or state possesses enough population to single-handedly crown a president. Candidates would instead be forced to campaign everywhere, earning individual votes in rural towns, suburban neighborhoods, and central cities alike. Moreover, the risk of localized recounts is a small price to pay compared to the chronic delegitimization that accompanies split outcomes between the popular and electoral results. Our technology and legal frameworks have advanced considerably since 1787; we can manage nationwide vote tallies just as we do for gubernatorial and senatorial elections across large, populous states.

A system that discounts the votes of tens of millions of citizens simply because of where they reside cannot endure in an era that values equal representation. By advocating for a constitutional amendment or state-level compacts that support a direct popular vote, you can help restore the fundamental democratic promise that every American’s voice weighs the same.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Constituent

Distance learning has become a realistic option for many schools, letting students join classes through video conferencing and online assignments. Learning from home is not ideal for every student or every subject, but schools should still offer it as a choice. Used thoughtfully, remote attendance can widen access to education, help students deal with personal challenges, and build skills that matter in college and the workplace.

To begin with, attending class from home keeps students from falling behind when they cannot safely or reasonably get to school. Consider a student recovering from an illness. That student may feel well enough to listen to a lesson and finish assignments but not well enough to spend a full day in a crowded building. In a traditional system, he or she might miss several days of instruction and then struggle to catch up. With a remote option, the student can join the class, ask questions, and stay connected to the material. Distance learning also helps students who live far from school or have transportation problems. Rather than losing instructional time to a missed bus, bad weather, or a family emergency, they can keep learning from home.

Remote learning can also give some students a more productive environment. Not everyone learns best in a busy classroom. Students with anxiety, chronic health conditions, or trouble concentrating amid noise may take part more confidently from home. A student who rarely raises a hand in a large class, for instance, might feel far more comfortable asking a question in a chat or speaking in a small online discussion. Digital tools add flexibility as well. Recorded lectures let students pause explanations, rewatch difficult sections, and review notes before a test. None of this means online learning is automatically easier; it simply gives students more ways to engage with the information.

In addition, distance learning encourages independence and technological competence. Students who attend remotely have to organize their own schedules, submit work electronically, communicate clearly with teachers, and solve basic technical problems. These skills carry over to modern workplaces, where people routinely collaborate through email, video meetings, and shared online documents. By learning to manage responsibilities outside a physical classroom, students can arrive at college and their future careers better prepared.

Still, schools should not treat online attendance as a full replacement for in-person education. Classrooms offer social interaction, immediate help from teachers, and hands-on experiences that are hard to duplicate on a screen. Laboratory experiments, team sports, art projects, and casual conversations with classmates are often more meaningful face to face. Some students also lack reliable internet access or a quiet place to work at home. For this reason, schools that offer remote options need to provide devices, technical support, and regular check-ins.

Overall, students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home, as long as distance learning stays a well-supported choice and not a requirement. It can keep students connected during difficult circumstances, accommodate different learning needs, and strengthen independent-learning skills. A flexible education system accepts that students do not all face the same challenges, and it offers them more than one path to success.

Dear Principal Harris,

I am writing to urge you to adopt Policy 1, which lets students carry phones and use them during lunch and free periods, provided they stay off during class. I understand why a total ban is tempting. Phones can distract, and anyone who has watched a student sneak a glance at a screen during a lesson knows it. But I believe a complete ban would solve a narrow problem by creating several bigger ones, while Policy 1 addresses the distraction directly without them.

Consider safety first. Parents want to reach their children, and children sometimes need to reach home. If a bus breaks down, practice is canceled, or a student feels sick and needs a ride, a phone makes a five-minute problem out of what might otherwise be an hour of confusion. Waiting in line at the front office to borrow the landline is slow, and in a real emergency, slow matters. Policy 1 keeps that lifeline in every student's pocket, and the rule that phones be turned off in class means it never has to compete with a teacher's voice.

Second, a ban is hard to enforce, and enforcement itself takes a toll. Teachers would end up spending time searching for hidden devices, confiscating them, and arguing with students and sometimes parents. Most students would still bring phones and hide them, which turns an ordinary object into contraband. Policy 1 sets a clear and reasonable line: use them at lunch, silence them in class. Rules that students see as fair are far more likely to be followed than rules they see as punishment. I would also argue that a student who learns to put a phone away for forty-five minutes is practicing a skill that no ban could teach, which is self-control.

That brings me to my third point. Our students will graduate into a world where phones are everywhere, at jobs, in college lecture halls, and in meetings. Learning when a device is appropriate and when it is rude or unproductive is part of growing up. A school that removes phones entirely leaves that lesson untaught, whereas a school that sets boundaries gives students daily practice in respecting them.

There is also something to be said for lunch itself. After hours of focused work, students need a break, and for many of them, a phone is part of how they relax. They listen to music, text a sibling, check a schedule, or look up something that came up in conversation. Some students who feel awkward in crowded cafeterias find it easier to ease into a social setting with a phone in hand. I would not claim that phones improve every lunch table, and I admit that some students may stare at screens instead of talking. Still, forcing conversation by taking away the alternative rarely produces friendships.

To make Policy 1 work, I would suggest a few simple supports: a clear consequence for phones that appear during class, such as holding the device until the end of the day for a first offense, and a visible reminder in each classroom, such as a poster or a basket by the door. Teachers would keep the authority to enforce the rule, and students would know exactly where they stand.

A ban promises a distraction-free school, but in practice it would likely deliver resentment, hidden phones, and a loss of safety. Policy 1 protects learning where it matters most, in the classroom, while trusting students with a tool they will have to manage for the rest of their lives. I respectfully ask you to choose it.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

Few objects have woven themselves into daily life as quickly as the cell phone, and few have proven as dangerous behind the wheel. The question of whether drivers should be allowed to use phones in any capacity deserves a more careful answer than a simple yes or no, but the evidence points toward a firm restriction: drivers should not handle or interact with phones while a vehicle is in motion.

Start with what driving actually demands. It requires the eyes to scan the road, the hands to steer, and the mind to anticipate what other drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians might do next. Texting seizes all three at once. A glance at a message that lasts five seconds is enough, at highway speed, to cover the length of a football field with no one watching the road. Researchers have repeatedly found that distracted drivers react more slowly than people who are mildly intoxicated, yet nobody seriously argues that a few drinks should be acceptable if the driver is careful. The comparison is uncomfortable, but it holds up.

The common defense is that people can multitask. They cannot, at least not in the way they imagine. What feels like doing two things at once is really the brain switching rapidly between them, and each switch costs a fraction of a second of attention. Those fractions are precisely what separate a near miss from a collision. Even hands-free calls, often promoted as the safe alternative, pull cognitive focus away from the road. Drivers on a call may stare directly at a stop sign and still fail to register it. The hands are free, but the mind is not.

That said, an absolute ban on every conceivable phone function would be hard to defend and harder to enforce. A phone mounted on the dashboard that provides turn-by-turn navigation is arguably no more distracting than a built-in car display, and it can keep a driver from fumbling with a paper map or making a panicked wrong turn. A reasonable standard would allow voice-activated navigation set up before departure, and perhaps emergency calls placed through voice commands. The principle should be that nothing requires the driver to look at, touch, or mentally engage with the device while moving. The line is drawn at attention, not at the mere presence of technology.

Critics sometimes frame such rules as government overreach into private habits. But driving is not a purely private act. A driver who drifts into another lane imposes the consequences on strangers who never agreed to share that risk. Societies already regulate seat belts, speed, and alcohol for exactly this reason, and the laws are widely accepted because the harm is visible and preventable. Thousands of people die each year in crashes involving distraction, and many of those deaths involve young drivers who grew up believing a phone is an extension of the hand.

Enforcement is admittedly imperfect, and law alone will not change a deeply ingrained habit. Penalties must be meaningful, and public campaigns should treat texting while driving with the same social stigma now attached to drunk driving. Technology can help too: phones that automatically silence notifications once they detect motion make the safe choice the default.

Convenience is a poor trade for a human life. A message can wait ten minutes; a collision cannot be undone. Drivers should be barred from using phones in any way that takes their eyes, hands, or focus from the road, with narrow exceptions for tools that truly support the task of driving.

Seeking advice from multiple individuals is a common practice, and for good reason. When faced with a difficult decision, talking to more than one person can provide a range of perspectives, ultimately leading to a more informed choice. This is because different people bring unique experiences, knowledge, and viewpoints to the table, which can help identify potential pros and cons of a particular option. For instance, consider someone who is trying to decide whether to pursue a career in a creative field or a more traditional, stable profession. By speaking with a artist, a business consultant, and a family member, they may gain a deeper understanding of the financial implications, creative fulfillment, and personal satisfaction associated with each path.

One of the primary benefits of seeking multiple opinions is that it allows individuals to consider a wider range of factors. When we only consult with one person, we may be limited to their particular area of expertise or biased perspective. In contrast, gathering advice from multiple sources can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the situation, highlighting potential pitfalls and opportunities that might have otherwise gone unnoticed. For example, a person considering a move to a new city might talk to a friend who lives there, a real estate agent, and a job recruiter. The friend could offer insights into the local culture and community, while the real estate agent could provide information on the housing market and cost of living. Meanwhile, the job recruiter could discuss the local job market and potential career opportunities, helping the individual make a more informed decision about their relocation.

Seeking multiple opinions can also help individuals avoid the pitfalls of groupthink and confirmation bias. When we only consult with people who share our views or values, we may be more likely to overlook potential flaws in our decision-making. By seeking out diverse perspectives, we can challenge our own assumptions and consider alternative viewpoints, leading to a more nuanced and thoughtful decision. Additionally, talking to multiple people can provide a sense of accountability and support, as individuals are more likely to feel confident in their choice when they have considered a range of opinions and weighed the potential consequences.

In some cases, seeking multiple opinions can even help resolve internal conflicts or mixed emotions. When we are torn between two or more options, speaking with different people can help clarify our thoughts and feelings, allowing us to identify the underlying values and priorities that are driving our decision. For instance, a person considering a major life change, such as a divorce or a career switch, may talk to a therapist, a trusted friend, and a family member. Each of these individuals can offer a unique perspective on the situation, helping the person to process their emotions and make a decision that aligns with their long-term goals and values.

Ultimately, seeking multiple opinions is a valuable strategy for making better choices, as it allows individuals to gather a range of perspectives, consider multiple factors, and avoid the pitfalls of biased thinking. By talking to different people and weighing their advice, we can make more informed decisions that take into account a variety of viewpoints and potential outcomes. Whether we are facing a major life decision or a smaller, everyday choice, seeking multiple opinions can provide a deeper understanding of the situation and help us choose the best path forward.

I am writing because I heard about the possible new policy that would require students to have at least a B average to play sports or join clubs and activities. I understand why you want students to do well in school, but I think this rule would hurt more than it helps, especially for students who have a C average. I believe students should not be kept out of activities just because their grades are not Bs.

First, a C average does not always mean a student is lazy or not trying. Some students work really hard and still get Cs in difficult classes. Others may have test anxiety, learning differences, or problems at home that make school harder. I have a friend who stays after school for math help and does all her homework, but she still gets a C because she struggles on tests. Track is the one thing that keeps her excited about coming to school. Taking that away would not suddenly make her math grade go up. It would probably make her feel worse and less motivated.

Second, sports and activities actually help students keep their grades up. When students know they have practice or rehearsal after school, they learn to manage their time. They use study hall or lunch to finish work because they know they will not have time later. Being on a team also teaches responsibility, discipline, and commitment, which carry over into the classroom. The students who have C averages often need that structure the most, so removing them from activities could make their grades drop even more.

Third, activities are not just extra things for fun. For a lot of students, they are a way to deal with stress, make friends, and feel good at something outside of academics. If a student struggles in science but is a strong basketball player or a good musician, taking that away can make them feel like they are failing at everything. That kind of feeling can make a student give up on school altogether.

I also think a strict B average rule is unfair because classes are not all the same. A C in an honors or advanced class can take more effort than an A in an easier class. If we make one blanket rule, students might start choosing easier classes just to protect their eligibility. That would push students away from challenging themselves, which is not what school should be about.

Instead of banning students with C averages, I think the school should offer more support. For example, students below a C could meet with a teacher or tutor once a week, or they could have a probation period before losing their activity. That way, students stay involved while still being held accountable. The goal should be to help students improve, not to take away the programs that keep them connected to school.

Dear Senator [Last Name],

My name is [Name], and I am a student in your district. I am writing to ask you to support changing the way we elect the president from the Electoral College to a national popular vote. I think every person's vote should count the same, and right now that is not what happens.

The biggest problem with the Electoral College is that a candidate can get the most votes from the American people and still lose. According to Bradford Plumer in "The Indefensible Electoral College," this happened in 2000 and again in 2016. That seems backwards to me. In my civics class we learn that democracy means the majority decides, but the Electoral College can overrule the majority. If a team scored the most points in a game but still lost, people would say the rules were broken.

Another problem is how campaigns are run. The Office of the Federal Register explains that forty-eight states and Washington, D.C. use a "winner-take-all" system, so the winner of a state gets all of its electoral votes, even if the race is close. Plumer points out that because of this, candidates spend almost all their time in a few "swing states" and ignore everyone else. That means if I lived in a state that always votes one way, my vote would hardly matter to the campaigns. This can make people feel like voting is pointless, which Plumer says lowers turnout across the country. A popular vote would give candidates a reason to talk to voters everywhere, because every vote would count toward the total.

I know there are good arguments on the other side. Judge Richard Posner, in "In Defense of the Electoral College," says it protects federalism and forces candidates to build broad coalitions across big and small states instead of just running up huge totals in crowded cities. I understand this concern, and I do not want rural areas to be forgotten. However, under the current system candidates already ignore many small states and focus on a few swing states, so the system does not really protect small states the way Posner says. With a popular vote, a farmer in a small town would count the same as a person in a big city, and candidates would have to care about both to get the most votes overall.

Posner also says the Electoral College gives a clear winner quickly and keeps recounts inside individual states instead of a giant national recount. That is a fair point, because a national recount sounds complicated. But the Federal Register says the electoral system already has 538 electors and a state-by-state process, and that did not stop close races in 2000 from becoming a mess. Also, a national election would probably have bigger margins than a single state, so a recount would be needed less often. If a recount did happen, I think it is worth the trouble to make sure the result is right. We should not keep an unfair system just because it is easier.

Finally, Plumer mentions "faithless electors," who could vote against what their state's voters chose. Even if this does not happen often, it is risky to let a few people possibly ignore the voters. A popular vote would remove that problem completely.

For these reasons, I hope you will support moving to a national popular vote for president. Every citizen should have an equal voice, and the person with the most votes should win. Thank you for taking the time to read my letter.

Sincerely,
[Name]

Extracurricular activities are a vital part of the high school experience, offering students a chance to explore their passions and interests outside the traditional classroom. From the thrill of competition on the sports field to the creativity of designing yearbook pages, or debating school policies on the student council, these activities often bring out the best in students. However, the principal's decision to make participation in at least one extracurricular activity mandatory is a step in the wrong direction. This policy, although well-intentioned, fails to consider the diverse personal obligations of students, undermines the genuine enthusiasm that makes clubs thrive, and introduces unnecessary stress into already demanding schedules.

The reality is that students' lives outside of school are complex and varied. Once the final bell rings, high schoolers do not all follow the same path. Many have to commute to part-time jobs to support their families financially, while others have critical responsibilities at home, such as caring for younger siblings or assisting elderly relatives. By imposing a mandatory after-school commitment, the school is placing an unfair burden on these students. They may be forced to choose between meeting their family obligations and satisfying the school's requirement, potentially sacrificing their academic performance in the process.

Moreover, compulsory participation in extracurricular activities undermines the very nature of what makes them valuable: the freedom to choose. When students are given the autonomy to pursue their interests, they are more likely to be genuinely engaged and enthusiastic. In contrast, forcing students to participate in an activity can lead to disengagement and resentment. A student council, for example, that is filled with apathetic participants will struggle to foster meaningful leadership and creativity. Similarly, sports teams and creative clubs rely on dedication and positive energy to thrive. Summer break gives students something school rarely does: long stretches of unstructured time. Schools that assign summer projects want to protect learning during that time, but the question of who designs the project matters a great deal. Although teacher-designed projects offer clear structure, summer projects should be student-designed, because they build motivation, teach independence, and produce deeper learning than assignments students complete only for a grade.

The strongest argument for student-designed projects is motivation. During the school year, teachers can rely on deadlines, daily reminders, and classroom routines to keep students working. In summer, those supports disappear, and a project that feels like a chore is likely to be postponed until the last week of August. A student who chooses her own topic has a reason to start early. A girl who loves baking might research how altitude, humidity, and ingredient ratios affect bread, keeping a journal of experiments. A teacher-assigned book report would probably get a rushed weekend of effort; the baking project could fill the whole summer, and she would be practicing measurement, chemistry, and writing along the way.

Student-designed projects also teach skills that teacher-designed ones cannot. Planning a project means setting goals, breaking work into steps, finding resources, and managing time without an adult watching. These are the habits colleges and employers say they value most, yet students seldom practice them when every assignment arrives with a rubric. A student who decides to build a simple website for a local animal shelter must figure out what the shelter needs, learn basic coding, and fix problems when something fails. That experience teaches self-direction in a way a worksheet packet never could.

Critics argue that students, left alone, will choose easy projects or none at all, and that teachers are better able to ensure academic rigor. This concern is reasonable, but it can be addressed without taking the design away from students. Schools can require a proposal in June that a teacher must approve, with criteria such as a clear question, a plan, and a final product. Teachers can offer guidelines, sample ideas, and a mid-summer check-in by email. In this model, the teacher acts as a coach and quality-control reviewer rather than the author of the assignment. Students still own the idea, but the school still ensures that real learning takes place.

Another concern is fairness. Students with fewer resources, such as money for materials or access to museums and travel, may struggle to design ambitious projects. Yet student-designed does not have to mean expensive. A student can interview grandparents about family history, track the plants growing in a neighborhood park, or teach herself a programming language using free library resources. In fact, open-ended projects are often fairer than assigned ones, because students can build on their own circumstances, languages, and communities instead of being measured against a single narrow task that may not fit their lives.

Finally, student-designed projects make learning feel valuable rather than obligatory. When students return in the fall and present what they discovered, they share work that reflects their own curiosity, and classmates often become inspired by one another's ideas. A room of students describing experiments, stories, and inventions is far more energizing than a stack of identical assignments.

In conclusion, summer projects should be student-designed, with teacher guidance and approval. This approach motivates students, develops independence, and accommodates different interests and backgrounds. If the goal is to keep students learning over the summer, the best strategy is to let them pursue questions they actually care about.

Dear Principal,

I am writing about your idea to require all students to perform community service. I know there are strong opinions on both sides, but I believe students should be required to do a small amount of community service before they graduate.

Some of my friends already volunteer, and they get a lot out of it. My friend Dana tutors elementary school kids at the library twice a month. She says it can be frustrating when a kid doesn’t understand something, but when it finally clicks, she feels like she actually made a difference. Another friend spends Saturday mornings picking up litter with his soccer team. He complains about it sometimes, but he also notices that the park stays cleaner because people see them out there. These examples show that service doesn’t have to be huge to matter.

I also know students who think community service takes too much time. They have homework, sports, jobs, and family responsibilities. I get that. But that’s why the requirement should be reasonable—maybe 20 or 25 hours per year, with flexible options. If it’s required, the school can help set up opportunities during lunch, after school, or on weekends so students are not left trying to figure it out alone. A small requirement would not ruin anyone’s schedule.

Requiring service also makes it fair. Right now, the students who volunteer are usually the ones whose parents push them or who already have connections. Other students never get asked or don’t know where to start. If the school requires it, everyone gets the same chance. The school could keep a list of approved places, like the food bank, animal shelter, nursing home, or elementary school. Students could choose something that fits their interests. For example, someone who likes working with kids could tutor, and someone who likes being outside could clean up a park.

I had an experience like this last fall when my class helped at a food bank. I’ll be honest—I didn’t want to go. I thought it would be boring and I had a lot of homework. But I went because it was part of a class project. Once I got there, I saw how many families depended on the food we sorted. I worked with people I usually don’t talk to, and we actually had fun. If it had been optional, I probably would have skipped it. That one afternoon changed how I think about my own town.

I understand that forcing students to volunteer might make it feel like a chore. But I think the benefits are bigger than that. If we keep the requirement small and give students choices, it can teach us responsibility and show us that we are part of something larger than ourselves. We might complain at first, but many of us will end up glad we did it.

Thank you for listening to our opinions. I hope you will consider making community service a graduation requirement with a flexible, reasonable number of hours.

Sincerely,  
Jordan M.

The question of whether summer projects should be assigned by teachers or shaped by students has drawn plenty of attention in schools. Some people value teacher-designed assignments for their structure and clear expectations. However, I believe student-designed projects are the stronger option for keeping students learning over the summer. When students have real control over what they study and how they approach it, they engage more deeply with content and build important life skills along the way.

One clear advantage of student-designed projects is that they allow students to follow their own interests, which makes learning feel less like an obligation. A student who loves environmental science, for example, might choose to survey local wildlife or plan a small sustainable garden. Because the topic matters to them personally, they are more likely to put real effort into research and problem-solving. Teacher-designed projects can be well organized, but they cannot always match the wide range of interests in a classroom. When assignments feel disconnected from students' passions, the work can become superficial.

In addition to boosting motivation, student-designed projects push students to think critically and solve problems independently. Designing a project from scratch means setting a goal, planning steps, adjusting when things go wrong, and reflecting on the results. A student working on an astronomy project might struggle to gather data or build a model, but working through those difficulties builds resilience and resourcefulness. These are exactly the habits students need in college and in the workplace, where problems rarely come with a ready-made set of instructions.

Student-designed projects also give teachers a practical way to support different learning styles and needs. When students can choose their own topics and methods, they can shape the project around their strengths. A student with a learning disability, for instance, might incorporate assistive technology or break the project into smaller steps. That flexibility helps more students participate fully and feel successful. It also sends the message that there is more than one way to demonstrate understanding.

Of course, teacher-designed projects may offer useful consistency and ensure that everyone covers specific material. Still, the benefits of student choice are hard to ignore. Student-designed summer projects encourage curiosity, strengthen independent thinking, and make room for a wider range of learners. By trusting students to take ownership of their education during the break, schools can help them return in the fall not only with new knowledge, but also with greater confidence in their ability to learn on their own.

I am writing to share my thoughts on the proposed changes to our school's cell phone rules. Between the two options being considered, I strongly believe Policy 1 is the better path forward. Allowing students to carry their phones and use them during lunch or free periods—while keeping them turned off and put away during instructional time—strikes the right balance between classroom focus and everyday practicality.

First, having access to our phones matters for student safety and daily communication. After-school schedules shift constantly. An athletic practice might get canceled due to rain, a ride home might run late, or a student might need to confirm a ride to a medical appointment. Expecting hundreds of students to queue up at the front office to make simple phone calls places an unnecessary burden on the office staff. More importantly, in the rare event of an urgent family situation or campus emergency, being able to reach parents directly offers peace of mind that cannot be replaced. Policy 1 preserves that vital line of communication without compromising the classroom, since devices remain off throughout instructional periods.

Second, Policy 1 is far more realistic to enforce. While a total ban sounds straightforward on paper, in reality it turns teachers into hall monitors who must constantly search for hidden screens and handle endless confiscations. Many students would inevitably sneak their phones in anyway, driving the behavior underground and wasting valuable class time on arguments. On the other hand, when students know they have an approved window at lunch to check their messages, they feel much less tempted to take a risky look under their desks during a lecture. When rules feel reasonable, students are far more inclined to cooperate.

Just as importantly, Policy 1 helps us build personal responsibility. In college or any future workplace, no one is going to confiscate our devices at the entrance. Instead, we will be expected to know when it is appropriate to check our screens and when our undivided attention is required. High school should be a place where we practice that kind of self-discipline, not an artificial environment that pretends technology does not exist. Setting clear boundaries treats students like maturing young adults and gives us the opportunity to live up to that expectation.

I understand the concern that phones can easily disrupt learning, and I agree that ringing devices and texting during class harm academic focus. However, Policy 1 directly tackles that issue by requiring phones to be turned off during instruction, and straightforward consequences—such as having a device held in the office until dismissal—can quickly deter repeat offenses. 

Ultimately, Policy 1 protects instructional time while acknowledging the realities of daily life. It encourages mutual trust, keeps families connected, and saves teachers from having to police an impractical ban. Driverless cars have the potential to change transportation in major ways, but they should not be widely used until their safety problems are solved. Although autonomous vehicles could prevent many accidents and help people who cannot drive, the technology is still not reliable enough in difficult situations. There are also important questions about who would be responsible if a driverless car caused a crash. For these reasons, driverless cars should continue to be tested, but they should not replace regular cars yet.

One strong argument for driverless cars is that they could save lives. According to the article, human error causes more than 90 percent of traffic accidents. Drivers may text while driving, fall asleep, speed, or drive while impaired. A computer would not get distracted by a phone or become tired after a long day. Driverless cars use laser radar, cameras, GPS, and sensors to notice obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals. If these systems work correctly, they could react more consistently than many human drivers. Fewer accidents could also lower insurance costs and make roads safer for everyone.

Driverless cars could also help people who have trouble driving themselves. Elderly people, disabled passengers, and people with medical conditions might be able to travel more independently in an autonomous vehicle. Instead of depending on family members, buses, or taxis, they could use a driverless car to get to work, school, appointments, or stores. Sergey Brin imagines driverless public transportation that would use less fuel and require less parking space. This could reduce pollution and make crowded cities easier to travel through.

However, the article also explains why these cars are not ready for full use. Their sensors can have trouble in heavy rain, snow, or fog. They may also struggle in construction zones where lane markings are missing or changed. Human drivers can sometimes understand confusing situations by using judgment and experience, but a computer may not know what to do if its sensors cannot clearly read the road. A mistake in bad weather or a construction zone could lead to a serious accident.

Another concern is that semi-autonomous cars still need people to take control during emergencies. Studies show that when a computer is driving, passengers quickly stop paying close attention. If the car suddenly needs help, the human driver may react too slowly. In that situation, the technology could actually create a new danger because people may trust it too much.

Finally, no one has clearly decided who is legally responsible when a driverless car crashes. Would it be the owner of the car, the automaker, or the software developer? Until those questions are answered, victims of accidents might have difficulty receiving justice.

Driverless cars offer exciting benefits, especially safer roads and more independence for people who cannot drive. Still, their weaknesses in dangerous conditions and the unanswered legal questions show that they need more development. The goal should be safer transportation, not rushing new technology onto the road before it is truly ready.

When my cousin Daniel was deciding between two college offers, he did what most people do first: he called his father. His dad, an engineer who had paid off his own student loans over eleven years, told him to take the cheaper state school without hesitation. It was sound advice, and Daniel nearly followed it. Then he talked to a professor from his high school, who pointed out something his father had not considered: the pricier private university had a co-op program that placed nearly every student in a paid job in his field before graduation. That single detail changed the math. Daniel ended up at the private school, graduated with less debt than anyone predicted, and had a job offer in hand by spring.

His story shows the central value of asking more than one person. Every advisor sees the problem through a particular window. A parent sees risk because a parent's job is, in part, to prevent disaster. A friend may see loyalty and excitement. A coworker sees office politics and promotion ladders. None of these views is wrong, but each is partial, and the gaps are invisible to the person who holds the view. Daniel's father wasn't careless; he simply didn't know co-op programs existed in the form the professor described.

Different opinions also expose bias, both the advisor's and our own. If three people tell you to quit a job and one urges you to stay, you can ask why that one disagrees. Perhaps she is the only one who has seen your manager's plans for the department. Or perhaps she depends on you to cover her shifts. Either way, the disagreement gives you something to investigate, which a chorus of agreement never would. And when everyone does agree, especially people with different backgrounds and no shared stake in the outcome, you can trust the conclusion more than any single voice could earn.

There is a quieter benefit, too. Explaining a dilemma over and over forces you to sharpen it. The first time Daniel described his situation, he rambled about tuition and homesickness. By the third conversation he had realized that what he really cared about was whether a school would lead to work he liked, and money was just the constraint around that. Hearing his own summary shift from one retelling to the next showed him what he valued. Advisors don't only supply information; they act as mirrors, and several mirrors at different angles show more of the face.

None of this means more voices are always better. Ask twenty people and you may drown in contradiction, or you may simply shop around until someone says what you already wanted to hear. That is not seeking advice; it is seeking permission. The skill lies in choosing a few people who differ from one another in experience and temperament, then weighing what each says against what they know and what they stand to gain. A cautious relative, an optimistic friend, and someone who has actually done the thing in question make a better panel than three people who think alike.

In the end, the decision still belongs to the person making it. But a choice informed by several perspectives rests on a wider base of facts, has been tested against honest disagreement, and has been clarified by repeated explanation. Daniel's father still jokes that he was almost responsible for the worst financial decision of his son's life. He says it fondly, because the second opinion proved him partly wrong and made the final choice better.

Summer break can be a welcome relief, but it often comes with a hidden cost. Research on the "summer slide" shows that months away from the classroom cause many students to lose ground in both reading and math. While schools are right to assign summer work to counter this drop-off, the real debate centers on who should create these assignments. Although teacher-designed packets offer an easy, predictable framework, summer projects should ultimately be student-designed within broad teacher guidelines. When students take ownership of their work, they stay more engaged and learn far more deeply.

The biggest factor during the summer is personal motivation. Unlike the regular school year, summer work happens without bells, daily attendance, or teachers standing nearby to answer questions and keep everyone on task. A generic assignment, like twenty pages of math worksheets or a standard report on a book nobody wanted to read, usually gets shoved under a bed until the final week of August—or simply ignored. On the other hand, an assignment a student actually chose gives them a reason to stick with it. Consider a student passionate about basketball who decides to analyze team shooting percentages and write an article on how shot selection affects winning streaks. That student is voluntarily practicing data analysis, research, and persuasive writing without feeling like school has invaded their vacation. When interest drives the work, effort naturally follows, and that sustained effort is what actually prevents learning loss.

Designing a project also forces students to develop independence in ways traditional homework rarely does. Managing a project from scratch means defining a goal, mapping out a schedule, finding resources, and problem-solving along the way. These self-regulation skills are essential for college and adulthood, yet typical classroom assignments provide few chances to practice them. A student who chooses to build a backyard raised-bed garden, for instance, has to figure out which crops thrive in their local climate, draft a budget for materials, monitor soil conditions, and adjust when plants struggle or pests arrive. That kind of hands-on decision-making teaches practical problem-solving that no pre-printed packet could ever replicate.

Naturally, skeptics worry that students given free rein might pick trivial topics or look for the easiest way out, making it harder for teachers to evaluate work fairly. These concerns make sense, but they call for thoughtful guidance rather than total teacher control. In late spring, teachers can have students submit short proposals outlining their main question, goals, and working timeline. Teachers can also set baseline criteria—such as requiring a research component, a log of weekly progress, and a final presentation—or offer broad categories like scientific inquiry, community service, or creative arts. This approach keeps academic standards high while letting the teacher serve as an advisor instead of an assigner of busywork.

Finally, student-driven projects make returning to school in the fall much more rewarding. Sharing a self-directed project lets classmates learn from each other's interests and gives teachers a quick window into who their new students are. An identical worksheet packet is simply stamped, graded, and forgotten. If the true goal of summer learning is intellectual growth, engagement matters far more than uniformity. When students are empowered to follow their own curiosity, summer becomes a genuine opportunity to learn.

Dear Senator,

I urge you to support changing presidential elections to a national popular vote. The Electoral College was created as a constitutional compromise, but a system that made sense at the nation’s founding no longer gives every citizen’s vote equal influence. In a democracy, the candidate who receives the most votes from Americans should become President.

The Federal Register explains that the Electoral College has 538 electors and requires 270 electoral votes to win. Each state receives electors based on its members of Congress: its House delegation plus two senators. This arrangement gives smaller states somewhat more influence per voter than larger states. More importantly, nearly every state awards all of its electoral votes to the candidate who wins that state, even if the margin is only a few votes. Thus, millions of votes for the losing candidate in a state do not affect the final result.

This winner-take-all approach has produced outcomes that conflict with the public’s overall choice. Bradford Plumer notes that candidates who won the national popular vote lost the presidency in both 2000 and 2016. That possibility undermines public confidence because voters can reasonably ask why a candidate with fewer votes nationwide should receive the country’s highest office. A popular-vote system would establish a simple and fair principle: every vote would count equally, whether it came from a rural county, a small state, a large city, or a suburban community.

The current system also distorts campaigning. According to Plumer, candidates focus heavily on a small number of competitive “swing states” while largely ignoring states considered safely Democratic or Republican. As a result, voters in many states receive fewer campaign visits, less attention to local concerns, and less incentive to participate. Under a national popular vote, no state would be “safe” in the same way. A candidate would have a reason to seek votes everywhere, including among supporters in states the candidate is unlikely to win outright.

Supporters of the Electoral College, including Judge Richard A. Posner, argue that it protects federalism, encourages broad coalitions, and prevents candidates from relying only on large urban areas. Those are serious concerns. However, a popular vote would not erase the importance of states or regions; candidates would still need support from diverse communities to gain a national majority or plurality. Nor could a candidate win solely by appealing to cities, since even the nation’s largest metropolitan areas do not contain enough voters to decide an election alone. Rural, suburban, and small-town voters would remain essential parts of a nationwide coalition.

Posner also argues that the Electoral College allows disputes to be resolved within individual states rather than through a national recount. Yet close elections are rare, and modern election standards could provide clear procedures for a nationwide recount when necessary. Avoiding a difficult recount should not justify a system that can reject the choice of most voters. Moreover, the possibility of “faithless electors,” identified by Plumer, adds another unnecessary layer between citizens and the outcome.

The Electoral College was intended as a compromise, not as an unchangeable rule immune from reconsideration. Our presidential election system should reflect the fundamental democratic belief that each citizen’s vote deserves equal weight. I ask you to support efforts to move the United States toward election of the President by national popular vote.

Sincerely,  
A Concerned Constituent

The idea of driverless cars is often presented as an exciting and unavoidable part of the future. However, the article “Driverless Cars Are Coming” shows that this technology still has serious risks and unanswered questions. Although autonomous vehicles could provide important benefits, I believe their widespread development and use should be slowed until safety, technological, and legal concerns are resolved. The possibility of fewer accidents is promising, but it does not justify placing unreliable technology on public roads.

Supporters of driverless cars have strong reasons for their optimism. According to the article, human error causes more than 90 percent of traffic accidents. Drivers may text, become tired, or drive while impaired, all of which can lead to deadly mistakes. A computer-controlled vehicle would not get distracted, fall asleep, or make the choice to drive after drinking. As a result, driverless cars could reduce crashes, save lives, and possibly lower insurance costs. They could also give elderly and disabled people more independence by providing transportation when they cannot drive themselves. These are meaningful advantages, and they show why research on autonomous vehicles should continue.

Still, the benefits of driverless cars depend on the technology working safely in all kinds of real-life situations. The article explains that current sensors can have trouble in heavy rain, snow, fog, and unmarked construction zones. These conditions are already difficult for human drivers, so a vehicle that cannot respond correctly in them could create even more danger. A car may have cameras, laser radar, GPS, and computer sensors, but those tools are only useful if they can accurately understand what is happening around the vehicle. If a sensor cannot recognize a lane marking or obstacle during a storm, the consequences could be serious.

Another concern is that autonomous software can have glitches or become the target of cybersecurity threats. A mistake in the software could cause a vehicle to react incorrectly or fail to react at all. Even worse, if someone were able to hack a driverless car, they could put passengers and others on the road at risk. Unlike a human driver’s mistake, a software problem could potentially affect many vehicles using the same system. Before driverless cars become common, companies must prove that their technology can resist these dangers.

Semi-autonomous cars also create a difficult situation for drivers. The article states that these vehicles still require humans to remain alert and take control in emergencies. However, studies show that people quickly lose focus when a computer is doing the driving, which slows their reaction time. This creates a dangerous middle ground: the car is not fully capable of handling every situation, but the person behind the wheel may no longer be ready to respond. Asking drivers to pay close attention while rarely needing to act may not be realistic.

Finally, important legal and ethical issues remain unsettled. If a driverless car causes an accident, it is unclear who should be responsible: the owner, the automaker, or the software developer. Without clear rules, accident victims may have difficulty receiving fair treatment. Companies also need to be held accountable when flaws in their systems cause harm.

Driverless cars may someday make travel safer and more accessible, but that day has not arrived yet. Research should continue because the potential benefits are valuable. However, autonomous vehicles should not be rushed into widespread use until they can handle dangerous weather, avoid software and cybersecurity failures, keep drivers prepared for emergencies, and operate under clear legal rules. Society should move carefully toward this future instead of allowing excitement about new technology to outweigh public safety.

Dear Principal,

I believe students should be required to perform community service, but the requirement should be reasonable and flexible. Community service can teach lessons that are hard to learn in a classroom. It helps students understand that they are part of a larger community, not just people who go to school, do homework, and spend time with friends.

For example, my friend volunteers as a tutor for younger students at an elementary school. At first, she said she was nervous because she did not think she would know how to help children who were struggling with reading. However, after a few weeks, she learned how to explain things more patiently. She also told me that one student she worked with began raising his hand more in class. My friend felt proud because she could actually see that her time made a difference. She learned responsibility and patience, but the younger student also got extra help.

Community service can also improve the place where we live. Some students in our town have helped clean up litter near parks and sidewalks. It may not sound exciting, but when people see trash everywhere, they may think nobody cares about the neighborhood. Cleaning it up makes the area safer and nicer for everyone, especially little kids and older people who use the parks. If more students helped with projects like this, our community could benefit in many small but important ways.

I understand why some students do not want a requirement. Many students already have sports, jobs, family responsibilities, and difficult classes. Students could choose from different options, including tutoring, helping at food drives, visiting nursing homes, cleaning up public spaces, or assisting at school events. Students with jobs or family duties could have more time to complete the hours or be allowed to do service connected to responsibilities they already have.

A requirement might also encourage students who would never volunteer on their own to try it. At first, they may only do it because they have to, but they could discover that they enjoy helping. Not every student will suddenly love community service, but most people can find one activity that matters to them.

School is supposed to prepare us for life, not only for tests and college applications. In adult life, communities depend on people who are willing to help others. Requiring a fair amount of community service would teach students that their actions can have a positive effect. For these reasons, I believe all students should complete community service, as long as the program gives them choices and respects their other responsibilities.

Drivers should not be able to use cell phones while operating a vehicle, except in a true emergency when there is no safer choice. Cell phones are useful for communication, directions, and entertainment, but driving requires a person’s full attention. Even a short glance at a screen can be enough time for a car to drift, miss a stop sign, or fail to notice someone crossing the road.

Many people think texting is the only dangerous phone activity. Texting is definitely one of the worst because it takes a driver’s eyes, hands, and mind away from driving at the same time. However, other types of phone use can also be risky. Changing a song, answering a call, checking a notification, or typing an address into a map may only take a few seconds, but traffic can change quickly. At 55 miles per hour, a car travels a long distance in just five seconds. A driver who looks down during that time could pass through an intersection without noticing a red light or a stopped vehicle.

Some people argue that hands-free calling should be allowed because the driver can keep both hands on the wheel. While that is better than holding a phone, it does not solve the whole problem. A phone conversation can distract someone mentally. When a person is listening carefully, arguing, or thinking about what to say next, they may not notice hazards around them as quickly. Talking to a passenger is different because a passenger can see the road and may stop talking when traffic becomes difficult. A person on the phone cannot do that.

Navigation is another common reason people use phones in cars. Maps can be helpful, especially when drivers are traveling somewhere unfamiliar. Still, drivers should enter the destination before they start the car or after they pull over safely. A phone could be mounted where it can give directions by voice, but the driver should not be tapping, searching, or reading messages from it while moving. The goal should be to keep the phone from becoming the main focus.

There should also be clear laws and consequences for distracted driving. Fines or penalties may seem strict, but they can remind people that using a phone is not a harmless habit. Drivers are responsible not only for themselves, but also for passengers, pedestrians, cyclists, and other drivers. One distracted choice can affect many people.

Of course, emergencies are different. If someone is in danger, sees a serious crash, or needs urgent help, using a phone may be necessary. In most normal situations, though, the safest choice is simple: wait until the vehicle is parked. A message, call, or video can wait, but a life may not.

In recent years, distance learning has changed from a rare alternative into a common educational option. Although some people argue that learning from home cannot match the energy and interaction of a traditional classroom, I believe students benefit from having the choice to attend classes online or through video conferencing. When it is used thoughtfully, distance learning can make education more flexible, accessible, and responsive to students’ individual needs.

One important advantage is flexibility. A regular school schedule does not work equally well for every student. Some students may be recovering from an illness, traveling with family, caring for relatives, or pursuing demanding activities outside school. With online classes, they can stay connected to their coursework instead of missing lessons and struggling to catch up later. For example, a high school gymnast who has afternoon practices could watch a recorded biology lecture in the evening and participate in a live class discussion the next morning. This type of arrangement can lower stress while still holding students responsible for completing their work.

Distance learning can also give students access to classes and teachers that their local schools cannot provide. A small or rural school may not have enough students or funding to employ a full-time teacher for Latin, advanced computer science, or music theory. Through video conferencing, however, students could join a class taught by a qualified instructor in another district. This allows schools to offer more opportunities without needing every subject taught in the same building. Online learning may also help students with disabilities, chronic health conditions, or severe anxiety. Features such as closed captioning, screen readers, recorded lessons, and a quieter learning environment can make participation easier. In this sense, distance learning does not need to replace in-person school; it can fill gaps that traditional schools sometimes cannot.

Another benefit is that learning from home can help students become more independent. Students who organize their schedules, submit assignments online, and communicate with teachers through email or chat gain skills that will be useful in college and future jobs. For instance, a student who watches a recorded lesson, takes careful notes, and asks questions during a video conference is learning how to manage responsibilities without constant reminders. These habits encourage self-discipline and digital responsibility, both of which are increasingly important in modern life.

Of course, distance learning is not perfect. Students may miss face-to-face friendships and group activities, while others might struggle to stay motivated at home. Reliable internet access is also a serious concern for some families. Still, schools can reduce these problems by providing devices and internet support, scheduling regular teacher check-ins, and offering blended programs that combine online and in-person learning. The purpose should not be to require every student to learn from home, but to make it a realistic option for those who need or prefer it.

Overall, students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home. Distance learning provides flexibility, expands access to courses and support, and helps students develop useful independent-learning skills. When schools offer it as one option among several, they can better meet students’ different circumstances and help more learners succeed.

I disagree with the decision to make every student participate in an extracurricular activity. Clubs, sports, and student organizations can be great experiences, but forcing students to join them would not make those experiences better. Instead, it could create stress for students who already have busy lives and make activities less meaningful for the students who actually want to be there.

First, many students have responsibilities outside of school that teachers and principals may not see. Some students have jobs after school to help their families pay bills or save money for college. Others babysit younger siblings, help take care of relatives, or spend time commuting home. If every student had to join a sport, club, or organization, these students might have to give up important responsibilities or become exhausted trying to do everything.

For example, one of my classmates works at a grocery store several afternoons a week. He does not work because he wants extra spending money; he works because his family needs help. If he were required to join an extracurricular activity, he might have to choose between keeping his job and meeting a school requirement. That is not a fair choice. School should support students, not add another problem to their lives.

Also, students should have some control over how they spend their free time. After a full day of classes, homework, tests, and projects, some students need time to rest. Others may prefer activities that are not connected to school, such as taking music lessons, volunteering at a church, helping at a family business, or practicing art at home. These are still valuable activities, even if they are not officially listed as a school club.

Mandatory participation could also hurt the activities themselves. Teams and clubs work best when members care about what they are doing. Imagine being on the yearbook staff with students who only joined because they had to. They might not attend meetings, finish their assignments, or take the work seriously. The same could happen in sports or student council. Coaches and club leaders would have to spend more time managing unwilling students instead of helping interested students improve.

I do think schools should encourage extracurricular activities. They help students make friends, learn leadership, and discover interests they may not find in regular classes. The school could hold a club fair, make joining easier, provide late buses, or recognize students who participate. Counselors could also help students find activities that fit their schedules.

However, encouragement is different from forcing everyone to participate. Students have different family situations, schedules, and needs. Extracurricular activities should be opportunities, not requirements.

In the past few years, almost every student had to try online school in one way or another. While some people couldn't wait to get back into the building, a lot of kids actually realized that learning from home worked better for them. In my opinion, schools should definitely offer distance learning as an option for students. It does not mean everyone has to stay home, but having it as a choice gives students more flexibility, lowers stress, and helps people with different learning styles succeed.

First of all, distance learning is a lifesaver when it comes to health and personal issues. In a regular school year, if you catch a bad cold or have a family emergency, you might miss three or four days in a row. By the time you get back, your desk is piled high with missing worksheets, and you have to spend your lunch periods trying to catch up on quizzes. If online learning is an option, students who are sick in bed can still watch the live stream or check the recorded lesson if they feel up to it. That way, nobody falls completely behind just because life happens. It is also amazing for students who have chronic illnesses and cannot safely be around hundreds of other kids every single day.

Another major benefit is that the traditional classroom is not the best environment for everyone. High school can be super loud and distracting. There are always people whispering in the back, phones going off, or drama happening in the hallways. For students who have social anxiety or ADHD, sitting in a crowded room for seven hours can be completely exhausting. At home, you can control your space. You can sit in a quiet bedroom, wear comfortable clothes, and actually focus on what the teacher is saying instead of worrying about who is looking at you. Some of my classmates who were really quiet in person actually participated way more in the chat box during video calls because they felt less judged.

Finally, attending classes from home saves a lot of time and energy. Most teenagers are constantly sleep-deprived because school starts ridiculously early. For a lot of us, that means waking up at 5:30 in the morning just to catch a bus and ride it for forty-five minutes. When you learn from home, you cut out that whole commute. That extra hour of sleep might not sound like a huge deal to adults, but it makes a massive difference in how well you can pay attention during first period. 

Of course, some students need the routine of in-person classes, and they miss seeing their friends or doing hands-on activities like science labs and sports. That makes sense, which is why distance learning should be an option rather than something forced on the whole school. Giving students the freedom to choose what works best for their own mental health and study habits would make school a much better experience for everyone.

Dear Principal,

I respectfully urge you not to require a B average for students to take part in sports and other activities. Academic success should always be a priority, but this policy would shut out many of the students who need activities most. A better approach would be to give struggling students academic support while still letting them stay involved.

To begin with, activities often help students do better in school instead of pulling them away from it. Whether they play on a team, perform in band, join debate, or act in the school play, students have to learn to manage their time. Practices, meetings, games, and performances push them to finish homework efficiently. For some students, wanting to stay on the team is the main reason they come to school every day and try in class. If one missed assignment could take away the activity that motivates them, they may become discouraged rather than improve.

In addition, a B average does not measure effort or potential. A student might earn a C because of difficult classes, a learning disability, family responsibilities, a job, an illness, or the challenge of adjusting to a new school. Someone in advanced courses may work far harder for a C than another student does for a B in easier classes. Judging everyone by a single number ignores these differences. Schools should encourage growth, not punish students who are still working toward higher grades.

Activities also teach lessons that a classroom cannot always provide. Sports build teamwork, perseverance, leadership, and discipline. Clubs give students chances to speak in public, solve problems, volunteer, and meet people who share their interests. These experiences build confidence and help students feel connected to their school. If students with C averages were removed from activities, many would feel isolated. Rather than improving their performance, they could lose the sense of belonging that helps them stay focused and responsible.

Of course, students should be expected to take their schoolwork seriously. Instead of a strict B-average rule, the school could use a system that combines support with accountability. For example, students whose grades fall below a C could be required to attend tutoring, meet with their teachers, turn in missing work, or follow an academic improvement plan. Those who still make no effort could face temporary restrictions. This approach would show that grades matter while giving students a fair chance to improve.

A school exists not only to honor students who are already succeeding but also to help every student become more successful. A B-average requirement would exclude many students who could benefit from encouragement, structure, and a sense of connection. I hope you will consider policies that support academic improvement without taking away the activities that inspire students to do their best.

Sincerely,  
A Concerned Student
