In recent years, distance learning has evolved from an emergency measure into a legitimate educational option. Although some argue that attending school in person is essential for social development and engagement, students can still benefit greatly from being able to attend classes from home. When implemented thoughtfully, online and video-conferencing classes provide flexibility, increase accessibility, and allow students to learn in ways that suit their individual needs.

One major advantage of distance learning is flexibility. Students are no longer bound by a rigid school schedule or lengthy commutes. This freedom is especially valuable for students with demanding extracurricular commitments, family responsibilities, or health challenges. For example, a student recovering from surgery can keep up with lessons from bed instead of falling behind for weeks. Likewise, a competitive athlete who travels for tournaments can attend class from a hotel room. By removing the need to be physically present, schools allow education to continue without interruption.

Distance learning also makes education more accessible. Students who live in rural areas, have disabilities, or experience social anxiety can participate fully from a comfortable environment. Video conferencing can include live captions, recordings, and screen-sharing tools that benefit students with hearing impairments or processing difficulties. A student with a compromised immune system, for instance, may otherwise miss valuable instruction to avoid exposure to illness. With distance options, that student can remain part of the class safely. This kind of inclusion is a clear benefit that traditional classrooms cannot always provide.

Furthermore, learning from home can support personalized instruction. Many online platforms allow students to pause, rewind, and review recorded lessons at their own pace. In a traditional classroom, a concept explained once may be missed; online, a student can revisit the material until it is understood. Additionally, some students find it easier to concentrate at home, away from hallway noise and peer distractions. Teachers can also use chat features and breakout rooms, giving quieter students more ways to contribute than in a large classroom discussion.

Of course, distance learning is not without challenges, such as the need for reliable internet and self-discipline. However, these problems can be addressed through school support and clear expectations. The benefits of flexibility, accessibility, and personalized learning outweigh the drawbacks when distance learning is offered as an option rather than a replacement. Therefore, students would indeed benefit from being able to attend classes from home. Schools should continue to expand distance learning opportunities, allowing more students to access education in ways that fit their lives and needs.

When people face a difficult decision, asking someone for advice can offer useful insight. However, seeking out several opinions often leads to an even better choice. Hearing from different people allows us to compare perspectives, notice recurring advice, and prepare for problems we might otherwise overlook.

One benefit of asking multiple people is that it exposes us to a wider range of experiences. Imagine trying to decide whether to switch careers. A person might talk with a veteran in the field to learn about long-term opportunities and with someone who recently entered the profession to understand the challenges of starting out. A career counselor could add a more neutral view about skills and qualifications. Each source fills in a different piece of the picture. Together, they provide a fuller understanding of both the advantages and the risks involved.

Another reason to gather several opinions is that it helps us spot patterns. When different people express the same concern, that warning becomes harder to ignore. When several people point toward the same solution, it can boost our confidence. For example, a friend of mine spent weeks deciding whether to go straight to graduate school. She talked with professors, alumni, and current students. While their experiences varied, most of them kept returning to the same idea: gain practical work experience before pursuing another degree. That consistency helped her feel more comfortable delaying graduate school and focusing on her career first.

Seeking multiple opinions also helps with planning for possible problems. Before making a large purchase, such as a house or a car, people often ask friends, family members, and professionals for advice. Each person may highlight a different concern. Someone considering a home might speak with a real estate agent about market conditions, a contractor about repair costs, and a financial advisor about budgeting. None of these experts alone can cover every angle, but together they reveal hidden expenses and maintenance issues that might otherwise come as a surprise. With this broader view, the buyer can make a more careful decision and prepare for challenges ahead.

In short, asking more than one person for advice can lead to a wiser decision. Multiple perspectives give us a richer understanding of the options, help us recognize patterns in what we hear, and allow us to anticipate difficulties before they arise. Whether the choice involves a career change, further education, or a major purchase, listening to a variety of voices can reduce uncertainty and build greater confidence. Ultimately, seeking several opinions is a practical way to make decisions that are more thoughtful and better informed.

Dear Senator,

I write to urge you to oppose any effort to replace the Electoral College with a direct national popular vote for president. While critics raise legitimate concerns, the Electoral College remains a vital safeguard of federalism, broad coalition-building, and electoral stability.

Critics such as Bradford Plumer argue that the system is undemocratic because a candidate can win the national popular vote and still lose the presidency, as happened in 2000 and 2016. They also note that the winner-take-all rule used in most states causes candidates to focus almost entirely on a handful of swing states while ignoring voters elsewhere, depressing turnout. These are serious objections. However, abandoning the Electoral College would create even larger problems. Judge Richard Posner explains that the Electoral College forces candidates to build broad national coalitions across large and small states rather than running up massive vote totals in densely populated urban areas or a single region. A national popular vote would encourage candidates to focus on the largest media markets and population centers, leaving rural and smaller states even more marginalized.

The Electoral College also reflects the constitutional design described by the Office of the Federal Register. It was established as a compromise between election by Congress and election by popular vote. Each state’s electors equal its congressional delegation, ensuring that states remain meaningful units in presidential selection. This federal structure helps preserve the voice of smaller states, which a pure popular vote system would diminish.

Furthermore, the Electoral College provides clearer and more manageable outcomes. Posner notes that it avoids nationwide popular-vote recounts by confining disputed vote counts to individual states. A close national popular election could require a chaotic nationwide recount, with every precinct in the country contested. The current system isolates problems, as the 2000 Florida recount demonstrated, rather than throwing the entire nation into uncertainty.

To be sure, the winner-take-all approach contributes to the swing-state focus critics decry. But that is a state policy choice, not a flaw in the Electoral College itself. The Constitution does not require winner-take-all; Maine and Nebraska already allocate electors by congressional district. States could adopt proportional allocation if they wish, addressing some concerns without abandoning the federal framework.

In short, while the popular vote has intuitive appeal, it would centralize presidential campaigns in urban population centers, erode the role of states, and invite national recount chaos. I respectfully ask you to support preserving the Electoral College.

Sincerely,  
[Your Name]  
[Your Address]

Dear Principal,

I am writing to express my strong support for Policy 1, which allows students to bring cell phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times, as long as they are turned off during class. While I understand the appeal of a complete ban, I believe Policy 1 is safer, more practical, and more educational than Policy 2.

First, allowing phones at school helps keep students safe and connected. In an emergency, whether it is a family situation, a sudden change in after-school plans, or a school-wide event, students need a way to reach their parents quickly. For example, if a student becomes ill or needs a ride home, a phone allows immediate communication. During a serious emergency, phones can also be a vital tool for receiving information and reassuring family members. A complete ban would cut off this important lifeline.

Second, Policy 1 teaches students responsibility. In the real world, people must learn to manage their devices wisely. By allowing phones during lunch and free time but requiring them to be off during class, students practice setting boundaries and following clear expectations. This is far more valuable than an all-or-nothing rule. If phones are banned entirely, some students may still bring them secretly, which creates unnecessary conflict and distrust between students and staff. Policy 1 gives students reasonable limits and encourages us to follow them.

Third, free time is exactly when phones can be used positively. During lunch, students can listen to music, catch up on messages, check assignments, or read. These activities help students relax and return to class more focused. Phones can also be used for quick research, taking photos of homework instructions, or setting reminders for upcoming deadlines. Banning them would remove these small but meaningful benefits.

Some may worry that phones distract students or lead to cheating. However, under Policy 1, phones are turned off during class, so instruction remains protected. Teachers can enforce this rule consistently. The answer to misuse is not to ban the tool entirely, but to teach appropriate use and hold students accountable.

In conclusion, Policy 1 offers the best balance. It keeps phones available for safety and communication, builds responsibility, and allows healthy breaks during free time while still protecting classroom learning. I urge you to adopt this policy.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

The modern classroom is no longer tethered to a physical address. With the maturation of video conferencing platforms and digital learning hubs, the choice to attend school from home has shifted from a novelty to a practical pathway. When institutions offer distance learning as an optional alternative, students stand to gain immensely. Far from diluting the educational experience, an off-campus model provides individualized flexibility, expands curricular access, and fosters self-directed discipline vital for the contemporary world.

Much of the value in remote education lies in the relief it offers from the one-size-fits-all rigidity of the conventional schoolhouse. Traditional campuses are sensory-heavy environments laden with social distractions, anxieties, and rigid schedules that rarely align with every adolescent’s circadian rhythm or cognitive style. For students managing chronic health conditions, neurodivergent profiles, or debilitating peer pressures like bullying, the home can serve as a sanctuary. Freed from commute times, classroom disruptions, and the performative social demands of hallways, these learners often discover they can absorb difficult material far more effectively. A teenager struggling with sensory overload in a thirty-person chemistry lecture can, through a screen, regulate their surroundings, pause recorded segments to digest intricate concepts, and engage without crippling apprehension.

Virtual classrooms also shatter geographic constraints. In small or underfunded districts, schools frequently lack the resources to offer specialized coursework, whether an advanced calculus sequence, niche computer programming, or less commonly taught foreign languages like Mandarin or Arabic. Distance learning bridges this divide instantly. A student residing in a remote farming community can attend the same seminar as peers in a well-endowed metropolitan center, democratizing access to elite instruction. Similarly, high-performing young athletes, performing artists, and adolescents who must work part-time to assist their households can mold their studies around demanding schedules rather than being forced to abandon one pursuit for the other.

Critics frequently counter that schooling from home fosters isolation and deprives young people of social development. This concern is valid when distance learning is treated as a blanket mandate, as demonstrated during emergency pandemic lockdowns. Yet as a deliberate, opt-in pathway, it operates quite differently. Most remote students actively seek social engagement outside school through community sports, clubs, and local volunteer initiatives, unencumbered by the exhaustion of eight-hour school days. More importantly, learning from a distance demands a high degree of autonomy. Tracking asynchronous deadlines, communicating clearly across digital channels, and organizing one’s daily schedule cultivate self-reliance—the very capabilities demanded by modern universities and an increasingly decentralized workforce.

Education should bend to serve the student, not the reverse. By offering remote learning as a genuine choice, schools validate the reality that people learn differently and flourish under varied conditions. Embracing this option does not mean abandoning the physical classroom, but rather enriching the educational landscape so that every student can discover an environment where they truly thrive.

The use of cell phones while driving has become a controversial topic in recent years. With the majority of the population owning a cell phone, it's not uncommon to see people using their phones while behind the wheel. However, the question remains, should drivers be allowed to use their cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle? In my opinion, drivers should not be able to use cell phones while driving, except in emergency situations.

One of the main reasons cell phone use should be prohibited while driving is that it can be a significant distraction. When you're driving, you need to be fully focused on the road and your surroundings. Using a cell phone takes your attention away from the road, which can lead to accidents. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, distracted driving was responsible for 3,166 deaths in motor vehicle crashes in 2017. This statistic is alarming and highlights the importance of minimizing distractions while driving.

Texting, in particular, is a hazardous activity to engage in while driving. It requires you to take your eyes off the road and your hands off the wheel, which can be disastrous. Even if you're just checking a text or responding to a message, it can take several seconds, and in that time, you can crash or fail to react to a hazardous situation. Moreover, texting is not the only way cell phones can be a distraction. Talking on the phone, browsing social media, or using apps can all take your attention away from driving.

Some people might argue that using a cell phone while driving is necessary in emergency situations. For instance, if you need to call for help or report an accident, having a cell phone can be lifesaving. In such situations, using a cell phone is justified. However, these situations are rare, and the benefits of allowing cell phone use in emergency situations can be achieved through the use of hands-free devices or by pulling over to a safe location.

Another argument against banning cell phone use while driving is that it can be helpful for navigation or listening to music. While this is true, there are alternative solutions that don't require you to physically interact with your phone. For example, you can use a GPS device or a music player that doesn't require you to touch it while driving. Additionally, many cars now come equipped with Bluetooth technology, which allows you to make hands-free calls and stream music.

In conclusion, the risks associated with using cell phones while driving far outweigh any potential benefits. The distraction caused by cell phones can lead to accidents, injuries, and even fatalities. While there may be situations where using a cell phone is necessary, these situations are rare, and alternative solutions can be found. Therefore, drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle, except in emergency situations. By prohibiting cell phone use while driving, we can reduce the number of accidents on the road and make our roads safer for everyone.

I am writing to share my thoughts on the possible new rule that students would need at least a B average to play sports or join clubs. I understand why you might want to push students to do better in school, but I respectfully disagree with this policy. I think it would hurt more students than it helps, especially since a lot of us are doing okay with a C average.

First, a C average is not the same as failing. Many students work really hard just to keep a C in tough subjects like math, science, or English. For example, my friend Marcus has a C+ overall, but he goes to tutoring twice a week and stays after school to get help from his algebra teacher. He plays on the basketball team, and that is one of the main things that keeps him motivated to show up every day. If this policy goes through, Marcus would be kicked off the team even though he is trying to improve and is passing all his classes. That does not seem fair or encouraging.

Second, being in sports and activities actually helps students do better in school, not worse. When you are on a team or in a club, you have to manage your time because practice or meetings take up part of your afternoon. Coaches already check our grades and make us sit out if we are failing a class. That system works. If you raise the bar to a B average, a lot of students who are passing but not getting Bs would lose that support and structure. Then they might just go home and stare at their phones or play video games, which definitely would not help their grades go up.

Third, not everyone is naturally good at every subject. Some students are amazing at music, art, or athletics even if they struggle with reading or math. Those activities are often the reason they come to school at all. If we take that away unless they have a B average, some kids might stop caring about school completely. They might think, “Why bother if the one thing I love is taken away?” That would make things worse, not better.

I am not saying grades do not matter. They do, and I think we should keep pushing students to improve. But requiring a B average is too strict. A better idea might be to require students to pass all their classes with at least a C and to attend tutoring or a study hall if they are struggling. That way, students get the help they need without losing the activities that keep them involved in school.

Thank you for listening to student opinions on this. I hope you will consider a more flexible approach.

Sincerely,
Jordan Lee

I am writing to share my thoughts on our school's upcoming decision regarding cell phone rules. Between the two options under review, I strongly believe that Policy 1—which permits students to keep their phones and use them during lunch and passing periods, while keeping them silenced and put away during instructional time—is the far better approach. It addresses real safety concerns, fosters personal responsibility, and avoids the enforcement headaches that an outright ban would inevitably bring.

First and foremost, cell phones serve as an essential communication tool for many families. On any given afternoon, sports practices get rescheduled, work shifts shift unexpectedly, or a sibling needs to be picked up. Being able to check in with a parent during lunch or right after the final bell prevents confusion and unnecessary panic. In serious emergencies, like severe weather alerts or unexpected campus lockdowns, having a direct line of contact with home provides immediate peace of mind. Forcing hundreds of teenagers to line up for a single front-office landline simply does not reflect how families coordinate today.

Beyond logistics, Policy 1 helps students develop the digital self-discipline we will need long after high school. In college lecture halls and professional workplaces, nobody collects phones at the door. Adults are expected to know when to engage with technology and when to put it away. By establishing clear boundaries—permitting phones during personal downtime but strictly prohibiting them when instruction begins—the school treats us as young adults capable of learning that balance. An absolute ban assumes students cannot be trusted at all, whereas a balanced policy sets an achievable standard and holds us accountable to it.

Practical enforcement is another major factor to consider. If the school adopts Policy 2, phones will not simply disappear from campus; they will just be hidden in pockets, boots, and backpacks. Teachers would have to spend the first ten minutes of every class acting like security guards, searching bags and issuing disciplinary referrals. The rise of digital communication has revolutionized the way we approach education. With many institutions now offering distance learning options through video conferencing and online platforms, students can attend classes from the comfort of their own homes. This shift has significant benefits, including the creation of personalized learning environments, increased educational accessibility, and the development of essential self-management skills.

One of the primary advantages of distance learning is its ability to cater to diverse learning styles and individual needs. Traditional classrooms can be overwhelming, with rigid schedules and a uniform pace that may not suit every learner. In contrast, studying from home allows students to create a quiet, comfortable workspace that minimizes distractions and optimizes focus. Virtual programs often incorporate asynchronous resources, such as recorded lectures and digital discussion boards, enabling students to review complex concepts at their own pace. This leads to deeper comprehension and reduced academic anxiety, as students are no longer forced to keep up with the fast-paced nature of in-person lectures. For instance, a student who needs more time to understand a particular concept can pause and rewind recorded lectures, ensuring they grasp the material before moving on.

Distance learning also plays a crucial role in enhancing accessibility and equity in education. Many individuals face significant obstacles when it comes to physical attendance, including chronic illnesses, physical disabilities, and severe social anxiety. Furthermore, students living in remote or rural areas often lack access to specialized coursework or advanced placement classes. By providing an online attendance option, these geographical and physical barriers are dismantled, ensuring that vulnerable or isolated populations receive a high-quality education without compromising their health or well-being. The elimination of lengthy daily commutes also allows learners to allocate more time to rest, study, and family life, leading to a better work-life balance.

Some argue that remote education limits social interaction and discourages student accountability. However, this criticism overlooks the fact that virtual formats do not eliminate collaboration; rather, they reshape it. Group projects conducted via video conferencing and collaborative cloud software mirror the modern professional landscape, where remote teamwork has become the norm. As students manage their own schedules and navigate online platforms independently, they develop critical organizational habits, digital literacy, and personal responsibility. For example, a student working on a group project online must communicate effectively with their teammates, set deadlines, and manage their time wisely, all of which are essential skills in the modern workplace.

In conclusion, offering students the option to attend classes remotely is a forward-thinking policy that has numerous benefits. Rather than replacing physical schools, distance learning serves as a complementary alternative, empowering students to take ownership of their education. By accommodating unique learning preferences, bridging equity gaps, and instilling essential digital and personal skills, remote education prepares students for success in an increasingly digital world. As we continue to navigate the complexities of modern education, it is essential that we prioritize flexibility, accessibility, and student autonomy, recognizing that distance learning is not only a viable option but a valuable addition to traditional educational models.

Distance learning has moved from a rare experiment to a common feature of modern education. Critics worry that students who learn from home will lose focus, social connection, and discipline. Yet when schools offer it as an option rather than a requirement, distance learning benefits students by giving them flexibility, access to opportunities, and a learning environment that can fit their individual needs.

The strongest argument for distance learning is flexibility. Students do not all live the same lives. Some are competitive athletes or performers who travel for training and competitions. Others care for family members, hold part-time jobs, or live with chronic illnesses that make daily attendance difficult. For these students, a rigid schedule in a physical building can mean falling behind or dropping out. Online classes and recorded video lectures allow them to keep up with coursework without sacrificing their health or responsibilities. A student recovering from surgery, for example, can continue learning from home instead of missing weeks of instruction and struggling to catch up.

Distance learning also expands access. Students in rural areas often attend small schools that cannot afford to offer advanced courses such as calculus, physics, or foreign languages. Through video conferencing, those students can join classes taught by qualified teachers elsewhere. This opens doors to college preparation that geography would otherwise close. Even in large urban districts, a student who wants to study a niche subject can find it online when it is not offered locally. In this way, distance learning promotes equity by reducing the effect of where a student happens to live.

In addition, some students simply learn better at home. A classroom can be noisy and distracting, and for some students it is also a source of anxiety or bullying. A student who is bullied or who suffers from severe social anxiety may find it nearly impossible to concentrate at school. At home, that student can work in a calm space, move at a comfortable pace, and pause or replay a lesson to review difficult material. Self-paced learning also builds valuable skills such as time management, independence, and self-motivation, which are essential in college and in the workplace.

Opponents are right that distance learning has drawbacks. Students may miss the friendships, teamwork, and face-to-face guidance that a school provides, and those without reliable internet or a quiet workspace may be disadvantaged. Some teenagers lack the self-discipline to stay engaged without direct supervision. These concerns are real, but they are reasons to design distance learning carefully, not to reject it. Schools can lend laptops and provide internet hotspots, require regular check-ins with teachers, and encourage online students to join clubs, sports, and in-person events. Because the program is optional, students and parents can choose it only when it suits them, and students who struggle can return to the classroom.

In conclusion, students benefit from being able to attend classes from home when the option is thoughtfully offered. It supports students with unusual schedules or health challenges, brings advanced courses to communities that lack them, and provides a more comfortable setting for those who struggle in traditional classrooms. Although it cannot replace the social value of school for everyone, it can serve as a powerful alternative. Education should adapt to the needs of students, and distance learning is one effective way to do that.

Dear Senator,

I am writing because I believe we should keep the Electoral College. Some people want to change to a national popular vote, but I think that would create more problems than it solves.

The Electoral College was set up as a compromise, not a mistake. According to the Office of the Federal Register, the Founders created it as a middle ground between letting Congress pick the president and letting a direct popular vote decide. Each state gets electors based on its number of House members plus its two senators, and a candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win. That means states matter as states, not just as piles of individual votes.

I know critics like Bradford Plumer say the system is undemocratic because a candidate can win the popular vote and still lose, like in 2000 and 2016. They also argue that winner-take-all pushes candidates to focus only on swing states and ignore the rest of us. I understand that frustration. If you live in a safe red or blue state, it can feel like your vote does not count. But switching to a national popular vote has its own problems.

Judge Richard Posner makes a good point that the Electoral College forces candidates to build broad support across different regions. Without it, a candidate could win just by running up huge vote totals in big cities or in one part of the country and ignoring smaller or rural states. A national popular vote might make campaigns spend all their time in dense media markets and not in places like our state. That seems less fair, not more.

Another thing is that the Electoral College keeps messy recounts contained. If there is a close election, a recount happens in a few states, not in all fifty states at once. A national popular vote would mean every questionable ballot in every precinct nationwide could be fought over, which could make elections drag on and feel even more chaotic.

I also think the swing state problem is real, but it is not a reason to throw the whole system out. We could encourage more states to split electoral votes like Maine and Nebraska do, as the Federal Register explains. That would give candidates a reason to compete in more places while still keeping the Electoral College’s structure.

In the end, I would rather keep a system that asks candidates to win across many types of states, not just many types of people in one region. Please oppose any move to replace the Electoral College with a national popular vote.

Sincerely,  
[Student Name]

Dear Principal,

I am writing to share my concerns about the proposed policy that would require students to maintain at least a B average in order to participate in sports and other school activities. I understand that the policy is meant to encourage students to take academics seriously. However, I believe it would hurt many students instead of helping them improve.

A C average should not automatically be treated as failure. In many classes, a C means that a student has shown satisfactory understanding of the material. Some students work very hard to earn C’s while facing challenges that other students may not see. They may have learning disabilities, language barriers, jobs, family responsibilities, or mental health concerns. For one student, a C may reflect a lack of effort, but for another, it may represent real progress and determination. Removing that student from activities would be unfair and discouraging.

Also, extracurricular activities can actually help students do better in school. Sports, music, theater, clubs, and student government teach valuable skills such as responsibility, time management, teamwork, and discipline. Students who have practice after school or a club meeting to attend often learn to organize their time more carefully. Activities can also give students a reason to come to school, complete their assignments, and stay connected to teachers and classmates. If students with C averages lose the activities they care about, they may lose the motivation and structure that could help them raise their grades.

A B-average requirement would also ignore talents that do not always appear on a report card. A student who struggles in math might be an excellent athlete, a dedicated member of the band, or a talented stage manager for the school play. Another student may not earn top grades but may be a caring leader who helps younger teammates and contributes positively to the school community. These experiences build confidence, creativity, leadership, and social skills. They are important parts of education, even though they cannot always be measured by a letter grade.

In addition, a strict policy could cause some students to feel disconnected from school. For certain students, a team, club, or performance group is where they feel accepted and successful. It may be the main reason they continue coming to school and trying to improve. If they are excluded because their average is below a B, they may feel that there is no place for them here. Rather than motivating them, the policy could lead to frustration, lower effort, or even dropping out.

Of course, academics should remain a priority. Students who are struggling should receive help and be expected to work toward improvement. However, support would be more effective than exclusion. The school could require tutoring, study halls, progress reports, or academic probation for students with lower grades. This approach would keep high expectations while giving students the assistance they need to meet them.

For these reasons, I urge you not to require a B average for participation in activities. Students should be encouraged to improve academically, but they should not lose the opportunities that may help them succeed.

Sincerely,  
A Concerned Student

As the school considers updating its cell phone policy, I want to explain why I believe Policy 1 is the stronger choice. This option would let students bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free periods, as long as they are turned off during class. It offers a sensible balance between responsibility and freedom.

For many students, phones are no longer just entertainment. We use them to track assignments, set reminders, check bus schedules, and communicate with parents or guardians about rides, jobs, or family plans. Allowing phone use during breaks respects these everyday needs while still protecting class time from distractions. It also gives us a chance to practice managing when and how we use our devices, a skill that will matter long after high school.

A complete ban, by contrast, feels overly strict and hard to enforce. Students sometimes need to reach family members quickly, whether because of an emergency or a last-minute change in plans. Not having access to a phone can add stress rather than relieve it. In addition, banning phones entirely may push students to hide them and use them secretly, which could lead to more distractions and discipline problems than a clear, limited-use policy would create.

Policy 1 also encourages accountability. When the school sets clear rules and teaches students about appropriate phone use, we learn important lessons about digital citizenship, cyberbullying, and knowing when to put technology away. These are conversations that should happen in school, not avoided. If phones are completely forbidden, we miss the opportunity to build those habits with adult guidance.

I understand the worry that phones can take attention away from learning. That concern is exactly why Policy 1 works: it keeps classrooms free from phones but allows reasonable use during unstructured time. Rather than pretending phones do not exist, the school can help students learn to use them thoughtfully. For these reasons, I hope you will choose Policy 1. It is a realistic, respectful approach that supports both our education and our growth as responsible young adults.

Whether by competing on a track team, designing layouts for the yearbook, or debating school policy on the student council, students frequently discover lifelong passions beyond the traditional classroom. In an effort to foster these benefits school-wide, the principal has decided that every student must participate in at least one extracurricular program. Dear Senator,

I urge you to support changing presidential elections to a national popular vote. The Electoral College was created as a constitutional compromise, but a system designed for the nation’s founding era no longer serves modern voters fairly. Every citizen’s vote should carry the same weight, regardless of whether that voter lives in a closely contested state, a rural state, or a heavily populated city.

According to the Office of the Federal Register, the Electoral College contains 538 electors, and a candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win. Each state receives electors based on its number of representatives and senators, and nearly every state awards all of its electoral votes to the candidate who wins that state’s popular vote. This winner-take-all arrangement creates serious inequality. A vote for the losing candidate in a state effectively earns no electoral representation, even if that candidate receives millions of votes. Meanwhile, a small margin in a competitive state can determine the entire outcome.

The most troubling result is that the candidate preferred by the most Americans can lose the presidency. Bradford Plumer notes that this occurred in both 2000 and 2016. In a representative democracy, that outcome is difficult to defend. The presidency is the only office that represents the entire nation, so it should be awarded to the candidate who receives the most votes from the entire nation. A national popular vote would establish a clear and understandable principle: one person, one vote.

The current system also distorts campaigning. Plumer explains that candidates focus their time, advertisements, and policy promises on a relatively small number of swing states. Voters in states considered safely Democratic or safely Republican are often ignored because campaigns assume their electoral votes are already decided. This means a voter in a competitive state may receive far more attention than a voter elsewhere, even though both are citizens of the same country. Under a popular-vote system, candidates would have reason to seek votes everywhere—small towns, suburbs, cities, and states that are currently treated as political afterthoughts.

Supporters of the Electoral College, including Judge Richard A. Posner, argue that it protects federalism and forces candidates to build broad coalitions instead of simply winning huge margins in urban areas. They also contend that it avoids the difficulty of a nationwide recount. These concerns deserve consideration. However, candidates already need support from many different communities to win a national majority or plurality of votes. Large cities contain many votes, but so do rural regions, suburbs, and smaller cities across the country. No candidate could realistically ignore most Americans and still win the popular vote.

Recounts are also not a sufficient reason to preserve an unfair system. Modern election procedures can establish consistent national standards for recounts when margins are extraordinarily close. More importantly, the possibility of a difficult recount should not outweigh the principle that the candidate with the most votes should win.

The Electoral College was a compromise, not an untouchable ideal. Our election system should encourage participation, treat voters equally, and reflect the will of the people. I ask you to support reforms that move the United States toward electing its president by the national popular vote.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Constituent

Dear Principal Johnson,

I am writing to share my opinion about the cell phone policy. I think Policy 1 is the better choice. Students should be allowed to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and free times, as long as they are turned off during class. I believe this policy is fair, safer, and more realistic than banning phones completely.

First, phones are important for safety and emergencies. If something happens at school or on the way home, students need a way to contact their parents. Last year, my bus broke down and we were stuck for almost an hour. A lot of kids were worried, and the ones who had phones could at least tell their families what was going on. If phones were not allowed at all, students would have to wait for the office to call home, and that could take a long time. Also, many students have parents who work late, so they have to text them about changing plans after practice or club meetings. Having a phone makes that much easier.

Second, Policy 1 teaches responsibility. If the school bans phones completely, students never learn how to use them the right way. But if we are allowed to use them at lunch and turn them off in class, we have to make good choices and follow rules. That is kind of like real life. Someday we will have jobs where we can't be on our phones all the time, but we will still have them with us. Learning to put a phone away when it's time to focus is a skill that helps. If someone breaks the rule, the school can give a consequence like taking the phone until the end of the day, so there is still a way to enforce it.

Third, a total ban would be really hard to enforce. I know that if phones are banned, a lot of students will still bring them and hide them in their backpacks or pockets. Then teachers would spend class time trying to catch people instead of teaching. That would make students and teachers frustrated. With Policy 1, there is a clear time when phones are okay and a clear time when they are not, so there is less sneaking around. Students would probably be more willing to follow the rule because it feels fair.

Some people might say phones are a distraction and that students would cheat or get into drama online. I understand that concern, and I agree phones should not be out during class. That is why the turned-off rule is so important. But lunch and free time are supposed to be a break. Students can talk to friends, listen to music, or just relax for a few minutes so they are ready to learn again. Honestly, it might even help some students who feel stressed or who are shy and don't want to sit alone at lunch.

In conclusion, I think Policy 1 is the best option because it keeps students safe, teaches responsibility, and is easier to enforce than a full ban. Phones can be a problem if they are used at the wrong time, but we can solve that with clear rules instead of taking them away completely. Thank you for taking the time to read my letter and for thinking about what students need.

Sincerely,
A concerned student

I am writing to urge you to adopt Policy 1, which allows students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times as long as they are turned off during class. While I understand the concerns about distraction, this policy is more realistic, more educational, and more beneficial for students than a complete ban.

First, allowing phones during free time supports student safety and family communication. Many students use lunch or study hall to confirm after-school plans, arrange rides, or check messages from parents about schedule changes. In an emergency, having a phone available can help a student reach family quickly. A total ban would cut off this important line of communication during the very times when students are most likely to need it.

Second, Policy 1 teaches students how to manage technology responsibly. In college and in most workplaces, people are expected to keep their phones put away during meetings or classes but may use them during breaks. A total ban does not teach self-control; it simply removes the temptation. By allowing phone use at appropriate times, the school helps students practice making good decisions. They learn that there is a time to focus and a time to relax, which is a valuable life skill.

Third, lunch and free periods are meant to be times when students can recharge. For many students, listening to music, texting a friend, playing a short game, or checking social media during lunch provides a mental break that helps them return to afternoon classes with more energy. Taking away phones entirely would make lunch feel more restrictive and could increase student resentment. It might also push phone use into secret, making discipline problems worse rather than better.

Some people worry that phones will distract from learning, but Policy 1 already addresses that concern by requiring phones to be off during class. Teachers can enforce this clear rule. A complete ban, on the other hand, is harder to enforce fairly and may lead to constant rule-breaking, lost phones in lockers, or conflicts between students and staff.

In conclusion, Policy 1 is the stronger choice because it balances safety, responsibility, and student well-being. It allows students to stay connected during free time while preserving a focused classroom environment. I encourage you to adopt Policy 1 as a fair and practical solution for our school.

A Student

Extracurricular activities have long been valued as essential components of a well-rounded secondary education, offering students invaluable lessons in leadership, teamwork, and discipline. However, the principal's decision to mandate that every student participate in at least one extracurricular activity is a well-intentioned but misguided policy. By compelling involvement, the school overlooks the complexities of students' personal lives, undermines the passion that drives these organizations, and deprives adolescents of the autonomy they need to develop into mature decision-makers.

For many students, life outside the classroom is already a juggling act. Between navigating rigorous academic schedules and fulfilling responsibilities at home, some students are barely keeping their heads above water. Many work part-time jobs to support their families financially, while others care for younger siblings or aging relatives. Adding a mandatory after-school commitment to the mix forces these students into an impossible dilemma. They must choose between fulfilling essential family duties and complying with school policy, which can lead to increased stress, decreased rest, and compromised academic performance. This is not to say that extracurricular activities are inherently bad; on the contrary, they can be incredibly enriching. But for students who are already Shouldering significant responsibilities, mandatory participation can be a burden rather than a benefit.

The quality of extracurricular organizations also suffers when participation is mandatory. The vitality of any club or team hinges on the genuine enthusiasm and dedication of its members. When students are forced to join, their engagement is often lackluster, and they may even exhibit apathy or resentment. This can be discouraging for peers who joined out of genuine interest, and it can also create more work for advisors and coaches, who must manage disengaged attendees rather than mentoring motivated participants. True dedication cannot be forced, and attempting to do so can dilute the experience for everyone involved. Moreover, when students are given the freedom to choose, they are more likely to discover their true passions and interests, which can lead to a more meaningful and lasting commitment.

Ultimately, preparing adolescents for adulthood requires giving them the freedom to govern their own time. Learning how to prioritize commitments, pursue independent hobbies, and make choices about how to spend one's time are essential life skills. By mandating extracurricular participation, the school is depriving students of the opportunity to develop these skills. Instead of fostering a sense of autonomy and self-direction, the policy may inadvertently create a sense of resentment and rebellion. As students navigate the challenges of adolescence, they need the freedom to make choices about their own lives, to explore their interests, and to develop into capable, independent individuals. By abandoning the mandatory participation policy, the school can help students achieve these goals, and truly provide them with a well-rounded education.

I agree with the principal's decision, though I think its success depends on how the school carries it out. A requirement sounds like a burden at first, but for most students it would open a door they might never have walked through on their own.

Consider how many teenagers spend their afternoons. Some go home and scroll through their phones until dinner. Others drift between a couch and a refrigerator. There is nothing wicked about this, but it is a waste of what could be the most formative hours of the school day. An extracurricular activity gives those hours a shape. A student who has to be at yearbook meetings on Tuesdays and Thursdays learns to plan around a schedule, and that habit carries over into homework in a way that lectures about time management rarely manage to achieve.

The social benefits matter just as much. Every school has students who eat lunch alone, not because they are unlikeable but because nobody has given them a reason to talk. When I was a freshman, I knew exactly four people in a building of nearly two thousand. Joining the stage crew for the fall play changed that within a month. Hauling plywood and arguing over paint colors with juniors and seniors, I made friends I never would have met in algebra. A requirement would push every shy student toward that kind of experience, and it would give them a ready-made topic of conversation: the thing they are all working on together.

Skeptics argue that students already have enough pressure. They point to those who work part-time jobs, care for younger siblings, or struggle to keep their grades up. This is a fair concern, and the policy should account for it. But "at least one activity" is a flexible standard. A student with a job might fulfill it through a weekly club that meets during lunch. Someone who looks after a little brother could join a short-season team or a service project that meets only a few times a semester. If the school defines "activity" generously and grants reasonable exemptions, the rule would not crush anyone.

Another objection is that forced participation produces halfhearted participation. Some students will, no doubt, sit in the back of a meeting and count the minutes. Yet I have seen reluctant people surprise themselves. A friend of mine joined the debate team only because his counselor insisted, and he ended up traveling to state competitions and applying to colleges with a confidence he had never shown before. Interest often follows involvement rather than preceding it. You cannot know you enjoy something you have never tried.

There is also a practical payoff. Colleges and employers look for evidence that a young person can commit to something, work with others, and see a project through. A transcript full of grades says one thing about a student; a record of leading a fundraising drive or editing a section of the yearbook says something richer. By requiring participation, the school gives every graduate at least one concrete story to tell.

Finally, schools are meant to teach more than facts. They are supposed to produce capable, curious, connected adults. Classes cover the first part well, but clubs, teams, and committees cover the rest. If the principal allows choice, offers a wide variety of options, and remains flexible for students with real obstacles, this policy could make the whole school feel less like a place people attend and more like a community they belong to. That is a goal worth supporting.

The debate about whether summer projects should be teacher-designed or student-designed has sparked intense discussion among educators and scholars. While some argue that teacher-designed projects provide structure and accountability, I firmly believe that student-designed projects are more effective in promoting continuous learning during the summer break. This stance is grounded in the idea that student autonomy and self-directed learning are essential for fostering a deeper understanding of academic concepts and developing crucial life skills.

Firstly, student-designed projects allow learners to explore topics that genuinely interest them, thereby increasing their motivation and engagement. When students are given the freedom to choose their own projects, they are more likely to invest time and effort into researching and learning about the subject matter. For instance, a student passionate about environmental conservation might design a project that involves conducting a local wildlife survey or creating a sustainable garden. This autonomy enables students to take ownership of their learning, leading to a more meaningful and enjoyable experience. In contrast, teacher-designed projects might not always align with students' interests, potentially resulting in a lackluster effort and a shallow understanding of the material.

Moreover, student-designed projects promote critical thinking, problem-solving, and creativity – essential skills for success in the 21st century. When students are responsible for designing their own projects, they must navigate the challenges of planning, executing, and evaluating their work. This process helps them develop a growth mindset, as they learn to overcome obstacles, adapt to new situations, and reflect on their progress. For example, a student designing a project on astronomy might encounter difficulties in collecting data or building a model, but by persevering and finding solutions, they develop resilience and resourcefulness. These skills are invaluable in both academic and professional contexts, as they enable individuals to approach complex problems with confidence and ingenuity.

Another significant advantage of student-designed projects is that they cater to different learning styles and abilities. By allowing students to choose their own topics and approaches, educators can accommodate diverse needs and preferences. For instance, a student with a learning disability might design a project that incorporates assistive technology or adaptive methods, ensuring that they can participate fully and effectively. This inclusivity is essential for creating a supportive and equitable learning environment, where all students feel valued and empowered to succeed.

In conclusion, student-designed summer projects offer a moreeffective and engaging way to promote continuous learning during the break. By giving students the autonomy to choose their own topics and approaches, educators can foster a deeper understanding of academic concepts, develop crucial life skills, and cater to diverse learning needs. While teacher-designed projects might provide structure and accountability, they often lack the flexibility and creativity that student-designed projects offer. As educators, we should strive to create learning environments that empower students to take ownership of their education, explore their passions, and develop into capable, confident, and curious individuals.

The use of cell phones while driving has become a controversial issue in recent years. With the majority of people owning and operating cell phones, it's not uncommon to see drivers talking or texting on their phones while behind the wheel. However, I strongly believe that drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

First and foremost, using a cell phone while driving is a significant distraction. When a driver is talking or texting on their phone, they're not fully focused on the road, which can lead to accidents. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, distracted driving claimed the lives of 3,166 people in the United States in 2017 alone. These numbers are alarming, and it's clear that something needs to be done to prevent such tragedies. By banning the use of cell phones while driving, we can significantly reduce the number of accidents caused by distracted driving.

Another reason why drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones is that it impairs their ability to react quickly to situations on the road. When a driver is distracted by their phone, they may not be able to stop in time or react to a sudden change in traffic. This can lead to a domino effect, causing a chain reaction of accidents. Moreover, using a cell phone while driving slows down a driver's reaction time, which can be fatal in situations where every second counts.

Some may argue that hands-free devices or Bluetooth technology can solve the problem of distracted driving. However, research has shown that even hands-free devices can be distracting, as the conversation itself can take a driver's attention away from the road. Furthermore, using a cell phone while driving can be addictive, and many people find it difficult to resist the temptation to check their phone or respond to a text message, even if it means putting themselves and others at risk.

In addition to the safety risks, allowing drivers to use cell phones while driving can also set a bad example for young and inexperienced drivers. If experienced drivers are using their phones while driving, it can give the impression that it's safe and acceptable to do so. This can lead to a culture of distracted driving, where drivers feel that it's okay to use their phones while behind the wheel.

To address the issue of cell phone use while driving, many countries and states have implemented laws and regulations. For example, some states have banned texting while driving, while others have implemented hands-free laws. However, I believe that a complete ban on cell phone use while driving is the most effective way to prevent accidents and ensure road safety.

In conclusion, drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle. The risks associated with distracted driving are too great, and the consequences can be fatal. By banning the use of cell phones while driving, we can significantly reduce the number of accidents caused by distracted driving and create a safer driving environment for everyone. It's time for us to take action and make our roads safer by keeping our eyes on the road and our hands on the wheel.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge you to support changing the way Americans elect their president so that the candidate with the most votes nationwide wins. The Electoral College began as a constitutional compromise, but it no longer gives citizens an equal voice. A national popular vote would make presidential elections fairer, push candidates to campaign in every part of the country, and ensure that the winner reflects the choice of the most voters.

To begin with, the Electoral College does not count every vote equally. The Office of the Federal Register explains that each state's electors equal its number of House members plus its two senators. Because every state gets two electors for its senators no matter how small it is, less populated states carry more weight than their populations would justify. Even more troubling, forty-eight states use a winner-take-all system. A candidate who wins a state by a narrow margin usually takes all of its electoral votes, which means that the ballots cast for the runner-up, sometimes millions of them, have no effect on the outcome there.

This arrangement can also put someone in the White House who did not win the most votes. Bradford Plumer points out that this happened in both 2000 and 2016. When the winner of the national popular vote can still lose the presidency, it is fair for citizens to wonder whether the system respects majority rule. A government earns legitimacy when each person's ballot carries the same weight, whether that person lives in a big city, a rural county, or a small state.

The system also leads campaigns to overlook much of the country. Since most states reliably favor one party, candidates spend their time, advertising money, and promises on a handful of swing states. Plumer argues that voters in "safe" states feel ignored, and that this can lower turnout. Under a national popular vote, every additional ballot would matter, wherever it was cast. Candidates would have a reason to seek support in all fifty states, including places that now get little attention because the result seems predictable.

Supporters of the Electoral College raise serious points. Judge Richard A. Posner argues that it protects federalism, keeps candidates from winning simply by piling up votes in densely populated areas, and forces them to build broad coalitions. He adds that it produces a quick, decisive winner and limits recounts to individual states instead of the whole nation. These concerns deserve a real answer. Still, a popular vote would not force candidates to ignore rural or small-state voters. Those voters are numerous, and their ballots would count just as much as anyone else's. A candidate would still need support from many kinds of communities to win a national majority or plurality. As for recounts, the risk could be reduced through consistent national election standards, better ballot procedures, and automatic recounts when an election is extremely close.

The Electoral College was an understandable compromise when the nation was founded, but its winner-take-all structure now distorts campaigns and can contradict the people's choice. I respectfully ask you to support reforms that move the United States toward electing its president by national popular vote. The president should be chosen by the Americans who vote, not by a system that can override their collective decision.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Constituent

Cell phones have become an ordinary part of daily life, giving people instant access to communication, directions, and emergency assistance. However, the same devices that are useful in everyday situations can become dangerous when used behind the wheel. Although phones provide convenience and a sense of security, drivers should not be allowed to use them in any capacity while operating a vehicle. Even hands-free phone use divides a driver’s attention, and the consequences of that distraction can be severe or fatal.

The main reason for a complete ban is that cell phone use creates cognitive distraction. Driving is not an automatic task; it requires drivers to constantly observe their surroundings, make quick decisions, and react to changing conditions. A person talking on the phone may still have both hands on the wheel and eyes facing forward, but his or her mind is partly focused on the conversation. Studies of inattentional blindness suggest that people can look directly at something without fully recognizing it when their attention is directed elsewhere. For example, a driver on a hands-free call might fail to notice a child near a crosswalk, a car braking suddenly, or a traffic signal changing. Unlike listening to music, a phone conversation is interactive. It requires listening, thinking, and responding, all of which take mental energy away from driving.

Texting, dialing, scrolling, and looking at a screen are even more dangerous because they add manual and visual distractions to the mental distraction already caused by the phone. Texting can take a driver’s eyes off the road for several seconds. At highway speeds, a vehicle can travel the length of a football field in that amount of time. During those few seconds, traffic can slow down, a pedestrian can enter the roadway, or another driver can make an unexpected move. Even voice commands and built-in phone systems are not completely safe. While these features may reduce the need to hold a device, they still require drivers to think about the phone instead of giving full attention to the road. Allowing limited use may also encourage people to believe they can safely handle more distractions than they actually can.

A strict prohibition is also justified because distracted driving affects more than the person using the phone. Thousands of people are killed or injured each year in crashes connected to distracted driving, and many of those collisions involve cell phones. These crashes can harm passengers, pedestrians, cyclists, and other drivers who have no control over someone else’s decision to use a phone. Unlike poor weather or mechanical failure, phone-related distraction is usually preventable. A clear rule would make expectations simple: when a vehicle is moving, the driver’s attention should remain on driving. It would also make enforcement easier because officers would not have to decide whether a particular type of phone use was safe enough.

Of course, emergencies may occur, and people sometimes need to contact family members, employers, or emergency services. In most situations, however, drivers can pull over safely before making a call or sending a message. The small inconvenience of stopping is far less important than protecting lives.

In conclusion, the benefits of cell phone communication do not outweigh the risks of using a device while driving. Because phones distract drivers mentally, visually, and physically—even when used hands-free—drivers should not be permitted to use them in any capacity while operating a vehicle. A total ban would promote safer habits, reduce preventable crashes, and keep drivers focused where they need to be: on the road.

Cell phones have become essential tools for communication, navigation, work, and emergency help. Because they are so common, many drivers assume they can safely make a call, follow directions, or send a quick message while behind the wheel. Still, drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle. Even phone use that seems harmless splits a driver's attention, slows reaction time, and puts passengers, pedestrians, and other motorists at risk.

The main problem is distraction. Safe driving demands constant awareness of traffic lights, road signs, nearby cars, weather, cyclists, and people crossing the street. A driver may have to brake or swerve with almost no warning. Glancing at a screen for just a few seconds can mean covering the length of a football field without really watching the road. Texting is especially dangerous because it takes a driver's eyes, hands, and mind all at once. Voice calls and hands-free devices are not risk-free either, since a conversation pulls at the driver's mental focus. Someone absorbed in a phone call may be looking at the road and still miss a car braking ahead or a child stepping toward a crosswalk.

Some people argue that hands-free technology should be permitted because it lets drivers keep both hands on the wheel. It is true that these devices reduce the need to hold a phone, but they do not remove mental distraction. The brain cannot give full attention to a serious conversation and to complicated driving conditions at the same time. Drivers using speakers may even become overconfident, believing they are safer than they really are. Navigation apps are certainly helpful, but the destination should be entered before the car starts moving. If a driver needs to change a route, answer a call, or read a message, the responsible choice is to pull over in a safe spot.

A complete ban would also set a clearer expectation for everyone. Laws that allow some kinds of phone use while prohibiting others are hard to enforce and easy to misunderstand. A simple rule, no phone use while the vehicle is in operation, would be much easier to follow. Over time, it could shift behavior the way seat belt laws and drunk driving penalties made those safety habits widely accepted. Drivers can help themselves by preparing before they leave, silencing unnecessary notifications, and turning on "do not disturb" settings to avoid temptation.

Emergencies deserve some practical consideration. If a driver witnesses a crash or suffers a medical emergency, calling for help may be necessary. Even then, the driver should stop in a safe location first whenever possible. The point is not to keep people from getting help, but to keep everyday convenience from becoming a deadly distraction.

In the end, driving is a serious responsibility and should not be mixed with constant digital communication. Since even brief phone use can weaken attention and endanger lives, drivers should not use their phones in any capacity while actively driving. The few minutes saved by answering a text or taking a call are never worth the cost of a preventable crash.

Dear Senator,

I believe the United States should change presidential elections to a national popular vote. The Electoral College was created as a compromise by the Founding Fathers, but the country has changed greatly since then. Today, the system can allow the candidate preferred by fewer voters to become president, gives too much attention to a few states, and makes many Americans feel that their votes do not matter.

According to the Office of the Federal Register, the Electoral College has 538 electors, and a candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win. Each state receives electors based on its number of representatives plus two senators. In 48 states, the system is winner-take-all, meaning that the candidate who wins even by a tiny margin receives every electoral vote in that state. This makes the actual number of votes almost less important than where the votes are cast.

This is unfair because a president should represent the choice of the most voters nationwide. As Bradford Plumer explains in “The Indefensible Electoral College,” candidates have won the popular vote but lost the presidency, including in 2000 and 2016. When this happens, citizens may reasonably question whether the election was democratic. If millions more people support one candidate, that candidate should not lose simply because electoral votes are distributed state by state.

The winner-take-all system also causes campaigns to focus heavily on swing states. Plumer points out that candidates often ignore states that are safely Democratic or Republican. For example, a voter in a closely divided state may see many campaign visits, advertisements, and promises, while voters in states that are expected to go one way receive much less attention. A popular-vote system would encourage candidates to seek votes everywhere, because every individual vote would add equally to their total. This could also increase turnout, since people would have more reason to believe their vote matters even if they live in a state dominated by the other party.

Supporters of the Electoral College, such as Judge Richard A. Posner, argue that it protects federalism and forces candidates to build broad coalitions instead of only appealing to large cities. They also argue that it creates clearer results and prevents a nationwide recount. These are serious concerns. States do have different needs, and a close popular-vote election could be difficult to recount.

However, changing to a popular vote would not mean candidates could ignore rural or small-state voters. Rural voters make up millions of people, and their votes would still count exactly the same as urban voters’ votes. Candidates would need support from many different groups to win a national majority or plurality. Also, recount rules could be planned at the national level, just as states already have rules for close elections. It is better to improve recount procedures than to accept a system where the person with fewer votes can become president.

The Electoral College may have been a reasonable compromise at the country’s founding, but it no longer treats every voter equally. I urge you to support efforts to move toward a national popular vote for president. Our democracy should make the candidate with the most votes the winner.

When facing an important decision, people often turn to others for guidance. While it may be tempting to rely on a single trusted friend or advisor, seeking multiple opinions generally leads to a better choice. Consulting several people exposes a decision-maker to diverse perspectives, uncovers hidden risks, and reduces the influence of personal bias, ultimately producing a more balanced and informed outcome.

One key advantage of seeking multiple opinions is that it broadens the range of information and viewpoints available. Different people bring different experiences, values, and areas of expertise to the same question. For example, a person deciding whether to accept a job offer might ask a former manager about career advancement, a friend in the same industry about workplace culture, and a financially savvy relative about salary and benefits. Each person notices details the others might overlook. What one advisor considers unimportant may be exactly the warning sign another person highlights. By combining these perspectives, the decision-maker can form a fuller picture than any single opinion could provide.

In addition, multiple opinions help uncover risks and weaknesses that a single advisor may miss. A person who is enthusiastic about a plan may focus on its benefits and ignore potential problems. For instance, someone planning to open a small restaurant might ask a successful restaurant owner, an accountant, and a customer who frequently dines out. The owner may emphasize long hours and staff management, the accountant may point out hidden costs such as permits and insurance, and the customer may stress the importance of location and convenience. Each opinion reveals a different challenge. Armed with this information, the person can adjust the plan, choose a safer location, or set aside a larger emergency fund. Without these varied insights, the decision might be built on incomplete or overly optimistic assumptions.

Seeking multiple opinions also reduces the danger of personal bias, both in the advisor and in the decision-maker. A single advisor may have a strong personal preference or an emotional stake in the outcome. For example, a parent may urge a student to choose a particular university because it is close to home, while a friend may recommend another school based on social life, and a teacher may focus on academic reputation. If the student listens only to one of these voices, the choice may reflect that person’s priorities rather than the student’s own needs. Comparing several opinions allows the student to sort through conflicting advice, ask follow-up questions, and identify which factors truly matter.

Of course, gathering too many opinions can sometimes create confusion or delay action. However, the solution is not to avoid consultation altogether but to seek advice from a small, carefully chosen group of people with relevant knowledge. When done thoughtfully, the process strengthens rather than weakens decision-making.

In conclusion, seeking multiple opinions helps people make better choices by expanding their understanding, exposing hidden risks, and balancing emotional or biased advice. Whether choosing a career, making a major purchase, or planning a new venture, a decision-maker benefits from listening to several voices before acting. A single opinion may offer comfort, but multiple perspectives offer clarity.

Drivers Should Keep Their Hands Off Their Phones

I think drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any normal capacity while driving. The only exception should be a true emergency, like calling 911 after witnessing a crash or if someone in the car is in danger. Otherwise, phones should stay out of reach.

The main reason is that phones split your attention. Driving requires constant small decisions. When I ride with my mom and she glances at a text at a red light, she sometimes doesn’t notice the light turn green, or she brakes late because she looked down for one second. That one second is enough for a child to run into the street or for the car ahead to stop suddenly. Even hands-free calls are not safe because your brain is focused on the conversation, not on the road. I have heard people say talking to a passenger is the same, but a passenger can see traffic and usually stops talking when something dangerous is happening. A person on the phone cannot see what you see, so they keep chatting while you miss your exit or drift into another lane.

Texting is obviously the worst. It takes your eyes off the road, your hands off the wheel, and your mind off driving. I know people my age who think they can send a quick reply at a stop sign, but the problem is they keep thinking about that reply after they put the phone down. Maybe the message made them mad or excited, and now they are not paying attention. Even just hearing a notification buzz can make you wonder who texted, and that curiosity is a distraction.

Some people argue that using a phone for GPS is necessary. I get that, because almost everyone uses maps now. But even GPS should be set up before the car moves and placed in a mount. Drivers should not be touching the phone to type an address while moving. If they need to change the route, they should pull over. That is not too much to ask when a mistake can cost someone’s life.

I know a total ban sounds strict. People say they need to be reachable for work or family. But no call or text is more important than getting home safely. If it is urgent, a driver can pull into a parking lot and return the call. That small delay is worth it. My uncle got rear-ended by a teenager who was checking Snapchat at 40 miles per hour. Nobody died, but my uncle’s neck still hurts years later. The teenager said it was “just one quick look.” That quick look changed two people’s lives.

So I believe cell phones should not be used while driving except for true emergencies. Keep the phone on silent or in the glove box. If you must use it, pull over. Driving is already dangerous enough without adding a screen to the mix.
