Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge you to support a national popular vote for president. The Electoral College began as a constitutional compromise, and it has defenders, but it no longer fits the basic democratic principle that every citizen's vote should carry equal weight. The president should be the candidate chosen by the most voters across the country, not the one who happens to assemble the right combination of states.

According to the Office of the Federal Register, each state receives a number of electors equal to its representatives plus its two senators, for a total of 538, and a candidate needs 270 to win. In forty-eight states and Washington, D.C., all of a state's electoral votes go to whoever wins that state's popular vote, no matter how narrow the margin. As a result, millions of votes never affect the outcome. A candidate who carries a large state by one vote earns the same reward as one who carries it by a million.

This system can also produce results that contradict the will of the nation. Bradford Plumer points out that candidates who won the national popular vote still lost the presidency in 2000 and 2016. Outcomes like these make it hard for citizens to believe their votes truly matter. Under a national popular vote, every ballot would count toward a single total, whether it was cast in a fiercely contested state or in one that reliably favors a single party.

The Electoral College also distorts the way campaigns are run. Because most states are considered safely Democratic or Republican, candidates spend their time, advertising money, and promises on a small group of swing states. Voters elsewhere are often ignored, since campaigns assume their states are already decided. Plumer argues that this neglect can depress turnout, because people may feel their vote is pointless when the result seems certain. A popular vote would give candidates a reason to seek supporters everywhere, in cities, suburbs, small towns, and every state.

Defenders of the Electoral College, such as Judge Richard A. Posner, make serious arguments. They say it protects federalism and forces candidates to build broad coalitions instead of piling up huge margins in densely populated areas. They also note that it usually produces a quick, clear winner and confines recounts to individual states. I take these concerns seriously, but I do not think they justify the current system. Rural and small-state voters would still matter under a national popular vote, because their ballots would count toward the same total, and a candidate would still need support from many kinds of communities to win. As for recounts, states already know how to handle close elections, and clear national procedures could be established for a tight presidential race.

The possibility of "faithless electors," which Plumer also raises, is one more reason for reform. Such electors are rare, but no single person should be able to override the choice of a state's voters. The presidency is too important to depend on a process in which electors, rather than citizens, can decide the result.

The Electoral College may have been a sensible compromise when the nation was founded, but our democracy should keep improving. By supporting a national popular vote, you would help ensure that every citizen has an equal voice and that the candidate backed by the most Americans becomes president.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Constituent

The classroom, for generations, has been a fixed point on the map: a room with desks, a board, and the daily ritual of travel. Distance learning changes that entirely, letting the room come to the student. While it is not a perfect replacement for every school experience, the benefits for many students are substantial and, in some cases, life-changing. The ability to attend classes from home offers a kind of freedom that traditional schooling cannot easily match, and that freedom often translates directly into better learning.

One of the most obvious advantages is flexibility. Not every student functions at full capacity at eight in the morning, nor can every family build a schedule around a single bus route. With online or video-conferencing classes, a student can review a recorded lecture after a difficult night or pause a math lesson to work through a problem without the pressure of keeping up with the room. For students who are serious athletes, actors, or musicians, the traditional seven-hour school day can feel like a wall blocking their training. Distance learning allows them to pursue demanding practice schedules while still completing rigorous academic work. A competitive swimmer, for instance, could attend an English seminar from a hotel room during a national meet and not fall behind. That kind of accommodation is not special treatment; it is simply matching the structure of education to the reality of a student’s life.

Health and accessibility present another powerful argument. A student with a compromised immune system, a mobility impairment, or severe anxiety may find the physical school environment exhausting or even unsafe. For these learners, attending class from a comfortable home setting can remove barriers that have nothing to do with intelligence or effort. A teen recovering from surgery, for example, could participate in discussions through video conferencing instead of missing six weeks of school and scrambling to catch up. In such cases, distance learning is not a convenience. It is the difference between staying connected and disappearing from the classroom altogether.

Critics sometimes argue that learning from home weakens social development, and there is some truth to that. Schools are where friendships form and students learn to navigate group dynamics. However, the choice does not have to be absolute. Many distance learning programs include scheduled in-person labs, field trips, or social gatherings. A hybrid approach can preserve the best of both worlds. Moreover, video discussions and online group projects can create their own surprising forms of connection. A quiet student who rarely speaks in a crowded room may find that typing a thoughtful response in a chat is less intimidating, allowing instructors to see a depth that would otherwise go unnoticed.

Perhaps the strongest reason to support distance learning is that it expands educational opportunity. A rural school cannot always offer advanced physics, Mandarin, or creative writing. But through an online consortium, a student in a small town can take a calculus course taught by an expert three hundred miles away. That student is no longer limited by what a single building can provide. In this sense, distance learning does not isolate students; it connects them to a wider world of knowledge. For these reasons, schools should continue to offer and refine distance learning options. The goal of education is not to produce students who are good at sitting in rows, but to help each learner grow, and sometimes that growth happens best at home.

I believe the school should adopt Policy 1: students should be allowed to bring their phones to school and use them during lunch and other free periods, while keeping them turned off during class. This policy recognizes that phones are a normal part of students’ lives without allowing them to interfere with learning.

The most important reason is safety. Many students walk home, ride buses, participate in after-school activities, or have parents whose schedules change unexpectedly. Although the office phone is available, it is not always practical for hundreds of students to depend on one office, especially after school or during a busy dismissal.

Allowing phones during lunch and free time could also make the school day more manageable. Students often use those breaks to check messages from parents, look up club information, review a schedule, or coordinate transportation. For example, a student who has a dentist appointment after school might need to confirm who is picking them up. Another student may need to contact a coach about a practice location. These are reasonable uses of a phone that do not disrupt instruction.

At the same time, the rule that phones must be off during class protects the learning environment. Teachers should not have to compete with ringing phones, games, social media, or constant notifications. A clear consequence for using a phone in class—such as having it held until the end of the day—would encourage students to follow the rule. This creates a fair balance: students have access to their phones when it is appropriate, but classroom time remains focused on education.

A complete ban may sound simpler, but it would probably be difficult to enforce. Some students would still bring phones secretly, which could lead to arguments, confiscations, and wasted time. Policy 1 is more realistic because it sets reasonable boundaries instead of treating every phone as a problem. When students understand why a rule exists and see that it is fair, they are more likely to respect it.

Phones can also be useful in unexpected situations. During a lockdown, severe weather event, or transportation delay, students may need information quickly. While school staff should always lead during emergencies, allowing students to have phones can provide reassurance to families and an additional way to communicate when appropriate.

Students should not be on their phones all day, and school should remain a place for learning, conversation, and participation. However, banning phones completely would ignore the practical role they play in students’ safety and daily responsibilities. Policy 1 offers the better solution because it allows responsible use while keeping classrooms free from distractions.

Sincerely,  
A Concerned Student

Requiring every student to join an extracurricular activity may sound like a simple way to create a more involved school community, but it is not a fair rule. Sports teams, clubs, student government, and yearbook programs can be valuable experiences. They help students make friends, explore interests, and build skills that do not always appear in a classroom. However, an activity is most beneficial when a student chooses it willingly. Schools should strongly encourage participation and make opportunities available, but they should not force every student to join.

Students have very different responsibilities outside of school. Some care for younger siblings while their parents work. Others have jobs that help their families pay bills or save for college. A student who works several evenings a week at a grocery store may not have the time or energy to attend soccer practice, debate meetings, or yearbook deadlines. That job may already be teaching the student responsibility, communication, and time management. It would be unfair to treat that student as less involved simply because the school does not count paid work as an extracurricular activity.

Mandatory participation could also create stress for students who are already overwhelmed. High school coursework can be demanding, especially for students taking advanced classes or trying to improve grades in subjects they find difficult. Imagine a student who struggles with math and spends extra hours each week meeting with a tutor. If that student is required to join a club as well, the rule could turn a helpful school activity into another source of pressure. Instead of enjoying a drama club or robotics team, the student might attend only to meet the requirement, contributing little and resenting the experience.

Forcing students to participate may even weaken the activities themselves. Clubs and teams depend on members who are interested and motivated. A student council meeting is more productive when students attend because they want to improve school events, not because they need a signature on a participation form. Coaches also need athletes who are committed to practice. If students join a sport only because they have no other option, they may quit quickly or create frustration for teammates who genuinely care about the season.

This does not mean schools should ignore students who are disconnected from campus life. Many students do not join activities because they are shy, do not know what is offered, or cannot afford fees and equipment. Schools can address those problems without creating a universal requirement. They could hold an activity fair, provide late buses, waive club fees, and invite students personally to try programs that match their interests. Teachers and counselors could help a quiet student find a low-pressure club, such as art, chess, gardening, or volunteering.

Extracurricular activities are important because they give students chances to discover who they are beyond grades and test scores. Yet choice is what makes that discovery meaningful. A school should open as many doors as possible, but it should not force every student through the same one.

Although extracurricular activities can enrich a student’s education, schools should not require every student to participate in one. Sports teams, clubs, student government, and yearbook staffs offer valuable opportunities for friendship, leadership, and personal growth. However, making participation mandatory ignores the different responsibilities, interests, and needs of individual students. Schools should encourage extracurricular involvement strongly, but they should allow students and families to decide what is realistic and meaningful.

First, many students already have important obligations outside of school. Some students work after classes to help support their families or save for college. Others care for younger siblings while their parents are at work. A student who spends several hours each evening babysitting may not be able to attend soccer practice, debate meetings, or rehearsals. Requiring that student to join an activity could create stress rather than provide an enjoyable experience. Instead of learning responsibility through a club, the student might have to choose between meeting family responsibilities and obeying a school rule.

In addition, students benefit most from activities when they choose them voluntarily. Someone who loves writing may enjoy contributing to the school newspaper, while another student may feel proud of playing in the band. Their effort is stronger because the activity matches their interests. In contrast, a student forced to join a club simply to meet a requirement may attend meetings without participating, contribute little, and make the experience less positive for others. For example, a student who dislikes public speaking might join student council only because it is convenient, but that student may not be motivated to help organize events or represent classmates. Mandatory participation can turn activities meant to build enthusiasm into another assignment to complete.

Furthermore, students need time for rest, homework, and independent interests. High school classes can already be demanding, especially for students taking advanced courses or preparing for important exams. If every student must add an official activity to an already busy schedule, some may lose sleep or struggle academically. Free time is not wasted time. Students may use it to read, exercise, create art, care for family members, or explore interests that are not offered by the school. These experiences can also teach discipline and creativity, even if they do not appear on a club roster.

Rather than requiring participation, schools should make extracurricular activities accessible and appealing. They can offer a wider variety of clubs, provide late buses for students without transportation, and recognize students who contribute to their communities outside school. Teachers can explain the benefits of involvement and help shy or uncertain students find activities they may enjoy. These approaches would increase participation without punishing students whose circumstances are different.

Extracurricular activities are valuable, but they should remain opportunities, not obligations. Students develop responsibility in many ways, both inside and outside school. By encouraging involvement while respecting personal choices and family responsibilities, schools can create a community in which students participate because they want to, not simply because they have to.

Police officers may have trouble proving what the driver was doing. A simple rule—do not use a phone while the vehicle is moving—would leave less room for excuses. Drivers could set up navigation, playlists, or messages before they start the car. If they need to answer a call or send a text, they should pull into a parking lot or another safe place first.

Dear Principal,

I'm writing to express my concerns about the possible policy change that would require students to have at least a grade B average to participate in sports and other activities. I understand that the goal is to encourage students to work harder and achieve better grades, but I strongly believe that this policy would be unfair and have negative consequences for many students.

Firstly, I think it's unrealistic to expect all students to have a B average. Every student learns at their own pace, and some may struggle with certain subjects due to various reasons such as learning difficulties or personal issues. By setting a B average as a requirement, we would be excluding many students who are capable and enthusiastic about participating in activities, but may not be academically gifted. For instance, I have a friend who is an excellent soccer player, but he struggles with math and science. He works hard to keep his grades up, but a B average is just out of his reach. If this policy is implemented, he would be denied the opportunity to play the sport he loves, which would be devastating for him.

Another reason I'm against this policy is that it would create an uneven playing field. Students who come from more affluent families or have better resources may have an advantage when it comes to getting good grades. They may have access to private tutors, online resources, and other tools that can help them achieve better grades. On the other hand, students from lower-income families may not have the same resources, making it harder for them to compete. This policy would essentially penalize students who are already at a disadvantage.

Furthermore, I believe that participating in activities is essential for a well-rounded education. Sports and clubs teach us important life skills such as teamwork, leadership, and time management. They also provide an outlet for stress and anxiety, which can actually help us perform better academically. By denying students the opportunity to participate in activities, we would be taking away a crucial part of their educational experience.

I also think that this policy would be counterproductive. If students are struggling academically, taking away their opportunities to participate in activities would only make things worse. Many students participate in activities because they enjoy them, and it gives them a sense of purpose and motivation. If we take that away, they may become disengaged and demotivated, leading to even poorer academic performance.

Instead of implementing this policy, I think we should focus on providing more support for students who are struggling academically. We could offer extra tutoring, mentoring programs, or study skills workshops to help students improve their grades. We could also encourage teachers to provide more feedback and guidance to help students understand what they need to work on.

In conclusion, I strongly believe that requiring a B average to participate in activities is not the right solution. It would be unfair, create an uneven playing field, and take away important opportunities for students to develop essential life skills. I urge you to consider alternative solutions that would support students who are struggling academically, rather than penalizing them. I hope you will take our views into consideration and make a decision that is in the best interest of all students.

Driverless Cars: A Future Worth Pursuing

Imagine a world where no one has to fear a distracted driver swerving across the center line, where an elderly neighbor can visit family without asking for a ride, and where cities are not overwhelmed by endless parking lots. According to the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming," this scenario may be closer than many realize. While the technology certainly faces real hurdles, the development of autonomous vehicles should continue because of their incredible potential to save lives, expand personal independence, and conserve resources.

The most compelling argument in favor of driverless cars comes down to basic safety. The article highlights that human error causes over 90 percent of traffic accidents, with texting, drowsiness, and impaired driving among the leading culprits. These mistakes are not rare flukes; they happen every day and cost thousands of lives. In contrast, a computer never gets sleepy after a double shift, never glances down at a text message, and never gets behind the wheel intoxicated. Relying on laser radar, cameras, GPS, and complex sensors to track obstacles, lane markings, and signals, autonomous cars can monitor the roadway without blinking. Eliminating even a fraction of human-caused collisions would be a massive victory for public safety, and fewer wrecks would also help lower insurance costs for families.

Beyond safety, autonomous vehicles offer life-changing mobility for people who cannot drive today. The article notes that driverless systems could provide reliable transportation for elderly and disabled passengers. For someone who has lost the ability to drive due to age or physical limitations, a self-driving car represents the difference between feeling isolated at home and staying engaged with their community. 

Furthermore, Google cofounder Sergey Brin envisions a future where autonomous public transit uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today's vehicles. If communities shift toward shared driverless fleets, cities could drastically reduce smog, conserve energy, and repurpose acres of asphalt into parks or housing. 

Critics, of course, raise valid concerns that cannot be ignored. The article explains that current sensors struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, and unmarked construction zones, while software remains vulnerable to glitches and cybersecurity threats. Additionally, when semi-autonomous systems require a human to intervene during an emergency, studies show that inattentive passengers react too slowly. There is also the lingering legal headache of figuring out who pays for a crash—the owner, the carmaker, or the programmer. 

Yet these problems are reasons to refine the technology, not abandon it. Sensor systems can be tested and upgraded for harsh weather, software security can be fortified, and lawmakers can establish clear liability rules before driverless cars flood the market. In fact, human inattention in semi-autonomous cars only proves that full autonomy is the safer end goal. Major innovations like airplanes and modern automobiles faced comparable safety and legal hurdles when they were first invented, and society moved forward through careful engineering rather than giving up.

In conclusion, driverless cars hold the promise of drastically reducing fatal crashes, helping the elderly and disabled lead more independent lives, and making our transportation systems far more efficient. The challenges mentioned in the article are serious, but they are problems that can be solved with time, testing, and smart regulations. Walking away from autonomous vehicles would simply mean accepting thousands of preventable deaths each year, and that is a cost society cannot afford.

Driverless Cars Need to Slow Down

Driverless cars sound exciting. No more parking stress, fewer accidents, and rides for people who cannot drive. But after reading "Driverless Cars Are Coming," I think we should not rush into developing and using them on regular roads. The technology is not reliable enough yet, and the legal problems are too big to ignore.

First, the sensors and software can fail in normal weather and road conditions. The article says current sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or unmarked construction zones. That is a huge problem because those conditions happen all the time. If a car cannot see lane lines in a construction zone or loses track of the road in a storm, it could cause a serious crash. A human driver might also struggle in bad weather, but at least people can slow down and make careful choices. A computer that gets confused is unpredictable.

Second, semi-autonomous cars may actually make drivers less safe because they lose focus. The article explains that these systems still need a human to stay alert and take over in an emergency. But studies show that passengers quickly lose focus when a computer is driving, and that slows their reaction times. If someone thinks the car is handling everything, they might start texting or daydreaming. Then, when the car suddenly beeps and asks them to take over, they are not ready. That sounds even worse than just driving yourself, because you have a false sense of security.

Finally, if a driverless car crashes, no one knows who is legally responsible. The article says it is unclear whether the owner, the software developer, or the automaker should be held responsible. This matters because accidents will happen. If a family is hurt by a driverless car, they should not have to wait years while lawyers and companies argue about fault. Until the law has clear answers, putting these cars on public roads is unfair to everyone else.

I understand the supporters' point that human error causes over 90 percent of accidents, and driverless cars could reduce crashes and help elderly or disabled people. Those are good goals. But a technology can be a good idea someday and still be too dangerous today. We should improve the sensors, test the software much more, and create clear legal rules first. Otherwise, we are treating public roads like a giant experiment.

In conclusion, I am against developing driverless cars for widespread use right now. The article shows that they have trouble with weather, make human drivers less focused, and raise unanswered legal questions. Maybe in the future they will be safe, but for now, we should slow down.

When faced with a difficult decision, it is common for individuals to seek advice from others. While talking to one person may provide some insight, seeking multiple opinions can be even more beneficial in making a better choice. This approach allows individuals to gather a diverse range of perspectives, weigh the pros and cons of different options, and ultimately make a more informed decision.

One of the primary reasons seeking multiple opinions is helpful is that it exposes individuals to different viewpoints and experiences. For instance, when considering a career change, talking to multiple people in the desired field can provide a well-rounded understanding of the profession. A person may speak with a seasoned professional who can offer valuable insights into the industry, as well as a recent entrant who can share their experiences navigating the job market. Additionally, consulting with a career counselor can provide a more objective perspective on the skills and qualifications required for the new career. By gathering information from multiple sources, individuals can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the potential benefits and drawbacks of their decision.

Another advantage of seeking multiple opinions is that it allows individuals to identify patterns and inconsistencies in the advice they receive. For example, if multiple people caution against a particular course of action, it may be a sign that the decision is not the best one. On the other hand, if several people recommend a similar approach, it can increase confidence in the chosen path. This was the case for a friend who was considering whether to attend graduate school. After speaking with several professors, alumni, and current students, she realized that the majority of them emphasized the importance of gaining practical experience before pursuing further education. This consistent message helped her decide to delay graduate school and focus on building her professional skills first.

Seeking multiple opinions can also help individuals to anticipate potential pitfalls and develop contingency plans. When considering a major purchase, such as a house or a car, it is common to seek advice from friends, family, and experts. By talking to multiple people, individuals can learn about potential issues that may arise, such as hidden costs or maintenance requirements. For instance, a person considering buying a house may talk to a real estate agent, a contractor, and a financial advisor. Each of these individuals can provide unique insights into the process, from the current market conditions to the potential for renovation and repair costs. By gathering this information, the individual can make a more informed decision and prepare for potential challenges that may arise.

In conclusion, seeking multiple opinions can be a highly effective way to make better choices. By gathering a diverse range of perspectives, weighing the pros and cons of different options, and identifying patterns and inconsistencies in the advice received, individuals can make more informed decisions. Additionally, seeking multiple opinions can help individuals anticipate potential pitfalls and develop contingency plans. Whether considering a major life change, a career shift, or a significant purchase, talking to multiple people can provide valuable insights and increase confidence in the chosen path. Ultimately, seeking multiple opinions is a key component of making well-informed decisions that can have a lasting impact on one's life.

Drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity that requires their hands, eyes, or attention while operating a vehicle. A narrow exception for truly hands-free navigation, set up before the trip begins, is reasonable. Beyond that, the evidence and common sense point toward a firm restriction.

Consider what driving actually demands. A car moving at fifty miles per hour covers about seventy feet every second. Glancing at a text for even four or five seconds means traveling the length of a football field essentially blind. No one would accept a driver who closed their eyes for that long, yet we tolerate the equivalent every day because the phone feels harmless. It isn't. Federal estimates attribute thousands of deaths each year in the United States to distracted driving, and researchers widely believe the true figure is higher, since drivers rarely admit to fiddling with a phone after a crash.

The common defense of hands-free calling deserves a closer look. Many people assume that keeping both hands on the wheel solves the problem. But studies using driving simulators and real traffic data have repeatedly found that the cognitive load of a conversation degrades performance regardless of whether the phone is held. The brain does not neatly split attention between a spoken exchange and a developing hazard. Reaction times slow, drivers miss exits and signs, and their eyes fixate on a narrower portion of the road. A conversation with someone who isn't in the car is different from talking to a passenger, too. A passenger can see the traffic, pause when a truck merges, and share the situational awareness. A caller cannot.

Opponents argue that a total ban infringes on personal freedom and ignores modern life. People use phones for directions, music, and emergencies, and many jobs depend on constant availability. These concerns are real, but they carry less weight than they seem to. Freedom to use a device ends where it endangers strangers who never agreed to share the risk. A pedestrian in a crosswalk or a child in another car has no say in the driver's choice to answer a message. As for convenience, nearly every practical need can be handled in advance: set the route before pulling out, choose the playlist, silence notifications. For genuine emergencies, pulling over is almost always possible and takes under a minute.

Enforcement is the usual objection to any ban, and it is fair to acknowledge that rules alone do not change behavior overnight. Yet seat belt laws and drunk driving penalties faced the same skepticism and eventually shifted social norms dramatically. Phone-blocking technology that activates while a vehicle is in motion, already built into many devices as a "driving mode," could reinforce the law without relying solely on police. Pairing clear penalties with these tools would make compliance easier rather than merely punishing failure.

There is also a cultural dimension. Part of what makes phone use behind the wheel so persistent is the belief that "I'm a good driver, so it's fine for me." Nearly every driver thinks this, and statistically they cannot all be right. A strict standard removes the guesswork and the self-flattery. It says that nothing on that screen is worth the risk of a life.

Phones are woven into modern existence, and no one is asking people to abandon them. But the car is a place where a moment's inattention can be irreversible. Treating that space as one where the phone simply stays out of the equation is a modest demand, and one that society can and should make.

Dear Principal,

I respectfully urge you not to require students to maintain a B average in order to participate in sports, clubs, music, and other school activities. Academic success should always matter, but a strict B-average rule would punish many students who need activities most and could actually make it harder for them to improve in school.

For many students, athletics and clubs are not distractions from education; they are reasons to stay connected to school. A student who struggles in algebra may still feel successful on the soccer field, in the marching band, or on the robotics team. That sense of belonging can motivate students to attend class, ask for help, and keep trying when schoolwork becomes difficult. If participation is taken away after a C average, some students may feel that they have failed at everything, not just one subject.

Activities also teach important skills that grades do not always measure. On a team, students learn responsibility because others depend on them. In drama, debate, student government, and community-service clubs, they practice communication, leadership, and cooperation. These experiences can build confidence and prepare students for jobs and college. A student with a C average may still be a dedicated teammate, a talented musician, or a reliable volunteer. It would be unfair to ignore those strengths.

In addition, a B average is not equally easy for every student to earn. Some students take advanced classes, work after school, care for younger siblings, or face challenges at home. Others may be improving steadily but have not yet raised every grade to a B. A student who moves from failing grades to mostly Cs has made real progress and should be encouraged, not excluded. The proposed rule could especially harm students who already have fewer supports outside school.

Instead of banning students with C averages from activities, the school could use participation as motivation for improvement. Students who are struggling academically could be required to attend tutoring, meet regularly with teachers, complete missing work, or create an academic improvement plan. Coaches and activity sponsors could check grades and encourage students to use study time wisely. This approach would hold students accountable while still allowing them to benefit from the activity they value.

Of course, students should not ignore their academic responsibilities. If someone is failing several classes or refusing to do assigned work, temporary restrictions may be appropriate. However, a C average usually means that a student is meeting basic expectations, even if there is room to improve. A single standard of a B average would turn participation into a reward only for students who are already succeeding academically.

Our school should help students grow in every area, not force them to choose between learning and belonging. Please consider policies that provide support and accountability rather than exclusion. Keeping students involved may be one of the best ways to help them achieve higher grades in the first place.

Sincerely,  
A Concerned Student

As the school's cell phone policy comes under review, it is essential to consider the potential impact of each proposed policy on the student body. In my opinion, Policy 1, which allows students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch periods and other free times, is the more sensible approach. By permitting students to have their phones with them, albeit with certain restrictions, the school can strike a balance between minimizing distractions during class time and acknowledging the importance of mobile devices in modern life.

One of the primary concerns with Policy 2, which prohibits students from having phones at school altogether, is that it may be overly restrictive and unrealistic. Many students rely on their phones to stay in touch with parents or guardians, particularly in emergency situations. For instance, a student may need to contact a parent to inform them of a change in after-school plans or to request a pickup due to illness. By banning phones entirely, the school may inadvertently create more problems than it solves, such as forcing students to leave campus to make a phone call or causing undue worry for parents who are unable to reach their children. In contrast, Policy 1 allows students to maintain this vital line of communication while still ensuring that classrooms remain phone-free zones.

Another significant advantage of Policy 1 is that it promotes a sense of responsibility and trust among students. By allowing them to use their phones during designated times, the school is, in effect, giving them the autonomy to manage their own time and make responsible choices. This, in turn, can help to foster a more positive and mature attitude towards phone use, as students learn to balance their desire to stay connected with the need to focus on their schoolwork. Moreover, this approach acknowledges that mobile devices are an integral part of modern life and that students will inevitably need to learn how to use them wisely. By incorporating phones into the school environment in a controlled manner, the school can help students develop essential skills, such as self-regulation and time management, that will benefit them in the long run.

In addition to these practical considerations, it is also worth noting that a blanket ban on phones, as proposed in Policy 2, may be difficult to enforce effectively. Students may still find ways to sneak in phone use, potentially leading to a cat-and-mouse game between students and teachers. This could not only create disciplinary issues but also undermine the authority of the school and the credibility of the policy. In contrast, Policy 1 offers a more pragmatic and flexible approach, one that recognizes the complexities of the issue and seeks to find a workable solution that balances competing interests.

Ultimately, the key to a successful cell phone policy is finding a balance between minimizing distractions and acknowledging the importance of mobile devices in modern life. Policy 1, with its emphasis on responsible phone use during designated times, offers a sensible and realistic approach that promotes student autonomy, trust, and responsibility. By adopting this policy, the school can create a more positive and inclusive environment that recognizes the needs and realities of its students, while also ensuring that classrooms remain focused and productive learning spaces.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge you to support changing presidential elections to a national popular vote. The Electoral College was created as a compromise by the Founding Fathers, but it no longer represents the fairest way to choose a president. In a democracy, the candidate who receives the most votes from citizens should win.

According to the Office of the Federal Register, the Electoral College has 538 electors, and a candidate needs 270 electoral votes to become president. Each state gets electors based on its number of representatives and senators. Although this system may have seemed reasonable when it was created, it can give some voters more influence than others. Most states use a winner-take-all system, meaning that even if a candidate wins a state by only a few votes, that candidate receives all of the state’s electoral votes. Millions of votes for the other candidate then do not affect the final result.

This problem has had real consequences. Bradford Plumer explains that candidates have won the national popular vote but lost the presidency, including in 2000 and 2016. It is hard to call an election democratic when more Americans vote for one candidate but another candidate becomes president. A popular vote would make every individual vote count equally, whether a person lives in Texas, California, Ohio, or a small rural state.

The current system also changes how candidates campaign. Plumer points out that campaigns focus mostly on swing states, where either party has a chance of winning. Voters in states that are considered safely Republican or safely Democratic may be ignored because candidates assume the outcome is already decided. For example, a voter in a safe state might not see many campaign visits, advertisements, or attention to local concerns. Under a popular-vote system, candidates would have a reason to seek votes everywhere, because gaining more votes in any state would help them.

Supporters of the Electoral College make important arguments. Judge Richard Posner argues that it protects federalism and forces candidates to form broad coalitions instead of only focusing on large cities or one region. He also says it can provide a fast, clear result and prevent a nationwide recount. These are reasonable concerns. However, a popular vote would not mean that rural or small-state voters would disappear. Their votes would count just as much as anyone else’s. Candidates would still need support from many different kinds of communities to earn the most votes nationwide.

Recounts are also not a reason to accept an unfair result. Close elections can require careful counting, whether the dispute happens in one state or across the country. We should improve election procedures instead of keeping a system that can overrule the choice of the majority.

The Electoral College is a historical part of our government, but history alone is not enough reason to keep it. Our country should choose its president by the principle of one person, one vote. Please support efforts to move toward election by national popular vote.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]

Dear Principal Davis,

As our school re-evaluates its approach to mobile technology, I appreciate that you are weighing multiple perspectives before setting a final rule. Deciding how to regulate devices in an environment built for learning is no small feat. While I understand the instinct behind a comprehensive ban, I urge you to adopt Policy 1, which permits students to carry phones and use them responsibly during lunch and free periods, while keeping them strictly turned off during instruction.

A total ban assumes that the easiest way to solve distraction is through complete eradication. In reality, modern smartphones are far more than entertainment consoles; they have become integral tools for daily coordination. Many students rely on them to communicate last-minute schedule shifts with working parents, coordinate carpools after sports practices, or check messages regarding shifts at part-time jobs. When schools forbid these devices entirely, families bear the brunt of the inconvenience. If a parent needs to alert a child about an altered pickup routine or a family emergency, the front office staff will suddenly be overwhelmed with mundane relay calls that students could easily handle themselves in the cafeteria.

Beyond convenience, Policy 1 serves an essential pedagogical purpose: teaching self-regulation. When students graduate, neither college professors nor workplace supervisors will confiscate their devices or manage their focus for them. Expecting adolescents to navigate the boundary between focused work and digital downtime requires practice, not enforced absence. Allowing phone access during personal breaks, paired with clear, non-negotiable expectations during class hours, mirrors the expectations of the adult world. It treats students as capable of learning restraint while establishing that instructional time remains sacred.

From an enforcement standpoint, an outright prohibition also creates more friction than it resolves. Complete bans inevitably foster an adversarial atmosphere between students and faculty. Teachers are forced to act as monitors, policing pockets and inspecting backpacks, while students simply become more covert, concealing screens under desks or taking suspiciously long trips to the restroom. Conversely, a policy that permits phones during lunch removes the desperate impulse to sneak glances during class. The rule becomes straightforward and equitable: keep the phone silenced and out of sight during class, or lose the privilege. Most students are willing to respect that clear trade-off.

Restricting phone use exclusively to free times strikes an effective balance between protecting classroom focus and acknowledging modern realities. By adopting Policy 1, you can safeguard instructional integrity without placing an impractical burden on our staff or treating students as incapable of self-discipline. Thank you for your leadership and for considering the student perspective on this vital matter.

Sincerely,

Alex Morgan

Distance learning, which allows students to attend classes from home through online platforms or video conferencing, has grown increasingly popular. Although some people worry that this model lacks the personal interaction and structure of a traditional classroom, I believe the benefits for students are substantial. The main advantages include greater flexibility, broader accessibility, and fewer distractions.

One of the strongest arguments for distance learning is the flexibility it provides. Many students have demanding schedules because of part-time jobs, family responsibilities, or ongoing health issues. Attending class from home lets them organize their time more effectively and fit school around the rest of their lives. A student who works in the evening, for example, can take morning classes online instead of being forced to choose between employment and education. This kind of flexibility can make a real difference for learners who find a traditional schedule difficult to manage.

Distance learning also makes education more accessible. In remote or underserved areas, students often lack access to high-quality courses and teachers simply because of where they live. Online classes help close that gap by offering the same opportunities regardless of location. Students with mobility challenges or chronic illnesses also benefit, since they can participate fully from home without the strain of commuting. As a result, these students are less likely to fall behind, and their presence can add valuable perspectives to the class.

Another advantage is the chance to reduce distractions. Traditional classrooms can be noisy and crowded, with side conversations and other interruptions that pull attention away from the lesson. At home, students can create a study environment that suits their own needs, which often leads to better focus. For instance, a student who is easily distracted by peers might set up a quiet workspace at home and concentrate more deeply on the material.

Of course, distance learning is not without challenges, including less face-to-face contact and a greater need for self-discipline. Schools can address these issues by scheduling regular virtual office hours and checking in with students to keep them engaged and motivated.

Overall, the advantages of attending classes from home clearly outweigh the drawbacks. Distance learning allows schools to serve a wider range of students, supports stronger academic outcomes, and prepares young people for a world where remote work and digital communication are common. As technology becomes an even bigger part of daily life, offering distance learning is not just a useful option; it is a necessary step in helping students build the skills and adaptability they will need for the future.

When faced with important life decisions, individuals often seek guidance from multiple sources. This approach is particularly useful when choosing a career path, navigating complex relationships, or making significant financial commitments. While consulting a single trusted mentor or friend can be a good starting point, relying solely on their advice can be limiting. Gathering multiple opinions is crucial for making informed decisions, as it helps counter personal bias, exposes hidden blind spots, and enables the decision-maker to form a well-rounded conclusion.

One of the primary benefits of seeking multiple opinions is that it acts as a safeguard against individual bias. Each person's perspective is shaped by their unique experiences, fears, and aspirations, which can influence the advice they offer. For example, a young professional considering a career change might consult an older relative who prioritizes job security, only to receive a cautionary warning about the risks of switching careers. In contrast, speaking with an entrepreneurial peer might yield enthusiastic encouragement to take the leap. By considering both viewpoints, the individual can weigh the pros and cons of each option and find a middle ground that balances caution with innovation. This nuanced approach helps to neutralize extreme attitudes and fosters a more realistic understanding of the situation.

Complex decisions often involve multiple facets that require distinct forms of knowledge and life experience. The process of synthesizing diverse advice also empowers the decision-maker by encouraging active engagement with the evidence and promoting critical thinking. When individuals seek counsel from only one person, there is a risk of outsourcing responsibility and passively adopting their mentor's judgment. In contrast, considering multiple viewpoints forces individuals to weigh conflicting arguments, reconcile differing priorities, and clarify their personal values. This intellectual exercise instills greater confidence in the ultimate choice, ensuring that the final outcome reflects deliberate ownership rather than blind deference.

Ultimately, seeking multiple opinions transforms the decision-making process into a rigorous and enriching assessment. By offsetting individual biases, uncovering overlooked factors, and fostering independent critical thinking, a diverse range of perspectives equips individuals to make more informed choices. As a result, the decision-making process becomes more collaborative, nuanced, and effective. By embracing the diversity of opinions and experiences, individuals can navigate complex decisions with greater confidence and clarity, leading to more satisfying and successful outcomes.

I think students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home, as long as it is an option and not a requirement. Some students do better in a regular classroom, but others have situations where learning from home is the better choice, and schools should make room for both.

One big reason is that distance learning helps students who can't always make it to school. For example, a student who is sick for a long time, like someone going through treatment for an illness, would fall way behind if they had to miss weeks of class. With video conferencing, they could still hear the lesson, ask questions, and turn in work. The same goes for a student who breaks a leg or has surgery. Without distance learning, they might have to rely on a pile of worksheets, which isn't the same as actually being taught.

Another reason is that it can help students who have problems at school that make it hard to focus. Some students get bullied, and going to school every day makes them anxious. Others get overwhelmed in crowded hallways and loud classrooms. At home, they might be calmer and able to pay attention to the lesson. I know a kid who struggled a lot with anxiety in middle school, and when she did classes online for a semester, her grades went up because she wasn't dreading the day so much.

Distance learning can also save time and give students more flexibility. Some students live far from school and spend an hour or more on the bus each way. That is two hours that could be used for homework, sleep, or helping their family. Other students have jobs or take care of younger siblings. Being able to log in from home could make it possible for them to stay in school instead of dropping out.

Of course, there are some downsides. Some people argue that students will get distracted at home by their phones, video games, or TV. That is a fair point, and I think it's true that some students wouldn't stay on task. Also, not everyone has good internet or a quiet place to work. And being in a classroom helps you make friends and learn how to work with other people. But I think these problems can be handled. Schools can require students to keep their cameras on, turn in assignments on time, and check in with teachers regularly. Schools could also lend out laptops or hotspots to students who need them. If a student isn't doing well with distance learning, they could be moved back to in-person classes.

Because of these problems, I don't think distance learning should replace regular school for everybody. Students need social time and hands-on activities, like labs in science class, that are hard to do at home. A good solution would be to let students choose distance learning when they have a real reason, and to check up on how they are doing.

In conclusion, I think students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home. It helps students who are sick, anxious, far away, or busy with responsibilities, and it keeps them from falling behind. Even though it has some drawbacks, like distractions and unequal access to technology, schools can fix a lot of that with rules and support. Giving students the option makes school fairer and gives more people a chance to succeed.

Dear Principal,

I believe the school should adopt Policy 1, allowing students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times while requiring them to be turned off during class. This policy recognizes that phones can be useful tools for students and families without allowing them to interfere with learning. A complete ban may seem simpler, but it would create unnecessary problems and would be difficult to enforce fairly.

First, phones are important for communication and safety. Many students arrange rides, after-school activities, jobs, sports practices, and family responsibilities through their phones. If a practice is canceled, a bus is late, or a parent needs to share an important message, students should be able to receive that information once class is over. Phones are also valuable in emergencies. Although students should always follow school safety procedures, having access to a phone during lunch or after school can help them contact a parent or guardian quickly when needed. Banning phones entirely would make ordinary communication much harder for families.

Second, allowing phones during free time gives students a reasonable amount of independence. Lunch and study breaks are times when students can relax, socialize, and manage personal responsibilities. Some students may use their phones to check homework assignments, review a school calendar, listen to music with headphones, or communicate with family members. Others may choose to play games or use social media briefly. As long as these activities do not disrupt others or violate school rules, students should be trusted to make responsible choices during their own free time. School should help students learn self-control, not remove every opportunity to practice it.

At the same time, the rule that phones must be turned off during class protects the learning environment. Teachers need students’ attention, and notifications, texting, and social media can easily become distractions. Policy 1 makes the expectation clear: class time is for learning, while free time can include personal phone use. If a student breaks the rule by using a phone during class, the school can apply consequences such as confiscating the device until the end of the day or contacting a parent. This approach addresses misuse directly instead of punishing all students, including those who follow the rules.

A total phone ban could also create conflict. Students may try to hide phones because they need them for transportation or family communication. Teachers and administrators would then spend valuable time searching for devices and deciding whether students had violated the policy. Policy 1 is more realistic and easier to enforce because it focuses on when and how phones are used rather than demanding that students leave them at home.

For these reasons, Policy 1 is the better choice. It supports safety, communication, and student responsibility while still protecting classroom instruction. By allowing phones during free periods but not during lessons, the school can create a balanced policy that benefits students, families, and teachers.

I believe Policy 1 would be better for our school. Students should be allowed to bring their phones and use them during lunch and other free times, as long as they are turned off and put away during class. This policy would give students some freedom while still protecting learning time.

First, phones can be important for safety and communication. Many students ride the bus, walk home, stay after school for sports, or have changing rides. If a practice gets canceled or a parent is running late, it is helpful to be able to contact family members quickly. Without phones, students would have to use the school office phone, which could be crowded or unavailable. Also, in an emergency, students and parents often feel safer knowing they can reach each other. Phones should not replace school safety procedures, but they can still be useful.

Second, lunch and free periods are not class time. Students need breaks during the day, and checking a phone for a few minutes can help them relax. Some students use their phones to listen to music, read, play games, check sports scores, or message friends. Others might use them for productive reasons, such as checking homework assignments, looking at the school calendar, or emailing a teacher. Banning phones completely would treat all phone use as a problem, even when students are using them responsibly.

That is why the rule about turning them off during class is important. Teachers should be allowed to collect a phone or give consequences if a student uses one during instruction. The school could also require phones to stay in backpacks, lockers, or a phone holder during class. This would make the rule clear and easier to enforce.

Policy 2 seems too strict. Students would probably still try to bring phones secretly, which could create more arguments between students and staff. A total ban might also punish students who follow the rules because of a smaller number of students who misuse phones. Instead of banning phones completely, the school should teach students how to use technology responsibly.

Policy 1 is a fair compromise. It keeps phones away during class, when learning needs students’ full attention, but allows them during lunch and free time, when students have more choice. It would support safety, communication, and responsible behavior without causing an unnecessary complete ban. I hope you will choose Policy 1.

I strongly support our principal’s decision to require every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. While some classmates will probably complain about having another obligation piled onto their schedule, the upside of getting involved outside the classroom is well worth it. Joining a team, club, or committee builds practical life skills, creates a stronger sense of community, and pushes us to explore talents we might never have discovered on our own.

To start, extracurriculars teach lessons that simply cannot be found in a textbook. Take the yearbook staff, for instance. Working on the yearbook forces students to manage tight deadlines, collaborate under pressure, and take pride in producing something the whole school reads. Serving on the student council offers real-world practice in public speaking, compromise, and leadership. Even joining an athletic team teaches crucial habits, from physical discipline and time management to handling tough losses with grace. These are the exact qualities colleges look for and employers value most. When participation is mandatory, everyone gets the opportunity to build these strengths, not just the students who already feel confident enough to sign up.

Beyond skill-building, activities give students a real anchor at school. It is surprisingly easy to drift through the day going from class to class, keeping to yourself, and heading straight home the second the final bell rings. That routine can leave people feeling isolated and disconnected. When a quiet or new student joins the drama club crew or the marching band, they immediately enter a circle of peers working toward a shared goal. Feeling like you belong somewhere on campus makes a huge difference; students who feel connected tend to show up more consistently, care more about their classes, and stay out of trouble. Requiring an activity guarantees that nobody gets completely overlooked.

Just as importantly, this policy gives teenagers a gentle push out of their comfort zones. Left entirely to ourselves, most of us stick to what feels safe, which usually means scrolling on our phones or hanging out with the same small group. A student who has never picked up a paintbrush might join the art club just to fulfill the rule and discover a genuine passion for painting. Someone else might try track and field and fall in love with running. Because the school offers dozens of choices—from robotics and debate to sports and volunteer clubs—students still have the freedom to pick something that matches their personality.

Of course, critics point out that some students already have full plates with part-time jobs, heavy homework loads, or family responsibilities. While that is a valid concern, it is a problem that can be solved with flexibility rather than by scrapping the policy altogether. The administration could easily offer clubs that meet during lunch or once every two weeks, or even count outside community service and job hours toward the requirement. Since the rule calls for just one activity, the time commitment remains reasonable. In fact, learning to juggle a single club alongside classes often helps students become better, more disciplined managers of their time.

In the end, school should be about developing the whole person, not just training people to pass standardized tests. The principal’s policy encourages us to grow socially, emotionally, and practically. With a little common-sense flexibility for students with unique situations, this requirement will make our school a livelier, more supportive place for everyone.

Driverless cars should continue to be developed because they could save lives, give more people access to transportation, and make travel more efficient. The technology still has real weaknesses, but those weaknesses are reasons to test and improve autonomous vehicles carefully rather than to give up on them. With strong safety standards, cybersecurity protections, and clear laws, driverless cars could become a major benefit to society.

The best argument for driverless cars is their potential to reduce traffic accidents. The article points out that human error causes more than 90 percent of crashes, often because drivers text, grow drowsy, or drive while impaired. An autonomous vehicle does not get tired or look down at a phone. It uses laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors to watch the road at all times, detecting obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals. If this technology prevents even a portion of the crashes caused by human mistakes, it could save many lives and lower insurance costs for families.

Driverless cars could also help people who have trouble driving themselves. Elderly and disabled people often depend on relatives, public transportation, or expensive ride services to get around. Autonomous vehicles could give them more independence by making it easier to reach jobs, schools, medical appointments, and social events. The benefits could reach beyond individuals as well. Google cofounder Sergey Brin imagines driverless public transportation that uses half the fuel and half the parking space of today's cars. If fewer people needed to own a car, cities might see less congestion and pollution, and the land now used for parking could become parks, housing, or businesses.

Critics are right that the technology is not perfect. According to the article, sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, and construction zones without clear markings, and software can suffer from glitches or cyberattacks. These problems are serious, since a computer error could endanger passengers and pedestrians. Still, human drivers also make poor decisions in bad weather and unfamiliar conditions. The answer is to require thorough testing before fully autonomous cars become common. Manufacturers should have to show that their vehicles can handle difficult conditions, resist hacking, and pull over safely or alert a human when the system cannot continue.

Another worry is who should be responsible after an accident. The article notes that it is unclear whether the owner, the automaker, or the software developer should be held legally liable. That uncertainty is a challenge, but it is not a reason to halt development. Governments can write rules that assign responsibility, require companies to carry insurance, and make sure crashes are investigated carefully. Laws have been adapted for other new technologies, and autonomous vehicles can be regulated in the same way.

Overall, driverless cars deserve continued development because their possible benefits outweigh their risks. They could reduce accidents caused by human error, offer independence to elderly and disabled people, and make transportation more efficient. Of course, they must be introduced cautiously, with careful testing and clear legal protections. If society takes on the remaining safety and ethical problems, driverless cars could lead to a safer and more accessible future.
