Dear Principal Harris,

I understand that you are deciding whether all students should be required to perform community service. I have friends on both sides of this question, and I have thought about it carefully. My conclusion is that students should be required to serve, but the requirement should be modest and flexible, with room for students to choose how they meet it.

Start with what my friends who already volunteer have told me. Marcus tutors second graders at the elementary school down the street twice a week. He says he signed up because a teacher suggested it, and he figured he would quit after a month. That was last year. Now he talks about a boy named Eli who could barely read in September and finished the spring with a stack of library books. Marcus has never been an enthusiastic student, yet he has become more patient and more confident in his own abilities. Nothing in a classroom taught him that.

Not every student would wander into an experience like that on their own, and this is the strongest argument for a requirement. Many teenagers are busy or nervous, or they simply never think to look for opportunities. A school expectation gives them the push. Once they are out picking up litter along the creek or sorting cans at the food pantry, they see their town differently. They notice who needs help and what a few hours of effort can change.

I do not dismiss the objections, though. My friend Dana works after school to help her family with expenses, and she plays in the orchestra on weekends. When she hears the word "required," she hears one more demand on a schedule that is already full. Other friends worry that forced volunteering feels like punishment and will make students resent the idea of helping at all. These are fair concerns, and a poorly designed program could create exactly that result.

That is why the details matter so much. I suggest a requirement of around twenty hours over the full four years of high school, which comes to only a few hours each semester. Students should be allowed to complete the hours during weekends, summers, or school breaks, so that no one has to give up a job or a practice. Service they already do through churches, sports teams, or family responsibilities, such as caring for a younger sibling or an elderly neighbor, should count. Dana, for instance, could meet the goal by playing music at a nursing home with her orchestra, something she might actually enjoy.

The school can also make the process easier by keeping a list of local organizations that need help and by organizing a few group service days. Cleaning up a park with classmates feels less like an assignment and more like an afternoon with friends who happen to be doing something useful.

A requirement like this asks very little of any one student, but across the whole school it adds up to thousands of hours of tutoring, cleanup, and support for people who need it. More important, it introduces students to a habit that many of them would carry into adulthood. Some will resist at first, as Marcus nearly did, and then be glad they stayed.

Thank you for considering my views. I would be happy to help the school put together a list of volunteer options if you decide to move forward.

Sincerely,
A concerned student

Drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle. I know that sounds strict, especially since almost everyone has a phone now, but driving already takes full attention. Adding a phone, even for a quick glance, takes your brain away from the road in a way that is not safe.

Texting and driving is the most obvious problem. You have to look at the screen, read the message, and think about what to type back. That is several seconds where you are not watching the car in front of you. At sixty miles per hour, a car moves about eighty-eight feet every second. If you look down for three seconds, you have basically driven the length of a football field without seeing anything. That is scary to think about. Even talking on the phone is bad, though. Some people think hands-free calls are fine, but they are still distracting. When you talk to a passenger, that person can see the traffic and pause if something dangerous happens. A person on the phone cannot see what you see, so they keep talking and pulling your focus away. I have seen my friend miss an exit because she was arguing with her boyfriend on speakerphone, and then she swerved across two lanes to catch it. Nobody got hurt, but it was close.

Another big excuse is using the phone for GPS or music. People say they need directions or want to change a song. But you can set your GPS and playlist before you start driving. If you need to touch the phone while the car is moving, that is still distracted driving. Looking down to type an address or scroll through songs is just as dangerous as texting. If something is that important, pull over first. It only takes a minute to stop in a parking lot or on a safe shoulder.

I understand that some people might say what about emergencies? If there is a real emergency, you should still pull over before calling 911. Calling while driving through traffic could cause another crash. It is hard to ignore a buzzing phone, but no notification is worth someone’s life. A lot of drivers think they can multitask, but the brain does not actually do two things at once. It switches back and forth quickly, and each switch means a moment where you are not fully focused on driving.

Cell phones are a normal part of life now, but cars are not the place for them. The rule should be simple: if the car is moving, the phone should be put away, on do not disturb, or in the glove box. If you need to use it, stop first. It might feel inconvenient, but it is better than causing a crash or living with the guilt of hurting someone. Drivers should not use cell phones in any capacity while driving because no one is good enough to drive safely while distracted.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge you to preserve the Electoral College. While many people criticize it as outdated or undemocratic, I believe it remains an essential part of our presidential elections because it pushes candidates to build broad national support rather than focusing only on large population centers.

Critics often point out that the Electoral College can allow a candidate to lose the popular vote and still win the presidency, as happened in 2000 and 2016. This is a serious concern, but it oversimplifies the Framers’ design. In “In Defense of the Electoral College,” Judge Richard A. Posner argues that the system prevents candidates from winning simply by running up huge vote totals in one region. Instead, it forces them to form coalitions across large and small states. Without this pressure, a candidate could focus narrowly on a few urban areas and ignore the rest of the country.

Another common objection involves “faithless electors” who might vote against their state’s popular choice. That risk, however, is quite low. According to the Office of the Federal Register, the Electoral College has 538 electors, and a candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win. Because the threshold is so high, a handful of faithless electors would rarely change the outcome.

The Electoral College also has practical advantages. Posner notes that it produces a clear, decisive winner quickly and avoids the chaos of a nationwide popular-vote recount. Disputes can be handled within individual states, which makes a smoother transition of power more likely. In addition, the system preserves federalism by giving smaller states a meaningful role and preventing larger states from dominating every election.

I understand the argument that the current winner-take-all system can lead campaigns to focus mainly on swing states. Bradford Plumer raises this point in “The Indefensible Electoral College,” and it is a legitimate weakness. However, the answer is not to abolish the system entirely. States such as Maine and Nebraska already allocate electors proportionally by congressional district, and that kind of reform could reduce the winner-take-all problem while keeping the benefits of the Electoral College.

In short, the Electoral College is not perfect, but its advantages—encouraging broad national coalitions, preserving federalism, and producing a clear result—outweigh its flaws. Rather than eliminating it, we should work to improve it. I hope you will support efforts to keep and reform this important institution.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

Almost everyone you see today has a cell phone in their hand or pocket. We use them for everything from talking to our friends and listening to music to checking the GPS so we do not get lost. Because phones are such a big part of everyday life, a lot of people naturally want to use them while they are driving. However, driving a car requires your full attention. Even though it is really tempting to check a message or change a song, drivers should not be allowed to use their cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle. 

The main reason is that driving takes a lot more focus than people think. When you are behind the wheel, you are in control of a heavy machine moving at high speeds. Things can change in a split second. A dog might run out into the street, a car in front of you might slam on its brakes, or a kid could cross without looking. If your eyes are looking down at your phone for even two or three seconds to see who texted you, you are basically driving completely blind during that time. Research we learned about in health class shows that taking your eyes off the road for five seconds at highway speeds means you travel the length of an entire football field. That is more than enough time for a terrible accident to happen.

Some people argue that hands-free setups, like using Bluetooth or speakerphone, should be totally fine because both hands stay on the steering wheel. It is true that having your hands on the wheel helps you steer, but your brain is still not fully on the road. This is called cognitive distraction. When you are having an intense conversation with someone, or trying to figure out how to give voice commands to your phone, your mind is picturing that conversation instead of scanning for hazards on the street. It is way different than talking to a passenger sitting next to you, because a passenger can see the traffic too and will stop talking if they see you need to focus on something dangerous. A phone cannot do that.

Using a phone while driving also puts innocent people at risk. If someone decides to drive recklessly, they aren't just endangering themselves, they are risking the lives of other drivers, passengers, and pedestrians. It is completely unfair for someone else to get injured or worse just because a driver felt like they needed to reply to a meme or check their notifications right away. 

In conclusion, there is almost nothing on a phone that is so urgent it cannot wait until you reach your destination. If something really is an emergency, the safest and smartest thing to do is just pull over into a parking lot and put the car in park before picking up the phone. Making roads completely phone-free would save lives, prevent thousands of crashes every year, and make everyone feel a lot safer when they are out traveling.

In today's world, smartphones have become an integral part of daily life, serving as personal assistants, entertainment hubs, and primary communication channels. However, their increasing presence in environments that demand intense focus, such as operating a motor vehicle, poses significant risks. Driving requires an individual's undivided attention, quick reflexes, and constant situational awareness, making it imperative that drivers be prohibited from using cell phones in any capacity while behind the wheel.

One of the most significant dangers of mobile phone use while driving is the manual and visual distraction it causes. Tasks like texting, browsing music, or holding a phone to talk necessitate taking hands off the steering wheel and eyes off the road. At highway speeds, this brief distraction can have devastating consequences, as a driver can cover the length of a football field without seeing the road ahead. In this short window, a pedestrian may step into the crosswalk, a leading vehicle may slam on its brakes, or unexpected debris may appear, transforming a routine commute into a fatal collision. Empirical safety data consistently shows that manual phone use substantially increases crash risks, highlighting the need for strict bans on handheld operation.

However, a comprehensive policy must also address hands-free use, as many motorists mistakenly believe that Bluetooth headsets, dashboard integrations, and voice-to-text systems eliminate the risks associated with mobile communication. Research in cognitive psychology reveals that this assumption is misguided. The human brain is incapable of efficiently multitasking two complex, high-demand processes simultaneously, making it difficult to engage in a phone conversation while safely operating a vehicle. This cognitive overload leads to inattentional blindness, where drivers may look directly at obstacles without registering them. Unlike a passenger who can intuitively pause conversation during challenging driving maneuvers, a remote caller remains unaware of road conditions, continually drawing the driver's cognitive focus away from safe operation.

Some argue that mobile connectivity is essential for modern logistics, particularly regarding real-time navigation. While navigation applications are undoubtedly valuable, this utility does not justify interactive use while driving. Route mapping can be configured before a journey begins, allowing audio directions to guide the trip without requiring manual adjustments or persistent visual monitoring. If an urgent call or message arises, the responsible course of action is to pull over in a safe parking area before engaging with the device. Personal convenience should never take precedence over collective roadway safety.

Ultimately, operating a motor vehicle is a shared public responsibility that carries inherent life-or-death consequences. Both handheld and hands-free cellular use degrade human reaction times and impair spatial judgment, comparable to driving under the influence of alcohol. To preserve human life and establish a definitive standard of safety, society must adopt a zero-tolerance approach. By prohibiting cell phone use in any capacity while driving, we can significantly reduce the risk of accidents and create a safer driving environment. This measure may require some adjustments to our daily habits, but the benefits to public safety far outweigh any perceived inconvenience. Moreover, it is our collective responsibility to ensure that the roads are safe for everyone, and this can only be achieved by prioritizing safe driving practices over personal convenience.

Dear Principal,

I was really excited to hear that you're reconsidering the school's cell phone policy. I think it's a great opportunity for us to make some changes that could really benefit the students. After thinking about it, I strongly believe that Policy 1 is the way to go. Allowing students to bring their phones to school and use them during lunch and free periods, as long as they're turned off during class, makes a lot of sense to me.

First of all, having our phones with us can be really helpful in case of an emergency. If something happens during lunch or between classes, we can quickly call or text our parents or guardians to let them know what's going on. This can be especially important for students who have medical conditions or other special needs. With Policy 1, we would have the security of knowing that we can get in touch with someone if we need to.

Another reason I think Policy 1 is a good idea is that it teaches us responsibility. If we're allowed to use our phones during certain times, we have to make sure we're following the rules and turning them off when we're in class. This helps us learn how to balance our freedom with our responsibilities, which is an important skill to have in life. Plus, it's not like we're going to be using our phones during class anyway - the teachers would still be in charge of making sure we're paying attention and doing our work.

On the other hand, I think Policy 2 is too strict. Not allowing us to have our phones at all would be really inconvenient and frustrating. Many of us use our phones to take pictures of notes or assignments on the board, or to listen to music during lunch. These are things that help us learn and relax, and they're not distracting us from our schoolwork. Furthermore, if we're not allowed to have our phones at all, we might be more likely to sneak them out during class, which could lead to more problems than if we were just allowed to use them during our free time.

I also think that Policy 1 would help us stay connected with our families and friends. Let's face it, a lot of us have busy schedules and can't always see our families or friends outside of school. Being able to text or call them during lunch or between classes can help us stay in touch and feel more supported. This can be especially important for students who are going through tough times or who have a lot on their plates.

Lastly, I think it's worth considering that many of us are already responsible with our phones. We're not going to be using them to cheat or disrupt the class, and we're not going to be texting or calling during lessons. By allowing us to use our phones during certain times, you would be showing us that you trust us to make good choices and follow the rules.

In conclusion, I really believe that Policy 1 is the way to go. It's a fair and reasonable policy that takes into account our needs and responsibilities. I think it would make a big difference for a lot of students, and it would help us stay safe, connected, and responsible. Thank you for considering our opinions and for being open to making changes to the cell phone policy.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to ask you to support keeping the Electoral College for electing the president. I know this is not the most popular position right now, especially after elections where the person who won the most individual votes did not become president. I get why people are upset. But after reading about how the system works, I think the Electoral College still does an important job, and we should not replace it with a national popular vote.

The Electoral College is not a place; it is a process the Founders created as a compromise between letting Congress pick the president and letting a simple popular vote decide. Each state gets electors based on its number of representatives and senators, and a candidate needs 270 electoral votes to win. Most states use a winner-take-all system, which means a candidate has to think about winning whole states, not just piling up votes in one area.

One of the strongest reasons to keep the Electoral College is that it forces candidates to build broad support. Judge Richard Posner argues that without it, a candidate could win just by running up huge vote totals in big cities or one region of the country. If we switched to a direct popular vote, candidates would have little reason to visit small states or listen to rural voters. The Electoral College makes it harder to win by focusing only on the most densely populated places. That is still important in a country as large and varied as ours.

I understand the counterargument. Critics like Bradford Plumer say the Electoral College is undemocratic because a candidate can lose the popular vote and still win the presidency, as happened in 2000 and 2016. They also point out that winner-take-all makes candidates focus only on swing states, while voters in safe states get ignored. That is a real problem, and I do not want to pretend it is not. But the answer is not to get rid of the whole system. We could encourage more states to use the district method like Maine and Nebraska, which would give more voters a reason to participate without losing the federalist structure.

Another practical point is that the Electoral College keeps election disputes from becoming national chaos. If we had a very close popular-vote election, a nationwide recount could drag on for months. Under the Electoral College, recounts are usually confined to individual states. That is a real benefit when the country needs a clear winner.

I know the system is not perfect. Losing the popular vote but winning the presidency feels unfair to many people. But the United States was designed as a republic made up of states, not just one giant national district. The Electoral College balances state power and popular power, and that balance still matters. I hope you will consider supporting it.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

Dear Principal,

I respectfully oppose the proposed policy requiring students to maintain at least a B average in order to participate in sports and other extracurricular activities. Academic achievement should always matter, and students should be encouraged to do their best in class. However, banning students with C averages from activities would likely hurt the very students the policy is intended to help. A better approach would be to require students to remain academically eligible while providing tutoring, progress checks, and support for those who need it.

First, activities often motivate students to improve their grades. Many students work harder in school because they want to stay on a team, perform in a concert, participate in a club, or represent the school in a competition. If a student knows that one low grade could immediately remove them from an activity they enjoy, that student may feel discouraged instead of motivated. Sports and clubs give students a reason to attend school regularly, manage their time, and set goals. For some students, being part of a team is what keeps them connected to school.

Second, a C average does not mean that a student is not trying or does not deserve opportunities. Students have different strengths, learning needs, and responsibilities outside of school. One student may spend hours each week caring for younger siblings or working after school to help support a family. Another may struggle with a difficult subject but excel in art, athletics, leadership, music, or technology. Requiring a B average would treat all students as if they have the same circumstances and talents. School activities should help students develop their abilities, not punish them for having different challenges.

In addition, extracurricular activities teach important lessons that cannot always be learned in a classroom. Athletes learn discipline, teamwork, perseverance, and responsibility. Members of drama clubs learn confidence and cooperation. Students in debate, robotics, band, and student government practice leadership, communication, and problem-solving. These skills can improve academic performance as well. For example, a student on a sports team must plan homework around practices and games, which can encourage better organization. Removing activities from students with C averages could take away an important source of growth and confidence.

Instead of setting a B-average requirement, the school could create a more balanced policy. Students could be required to pass their classes or maintain at least a C average. Those whose grades fall below that standard could attend mandatory tutoring, meet regularly with teachers or counselors, and complete academic progress reports. Coaches and activity advisers could also check in with students about missing assignments. This system would make academics a priority while still allowing students to benefit from participation.

Our school should expect students to work hard, but it should also give them the support needed to succeed. A B-average requirement would exclude many students who could improve through the motivation and structure that activities provide. I urge you to choose a policy that promotes both academic responsibility and student involvement.

The glow of a screen has become a kind of gravitational field. It pulls at attention even when hands are on the wheel. Allowing drivers to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle is a dangerous concession, not a harmless convenience. The evidence from cognitive science and traffic safety makes one point clear: the problem is not just where a driver’s hands are; it is where the mind goes.

Many people imagine that hands-free devices solve the issue. They do not. A driver speaking through a Bluetooth headset may keep both eyes on the road, but the brain is still scheduling, listening, and responding to a remote conversation. This is not multitasking; it is rapid attention switching. A driver absorbed in a call can miss visual cues, including red lights and pedestrians stepping off a curb. Studies have shown that the impairment from phone conversation is comparable to driving with a blood alcohol concentration at the legal limit. The hands-free distinction is largely a marketing comfort, not a safety boundary.

Texting is even more blatant. Sending a short message takes a driver’s eyes off the road for several seconds. At highway speed, that is the length of a football field traveled blind. No status update, emoji, or quick reply is worth that risk. But the temptation is real because phones are designed to be habit-forming. They ping, vibrate, and glow. A policy that permits any use while driving leaves a gray zone in which a driver can rationalize glancing at a notification, switching a playlist, or reading a fragment of a message. Each glance erodes the attention required for safe driving.

Some argue that navigation apps and emergency calls justify phone use. Yet these functions can be configured before a trip begins, with audio directions set and the phone placed in a mount. If a true emergency arises, a driver should pull over. The road is not a place for managing digital life. Allowing cell phones in any capacity invites a slippery slope from voice command to one-handed typing under the steering wheel.

Ultimately, the vehicle should remain a space of focused attention. Drivers should not be permitted to use cell phones while the car is moving. Not because phones are inherently evil, but because driving requires a kind of presence that phone use, even legal hands-free use, quietly destroys. The cost is measured in lives, and it is far too high.

Every June, backpacks are emptied of crumpled notebooks and replaced with a familiar burden: the summer assignment packet. For generations, this ritual has meant uniform reading lists, identical packets of math problems, and standardized reflection prompts designed entirely by teachers. While the intention—combating summer learning loss—is reasonable, the delivery method is fundamentally flawed. If schools genuinely want students to remain intellectually engaged during their break, summer projects should be designed by the students themselves.

The most compelling argument for student autonomy lies in the nature of motivation. During the school year, learners move through a conveyor belt of mandatory curricula, bells, and pre-packaged assessments. By the time July arrives, mental fatigue is palpable. Imposing another rigid, teacher-designed task often yields resentment rather than enrichment; assignments are either shoved aside until the night before classes resume or completed via superficial shortcutting. In contrast, when students possess the freedom to design their own inquiry, curiosity replaces compliance. A teenager indifferent to an assigned novel might spend weeks writing and scoring an original short film, researching the water quality of a local watershed, or building a functional computer from salvaged components. These self-directed endeavors demand planning, problem-solving, and perseverance—the very cognitive habits educators hope to preserve over the break.

Student-designed projects also accommodate the starkly uneven realities of students’ summer lives. Teacher-directed initiatives often inadvertently make assumptions about access, requiring specific technologies, quiet study environments, or purchases that strain family budgets. Summer schedules look drastically different across households. One student might have months of leisure, while another works thirty hours a week at a grocery store or cares for younger siblings. A flexible, self-designed framework allows learners to build rigorous projects around their lived circumstances. The working student might analyze retail supply chains or study local labor trends; the student caring for family could design and document a weekly literacy program for their younger brothers and sisters. Such adaptability ensures that academic growth is integrated into authentic life rather than treated as an alien imposition.

Skeptics often worry that autonomy invites indolence, assuming teenagers will pitch trivial topics that require minimal effort. However, allowing students to design their work does not mean removing accountability. Teachers can still establish clear evaluative criteria, requiring a formal project proposal in May, evidence of research, and a tangible final product to present in the fall. The educator’s role shifts from a dispenser of chores to an advisor who refines ideas and ensures adequate rigor.

Summer should not be a cognitive vacuum, but neither should it merely extend the classroom’s four walls into the warmest months

Summer break is a valuable pause, but it also carries a well-documented risk: students who spend three months away from academic work often return having forgotten material. Schools that assign summer projects are right to address this problem. The remaining question is who should design those projects. Although teacher-designed assignments offer structure, summer projects should be student-designed, with teacher guidance, because students learn more and work harder when the project reflects their own curiosity.

The strongest argument for student-designed projects is motivation. Summer is the one time of year when students are free from daily classroom demands, and an assignment that feels like a chore is likely to be postponed until the last week of August. A teacher-designed packet of worksheets or a required essay on a assigned novel is easy to rush through or copy from a classmate. By contrast, a student who chooses to build a working birdhouse, write a short documentary about her grandmother's immigration story, or code a simple game has a personal reason to keep going. When the topic belongs to the student, the work stops being something to finish and becomes something to be proud of.

Student design also builds skills that teacher-designed projects cannot. Planning a project requires a student to set a goal, break it into steps, estimate time, and solve problems along the way. These are the same executive skills that employers and colleges value, yet students rarely practice them when a teacher hands over a list of instructions. A student who decides to study water quality in a local creek must figure out what to measure, how to collect samples, and how to present the results. If something goes wrong, she must adapt. That experience of managing uncertainty is a form of learning that a pre-written assignment removes.

Critics argue that students, left alone, will choose easy projects or none at all, and that teachers are better able to ensure academic rigor and alignment with the curriculum. This concern is reasonable, but it does not require teachers to design the project themselves. A better model is a proposal system: before the school year ends, each student submits a plan describing the topic, the learning goals, the materials needed, and a timeline. Teachers review each plan, require revisions when the work looks too thin, and make sure it connects to a subject such as science, writing, or math. A student who proposes to "watch cooking videos," for instance, could be asked to test and document recipes while calculating ratios and nutrition information. In this way the teacher protects rigor while the student keeps ownership.

Student-designed projects also address fairness. Not every family has the same resources over the summer. A teacher-designed project that requires a trip to a museum or expensive supplies can disadvantage students who cannot afford them. When students design their own projects, they can build on what is available to them, whether that means interviewing relatives, studying plants in a neighborhood park, or writing a family cookbook. Teachers can then help adjust ideas to fit each student's circumstances, something a single assignment for the whole class cannot do.

In conclusion, the purpose of a summer project is not simply to fill time but to keep students thinking and learning. Teacher-designed assignments may be efficient, but they often produce minimal effort and little curiosity. Student-designed projects, supported by teacher review and clear standards, encourage motivation, teach planning and problem-solving, and respect differences in students' resources. Schools that want students to return in the fall not only retaining knowledge but also eager to learn should let students take the lead.

Dear Principal [Name],

I am writing to urge you to adopt Policy 1, which would allow students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times, as long as they are turned off during class. I believe this policy balances the need for a focused learning environment with the realities of student life, and it teaches responsibility in a way that a total ban cannot.

First, allowing phones during free time addresses real safety and family needs. Many students have parents who work late, siblings who need pickup arrangements, or medical conditions that require communication. If a student misses a bus, stays after for an activity, or feels unwell, a phone allows them to contact a family member right away rather than waiting in line at the office. In a genuine emergency, immediate access to a phone can matter enormously. A total ban would remove that option for every student, even though most of them would never misuse it.

Second, Policy 1 protects instructional time just as effectively as a ban when it is enforced well. The concern behind a ban is that phones distract students from learning. That concern is valid, but Policy 1 directly addresses it by requiring phones to be off during class. Teachers would have a clear, simple rule, and consequences for violations, such as having the phone held until the end of the day, could be consistent across classrooms. A ban, by contrast, is often difficult to enforce, because many students would still carry phones secretly. This leads to hidden use, constant searching and confiscation, and a tense relationship between students and staff. A reasonable rule that students view as fair is far more likely to be followed than a strict prohibition they see as excessive.

Third, this policy teaches self-discipline and responsible technology use. Students will spend their adult lives surrounded by devices, and they will need to know when to put them away, whether in a meeting, a job interview, or a workplace. School is an ideal place to practice this skill. By trusting students to use phones appropriately at lunch and then silence them for class, we help them build habits they will need after graduation. Banning phones entirely avoids the problem rather than teaching students to manage it.

Finally, free-time phone use can benefit student well-being. Lunch and breaks are meant for relaxation. Some students use that time to call family, listen to music, check schedules, or connect with friends. Others use phones to photograph assignments, set reminders, or coordinate group projects. These are practical, harmless uses that make school life smoother. If we worry that phones will replace face-to-face conversation, the school can designate phone-free tables or zones in the cafeteria so students have options.

Some will argue that any phone presence leads to cyberbullying or inappropriate content. These risks exist, but they exist outside school as well, and a ban does not eliminate them; it only moves them to the bus ride or the evening. A better response is clear conduct rules, with firm penalties for harassment, and education about digital citizenship.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask you to adopt Policy 1. It keeps classrooms focused, supports student safety, and prepares us to use technology responsibly. Thank you for considering my perspective and for working to make our school a better place.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]

The ubiquitous presence of cell phones in modern life has led to a contentious debate about their use while driving. As the world grapples with the implications of this technology on road safety, it is imperative to examine the merits of allowing drivers to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle. The argument in favor of permitting cell phone use hinges on the idea that responsible drivers can multitask effectively, and that the benefits of having access to emergency services, navigation, and communication outweigh the potential risks. However, this perspective is fundamentally flawed, as it underestimates the cognitive and physical demands of driving and overestimates the ability of drivers to manage distractions.

The human brain is not equipped to handle the dual tasks of driving and using a cell phone simultaneously. Research has consistently shown that engaging in conversations, texting, or browsing while driving significantly impairs reaction times, reduces situational awareness, and increases the likelihood of accidents. Even hands-free devices, which are often touted as a safer alternative, can still divert a driver's attention away from the road, leading to a state of "inattention blindness." This phenomenon, where drivers fail to notice critical events or hazards, can have devastating consequences, particularly in high-risk situations such as merging onto a highway or navigating through intersections.

Moreover, the notion that drivers can responsibly use cell phones is belied by the alarming statistics on distracted driving. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, distracted driving claimed the lives of over 3,000 people in the United States in 2020 alone, with cell phone use being a primary contributor to these fatalities. These numbers are a stark reminder that the risks associated with cell phone use while driving far outweigh any perceived benefits. Furthermore, the widespread availability of alternative solutions, such as voice-activated assistants and phone mounts, makes it increasingly unnecessary for drivers to physically interact with their devices while on the road.

In light of these findings, it is clear that drivers should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle. Instead, drivers should be encouraged to adopt responsible habits, such as pulling over to a safe location to make calls or send messages, or designating a passenger to handle communication tasks. By taking a proactive approach to mitigating the risks of distracted driving, we can work towards creating a safer and more attentive driving culture. As policymakers and individuals, we must prioritize road safety and take concrete steps to address the dangers posed by cell phone use while driving. Ultimately, the preservation of human life and the prevention of avoidable tragedies must take precedence over the convenience and connectivity provided by cell phones.

I recently heard that you're thinking about changing the school policy so that students need to have at least a B average to participate in sports and other activities. I strongly disagree with this idea and I think it would be really unfair to a lot of students, including me.

First of all, I think it's great that our school offers so many different activities and sports teams. Another reason I don't think this is a good idea is that it's not always fair to judge someone's abilities or potential based on their grades. To combat the phenomenon known as the "summer slide"—the documented loss of academic skills over break—many schools mandate summer projects. While the goal of keeping students intellectually active is commendable, the format of these assignments often dictates their success. Historically, educators have assigned uniform, teacher-designed tasks, such as mandatory reading lists or standardized packets. However, to maximize engagement and cultivate meaningful personal growth, summer projects should be student-designed. Granting learners agency over their summer work nurtures intrinsic motivation, builds vital self-direction skills, and transforms an obligation into an authentic learning experience.

The primary benefit of student-designed projects is the awakening of genuine curiosity. Traditional, top-down assignments often feel punitive, reinforcing the perception that learning is an unwelcome intrusion into vacation time. When forced to read the same predetermined novel or solve identical math worksheets, students tend to engage in passive compliance rather than active inquiry. In contrast, self-directed projects allow individuals to pursue their distinctive passions. For instance, a student fascinated by technology might choose to program a basic video game, while another interested in civic engagement might volunteer at a community garden and document local food insecurity. Because these endeavors originate from personal interest, students invest significantly more time, effort, and creative energy into them than they ever would into a generic worksheet.

Furthermore, conceiving and executing an independent project develops critical life skills that structured school environments rarely demand. When a teacher provides the rubric, timeline, and topic, the critical planning phase is effectively outsourced. Conversely, requiring students to design their own projects forces them to practice executive functioning. They must define a feasible scope, set milestones, locate appropriate resources, and manage their time over several unstructured months. A high schooler seeking to write a collection of short stories must learn to draft an outline, establish a writing schedule, and edit their work without the scaffolding of daily class bells. These competencies—self-regulation, initiative, and problem-solving—are precisely the qualities needed to succeed in higher education and the modern workforce.

Skeptics may argue that without teacher oversight, student-designed projects lack academic rigor and encourage low-effort choices. Critics worry that without prescriptive guidelines, students will select frivolous topics simply to evade meaningful work. However, autonomy does not mean an absence of standards. Schools can easily institute broad evaluative frameworks that require students to submit project proposals in June and reflect on their progress in September. By establishing criteria for depth, documentation, and effort—while leaving the content entirely up to the learner—educators preserve academic integrity without stifling individual creativity. 

Ultimately, the purpose of summer education should not be to replicate the rigid mechanics of the classroom, but to demonstrate that learning extends beyond the schoolhouse walls. Teacher-designed assignments too frequently foster resentment and fatigue. By entrusting students with the design of their own summer projects, schools affirm that education is a personal pursuit rather than an external imposition. In doing so, they foster independent thinkers who view the summer break not merely as an escape from school, but as a valuable landscape for self-discovery.

Dear Principal Adams,

I’m writing because I know you’re deciding whether to make community service a requirement for all students. I understand why this idea is on the table. A lot of my friends do great things—my friend Jake tutors elementary school kids in reading, and a group of kids from my class spends Saturday mornings picking up litter at the park. They say it feels good to help. I agree that community service is valuable, but I don’t think it should be required.

The main reason is that students already have very full schedules. Many of us have homework, sports, music lessons, and family duties after school. I play soccer three days a week, and on those days I get home around 6:00, eat dinner, and still have to study. My friend Dana works at her family’s restaurant three nights a week to help pay bills. If the school added 20 or 30 hours of required service, students like Dana and me would have to give up something important. That could mean less sleep, worse grades, or quitting activities that keep us healthy and motivated.

Requiring service also changes why people do it. Right now, students who volunteer do it because they actually care or because they want to see the community improve. My friend Jake is patient with the kids he tutors because he chose to be there. If a student is forced to tutor just to check a box for graduation, that student might show up annoyed or not try hard. The elementary kids would notice. The same goes for litter cleanup—if someone is forced to pick up trash, they might do a sloppy job, and the place still looks messy. Volunteering works best when it’s voluntary.

I know some people worry that if service isn’t required, not enough students will participate. But I think the school can encourage service without forcing it. For example, you could set up a volunteer fair where local groups come and explain what they need. You could give students recognition—like a certificate or an honor roll mention—for completing a certain number of hours. You could even offer service opportunities during school hours, like a half-day where homerooms choose a project, so nobody has to miss work or practice. That way students get a chance to help and see if they like it, but they aren’t punished for having other responsibilities.

I know the goal is to help the community and teach us responsibility. I want that too. But a requirement would make service feel like homework. It would be better to make it easy and rewarding for students to volunteer on their own. That way the people who help are there for the right reasons, and the community gets our best effort.

Thank you for listening.

Sincerely,
Alex Martinez

The vision of driverless cars is often presented as a sleek, inevitable future, but the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming" makes clear that this future carries serious unresolved risks. While autonomous vehicles may offer real benefits, I believe their widespread development and deployment should be slowed until major safety, technological, and legal problems are addressed. The promise of fewer accidents is not enough to justify putting unready technology on public roads.

Supporters of driverless cars make a compelling point: the article notes that human error causes over 90 percent of traffic accidents, often due to texting, drowsiness, or impaired driving. A computer driver that never becomes distracted could dramatically reduce crashes, save lives, lower insurance costs, and provide new mobility for elderly or disabled passengers. These benefits are significant and should motivate continued research. However, they depend on autonomous systems performing reliably in the real world, and the article shows that this is not yet the case.

One major problem is that current sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or unmarked construction zones—precisely the conditions where driving is most dangerous and reliable judgment matters most. In addition, the software that controls these vehicles remains vulnerable to glitches and cybersecurity threats. A system that can fail suddenly or be hacked introduces new risks that human drivers do not face.

Even more troubling is the problem of semi-autonomous driving. The article explains that these features require human drivers to stay alert and take over in emergencies, yet studies show that passengers quickly lose focus when a computer is driving, which slows their reaction times. This creates a dangerous middle ground: the car is not fully autonomous, but the human is not fully attentive. Finally, legal and ethical questions remain unresolved. When an accident occurs, it is unclear whether the vehicle owner, the software developer, or the automaker should be held legally responsible. Without clear accountability, victims may struggle to receive fair treatment, and manufacturers may have little incentive to fix flaws promptly.

To be clear, driverless car research should continue. The potential to reduce human error and expand mobility is worth pursuing. But until autonomous vehicles can handle bad weather reliably, resist cyberattacks, keep human drivers genuinely engaged, and establish clear liability rules, their development should not be rushed. We should proceed with caution rather than allowing an appealing future to blind us to present dangers.

Dear Principal,

I believe students should be required to perform some community service, but the requirement should be reasonable and flexible. Community service can help students understand that they are part of a larger community, not just people who come to school, do homework, and go home. At the same time, students have sports, jobs, family responsibilities, and difficult classes, so the school should not require an extreme number of hours.

One reason community service should be required is that it teaches responsibility in a way that regular classes cannot always teach. In history or English class, we can learn about problems in society, but helping in person makes those problems feel more real. For example, one of my friends tutors younger students at an elementary school. She told me that some of the children are embarrassed to ask questions in class because they do not want to look behind everyone else. When she works with them one-on-one, they become more confident. My friend has also learned patience and how to explain things clearly. Both she and the students benefit.

Community service can also improve our school’s relationship with the neighborhood. People sometimes complain that teenagers only care about themselves or make messes in public places. If students helped clean parks, collected food for families, visited nursing homes, or volunteered at local events, people would see students differently. More importantly, we would actually make a difference. A group picking up litter might seem small, but if every student helped for even a few hours, the results could be noticeable.

I understand why some students do not want a requirement. Some students already have after-school jobs to help their families. Others take care of younger siblings or have practices and homework every day. It would be unfair if community service caused them to lose income, fall behind in class, or miss important responsibilities. That is why the program should allow different choices and schedules. Students could complete a small number of hours over the whole year, maybe ten to fifteen hours. They could choose activities on weekends, during school-sponsored service days, or through approved organizations. Students who have major family or work responsibilities could ask for an alternative assignment or an exemption.

Also, students should be able to choose service that matches their interests. Someone who likes animals could help at a shelter. Someone interested in medicine could make care packages or help with a health fair. A student who enjoys art could paint signs for a community center. Giving students choices would make the requirement feel less like punishment and more like an opportunity.

Requiring a reasonable amount of community service would not solve every problem in our town, but it would teach students useful lessons about empathy, responsibility, and teamwork. I hope you will create a flexible requirement that respects students’ busy lives while still encouraging everyone to contribute.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Student

When faced with a significant dilemma, the temptation to find a single, definitive voice can be strong. We want someone wise to point an unambiguous finger toward the right path and relieve us of the burden of uncertainty. Yet trusting only one person’s counsel often means inheriting their blind spots along with their wisdom. Consulting multiple people transforms decision-making from a game of chance into an act of triangulation, allowing us to map out a problem in all its dimensions.

Every advisor speaks from the vantage point of their own history, anxieties, and temperament. Consider someone contemplating leaving a stable, decade-long corporate career to join a fledgling startup. An older relative who weathered economic recessions will almost certainly emphasize security, warning against the volatility of an unproven enterprise. A peer who recently launched their own company might offer the opposite prescription, viewing hesitation as cowardice and urging immediate reinvention. Neither person is necessarily wrong, but neither is offering an objective truth. One is projecting a deep-seated need for safety, while the other is projecting an appetite for risk. By listening to both, the seeker can strip away the personal baggage inherent in each reaction, arriving at a clearer assessment of the actual trade-offs involved—balancing cash reserves against professional stagnation.

Moreover, different people illuminate entirely distinct facets of the same issue. When navigating a complex medical diagnosis, for instance, relying solely on a surgeon’s advice might frame the solution exclusively through the lens of operative intervention. Consulting a physical therapist or a nutritionist introduces alternative modalities that might otherwise remain invisible. It is not a matter of pitting experts against each other to see who wins an argument. Rather, diverse perspectives expose the hidden assumptions that quietly constrain a problem. One advisor asks about immediate financial costs, another about emotional endurance, and a third about long-term lifestyle changes. Together, they construct a comprehensive ledger of possibilities that a single mind, no matter how sharp, would inevitably narrow.

Ultimately, gathering several opinions is not about conducting an informal poll or surrendering autonomy to a consensus. True clarity rarely emerges from an average. Instead, hearing divergent perspectives forces the decision-maker to articulate what actually resonates with their own values. When two trusted mentors give contradictory advice, we are suddenly compelled to evaluate the underlying principles behind their recommendations. In having to choose which rationale carries more weight, we discover our own conviction. Seeking multiple viewpoints does not dilute our judgment; it refines it, ensuring that whatever choice we make is rooted in awareness rather than accidental oversight.

The decision by the principal to mandate participation in at least one extracurricular activity for all students has sparked a debate among educators, parents, and students. While some may view this decision as an opportunity for students to explore new interests and develop valuable skills, I strongly disagree with this policy. Forcing students to participate in extracurricular activities can lead to undue stress, stifle creativity, and create an uneven playing field.

One of the primary concerns with this policy is that it can lead to an increase in stress levels among students. Many students already struggle to balance their academic workload with other responsibilities, such as part-time jobs or family obligations. Adding an extracurricular activity to their plate can be overwhelming, leading to burnout and decreased motivation. For instance, a student who is already struggling in a particular subject may find it challenging to dedicate time to a sports team or club, potentially compromising their academic performance. Furthermore, students who are not interested in the available extracurricular activities may feel pressured to participate in something that does not align with their passions, leading to a lack of engagement and enthusiasm.

Moreover, mandating extracurricular participation can stifle creativity and autonomy among students. By forcing students to participate in a particular activity, the principal's decision undermines the freedom of students to explore their interests and make choices about how they want to spend their time. Many students may have unique talents or hobbies that are not represented by the available extracurricular activities, and by not providing alternative options, the school may be neglecting the diverse needs and interests of its student body. For example, a student who is passionate about photography may not find an outlet for their creativity in a traditional sports team or club, and may be forced to participate in an activity that does not allow them to express themselves.

Another issue with this policy is that it can create an uneven playing field, where students from more affluent backgrounds have an advantage over their less privileged peers. Students from wealthier families may have access to private coaching, equipment, or training that gives them an edge in competitive extracurricular activities, such as sports or debate teams. In contrast, students from lower-income families may not have the same resources or opportunities, putting them at a disadvantage. This can lead to a lack of diversity and representation in extracurricular activities, as well as a perpetuation of existing social and economic inequalities.

In conclusion, while the principal's decision may have been made with the best intentions, I firmly believe that mandating extracurricular participation is not the right approach. Instead of forcing students to participate in activities they may not be interested in, the school should focus on providing a range of options and opportunities that cater to diverse interests and needs. By doing so, the school can foster a more inclusive and supportive environment that encourages students to explore their passions and develop valuable skills, without compromising their academic performance or well-being. Ultimately, students should be given the freedom to choose how they want to spend their time, and the school should prioritize providing resources and support to help them make informed decisions.

Dear Principal,

I am writing to share my opinion about the possible policy that would require students to have at least a B average to play sports or join other activities. I understand that you want students to take their grades seriously, and I do too. But I think this policy would hurt a lot of students more than it would help them, so I am against it.

First, a lot of students with a C average are not lazy. Some of us work hard and still find certain subjects difficult. For example, I study for math almost every night and I still usually end up with a C. If I got kicked off a team because of that, it would feel like I was being punished for something I am already trying to fix. A C is a passing grade, and it means we understand most of the material. It does not seem fair to treat it like a failure.

Second, activities are often the reason students come to school in the first place. Many kids stay motivated because they have practice after school or a club meeting they care about. If those things are taken away, some students might stop caring at all. They could end up with more free time and nothing to do, which might lead to trouble or just sitting around on their phones. Being on a team also teaches us things that a classroom does not, like how to work with others, be on time, and keep going when something is hard.

Third, sports and clubs actually help many students stay organized. When I have practice until five o'clock, I know I have to start my homework right away because I do not have time to waste. On days when I have nothing going on, I put it off and it takes me twice as long. Students who are busy often learn better time management than students who have all afternoon.

I also think the policy would not be equal for everyone. Some students have a harder time getting a B because they do not have help at home, have to take care of younger siblings, or work part-time jobs. These students might need activities the most, but they would be the first ones to lose them. A student with a tutor and a quiet house has a much easier path to a B than a student without those things.

That said, I do think there should be some kind of academic expectation. Instead of a B average, maybe the school could require a C average and passing every class. If a student drops below that, they could be put on a warning period and be required to go to study hall or get tutoring for a few weeks. If their grades still do not improve, then they could be suspended from the activity until they do. This way, students are encouraged to do better without being cut off right away.

In conclusion, I think requiring a B average is too strict and could push students away from school instead of helping them. A policy that offers support and a fair chance would work better. Thank you for taking the time to listen to student opinions, and I hope you will consider these ideas.

Sincerely,
A concerned student

Summer projects should mostly be student-designed because students learn more when they have a real interest in what they are doing. Teachers can still give rules and help students make a plan, but they should not make every student complete the exact same project. Summer is a break from regular school, so projects should encourage students to explore instead of making them feel like they are just doing extra worksheets.

One reason student-designed projects are better is that students can connect learning to their own lives. For example, a student who likes cooking could create a cookbook with recipes from family members. While doing that project, the student could practice reading, writing, measuring ingredients, and maybe learning about the history of different foods. Another student might be interested in sports and keep track of statistics for a favorite baseball team. That student would use math by calculating averages and percentages. Both students would be learning, but they would probably be more motivated than if they had been assigned the same book report or packet of problems.

Student-designed projects can also help students become more responsible. In school, teachers usually decide the topic, the steps, and the deadline. During a summer project, students could practice setting goals for themselves. For instance, someone who wants to learn photography could decide to take pictures every week, research how lighting works, and make a small photo display at the end of the summer. They would have to plan ahead instead of waiting until the night before it is due. Those planning skills are important in high school, college, and jobs.

Some people may say teacher-designed projects are better because teachers know what students need to learn. This is true to some extent. If every student had complete freedom, some might choose projects that are too easy or might not do much work at all. However, teachers can solve this problem without choosing the project for everyone. They could require that each project include certain parts, such as research, a written reflection, and a final presentation. Teachers could also approve project ideas before summer begins. That way, students would have choices, but the projects would still be educational.

For example, a teacher could tell students that their project must answer a question, use at least two sources, and show what they learned in a creative way. One student could investigate why local streams get polluted, while another could learn about a musician, build a small garden, or interview an older relative about family history. The topics would be different, but the learning standards would still be clear.

Overall, summer projects should be student-designed with teacher guidance. Students are more likely to work hard when they care about the topic, and they can develop independence at the same time. A summer project should keep students learning, but it should also give them the chance to discover what they enjoy.

Extracurricular activities can enrich a student's education, but schools should not require every student to take part in one. Sports teams, clubs, student government, and publications give students a chance to make friends and build leadership skills. Still, a mandatory rule ignores the different responsibilities, interests, and circumstances students deal with outside the classroom. Schools should encourage involvement and make activities easy to join, but they should not force anyone.

To begin with, many students already carry heavy obligations beyond school. Some work part-time jobs to help their families pay bills or to save for college. Others look after younger siblings while their parents work late shifts. A student who spends several hours every afternoon at a job may simply have no time for soccer practice, yearbook meetings, or student council events. Adding another commitment could leave that student stressed and hurt his or her grades. School should help students succeed, not penalize them for responsibilities they cannot avoid.

A requirement could also push students into activities they do not care about. Programs work best when members join because they are interested. A student who loves writing might pour energy into the school newspaper, and one who likes science might thrive in robotics club. A student who signs up only to satisfy a rule, however, may show up reluctantly, contribute very little, and take a spot from someone who really wants it. Clubs depend on enthusiasm and teamwork, so unwilling members can make the experience worse for everyone.

Some people argue that a requirement would help shy or isolated students find friends, and that is sometimes true. A student who tries drama club or basketball might discover talents and friendships that would otherwise stay hidden. Even so, forcing participation is not the best way to build a sense of belonging. Students who are anxious or uncomfortable in groups could feel even more alone if they must attend an activity they never chose. A better approach is for counselors and teachers to recommend programs that fit each student's interests and to offer low-pressure options, such as activity fairs or short trial sessions.

Students can also grow in important ways outside official school activities. Volunteering at a community center, caring for relatives, taking music lessons, taking part in a religious group, or working on an independent art project can all teach responsibility, communication, and perseverance. Learning does not happen only on campus or on a club roster. If the goal is to raise well-rounded citizens, the school should respect these other kinds of involvement.

Instead of imposing a rule, the principal could make activities more welcoming and practical. The school might provide late buses, lower participation fees, advertise clubs more clearly, and hold some meetings before school or online. Changes like these would let more students join because they want to.

Extracurricular activities are valuable, but that value comes from choice and commitment. Students should be encouraged to explore sports, clubs, and leadership roles, and they should also be free to balance school with work, family, and personal interests. A supportive school offers opportunities without taking away the freedom to choose.

Making an important decision can be difficult because no single person sees every part of a problem. Whether someone is choosing a college, considering a new job, making a medical decision, or solving a conflict with a friend, seeking multiple opinions can lead to a better choice. Different people bring different experiences, knowledge, and priorities. By comparing their advice instead of relying on only one voice, a person can recognize blind spots, weigh possible consequences, and make a decision that fits their own needs.

First, multiple opinions provide information that one adviser may not know. For example, a student deciding between two colleges might ask a teacher, a parent, a recent graduate, and a guidance counselor for advice. The teacher may focus on academic programs, while the parent may be concerned about cost and safety. A recent graduate may describe what campus life is actually like, and the counselor may know about scholarships or career opportunities. None of these perspectives is necessarily wrong or complete by itself. However, together they give the student a more realistic picture of each school. The student can then make a choice based on academics, finances, social life, and future goals rather than on one factor alone.

Seeking several opinions can also protect people from bias. Everyone has personal preferences that affect the advice they give. A friend who loves living in a large city may encourage someone to accept a job in a crowded urban area, even if that person prefers quiet surroundings. Meanwhile, a family member might advise staying close to home because they do not want the person to move away. Listening to both opinions can help the job seeker notice that each recommendation reflects the adviser’s values as well as the facts. The final decision-maker can then ask, “What matters most to me?” Rather than copying another person’s choice, they can use the advice to clarify their own priorities.

In addition, different opinions can reveal risks that might otherwise be overlooked. Consider someone thinking about starting a small business. An enthusiastic friend may focus on the exciting possibilities of being independent, while an accountant may explain the costs of taxes, insurance, and rent. A customer might offer insight into whether there is real demand for the product. Hearing these viewpoints does not mean the person must abandon the idea. Instead, it allows them to prepare more carefully by saving money, researching competitors, or beginning with a smaller version of the business. Advice is especially valuable when it comes from people with relevant experience, because they can point out practical problems that are not obvious to beginners.

Of course, asking for many opinions does not mean allowing others to make the decision. Too much advice can become confusing, especially when people strongly disagree. The person seeking guidance should consider the credibility of each source and focus on advice that relates to their goals. Ultimately, they must take responsibility for the outcome.

Seeking multiple opinions improves decision-making because it broadens knowledge, reduces the influence of bias, and exposes possible risks. When people listen carefully to several informed perspectives and then reflect on their own values, they are more likely to make choices that are thoughtful, realistic, and personally meaningful.

Driverless cars should continue to be developed because they have the potential to make transportation safer, more efficient, and more accessible. Although the technology still has important weaknesses, the possible benefits are too significant to ignore. Instead of abandoning autonomous vehicles because they are imperfect, companies and governments should improve the systems, test them carefully, and create clear laws before they become common on public roads.

The strongest argument for driverless cars is safety. According to the article, human error causes more than 90 percent of traffic accidents. Drivers text, become drowsy, speed, or get behind the wheel after drinking. A computer does not get tired during a long trip, become distracted by a phone, or make an emotional decision in traffic. Autonomous vehicles use laser radar, cameras, GPS, and computer sensors to identify obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signals. If these systems are properly designed, they could prevent many of the crashes caused by careless or impaired drivers. Fewer accidents would mean fewer injuries and deaths, as well as lower insurance costs for families.

Driverless transportation could also help people who cannot easily drive themselves. Elderly people, people with disabilities, and others who are unable to operate a car could gain more independence. Rather than depending on relatives, public buses, or expensive rides, they could travel to work, school, appointments, and stores more easily. Sergey Brin imagines a future in which people may not need to own cars at all because driverless public transportation could serve more passengers. This type of system could use half the fuel and half the parking space of today’s cars. In crowded cities, reducing fuel use and freeing up parking areas would improve both the environment and the quality of life.

Critics are right to point out that autonomous vehicles are not ready to operate without limits. Sensors may struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or construction zones without clear lane markings. Software can also have glitches, and connected vehicles could face cybersecurity threats. These concerns show why driverless cars must be introduced gradually. Manufacturers should test them in difficult weather and unusual road conditions, while engineers strengthen protection against hackers. Governments should also establish rules about who is legally responsible after a crash. Whether responsibility belongs to the owner, automaker, or software developer should be decided before fully autonomous cars become widespread.

The article also explains that semi-autonomous cars can create a special danger because human drivers may stop paying attention while the computer controls the vehicle. This problem supports the need for caution, not the end of development. Cars should not be marketed as fully safe if they still require immediate human intervention. Until the technology can reliably handle emergencies, drivers must receive clear warnings and remain responsible for supervising the vehicle.

Driverless cars are not a perfect solution yet, but neither are human drivers. With careful testing, strong safety standards, and clear legal rules, autonomous vehicles could save lives, reduce traffic problems, and give more people the freedom to travel. The risks are real, but the benefits make continued development worthwhile.

Dear Senator [Last Name],

I am writing to urge you to support a move away from the Electoral College and toward electing our president by national popular vote. I know the current system has a long pedigree and some thoughtful defenders. But a method of choosing the nation's only truly national officeholder should rest on a simple principle: every citizen's vote counts equally, wherever it is cast.

The Electoral College began as a compromise. As the Office of the Federal Register explains, the Founders were choosing between letting Congress select the president and allowing a direct vote by qualified citizens. That was a reasonable solution for a young country with slow communication and deep suspicion of concentrated power. But the system we live with now is not the one the framers sketched. Forty-eight states and the District of Columbia award all of their electoral votes to whoever wins the state's popular vote, even if the margin is a sliver. Only Maine and Nebraska divide theirs by congressional district. The winner-take-all habit appears nowhere in the Constitution's design; it is a state-level choice that has hardened into the national norm.

The consequences are plain. Bradford Plumer points out that a candidate can win the most votes nationwide and still lose the presidency, as happened in 2000 and 2016. In those elections, millions more people preferred one candidate, yet the other took office. It is hard to tell citizens that their government rests on majority consent when the arithmetic says otherwise. Plumer also notes that winner-take-all rules push campaigns into a handful of swing states. Voters in reliably red or blue states, including many here, are largely ignored, because their outcome is treated as settled. A system that tells tens of millions of people their ballots barely matter is likely to depress turnout, and it distorts what candidates promise and where they spend their time.

Defenders raise serious points, and I want to answer them. Judge Richard Posner argues that the Electoral College preserves federalism and forces candidates to assemble broad coalitions rather than piling up enormous margins in dense urban areas or one region. I understand the appeal. But the current map does not actually force candidates to court small or rural states; it forces them to court competitive ones, which may be large or small and which change little from cycle to cycle. Under a national popular vote, a vote in rural Wyoming would count exactly as much as a vote in Los Angeles, and a candidate would have a reason to seek support in every community, because every additional vote would matter anywhere.

Posner also contends that the Electoral College yields a quick, decisive result and confines recounts to individual states rather than risking a nationwide recount. That worry deserves attention, and a popular-vote system would need clear, uniform standards for audits and recounts. Yet close national margins are rare, and the present arrangement is hardly immune to disputes; the 2000 election turned on a recount in a single state. Concentrating the stakes in one narrow battleground can make a contested result more explosive, not less. Plumer's reference to faithless electors, who could theoretically defy their states' voters, is another reminder that the system carries risks of its own.

A constitutional amendment is a high bar, and I recognize that. In the meantime, I hope you will support efforts such as the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which would commit our state's electors to the national winner once enough states join. Please consider backing that measure and speaking publicly for direct election of the president.
